# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr — The Age of Dubhan (An Aois Dhubhain)

# Chapter One: Of the Fire Banked in the North

*DE 1*

> **Part One · Of the Fire in the North and the Five Lights**
>
> *Loiscidh e, tha fàileadh dheth, agus chan e gual a th' ann.*
> It burns, it stinks, and it is not coal.
>
> — the surveyors of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, DE 2

## I. Of the Night near Midsummer

So the old people of the north tell it, in both their tongues, and they tell it the same way at the harbour wall of Caol mhòr and at the hearths of the hill farms: there was a man who had failed for ten years.

Every season had seen him fail. He had tried the spoil that the pits tip down the hillsides, the grey waste that will not burn for the stone in it, and the black slurry that settles in the sumps, and the dust swept up from the floors of the coal-sheds. These things he had boiled and dried, pressed them and baked them, mixed them with this and with that, with things the tellers do not name because they do not know them. Most of what he made would not light. What would light went out, or smoked a room blind, or cracked in the fire and threw its sparks across the floor. The tellers give no count of his trials. They say only that for years nobody thought to ask how the work went, because the answer was always the same.

Nobody in the south knew his name that summer. Nobody at Cathair dhearg was watching him, and the clerks of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, who counted every sack that came up out of the vein, had no line for what went down the tip. His name was Dubhan. His people were the Tuathaich, whom An Dealachadh had pushed to the island's northern edge, and the coal had never been theirs to inherit. What he had to work with was what the kingdom threw away.

The summer of that year came in dry and dear. In the north, at midsummer, the sky never goes wholly dark: the light goes down behind the hills in the north-west, and it runs along under the rim of the world as a green-grey band, and it comes up again in the north-east before a man has properly slept. On such a night, near the longest day, he banked his fire for the night as he had banked it on a hundred nights before. He set his crucible in the heart of it, packed with pit waste, and covered the whole with ash and turves so that it would burn low and long. Then he lay down beside it and slept.

That is all the telling gives of the night. There is no speech in it. The tellers do not say what he hoped, and they will not guess.

In the morning he raked the ash away. The crucible had not cracked. In it, where the waste had been, lay a cake of something black and close-grained and heavy for its size, with a dull skin on it like the bloom on a sloe. He broke it with a hammer on the hearthstone, and it broke clean. He laid a piece of it on the embers.

It took the fire slowly, the way good coal takes it, and it burned with a low red heat and a thick yellow smoke that stank of tar and bad eggs. There was no cracking and no spitting. At last it fell to a fine grey ash, and the ash was cold before the man had moved from where he knelt.

So, the tellers say, he broke another piece and laid it on, and watched that burn too.

The north keeps the day as the day the fire came. The years of this age are counted from that morning, which was 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1. It was a rough thing, what lay in the crucible, and it was no trade and no wealth to anyone. Nobody bought it or sold it. It was one man's answer to a need that the people who ruled the island had not yet looked in the face. In the north they still say of a thing that works at last after long failing, *thàinig an teine*, the fire came, and a child who is slow to walk and then walks is said to have banked his fire.

## II. Of the Dry Summer and the Fourth Floor

Of the kingdom as it stood that summer its own record has a great deal to say, and none of it is cheerful.

Mairead reigned at Cathair dhearg. She had come to the throne heir to a kingdom whose wealth was plainly running out, and the running-out had not stopped for her crowning. The lowest galleries of An Sloc Mòr lay under water, because the pumps cost more to run than the coal beneath them was worth; the minute of Comhairle nam Mèinnean called it a pause, and the pause was now in its tenth year. The yield of the upper galleries fell each quarter by a little. Its clerks entered the little in a firm hand.

Coal-fuel was dear everywhere. At Fèill Muileann òg its price had doubled in the autumn before, and the court of the fair had fixed a ceiling it could not hold. All that summer the dealers sold above it, and the court fined them, and the dealers paid the fines and put them on the price. At Cnoc fhiadhaich, in the pit country, the households still went up onto the spoil-heaps at dusk with baskets to pick out the black among the grey, and the watchmen posted there, being men of the town, still saw nothing.

In the capital the street-lamps that the humans had set up, which had burned coal since they were raised, were lit later in the evening that year and put out earlier in the night, and the lamp-men lit fewer of them in the lanes behind the fish-quays and under the walls. The poorer streets were darker than they had been in the memory of anyone living in them. People who had to go out after dark in those streets went in twos.

At Achadh dhomhain, where Comann nan Gualadairean kept its hall, the day of binding came round in the spring as it always had, and the masters sat in their places in the long room with the oath-stone on the table in front of them, and no family brought a son or a daughter to be bound. It had happened first in the year of Mairead's crowning, and in more years since than not. That first year the masters had waited until noon. This year they waited an hour, and then the clerk wrote the day into the book with nothing under it, and the masters went home.

The census had been published seven years before, openly, for the first time in the kingdom's history. It had changed nothing in the frame of things, except that the north now knew in print what it had known already.

In the north, Tional nan Tuathach sat at Caol mhòr under Daniel Frayne, as it had sat under one speaker or another since the first years after An Dealachadh, with no standing in any court of the kingdom and minute-books that ran unbroken from its first wet evening. It met that summer on its usual days. Its minutes speak of the herring, of the wool, of a roof at the school at Doire ghlas and of the price of coal. They say nothing of any fire in any crucible, because nobody had yet brought word of one to Caol mhòr.

And at Muileann chaol, in the eastern hills, the record of all these things was kept.

Leabharlann Muileann chaol stands above the river on the edge of the narrow mill town that has lived on it since the new kingdom was young. The old building, where the keeper and the chronicler have their rooms, is of the grey hill stone, with small windows and deep sills. The new wing, raised when the shires' chests were called in, is of stone from An Sloc Mòr, and it is darker, and it has four floors.

The shires' chests filled three of them. The fourth was empty. It had been left for what had not been sent, and in the summer of that year it was still waiting.

Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, who was Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd and had been since Tormod Pinn died at his desk, worked in the old building on the side that looked over the river. She was a woman of some fifty years that summer, small and straight, with ink in the creases of her right hand that no soap had moved in twenty years. The room had been Tormod Pinn's and still had his chair in it, which she did not use, and his inkstand, which she did. From her window she could see the paper-mill's wheel turning in the race, and beyond it, a mile down the valley, the ford at Àth dhomhain, where every reader bound for an Leabharlann crossed.

It was her habit, and she had made it the office's habit, to write at the foot of each year a note of what the year had kept from her. Her first such note had been about the census. The census clerks in the northern shires had been given their figures and had not counted them, and the figures they had been given were the figures of Tional nan Tuathach. The kingdom's first honest census had been honest in the north because the Tuathaich had done the counting for it. She had written that down in plain words, and nobody in the council had written to her about it, which she took for leave to go on.

In the months of that summer she was doing the thing that a chronicler does most of the time, which is reading. The shires' chests had come in over half a dozen years, and the copyists had been at the work of listing them ever since. That summer they finished the last of the lists. Ailig mac Thormoid, the eldest of the copyists, a thin man with a cough he blamed on the new wing's dust, brought her the tally on a single sheet in the second week of an t-Iuchar.

"One thousand and six chests," he said. "Every shire has sent something, except the ones that haven't."

"And the one that burned its chest in the yard."

"We've put Seann Tarr down as sent, keeper's orders. Sent to the fire." He laid the sheet on her desk. "The fourth floor is as it was."

She went up with him that afternoon, because she had not been up there since the spring. The stair in the new wing was steep and the treads were still sharp at the edges. On the first three floors the chests stood in their rows with their shire marks painted on the lids, and the air smelt of dry wood and old paper and a little of mice. On the fourth floor there was nothing. The windows had shutters and the shutters were closed, and the light came through their slats in bars across a floor that had been swept and had nothing on it to sweep. Their feet were loud on the boards.

"Mòrag used to say we would fill it in her lifetime," Ailig said.

"Mòrag used to say a great many things." Beathag walked the length of the room to the far wall and back. Nothing had been sent from the north. The minute-books of Tional nan Tuathach were at Caol mhòr, and the schools' registers were in the schools, and the vigil-books of Baile chrom were wherever the people of Baile chrom kept them, and no one had asked for any of them. That was the fourth floor, and the kingdom had built it on purpose. She had understood that from the first, and it still made her tired to stand in it.

On the way down Ailig said, "The carriers are late this week."

"The carriers are late every week."

"They say it's the price of fodder. Everything's the price of something."

## III. Of the Carrier's Word

Dòmhnall mac Ailein carried on the library road. He brought up paper and ink and lamp-oil from the landing at Ceann dhomhain, and the letters of the capital, and in winter the ration of coal for an Leabharlann, which grew smaller every year and dearer every quarter. He was a big slow man with a big slow horse, and he had been bringing things up the hill to Muileann chaol for longer than Beathag had been chronicler. Talk came out of him while he unloaded, and nobody at an Leabharlann had ever found a way to stop it.

It was he who first brought the word, on a hot afternoon in an Lùnastal, while he stacked reams against the wall of the yard.

"There's a thing in the north," he said, "that the Tuathaich have got hold of."

Beathag was in the yard because the carrier's cart was the nearest thing to news that came up the hill, and she had learnt long before to be there when it did. "What sort of thing?"

"A fire out of spoil." He set a ream down and straightened his back. "Out of the tip. I had it off a drover at the landing, and he had it off a boatman who'd been up the coast. There's a man up there, a Tuathach, has made a fuel out of what the pits throw away, and it burns."

"Everything burns if you put enough under it."

"That's what I said." He looked pleased at the agreement. "But the drover said no, it burns on its own, like coal. Stinks worse than a tannery, he said, but it burns."

"Who is the man?"

Dòmhnall thought about it. He was an honest carrier, which meant that he did not like to give a thing he had not been given. "The drover had a name for him. Dubhan, he said, or near it. It might have been Dubhain. The boatman said it one way and the drover another, and I've said it both ways since, so I couldn't swear."

"And where in the north?"

"The drover didn't know. The boatman had it from Caol mhòr, where some pedlar had a cake of the stuff on the market, but that's only where the boats are." He lifted another ream. "They'll tell you anything, the Tuathaich, in their own tongue, and nothing in ours. Or the other way about. I never know which."

She wrote it down that evening in her day-book, which was her own and not the kingdom's: *Dòmhnall mac Ailein: a fuel of the north made from pit waste, said to burn like coal. A man's name given with it, Dubhan or Dubhain. From a drover, from a boatman, from Caol mhòr.* She looked at it a good while, then underlined *from* three times, and went to bed.

The next week she asked Dòmhnall whether he had heard any more. He had not. The week after, he had heard that the fuel was made of tar, which she did not believe, and the week after that, that it was a trick of the Tuathaich to sell their spoil to fools, which she believed less. By the end of an Lùnastal the story had come up the library road four or five times in different mouths, and in every mouth it was a little larger and no nearer.

She said as much to Raghnall mac Mhuirich, the keeper, when she met him in the yard at the end of the month. He was three years younger than she, a tall stooping man who had been Mòrag nic Coinnich's deputy for most of his working life and had become keeper the summer before. He was still getting used to the room, and he spent his days as he had always spent them, in the stacks with a pencil behind his ear.

"The carriers have a fuel in the north," she said. "Made of spoil."

"So I hear. Ailig told me. Ailig tells me everything, eventually." Raghnall took the pencil from behind his ear and looked at it, as if it might have news of its own. "Have you seen any?"

"No."

"Has anyone you trust seen any?"

"Dòmhnall mac Ailein trusts a drover who trusts a boatman."

"Then there's nothing to keep." He put the pencil back. "Beathag, if there is a fuel, someone will write it down. Comhairle nam Mèinnean will write it down, or the court of the fair will write down that it was sold, or the Tuathaich will write it in their minute at Caol mhòr, and one day, if anyone sends the writing, it will come here and we will keep it. That is what we are for. An Leabharlann keeps. It does not chase."

"I am not an Leabharlann," she said. "I am the chronicler."

"You are the chronicler in an Leabharlann." He said it kindly. "It comes to the same in the end, when the council reads the bills."

## IV. Of the Pedlar at the Ford

The market of Muileann chaol is held in the yard of an Leabharlann, as it has been since the town was given its charter, and on the market day in the middle of an t-Sultain the yard was full of stalls under the chestnut trees: paper and pens and binders' thread, eggs and cheese from the hill farms, knives, pots, a man selling ribbons, a woman selling honey out of a crock with a spoon for tasting. The copyists came down from their tables to buy, because the market was the only day in the month when anyone came up the hill with anything but paper.

Beathag spent the morning at her desk with the shutters half closed against the sun, going through the letters of the northern maoir for the year, and she did not go down until the afternoon, when the stalls were being packed.

Ailig mac Thormoid met her at the foot of the stair. He had a slip of paper in his hand, one of the narrow slips the copyists use for marking a place in a chest, and he was excited, which was rare in him.

"There was a Tuathach at the market," he said. "A pedlar. Needles and pins and buttons, and a bit of lace from Doire ghlas. And he had a cake of the black stuff wrapped in sacking, the stuff Dòmhnall talks about."

"Where is he?"

"Gone. He went at noon. He was for the landing, he said, and the boats south." Ailig held out his slip. "He burned a piece of it for us, on the flagstone by the pump. He wanted a penny a look, and then he didn't, because everyone was looking anyway. I wrote down what he called it."

She took the slip. Ailig wrote a good copying hand and a poor hurried one, and this was the hurried one. It gave the name of the fuel, or of the man, it was not clear which, spelled a third way, different from both of Dòmhnall's.

"Is that how he said it?"

"That's how I heard it. He said it quick, in the northern way. I asked him to say it again and he said it again and it sounded different. Then he laughed and said we could call it what we liked, it'd burn the same."

"Did it burn?"

"It burned," Ailig said. "Slow. Red, with no colour at the edge, not like ours. And it stank." He wrinkled his nose at the memory of it. "The whole yard stank. The honey-woman packed up. The ash is still there by the pump, if you want it."

She went and looked at the ash. It was a small grey heap on the flagstone, fine as flour, and when she crouched and put her finger in it, it was cold and left a grey mark on her skin and nothing else. It smelt of old smoke. Anything in the world might have made it.

Then, because she was Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, she put on her boots and went down the valley to the ford.

It is a mile from an Leabharlann to Àth dhomhain, downhill all the way, on a road that the carts have worn into two stony ruts with grass between them. The afternoon was warm, and the dust of the road came up round her skirts, and the river on her left ran low and brown between its stones after the dry summer. At the ford the ferryman's boy was sitting on the bank with his feet in the water. Yes, he said, a Tuathach had come down with a pack, round about noon. He had waded over, because he said the ferry was dear, and gone on along the far bank towards the landing at Ceann dhomhain. He'd have caught the evening boat if it went, and it went most evenings.

"Did he have anything with him? A black thing, wrapped in sacking?"

The boy shrugged. "He had a pack. I didn't look in it. You don't, with the Tuathaich." He considered her. "He gave me a button."

She stood on the bank for some time, looking at the far side of the ford, where the road went up between alders and out of sight. It was three miles to the landing and the boat would have gone. She was fifty years old and she had come down in her indoor boots. She turned and walked back up the hill to an Leabharlann, and it was dusk when she came into the yard, and someone had swept the ash from the flagstone by the pump.

## V. Of the Letter to the Maor and the Foot of the Year

In the first week of an Dàmhair she wrote to the maor of Caol mhòr.

She wrote it three times before she was satisfied, and the copy she kept is the third. It is a short letter and a correct one. It says that the chronicler of the kingdom has heard report, from carriers and from a pedlar of the north, of a fuel made from the waste of the pits, burning in the manner of coal; that the report names a man of the north, whose name is variously given; that she has not seen the fuel and can find no one who has seen it made; and that she would be grateful if the maor, or any clerk of his, could send her a piece of it by the carrier, with a line to say where it came from and who had made it, so that she might set down in the record what was true. She signed it with her name and her office, and sealed it with the office's seal, which was pressed with coal ink as every seal of the kingdom was, and gave it to Dòmhnall mac Ailein for the landing and the post north.

"Caol mhòr," Dòmhnall said, looking at the direction. "That's a long way for a letter to go and come back."

"It is sixty miles and more. A letter can do it in ten days."

"A letter can," he said. "An answer's another thing."

No answer came in ten days, or in twenty. At the end of an Dàmhair the rains came in from the west, the first of the autumn, and the library road went to mud, and for a week Dòmhnall's cart could not get up the last hill and the reams came up on a sledge. The coal for an Leabharlann came up with them, the first of the winter's ration, and it was less than the year before and had cost the council more. Raghnall called the copyists together in the long room of the old building and told them that there would be no fire in the reading-room before the middle of an t-Samhain, and none after dark at all, and that anyone who wished to copy in the evenings could do it at home. Ailig coughed and said nothing. There had never been a fire in the stacks, and never a lamp, because of the old condition on the first loft of papers that nothing in it should be burned. The town had kept that condition when it had kept little else.

Beathag asked Dòmhnall each week whether there was a letter from the north for her, and each week he said there was not.

"They don't answer letters, up there," he said. "Not ours."

"The maor is the kingdom's man."

"Then he's a kingdom's man living among Tuathaich," Dòmhnall said. "And that's a man who has learnt not to answer letters."

In the middle of an t-Samhain she went to Raghnall. He was in his room, which had been Mòrag's, with a shawl round his shoulders and a book open on the desk in front of him, reading by the last of the daylight at the window. It was a little after three in the afternoon. He had not lit his lamp.

"I have had no answer from Caol mhòr," she said.

"I had not thought you would." He closed the book on his finger. "You want to write the fuel into the year."

"I want to write the year. The fuel is in it. Or the talk of the fuel is in it. I don't know which, and I don't know how to find out from here, and I don't know who else will, because Comhairle nam Mèinnean has sent no one north and its clerks will not write down what they have not counted. If I leave it out, the year is short by a thing that half the carriers of the library road are talking about. If I put it in, I am putting in a drover's tale."

"You can leave it for next year. If it is real it will still be real."

"And if it is real, the record will begin a year late, and someone at this desk after me will want to know why."

Raghnall looked at her over the book and said nothing. The light was going out of the window behind him while they talked, and his face was growing hard to see.

"You will not write what you have not seen," he said.

"No."

"And you will not leave it out."

"No."

"Then you had better find a way to do both," he said. "It is your office, Beathag, not mine. I only keep the rooms." He opened the book again, though he could scarcely have read it in that light. "Write what you have. Write that it is what you have. That is what the note at the foot of the year is for, isn't it? You invented it. Use it."

She wrote the note on 21 an t-Samhain, DE 1.

That was the day the office closed the year's record, as it did every year a month before the shortest day, so that the copyists could make the fair copy for the council before the roads closed. It was a still, grey day, and raw, with the smoke of the town lying flat in the valley and the mill-wheel stopped, because the dry year had left the race too low to turn it. By the middle of the afternoon the light in her window was gone. She lit her lamp early, an oil lamp with a glass chimney that had been Tormod Pinn's, and the room smelt of hot oil and of the damp coming through the shutters.

The year's record lay in front of her in its loose leaves, forty-one pages in her own hand. Mairead's reign, and the council's sittings, and the orders of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, and the price of coal-fuel at the fair and the ceiling unheld. The day of binding at Achadh dhomhain with nothing under it. The chests counted, one thousand and six, and the fourth floor empty. The watchmen at Cnoc fhiadhaich. The coal ration. The rains. It was a thin year, as the years had been thin for a long while, and every page of it was about something running out.

She turned to the foot of the last leaf, where the note would go, and sat a long time with the pen dry.

She had three spellings of the name, and she did not know which of them was right. There were Dòmhnall's two, as the drover said it and as the boatman said it, and there was Ailig's slip with the pedlar's word, written in a hurry by a man who had heard it said quick in the northern way. No letter had come from the maor. All else she had was a cold grey smear of ash that someone had swept away. She had not seen the fuel, and she had not seen it burn, and she had not spoken to anyone who had seen it made.

In the end she wrote two lines. The first says that a fuel made without the vein, from the waste of the pits, is reported out of the north this year, and that it is said to burn in the manner of coal, and it gives the name that goes with it as Dòmhnall's drover gave it, and then as his boatman gave it, and then, in the second line, as Ailig took it down from the pedlar at the pump. The second line says that the chronicler has not seen it.

Among the spellings she did not choose. She could not, and would not pretend to. All three she let stand side by side in the kingdom's record, the one word three ways in two lines, so that whoever came to the desk after her would know how the word had come up the hill: late, in pieces, by the mouths of carriers, with no one to vouch for it.

That is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record. There is no earlier one.

When she had written it she sat back and read the two lines over by the lamp, and then she read the whole leaf, and then she sanded it and laid it on the pile. The lamp was smoking a little and she turned the wick down. Outside the window it was full dark, though it was not yet five o'clock, and down in the town the few lamps that were lit made yellow points in the valley, and past them nothing, all the way to the north.

She thought of Raghnall in the stacks saying that an Leabharlann keeps and does not chase, and of the ferryman's boy with his feet in the water, and of the pedlar going along the far bank of the ford between the alders with his pack on his back and the black cake in it wrapped in sacking. She thought that somewhere in the north, far past the reach of her letters, a man whose name she could not spell had made a fire that burned.

*A chur san Leabharlann*, they say on the island: to put a thing in an Leabharlann is to settle it. She had put this in, and it was not settled at all.

She left the lamp to burn down, which she never did, and went to bed.

# Chapter Two: Of the Two Surveyors

*DE 2*

## I. Of the Order and the Northern Road

The order came down to Seumas mac Eachainn in the second week of an t-Sultain, in the drawing-room at Cathair mhòr where the surveyors of Comhairle nam Mèinnean kept their tables, and it came folded twice under the seal of the mine office. He was twenty-four that summer and had been four years a surveyor. He had measured the flooding in the lowest galleries of An Sloc Mòr with a weighted line and a lantern, and had written in his book, as he was told to write, that the water stood at a pause. In all his life he had never been north of the capital.

The order said that it was reported from the north that a fuel was being made without the vein, and burned; that two of its surveyors should go into the Tuathaich country and learn whether it burned as men said; and that they should report under their hands to Comhairle nam Mèinnean at Cathair mhòr and, by a fair copy, to the council's clerk at Cathair dhearg. It was signed by the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean and countersigned by a clerk of Comhairle na Rìoghachd, and that second name was what made the older surveyors look up from their tables when Seumas read it out.

"The council wants it," said Iain Ruadh mac Nèill. "Then the council can wait for it."

Iain Ruadh was the other surveyor named. He was fifty-seven, and the red that had given him his name had gone the colour of wet sand, except in his eyebrows, which still stood out on his face like two coals in ash. He had been a surveyor since before Seumas was born. In his time he had gone down every open shaft on the mountain and some that were not open, and he held that there was nothing on the island that could be learned about fire that the mountain had not already taught.

"It is pit waste," he said, "cooked in a pot by a man with time on his hands. They have been at it in the north since the humans went. It smokes, it cracks, it goes out. We will ride two days to watch it go out."

They rode for the capital the next morning, because the northern road began there, and lay a night at Cathair dhearg in a lodging-house near the bridge. Seumas's mother lived in the lanes below the bridge-foot on the south bank, and he went to her for an hour after dark. She asked him what the mine office wanted with the Tuathaich, and he said it wanted to know about a fire. She said the lamp-houses were talking of leaving half the streets dark for the winter, and that the lamp-lighter two doors down had not been paid since Lùnastal. He told her the price of coal was not his masters' doing. She said she had not said it was.

In the morning they rode out past Cathair dhomhain and its harbour, with the stubble of the barley on either hand. It was a mild grey day with the wind in the west and rain in it now and again, never enough to wet a man through. The road was the old one, broad, rutted by carts, walled here and there where the farms were Dia-thìrich and the fields were worth a wall. At Ceann gheal they watered the horses and ate bread and cheese standing up. After that the country rose into long bare ridges with the road going over them one by one, and the farms grew smaller and farther apart, and the walls gave way to banks of turf with gorse along them.

Iain Ruadh rode a big bay mare that knew the road better than he did and let her choose her pace. He talked when he wanted to and was silent when he did not, and Seumas learned by the middle of the afternoon that the silences meant nothing. What the old man talked of was the mountain: which galleries had been good in his father's time, which seams had gone thin, how the colour of a flame told a surveyor what a coal was and where it had been cut. Coal of An Sloc Mòr burned with a dark edge to its flame, blue and green and a red like a wound, and a man who had seen it would know it anywhere.

"That is what they cannot make," Iain Ruadh said. "They can make a thing that burns. Any fool can make a thing that burns. They cannot make the edge."

They lay that night at Tobar dhomhain, which was a well, a farm, a smithy and an ale-house, and the ale-house had one room for travellers with a bed in it and a bench. Iain Ruadh took the bed. Seumas lay on the bench under his coat and listened to the wind in the thatch and thought of the order in his saddle-bag and the second name on it.

They crossed the boundary stones in the middle of the next morning.

Seumas had known they were there, as everyone knew. Stones had been set on the north roads in the first year after An Dealachadh, where the Tuathaich country began, and no wall had followed them. He had thought there would be more to see. There were two stones, one on either side of the road, grey, shoulder-high, rough-dressed, with lichen yellow on their northern faces and nothing cut in them at all. A sheep was lying in the lee of the western one. It got up as the horses came near and walked a little way off and lay down again.

Iain Ruadh did not look at the stones. His mare did not slow. Seumas reined in, because it seemed to him that a man ought to, and sat for a breath or two between them, and then felt foolish and rode on to catch up.

"I crossed here the first time in my twenties," the old man said, without turning his head. "I thought there would be someone to ask my business. There never is."

North of the stones the road was the same road. The ridges went on. The farms were no poorer than the farms behind them, though they were built differently, with the house and the byre under one long roof and the doors painted, and the walls whitened with lime. At Àth fhionn a woman was lifting potatoes in a field by the ford, with two children picking behind her into a basket. Seumas called a greeting in Dia-thìris. She straightened and answered him in Dia-thìris, civilly, and when he had ridden past he heard her speak to the children in the humans' tongue, and the elder of the two laughed.

## II. Of the Harbour at Caol mhòr

They came down into Caol mhòr in the evening, with the light going copper over the sea to the west and the strait below them full of it. The town lay along the shore and up the slope behind, grey houses and white ones, and the harbour was crowded with boats come in for the night, their sails brailed up and their masts rocking together. There were three church towers that Seumas could count from the road, square and plain, and as they came down a bell began in one of them and was taken up by the second and then the third, not quite together, so that the sound came down the hill in pieces.

"Evening prayer," said Iain Ruadh. "They keep hours like a druid school."

They found a lodging at an inn on the harbour front whose sign was a painted boat. The landlord was a big soft-spoken man named Harker who spoke to them in Dia-thìris and to his wife in the other tongue, and who gave them a room over the tap with two beds and a window on the water. Seumas asked him, as they sat to their supper, whether he knew anything of a new fuel that was burned in the north.

Harker considered the question. "I know there's talk of one," he said.

"Have you seen it?"

"I've seen a good many things." He took their plates. "There's more fish if you want it."

That was the first answer, and it was the pattern of the rest.

They spent four days at Caol mhòr. They went first to the maor, An Crùn's officer for the shire, a thin Dia-thìreach of the south who had held the post eleven years and plainly meant to hold it no longer than he must. He received them in a cold room above the harbour office with a fire of driftwood in the grate. He had heard of the fuel, he said. An Leabharlann had written to him about it. He had asked, and been told nothing. He doubted they would fare better; they were welcome to try, and he would give them a letter.

The letter got them into places and got them nothing there. They went to the harbour master, who showed them his book of dues and said there was no line in it for any fuel but coal and turf and wood. They went to a cooper's yard, a smith's, a rope-walk along the shore. On the second day they went to the market, because Iain Ruadh remembered that a pedlar had been said to carry the stuff there. The market was fish and wool and cabbages and a man mending pots; the pedlars had cloth and needles and cheap ribbons and tin whistles; and when Seumas asked after a black cake that burned, a woman selling eggs said that there was a man who had sold such a thing the winter before, and that he had not come this year, and that she did not know his name.

Everywhere it was the same. They were answered civilly and at once, in good Dia-thìris, and the answer was never a lie and never any use. A man asked a question in Dia-thìris would give it back smooth and turned over, like a stone out of the burn. Then, as the surveyors went away, they would hear behind them the other tongue, quick and low, and sometimes a laugh, and sometimes nothing.

"They speak it among themselves to keep us out," Seumas said on the third evening. He had drunk two cups of Harker's ale, which was strong.

"They speak it among themselves because it is theirs," said Iain Ruadh. "They speak ours to us because it is ours. On the whole island there is no better-mannered people. I have been coming here thirty years and I have never once been told a thing I wanted to know."

"You don't think it's there."

"I think a man in the north has cooked some pit waste, and the whole coast is pleased with him for it, and it will be out by the new year." The old man looked into his cup. "I think they are proud of him. That is why they will not show us."

Seumas lay awake that night and listened to the boats knocking in the harbour. He was a Dia-thìreach of the capital and a servant of the mine office, and he had not thought of himself, before this week, as anything a people would keep a thing from. He found he did not like it. Turning over towards the wall, he found also that he did not blame them.

On the fourth morning a boy came to the inn with a message. It was written in a good round hand in Dia-thìris, and it said that if the gentlemen of Comhairle nam Mèinnean wished to see a fire, the mill yard at Doire ghlas would be scouring on the morrow and they might come at the tenth hour. It was signed M. Greaves, manager.

"Who is this?" Seumas asked Harker.

"Martha Greaves," said Harker. "She has the big mill at Doire ghlas, the one Tional nan Tuathach built."

"How does she know we are here?"

Harker looked at him with a patient kindness that Seumas remembered for a long time afterwards. "Sir," he said, "everyone knows you are here."

## III. Of the Mill Yard at Doire ghlas

Doire ghlas lay a little under ten miles east of Caol mhòr, on a road that ran inland from the strait through small fields and then up among low hills with oak woods on them. The oaks were old and grey-barked and bent by the west wind, and the road went through the edge of them for a mile before it came out above the village. Seumas had heard it called a village and had expected a village. It was as big as Caol mhòr, and seemed bigger, because it was built close about a great grove of the grey oaks in the middle of it, with the houses and chapels and the mills set around the grove like men round a fire, and nothing at all built under the trees.

"They will tell you it is a village," Iain Ruadh said. "Let them."

The mills stood at the eastern edge, where a stream came down off the hill and had been led in a stone race along the backs of them. There were three, long stone buildings with slate roofs, and the noise of their looms came out of their windows and filled the road. Carts of fleece stood in the lane. A smell of wet wool and lanolin and something sourer hung over everything, and under it, when the wind turned, Seumas caught another smell that he did not know.

Martha Greaves met them at the yard gate herself. She was a square, grey woman in her fifties in a dark stuff gown with the sleeves pinned back and an apron over it, and she had ink on her right hand and a pencil through the knot of her hair. She greeted them in Dia-thìris, gave them each her hand, asked after their journey and their lodging and the health of the maor, and said that she had kept them no more than a quarter-hour, which was true.

"You'll want to see the scouring," she said. "Come this way. Mind the channel, it's hot."

The scouring-house was a lean-to along the yard wall, open on the yard side, with three great coppers set into a brick range. The raw fleece came in at one end, was boiled in the first copper with soda and stale urine, lifted steaming on forks into the second and the third, and went out at the other end grey and wet and clean to the drying lofts. Four women worked the forks, with their skirts kilted and their arms red to the elbow. The steam rolled up under the roof and out across the yard.

Under the coppers were the fires.

Seumas went down on one knee on the wet brick to look at the nearest, and Iain Ruadh, after a moment, lowered himself stiffly beside him. The fire-door was open. The fire inside was low and steady and very hot; Seumas felt it on his face at arm's length. It burned yellow, a heavy smoky yellow with red at the root, and the smoke went up the flue fat and brown and came down again in the yard as a smell. It was a smell of tar and bad eggs and something like singed hoof, and it got into the back of the throat and stayed there.

There was no edge on the flame. He looked for it, as he had been taught to look. There was none of the blue, none of the green, none of the dark red. It was a plain flame.

"How long has it been burning?" Iain Ruadh asked.

"Since the fifth hour," said Martha Greaves. "It will burn till the fourth hour of the afternoon, when we draw the fires. The girl banks it at noon with two more cakes."

"Two."

"Two."

Iain Ruadh said nothing more. Seumas knew what he was thinking, because he was thinking it himself. A fire of the mountain's coal that would hold three coppers at the boil from the fifth hour to noon would have eaten a scuttle an hour. He looked round the yard for a coal-heap and did not see one. Against the wall of the scouring-house, under a sheet of tarred canvas, there was a low stack of something dark.

"May I?" he said.

Martha Greaves lifted a corner of the canvas for him.

The cakes were about the size of a small loaf, flattened, and blacker than any coal he had seen, a dull black that took no light. They had been pressed in some kind of mould; there was a ridge round the edge of each where the mould had joined. He picked one up. It was lighter than coal of its size and a little greasy, and it left a black bloom on his fingers that would not rub off on his trousers. He smelled it. It smelled of the fire, fainter.

"Where is it made?" he asked.

"In the north," said Martha Greaves.

"By whom?"

"By the man who makes it." She let the canvas fall. "You may take that one with you. It will tell you more than I can."

"Is it sold?"

"We buy it."

"From whom?"

She looked at him. She had grey eyes and a broad plain face that had been handsome, and was still good to look at, and there was nothing in it at all that he could read. "From the man who sells it to us," she said. "Will you take some tea, gentlemen? The kettle is on in the counting-house."

They took the tea. The counting-house was a small room at the corner of the yard, with a desk and two ledgers and a clock that ticked loudly and a window on the grove, and there was a fire in the grate there too, of peat. Martha Greaves poured for them and sat down at her desk and talked to them for half an hour about the price of fleece, and the rule of Tional nan Tuathach for its mills, and the carts on the long road to Fèill Muileann òg, and the weather, and the harvest, and the health of the Tuathaich minister of Doire ghlas, who was ninety and had baptised her. She spoke of the fuel only when they asked, and then she told them what they could see for themselves: that it had heated the coppers since the spring, that it cost less than coal, that the women disliked the smell and had stopped mentioning it.

When Iain Ruadh asked her directly how many mills of the north were burning it, she said she could answer only for her own mill.

When Seumas asked her, at the last, whether the surveyors might be let see the place where it was made, she put down her cup.

"Mr mac Eachainn," she said. She said his name the Tuathaich way, with the stress in the wrong place, and he did not think she did it by accident. "You have seen it burn. You have held it in your hand. Take it home and burn it on your own hearth. What else is there that your masters would want to know?"

He did not answer. He found he did not know what to answer. She waited a civil while, and then she stood up, and so they stood up too.

She walked them to the gate. On the way across the yard they passed the scouring-house again, and the women at the forks did not look round. At the gate Martha Greaves gave them each her hand again, and wished them a good road, and said that she hoped they would find Caol mhòr comfortable, and that Harker kept a fair house. Then she went back into the yard, and the gate was shut behind her, and the noise of the looms closed over everything.

They rode back towards the strait in the long light of the afternoon. The cake was in Seumas's saddle-bag wrapped in a page of the maor's letter, and every time the wind came round behind them he could smell it.

"Well," said Iain Ruadh at last. "It burns."

## IV. Of the Three Clauses

On 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2, the two surveyors sat down in the room over Harker's tap to write their report, with the window open on the harbour and a jug of ale between them and the cake from Doire ghlas on a plate on the sill.

They had burned half of it the night before in the grate of that room, with Harker's leave and to his wife's great displeasure. It had taken a long time to catch. Once caught it had burned for three hours and a half, low and hot and yellow, while they sat on their beds with their coats on and the window open and timed it by Iain Ruadh's watch. The smell had gone down the stairs and into the tap, where a fisherman had made a remark in the humans' tongue that set the whole room laughing. In the morning there was a little grey ash in the grate, less than Seumas had thought, and a black bloom on the ceiling above it the size of a man's two hands.

The order required that they report under their hands. Iain Ruadh, as the elder, had the right of the first draft, and he took it. He wrote for most of an hour in a small, square, old-fashioned hand, and then pushed the paper across.

Seumas read it twice.

It was a good report as reports of the mine office went. It set out the order and the road and the dates. The names of those they had called on at Caol mhòr were there, and what each had said. It described the mill yard at Doire ghlas and the coppers and the fire under them. It gave the hours of burning and the size of the cake and the weight of the ash. And it ended with a paragraph which said that the surveyors had not been shown the making of the fuel, nor the place of its making, nor told the name of the maker, nor the quantity made; that its nature and its lasting could not be judged by one mill and one cake; and that it must be accounted unproven.

"It is true," Iain Ruadh said, watching him. "Every word."

"It is true," Seumas agreed.

"Then sign it."

Seumas did not sign it. He sat with the paper in front of him and looked out of the window at the boats. A man was baiting lines on the deck of the nearest, and a gull stood on the rail beside him and waited. After a while Seumas said, "We were not sent to learn how it is made."

"We were sent to learn whether it burns as men say."

"And it does."

"We saw one fire, boy. In one yard. Shown us by a woman who told us nothing and meant to."

"We saw three fires. We burned one ourselves." Seumas put his finger on the last paragraph. "If this goes to Cathair mhòr, they will read the last word and no other. Unproven. They will file it and forget it, and next year someone will ask again, and someone will ride up here again, and be given tea."

Iain Ruadh was silent a long time. The gull on the rail stretched its wings and settled them.

"And what would you write?"

Seumas took a clean sheet. He knew the words already; he had been carrying them since the scouring-house, when he knelt on the wet brick and looked for the edge of the flame and did not find it. He wrote them in Dia-thìris, in the plain hand the mine office taught its clerks, below the heading and the order and the names:

> *Loiscidh e, tha fàileadh dheth, agus chan e gual a th' ann.*
> It burns; it stinks; and it is not coal.

Then he copied Iain Ruadh's account of the road and the town and the yard and the hours below it, word for word, and left out the last paragraph.

Iain Ruadh read it through. He read it a second time. He picked up his cup and found it was empty and put it down.

"They will think we were drunk," he said.

"They will read it."

"They will read the first line," said the old man, "and no other." But he took the pen. He signed first, as the elder, in his small square hand, and Seumas signed under him. Then they made the fair copy for the council's clerk, and signed that too, and Iain Ruadh folded both and sealed them.

When it was done he took from his saddle-bag the little tin that every surveyor of the mountain carries, with a thumb of coal from An Sloc Mòr in it for the matching of samples, and laid the coal on the last embers of the cake in the grate. It lay there a while and then caught. The flame came up round it thin and bright, and along its edge ran the colours of the mountain, blue and green and a red like a wound, so that for the time it burned the whole dull hearth had a rim of light on it.

"There," the old man said, and watched it until it was ash. "That is what I mean by an edge."

## V. Of the Unlit Lamps

They rode south two days later and came to Cathair dhearg on the evening of the second day, with rain. Iain Ruadh went on alone the next morning by the road east to Cathair mhòr, with the copy for Cathair mhòr in his saddle-bag, and Seumas stayed in the capital to put the fair copy into the hands of the council's clerk, as the order said, and to wait upon the council in case it wished to ask him anything.

He put it into the clerk's hands the same day, in a small panelled room off the passage below the council chamber, and the clerk, a courteous young man with a cold, gave him a receipt for it and wrote his lodging in a book. Then Seumas waited.

He waited nearly the whole of an Dàmhair. He lived at his mother's house in the lanes below the bridge-foot, and walked up every second morning to the panelled room to ask whether he was wanted, and every second morning the courteous young man, whose cold got better and then worse again, told him that he was not wanted yet. In between he walked the town. He walked out to the quays of Ros dhomhain and watched the coal-boats that had once come in loaded going out light. He walked round the precinct walls and past the temple of Macha, where the two horses of the rite were led out in the afternoons to graze the temple green. Walking was all there was to do with the days, and in the evenings he sat by his mother's fire, which was of turf and driftwood now, and told her about the grey oaks at Doire ghlas and the three bells at Caol mhòr, and did not tell her about the cake.

On 27 an Dàmhair, DE 2, there came a letter for him from Cathair mhòr, in Iain Ruadh's small square hand.

It was short. It said that the old man had come safe to Cathair mhòr and delivered the report, and that the master had read it at his table in Iain Ruadh's presence and passed it to the chief clerk, and that the chief clerk had filed it in the press among the surveys of that year. There had been no minute made of it. There had been no question asked. It said that Iain Ruadh had been sent the week after to measure the water in the lower galleries again, and that it stood where it stood, and that he had written that it was at a pause. It ended: *They read the first line. I told you so. I. R.*

Seumas read it by the window of the panelled room, where the clerk had given it to him with his daily word that the council did not want him yet. When he had finished he folded it and put it inside his coat. The clerk asked, out of courtesy, whether it was bad news. Seumas said it was not news at all.

As he came down the steps into the lane there was a woman on the lowest step with three children beside her, the eldest a girl of ten or eleven holding the youngest on her hip. The woman had a paper in her hand. Seumas knew her; it was the wife of the lamp-lighter two doors from his mother's, and the paper was a petition, written out for her by the scribe at the bridge-foot for a copper, and it asked that her husband, who had lit the lamps of the south bank for nineteen years, be given other work of the town's, any work, since the lamps he lit were to be lit no longer. A porter of the council house was telling her, not unkindly, that the petitions of the lamp-houses went to the lamp-houses and not to the council, and that the lamp-houses had already said no.

"They sent me here," the woman said.

"Then they were wrong to," said the porter.

Seumas stood on the step above them. He thought of the receipt in the clerk's book, with his lodging written beside it. He had nothing in his hand to give her but Iain Ruadh's letter, and it was no use to anybody. After a while the woman put the petition away in her shawl and took the youngest child from the girl and went off down the lane towards the bridge, and the other two followed her.

He walked home late, after dark, the long way, because he did not want to go in.

The lamp-houses had made their order that day. It was pinned up at the bridge-foot, and the watch had it by heart: the lamps of the main streets, the precinct, the bridge and the quays to be lit as before; the lamps of the lanes on the south bank, and of the streets behind the tannery and the fish-market, and of the lower town along the river, to be left unlit until the price of coal should fall. Seumas had seen the lamps of his mother's lane burning every night of his life when he was in the capital. He walked down the lane now and counted them, because he was a surveyor and it was the thing he knew how to do.

There were eleven iron posts in his mother's lane, and eleven dark heads on them, with the rain running off the glass. There were nine in the next lane, and fourteen in the one after, and six in the steep little lane that went down to the water-stairs, where he nearly fell. He counted them in his head and then, when the numbers grew too many, in the notebook he carried for the galleries, writing by feel in the dark: lane, lamps, lane, lamps. Behind the fish-market there were thirty-one. Along the river road there were fifty-two, and the river beside them was black and loud with the rain.

From the river road he could see the bridge. It was lit from end to end, as the order said, twenty lamps in two rows, and each of them had a coal flame in it, and each flame had the dark edge of the mountain's coal round it, blue and green and a red like a wound, so that the whole bridge hung over the black water with a coloured light on it. It was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen, and it was burning coal that the poorer streets of the capital could not have.

He stood on the river road and looked at it for a long time.

While he stood there he heard a shout from the far end of the bridge, and then running feet, and then the rattle of the watch. A man came off the bridge towards the south bank at a run, out of the light and into the dark of the lanes, and was gone. Two of the watch came after him as far as the bridge-foot and stopped there, where the lamps stopped, and one of them spoke a word to the other and they went back. A little later Seumas passed them at the bridge-foot, under the last lit lamp, where one of the watch had his book open against the post and was writing in it by the coloured light. A carter coming home had been knocked down on the bridge and his purse taken, and the thief had gone into the south-bank lanes, where there was no light to follow him by. The watchman wrote that down, and the hour, and put the book away.

Seumas went on into the dark. At his mother's door he took out his notebook and, by the light of her window, added up the lamps he had counted. It came to a hundred and forty-three. He wrote the figure under the column and drew a line beneath it, as he would have done for any measure of the mine office's, and then he stood for a while in the rain with the book open in his hand, with no one to send it to.

# Chapter Three: Of the Last Cartload and the Crowning

*DE 3*

## I. Of the Last Cartload

Cùirt na Fèille sat in the upper room of the toll-house at Muileann òg, over the arch where Rathad na Fèille came in, and in winter the room smelled of wet wool and lamp-soot and the river. The court kept the fair's measures and heard the fair's debts, and on market days through the year it kept the town's as well, because there was no other court in Muileann òg and nobody had seen a reason to make one. Its clerk in those years was Ùna nic Ailein. She was not yet thirty. She had come to the desk at seventeen to cut quills for old Seonaidh Crùbach, and when his eyes failed she had read the day-book aloud to him every evening until he died, and after that the justice had given her the key of the press without asking the council's leave, which was how most things at Muileann òg were done.

On 22 am Faoilleach, DE 3, it had rained since before light, a thin rain driven sideways off the plain. The market was small, as it always was in am Faoilleach: a few carts of turnips, two drovers with lean beasts, a woman selling eels from a tub. Ùna had the window open a hand's breadth for the light and kept her ink-horn under her palm against the wind.

A little before noon the coal cart came in under the arch.

She heard it before she saw it. Every child in the town knew the sound of Uilleam mac Dhùghaill's cart, because the near wheel had a split felloe bound with iron and it rang on the setts twice to every turn. He had carried coal down Rathad na Fèille from the yards at Cathair dhearg for thirty-one years. His father had carried it before him, when the loads came to the fair from the wagons of Comhairle nam Mèinnean and a cart went back and forth four times in a market week. In Ùna's first years at the desk Uilleam had still come every market day. Then it was every other. In the autumn before last, when Comhairle nam Mèinnean cut its sales and the price at the fair doubled, the court had fixed a ceiling, and Uilleam had sold under it twice and then stopped coming at all until the court looked away.

He stopped under her window. The load was covered in sacking, black with rain. He climbed down slowly, one hand on the shaft, and looked up at her.

"Is he in?" he said.

"He is in."

"Then I'll sell it whole, and I'll sell it here, and you can write it."

Fionnlagh mac Gille-Chaluim, justice of Cùirt na Fèille, came down to the arch in his old brown cloak and stood in the rain to see it done, as the rules asked. He was past seventy and had kept the court for twenty years. He lifted a corner of the sacking and looked at the coal underneath: small stuff, most of it, the size of a hen's egg and smaller, and some slack at the bottom that would be lost in the grate. There was no great lump in it anywhere. He dropped the sacking back.

"Whose yard?"

"The capital's. The last of what they'd let me have."

"Price?"

Uilleam told him. Ùna, above them, wrote it down before the justice answered, because she knew he would not argue. It was more than a third over the ceiling that was still painted on the board by the door.

The buyer was Màiri nic Leòid, who kept the brew-house by the ford and had a copper to boil. She had come up the street under a sack of her own with her son behind her pushing a barrow, and she counted the coin out on the step of the toll-house with the rain running off her hood onto the stone. When the boy had shovelled half the load into the barrow he took it off and came back for the other half, and Uilleam stood by his horse and did not help him. The horse was old too. Its breath smoked.

When the cart was empty Uilleam came up the stair and stood dripping in the doorway of the court-room with his hat in his hands. He had never come up before. The carters paid their dues at the window below.

"Put it in," he said. "The whole load, and to her, and the price. And put it that it was the last."

"I'll write what was sold," Ùna said. "How do I know it was the last?"

"Because I'm telling you. The yard won't sell by the cart any more. They'll sell by the sack at the gate, to anyone who walks up, and dear, and a man with a cart can't make a living of sacks." He turned his hat round once. "Put it that I said so."

She wrote the sale in its line, as every sale of coal-fuel had been written in that book since the fair was first held: the day, the seller, the buyer, the load, the price, the justice's mark. Then, in the margin, in smaller letters, she wrote: *The carter says this is the last load sold at this court by the cartload. The yard at Cathair dhearg sells now by the sack.* She turned the book round so that he could see it. He could not read. He looked at the marks a long while all the same.

"That's it, then," he said, and went down.

The justice came up after him and read the margin with his finger. He did not tell her to strike it. He went to the door, and took his knife, and scraped at the painted ceiling on the board until the figures were a grey smear.

"No sense keeping a price nobody sells at," he said. "Write that too."

She wrote that too. Afterwards, when the market had packed up and the lamps were lit, she turned back through the book to see how many cartloads there had been. In the first years of the fair they filled a page a day. Ten years back they filled a page a week. She found Uilleam's name on the last seven, one under another, like a man going down a stair.

Uilleam mac Dhùghaill sold his cart that spring to a man who carried grain from Muileann ghlas, and kept the horse, and did not come to the fair again that anyone at the court remembered.

## II. Of the Sack and the Lump

The day-book of Cùirt na Fèille for that year is in an Leabharlann now, and a reader who turns its pages can watch the coal go out of it.

In am Faoilleach there is the cartload. Through an Gearran and am Màrt there is no coal at all; the town bought what it bought at the capital, those who could get there, and those who could not burned turf and furze and cold wood from the hedges, and the court was asked twice to settle quarrels over hedges. In an Giblean a man from Cnoc leathan came with eleven sacks on a pack-horse and sold them one at a time from the step of the toll-house, which the court allowed, since the rules said nothing against it, and Ùna wrote the eleven sales in eleven lines. After that the sacks came irregularly, three or four in a market day, carried by whoever had got them. The price in the book goes up by a little every month. Nobody in the book complains of it. The court had already given up the ceiling, and there was nobody to complain to.

What the book does not show is the town. Ùna walked home every evening through the lanes below the toll-house, where the weavers' cottages stood in two rows back to back, and she saw the chimneys smoking less. The women took their bread to the baker's oven instead of their own. Old men sat in the brew-house late because Màiri nic Leòid kept the copper going and the room was warm, and some of them paid for one cup in an evening and made it last till she put them out. In the rows where there were children the doors were kept shut by day, which nobody in Muileann òg had done in Ùna's lifetime. The spring was mild and wet. People said it was lucky, and it was.

On Bealltainn a boy came into the court from one of the small houses of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail in the hills to the west. He was a custodian's boy, in a grey tunic, and he had walked since before dawn. He had money in a knotted cloth and asked, with great care for his manners, for a piece of coal.

"How much?" Ùna said.

"A piece. For the altar. For tonight." He held his hands apart to show her, about the size of a loaf. "Our custodian says the fire of Bealltainn must be lit from a coal of the vein, and we have none left in the house, and the pits send no more to houses of our size."

There was no coal in the market that day. Ùna sent down to the man from Cnoc leathan, who had one sack left over from the week before and had kept it back to burn at home; he came up grumbling and opened it on the floor of the court-room, and the justice turned the pieces over with his foot until he found one big enough, a black lump with a seam of colour in its broken face that took the lamplight and showed a flash of blue and red when he turned it. It was the kind the old people called a good coal, the kind that had once come by the wagon.

The boy paid. It was more than a cart-horse cost at Lùnastal the year before. He wrapped the lump in the cloth the money had come in, and put it inside his tunic against his chest, and went off down the west road at a trot.

Ùna wrote the sale. Then she sat with the pen in her hand. The rules of the court said that coal-fuel was entered by the load, the sack or the basket, and this was none of them. She wrote: *One lump, for an altar.* It is the first such entry in the book. There were four more before the end of that year, and in each the buyer gives the name of a house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, and in each the justice picked out the piece himself.

"They'll be buying it by the lump for the altars when there's none to be had for the grate," he said to her that evening, when she read him the day's lines. "I've seen that coming for ten years. It's a strange thing to see it come."

She asked him what else he had seen coming.

"Nothing I'd put in a book," he said.

## III. Of the Crowning at Cathair dhearg

In the summer word went round Rathad na Fèille that Mairead's reign had ended, and that there would be a crowning at Lùnastal, the first in fifteen years. The court shut for the day of the feast by the justice's order. Half the town went up to the capital to see it, and Ùna went with them.

They went up the day before in the carrier's wagon, twelve to a bench, and slept in the carrier's loft in the lane behind the tannery, and were in the streets before light. Rathad na Fèille was full all the way up. There were families walking with their children on their shoulders; there were two priests of Òrd Mhacha from the house at Cnoc òg with a bundle of green boughs; there were drovers with no beasts, and a man selling cold mutton pies from a board hung round his neck, who had sold out before they reached the bridge. The long light of the day before the feast lay yellow across the barley. From the brow of the last hill they could see the smoke of Cathair dhearg over the river, less of it than Ùna remembered.

What follows is told as she wrote it that night in a letter to the justice, who had stayed at home. The letter was kept among the court's papers and came to an Leabharlann with the day-books.

"We stood nearly five hours," she wrote, "in the street below the temple, the one that goes up from the bridge, and I could see the temple steps between a woman's hat and a lamp-post. Nobody sat. There were soldiers of the palace in the street to hold a lane open, and they were as tired as we were by noon, and gave the children water from their own flasks.

"The regalia came out first. Òrd Mhacha keeps them, as you know, and we saw how little anyone else has handled them, for the priests carried them down the steps as if they were carrying a sleeper. There was a circlet, and a mantle of red wool that trailed on the stone, and something in a box that I could not see. People said different things about what was in the box, and I will not write them.

"Then the horses. I had not thought there would be real horses. A priest led out a grey mare and another a black horse, from the stable on the south side of the temple yard, and they were brought to the foot of the steps and stood there, one on each side. The grey was restless and the black was not. People round me were saying their names, Liath Macha and Dubh Sainglenn, and a woman behind me told her son they were not the same horses as at the last crowning, only the same names, and he asked how she knew, and she said her mother had told her the grey was the restless one then too.

"Cathal came down between the horses. I was too far off to see his face, only that he walked slowly. The priests set the mantle on him at the foot of the steps and the circlet on him at the top, and between the two the grey mare put her head down and pulled at her rope and the priest had to lean on it. Nobody laughed. I think some wanted to.

"He did not speak. I had expected him to speak. The priests spoke, and the chief of them read the old words of the rite, which I could not hear for the crowd, and then turned to the street and said in a loud voice that the kingdom had its king, and the street shouted, and the black horse threw up its head at the noise. Then Cathal went into the temple and the doors were shut, and that was all we saw of him. People stood a long time after, as though something more would happen. It did not. By and by they began to go home.

"I stood beside a man at the lamp-post the whole afternoon. He told me, when we had stood there long enough to talk, that he cut dies at the mint, and that he would be cutting the new king's dies before the month was out. His name is Gille-Easbaig Bàn. His hands are black at the nails, which he says is the ink and no washing takes it off. I asked him was it hard to cut a king's face when you had only seen it at a distance from behind a lamp-post, and he said the face is the easy part, the council sends a drawing; the hard part is the seal.

"He told me the seal of every coin is pressed with an ink ground from coal dust, as it has been since Fearchar Bonn struck the first coin of the kingdom, and every die-cutter since has been a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, and he is the first who is not. He learned his trade at the silver-smiths' in the eastern hills. So he must make the ink himself as Fearchar Bonn's men made it, from a recipe on a card that hangs by the grinding-stone, and the recipe says it must be good coal of the vein, with the colour in it, ground fine and bound with gum. He said the mint sent to Comhairle nam Mèinnean for coal of that sort and got back a price. He said the price for the little pot of ink the new dies want is as much as the mint pays him in a year. I asked him was that true or only a way of speaking. He said he had worked it out on the back of their letter, and it was true.

"I asked him why they did not use some other ink, since the coin would be as good. He looked at me as though I had asked why they did not crown the king in a barn. Then he said, 'Because a clipped coin has to show the colour at its edge. That's how you know it's the kingdom's.' I said that if coal went on the way it was going there would soon be no colour to show. He said that was the council's business and not a die-cutter's, and he would cut what he was told. Then the woman with the hat moved, and I could see the steps better, and we did not talk any more.

"Walking back to the loft at dusk I went by the streets below the tannery, where the lamps have been left dark since the autumn before last. The lamp-posts are there still, with the glass in them. Someone had hung a green bough from Lùnastal on one. It was too dark to see what was on the others. We go home in the wagon tomorrow. I have written it all down so that you will know it as well as if you had stood there, which I think is better than standing, for my feet are raw."

She sent the letter by a drover going south that night and came home herself the day after. The justice had it read to him twice.

## IV. Of the New Dies and the Ruled Line

The mint's day-book for that month is short. It says that on 30 an Lùnastal, DE 3, Gille-Easbaig Bàn delivered the dies for the coinage of the reign, face and seal, and that they were proved and found good. The coal ink for the seal was ground in the mint from coal bought of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, and the clerk set down the price, which is what Gille-Easbaig had told Ùna at the lamp-post. The first coins struck from the new dies showed the colour at the edge. No one else is named. In all that book it is the first entry in which the die-cutter is not called a pupil of anyone.

The new coin came down Rathad na Fèille in the purses of carriers and drovers through an t-Sultain, and by the time Fèill Muileann òg opened in an Dàmhair half the coin that crossed Ùna's table had Cathal's head on it. She held one of the first up to the window. It was bright, and a little thinner than the old, or she thought so; and when she turned it on its edge the thin dark rim showed where the seal-ink had been pressed, and when she tilted it in the light there was a thread of colour in the black, very small, blue going to red.

The fair ran eleven days that year. It was thinner than any year Ùna had kept its books. The coal-sellers' row, which in the old days had run the whole length of the lower field from the ford to the elm with its wagons in a line and its men black to the elbow, had four booths standing in it, and two of those sold turf. Cnoc leathan let fewer beds. The fire-watch walked the stalls every night as it had done since the burning, with buckets and a bell, and found little enough to watch; the booths were dark by nine for want of fuel to keep a brazier. But the cattle came, and the salt, and the cloth, and the court sat from first light every day in the upper room with its window open onto the noise, and Ùna wrote until her hand ached and the justice slept upright in his chair by the stove after noon and woke when anyone raised a voice.

On the northern day the Tuathaich goods came in.

It had been so since Daniel Frayne's first year in the speaker's chair of Tional nan Tuathach: one day of the fair given to goods of the north, sold through Dia-thìreach factors under the makers' marks. The factors stood at their booths along the upper field with the bales behind them, and the Tuathaich who had brought the bales down stood behind the factors and did not speak unless they were spoken to. There was grey twill from Doire ghlas with the white thread at the selvedge, and heavy cloth from Baile chiar, and knitted things in baskets, and fish salted in kegs from the northern coast. The buyers from the south walked the booths and fingered the cloth and asked the factors the price. The factors turned round and asked the makers, in the northern tongue, and then turned back and said the price in Dia-thìris, a little higher. Ùna had watched it done for ten years. It went quickly when it went well.

A little after noon the factor Coinneach Liath came up the stair of the toll-house with a man behind him.

The man was a Tuathach. He was of middle age, square and brown, in a jacket of Doire ghlas twill gone thin at the elbows, and he carried a creel on his back with a sacking cover lashed down over it. He stood in the doorway. Coinneach Liath came to the table, and leaned on it, and said that he had a sale to enter and did not know how to enter it.

"What goods?" said Ùna.

"Fuel."

"Coal-fuel goes in by the sack or the basket. Or the lump." She turned the book to the page. "Which?"

"It's not coal."

The justice woke. He looked at the factor, and then past him at the man in the doorway, and said, "Let's see it."

The man set the creel down on the floor and unlashed the cover. Inside, packed close like peats, were cakes of something black: flat and squarish, a little bigger than a man's hand, rough on the faces, with a dull shine where they had rubbed on each other. The man took one out and held it up. Ùna saw that his palm was grey with the dust of it.

"What is it?" said the justice.

The man answered him in Dia-thìris, slowly and correctly, the way northern people spoke it at the fair when they wanted no mistake. "It's made from the waste. What the pits throw out. It's burned in the north for a year and more."

"Made by whom?"

"Made in the north."

"Does it burn?"

The man looked at the stove. The justice nodded, and Ùna got up and opened the stove door, and the man crouched and put the cake in on top of the embers of the turf, and they waited. For a while nothing happened. Then the edges of the cake began to glow, a dull red with no flame, and a thick yellowish smoke curled out of it and up the flue, and some of it came back into the room. It had a smell that Ùna had never smelled in her life: sour, oily, like a tannery and a pitch-pot together. Coinneach Liath put his sleeve over his nose. The justice did not. He held his hands out to the stove door and kept them there.

"It's hot," he said, after a while.

"It's hot," the man agreed. "It lasts."

"And it stinks."

"It does."

The justice sat back. "Well," he said to the room, "it's not coal. What's it called?"

The man shrugged. "In the north the women call it the black cake. Some call it after the man who first made it." He looked at Ùna's pen. "Black cake will do."

The factor named his price for the creel, which the man had told him in the northern tongue on the stair. A buyer was waiting at the foot of the steps, a woman of Muileann ghlas with a bakehouse, who had watched the smoke come out of the court-room window and come up to see what it was. She bought the creel whole. She paid in the new coin, and Ùna saw the dark rim on the pieces as they went across the table into the factor's hand, and from the factor's hand, when the factor had taken his part, into the Tuathach's. He looked at them no longer than it took to count them. He put them in his jacket.

Then there was the entry to make.

The day-book of Cùirt na Fèille is ruled by hand at the start of each year, one page for each kind of goods the fair has sold before, and the lines run across from the day to the price, and at the head of each page the kind of goods is written in the clerk's best hand. Ùna turned through them: grain, cattle, sheep, horses, wool, cloth, salt, fish, timber, stone, iron, coal-fuel. She went back to coal-fuel and looked at it: the cartload in am Faoilleach, the sacks, the five lumps for altars, and then nothing since the start of the fair. The justice watched her. So did the factor, and the Tuathach in the doorway, and the baker's wife of Muileann ghlas with her creel, who wanted to be gone.

"Put it under coal," said Coinneach Liath. "It's the same trade."

"It's not coal," said the justice. "We've just said so. And the man says it isn't. And I'll not have the clerks of the pits reading my book and finding their coal sold by the creel at half their price, and coming down here to tell me I've made a fool of their ledger."

"Then put it under sundries."

Ùna did not answer him. She took the ruler out of the drawer, and the lead, and turned to the back of the book, where there were clean leaves kept for the next year. She ruled a page as the pages at the front were ruled, across and down, and at the head of it she wrote *black cake*, and under that, smaller, *of the north*. Then she dipped the pen and wrote the sale in its first line: the day, the factor as seller, the maker not named, the buyer of Muileann ghlas, one creel, the price, and a space for the justice's mark.

She turned the book so that the justice could make his mark. He looked at the page a long time. The black cake in the stove had settled and was burning low and red, and the smell of it lay in the room.

"There's only the one line on that page," he said.

"There's only been the one sale."

He made his mark. The Tuathach picked up his empty creel and put the straps over his shoulders. At the door he stopped and looked back at the page from where he stood, though he was too far off to read it, and then he went down the stair into the noise of the northern day, and Ùna did not see him again at that fair. She had not asked his name. The rules of the northern day did not ask for it.

When the fair was over and the booths were down and the field was mud, she went back through the book to reckon the year, as she did every year in the last week of an Dàmhair, with the lamp lit early.
