The page of coal-fuel held the cartload, a run of sacks, and five lumps for altars. The page she had ruled at the back held one line. She sat and looked at both for a while in the lamplight. Then she wrote at the foot of the year, under the totals, in the place where the clerks of Cùirt na Fèille had always written the year's weather and the state of the roads: *Coal sold this year by the cart, by the sack, by the lump. A new fuel sold once, from the north.* She blotted it, and shut the press, and turned the key, and put out the lamp.

# Chapter Four: Of the Shipmasters' Works

*DE 4*

## I. Of the Salt-Sheds

Peigi nic Ascaill smelt the works before she saw them.

She had come down from Cathair dhearg in the second week of am Màrt, two days in the carrier's coach with a crate of lamp-glass on the seat beside her, and on the second afternoon, where the road tops the last rise above the southern coast, the wind came up off the sea and brought her a smell she had no name for. It was like tar, and like a wet hearth in the morning, and under both was something sour and sharp that made her eyes water. The carrier, a broad man from Muileann òg who had driven the coast road half his life, put his sleeve over his nose and said nothing until they were down among the first houses. Then he said, "That's them. The shipmasters. You can smell them from Tobar dhearg when it blows from the west."

Below them lay Seann Skell of the south, the great port of the southern coast: its harbour inside the long mole, the grey roofs going down to the water in steps, and on the height the house of Òrd Bhrìde with its lamp already lit in the west window against the dusk. Beyond the harbour, on the east side where the salt-pans had been, stood a row of long low sheds with tarred roofs, and at the end of the row a new chimney of red brick, still in its scaffolding, with smoke coming out of it at a slant.

Nobody had built anything so tall on that shore in the memory of the town. It was not yet as tall as it would be by the year's end, and already the gulls went round it.

Peigi had read about it at her desk in the capital. The company of shipmasters, Comann nan Sciobairean, had taken a lease of the old salt-sheds in the winter; the salt trade had long gone east, and the town was glad to be paid for sheds that had stood empty since the humans' time. On 20 an Gearran, DE 4, the company had set up its works there, the first works for the making of dubhan anywhere on the island outside the north. That was what the letter to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais said, in a clerk's round hand, and it said no more. It did not say who had shown them the making, or where they had it from.

She had also read the surveyors' report of two years before, which had come to an Leabharlann and to her own masters and been filed without a minute. Three clauses: it burns; it stinks; it is not coal. She had copied the three clauses into her pocket-book and underlined the first.

She was thirty-six that spring, a narrow woman with ink on her second finger that no soap would take off, and she had been engineer to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais for six years. In those six years she had watched the price of the lights' coal go up every quarter, and every quarter she had written to say so. The five towers of the island burned coal-lit flame, the flame with the dark coloured edge that only the island's coal gives, and the coal came dearer and poorer each year from the failing vein. At Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, the first of the five, the keeper had begun to bank the fire on calm nights to save it. Peigi had not written that to her masters. She had told the keeper she had not heard it.

She took a room at an inn on the quay where the landlady fed her fish and asked her no questions, and in the morning she walked round the harbour to the sheds.

The master of the company met her at the gate. He was an old salt-shipper with a white beard cut square and a coat too good for the place, and he knew who she was before she said it. He took her hand in both of his and said the whole town knew the lights' own engineer had come, and that the company was honoured.

"I've come to see it made," Peigi said.

"And so you shall," he said, "so far as there is anything to see."

He walked her through the first of the sheds. It was full of heaps: slack and spoil, the grey and black waste that the pits throw out and the heaps of the pit towns are made of, brought down the coast in the company's own hulls. Men were shovelling it into barrows. The floor was black and the light came in grey through the high windows, and the dust stood in the light like smoke. In the second shed the waste went into iron retorts, six of them in a row on brick furnaces, and there the heat met her at the door like a hand on the chest. Men in leather aprons tended the fires. The smell she had met on the hill was here at its root, and she breathed through her mouth.

The third shed was locked. There was a new padlock on it the size of a man's fist.

"The making-shed," said the master of the company. "Where the stuff is finished. You'll forgive us. Every house has one room it keeps."

In the fourth shed the finished dubhan stood in barrels, rows of them, new oak bound with iron, and at the far end a man had one open and was drawing it off into a can. It came out thick and black and slow, like treacle in cold weather, and it shone. The master had the man fill a small lamp from the can and light it on a bench, and it burned with a yellow flame, steady and a little smoky, and the smell of it was less than the smell of the shed.

Peigi watched the flame for a long time. She held her hand over the chimney and felt the heat, and turned the wick up and down, and held a sheet of her pocket-book behind it to see how the light fell. Then she asked the question she had come to ask.

"Where did you learn the making?"

"You'll take a glass of wine," said the master of the company.

He took her up to a room over the gate where there was a fire of driftwood and a table with a cloth on it. The wine was from the south-west coast, red and good, and he poured it himself. He talked about the harbour, and the price of hulls, and how the coal ships had had nothing to carry these five years, which was true. His father, he said, had carried coal for A' Chompanaidh of the humans from the west coast to the capital and been paid in human silver. Then he asked after the keeper at Tobar dhearg, whom he had known as a girl.

When she asked the question again, he filled her glass.

When she asked it a third time, he smiled and said, "We are shipmasters, engineer. We go a long way along the coast and we hear a great deal. We have a paper for the lease, and a paper for the harbour-due, and the maor has seen both. There's no law on the making. You'll find nothing wrong with us."

"I'm not looking for anything wrong."

"Then you'll find nothing," he said, and filled his own glass.

She went down to the yard afterwards and stood in the wind to clear her head. Men were rolling barrels down a plank onto a cart for the quay. Most were Dia-thìrich of the town, in the blue smocks of the harbour. Four or five were not.

She knew them for Tuathaich before she heard them speak, by the cut of their hair and the way they stood apart at the water-butt; and when one of them called to another it was in the humans' tongue, and the answer came back in Dia-thìris, as if the two tongues were one road with a ford in it. It was a rare thing in the south to see Tuathaich working at all. They do not come south, the council's old minute says; and here were five of them at the far end of the island, in a shipmasters' yard, with black to the elbow.

One of them was fitting a new tap to a barrel at the end of the plank. He was a young man, lean, with his sleeves rolled above the elbow and a burn scar on the back of one wrist, and he worked the tap into the wood with small turns of a wrench, listening to it. When it was in he tried it, closed it, wiped it with his thumb, and went on to the next. He did not look up. Peigi watched him fit three taps. Not one of them dripped.

"Who is that?" she asked the foreman, a Seann Skell man.

"That one? Ashby. Joe Ashby. From Caol mhòr, up north." The foreman shrugged. "They're good hands, the northern ones. They know the stuff."

"How do they know it?"

The foreman looked at her, and then at the gate-house window, and said he had barrels to see to.

Three more days she stayed. She saw the retorts filled and the spoil go in grey and come out black, and she saw the locked shed opened twice, each time for a man to go in with a lamp and come out again, and the door shut behind him. She counted the barrels in the fourth shed, and the carts on the quay, and the hulls in the harbour with the company's mark, a black ring, painted on their bows, and wrote it all down. On the fourth morning she took the coach back to the capital and wrote her report on the way, with the book on her knee and the coach lurching.

*The fuel burns clean enough for a lamp,* she wrote. *It may serve for the lights. The works will not say how it is made, and I think they will not say it to us or to anyone. They have Tuathaich hands who know the stuff. I asked where from and was given wine.*

She thought about striking the last line out, and left it.

## II. Of the Making-Shed

Her masters read her report and filed it. Nobody wrote to her about it. In an t-Ògmhios she found a reason to go south again: the lantern at Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg wanted new glass, and the glass-blowers of Seann Skell, who blow from the white sand of their own shore, were the best on the island and half the price of the capital's. She saw the glass ordered in a day. Then she walked over to the works.

The chimney was finished. It stood above the salt-sheds like a finger raised, and its smoke went up straight on still days and lay along the shore on windy ones, and the fishwives of the harbour said the herring tasted of it. The town had taken a petition to the maor about the reek. The maor had read it and answered that the company paid its harbour-due. That was the end of the petition.

The works had doubled since am Màrt. There were twelve retorts now, and two new sheds, and a jetty of its own where a hull with the black ring on her bow was unloading spoil into barrows. The master of the company was away up the coast. The foreman let her in without asking him, because she had been there before and it was a hot day and he was busy.

She did not go near the locked shed. She went and found the Tuathaich.

There were nine of them now. They worked the retorts at the far end, the hottest end, in shifts, and they ate together at noon in the shade of the jetty wall, bread and cold fish and a can of tea boiled over a dubhan lamp. Joe Ashby was among them. He had grown a beard since the spring, and his scar had a new one beside it.

Peigi sat down on an upturned barrel near them with her own bread. It was not a thing an engineer of the lights did, and the men went silent. After a while one of the older ones said something in the humans' tongue that made two of the others laugh. Joe did not laugh.

"He says," Joe said to her, in Dia-thìris, "that you've come to learn the making by sitting on it."

It was the first time she had heard him speak. His Dia-thìris was the north's, with the long vowels shorter, and quick.

"I came to ask about the taps," Peigi said. "I watched you in the spring. You fitted three and none of them dripped. The lights have barrels that drip at every tap on the island."

He looked at her for a while. Then he took a tap out of his apron pocket and passed it to her, and showed her how the thread was cut finer than the carpenters cut it, and how he wrapped it with tarred cord, and why the cord went on with the thread and not against it. It took him a long time to explain, because he did it with his hands more than with words, and she asked him to do it twice. The others went back to their bread.

"Where did you learn that?"

"Caol mhòr. There's boats at Caol mhòr. You learn taps on boats or you bail."

"And the dubhan? Where did you learn to work the retorts?"

"Here," said Joe.

"And before here?"

He took the tap back from her and put it in his apron pocket.

"Before here," he said, "I fitted boats at Caol mhòr."

That was all, and she did not ask him again. Peigi was no fool. She could see that the men at the jetty wall had stopped eating to listen, and that the foreman at the retort-house door had turned his head. Whatever there was to be told, it was not going to be told on an upturned barrel at noon to a woman from the capital with ink on her finger. She was not even sure that Joe Ashby knew it. He might have come south for the wage, as men go anywhere for a wage, and been set to the retorts because he was quick with his hands. The Tuathaich at the wall might have been hired off the quay for all she could tell. The company's hulls went up and down the whole coast.

In the afternoon one of the retorts burst.

She heard it from the yard, a crack like a mast going, and then the shouting. By the time she reached the retort-house door the men had the furnace raked out and were throwing sand on the floor, and a Seann Skell man was sitting against the wall with his arm held out in front of him and the skin of it gone white and wet. The stuff had come out of the split seam of the retort in a black spray. Joe Ashby had him by the shoulder and was pouring water over the arm from a bucket, slowly, and talking to him in Dia-thìris the whole time about nothing: the weather, the herring, the fishwives. The foreman had gone for the doctor.

Peigi looked at the retort. It had split along the lower seam where the rivets were, and she could see why: the iron had been heated too fast on one side, where the furnace door was, and had not had time to follow on the other. She said so to the foreman when he came back. He looked at her as if she had spoken in the humans' tongue.

"Bank the fire on the door side," she said. "Or put a baffle in. Anyone who has tended a tower furnace could tell you. The heat wants to go round."

The foreman said he would tell the master when he came back.

She went back to the inn and drew a baffle for the retort furnace on a sheet of her pocket-book, with the measures, and sent it round to the works in the morning with a boy, unsigned. Then she went back to the capital with the glass for Tobar dhearg packed in straw on the coach roof, and she did not know until the autumn that the company had fitted her baffle to every furnace in the row.

## III. Of Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche

In an t-Samhain she was in the south a third time, for the new glass was being set in the lantern at Tobar dhearg and she would not leave that to anyone. It rained for a week. On the evening appointed she walked into Seann Skell along the cliff path, with the gale at her back and the rain coming over her shoulder, to hear Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche read in Brìde's house.

Everyone knew it was to be read. The letter had been talked of in the south since the summer. Alasdair mac Ìomhair, Àrd-choimheadaiche of Òrd Bhrìde since before Cathal was crowned, had been asked by the custodians of four shires whether the new fuel was lawful to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, and had taken the whole of the summer and the autumn to answer. Some said he was waiting for the council. Some said he was waiting for the works to fail. The fishwives said he was waiting for the smell to go away.

On 25 an t-Samhain, DE 4, his answer was sent to every house of the order on the island, to be read aloud at the evening lamp, and at Seann Skell he read it himself.

The great house of Òrd Bhrìde at Seann Skell is the largest house of the order anywhere, and the oldest part of it is older than the kingdom: a long hall of grey stone with a roof of heavy slate, and at the far end, up three steps, Brìde's altar, with the coal flame burning in its iron cup as it had burned since before the humans came. It was the only fire in the hall. The rain beat on the high windows and the wind came under the door, and the people stood close in their wet coats and steamed. There were more of them than the hall was built for. Peigi stood at the back against the wall, where she could see the altar over the heads.

The coal on the altar was poor. She could see that from the back of the hall. The flame had the coloured edge still, the dark blue and the green that the old coal gives; but it was low in the cup and it burned unevenly, and every so often it spat. The custodians fed it with tongs from a small box, a lump at a time, and the box was not full.

Alasdair mac Ìomhair came out from the vestry in his grey robe with the letter in his hand. He was sixty-two that year, tall and stooping, with a long face and a voice that did not need to be raised. He stood beside the altar, where the light fell on the page, and waited until the hall was still. Then he read.

The letter was not long. It greeted the houses in Brìde's name. It said that a fuel was now made on the island out of what the pits cast away, by a man's hand and without the vein; that the custodians had asked whether the order might suffer it; and that he who wrote had taken counsel and prayed at the altar and read what the order had written since An Ceangal. Then it gave the ruling.

"It is not forbidden," read Alasdair mac Ìomhair, "since it is not coal. And it is not blessed, since it is not coal."

He lowered the page. For a breath nobody in the hall moved, and the rain came on the windows. Then a custodian in the front row, a young man from one of the eastern houses, said aloud, "That's the whole of it?"

"That is the whole of it," said Alasdair mac Ìomhair.

There was a stir through the hall like wind through barley. Somebody near Peigi laughed, and stopped. An old woman in front of her said to her neighbour, very clearly, "Then my lamp has no blessing on it and I'll have to put up with it," and the people round her smiled, because many of them had dubhan lamps at home already, bought off the works' carts that summer. They had wanted to know whether they had done wrong. The Àrd-choimheadaiche had told them that they had not done wrong, and that they had not done right either, and that the vein did not come into it.

Peigi thought it was the cleverest thing she had heard a priest say. She thought, too, that it left every house on the island free to go on as it liked, and every custodian free to quarrel about it for years. She said so to Alasdair mac Ìomhair himself, half an hour later, which she had not meant to do.

He had come down the hall after the reading to speak to the people, as the custodians did, and she had not moved fast enough to get out of his way. He stopped in front of her and asked, pleasantly, whether she was not the engineer of the lights, who had been seen at the works; and she said she was; and before she could stop herself she said that the letter was very clever and would be argued for years.

"I hope so," said the old man. "A letter nobody argues is a letter nobody reads." He looked down at her with his long face. "You have come about the lights."

"I've come about the glass at Tobar dhearg."

"You have come about the lights," he said again, as if she had not spoken. "Your towers burn the island's coal, and the island's coal is failing, and you have come to see whether the new stuff will burn in a lantern." He looked back up the hall towards the altar, where the custodians were feeding the flame a lump at a time from the small box. "The houses will ask me next whether a sea-light may burn it. They will ask whether a flame of Brìde's may be put out for it. I should be glad of more time than I had for this one."

"Would you forbid it?"

"I have just told the whole island," said Alasdair mac Ìomhair, "that I forbid nothing that is not coal." He smiled a little, and went on down the hall to the people waiting for him.

The letter was argued, as he said it would be. Within the month the school of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Caol shean had written that a fuel made from the vein's own waste could not be called wholly *not coal*, since the spoil had lain against the seam for a thousand years; and the houses of Òrd an t-Seabhaig round Cnoc bheag, who had never owned the Àrd-choimheadaiche's right to rule on anything, wrote that they had not asked his opinion and were glad to have it all the same. The letter was read in every house of the order that winter and copied into the books of most of them, and it was quoted at supper-tables in the south for a long time. At the works, where they had heard that Alasdair mac Ìomhair was to rule on the fuel and had feared the worst, the master of the company opened a cask of the south-west wine for the whole yard, Tuathaich and all, and the fishwives said that the smell that night was the smell of a company that had been let off.

## IV. Of the Twenty Barrels

On 24 an Dùbhlachd, DE 4, the works sold their first year's making.

Peigi had not meant to be there. The glass at Tobar dhearg was set and the lantern lit behind it, the keeper had signed for it, and she had her seat taken on the coach for the week before midwinter. Then the gale came back and the coast road flooded under the cliff at the ford below Tobar dhearg, and the coach did not run for three days. She spent the three days at the inn on the quay, writing letters to the capital that could not be sent, and on the fourth she walked round the harbour to the works because she had nothing else to do and could not keep away.

The harbour was full of the company's hulls, riding at the mole with the black ring on their bows, and between them the fishing boats of the south coast were rafted three deep, waiting to load. The skippers had come in from all along the shore, from Tobar dhearg and the coves to the east of it and from as far as the western end of the coast, for the word had gone up and down that the works would sell before the midwinter and that dubhan was cheaper than coal by a third. The south-coast boats had burned coal in their galley-stoves and their riding-lamps since the humans' time. For five years now they had been burning driftwood and fish-oil and going cold, and more than one had gone on the rocks for want of a lamp that would stay lit in a gale. So they came in for dubhan, and they came in numbers.

The barrels came down out of the fourth shed on a slide of greased planks and went onto the boats by tackle from the jetty, two at a time, swinging out over the water with a man on the guide-rope. On the quay a clerk of the company sat at a table under a sailcloth with his ledger and his box of money, and the skippers stood in the rain in a line to pay him, in coin and in fish and in promises. Up the slope from the quay a row of carts stood with their tails to the works, and these were for the capital: dubhan for the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg, bought by the barrel on the lamp-houses' account, to light the poorer streets that had been left dark for three winters to save coal.

Peigi stood by the jetty wall and watched the carts load. She counted them, because she always counted things. There were eleven carts, six barrels to a cart.

Above everything the chimney went up into the rain. Its smoke lay along the shore to the east, grey on grey, and in the thick air it looked taller than it was. It was the tallest thing on that coast. From the quay it stood higher than Brìde's house on the height above the harbour; and the fishwives, who had never forgiven it, said it was put up where it was so that the Àrd-choimheadaiche would have to look at it every morning.

At noon the master of the company came down onto the quay in his good coat to see the last carts off, and found her.

"The engineer," he said, and took her hand in both his again. "Stormbound with us. We are honoured twice." He looked at the carts. "Your baffle, I'm told. On every furnace. We've not split a retort since the summer." He did not say who had told him, and she did not ask.

"I'm glad of it," Peigi said.

"The company is grateful. If there were ever anything the company could do for the lights."

She had not known until he said it what she was going to do. She thought afterwards that she had known since the spring, since the lamp on the bench in the fourth shed, and had only been waiting for somebody to say it to her so that she could answer.

"Twenty barrels," she said. "On account, for the lights. For a trial."

The master of the company looked at her for a while with his head a little on one side, the way the gulls look. He knew as well as she did that an engineer of Comhairle nan Taighean-solais could not buy a barrel of lamp-glass without a letter from her masters, let alone twenty barrels of a fuel those masters had filed without a word. He knew too that she had no such letter, for if she had, she would have shown it to him in am Màrt.

"A trial of what?"

"Of whether it will burn a sea-light through a winter."

"And your masters have agreed to this trial."

"My masters," said Peigi, "will agree when they have the figures."

He laughed, a short bark, and called the clerk from under the sailcloth. The clerk wrote it in the ledger while the rain dripped off the edge of the cloth onto the page: *twenty barrels to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, on account, for the engineer*. Peigi signed it. Her hand was steady. Her name went down in the company's book below the skippers of the south coast and the lamp-houses of the capital, in the same black ink, and she noticed that there was coal-dust in the ink, and did not know why she noticed it.

"Where will you have them sent?"

She had not thought of that either. The towers were at the island's ends: Tobar dhearg on the southern cape a few miles along the shore, Baile ìseal far away on the eastern cape, the three others in the north. Tobar dhearg was the nearest and the easiest, and at Tobar dhearg every soul who worked the light would know by the next morning that the engineer from the capital was burning the new stuff under their tower, and so would the house of Brìde on the height. She thought of the keeper's face.

"Hold them for me," she said. "I'll write."

"Twenty barrels held for the engineer," said the master of the company. "Joe."

Joe Ashby came out from the fourth shed with his sleeves rolled and a lump of chalk in his hand. He had heard the whole of it; she could see that he had. He went along the row by the shed wall and counted off twenty barrels and rolled them out of the line, one at a time, onto the planks under the eaves where the rain did not reach. On the head of each one he chalked a mark. She went to look at it when he had done. It was a lantern: a square with a flame inside it, drawn in four strokes and a curl, the same on all twenty.

"That's the lights'," he said.

"The lights have no mark."

"They have now," said Joe Ashby. He put the chalk in his apron pocket, next to the taps, and went back into the shed.

The last of the carts for the capital went up the slope at the fall of the dark, their lanterns lit with the stuff they carried and swinging on the tail-boards. The fishing boats cast off from the mole one by one and went out past the light on the end of it into the rain, and the smell of their galley-stoves came back across the water, tar and wet hearth and something sharp; the smell of the works, going out along the coast in every boat. Peigi stood on the quay until the last lamp was out of sight round the headland. Then she went back to the inn and wrote to her masters.

It took her until past midnight. The letter said that she had bought twenty barrels of dubhan on her masters' account, without leave, at the works of Comann nan Sciobairean at Seann Skell of the south; and she gave the price, which was a third less than the price of coal for the same hours of light; and she said that she asked their leave to run a trial of the stuff in a spare lamp, in the yard below one of their towers, for a hundred nights, with a man to keep the log. If they would not give leave, she would pay for the barrels herself out of her wage, and they could stop it from her quarter by quarter.

She read it over. It named no tower. Of the chimney it said nothing, nor of the locked shed, the Tuathaich at the jetty wall or the wine. On the last line of the letter she wrote the date and signed it; and out of the window, over the harbour, the smoke of the works went up into the dark where she could not see it, and she could smell it still.

# Chapter Five: Of the Hundred Nights

*DE 5*

## I. Of the Barrels at the Slip

The twenty barrels came up the east coast at the end of an Gearran in the hold of a salt-boat of Àth bheag, which had carried salt down to Seann Skell of the south and had nothing to bring home. Her skipper took them because the engineer of Comhairle nan Taighean-solais paid the freight in coin and in advance, and because nobody told him what was in them. He found out off the southern cape, when the sun came out for an afternoon and warmed the staves. By the time he brought her round under the eastern cape and in to the slip at Baile ìseal his crew were sleeping on deck with their coats over their faces, and he told Peigi nic Ascaill, who stood waiting on the wet stones with her bag at her feet, that he would carry pigs for her next time, live ones, but not this.

"It keeps the weather out," Peigi said. "Put your head in a coal-cart and tell me which you'd sooner."

"The coal-cart."

"So would everyone. Help me get them up the slip."

Baile ìseal is a small place. It was some ninety souls that year, in low houses of grey stone along one street that runs down to the slip, with the dunes going away north towards the ford at Àth bheag and the cape going away south into the sea. The tower stands out at the end of the cape, a couple of miles below the town, where Torcall Clachair had it raised in An Aois Choigreach, sitting in a chair at the foot of the headland because he was too old by then to climb. Long before the tower the households of that coast kept a fire on the cape in turn, to bring their boats home in a storm, and the old people of Baile ìseal will still tell you that the light is there to bring boats home, whatever Comhairle nan Taighean-solais has painted over its door. The keepers of the light were the town's watch as well. Sea-thieves had come ashore on that coast within living memory and burned the salt-sheds at Àth bheag, and the town had no other watch but the woman in the lantern-room with a glass.

Peigi had the barrels carted out along the cape by a carter of Baile ruadh, whose family had carried the keepers' coal and meal since the light was lit, and who charged her twice his rate for the smell. He set them down in the yard at the tower's foot, in the lee of the coal-store, twenty black casks in two rows. The chalk on their heads had run in the salt-boat's hold, but the mark could still be read on most of them: a square with a flame inside it, four strokes and a curl. The carter asked what it was.

"The lights' mark," said Peigi.

"The lights have got no mark."

"They have now," she said, and paid him.

She had chosen Baile ìseal in the coach going home from Seann Skell at the year's end, with her pocket-book on her knee and the five towers written down the page. Tobar dhearg was nearest the works, and the whole south coast would have known by the next morning that the engineer of the lights was burning the new stuff under its tower, and so would the house of Brìde on the height above the harbour. The three towers of the north were far, and cold, and their keepers were not people she knew. Baile ìseal was as far from the capital as a tower can be and still be on the island. It kept Na Seann Spioradan, and had no house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail within a day's walk to take offence; and its old keeper, retired, still lived at the landward end of the yard wall. She had met him twice, years before, on her rounds, and remembered that he had corrected her arithmetic.

Her masters' answer had found her at the capital in am Faoilleach, and she carried it folded inside her coat and had read it enough times to have it by heart. Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, the secretary wrote, saw no objection to a trial of the engineer's burner in the yard of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, at the engineer's own charge and in her own time, on condition that the light was not touched and the keeper's duties in no way hindered. There was a second paragraph. The secretary had observed that twenty barrels of fuel had been entered to its account at Seann Skell by the engineer's hand, and would be glad to learn under what head.

Peigi had not answered the second paragraph. She meant to answer it with a hundred nights.

The keeper met her at the tower door that afternoon. Seonag nic Thòmais was some years younger than Peigi, broad in the shoulder and red with weather, with the keys of the tower on a strap across her chest and coal-dust ground into the knuckles of both hands. A copy of the secretary's letter had come to her too, and she had it in her apron pocket, and she took it out and held it up without unfolding it, the way a man at a fair holds up a paper that proves the cow is his.

"The yard's yours," she said. "That's what it says. The stair's mine."

"I've no wish to go up your stair."

"That's as may be." Seonag looked past her at the barrels. "That light's burned coal since before my mother was born. Murchadh kept it thirty-one years and I've kept it eight, and there's never been a night it went out. Whatever you've got in those, it doesn't come past the door."

"It won't," said Peigi. "I'll want a man to keep the log. Somebody who knows a light and isn't me. My masters won't take my word for a hundred nights, and it's right not to."

Seonag considered this. Something moved at the corner of her mouth.

"Murchadh," she said. "He's nothing to do all night but sit at his window and tell me I'm burning it too high. You can give him something else to look at."

## II. Of the Spare Lamp and the Log

Murchadh mac Coinnich was seventy-one that spring. His knees had gone, and he walked with two sticks and sat with both legs stretched out before him, but his eyes were as good as they had been when he first climbed the stair as a boy from Baile ruadh, and his hand was square and exact. He had the cottage at the landward end of the yard wall, two rooms and a peat fire, with a window that looked straight up the tower to the lantern. He heard Peigi out without a word, filling his pipe and not lighting it.

"What does it cost?" he said at the end.

She told him: a third less than coal, for the same hours of light, at the works' price; and the price of coal still climbing, and the price at the works falling.

"Who makes it?"

"A company of shipmasters at Seann Skell."

"That's who sells it," said Murchadh. "Who made it first?"

"A man in the north. A Tuathach. They call the stuff by his name."

"Dubhan," said Murchadh. "The carrier from Àth bheag talks of nothing else. He says it's made out of the muck the pits throw up, and it stinks like a burnt boot." He struck a light for his pipe at last. "Well. I'll keep your log. I'll write down what I see and not what you'd like to see, and I'll rule the book myself, and you'll pay me the lights' rate for an under-keeper, since that's what you're making of me."

"Agreed."

"And you'll not argue with what I write."

"I'll argue," said Peigi. "You needn't change it."

He looked at her for a while through the smoke and then nodded, as if that was the answer he had wanted.

The spare lamp was in the coal-store under sacking. It was the tower's storm-lantern, a great box of iron and glass with a silvered bowl at the back of it, which the keepers hung on the gallery rail on the nights when the main grate was drawn and cleaned of its clinker, so that the cape was never dark. It had a grate of its own the size of a man's hat. Peigi took the grate out and threw it on the heap, and in its place she set the burner that the fitters at the works had made to her drawing over the midwinter: a broad round wick in two rings, one inside the other, with a brass drum below it to hold the fuel and a pipe coiled twice round the foot of the chimney, so that the heat of the flame would warm the stuff on its way to the wick. The fuel came out of the barrel thick and slow, like treacle in the cold, and in a cold lamp it would not climb a wick at all. Warmed, it ran like oil. She had worked that out on the bench in the fourth shed at the works in the spring, with the master of the company watching her and not knowing what he was watching.

She had a stage built for it in the yard of old ship's timber from the beach, twenty feet high with a ladder, so that the lamp stood above the yard wall and showed to the sea over the lip of the cape. From the water it would be a second light below the tower's, low and a little to the landward side. She measured the angle three times and had the stage shifted a yard to the north, and the carpenter from Baile ìseal, who had built boats for forty years and never shifted anything a yard for a woman, did it without a word, because the keeper had told him to.

Murchadh ruled the log on the afternoon of the first day, at his table by the window, with a straight-edge and a pot of the keepers' ink. He gave each night one line across two pages. The headings were his own: the night and the day of the month; wind; weather; lit; out; wick; smoke; and at the far right, with the most room, *what the boats said*.

"The boats'll say nothing," said Peigi. "They'll not know it's there."

"They'll know," said Murchadh. "And they'll have opinions. You've never lived in a fishing town."

She lit it first on 4 am Màrt, DE 5, at dusk, with the wind light from the west and a clear green sky over the land. She warmed the coil with a spirit-cup, as she had practised at the works, and when the stuff began to run she touched a spill to the wick. It took, and crawled round the rings, and stood up in the chimney yellow and a little smoky; and then, as the coil warmed and the draught drew, it lengthened and brightened until it was nearly white, and the silvered bowl behind it caught it and threw it out over the wall. Peigi came down the ladder and walked out to the lip of the cape to look at it from as near the sea as she could get.

Above it, the tower's own light burned at the top of the stair: a coal flame in its great grate, red at the heart and ringed with that dark coloured edge that only the island's coal gives, and all of it made large by the glass. Below it, and to one side, her lamp burned yellow-white and steady, smaller, plainer, and in the clear air nearly as far-reaching. From where she stood she could see both. She stood there until her feet were cold.

When she came back Murchadh had lit his own lamp and had the log open.

*Night the first,* he had written. *Wind W, light. Clear. Lit at dusk. Wick took well. Smoke: some, black, going off to the E. Smell: bad. Boats: none out.*

"Smell's no heading," said Peigi.

"It is tonight," said Murchadh.

The burner clogged at two in the morning. The flame went down on one side and then the other, yellow, sullen, and a coil of black smoke went up the chimney and blackened the glass inside. Peigi went up the ladder in her coat with a lantern in her teeth and found the wick crusted over with a hard black char, like the crust on a burnt pot, which the stuff laid down as it burned. She trimmed it with the scissors and it came up again. At four it crusted again. She trimmed it again. At sunrise, when she put it out, she had slept an hour on a chair in Murchadh's kitchen, and her hands were black to the wrist.

*Out at sunrise,* Murchadh wrote. *Wick crusted twice, trimmed twice. Engineer up the ladder with scissors at two and four. Said a word I will not write.*

## III. Of What the Boats Said

The first fortnight was a fortnight of the wick. Peigi strained the fuel through sailcloth into the drum to take out the grit and the lumps, and it crusted less. She warmed the barrel it came from by the coal-store wall on the sunny afternoons, and it crusted less again. She had the tinsmith of Àth bheag make her a second pair of wick-rings, so that one pair could burn while the other was soaked clean in a pan of the stuff itself, and on the tenth night the wick burned from dusk to dawn with one trimming. Murchadh wrote *trimmed once* under *wick* without comment, and she saw him look at it afterwards with his head on one side.

On the eleventh night a squall came in off the sea after midnight, hard cold rain driven almost level, and the chimney-glass, which was hot as a kettle, cracked from top to foot with a noise like a pistol. The flame staggered and smoked and did not go out. Peigi had three spare glasses. She put one in with the rain running down her neck, and in the morning she had the tinsmith make a hood of sheet iron to go over the top of the lantern and keep the rain off the glass. After that the glasses held.

*Night the eleventh,* the log says. *Wind SE, strong, squalls of rain. Glass cracked at one. Lamp did not go out. New glass in by the engineer, who was wet.*

The nights grew shorter, and the lamp burned less of the stuff each night; Peigi counted it, a finger-mark on the dipstick in the drum each dawn, and wrote the figures in her pocket-book beside the tower's coal. She knew the tower's coal as well as she knew her own wage. Seonag's lad, a boy of Baile ruadh who carried coal up the stair in two buckets forty times a night on a bad night, told her one morning how many buckets had gone up, and after that he told her every morning, without being asked, and she gave him a coin at the month's end, which the keeper did not see.

The coal in those years was poor. It came from the bottom of the failing vein, dear and slaty, and it burned dull and left a great deal of clinker behind. When Murchadh first climbed the stair it had burned with a green edge and a blue heart, he said, and on a still night you could see the colours from the sea two miles off. Now the edge had gone muddy, and in the last year Comhairle nan Taighean-solais had written to all five keepers that the grate was to be kept low on clear nights and fed high only in thick weather. Seonag had read that letter out to Murchadh in his kitchen and then put it in the fire.

The fishing boats of Baile ìseal went out to the long lines in the spring, a dozen of them, open boats with a lugsail and four men, and they came home at dark or after. Murchadh had been right: by the fourth night they knew the lamp was there, and by the tenth they had opinions. He wrote them down in the wide space at the right, in their own words, as nearly as he could get them, with the teller's name when the teller would give it.

*A lamp in a yard,* one said. *Like a star fallen in the nettles,* said another. *Too low. No use to a ship in the open sea.* *Too white; it hurts the eyes.* *Where's the colour gone.* *It smells from half a mile out when the wind's off the land, you'd find the cape by your nose.* An old man who had not been to sea for twenty years came out along the cape on purpose to tell Murchadh that he would not have steered by it in his day, and Murchadh wrote that down too, with the old man standing over him to see that he spelled his name right.

Late in am Màrt the salt-boat came back up the coast and her skipper walked out to the cape to look. He stood at the foot of the stage with his hands in his pockets for a long time and said at last that it was a better light than it was a smell, and that was something. Murchadh wrote it in.

Peigi slept in the day in a room of the keeper's cottage that Seonag let her have, because there was nowhere else in the yard, and ate at the keeper's table, and the two women were civil to each other across the bread. Seonag did not come near the stage. In the evenings she came down the tower door to the yard at dusk with the keys on her chest, and stood a breath in the doorway, looking out to sea and not at the lamp, and went up again; and the tower light would come on above, red, and then fuller, as the lad fed the grate. In the mornings she came down black to the elbows and went to her bed without a word. Once, in the first week of an Giblean, Peigi heard her on the stair in the small hours, going up and down between the coal-store and the lantern with her own buckets because the lad was sick, and counted forty-four journeys before she fell asleep.

On the forty-first night the haar came in.

It came off the sea in the afternoon, grey and wet and thick as fleece, as it does on that coast in the spring when a warm air comes over the cold water; and it lay high on the cape, as a haar will sometimes, with a clear ribbon under it along the face of the water. The tower's light burned up inside it. From the slip you could see a red smear in the grey where it should have been, and nothing else. Peigi's lamp burned below it, in the clear ribbon, and from the slip you could see it plain.

Calum mac Iain's boat was the last in that night. He had gone out farther than the others after the lines, and the haar had found him on the way home. He told the story afterwards at the slip, where Peigi heard it, and he told it more than once, so that the log has two forms of it. In the first he was steering for the smear in the haar, which is all a sensible man could do, when he saw a light under it, low and white, and took it for somebody on the rocks with a lamp and came in to see who was drowning. In the second he knew very well what it was, and had been steering by it for half an hour, and would do it again. Either way he came round the cape with the white light on his right hand and the smear above it and found the slip without touching a stone.

The next morning he walked out to the yard and looked at the lamp for a while, burnt out and black-glassed in the daylight on its stage, and then went to Murchadh's window.

"You'll not write that," he said. "Don't let Seonag see it."

*Night the forty-first,* the log says. *Wind E, light. Haar, thick from the afternoon, lying high. Tower light lost in it from the slip. This lamp seen under it. Wick trimmed once. Boats: Calum mac Iain came in by this lamp and not by the tower. Asked me not to write it.*

Seonag read it all the same. She read the whole log at the end of every week. Murchadh left it open on his table on purpose.

On the eve of Bealltainn the young people of Baile ìseal lit their fire on the dunes north of the town, as they did every year, and put out the hearths of the houses and lit them again from it the next morning. A girl of the town came out along the cape on the morning of the feast with a shovel of the fire in a pail, as her mother had carried it out to the tower in Murchadh's time and her grandmother before that, and the lad took it up the stair to the grate. On the step of the stage she stopped, and looked at Peigi's lamp, and asked whether it was to have some too.

"It lights from a spill," said Peigi.

"It's to have some," said Murchadh from his window.

So the girl climbed the ladder with her pail, and Peigi, who thought it nonsense and knew better than to say so, took the spill and lit it from the Bealltainn coals, and put it in her pocket-book for that night, and lit the lamp with it at dusk. Murchadh wrote *lit from the Bealltainn fire* under *lit*. That was the fifty-ninth night.

## IV. Of the Seventieth Night

The gale came on the seventieth night out of the south-east, off the open sea. The glass had been falling all day in Murchadh's kitchen, and the swell had come in under a fine sky long before the wind did, so that the old men at the slip knew what was coming and kept their boats in. Two did not. They had gone out before dawn to lift lines they had shot the day before, far out to the south-east, and they were not back by noon, and by the middle of the afternoon the wind was up and the rain behind it.

By dusk it was a whole gale. The sea came up the cape in sheets and the spray went over the yard wall and rattled on the coal-store roof like shot. Peigi and the lad had lashed the stage to the wall with the carter's ropes in the afternoon, and she had wired the chimney-glass into the lantern at the top and bottom, and under the hood; and when she lit the lamp at dusk the flame lay over flat in the chimney, and smoked, and roared, and stood up again. She stayed on the ladder with it until she was sure. Then she went down and sat at the foot of the stage in her oilskin with her back to the timber and the dipstick in her lap, and Murchadh opened his window a hand's breadth against the weather so that he could see both lights at once, and sat at it with the log.

The trouble in the tower began a little after midnight. Peigi saw it from the yard before she understood it: the red of the tower light went dull, and then dark red, and then brown, like a coal dropped out of a grate on to the hearth. Smoke was coming out of the lantern's vents at the top, and blowing flat, and the wind was driving it down on to the gallery and round the glass.

She learned afterwards what had happened, from the lad. The roof of the coal-store had lifted in the first of the gale and let the rain in on the heap, and the coal that went up the stair from nine o'clock on was wet. The grate would not draw on it. The wind came down the vent at the top of the lantern as it will in a south-easter, the one wind the vent was never built against, and drove the smoke back into the room; and the poor coal of those years, wet, lay in the grate and smoked and sulked and would not blaze. Seonag raked it and fed it and raked it. She opened the vent and the wind came down it harder. She shut it and the grate died under her hands. The inside of the glass went black with soot. From the sea, the light of Baile ìseal was a red smudge, and then a brown one, and for the best part of two hours, from the second hour after midnight to the fourth, there was hardly any light at all.

Peigi went to the tower door. It was shut, and she could hear Seonag above, shouting to the lad for dry coal from the back of the heap, and the wind in the stair like a beast in a pit. She put her hand on the latch.

"Keep off my stair!" Seonag's voice came down the stone. She could not have seen who it was. She knew.

Peigi took her hand off the latch and went back to the stage.

Her own lamp was burning. It burned low and yellow when the gusts came, and long and white between them, and it smoked, and the smoke went off towards the land in a black rag; and every half-hour she went up the ladder and trimmed it, and Murchadh at his window called the time out to her and wrote it down, and every half-hour the lad came down out of the tower door with his buckets and looked at it and went up again with the dry coal. The drum held. The wire held. The hood held. The chimney-glass steamed and cleared and steamed. And all the while it showed out over the lip of the cape to the sea, low and plain, a second light below the tower, and for two hours the only one.

The first of the two boats came round the cape at about the third hour. Peigi did not see her. She saw a lantern on the water to the south, going up and down in the seas at a great distance, and then going behind the point, and she did not know until the morning that it had been Calum mac Iain's brother's boat. The second came in an hour after, with a torn sail and a man with a broken arm, and her skipper said at the slip in the morning, before he had his boots off, that he had not seen the tower since midnight and had steered for the white light under the cape because there was nothing else to steer for, and had not known what it was, and did not care.

At the fourth hour the tower light came back. Seonag had got dry coal from the back of the heap under the tarpaulin, and wedged the vent half-open with a bar so that the wind could neither blow straight down nor shut it, and at last the grate drew. The red came up through the soot, dull and then fuller, and by the first grey of dawn it was burning as it should. Peigi's lamp burned on below it until sunrise, and she put it out as the sun came up out of the sea to the east, far off, where Ceò Mhanannain lies along the edge of Muir Mhanannain; and then she sat down on the step of the stage because her legs would not hold her.

Seonag came down the stair when the sun was up. She was black from her hair to her boots, and her eyes were red, and her hands were cut about the knuckles from the rake. She stood at the tower door and looked across the yard at the lamp on its stage, dark now, with its glass black and its drum wet, and at Peigi on the step.

"It's lower than my light," she said.

"It is."

"A light that low's no use to a ship in the open sea."

"No."

Seonag looked at it a while longer.

"It didn't go out," she said, and went into the cottage and shut the door.

Murchadh had written the night up before either of them came in. His hand is as square that morning as any other in the book.

*Night the seventieth. Wind SE, a whole gale from dusk, rain. Lit at dusk. Out at sunrise. Wick trimmed every half-hour. Smoke: much, blown away to the land. The tower's light failed from the second hour after midnight to the fourth, for wet coal and a down-draught; the keeper kept at it. This lamp did not fail. Boats: two came in by it. They said nothing about it. They were too wet.*

## V. Of the Hundredth Night

After the seventieth night the lad came down out of the tower every evening at dusk, sent by the keeper, to ask whether the lamp was lit; and when it was, he went up again and said so. Seonag herself did not come.

A roofer came from Baile ruadh in the week after the gale and put the coal-store to rights, and a letter came from the secretary at Cathair dhearg in answer to the keeper's report of the night, asking for particulars of the wet coal and the down-draught, and saying nothing of the yard. Seonag gave Peigi the letter to read at breakfast. It was the first thing she had given her.

Peigi began to write her report in those weeks, a page or two in the day before she slept, at Murchadh's table while he sat by the fire. She had every night in her pocket-book beside the tower's: the fuel burned by the finger on the dipstick, the coal by the lad's count of buckets, the hours from dusk to dawn, the price of each at the works and at the pit-head. She did the sums three times, and Murchadh did them once in his head and found that she had carried a figure wrong in the second, and she did them a fourth time. At that rate the barrels would last the hundred nights and some over. By the end of the trial she had burned eleven of the twenty and some of a twelfth.

The nights shortened. By the start of an t-Ògmhios the lamp was lit late and put out early, and in the few hours between the sky in the north never went all the way dark, but lay green and pale along the edge of the land; and on the clear evenings, far out over the sea to the east, Ceò Mhanannain could be seen lying on the water where it always lies, grey, at the very edge of sight. Peigi had never lived where she could see it. On the calm nights, with the lamp trimmed and the drum full and nothing to do until the next trimming, she sat at the lip of the cape and looked at it. The straight way east had never been found through it. She thought, not for the first time, that a lamp is a strange thing to set against a sea like that, and that the people of Baile ìseal had been setting one there since An Aois Ailein.

The boats had stopped saying things. In the wide space at the right of the log, through the last weeks, the line goes on night after night, *boats: nothing*, and *boats: nothing*, and once *boats: Calum mac Iain asks when it's to go up the stair*, which Murchadh wrote down without a word and Peigi read without one.

On the ninety-sixth night Seonag came down out of the tower door at dusk and crossed the yard to the foot of the stage, where she had not stood in three months. She looked up at the lamp for some time, lit, the flame standing tall and nearly white in its chimney. Then she asked how the coil round the chimney foot was made, and how many turns it had, and why two and not three; and whether the drum would take a bigger charge; and how often the wick was changed in a week of bad weather; and what the stuff did to brass. They were an engineer's questions, and Peigi answered them one by one, as exactly as she could, with the lad standing by with his buckets forgotten in his hands. At the end of it Seonag nodded.

"The stair's still mine," she said.

"I know it is."

"Good," said Seonag, and went up to light her own.

The hundredth night was fair, with a light wind from the west and a long clear dusk. Peigi lit the lamp herself, with a spill, at the hour Murchadh called; she warmed the coil and touched the wick and watched it climb and stand, as she had watched it ninety-nine times before, and came down the ladder and stood a while at the foot. The tower's light came on above it, red, and fuller, as the lad fed the grate.

She trimmed the wick at midnight and at two. There was nothing else to do. She sat on the step of the stage with her coat round her and her back to the timber, and did not sleep, and watched the two lights go out over the sea, one high and one low, and the short night go grey in the north and then pale along the eastern water. When the sun came up she climbed the ladder and put the lamp out.

Murchadh had the log open on the table when she came in, and the pen in the ink. She had thought, in the night, that she might ask to write the last line herself. She held her tongue. It was his book.

He wrote it slowly, and blotted it, and turned the book round on the table so that she could read it.

*Night the hundredth. Wind W, light. Clear; Ceò Mhanannain on the sea to the E, as always. Lit at dusk. Out at sunrise. Wick trimmed twice. Smoke: some. Boats: said nothing about it. They have got used to it.*

# Chapter Six: Of the Boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich

*DE 5 – 6*

## I. Of the Engine in the Rope-Shed

In the summer that the trial lamp on the eastern cape ran out its hundred nights, some ninety miles to the west, at the other end of the south coast, a boatwright of Caol fhiadhaich bought an engine for the price of old iron. The boatwrights of the south-west tell it that way, as a bargain first and a quarrel after, and they begin it with the town.

Caol fhiadhaich stands at the head of its strait, a mile of broken water between the harbour wall and the skerries, where the tide runs one way under a wind blowing the other and the sea stands up in ridges. Its pilots had earned their bread there since An Aois Ailein, taking strangers through the rocks for a fee and an offering at the wolf-stone by the harbour mouth, as the houses of Òrd na Cloiche taught. Its own fishers had been the first to sail round into the southern sea, and the lane they opened still bore the town's name, Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich. That was long ago. In the humans' time the fleet could not pay the harbour dues in marks and sold half its boats to A' Chompanaidh, and the men who had sailed them went into the pits. The harbour wall was built afterwards, out of the town's share of the western tolls, and was better than the fleet it sheltered. By the summer of this tale the boats of Caol fhiadhaich were some thirty open hulls and a dozen decked ones, under sail and oar, and when the wind came into the south-west and stayed there they lay along the wall for a week at a time and the town ate its own salt fish.

Sorcha nic Dhùghaill kept the yard at the west end of the harbour, under the rope-walk. She had been bound to the guild at sixteen, at Ros dhomhain, and had served her seven years on the slips there before she came home to take the yard from her mother's brother, who had built boats in it for forty years and died with an adze in his hand, or so he had always promised he would. She was forty-one in that summer, broad in the shoulder, grey early, and known along the coast for two things: her hulls did not leak, and she did not lower her price for anyone, not for the pilots and not for the priests of Òrd na Cloiche.

In an t-Ògmhios she went up to Ros dhomhain to buy copper nails of the guild's stamp and to see a timber merchant about larch. It was a long day on the mail-cart, which changed horses twice on the road, and a long day back. In a chandler's yard behind the coal quay, among anchors and stove-in water-casks, she found an engine.

It had come out of a harbour launch, one of the little craft that had once towed the coal ships off the quay when the wind was foul. The launch had been laid up eight years, since the price of coal passed what a launch could earn in a day, and it had been broken up for its planking. The engine sat on two baulks of timber in the nettles with a sheet of tarred canvas over it, and the chandler wanted it gone. Sorcha put her hand on the flywheel and turned it. It moved, stiff with old grease, and something inside answered with a slow clank.

"What do you want for it?" she said.

"What would you do with it?" said the chandler. "It eats coal. You couldn't feed it."

"I didn't ask what it eats."

He named a price for old iron. She paid it out of the nail money, and went home without the nails.

It came down the coast road a week later on a wain drawn by four oxen, and took two days to do what the carrier did in one. The children of the harbour walked beside it the last mile. It was set down in the rope-shed at the back of the yard, where it was dry, and there it stood for a month while Sorcha went round it with a lamp and a notebook and took it apart as far as she dared.

She knew nothing of engines. Neither did anyone in Caol fhiadhaich. What she knew was that the south-coast boats had been burning dubhan all that year in their stoves and their lamps, since the works at Seann Skell sold its first making to them, and that the stuff came west along the coast in barrels on the coasters and could be bought on the quay. It burned, it stank, and it was cheap. An engine was a fire and a wheel, she reasoned, and the wheel did not care what the fire was made of.

The smith of the harbour, Seonaidh Bàn, a man who spoke some dozen words a day and made each of them count, came and looked at the firebox and the grate. He went away, and came back two days later with a burner of his own making: a trough of iron with a row of holes along it and a pipe and a cock to feed it from a tank. He had copied it, he said, from the stove of a coaster out of Seann Skell on the southern coast that lay in the harbour that week, and made it bigger.

"Will it serve?" said Sorcha.

"It'll burn," said Seonaidh Bàn. That was all she got from him that day.

## II. Of the Unbored Keel

The engine was the easy part. The hard part was the boat.

Lachann mac Neacail came to her about it before she went looking for him. He had a decked boat of thirty feet, *An Ròn Dubh*, built in that same yard by her uncle twenty years before, and she was a good boat, heavy in the bilge and dry, and slow. In any foul wind she was the last boat home, and Lachann was tired of it. He was a lean man with a face burnt the colour of a kipper, and he had lost a brother to the strait. He came into the rope-shed one evening, looked at the engine on its baulks for a long while, and said: "If you put that in a boat, put it in mine."

"She'd have to be opened," said Sorcha. "Aft. Through the post."

"Then open her."

Every apprentice of the guild learned the rule in his first year, before he was let near an adze, and learned it in the old tongue as the first wrights of the fellowship had said it: *Cha tollar an druim*, the keel is not bored. A boat's backbone was laid whole and kept whole. You fastened to it, you scarfed it, you might shape it; you did not put a hole through it below the water. The rule was older than the guild's charter, older than the humans' coming, and it had kept a great many boats afloat. Sorcha had had it beaten into her on the slips at Ros dhomhain at sixteen, and she believed in it.

To put a shaft out through the stern of *An Ròn Dubh*, to turn a screw behind her, the post had to be bored and the deadwood under it, a long hole slanting down and aft, and a tube of copper set in it packed with oakum and tallow so the sea would not come in. There was no other road for the shaft to go.

She sat up two nights with the lines of the boat laid out on the loft floor in chalk, working out the angle. On the third morning she had *An Ròn Dubh* hauled up the slip and chocked, and sent for the long auger.

The other yards came to watch. There were three besides hers in Caol fhiadhaich, and all of them were members of the guild, as she was: old Donnchadh Ruadh, who had been bound in the same year as the guild's present master and never let anyone forget it; the two brothers of the yard below the church of Òrd na Cloiche; and a young woman, Raonaid nic Coinnich, who had served her time only the year before. They stood at the head of the slip with their arms folded and said nothing while Sorcha set the auger and began to turn.

It took her the whole of a long day. The post was oak, and hard. Twice she stopped to sharpen the bit. Twice she crawled under the hull with a lamp and a plumb-line to see that she had not wandered. Towards evening the auger broke through into the light behind the post, and a curl of pale oak came out on the end of it and dropped on the shingle. Old Donnchadh picked it up and put it in his pocket. He did not say why.

The engine went into the boat a fortnight later, bedded on oak and bolted through her floors. The tank for the dubhan went forward of it, and the smith's burner under it. The shaft went out through the new hole in its copper tube, and the screw on the end of it was a two-bladed thing that Seonaidh Bàn had cast in bronze from a pattern Sorcha had carved in pine, and it was ugly, and it was true.

They tried her on an evening near the end of an Lùnastal, with no wind at all and the harbour flat as a plate. Half the town was on the wall. Lachann was at the helm. Sorcha was down in the well with the engine, and Seonaidh Bàn was beside her with the cock of the burner in his fist. He opened it. The dubhan caught with a soft thump and a smell like a tannery on fire, and a black smoke rolled up out of the hatch and over the wall, where the people on it coughed and swore and did not move back. They waited. It was a long wait. Then the engine gave a groan, and a clank, and another, and the flywheel turned, and turned faster, and the shaft began to turn in its tube.

*An Ròn Dubh* moved. She went out from the slip with her sails furled and her oars shipped, pushing a little wave in front of her, and she crossed the harbour in a straight line to the wolf-stone and turned, slowly, and came back. Nobody on the wall cheered. They watched her the way they would watch a dog walking on its hind legs.

At the wolf-stone the pilots were sitting on their bench as they did every evening, waiting for a ship that might want them. The eldest of them, Ailig Mòr, who had taken more hulls through the strait than any man living, watched *An Ròn Dubh* go by within an oar's length, stinking and clanking, with no sail on her. He took his pipe out of his mouth.

"That'll frighten the fish," he said.

"It frightened you," said Lachann from the helm, and the pilots laughed, and Ailig Mòr put his pipe back in his mouth and said nothing more that night.

## III. Of the Guild's Letter

Word went up the road to Ros dhomhain faster than the engine had come down it. A timber merchant told a chandler, the chandler told a warden of the guild, and the warden told the master.

The letter came on 7 an t-Sultain, DE 5, on the carrier's cart with the mail and a crate of hens. It was addressed to the members of Comann nan Saor-luinge at Caol fhiadhaich, all four yards together, and sealed with the guild's seal, the adze and the ship. Sorcha had it from the carrier's hand at the yard gate and carried it unopened to the net-loft over the fish-store, where the four yards met when they had anything to meet about, which was seldom. She waited until they were all there. Then she broke the seal and read it aloud.

It was not long. The master of the guild, Pàdraig mac an t-Saoir, wrote that he had heard with grief that a member of the guild at Caol fhiadhaich had bored the keel of a boat below the water to take an engine; that the rule of the unbored keel was the first rule of the fellowship and older than its charter; that the work was unlawful for any member of the guild; that it was to cease in every yard of the town; and that a member who went on with it would be struck from the roll, and fined, and his apprentices unbound. Below his name the wardens had set theirs, eleven of them. The letter used *his* throughout. There had not been a woman among the guild's masters since its charter was taken.

When she had finished there was a silence in the loft. The fish-store below them smelled of brine. Somebody's dog was barking on the wall.

"Well," said old Donnchadh Ruadh. "You bored it."

"I bored it."

"Does it leak?"

"No."

"Then he's wrong," said Donnchadh, "and he always was. He was wrong on the slip when we were boys." He took the curl of oak out of his pocket, the one he had picked up off the shingle, and turned it in his fingers. "But he's the master. What'll you do?"

"There are six skippers waiting on my slip," said Sorcha, "and there's another engine in a yard at Inis chrom that I can have for the carting. I'll do the work."

"And the guild?"

She folded the letter and put it down on the table.

It was Raonaid nic Coinnich, the youngest of them, who said it first, because she had the least to lose and the longest to lose it in. "If they strike one of us they'll strike all of us," she said. "There isn't a yard in this town that hasn't had a skipper through its gate this month asking for an engine. We'll all be boring keels by the spring, or we'll all be building for the dead."

The two brothers of the yard below the church looked at one another for a long time, as brothers do, and nodded together.

Donnchadh Ruadh put the curl of oak on the table beside the letter. "I was bound in the same year as Pàdraig mac an t-Saoir," he said. "Fifty-one years. I'd like to have got to the end of it." He stood up, slowly, as a man does whose knees have spent half a century on slipways. "Write it, then, Sorcha. You've the best hand."

She wrote it that night, on the loft table, with the lamp smoking. It said that the boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich had read the master's letter; that they held the work lawful and would go on with it; and that since the guild held it unlawful for its members, they were members no longer, and returned their papers with this letter. The four of them signed it. Sorcha went home and took down from the wall of her house the paper of her binding, which had hung there in a frame for twenty-five years with the guild's seal on it and her uncle's name as witness, and she took it out of the frame and rolled it up with the others. In the morning it all went up the road on the carrier's cart with the mail and a crate of hens going the other way.

A month later the guild's answer came. The four yards of Caol fhiadhaich were struck from the roll, and each was fined, and the fine laid on Sorcha's yard was the heaviest, being more than the yard would clear in a good season. None of them paid it. The guild had no bailiff in the south-west and no ship to send one in, and the maor of the shire, when the guild wrote to him, answered that a guild's fine was the guild's business.

## IV. Of the Wind in the South-West

The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich still tell of the autumn that followed, and they tell it as the season of *An Ròn Dubh*, though by its end there were two engine-boats in the harbour and a third on the slip.

Before she went out the first time, Lachann did what every skipper of that harbour did before a new season: he went down to the wolf-stone at dawn with a fish from the last catch and laid it at the foot of the stone, as Òrd na Cloiche had taught the harbour, and one of the pilots said the words over it. That morning it was Ailig Mòr. He looked at the fish, and then over his shoulder at the boat with her stack and her smell, and said the words all the same, and not any faster than usual.

Then he went down the steps and into *An Ròn Dubh*, and took her through the strait himself.

He had never been through it under power, nor had anyone. He had spent sixty years reading the strait by the set of a sail and the pull of an oar, and at first he steered her as if she were still a sailing boat, waiting for a wind that did not matter any more. At the second skerry the tide caught her on the bow and she swung. Lachann shouted to the engine and Seonaidh Bàn opened the burner, and the boat drove on across the tide as if it were a millpond, and Ailig Mòr said something in the old tongue of the pilots that nobody in the boat understood, and did not repeat. Beyond the skerries he handed the helm to Lachann and sat down on a fish-box and lit his pipe.

"I'll take you back in," he said. "Don't try it on your own."

The first weeks were hard. The burner fouled, and had to be pulled out and cleared with a wire, in a seaway, by a man lying on his belly in the stink. The copper tube in the stern wept a little at the packing, and Sorcha had *An Ròn Dubh* up the slip twice to repack it, and lay awake in between. The dubhan came west in barrels on the coasters from Seann Skell on the southern coast, and the coasters came when they pleased, and one week in an Dàmhair there was none to be had in the town at any price, and *An Ròn Dubh* lay at the wall with her sails bent on like any other boat and her engine cold, and the pilots made remarks. But the boat caught fish. She could go out when the others could not and come in when they could not, and she did not wait on the tide at the skerries, and the fish she brought in were the freshest on the quay.

The day the town remembers came late in an Dàmhair. The fleet had gone east to the banks off the south coast by the old lane, where the herring were thick that year, twenty boats and more, with *An Ròn Dubh* among them, and they had fished two nights and filled. On the third morning the wind backed into the south-west and rose, and by noon it was blowing a full gale up the coast, straight in the teeth of any boat that wanted to go home to Caol fhiadhaich.

The sailing boats did what they had always done. They ran for the lee of the nearest headland to the east, a good day's sail from home, and lay there at anchor with their catches salting in the hold, as their fathers had lain there before them, to wait out the wind. It might be two days. It might be a week. The fish would be salt fish by the time it was over, worth a third of fresh.

Lachann did not run for the lee. He put *An Ròn Dubh* head to the gale, with a scrap of sail on her to steady her, and opened the burner, and went home.

It took him from noon until an hour after dark, into a sea that broke green over the bow and ran aft along the deck and down the hatch onto the engine. Twice the burner guttered and twice his boy, a lad of fourteen, lay in the water in the well and kept it lit with his body over it. Once a sea took the scrap of sail clean out of its bolt-ropes. The engine groaned and clanked and hissed where the water hit the hot iron, and did not stop. At every sea *An Ròn Dubh* lifted her bow and seemed to stand still, and then the screw bit and she went on, a boat's length, and another, along a coast where every man aboard knew the rocks by name.

In Caol fhiadhaich they had seen the fleet go east three days before and had not looked for any of it back until the wind changed. Sorcha was in the rope-shed at dusk, cleaning the auger by lamplight, when a boy from the harbour came running and shouting that there was a light in the strait.

She went out onto the wall. It was nearly dark, and the rain was coming across the harbour in sheets, and the whole mouth of the strait was white. Out in it, low down, a light was moving. It came on steadily through the broken water between the skerries, into the wind, not tacking, not drifting, rising and falling with the seas and always coming on, and behind it, when the wind let her hear it, came the clank and grunt of the engine.

Ailig Mòr was on the wall beside her. He had come out without his pipe. He watched the light come in past the second skerry, where the tide ran hardest, and past the third, and he did not say a word until it had turned in under the wolf-stone and was in the smooth water of the harbour. Then he said, "He did it on his own, the fool," and went back to the pilots' bench out of the rain.

*An Ròn Dubh* came alongside the wall with her deck swept clean and her boy shaking with cold and a hold full of herring caught the night before. The catch was carried up to the market at Doire shean on the road that same night, and sold at dawn, fresh, the only fresh herring on the coast, at a price the fish-wives of Doire shean spoke of for years. The rest of the fleet came home five days after, when the wind went round, with salt fish.

That winter there were more skippers in Sorcha's yard than she had room for on her slip. Some came to talk and some came with money. The other three yards of Caol fhiadhaich were boring keels by an Dùbhlachd, and old Donnchadh Ruadh fitted his first engine with his own hands before the year was out, grumbling the whole while that he was too old for it. In am Faoilleach of the new year the yards of Inis chrom and Doire shean, a mile or two along the coast, sent to ask how it was done, and Sorcha showed them, and by an Gearran three yards of the south-west coast outside Caol fhiadhaich were doing the same work, and they too had left the guild, or been struck from it, depending on who told it.

The engines were the trouble. There was no one on the island making them for boats. Every laid-up launch in every harbour of the capital country had its engine bought out of it that winter, and the chandlers of Ros dhomhain, who had been glad to be paid for old iron in an t-Ògmhios, asked three times the price by am Màrt and five times by an Giblean. Seonaidh Bàn made burners all winter, a dozen of them, each a little better than the last, and said nothing about any of them.

## V. Of the Court at Ros dhomhain

The summons came early in an Giblean. The court of Comann nan Saor-luinge would sit at Ros dhomhain on the twenty-third of that month, and the boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich were called to it to hear its ruling on the matter of the engines. It said nothing more than that. The four yards talked it over in the net-loft and agreed that Sorcha should go for all of them, since it was her auger that had started it.

She went up on the carrier's cart the day before, through the green of the spring. The road ran north-east, inland from the coast, through the fields of the shire, where the sowing was done and the lambs were out, and over the low hills into the capital country, and at evening she came down into Ros dhomhain with its counting-houses and its warehouses and its slips, and smoke over all of it. She slept at the carriers' inn by the market. She did not sleep much.
