The guild hall stood above the slips, where it had stood since the wrights of Ros dhomhain took their charter in the first years of the kingdom: a long hall of stone with a roof of slate, and inside it a floor of oak worn into hollows by the feet of the apprentices bound there. Over the master's bench hung a board with the rules of the fellowship painted on it in the old tongue, and the first of them, in letters as long as a finger, was *Cha tollar an druim*. Sorcha had stood under that board at sixteen with her hand on the guild's adze and sworn to keep it.

The court sat at the fourth hour. The master was in his chair, with the eleven wardens on the bench on either side of him. Pàdraig mac an t-Saoir was a big white-haired man with the hands of a wright and the voice of a man who has spent his last twenty years talking to merchants. He did not look at Sorcha when she came in. The hall was fuller than she had expected: the masters of the Ros dhomhain yards in their good coats, a clerk of the merchants' houses, two men she did not know who sat together and took notes, and at the back a scatter of apprentices who had come to see the woman from the south-west who had bored a keel.

The master's clerk read the matter. The master read the ruling.

It was a careful ruling, and it took some time. The guild, he said, had considered the fitting of engines into boats at three sittings through the winter, and had taken counsel of its oldest members and of the charter itself. It found that the charter of the guild was given for the building of ships and boats and for the work of wood in them. An engine, the court found, was a work of iron, made by founders and smiths, and the setting of an engine in a hull, with the boring and fitting needful to it, was the work of an engineer. The fitting of an engine was therefore no shipwright's work at all, and lay outside the guild's charter. The guild had no rule over it, and the rule of the unbored keel did not reach it. So the boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich had broken no rule of the guild's, and they were readmitted to the guild, with all their papers and all their apprentices, and the fines laid on them were remitted.

He put the paper down and looked at her for the first time.

"The court has ruled," he said. "You may take your papers from the clerk, mistress. The guild is glad to have Caol fhiadhaich back."

Sorcha stood up. The whole hall had gone still. Through the open door came the sound of adzes on the slips below, and a gull, and she could hear her own heart.

She had thought on the cart, and in the inn, and lying awake, about what she would say, and had got no further than the first words. She looked up at the board above the master's head, at the letters as long as a finger.

"Master," she said, "in the autumn I bored the keel of *An Ròn Dubh* with my own auger, in my own yard, in front of three members of this guild. Your letter called it unlawful. You struck us from your roll for it, and you fined us. Now you tell me it was never your business. I bored that keel as a shipwright. I bedded the engine on oak as a shipwright, and I set the tube in the post, and I packed it, and it holds. If that's no shipwright's work, then I've no need of a shipwrights' guild. The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich thank the court. We won't come back."

There was a noise in the hall then, of a good many people talking at once, and the master struck his bench twice with the flat of his hand. When they were still he asked her whether that was the answer of all four yards, or her own.

"All four," she said. "I have it in writing, if you want it."

"The court doesn't want it," said Pàdraig mac an t-Saoir. He looked at her a while longer. He was not a fool, and he had been a wright before he was a master. "You were bound under that board," he said.

"I was. Twenty-five years I kept the rule. I kept it until it kept the boats in the harbour."

The clerk wrote that the boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich declined the guild's readmission. The master rose, and the court rose with him, and it was over. The two men who had sat together taking notes went out quickly, and one of them, she learned afterwards, was a clerk of Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, and the other had come from the dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast to see what the court would say about engines.

Outside the hall the evening was coming on, clear and cold, with a light wind out of the west. Sorcha walked down to the slips. The yards of Ros dhomhain were closing for the night. On the last slip, the one where she had served the first year of her time, a harbour launch lay chocked up with her planks sprung and her engine gone out of her; the hole in her stern where the shaft had once run was stopped with a wooden plug, and grass was growing out of the seam beside it. Sorcha stood and looked at it until an old watchman came along the slips with his lantern and asked her whether she wanted anything.

"No," she said. "I was looking at the post."

She went back to the carriers' inn, and ate, and asked the carrier what time he went south in the morning. Then she took out the yard-book that she carried everywhere, and under the day's date, below the price of the larch and the name of a skipper from Inis chrom who wanted an engine by Bealltainn, she wrote one line: *Court at Ros dhomhain. Declined.* She closed the book, and put out the lamp.

# Chapter Seven: Of the Last Coal Flame

*DE 6*

## I. Of the Warrant of Tobar dhearg

At Tobar dhearg they tell it from the keeper's side, since it was the keeper who walked. The custodians of the south coast tell it from the altar, and the fitters who came after tell it from the stair; but the village on the red well says that nobody else was near enough to see the thing whole, and that Ciorstaidh nic Artair never told it twice the same way, and so they tell it for her.

She was in her sixty-ninth year when the order came, and she had kept Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg for twenty-two of them. Before that she had kept it under her father for as long as she could remember. He had taught her to trim the grate before she could reach it, standing her on a salt-box, and to read the colour of the fire the way a fisherman reads a sky. On a night in an t-Ògmhios, twenty-two years back, a boat of Seann Skell had gone onto the reef below the light in a south-westerly, and he had gone down with a line to it, and the sea had taken him off the rocks. She went down after him with the same line. She brought four men in, one by one, and the fifth could walk. Comhairle nan Taighean-solais sent her his warrant in a month, with a letter regretting the loss of a servant of long standing, and that autumn she had a post driven into the reef with a bell on it that the swell rang. While she kept the light no boat had gone aground there. The village could tell you that before it could tell you anything else about her.

The tower stood out on the cape below the village, a stone drum older than anyone's grandmother, and on its top, inside the lantern-glass the humans had set there in the days of A' Chompanaidh, the fire burned in an iron grate. It had burned coal for more than a hundred years. It burned the island's coal, broken small, which when it catches shows every colour in the break and gives a flame that no other fuel gives: bright at the heart, and at the edge dark and coloured, like oil on water, green and violet and a red that is nearly brown. Seen from the sea it was a warm light, low and a little unsteady, and the south-coast boats knew it from any other light on the island by that, and some of their old men said they could tell it from a star at twenty miles.

The coal came by sea from Seann Skell in sacks. For three years it had come short. The master of stores wrote each quarter that the lights stood first on the kingdom's list after the altars, which was true, and that the lights' allowance was what Comhairle nam Mèinnean could spare, which was also true, and Ciorstaidh had learned to bank the grate on the short nights of summer and let it roar only in the long ones. She kept the tally of every sack in her own book beside the log. The druids of the village, who by old custom kept the light's log for Brìde's sake, wrote the weather and the ships; she wrote the coal, in a small hand, with the price when she could get it.

On 22 an Cèitean, DE 6, Comhairle nan Taighean-solais sat and had read to it the council's order that the five lights of the coast should be turned to dubhan, the first works of the kingdom to be so turned, and that the coal they burned should go to the altars. The copy came down the coast to Tobar dhearg eleven days later in a leather case, carried by a clerk who had never been to the south coast and was sick on the fish-cart from Seann Skell. He gave it to her at the tower door and stood waiting, as if she might have a reply.

She read it standing. It was short. The lights of Baile ìseal and Tobar dhearg, being nearest the works at Seann Skell, were to be turned first, in the summer; the others as the fitters could reach them. The engineer of the lights was being sent to fit the burners. The keepers would keep their warrants, their wages and their houses.

"It says nothing of the grate," Ciorstaidh said.

The clerk said that he believed the grate would be taken out.

"And the fire in it?"

He did not know. He had not been told about the fire.

She gave him bread and a cup of the well water, which he looked at doubtfully because it ran reddish from the rock and always had, and sent him back up to the village to find his cart. Then she climbed the stair, which had a hundred and nine steps and a rope along the wall worn to the colour of a chestnut, and sat in the lamp-room with the letter on her knee until it was time to feed the fire.

## II. Of the Custodians' Asking and the Deputy

The custodians of Tobar dhearg were three, an old man and two younger women, and their house stood by the well at the top of the village. They were of Òrd Bhrìde, as nearly all the south coast was, and they held the light's log as their predecessors had since before the humans came, when the beacon was a fire in a ring of stones on the cape and the log was notches on a stick. They had known the order was coming before the clerk was sick on the fish-cart. The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell had known it before the order was read.

The old custodian came down to the tower the next evening. He was a slow walker and she saw him on the path a long while before he reached her.

"The Àrd-choimheadaiche will not bless the new burners," he said, when he had his breath. "You know his letter."

Everyone on the south coast knew the letter. Alasdair mac Ìomhair had written it to every house of Òrd Bhrìde two years before, when the shipmasters' works first smoked at Seann Skell: the new fuel was not forbidden, since it was not coal, and not blessed, since it was not coal. It had been read out in every house, and argued over in every tavern that had a druid in it, and the fishermen had made a rhyme of it that was not repeated in front of custodians.

"He will not forbid them either," Ciorstaidh said.

"No. But the fire in the tower has been coal since A' Chompanaidh lit it, and before that it was a shore-fire of driftwood and wrack. It was Brìde's fire on this cape before there were clerks to own it. We have asked him that it not be let go out on a clerk's say, like a lamp in a kitchen. We have asked that it be carried to her altar at Seann Skell, and burn out there, where the flame first came from."

She looked at him a long time. The fire behind her ticked in the grate.

"And what does he say?"

"He says yes. He has written to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, and they have written back that they have no objection, provided the light is not dark a single night." The old man folded his hands. "They will send a man for the lantern. They offer one of their own clerks, or the Àrd-choimheadaiche will send a young custodian of the house there. It is ten miles, keeper, and in the heat."

"It is nine and a half," Ciorstaidh said, "and I have walked it every quarter for twenty-two years to argue for coal."

She said nothing more that night. The next morning she wrote to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, in the same small hand she kept the coal in, that she thanked them for the offer of a deputy and would not need one; that the flame was hers by her warrant until the burner was lit; and that she would carry it herself or it would go out on the cape in its own grate, and they might choose. The answer came in a fortnight and was a line long. The keeper was to arrange the matter with the Àrd-choimheadaiche as she saw fit.

The village says she was angry for a week after, and that nobody could tell with whom. The custodians thought it was the lights' masters. The clerk who had to carry the next letter thought it was himself. Her under-keeper, a Baile gharbh lad of nineteen whom she had taken on four years before because he could climb the stair twice without stopping, thought it was the coal, because she went at the grate that week as if it owed her money. He was the only one of them who ever said so to her face, and she told him he was nearer than the rest.

## III. Of the Tank at the Stair's Foot

The engineer of the lights came in the third week of an t-Ògmhios, off a works boat from Seann Skell that came round the cape in the early morning and stood off the landing-stones below the light, and the whole village came down to watch her land.

Ciorstaidh had heard of Peigi nic Ascaill, as every keeper had. She was a woman under forty who had run a dubhan lamp for a hundred nights in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, on the eastern cape, and had it hold in a gale when the tower's own coal flame blew out. Every keeper on the island had had that story by letter within the month, and every keeper had an opinion of it. Seonag nic Thòmais at Baile ìseal had refused, it was said, to let the thing up her stair at all, and now had it at the top of her stair by the council's order and was not speaking to anyone who had signed it. Ciorstaidh had rather liked the sound of Seonag nic Thòmais.

The engineer came up the landing-stones in a man's coat with the sleeves turned back, and stood at the foot of the tower and looked up at it with her head on one side, and the first thing she said to its keeper was that the stair would do.

"At Àth dhearg it won't," she said. "I've the drawings. The tank would stick at the second turn like a cork. But yours is wide. The humans built this one first and hadn't learned to be mean with stone yet."

"The tank?" Ciorstaidh said.

It was coming off the boat. It was a drum of riveted iron, taller than a man's waist and as wide as a well-head, and it took eight of the village men with poles and ropes to bring it over the landing-stones, and the boat's crew stood on the gunwale and shouted advice. After it came the burner in a crate, and the pipes in a bundle, and the glass chimneys in straw, and then the barrels. There were forty barrels, black, and they were rolled up the path and stood in a row against the tower's wall where the coal-sacks used to stand, and the smell came off them in the warm morning and went up the cape.

Ciorstaidh had smelt dubhan before. By then everyone on the south coast had. The works at Seann Skell sent it out in its barrels to the fishing boats and the lamp-houses, and it burned on the quays at night in the new lamps, and the whole harbour smelt of it in a wet wind. Up close it was worse. It was a thick smell, like a burnt pan and something from under a pit-heap, and it caught in the back of the throat.

"You'll stop noticing," said Peigi nic Ascaill, who had watched her face.

"I doubt it."

"You will. I did." The engineer looked at the barrels without much love. "It burns, it stinks, and it is not coal. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own surveyors wrote that four years ago, and nobody has improved on it."

They took four days over the fitting. The tank went up the stair on ropes, with the village men sweating under it and Ciorstaidh walking behind with a lantern, because the lamp-room was dark while the fire was banked for the day and she did not trust any of them on the turn. It sat in the room below the lamp-room, where the coal had been kept in the humans' time, and a pipe went up from it through the floor. The burner stood in the lantern-glass beside the grate. For four nights the grate burned as it always had and the burner stood cold beside it, a brass thing like a ship's bell turned over, with its row of wicks, and Ciorstaidh fed the coal and did not look at it.

On the third evening the engineer came up the stair after supper and sat on the step of the lamp-room while the keeper fed the fire. It was the longest day of the year or near it, and the sun was not down till late, and the grate was banked low for the short night.

"You keep it low," Peigi said.

"The coal comes short. Three years now. I bank it in summer. The boats know the light's lower in summer, and they know why." Ciorstaidh knocked the grate. The flame came up, and the colours came up with it along its edge, the violet and the green. "They say they can tell it from a star at twenty miles."

"Can they?"

"The old ones say so. I think they tell it from a star because it's where they've always seen it." She sat back on her heels. "Your lamp at Baile ìseal. The one that held."

"It held."

"And the tower's went out."

"In the gale. The draught came down the chimney and the coal was damp. It happens." The engineer looked at the fire. "Murchadh mac Coinnich kept the log for me. He was keeper there once. He was sorry it went out. Into the log it went, that the tower's went out and mine didn't, and then he wrote that he was sorry. He didn't sign that line."

Ciorstaidh said nothing to that for a while. Then she said, "Mine doesn't go out."

"No," Peigi said. "I've read your log. Yours doesn't."

They sat together without talking, and the light went down over the sea to the west, and the fire grew in the glass as the sky darkened, until from the cape it would have been the brightest thing on the whole south coast. Below, somewhere under the lamp-room, the dubhan in the tank ticked as it cooled. The engineer went down at the dark, and Ciorstaidh stayed and fed the grate until her under-keeper came up at midnight to take the second half.

They lit the burner on the fourth night for a trial, beside the coal, an hour only. It came up white. There was no other word for it. It was a steady, hard, white light without an edge, and it made the coal flame look like the fire in a cottage hearth, and it threw the shadows of the lantern-glass's iron bars out across the cape so that the whole village could see them lying on the grass. The boats that were out that night saw it and came in to ask what had happened. The engineer turned it down after the hour, and the grate burned on alone, and the old custodian, who had been at the foot of the tower all the while, went back up to the village without a word to anyone.

She had the day of the carrying set with the Àrd-choimheadaiche by letter: 19 an t-Iuchar, DE 6, a day with no feast on it, so that nobody could say it had been chosen for a sign. The burner would be lit that evening for good. Until then the grate would burn as it always had. The engineer went back to Seann Skell on the works boat to do what she could at Baile ìseal, where the burner had been lit the week before and was already being blamed for everything, and she promised to come back the day before the carrying to see the burner in, and to walk with the keeper if the keeper would have her. The keeper said she might suit herself.

## IV. Of the Road to Seann Skell

She did not sleep the night before, and had not expected to. All night she sat up in the lamp-room with the fire and let her under-keeper sleep through the whole of his watch, which he held against her afterwards, and she fed the grate with the last of the quarter's coal, a sack and a half, and let it burn as high as it would burn on a summer night, higher than it had burned since the coal began to come short. The boats that were out saw it and wondered, and some of them knew.

In the grey before dawn she took down the lantern. It was a closed lantern of brass and thick glass, a storm lantern of the humans' make with a little door in its side and a pot at its foot for a handful of coal, and it had hung in the lamp-room for as long as the tower had stood, for carrying the fire down to the landing-stones on nights when a boat came in blind. She had carried it down that stair with her father's line coiled over her shoulder. She filled the pot with the best of the coal she had kept back, broken small, and she took a coal from the grate with the tongs and laid it on the others, and closed the door, and watched through the glass until the new coals caught.

Then she let the grate go.

That is the part the village does not tell, because she did not tell it, and there was only the under-keeper to see, and he had been asleep. He woke to find the grate dark and cold enough to put a hand in, and the keeper sitting on the step of the lamp-room with the lantern on her knees, and the sun coming up out of the sea to the east. He said afterwards that she looked the way his grandmother had looked the morning after his grandfather was buried, sitting straight on a hard chair with her good shawl on. She told him to get the burner going the moment the sun was off the sea that night, and not a quarter-hour later, or she would hear of it at Seann Skell. He said she would hear of nothing else. She told him to mind his tongue.

The engineer had come on the evening boat and slept in the keeper's house. She was at the tower door with bread and a flask of the red water when the keeper came down the hundred and nine steps with the lantern held out a little from her body, the way you carry a thing that is hot or that someone might want to take off you. The flame burned inside the glass with the colours along its edge. The two of them set off up the path to the village.

It was a hot morning with a haze on the sea, and the whole of Tobar dhearg was out. They stood at their doors along the one street and round the red well. Nobody spoke to her, since she plainly did not want to be spoken to, and the children who ran after her were called back. At the well the three custodians of the village fell in behind, the old man in the middle, and so did a good many others, and when she went out of the village on the road north-west there were thirty people walking behind the keeper and her lantern, and the engineer in her man's coat among them, and the fish-cart following empty in case anybody fell down.

The road from the cape to Seann Skell runs along the coast behind the dunes, then inland round the marshes where the burn from Baile gharbh comes down, then out along the shore again to the town. It is nine and a half miles. It was a road she knew stone by stone. On it she had walked to Seann Skell every quarter for twenty-two years to wait on the master of stores and argue for coal, and walked home again with less than she had asked for.

She walked it that day without stopping, except twice at wells to drink. She did not hurry, and she did not give the lantern to anyone. At Baile gharbh the fishermen's wives were at their doors, and one of them came out with a cup of milk and held it up to her without a word, and she drank it and gave the cup back and went on. At the ford over the burn a carter coming the other way with a load of salt pulled his horse into the reeds and took off his cap and stood there holding it until they had all gone by. A child asked in a loud voice what the old woman was carrying, and its mother said *Brìde's fire*, and the child said, *but it's only a lamp*, and nobody laughed.

Past the marshes the road came out onto the shore again and the town was in sight: the roofs of Seann Skell along the bay, and the masts in the harbour, and the long grey roof of Brìde's house on the rise above the quays, which was the greatest house of Òrd Bhrìde on the island. And to the left of the town, down by the old salt-sheds, stood the chimney of Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell, the shipmasters' works, which was the tallest thing on the coast by then and could be seen from Baile gharbh on a clear day. It was putting out smoke that morning, as it put out smoke every morning, and the haze from it lay along the shore in the heat, and the smell of it came to meet them on the wind a mile before they reached the town.

Ciorstaidh looked at it once and walked on towards it. The engineer, who was walking at her shoulder by then, said afterwards that she had been ready for the keeper to say something about the chimney, and would have understood whatever it was, and that the keeper said nothing at all and only shifted the lantern to her other hand.

At the town's edge a young custodian of the house was waiting for them, a lad not much older than her under-keeper, sent down by the Àrd-choimheadaiche to meet her. He bowed to the lantern first and then to the keeper, and offered to carry it the last half-mile up the hill, since that was the steep part. She looked at him until he coloured, and then she thanked him, and asked him to walk ahead and show the way, since the streets had changed since last she came. They had not changed at all. He walked ahead.

## V. Of Brìde's Altar

It was late in the afternoon when they came up to Brìde's house, and the sun was on the west side of it, and the doors stood open. The people who had walked from Tobar dhearg stopped at the steps and did not go in, since the hall was for the custodians that day, and the townspeople who had come up to see stood with them. The engineer went in, because the Àrd-choimheadaiche had asked for her by name, and stood by the door with her coat over her arm.

The hall of Brìde's house at Seann Skell is long and narrow and cool, with a stone floor worn into shallow dips by the feet of those who have stood there, and a roof of dark timber held up by posts that were ships' masts once. At the far end, on a step of three stones, is the altar, which is a block of grey stone with a hollow in its top, and in the hollow burns Brìde's flame, which is fed with the vein's coal in measure and from it the order lights its first lamp of the year on the feast of Brìde. That day the altar-flame had been let burn low, and the hollow beside it was clear.

The custodians of four shires were standing in two rows down the length of the hall, one on each side, facing inward, in their grey. There were more than sixty of them. Some had come a long way. The custodians of Seann Bhral had walked from their town, and the houses of the farther shires had come by cart the day before and slept on the hall floor. They stood in their rows and did not speak, and they did not turn their heads as she passed.

Ciorstaidh nic Artair walked down the hall between them with the lantern held out before her. Her boots were loud on the flags. The engineer said that it was the only sound in the place, and that she had never heard boots so loud in her life, and that she could hear the old woman's breath as well, because it had been ten miles in the heat and she was sixty-eight.

At the foot of the altar the Àrd-choimheadaiche was waiting. Alasdair mac Ìomhair was a thin man in his middle sixties, with a long face and his grey hair cut short in the custodians' way, and he stood aside from the altar as she came and made room for her on the step. He did not offer to take the lantern. The custodians of Tobar dhearg, who had told him a good deal about their keeper by letter, may have warned him not to.

She went up the three stones and set the lantern down in the clear hollow beside Brìde's flame. She opened its little door.

The flame inside leaned towards the air, as a flame does when a door is opened on it, and seemed for a breath about to go out, and steadied. It burned up in the open with the colours along its edge, a little higher than it had burned in the glass, and it gave the altar step a warm light that was different from the light of the altar-flame beside it. Then it settled down to burn the coal that was left in the lantern's pot.

Nobody told her to go, so she stayed. She stood at the side of the altar step with her hands folded, and the custodians stood in their rows, and Alasdair mac Ìomhair stood across the step from her, and nobody spoke, and the coal burned.

It took longer than anyone had thought. The custodians had been told by the house, or had told each other, that it would be a matter of an hour. It was the best of the coal, broken small, and she had packed the pot as tight as it would go, as she packed the grate in winter. After the first hour the young custodians at the back of the hall began to shift on their feet. After the second, the light through the west windows had gone from yellow to red, and the long shadows of the ranks lay across the floor, and one of the Seann Bhral custodians, an old woman, sat down on the floor where she stood and nobody reproached her. The engineer stood by the door the whole time. She said later that she had meant to stay a quarter of an hour, and found at the end that she had not once thought of going.

The Àrd-choimheadaiche did not move, and neither did the keeper. What he thought of it he never set down in any letter that is open to an Leabharlann, and the custodians of the south coast have never agreed about it among themselves. Some say he prayed. Some say he was counting, and meant to write the time to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais. The keeper said afterwards to her under-keeper, when he asked, that the Àrd-choimheadaiche had stood on the altar step for three hours watching a lamp go out and had not once looked at the door, and that she could not ask more of any man than that, and would not have got it from the clerks of the lights.

At the end, in the last of the light, the fire in the lantern's pot went down to a few coals, and to one. The flame stood up off it very small, and the colours went out of its edge one after another, the red and then the green, until it was only blue. Then it shrank to a blue bead the size of a barleycorn, sitting on the coal, and it went on sitting there, a long time, while the hall got darker round it.

Then there was nothing on the coal.

A thin thread of smoke went up from the pot, straight in the still air, grey, and rose until it met the roof and hung there under the dark timber. Down the right-hand row one of the custodians let out a breath as if he had been holding it the whole while, and someone else coughed, and it was over.

Alasdair mac Ìomhair stepped forward then, and put out his hand to the lantern's little door, and looked at the keeper, and she nodded. He closed it. He said the words that are said at Brìde's altar when a lamp that has burned the vein's coal is let go out, which are short and old and are not written down outside the houses; and then he said, in the ordinary voice of a man talking across a table, that the flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg had come home to the altar it was first lit from, and gone out there, and that he thanked the keeper who had carried it.

"The order does not bless the new light," he said. "Nor does it forbid it. I have said so, and there is no more it can say. This it can bless." He laid his hand flat on the lantern, which was still warm. "This it blesses."

Ciorstaidh nic Artair said, "Thank you, lord," and then, "I'll have my lantern back, if the house doesn't want it."

He looked at her a while, and then he picked it up off the altar step and gave it to her, and the custodians broke their rows.

## VI. Of the Light Seen from the Quays

She would not stay in Brìde's house that night, though a bed had been made for her, and she would not go home on the fish-cart in the dark. She went down with the engineer to the harbour, where there was a lodging-house that took in keepers who came to argue for coal and had taken her in for twenty-two years, and the landlady gave her the room she always had, which looked south-east down the coast.

The harbour was full that night. Word had come down from Brìde's house ahead of them, and the fishermen had come in early, and the quays were crowded under the new dubhan lamps, which the works had set up along the harbour-front the year before and which lit the wet stones white and made the whole quay smell of the burnt pan. Down in the taverns along the harbour they were singing.

The song was new that night. The fishermen of the south coast, who had made a rhyme of the Àrd-choimheadaiche's letter, made a song of the carrying, the same evening; the harbour says it was first sung in a tavern under the quay wall by a skipper of Tobar dhearg whose father had been one of the four men brought in off the reef twenty-two years before, and that he made it as he sang it. It had a great many verses before the night was out, and by the end of the summer every harbour of the south coast had its own. Some were about the keeper, and some about the chimney of the works, and some were not fit to be sung in front of custodians. The verse that stayed, and is sung wherever the song is sung, is the first one, and it was the only one the skipper sang twice.

Ciorstaidh nic Artair heard it from her window. She had the lantern on the sill beside her, cold now, with its little door shut. Out beyond the harbour, far down the coast to the south-east over the dark of the marshes, where the cape stood out into the sea, a light had come up at sunset on the stroke, as she had ordered. It was small at that distance, and white, and very steady, and it did not flicker when the wind came off the sea. It had no colour at its edge.

The engineer, who had come up to say good night and had stayed at the door, said that the lad had lit it on time.

"He has," said the keeper. "The boats will see that at thirty miles."

"They will."

"They'll not know it from a star." She watched it a while. "They'll get used to it. You said I would."

Below the window, in the tavern under the quay wall, the skipper of Tobar dhearg sang his first verse again, and the whole room sang it with him, and it came up to her through the warm night, over the white lamps on the stones:

> *Dh'fhalbh an lasair às an tùr,*
> *tha solas ann, ach chan ann leinn.*
> The flame has gone out of the tower;
> there is a light there, but it is not ours.

# Chapter Eight: Of the Five Towers

*DE 7*

## I. Of the Carts to Muileann bheag

Two of the five lights had been turned by the end of the year before. Taigh-solais Baile ìseal on the eastern cape had burned a dubhan lamp in its yard for a hundred nights before it burned one in its tower, and Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the south coast had let its coal flame go to the altar in the high summer, in a lantern carried by its keeper. That left three: one on the northern point, one on the north-eastern cape, and one on the headland at Baile chrom in the far north-west, which was farther from the capital than any work the kingdom kept.

Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, went north in am Faoilleach with two of the board's fitters, a box of drawings and a letter under the board's seal. The letter said that Taigh-solais Muileann bheag was to be turned to dubhan before the spring gales. It did not say where the dubhan was to come from.

The other lights were fed from the south. The tanks for Baile ìseal and Tobar dhearg had gone out of Seann Skell on the south coast by boat, from the shipmasters' quay below the works, and the barrels that followed them went the same way. Muileann bheag stood on the north coast of the Tuathaich country, and a boat out of the southern Seann Skell must go round half the island to reach it. In am Faoilleach no master on that coast would take a laden hull round the western capes for any board's letter.

So the fuel for Muileann bheag came by cart. Peigi bought it at Caol mhòr, in the market by the harbour, where the black cake had been sold off the pedlars' barrows since the first year of the fuel and was now sold from a shed with a slate roof and a Tuathach behind a counter. She asked him where it was made. He said, in the Dia-thìrich tongue and politely, that it was made in the north. She asked where in the north. He said in the other tongue something to the man beside him, and the man laughed, and then he said to her again, in her own, that it was made in the north, and would she be wanting it in barrels or in the sack.

She took it in barrels. Twelve carts went out along the coast road on a grey morning with the wind off the sea, drawn by the small hill horses of the north, and a Tuathach walked at the head of each horse. The road ran some fifteen miles, low along the shore through the mill country, past the mill-dams frozen at their edges and the white fields, and it took the carts the whole of a short day. Peigi rode on the last cart with her feet on a barrel. The board's two fitters, who had never been north of the capital, sat together on the one in front and looked at the country as if it might bite.

The carters did not look at it at all. They talked among themselves in the humans' tongue, of a boat come in at Caol mhòr with her mast sprung and of the price of meal, and one of them sang. When the cart ahead stuck in a rut at a burn-crossing they all came back to it without a word from anyone, and put their shoulders to the wheels, and it came out. Peigi wrote in her notebook that night: *Carters of Caol mhòr, twelve, paid at the rate of the town. Good men.* Then she struck out the last two words, because the board did not want its engineer's opinions of carters, and wrote *Sound* over them.

Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stood on its point above a little mill town of grey houses, with the sea on three sides of it. It was the fourth of the five towers to be raised, and the first to burn coal, and under its foot the ash of an older shore-fire went down three yards into the red earth. The fire on that point was older than the humans and older than the kingdom. Its keeper that winter was a Dia-thìreach of the south named Calum Bàn, who had kept the light for nineteen years under the royal warrant and in all that time had been to church in Muileann bheag twice, at two funerals, and had stood at the back.

He met Peigi at the tower door with his hands folded under his arms against the cold. He looked at the carts and the carters, and at the board's two fitters, and last at her.

"They told me it would come by sea," he said.

"No boat would bring it."

"No," he agreed. "They wouldn't." He stood aside to let her in. "The coal came by sea. Every sack for nineteen years."

The work took nine days. The old coal-grate came out of the lamp-room in pieces, the board's men swearing at the bolts, which had rusted to their seats in the salt air; the tank went up the stair in the carters' arms, for the stair at Muileann bheag was wide and the tank was the small pattern, and two of the carters stayed on for the lifting and were paid for it. The burner was Peigi's own, the one she had drawn after the hundred nights at Baile ìseal, with a wider throat to it and a screw to clear the jet without putting out the flame. She fitted it herself. The board's men watched her, and Calum Bàn watched the board's men.

On the ninth evening, which was 26 am Faoilleach, DE 7, she lit it. The flame came up white and steady and threw its light out over the northern sea, where there was nothing to see but the dark water and, far out, the wall of grey that lay on the sea to the north in every weather. Calum Bàn stood at the glass and looked at it a long time.

"It's brighter," he said at last.

"Yes."

"It stinks."

"Yes. Less, in the tower. You'll not notice it in a month."

He did not answer that. In the morning he showed her the coal-store at the tower's foot, three-quarters empty, the last of it gleaming dully in the cold, and asked her what he was to do with it. She said she would write to the board. He said he would keep it, then, until the board wrote back, and locked the door on it, and put the key on the nail inside his own door where the other keys were.

The carts went back to Caol mhòr empty. Of the five lights, Taigh-solais Muileann bheag alone was fed thereafter by the road and not by the sea from Seann Skell, and its barrels came along the coast in Tuathaich carts from Tuathaich stores, and were paid for in the kingdom's coin at the market price, which that winter was a little under the price in the south.

## II. Of the Crane from Seann Tarr

The north-eastern cape was a harder matter.

Taigh-solais Àth dhearg stood on the high ground over the sea-passage in toward Seann Tarr, a stone tower raised by the townsmen of Àth dhearg in An Aois Choigreach and paid for, as the keepers still said, stone by stone. Its keeper, Iseabail Ruadh, had the light from her father, and kept on the shelf of the lamp-room the old daybook of Tormod mac Pheadair, who had written down every ship he saw from that gallery in the years when ships still came, and she would show it to visitors who asked. Peigi asked. The book was bound in sealskin gone black with handling. The last ships in it were a long time ago.

The tank for Àth dhearg had come round by sea from the southern Seann Skell and lay on the quay at Seann Tarr under a tarpaulin, the large pattern, for the light on the north-eastern cape was the strongest of the five. It came up the coast road to the tower on a dray behind four horses, and at the tower door it stopped. The stair of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg had been built by masons of the town who had built nothing but houses before it, and they had built it tight and turning, like the stair of a house. A man with a sack of coal on his shoulder went up it sideways. The tank would not go up it at all.

Peigi measured the stair. The board's men measured the tank. Then they measured the stair again, because they did not like the first answer.

"We cut the tank," said the elder of the board's men. "Two halves. Seam it up at the top."

"And it leaks at the seam into a lamp-room with a naked flame in it," said Peigi. "No."

"Then we cut the stair."

"Then the tower falls down," said Iseabail Ruadh from the doorway, "and I'll not be in it."

They stood about the dray in a wind that came straight off the sea with sleet in it. It was Iseabail who said, in the end, that the rope-walk at Seann Tarr had a crane for lifting the hemp-bales off the boats to the loft, and that the rope-makers owed the light a good turn, since their boats steered home by it every night of the winter.

So it was done that way, and it took a month more than the others.

The rope-makers of Seann Tarr were a guild of their own, the last that the old custom had chartered, and their master was a heavy slow man who came up to the tower to look at the thing before he promised anything. He walked twice round the tower, and looked up at the gallery, and looked at the tank on its dray, and said the crane could do it if the ground held. Then he went home and said nothing more for a week. At the end of the week the crane came.

It came up the three and a half miles of the coast road from Seann Tarr in pieces, the jib on one wain, the mast on another, the drum and the iron on a third, with half the rope-walk walking beside it. The weather had turned, as it turns there in am Màrt, from sleet to a hard bright wind, and Àth dhearg came out on the road to watch it pass, the children running ahead and the town's priest of Na Seann Spioradan standing at the gate of his house with his hands behind him. It took them two days to raise the mast on the rock below the tower and stay it with cables to rings the masons let into the stone. The master of the rope-walk would not let the board's men touch the cables. He said they were the rope-walk's cables and the rope-walk's knots and if they parted it would be the rope-walk's shame.

On the day of the lift the tank went up the outside of the tower in the slings, slowly, turning a little on its rope, with the sea behind it very blue and the gulls going round it as if it were a fish. Peigi stood on the gallery with Iseabail Ruadh. The board's men had taken out the great window of the lamp-room, frame and all, and it leaned against the parapet in its sacking. When the tank came level with the gallery rail it swung in the wind, out and back, and every man on the rock below leaned with it. Then the rope-makers on the drum let it down a hand's breadth at a time, and Peigi and the board's men caught it with their hands and walked it in over the sill.

Nobody cheered. The master of the rope-walk looked up at the gallery, and Peigi lifted her hand to him, and he nodded and turned to see to his cables.

The window went back in its frame; the glaziers of Àth dhearg sealed it; the burner was set; and on 25 am Màrt, DE 7, a month after the day she had meant to, Peigi lit the light on the north-eastern cape. Its beam went out over the passage, and at Seann Tarr that night, it is said, the boats came in by it as they always had, and nobody on the quay remarked that it was a different fire.

Iseabail Ruadh wrote that night in her own daybook, below the last line of her father's, that the light was turned to dubhan on this day, the tank being raised by the crane of the rope-walk at Seann Tarr. She named the rope-walk, and the board's engineer. Peigi read it over her shoulder and did not say anything.

The rope-makers would take no hire for the crane. The master sent word after it that the light owed them nothing, only let it burn.

That night at the inn at Àth dhearg Peigi wrote her letter to the board. Four of the five lights now burned dubhan. There remained Baile chrom. It was the farthest of the five, some twenty-five miles west of Caol mhòr on the headland at the edge of the Tuathaich country, and the board's fitters were wanted in the south, where the lamp-houses of the capital were putting in dubhan burners faster than there were men to fit them. The board had two fitters who could be spared, and they were the two she had with her, and they had been away from home since the new year and said so every evening.

She wrote to the board that she could not do Baile chrom before the autumn gales with the men she had. Then she took a second sheet and wrote, in her own name, to Tional nan Tuathach at Caol mhòr.

She knew no one at Caol mhòr, and one Tuathach fitter by name. Three years before, at the shipmasters' works at Seann Skell, there had been a man among the Tuathaich hands at the retorts, a lean man with his sleeves rolled and a burn on his wrist, who had shown her how to wrap a tap so that it did not drip and had chalked the lights' mark on her twenty barrels. He was of Caol mhòr, and he had gone home the winter after, as most of the northern hands went, when the rents of the south ate their pay.

She wrote: *To the speaker of Tional nan Tuathach at Caol mhòr, or to whoever keeps his letters.* Then, being tired, she crossed out the assembly's name, which she was not sure she had spelled as they spelled it, and left *the speaker at Caol mhòr*. She asked for four fitters of the town to turn the light at Baile chrom, the drawings and the burner to be sent them, the tank and fuel to come by sea. If a man named Ashby could be found, she would be glad of him. Who would pay them she did not say, because she did not know.

## III. Of a Week of Rain at Baile chrom

The letter came to Caol mhòr in an Giblean and lay on the speaker's table for a fortnight, because Daniel Frayne was ill that spring and read his letters slowly. When he had read it he sent for Joe Ashby. Frayne had been speaker of Tional nan Tuathach for more than twenty years, and he was past seventy.

Joe was fitting a winch on a herring boat at the harbour wall when the boy came for him, and he finished the winch first. Then he went up to the assembly's house in his working clothes and stood in the speaker's room with his cap in his hand while the old man read the letter out to him in the humans' tongue, turning it into that tongue as he went, word by word, with his finger on the line.

"She asks for you by name," said Daniel Frayne. "Do you know her?"

"At the works in the south," said Joe. "She bought barrels off us. I marked them for her."

"Did you speak to her?"

"About taps."

The old man looked at him over the letter for some time. He had a long face, grey and folded, and he breathed as if the room were short of air. "The board has no one to send," he said. "That's what this says. And it says nothing about pay." He put the letter down. "We'll pay you, then. The assembly will. Four men. Choose them yourself."

So in the middle of an t-Ògmhios four fitters of Caol mhòr went west along the coast road with their tools on a hand-cart and their food in a sack: Joe Ashby, and Will Tanner, who had worked in the Caol mhòr yards since he was a boy, and Ned Fowler and his cousin Abel, who had both been at the retorts in the south and come home. They walked the twenty-five miles in two days, sleeping the one night in a byre at a farm whose people gave them milk and would take nothing for it, and it began to rain on the morning they set out and did not stop until the work was done.

It was the rain of the far north-west in summer, which does not fall so much as stand in the air and soak through everything that stands in it. It came in off the open sea to the west, where there is nothing between the headland and the edge of sight, and it hid the sea, and the fields, and the road ahead. They came into Baile chrom at evening on the second day wet to the skin, and walked down its crooked street, which bends along the shore with the land, and the people in the doors looked at them and nodded, and a woman called to Will Tanner by name.

The boat from Seann Skell had come in two days before them and lay in the little bay below the headland, where there was a landing of stones but no quay. The tank lay on the landing under a sail, and the barrels were stacked beside it under another. The shipmasters' men who had brought her round had gone into the town to drink and had not come back. Joe went down and lifted the corner of the sail and looked at the tank, and put his hand on it, and came back up the path.

"Small pattern," he said. "It'll go up."

The keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom was a Dia-thìreach named Uilleam mac Dhòmhnaill, a spare man with a clipped grey beard, the last of a line of Dia-thìrich keepers who had kept that tower under royal warrant since the first years after An Dealachadh, a warrant that bade them report on the land as well as on the sea. In eleven years at Baile chrom he had come to know every family in the town by sight and some by name; he went to the town's houses when he was sent for and not otherwise, and the town left him to his tower.

He met the four of them at the tower door with a lamp in his hand, though it was not yet dark, because the rain made the evening dark. He looked at their wet coats and their hand-cart and the tools on it.

"You're the fitters," he said, in the Dia-thìrich tongue.

"We are," said Joe, in the same.

"From the board?"

"From Caol mhòr."

The keeper considered that, and then he stood aside. "The coal-grate's to come out," he said. "I've done what I could with the bolts. You'll want to eat first."

They ate in his kitchen at the tower's foot, bread and a piece of mutton, with the rain on the window. He did not eat with them. He sat at the end of the table with his daybook and wrote, and when Abel Fowler asked him what he was writing he said the weather.

They began in the morning. The grate came out in four days, piece by piece, down the stair on their shoulders, iron that had stood in the fire for more than a century and was burnt and scaled and heavier than it looked. The tank came up from the landing on the hand-cart with four men of the town pushing behind, and up the stair in the arms of all eight, turning at every turn, and Joe going first and backwards with his hands on the lip of it and his eyes on the next step. It went up. They set it on its bed and bolted it down and ran the pipe.

All that week the rain came in off the sea. It came in under the door of the lamp-room and down the inside of the glass where the old putty had shrunk, and Will Tanner spent a day raking the glazing out and setting new, swearing at the putty, which would not take on the wet stone. The coal-store at the tower's foot flooded to the ankle. The keeper came up the stair twice a day to see how they went on and went down again without a word. In the afternoons, when the light was worst, they worked by the lamp he had carried up the first night, and the smoke of it hung in the lamp-room with the smell of wet wool and oil.

On the fifth day the burner jammed. It was Peigi nic Ascaill's burner, sent round in the boat in a box of its own, with the drawings in a tin case beside it and a note on the drawings in a quick small hand: *The throat is wider than the old pattern. Do not trim it. Clear the jet with the screw, not a wire.* Something had been bent in the box on the voyage round the western capes, and the screw would not turn. Joe took the burner apart on the lamp-room floor on a piece of sacking and laid the parts out in rows. He sat over them most of the afternoon while the others worked about him. Then he took the bent part down to the town, where there was a smith who shod the horses and mended the boats' ironwork, and the two of them straightened it on the anvil with the door shut against the rain. The smith did not ask what it was for. Joe paid him out of his own pocket.

On the evening of 20 an t-Ògmhios, DE 7, which was the eve of the longest day, the burner was set and the tank was full and the glazing held. The rain still fell, thinner now, and in the west under the cloud there was a strip of yellow light over the sea.

The keeper came up the stair with his daybook under his arm. The four fitters stood back from the lamp. There was no one else in the lamp-room, and no one on the headland below but a few children of the town who had come up to watch the tower and stood in the wet grass.

"Who lights it?" said Uilleam mac Dhòmhnaill.

The others looked at Joe. Joe looked at the keeper. "It's your light," he said.

The keeper hesitated. Then he put down his daybook on the sill and took the taper Joe gave him and lit the flame. It came up blue and then white, and spread, and steadied, and the great lens took it and threw it out west over the sea in a long beam that the rain caught and showed, so that for a mile out the drops were lit like sparks. On the headland below the children shouted.

The keeper watched it a while. Then he picked up his daybook and went down the stair, and they heard his door close at the bottom.

In the morning, before they left, he gave them breakfast again, and shook each man's hand at the door, and said the work was good. He said it in the humans' tongue, which none of them had heard him speak all week, and he said it badly, and they thanked him in his own.

They walked home to Caol mhòr in two more days of rain. At the assembly's house the clerk paid them from the chest of Tional nan Tuathach for nine days' work and four days' walking, at the rate of the town, and entered it in the assembly's book: *To four fitters of this town, for the turning of the light at Baile chrom*, and their four names under it, and the sum.

## IV. Of the Paper at the Custom-house

The keeper's report reached the board at the end of the summer. Every keeper of the five lights sent one at each quarter-day, telling in a fair round hand what he had seen on the sea and on the land. The board copied the part that concerned the turning of the light and sent it round the kingdom to be pinned up where such things were pinned, that the shires might know their lights were turned. One copy came to Caol mhòr, because Baile chrom lay in the Tuathaich country, and the maor pinned it on the board outside the custom-house by the harbour, beside the notice of the fish-prices and the harbour dues.

Joe Ashby read it on his way home from the harbour, on an evening of an Lùnastal with the sun still high.

Will Tanner had seen it that morning and told him, and Joe had walked past the custom-house three times that day without looking. The fourth time he stopped.

It was a short paper. It said that Taigh-solais Baile chrom was turned to dubhan on the twentieth of an t-Ògmhios. It said the tank had come by sea from Seann Skell and was of the small pattern, and the burner of the new pattern drawn by the board's engineer. It said the coal-grate was taken out and the glazing of the lamp-room renewed. It said the light burned well and was seen by the boats. It said the town gave no trouble. It said the work was done by fitters from Caol mhòr.

Joe read it twice. Then he read the fish-prices beside it, and the harbour dues, and walked home.

His name was not in it. None of their names were. He had known it would not be; he had seen keepers' reports before, pinned on that same board, and they did not name fitters, or carters, or the men who carried things up stairs. Iseabail Ruadh's daybook at Àth dhearg named the rope-walk; he had not seen it, and would not have known it if he had. What he knew was that a Dia-thìreach keeper had stood beside him on the eve of midsummer and had lit the light because Joe gave him the taper, and had gone down his own stair and written *fitters from Caol mhòr*, and that the words were true.

He did not speak of it that night. His sister, with whom he lodged, said afterwards that he sat a long time at the table with a cup he did not drink, and then went out, and she heard him in the shed behind the house, at the bench, sharpening every tool he owned.

The Tuathaich of Caol mhòr have a way of telling it, when they tell it at all, which is short. They say that the Baile chrom light was turned by four men of the town, and they name them, and they say that the keeper's report named the town. Some say it as a grievance and some as a joke. Will Tanner says still that it was the only time Caol mhòr had been in a report of the kingdom's for anything but fish.

A week after, there was a letter for Joe at the assembly's house. It came from the southern Seann Skell and it was written in the same quick small hand as the note on the drawings.

Peigi nic Ascaill had left the board's service at the end of the summer, the letter said, and taken service with the shipmasters' works at Seann Skell as their master-fitter. The works were building a second range of retorts and wanted fitters through the winter, and the shipmasters paid better than the board and a great deal better than the assembly at Caol mhòr. She had had the Baile chrom report and knew who had done the work, for the assembly's clerk had written to the board for the fitters' pay to be made good and had named all four. She would take any of the four who would come, and she would take Joe Ashby first. There was a room over the forge at the works that a fitter might have.

The board did not make good the assembly's money that year, nor the next. The clerk entered the sum in the book as owed, and it stood in the book as owed.

Joe went south in an t-Sultain. Will Tanner would not go; he had a wife and a boat. The Fowler cousins went with him. They took the northern road to the capital and the south road from there to the sea, five days' walking, and came in to Seann Skell on the south coast on an evening of wind with the works' chimney standing up out of the town like a mast, taller than the house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, taller than anything on the coast, its smoke going out flat over the sea.

Peigi met them at the gate. She had been told they were coming and had come down from the office in her apron. She shook each man's hand, and she looked at Joe a moment longer than the others.

"You mended the burner," she said.

"The screw was bent."

"I know. I've changed the box." She turned to go in, and turned back. "The report named no one."

"No," said Joe.

"The assembly's book did."

He did not answer that. She took them in to see the new range, its brick half-raised in the long shed and its iron lying in the mud, and then the room over the forge.

## V. Of the Flame over the Hammer

At the foot of that year the lamp-makers of Muileann mhin began to make dubhan lamps.

They had made lamps for the pits since before anyone at Muileann mhin could remember. Muileann mhin was a river town east of the capital, on the Abhainn fhionn, a town of flour-mills and of the capital's order, and among the mill-wrights and the millers there had grown up a street of lamp-makers who made the coal lamps for every shaft on the island. They had been chartered as Comann nan Lòchran in An Aois Rìoghachd, and their mark was a flame over a hammer, stamped into the brass of every lamp they made. Of all the guild marks of the island it was the only one the humans' traders had ever copied.

There were fewer shafts now. When coal grew scarce in the old reign the lamp-makers had halved their making for want of coal to burn in the lamps they made, and the guild's minute-book of those years was a list of old lamps lent from pit to pit. In the autumn of this year the master of the guild had written to Seann Skell, to the shipmasters' works, for the drawing of a burner, and Peigi nic Ascaill had sent it.

In the last days of the year Peigi went up to the capital on the works' business with the lamp-houses, and at the shipmasters' asking took Joe with her to look at a pump the lamp-houses said did not draw. They came back by Muileann mhin because the master of the lamp-makers had written that he had something to show her.

It was 28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 7, a day of hard frost with the sun low over the river and the mill-wheels stopped with ice. The lamp-makers' street ran down to the water, a row of narrow shops with their doors open for the light and their forges going, and the sound of small hammers came out of every door. The master of the guild met them at the door of the guild's hall at the street's foot, an old man in a leather apron with burns on his forearms like a hewer's scars, and took them in.

On the long table in the hall stood a lamp. It was a pit-lamp of the old shape, the brass bowl and the gauze and the hook to hang it by, but the bowl was deeper, and in its throat was a small burner of Peigi's pattern, made smaller. Lit, it burned with a clean white flame behind the gauze and gave off a thin reek of dubhan.

"Twelve of them," said the master. "We made twelve this month. We've orders for a hundred, from the pits that are left and from the yards of Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn, and from the inns on the old roads."

Peigi bent to the lamp and turned it in her hands and looked at the burner. Joe looked over her shoulder. The work was fine.

"It's good," she said.

"It's good," the master agreed. He turned the lamp so that the bowl was toward her, and put his thumb on the brass where the mark should be. There was nothing there. "We can't stamp it."

The guild's charter, he explained, gave the mark of the flame and the hammer to the coal lamps of Muileann mhin. It said coal. It had been written when there was nothing else to burn in a pit, and the men who wrote it had seen no reason to say more. Some of the guild, the older masters, held that a lamp that burned dubhan was no coal lamp and could not bear the mark, and that to stamp it would be to break the charter. Others said the mark was the mark of the hands that made the lamp and not of the thing burned in it. They had argued it at the guild's table since the harvest.

"So we've written to the guild court," said the master. He took a paper from the table and gave it to her. "Asking leave to set the mark on them. I'd be glad of your name on it, as the one who drew the burner."

Peigi read the paper. Then she took the pen he held out to her and signed it at the foot, under his name and the names of the lamp-makers who were for it, *Peigi nic Ascaill, master-fitter of Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell, who drew the burner*. She held the pen out to Joe.

Joe looked at her.

"You mended one," she said.

He took the pen and wrote his name under hers in the humans' letters, *Joseph Ashby, fitter, of Caol mhòr*, and gave the pen back to the master, who looked at the name a long time, and then blotted it.

The petition went to the guild court at Muileann mhin that afternoon, carried by the master himself in his good coat. Peigi and Joe went on by the road to the south-east in the last of the light. Behind them, in the window of the guild's hall, the lamp without a mark burned on the long table, where the master had left it, and the street of the lamp-makers went on with its hammering into the frost of the evening, and the year ended.

# Chapter Nine: Of the Speaker and the Binders

*DE 8*

> **Part Two: Of the Roads, the Rails and the Plain Seal**
>
> *Cha b' fheudar dhomh riamh roimhe bliadhna a ghluasad 's mi beò innte.*
> Never before have I had to move a year I was living in.
>
> — Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, DE 15

## I. Of the Speaker's Last Night

The minute-book of Tional nan Tuathach has no entry for the first week of am Faoilleach in the eighth year. The clerk at Caol mhòr would not call the room to order while the speaker lay dying, and nobody asked him to. What the book leaves out, the mill-hands of Doire ghlas and the binders of Muileann leathan have kept between them, and they tell it much alike.

On the eighth of the month a boy came up the mill road at Doire ghlas on a pony as wet as himself, with a note folded small in his fist. Martha Greaves was in the carding-room with her sleeves pushed up, counting fleeces that the tally said were forty and her eyes said were thirty-eight. She took the note without looking at the boy and read it standing among the bales. It was in the eldest binder's hand, which she knew from thirty years of the delegates' accounts, and it said only that Daniel was asking for her, and that he had not asked for anyone before.

She finished the count first. It was thirty-eight. She wrote the two missing fleeces against the carrier's name, put on her coat, and told the overseer he had the mill until she came back, and that if he let the east wheel run dry again she would know.

The road from Doire ghlas to Muileann leathan runs east under the grey oaks and then out along the edge of the coast, some seven miles. The cart took the better part of the afternoon. It rained the whole way, the fine sideways rain that comes in off the sea to the north in the dead of winter and finds its way in at the collar however the collar is buttoned. Martha sat beside the carter with the oilcloth over her knees and kept her own counsel. Fifty-nine that winter, broad in the shoulder, grey, and known in every northern town as a woman who read a ledger faster than most people read a name, she had managed the mills at Doire ghlas since the year the delegates' money built them. For eleven years she had sat in Tional nan Tuathach as delegate for the mill-town and had never once spoken in it for longer than it took to give a figure.

Muileann leathan stands on its stream inside an old wall, with the keep of the Dia-thìrich governors at one end and the church of the northern congregations at the other, and the mill that gives the town its name squatting broad and low across the race between them. The bindery was a narrow house under the wall, down a lane that smelt of wet stone and flour. A lamp was lit in the upper window.

The binders were in the workroom below, all of them, though there was no work on the benches. There were eleven. They had been boys and girls when Daniel Frayne first taught them to fold a sheet and sew a gathering, in the years when no guild in the south would take a Tuathach apprentice for that craft, and now the youngest of them was going grey. They sat among the standing presses and the sewing frames with their hands in their laps, and the room smelt of paste, hide and cold glue. The eldest binder, a lame woman who had sewn her first gathering for him at twelve, got up when Martha came in.

"He's awake," she said. "He's been awake since noon, waiting on you. He'd not let us send before."

"Why not?"

"He said you'd a mill to run."

Martha went up. The stair was steep and bare, and the room at the top was hardly wider than the bed. Daniel Frayne lay propped against a bolster with his hands laid flat on the blanket, the way he had laid them flat on the speaker's table at Caol mhòr for twenty-three years when he meant to keep them still. He was seventy-three, and the skin of his face had gone thin and yellow over the bone. There was a dubhan stove in the corner, one of the little iron ones the pedlars sold, and it gave off a steady heat and a smell like a tarred rope smouldering.

"Martha," he said.

"Daniel."

"Sit. The chair's sound, whatever it looks."

She sat. Through the small window, past the roofs and the wall, she could see the headland where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stood, and its lamp had just been lit. The light had been turned to dubhan the winter before, fed by carts from the north, and it burned whiter and steadier than the coal flame had. She had not got used to it.

"You'll want to know what I want," he said.

"I'd guessed you wanted something."

He nearly laughed, and it cost him, and he waited till his breath came back. "The books," he said. "The minute-books. The first twenty years are coming out of their boards. Walter's paste was flour and fish-glue, and there's nothing left of it but dust and a smell. I've been meaning to rebind them since before you were a delegate. Every year there was something the room wanted more."

"The clerk's been keeping the loose leaves in order. I've seen him at it."

"The clerk's been keeping them in a drawer with a stone on top." He moved one hand on the blanket, an inch, and put it back. "I want them done. All of them. From the wet afternoon onward. By my own, down there. They know the work. They'll do it for the cost of the thread if the room lets them, and more carefully than anyone in Cathair dhearg would do it for gold."

"That's for the speaker to ask."

"Yes," said Daniel Frayne. He looked at her with his pale eyes and said nothing more about it, and she understood that he had said all he meant to on that head. It was his way in the chair as well. He put a thing on the table and let it lie there until someone picked it up.

They talked a little after that, of small things. He asked after the mill and the price of fleece. She told him about the two fleeces short at the carrier's, and he said the carrier's father had been a thief before him and his grandfather a thief under the humans, and that it showed a proper respect for a trade to keep it in the family. Then he slept, and woke, and asked for water, and slept again.

The eldest binder came up with a candle at about ten and sat on the top step. Martha did not go down. Toward the small hours his breathing changed and slowed, and grew loud, and then far apart. The lame woman came and stood at the foot of the bed with her hand over her mouth. The rain had stopped. Out on the headland the white lamp of Muileann bheag turned and turned, and its light came round in the window at each turn, and went.

He died a little before light on 9 am Faoilleach, DE 8. Martha heard the breath go out and not come back, and she waited a long while to be sure. Then she folded his hands one over the other, since there was no longer any need to keep them flat, and went down the stair to tell the others, who already knew.

## II. Of the Burial at Muileann leathan

They buried Daniel Frayne four days later in the churchyard of Muileann leathan, at the east end of the town, under the wall where the wind comes over from the sea.

The church there is the largest in the north after Doire ghlas, a long grey building with a squat tower, raised on the stones of a Dia-thìreach hall that stood on the spot before An Dealachadh. Eaglais nan Tuathach has kept it since those years. It was full that morning, and the lane outside was full, and the people who could not get in stood along the churchyard wall in their dark coats with the rain dripping off their hat-brims. They had come from all along the coast: fishing families from Cathair gheal, millers and weavers from Doire ghlas, carters, harbour-men from Caol mhòr, a knot of hewers from the western hill towns who had walked two days and stood a little apart, with the black of their trade still in the lines of their knuckles.

The binders carried him. There were eleven of them and the coffin wanted six, so they took it in turns down the length of the lane, stopping at every twenty paces to change, and the crowd waited each time without a word. The eldest binder walked in front with her stick. Martha walked behind with the clerk of Tional nan Tuathach, a thin nervous man called Thomas Rook who had brought the speaker's chair-cushion wrapped in a cloth under his arm and did not seem to know what to do with it.

The priest read in the humans' tongue, which was the tongue of the northern churches and of most northern kitchens, though every soul in the church could have followed him as well in Dia-thìris. He read the psalm the north keeps for its dead, of the waters and the hills, and then he spoke briefly of Daniel Frayne's life, and said that he had taught the children of this town a trade when no one else would, and had kept the northern delegates' books in good order for twenty-three years, and had never been heard to raise his voice in either work. Then the schoolchildren of Doire ghlas, whom their teacher had brought seven miles in two carts that morning, stood up in the gallery and sang the hymn of the sea road, and some of the fishing families sang with them. Martha found she did not trust herself to sing and did not try.

At the grave the ground was soft and heavy, and the diggers had laid planks along the edge. The binders let the coffin down on their own straps. When the priest had done, each of them in turn stooped and dropped something into the grave before the earth went in. Martha, at the foot, saw that it was thread: a short length of linen binding-thread from each of them, waxed and cut, the kind he had taught them to draw through the fold.

When it was over the crowd stood about in the lane and would not go home. The women of the town brought bread and hot broth out of their kitchens, and people drank it standing under the eaves. Martha found herself backed against the churchyard wall with a cup in her hands and a ring of delegates round her, pretending to talk of the weather.

Peter Hale was one of them, the delegate of Caol mhòr, thirty-eight years old, long-armed and fair, and he kept the tally on the Caol mhòr fish-quay as his great-grandfather Walter Hale had kept the humans' harbour books before the northern towns had any gathering of their own. He had a way of standing straight as a mast when he was nervous. He was standing so now.

"Mistress Greaves," he said.

"Peter."

"The room will sit at Caol mhòr at the month's end. For the chair."

"I know when the room sits. I've sat in it eleven years."

"They'll put your name," he said. "Cathair gheal's said so, and the hill towns, and I'd put it myself if nobody else did."

"Then somebody had better put another one beside it," said Martha, "for I've two hundred looms and a carrier who can't count to forty, and I'm no talker."

"Daniel wasn't a talker."

"Daniel was a bookbinder. It's a trade for a patient man." She drank off the broth and gave him the cup to hold. "Ask Mistress Marsh. She stands up in front of forty children every morning and makes them listen. That's a gift."

Ellen Marsh had come up behind him while they spoke, with her two carts of children marshalled along the wall by the older girls. She was a narrow dark woman of fifty-two, the teacher at Agnes Pike's old school in Doire ghlas, with ink on her middle finger that never quite washed off, and a dry voice that carried to the back of any room without being raised.

"Mistress Marsh is not a delegate," she said, "and would be no use to you in the chair, for she'd make the council parse its own letters before she answered them." She looked at Martha. "They've asked you already, Martha. They're only waiting now for you to hear it."

Martha said nothing. Down the lane the eldest binder was standing at the door of the bindery with her stick, looking out at the crowd, and behind her the workroom was dark. It came to Martha then, with the broth still burning in her throat, that whoever sat in the chair would be the one to ask for the books, and that she had sat by his bed and told him so herself.

## III. Of the Chair at Caol mhòr

Tional nan Tuathach sat at Caol mhòr on the last day but one of am Faoilleach, in the long low room over the net-lofts by the harbour where it had sat since Walter Hale's wet afternoon. The humans' harbour office had stood below it once. The room still smelt of damp wool and fish-scale, and would until the sea dried up. A fire of driftwood and turf burned in the grate at one end and did nothing for the other. There were benches along both walls and a trestle down the middle, and at its head the speaker's chair, a plain high-backed thing of ship's oak. Thomas Rook had laid the cushion back on it, and nobody had sat down there.

Forty-four delegates came, which was more than had come to any sitting in years. The fishing towns came, and the mill towns, and the farms of the northern shires, and the pit towns of the western hills, whose hewers still worked their own seams under their own captains and paid An Crùn its fifth by the old ruling, to a Comhairle nam Mèinnean that entered it as arrears. Thomas Rook read the notice of Daniel Frayne's death into the minute in his careful clerk's voice, and the day and the place of his burial, and the room stood for the space of a breath and sat down again.

Then an old fisherman from Cathair gheal got to his feet without being asked and said, "I put the name of Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas," and sat down again, as if that settled it.

Martha stood up at once. She had meant to speak calmly, and found that she was angry, and could not have said at whom.

"I have a mill," she said. "Two mills, and a dye-house, and three hundred people who eat by them. I've no learning past the figures. I've never stood up in this room longer than it takes to read a row of figures. There are men and women on these benches who can talk a council clerk into a stupor and out again. Put one of them."

"Daniel had a bindery," said the old fisherman from where he sat.

"Daniel had eleven binders who could run it without him."

"And you've an overseer," said Peter Hale, "who let the east wheel run dry in an t-Samhain, and you've not sacked him."

There was laughter at that, not unkind, and Martha had nothing to say to it. The room had heard her, and went on as if it had not.

A delegate of the farm towns put a second name, the name of a Ceann mhòr carter, a big genial man who had spoken in the room more often than anyone. The carter got up and said with great good humour that he withdrew it, since he could not read, and that he would sooner see a speaker who could add. Nobody else put a name. Thomas Rook looked down the trestle at the rows of faces, and then at Martha, and asked the room in the old form whether it would have Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas in the chair.
