The hands went up along both walls, the fishermen's and the millers' and the hewers', and he did not trouble to count them.

She sat down in Daniel Frayne's chair on the cushion he had sat on, and found that it was too high for her, and that her feet did not lie flat on the floor. She kept them still.

The room waited for her to speak. She had no speech. She looked down the trestle, over the ink-pots and the delegates' hats laid in a row, to the fire at the far end, and then she said what was in her mind.

"Daniel asked me for a thing on his last night," she said. "He asked me to ask the room for it. So I'll do that first, and then we can get on."

She told them. She spoke in the humans' tongue, as the room mostly did, and when an old woman from the western coast, who kept Dia-thìris by preference and made a point of it, called out that she had not caught the last of it, Martha said it again in Dia-thìris without a pause and without apology, and went on. The first books were coming apart. The clerk kept the loose leaves in a drawer with a stone on them. Daniel's binders at Muileann leathan would rebind the whole run from the first meeting for the cost of their thread and board, and he had wished it done.

Thomas Rook went to the press at the side of the room, a tall cupboard with a lock, and brought out the first of the books and laid it on the trestle before her. It was a thick ledger in a split calf cover. When she opened it the front board came away in her hand, and a gathering of pages slid out after it and fanned across the table. The delegates at the near end leaned to look. The ink on the top leaf was brown and small and cramped, and it gave the day, and under it the names of the towns that had come.

"There's sixty-odd of these," said Thomas Rook, "and the first twenty are like that one, or worse."

A delegate of the fishing towns asked who paid, and how much, and for how long the room would be without its books. They were fair questions, and Martha found that they steadied her, since they had answers and she could get them. She said that she would have the binders' reckoning for the next sitting, and that if the room's purse could not meet it, the mills at Doire ghlas would, and the room could argue with her afterwards about whether it ought to have let them.

It was moved and carried that the matter lie over to the next sitting for the binders' figures. Thomas Rook wrote it in. Then the room got on, as she had said it would: a quarrel between two fishing towns over a mooring, the price of seed-oats, a letter from Comhairle nam Mèinnean about the western pits that nobody could make head or tail of. Martha heard them all out with her feet off the floor, and kept the minutes short.

When the sitting rose at dusk, the delegates went down the outside stair into the wind, and she stayed. She sat on in the chair with the loose pages of Walter Hale's book in front of her, gathering them square, until Thomas Rook coughed from the door and said he would be locking up. The minute-book for that day records her first sitting as speaker. It is the shortest minute of the year.

## IV. Of the Minute of the Second Set

The room sat again on 24 an Gearran, DE 8, in a hard gale from the south-west that shook the net-lofts beneath the floor and set the lamps swinging on their hooks.

The binders' reckoning had come to Martha at Doire ghlas a week before, in the eldest binder's upright hand, on a single sheet. She had gone through it at her desk in the counting-house one evening with the mill quiet below and a pot of tea going cold at her elbow. It was a good reckoning. It set down the number of books, which was sixty-three, and the number of leaves in each so far as the clerk's drawer allowed, and the linen and the board and the hide and the paste by weight, and the days of work, and at the foot a sum so small that she went through it twice to find the mistake. There was none. The binders had charged nothing for their hands.

She read it to the room. It passed without a division, and Martha said that the mills at Doire ghlas would give the hide.

The eldest binder had come herself to hear it, seven miles by cart and then the long road round the head of the strait to Caol mhòr, and she sat on the bench by the door with her stick across her knees. When the vote was taken she got up and came down the room, and laid a second paper on the trestle before the chair, folded twice.

"There's one thing more," she said, "if the speaker will have it read."

Martha unfolded it. It was the wording of a minute, written out fair so that the clerk could copy it straight. It said that the books of Tional nan Tuathach were to be rebound by the binders of Muileann leathan and kept thereafter in the delegates' press at Caol mhòr; and that a second set of the same was made, and was hidden elsewhere; and that this minute should stand as all the gathering knew of it.

She read it through twice. The gale drummed on the roof. Then she looked up at the eldest binder, who looked back at her with no expression at all.

"Made," Martha said. "Not to be made."

"Made," said the eldest binder.

"Since when?"

"Longer than you've been in that chair, Mistress."

Martha read it out to the room. There was no sound at the end of it but the wind and the swing and creak of the lamps. Forty faces looked at her along the trestle, and she looked at them. She saw Peter Hale sitting stiff as a mast, and the old fisherman of Cathair gheal with his eyes shut, and the hewers of the western hills side by side on their bench with their black knuckles folded, and she could not tell from any face whether it knew more than she did.

"Is there anybody in this room," she said, "who knows where?"

Nobody answered.

She sat for a while with the paper under her hand. She thought of Daniel Frayne with his palms laid flat on the blanket, putting a thing on the table and letting it lie. The census figures had once been read out in this room, and he had written two words under them. She thought, because she was a mill manager and could not help it, of the kingdom's clerks at Cathair dhearg, and what a speaker of Tional nan Tuathach might one day be asked across a table by a man with a pen, and of what it would be worth then to be able to say that she did not know.

"Then I shan't ask," she said. "Thomas, write it as it's written."

Thomas Rook copied it into the book, word for word, while the room watched his pen. When he had done he turned the book round on the trestle and held out the pen to her, and Martha Greaves signed the minute under the line that said a second set was made and hidden elsewhere. Her hand was steady. She blotted it herself.

The eldest binder took back her paper and folded it into her sleeve. "Thank you, Mistress," she said, and went back to her bench by the door and sat down.

The last business of the sitting was the carrying. The books could not go to Muileann leathan, for the bindery had been Daniel's house as well as his shop and his kin were clearing it, and there was no room in it now to lay out sixty-three books and their loose leaves on a table at once. Ellen Marsh had written from Doire ghlas to say that her schoolroom was long and dry, with a good north light and a stove that drew, and that the children could be taught in the church meanwhile, since the priest had said he would be glad of the noise. The binders could come to it from Muileann leathan in a morning, and Caol mhòr could send the books to it in a day.

The room thanked Mistress Marsh by a vote, and it was moved that the delegate of Caol mhòr carry the books to Doire ghlas and back, since his great-grandfather had written the first of them. Peter Hale went red to the ears and said that he would.

## V. Of the Schoolroom and the Press

Peter Hale brought them in the first week of am Màrt, in a hired cart with the tilt laced down and the books packed upright in three tea-chests lined with oilcloth, and he walked beside the horse the whole nine miles from Caol mhòr with one hand on the tailboard. At Doire ghlas the children had been let out early to see the books come in, and they stood in two lines under the grey oaks outside Agnes Pike's school in their pinafores and boots, and watched him lift the chests down as if they held a king's regalia. Ellen Marsh did not shoo them off. She said that they might as well see the town's history carried in the door once, since it was so seldom that any of it was.

The schoolroom was what she had said: long, whitewashed, with tall windows to the north and a black iron stove at the end. The benches were pushed back and the children's tables set end to end down the floor. The binders came over from Muileann leathan the next morning in two carts with their standing presses and sewing frames lashed down under sacking, and by noon the schoolroom smelt of paste and warm glue and the stove, and nobody who went in could tell any longer that it had ever been a school, except for the alphabet painted round the top of the walls in the humans' letters, and under it the same in Dia-thìris.

Martha came over from the mill most evenings when the looms were stopped. It was a short walk under the oaks. She told herself she came to see that the hide was the hide she had paid for, and after the first week she stopped telling herself anything. She would sit on the end of a bench with her coat still on and watch them work by the lamps until Ellen came in from her rooms at the back with a pot of tea and sat beside her.

The binders took the books apart first, all of them, before they put any together. They cut the old stitching, lifted the gatherings out of the boards and laid them flat on the tables in order, sixty-three rows of loose pages under weights, so that the whole long record of the room lay open down the length of the floor at once. Martha walked the length of it one evening from the stove to the door, and it took her twenty paces, and she thought that it was seventy-seven years.

When they came to take Walter Hale's first book out of its boards, the eldest binder called Martha and Ellen over to the table under the lamp.

"Look here," she said.

She had slit the old spine, and turned back the first gathering, and at the inside of the fold, between the stitching and the first page of minutes, there was a row of narrow stubs where leaves had been cut out close with a knife. On the stubs, at the edge, were the ends of ruled columns, and a few figures in a neat brown hand, and on one of them the tail of a word in the humans' tongue.

"It's a harbour ledger," said the eldest binder. "Tonnage and dues. He cut out what he'd written for the humans and used the rest."

Martha bent close. The figures on the stubs were the same brown and the same hand as the minute that followed. Walter Hale had been a harbour clerk under the humans. When the humans' harbour office closed and the Tuathaich came together in the room above it, he had taken the ledger he had in his desk, cut out his old masters' accounts, and written the first day of Tional nan Tuathach on the next clean page. On that page the ink was a little blotted, as if the pen had been wetted too full.

"He hadn't a new book," said Ellen Marsh.

"He hadn't anything," said Martha. "None of them had." She straightened up. "Keep the stubs in."

"I'd meant to," said the eldest binder.

They went on through am Màrt and into an Giblean. Gathering by gathering the old pages were mended where they were torn, backed with fine paper where they were weak, pressed flat, and sewn onto new cords with the waxed linen that Daniel Frayne had taught them to draw. The boards were covered in the brown hide from the Doire ghlas tannery, and the eldest binder cut the lettering on each spine herself with a hot tool, the years and nothing else. The finished books stood in a row on the long shelf under the window, and every day the row was a little longer.

The children came in and out. The eldest binder let them, provided they kept their hands behind their backs, and a few of the older girls were set to fold and trim the backing paper and did it well. One wet afternoon Martha found a boy of nine standing at the table where the minutes of the census year lay spread under their weights, reading them upside down with his lips moving.

"What's that say, missus?" he asked her, pointing.

She looked. It was a page in Daniel Frayne's small upright hand, with rows of figures read out from the kingdom's paper, and underneath, alone on the line, the two words.

"Now written," she said.

"What's now written?"

"That's the question," said Martha, and after a while, since he was still waiting, she told him about the census, and the northern towns set down at half the measure, and the room in Caol mhòr where it was read out, and the speaker who sat with his hands flat on the table and would not raise his voice. The boy listened with his hands behind his back, as he had been told. When she had done he said that he thought the speaker ought to have shouted, and went off to fold paper.

Ellen had been listening from the stove. When the boy was gone she came and stood by Martha at the table and looked down the long rows of pages.

"It's all what was decided," she said. "Motions and votes and letters sent and letters received and filed. The price of seed-oats. Every page of it."

"That's what minutes are."

"I know it." Ellen touched the edge of the census page with one ink-stained finger, lightly, not to disturb the weights. "There's not a line in seventy-seven years of what happened to anybody."

Martha did not answer that. She had no answer ready, and she was not a woman who said things she had not thought out. After a time Ellen went back to the stove and poured the tea, and the binders worked on.

The last book was finished on the twenty-sixth of an Giblean, a clear cold morning with a high wind. It was Daniel Frayne's own last book, which ended in the middle of a page with the room's business for the last week of an Dùbhlachd, and after that the first minute in Thomas Rook's hand of the speaker's death. The eldest binder cut the spine with the two years it held and set it on the shelf at the end of the row. Then she stood back, leaning on her stick, and looked at the sixty-three books together for a long time, and said that it would do.

Peter Hale came for them the next day with the same cart and the same tea-chests. The children lined up under the oaks again to see them go, and Ellen Marsh stood in the door of her school and watched until the cart had gone out of sight among the trees. Then she went in and began to push the benches back into their rows.

Martha rode in the cart. It was a bright blowing day, with the rain gone east, and the road ran down through the oak country toward the head of the strait, and they came into Caol mhòr in the middle of the afternoon with the tide out and the fishing boats lying over on the mud. Peter Hale carried the chests up the outside stair one at a time. Thomas Rook had the press open and had scrubbed its shelves.

Martha laid the books in herself. She took them out of the chests one by one, in order, reading the years on each spine before she set it in its place, beginning at the top left with Walter Hale's harbour ledger in its new brown hide and ending low on the right with Daniel's. It took a long time, and neither of the men offered to help. When the last was in she ran her hand along the spines once, top shelf to bottom, the way she ran it along a row of bolts in the warehouse to be sure the count was right. It was right. She shut the doors of the press and locked them, and took the key off the lock, and put it on the ring at her belt with the keys of the mills.

"There's a minute wants writing," said Thomas Rook.

"Write that the books are laid in the press," said Martha. "Sixty-three of them, rebound by the binders of Muileann leathan, at the cost of their thread. Write the day."

He wrote it. He did not ask whether he should write anything more, and she did not tell him to, for there was nothing more that she knew.

She went down the stair afterward and stood a while at the harbour wall in the wind with her coat buttoned to the chin. The tide was on the turn and the boats were beginning to lift. Across the strait the evening came up grey off the water, and along the harbour front the lamps were being lit in the windows, one and then another. The key knocked against the others at her belt when she moved. She stood there until the first boats were afloat, and then she went to find the carter for the road home.

# Chapter Ten: Of the Coal Line and the Salt Road

*DE 8 – 9*

## I. Of the Yard at Muileann chrom

The yard families of Muileann chrom lived in three rows of slate-roofed houses between the sidings and the river, where Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn had put them when it laid the new lines in the kingdom's thirteenth year of the old count. Comhairle nam Mèinnean counted them apart from the rest of the town, and in time they counted themselves apart. They married among the rows, they buried in their own corner of the burial ground below the mill, and they kept their own hours, which were the hours of the trains. A child of the rows learned to tell the coal engines one from another by the note of their breath before she learned her letters, and a man of the rows who could not tell you the gradient of every mile of Slighe a' Ghuail between the yard and the sea was thought a little slow.

Eachann mac Ruairidh was forty-three that spring and had driven coal on the line for twenty years. He was a short, broad man with a burn-scar across the back of one hand from a gauge-glass that had burst when he was a fireman, and he had the habit, which his wife said was the only vain thing about him, of cleaning his boots every night whatever the day had been. He lived in the middle row with Seonaid nic Dhòmhnaill, who had come to the yard as a girl from the drovers of Achadh mhòr, their two daughters, and his father.

His father was Ruairidh mac Eachainn, and he had driven for forty years. He had been a fireman on the first trains the kingdom ran up to An Sloc Mòr, when the rails were still the humans' rails and the timetable was still the humans' timetable, and he had been a driver on the same run before Eachann was born. In the year the yard stopped the trains for three days over the cut in wages, Ruairidh had stood on the line with the rest and had not been among the eleven dismissed on the fifth day, and he never said whether he had been lucky or careful. Now he sat on a chair outside the door of the middle row in all weathers but rain, with a blanket over his knees, and listened to the engines, and could tell you from the sound of a train leaving the yard whether the fireman knew his work.

In the last days of an Gearran, in the eighth year of Linn an Dubhain, which nobody then called by that name, Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerk at the yard pinned a notice to the door of the engine-shed. Comhairle nam Mèinnean had bought an engine of the new kind from the shipmasters' works at the southern Seann Skell, and would try it on Slighe a' Ghuail. A driver was wanted to learn it. The notice said that the man chosen would be paid at the driver's rate during his learning, and it did not say what would be paid to anyone afterwards.

The older drivers read it and went back to their engines. Two of the younger ones put their names down and took them off again the same evening after talking to their fathers. Eachann read it three times, went home, cleaned his boots, and said nothing about it at supper. His father said nothing either, which was how Eachann knew he had heard.

"You'll put your name to it," Seonaid said, when the girls were in bed.

"Somebody will."

"That is not what I asked."

"Then yes," he said. "I will."

In the morning he wrote his name under the notice, alone, and the clerk took it down at noon.

The engine came up from the south in the middle of am Màrt. Slighe a' Ghuail did not run to the southern Seann Skell, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean would not wait for rails to be laid, so the works sent it by the old road on a low wagon with iron wheels, drawn by twelve horses. The horses were hired from the stables of Òrd Mhacha at Muileann chrom, which kept the best draught-beasts in the central country, and a priest of the order walked at the head of the leaders the whole two days, as the order's custom was whenever its horses hauled for the kingdom. It rained on the first day. On the second the wagon stuck in the ford below the town, and the priest stood in the water to his thighs speaking to the horses in the old words until they took it out. Half the yard went down to the ford to watch. Eachann went with them.

The engine was smaller than he had expected, a long box of dark-painted iron on eight wheels, with a cab at each end and no chimney. There was no firebox and no boiler, and no place in the cab for a fireman to stand. On its side, where Comhairle nam Mèinnean's number would go, someone at the works had chalked a word in the humans' tongue that nobody at the ford could read, and the priest of Macha wiped it off with his sleeve before the wagon came up the bank.

"What does it drink?" somebody asked.

"The black stuff," said a man who had been to the south. "Out of a barrel."

"And what does it eat?"

"Nothing. That is the whole trick of it."

The tank came three days after, on its own wagon, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's men set it on stone piers at the end of the long siding and filled it from barrels brought up by cart from the southern Seann Skell. It was the first dubhan tank Comhairle nam Mèinnean owned. The children of the rows stood under it and sniffed, and made faces, and came back the next day to sniff again. Dubhan in those years had a reek that nobody who smelled it ever forgot, something between a tar-boiler and a wet dog, and it clung to cloth. Seonaid said she could tell from the doorway what her husband had been doing all day, and in the end she made him leave his jacket in the wash-house.

Two fitters from the works came with the engine to teach it. One was a Dia-thìreach of the south coast, a thin, sour man who knew the engine as a priest knows a psalm and could not explain one word of it. The other was a Tuathach from Caol mhòr named Will Garside, who had come south to work at the shipmasters' works when they first took on northern hands. He spoke Dia-thìris with a northern burr and the humans' tongue with his own people, and he would shift from one to the other in the middle of a sentence when he was thinking hard. He was a patient teacher, and had Eachann take the engine's heart out and put it back on the first day, and on the second, and on the seventh, until Eachann could do it in the dark.

"You drove coal," Will said to him once, on the siding, while the rain came off the hills.

"Twenty years."

"Then you'll be wanting to feed it. You'll put your hand out for a shovel that isn't there. Every coal man does it. Leave your hand where it is."

Eachann did it for a week and then stopped. What he could not stop was listening for the fire. A coal engine talked to its driver the whole way: the roar when the door opened, the sigh of the safety-valve, the change of note on a gradient that told you before any gauge did that you were short of steam. The dubhan engine beat. It beat under his feet like a heart that had been running too long, steady and hard, and the beat went up when he opened it and down when he closed it and told him nothing else at all. For the first fortnight he drove with his head on one side like a dog listening at a door, and Will laughed at him and then did not laugh, because the listening was what made him careful.

By the middle of an Giblean he had taken the engine to An Sloc Mòr and back, empty, twice, with the sour fitter beside him and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's engineer, Niall mac Leòid, riding behind in a brake-van with a notebook. By the end of the month he had taken it without the fitter. The engineer wrote in his notebook that the man could drive it. He did not give Eachann any paper that said so, and Eachann did not ask for one.

His father came down to the siding once in all that month. He stood at the end of the platform with his stick and watched Eachann bring the engine in, and when it stopped he looked at it a long while, at the place where the chimney should have been, and at the cab where there was no fire.

"It's clean," he said at last.

"It is."

"A clean engine," his father said, and went home.

## II. Of the Engine that Carried No Coal

On Bealltainn, the first day of an Cèitean, Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn ran its first dubhan train on Slighe a' Ghuail from the yard at Muileann chrom to Cathair dhearg.

The fires of the feast had been lit on the hills about the town the night before, as they were every year, and the cattle of the hill farms driven between them for luck, and at dawn there was still smoke going up from three hilltops into a sky the colour of pewter. In the yard they filled the four tank-wagons from the tank on the piers by hand-pump, the men taking turns at the handle, and the reek of the stuff lay over the sidings so thick that the women of the rows shut their windows. There was no coal on the train. There was dubhan for the lamp-houses of the capital, and a brake-van at the tail with Niall mac Leòid in it, and that was all.

A few people came to see it off: the clerk, the yard foreman, the families of the rows who were not at work, the priest of Macha who had walked the engine up from the ford, and who said a blessing over it that was the blessing for a horse setting out on a long road, since no one had yet made one for an engine. Will Garside had gone back south a week before. Eachann's daughters stood on the wall of the rows and waved. His father was not there. His chair stood outside the door of the middle row with the blanket folded on it.

Eachann opened the engine, and the beat came up under his feet, and the train went out of the yard.

It is thirty-one miles from the yard at Muileann chrom to the goods-sheds at Cathair dhearg by Slighe a' Ghuail, and the line goes west the whole way, down the valley of the river and out onto the long slope of the capital's country. Eachann had driven it more times than he could count, and had never seen it. With no fire to feed and no fireman to watch, he had nothing to do with his eyes but look out of the window, and he found that the road he knew by its gradients and its signals and its places to take water had fields beside it, and people in the fields. At Cnoc ghorm the women of the line-side houses were hanging washing on the line behind their houses and did not look up; a coal train went by them six times a day, and they had not yet learned that this one was different. Past the bend below Cuan chrom the old coal road came down beside the line for a mile, and Eachann saw the roof of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr above it with a cart standing at the door. A little after that the line crossed a burn, and a boy fishing from the bridge dropped his rod and stood staring after the train with his mouth open, because it had no smoke.

That was what people saw, all the way down the line: no smoke. At every crossing where the road went over the rails there was someone standing to look, and they looked at the place above the engine where the smoke should have been, and then at the cab, and then at each other. A carter near Muileann mhin pulled his horse off the road and stood at its head, and as the train went past he took his cap off, though whether it was to the engine or to Eachann or to the day, he did not say.

Muileann mhin was where the lamp-makers were. That winter Comann nan Lòchran had begun to make lamps for dubhan, and had asked leave of the guild court to set on them the mark it had always set on its lamps, the flame over the hammer; the court was still arguing it. As the train came by the town's end, Eachann saw that the lamp-makers had come out of their shops and were standing in a row along the fence of the last field, some thirty of them in their leather aprons, to see the fuel their lamps would burn go by on its way to the capital. Nobody waved. One of them raised a lamp above his head as the engine passed, a new one, unlit, the brass bright in the grey light.

The goods-sheds at Cathair dhearg lay on the eastern edge of the capital, by the coal-yards, and the lamp-house men were waiting there with their carts and their barrels. They were men of the capital's poorer streets, where the lamps had been left dark to save coal six years before and had been lit again when the first dubhan came up from the south by road. The reek was nothing new to them, and nobody made faces at it. The dubhan was drawn off into their barrels by the tank-wagons' taps and loaded the barrels on their carts, and their foreman signed Niall mac Leòid's paper, and it was all done by a little after noon.

Eachann ate his bread in the cab. When he had finished, the lamp-house foreman came and stood by the step and looked up at him.

"Is it true there's no coal in her at all?"

"None."

"Not even to start her?"

"Not a lump."

The foreman shook his head. "My grandfather lit the lamps in Cathair dhearg when the humans put them up," he said. "Every night of his life he carried coal up a ladder. I carried coal up a ladder. My boy has never carried a lump of it, and he's twelve." He looked at the engine a while longer. "I don't know what I think," he said, and went back to his carts.

The train went home empty. There was nothing at the capital that anybody wanted carried to Muileann chrom, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean had not thought to find anything, and so the four tank-wagons rolled east behind the engine with their taps shut and nothing in them but the smell. On the long pull up the valley Eachann opened the engine to its full and felt the beat come up hard under his boots, and the engine took the bank below Cnoc ghorm without slowing, where a coal engine bringing the empties home would have been down to walking pace and the fireman sweating at the door. Eachann had not known it could do that. He sat with the knowledge for a while and did not know what he thought about it either.

He brought the train into the yard at dusk. The feast-fires were smoking still on the hills, and the smoke of them lay in the valley, and the yard lamps, which burned oil, were lit along the sidings. The families had gone in to their suppers. The foreman signed him off. Niall mac Leòid climbed down stiffly from the brake-van, shook Eachann's hand, said that Comhairle nam Mèinnean would be pleased, and went off to find a bed at the inn by the mill.

His father was standing at the end of the long siding, by the tank on its piers, leaning on his stick.

Eachann climbed down. For a while neither of them said anything. The engine ticked as it cooled. Somewhere in the rows a child was crying and being hushed.

"She took the bank below Cnoc ghorm coming home," Eachann said, "and never slowed."

"I heard her come in," said his father. "From the house. I took her for the mill."

"Come up," Eachann said. "I'll take her down to the points and back. It's no distance. You can stand where the fireman stands."

"There's no fireman."

"Then stand where he would."

His father looked at the engine. In the half-dark it was only a long shape against the lamps, with no glow at the cab door and no steam at the valves, and nothing about it that moved.

"Forty years," Ruairidh said, "I had a fire at my knee. When she was hungry I knew it, and when she was full I knew it, and on the bank below Cnoc ghorm, going up in the dark with a full train, I could look at the fire and tell you whether we'd make the top. That was a thing I knew." He shifted his weight on the stick. "I'll not ride behind a thing I can't see into."

"It's the same line, Athair."

"It is," said his father. "I'll walk it."

He turned and went back up the siding towards the rows, slowly, with the stick, and Eachann stood by the engine until he had gone in at the door of the middle row, and then he went and cleaned his boots.

## III. Of the Salt Road

The summer went on, and the new engine ran to Cathair dhearg twice in the week and came back empty twice in the week, and the coal engines ran as they always had on the trains from An Sloc Mòr and stood idle more often in the siding between runs, because there was less coal to carry each season than the season before. In an t-Ògmhios Comhairle nam Mèinnean took a second fireman off the roll and did not put anyone on in his place, and a man of the first row who had been a fireman nineteen years went down to the river landing to see if the boats wanted hands.

In an Lùnastal a boy of the rows was killed. His name was Ailean mac Mhathain and he was fourteen, and he had been set to work with the shunting gang that summer because his father had broken a leg. The yard was moving the dubhan tank-wagons from the long siding to make room for a second tank, and the gang was moving them by rope and pinch-bar because the small coal engines were busy on the train from An Sloc Mòr and Comhairle nam Mèinnean would not use the new engine for shunting. A wagon ran on the wet rail further than they meant it to. The boy was between it and the next. They buried him in the corner of the burial ground below the mill on the day after, and the whole of the rows walked behind him, and Eachann, who had been on the Cathair dhearg run that day and was not told until he came home, walked with them. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerk wrote the death in the yard book as an accident in the changeover. The women of the rows said that in the old days the boy would have been listening for an engine and would have heard it, and that nobody had yet learned to listen for a wagon pushed by men; and that was the only thing ever said about it that anyone wrote down, for Seonaid put it in a letter to her mother at Achadh mhòr, and the letter was kept.

Of the salt the salt-carters of Àth bheag tell it this way.

The pans had been dug on the flats below the town in the kingdom's thirty-second year of the old count, and since then Àth bheag had salted the whole eastern seaboard and a good part of the country inland. The salt went inland the way everything had gone inland from that coast since before there was a kingdom: by the old drove road that runs south out of Àth bheag along the shore, past the tower of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and the little town beside it, and then turns west away from the sea into the farm country. It went in carts drawn by oxen, six beasts to a cart, and the drovers of the east coast who owned the oxen took the salt in and brought back grain, and hides, and whatever else the inland towns had to sell. It was slow. A laden ox-cart makes ten or twelve miles in a day if the road is dry, and less if it is not, and on that coast it is seldom dry. But it had always been slow, and the drovers and the salt-masters had grown old together with it, and nobody had asked for it to be faster.

In the autumn of that year a salt-master of Àth bheag bought a lorry. He bought it from the shipmasters' works at the southern Seann Skell, where the fitters had begun to set their engines under carts, and it came up the coast road on its own wheels with a fitter driving and a barrel of dubhan roped behind the seat. The drovers came down to the ford of the Abhainn dhubh to look at it, and walked round it, and one of them kicked its wheel, and they went back to the alehouse and laughed about it for a week.

On the eleventh day of an Dùbhlachd it went out with its first load of salt. The salt-master's son drove it. It went down the drove road past Baile ìseal in the early morning, when the lamp was still burning in the tower, and the keepers came out on the gallery to watch it pass, and a man of Baile ìseal who was mending his boat on the shingle said afterwards that it made a noise like a hen-house on fire and went faster than a horse at the trot. By noon it had passed three ox-carts that had set out the day before. The drovers walking at the heads of their teams pulled over into the ditch to let it by, and stood in the ditch and watched it go on up the road, west into the farm country, with the salt-master's son sitting up high in the cab and not looking back.

"We knew then," an old drover of Àth bheag used to say, "and we did not know. We said to each other, one lorry. One lorry is a toy. And we went on to the next town at the pace of the oxen, and when we got there the lorry had sold its salt and gone home."

The lorry came to Muileann chrom two days later, with a second load. It was the salt-master's thought that if salt could come to the yard by lorry it could go on to the capital by rail, faster than any ox-cart could take it by the western roads, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean, which had been sending four tank-wagons home empty twice a week since Bealltainn, was glad to hear it. The salt went into a covered wagon behind the empty tanks, and on the next run Eachann drove it west, and brought it into the goods-sheds at Cathair dhearg, and a salt-merchant of the capital signed for it. It was the first load the new engine had ever carried towards the capital that was not dubhan, and the first time since the spring that it had pulled anything that paid.

Eachann told his father that night. "Salt," he said. "From Àth bheag. Came up by lorry, went down with me."

His father thought about it. "The drovers won't like that."

"No."

"They were an ox people," his father said, "the Àth bheag men. You could hear them singing to the beasts from the other side of a hill. My father knew some of their songs." He was quiet a while. "I don't remember any of them," he said.

That winter the drovers of the east coast began to sell their oxen. They did not sell them all at once. A man with three teams sold one, and then a second when the salt-master bought another lorry, and kept the last for the hay and the carting on his own ground. A man with one team kept it longer than was wise, and then sold it at a worse price than his neighbour had got. The beasts went to the farms inland and to the butchers of the market towns, and the carts stood in the yards with their shafts on the ground. In am Faoilleach of the ninth year the last ox-drove went out of Àth bheag with salt on the old road, four carts and twenty-four beasts, driven by an old man named Murchadh Bàn and his two grandsons, and it took five days to reach the inland towns in the rain; and when it came home the old man sold the oxen at the ford and did not buy others.

## IV. Of the Drovers at An Sligeanach Fad' às

Seonaid's brother was Uilleam mac Dhòmhnaill, and he had been a drover all his life, as their father had been. The drovers of Achadh mhòr were a different people from the drovers of the east. They were a southern family of families, who drove the oxen of the granary country and hauled its grain, and who had driven the cattle up from the east coast every autumn to the great fields of Achadh mhòr, where the stubble fattened them, and sold them on in the spring. They were wealthier than the eastern drovers and prouder, and a family of them had bought An Sligeanach Fad' às ten years before and built a second hall on it for the drove trade, so that it had become the greatest house on the old mining roads.

Uilleam wrote to his sister at the turn of the year. The letter was short, because he did not like writing, and Seonaid read it aloud at supper. There were no oxen coming from the east this spring, he said, because the eastern men had sold their teams; there was nothing to drive to the fields and nothing to drive away from them; and the grain of Achadh mhòr was going to the southern Seann Skell by lorry already, for the works there had begun to sell lorries to anyone who would pay. The family was meeting at the Sligeanach on the twenty-second day of am Màrt to settle what they would do. He did not say what that would be. He asked Eachann to come, if Comhairle nam Mèinnean would let him go, since Eachann knew engines.

Comhairle nam Mèinnean let him go for two days. He went south by the carrier's cart on the old road, twenty-one miles through the farm country in a thin rain, and came to the Sligeanach in the late afternoon of the day before the meeting.

It stood by itself on the southern road a little way out of Achadh mhòr, a long, low house of grey stone with a slate roof, and the second hall built out at the back of it, and behind that the ox-yards, walled, where two hundred beasts could stand at a time. It was the oldest house under Sìth an Rathaid, the law which says that no feud may be followed under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door, and the keepers of the waypoint houses had first set that law down here in An Aois Ailein. The carriers say that one is never nearer to An Sligeanach Fad' às than halfway, wherever one starts, and it has had that name from the saying for longer than it has had its stone walls.

When Eachann came in by the road that afternoon, the ox-yards were empty. There was a new thing in the forecourt, between the door and the road: an iron tank on stone piers like the one at the yard in Muileann chrom, only smaller, painted green, with a hand-pump beside it and a board nailed to the pump with the price chalked on it by the gallon. A lorry was drawn up at it, and a boy of the house was working the handle, and the reek of dubhan hung over the forecourt in the rain. Inside, the old hall was lit by the lamps it had always had, oil lamps with wicks on chains from the beams, and the fire was a fire of peat.

Uilleam met him at the door. He was a big, fair man, going grey, with a drover's hands and a drover's way of standing with his weight back, as if he had a beast on a rope in front of him.

"You smell like a lorry," Uilleam said.

"I drive one on rails."

"So I hear." He took Eachann's wet coat and hung it by the fire. "We're all going to smell like it soon enough."

The meeting was in the morning, in the second hall. There were some forty of them, the heads of the drover families of Achadh mhòr and their sons, and the landlord of the Sligeanach, who was one of them, and a man from the works at the southern Seann Skell in a good coat who had come with papers. Eachann sat at the back and held his tongue, for he was no drover and it was not his meeting; he listened, and afterwards he could tell Seonaid all of it.

It was not a long meeting. There were no oxen coming from the east, and there would be none next year. The grain would go to the southern Seann Skell and to the capital whether the drovers hauled it or not; the only question was whether it would go in their lorries or in someone else's. An old man named Aonghas Mòr, the eldest of the families, spoke for keeping the oxen one more year, to see. Nobody answered him. When he had sat down, the landlord said that he had put a tank of dubhan in his forecourt that winter, and that he had sold more fuel off it since Samhain than he had sold beds, and that if the families bought lorries he would sell them their fuel and their dinners at the same door, and the house would stand as it had always stood. The man from the works laid out his papers.

By noon they had agreed. Each family would sell its teams at the Sligeanach that day, to the butchers and farmers who had come for the purpose, and the works would take the price of the oxen against the price of lorries, the rest to be paid over three years from the grain. Uilleam put his mark to the paper with the others. His hand was steady.

The sale was held in the ox-yards in the afternoon. The rain had stopped and a low sun came in under the cloud, and the yards were full again for the last time, with the beasts of every drover family of Achadh mhòr, great red and brindled oxen with their horns tipped in brass, steaming in the cold. Buyers came from all over the granary country. Eachann stood by the wall with his brother-in-law and watched the lots go through.

Uilleam's were the last. There were six of them, one team, and he had raised the youngest from a calf. He went into the pen before the auctioneer called them and walked down the line of them with his hand on their backs, speaking to them in the words the drovers use to their beasts, which are older than the road; and then he came out and shut the gate and did not look at them again while they were sold. They went to a farmer from the hills west of Achadh mhòr, who wanted them for ploughing, and the price was a fair one.

"He'll work them," Uilleam said, when it was done. "That's something. He won't eat them."

"No."

"My father drove the east road forty years. His father before him. We had the cattle up out of the east every autumn, every year, since there were drovers." He stood looking at the empty pen. "Your father still won't ride the thing?"

"He won't."

"I wouldn't either," Uilleam said, "at his age." He turned from the pen. "But I'm not his age. Come and look at the lorry and tell me what I've bought."

The lorries stood in a row in the road beyond the forecourt, eleven of them, painted the same dark green as the tank, which was the colour the works painted everything. The man from the works had driven one up and brought the others with fitters in the morning. They were high, ugly, square-built things with open beds for the grain and a cab over the engine, and in the evening light, with the empty ox-yards behind them, they looked to Eachann like beasts of some kind themselves, waiting to be led. He went over Uilleam's with the fitter while the light lasted. He showed his brother-in-law where the engine's heart was, and how to know from the beat when it was labouring, and which of the fitter's answers to believe, and Uilleam listened to him as he had never listened to him in the twenty years since Seonaid had married into the rows.

When it was too dark to see, they came back across the forecourt. The landlord's boy was at the pump again, filling the lorries one after another from the green tank, and working the handle with his whole body, and the landlord stood beside him with a slate, chalking the gallons. On the wall of the forecourt behind him there was an older slate, fixed to the stone, where the house had kept the tally of beasts through the ox-yards for as long as anyone could remember, and the last figures on it were still there, in the landlord's hand, from the autumn. The landlord saw Eachann looking at it.

"I'll wash it off in the morning," he said. "I'll want it for the barrels."

Inside, the lamps on their chains were lit, and the fire of peat was built up, and the drovers of Achadh mhòr sat down together in the old hall to eat, as they had eaten there every spring on the day of the sale since the house was theirs. Somebody began one of the droving songs, and some of the older men took it up and some did not. Out in the road the lorries stood in their row in the dark, with the rain coming on again and running off their square cabs, and the reek of their fuel drifted in under the door every time it opened, and nobody got up to shut it.

# Chapter Eleven: Of the Wick over the Door

*DE 9 – 10*

## I. Of the Roads Before the Lamps

The old mining roads of the kingdom had been made for coal, and coal had kept them, in the years when Comhairle nam Mèinnean's carts went out from every pit-mouth to every market town and a house on the road could live well enough selling beer and oats to the men who drove them. There were inns along every one of the roads, a day's walk or a day's drive apart, and a carrier who knew the roads knew the inns by name before he knew the towns they stood near: the Lion on the north-east road, An Sligeanach Fad' às on the east road, An Taigh-seinnse Òir and An Taigh-òsta Grianach each on its own way south, and a dozen smaller ones between, kept by families who had kept them for longer than any coal charter had run. They lit their yards and their taprooms with oil in glass, on a wick that wanted trimming every hour past dark, and a house was judged along the roads by how clean it kept its wicks and how far its light carried into the yard, so that a carrier coming in tired and late could see, from a mile off in the winter dark, whether there would be a fire and a bed for him or not.

In the ninth year of Linn an Dubhain, though nobody yet called it that, the light along the roads changed inside a single turn of the seasons, and it changed in every house at once, though no house changed on the same day as its neighbour. The Muileann mhin lamp-makers, who had been given leave the autumn before to set their own mark on the lamps they made, now sent them out along every road that a lorry could reach, small round-bellied things of brass and glass with a wick of their own kind that needed no trimming and burned steady in a wind that would have guttered oil to nothing. A house that put in three or four of them at the door and along the yard wall had light enough to see a cart come in from the top of the hill, and light enough, more than one landlord said, to count the coin by without a candle at the till. The lamps cost money that not every house had lying by, and the barrels of dubhan to fill them cost more again, carted out from the depots that were only then opening at the market towns; so the roads did not change together, and for a season and more a carrier travelling from the north-east to the south-west of the kingdom passed from a house lit like a market fair into one still lit as his grandfather's inn had been lit, sometimes within the same day's driving.

The carriers themselves said little about it at first, being men and women whose trade was to move goods rather than to remark on them. They were the ones who saw it whole, house by house, season by season, in a way that no single landlord and no clerk of Comhairle nam Mèinnean ever did, and it is chiefly from what they told afterwards, and from the account-books of the houses themselves, that the change along the roads is known at all. A carrier of the south-west road, asked years later what she remembered first of the new lamps, said only that she remembered the smell of them before she remembered the light, the tar-and-wet-dog reek that clung to a coat left too near the door, and that for a whole season she judged an inn's newness by how strongly it smelled rather than by how brightly it burned.

They judged the houses by other small signs too, that a clerk of Comhairle nam Mèinnean riding the same roads would never have troubled to note. A house that had put in the new lamps kept its stable-boy later, because a lorry could come up the road at any hour and a carrier who saw light from a mile off would drive on to reach it rather than stop short at a darker house nearer by; a house that had not put them in kept its old custom of shutting the yard gate at full dark, because there was no longer any light by which a late traveller could be seen coming, or trusted, once the gate was shut. A landlady who had hung the lamps might tell you, if you asked her over her accounts, exactly what week her trade had turned; a landlady who had not would tell you only that trade was much as it had always been, in a voice that did not always believe itself. The carriers carried both kinds of answer from house to house all that year, along with the grain and the barrels and the letters that were their ordinary trade, and a house's name came, before the year was out, to mean as much for its light as for its beer.

## II. Of the Yellow Lion

On the north-east road, two days' driving out of the capital where the road climbs onto the high moor, stood the house called An Leòmhann Buidhe, which had stood on that spot, by its own reckoning, since before the humans came. It was not a large house. It had a taproom, a kitchen, six rooms for travellers and a long low stable that had held more horses in its day than it held now that half its custom came by lorry, and its landlord was a heavy, slow-spoken man who had kept it from his father and meant to leave it to his son, and who had, until that year, never in his life put anything new into the house that the house had not asked for first.

He hung the new lamps in the spring, four of them along the yard wall and two either side of the taproom door, because a carrier had told him plainly, the autumn before, that houses without them would lose their custom to houses with them inside two years, and he was not a man to lose custom out of stubbornness. The lamps burned clean and steady and lit the yard farther than the old oil ever had, and within the month the taproom was fuller of an evening than it had been in years, men coming in off the road simply to sit where the light was good.

But over the door itself, where an oil lamp had burned since before his father's time, he did not take the old one down. He filled it, and trimmed it, and lit it every evening with the same care he had always given it, so that a traveller coming up the road at dusk saw, above the four new lamps burning steady along the wall, one small wavering flame that had to be watched and tended and could not be trusted to burn the night through on its own.

A carrier who lodged there that summer asked him why, when the new lamps cost him nothing to keep once they were filled and the old one cost him an hour of trimming every night of his life.

"My grandmother lit that one," the landlord said, "the night my grandfather came home from the sea he'd been given up for lost in, and she kept it lit every night after, in case he was late again. I don't believe the wick's been out a night since, bar the one when the glass cracked in a frost and we had it mended by morning." He looked up at it, where it burned above the new lamps' steadier light. "The new ones I keep for the road. That one I keep for the house."

He never gave a fuller reason than that, and none was asked of him again, but other houses along the road began to do the same in the months after, keeping one old wick burning among the new lamps, over a door or in a window that faced the road, and the custom spread faster than anyone could account for from a single inn's grandmother. Some of the houses that took it up had no grandmother's story of their own to hang it on, and lit a wick over the door only because the house up the road had one and looked the better for it; a carrier who lodged at three such houses in a week said that by the second he had stopped asking what each lamp was kept for, since the answer was as often "because the Lion does" as it was any tale of a father lost at sea. Within a year or two a wick lamp kept burning that way, of no more use than the memory it was lit for, or of no memory at all beyond the fashion of keeping one, was called along every road in the kingdom a Leòmhann, after the house where a carrier first thought to ask why, and the word outlived the reason for it in most of the mouths that used it.

## III. Of the Carriage that Needed No Horse

At the southern Seann Skell, where the shipmasters' works had grown in six years from a leased row of salt-sheds into the largest yard of its kind on the coast, the fitters who served under Peigi nic Ascaill had by the ninth year of the count learned to build the dubhan engine into almost anything that moved on wheels: lorries first, then a fishing boat's donkey-engine, then, that spring, a farm cart for a miller of the shire who wanted his grain in to market before his neighbours' horses were harnessed. It was Peigi who thought first of the carriage, or so the works always said afterwards, though she herself, when asked, only said that the Àrd-choimheadaiche had asked her outright whether a man might ride without a horse as well as a cart of grain might, and that she had not been able to think of a reason to tell him no.

Alasdair mac Ìomhair, Àrd-choimheadaiche of the order of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, kept a closed carriage of the old kind for his journeys among the houses of his order, drawn by a pair of matched greys that were, by that year, old themselves and failing in wind on the long climbs to the hill houses. The works fitted a lorry's engine under the carriage's own frame, boxed it in behind a panel so that it showed nothing from the road but a low hum and a smell, and set the driver's seat where the coachman's had always been, with reins for nothing now but a wheel. It took the fitters the better part of a month, working evenings on it besides their ordered work, and Joe Ashby, who had come to the works two years before with two other Tuathaich hands and stayed on as one of Peigi's best, did most of the fitting of the engine itself, though the works' book, when the carriage was shown, named the works and not the man.

On the day it was ready the custodian came down from Seann Skell's house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail to try it, in his working robes rather than his formal ones, and stood a long while looking at it before he got in.

"It has no horse in it at all," he said.

"No, my lord," said Peigi.

"Then what does it eat, going up the hill to Tobar dhearg?"

"The same as a lorry eats. A barrel behind, and it goes as far as the barrel lasts, and no farther, unlike a horse, that can be fed from any field along the road if the barrel runs dry."

He considered that, and got in, and Joe drove him, the custodian sitting very upright with his hands folded and his eyes on the road the whole way. The road out of Seann Skell climbs for the first two miles before it levels toward the coast, a grade that the old greys had taken at a walk for years, resting twice, and the carriage went up it without slowing, so that the custodian, glancing out at a milestone he knew well, remarked only that he had not thought to see that stone again so soon. Joe said nothing to that, having been told before he ever put his hand to the engine that the custodian's habit was silence on a journey and that a driver who filled it with talk would not be asked twice, and the two of them went the rest of the road that way, the engine's hum under the floor the only voice in the carriage, until they came in sight of Brìde's house at Tobar dhearg, where he was expected that evening for the eve of a small feast that fell in an t-Ògmhios. The custodians and the novices of the house came out at the sound of the engine, having never heard one on that road before, and stood in a line along the steps to see him step down from a carriage that had come the whole nine miles from Seann Skell without a horse ahead of it.

"It is not forbidden," the custodian said, to no one in particular, looking back at the carriage as it stood ticking and cooling in the yard, the phrase he had used five years before of the fuel itself and had never since had cause to take back or to add to. "I do not know that it is blessed, either." He went in to the feast, and the carriage stood in the yard of Brìde's house overnight with a boy set to watch it, in case it should do something no one had thought to warn him of, and did nothing at all but grow quiet and cold, as any engine does, once its fire is out.

Within a few years the council kept such carriages of its own, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean after it, and a carriage that needed no horse ceased to be a thing anyone in the capital troubled to remark on; but it is remembered along the roads as the custodian's carriage first of all, the first one anyone had seen, and the fitters at Seann Skell kept, for a long while after, the panel from its first engine-box, with the mark Joe Ashby had chalked on the inside of it where no report would ever find it, and the mark was his own initials, and nothing more.

## IV. Of Am Buabhall Fortanach

There was no house on the south-west road better known, nor better loved by the carriers who used it, than Am Buabhall Fortanach, the Lucky Buffalo, which stood at a crossing of two roads near Doire shean where five could put up for the night in comfort and thirty could crowd the taproom on a market eve without anyone going without a seat. It had been built by the landlady's grandfather's grandfather in the years when the south-west road first carried coal down to the coast in any quantity, and it had prospered on that coal for four generations, through droughts and through the wars of a kingdom the house had outlasted twice over, and its account-books, kept in an unbroken line back to the house's founding, were the pride of the family that kept it, each ledger signed at its close by the landlady of the year and handed to her daughter or her niece when the house passed on.

By the ninth year of the count the house was kept by Oighrig nic Iain, who had taken it from her aunt six years before, a tall, dry-spoken woman with a scar on one forearm from a kitchen fire in her girlhood and a way of running her thumbnail along a column of figures that every carrier who had watched her cast an account knew and dreaded, because it meant she had found an error and would not let it stand uncorrected for politeness' sake. She had heard of the new lamps the same autumn as every other landlady on the roads, and unlike most of them she had not hurried. Her account-books told her, plainly enough, what the new light would cost her: the lamps themselves, brass and glass and the Muileann mhin mark on each one, more than she cared to reckon at first sight; the barrels of dubhan, carted from a depot two days off, at a price that the depot's own clerk admitted might fall in a year or might not; and against all that, no certain gain, only the word of carriers passing through that a house without the new light would lose its custom to a house with it, which was a thing said easily enough by people who did not keep the books.

"I will hang them," she told her cousin, who fitted lamps for half the houses of that road and had asked her three times that year already, "when I have seen one house on this road ruined by hanging them, or one house on this road ruined by not."

"You'll wait a long while for either," he said.

"Then I'll wait a long while."

Neither happened, in the year and more she waited, but her custom did not fall either, for Am Buabhall Fortanach was the kind of house that carriers went out of their way for whether its yard was bright or not, and she went on filling her oil lamps and trimming her wicks and casting her accounts by their light, while house after house along the roads about her put in the new light and told her, when they met at the fair or the market, that she was a fool to wait, or a wise woman to wait, according to how their own reckoning had gone that season. A carrier who put up at her house most weeks of that trade said afterwards that he never once heard her answer the talk with more than a shrug and a line about counting at the year's end rather than at the fair, and that he had taken her for simple stubbornness until he saw her books himself, and understood that she had never once, in all that waiting, stopped reckoning.

Her own book changed her, in the end, and neither a season's takings nor any carrier's word. In the autumn of the ninth year, closing the ledger for the year past as her aunt had taught her and her aunt's mother before that, she found, ruled up in her own hand at the year's foot, that the house's trade in oil, which had held steady or grown a little every year of her keeping, had fallen for the first time since the ledgers began, by a sum small enough that no single month's entry showed it plainly, but real once the year was cast up whole. It was the first year in four generations that the house's oldest trade had gone backward, and she sat a long while with the book open before her and the last of the day's oil light burning low on the sill, and then she wrote, beneath the year's total, a line that stayed in the book after: *the light is going out from under us, whether we hang the new lamps or not; better to hang them ourselves than have the road hang them for us.*

She sent for her cousin the next week. He came with six lamps for the yard and two for the taproom, and fitted them himself over three days, working from a ladder while she stood below him with the account-book still under her arm, as though she meant to enter the cost of each lamp the moment it was hung rather than wait for the week's end. On the second evening, with half the yard already bright and the other half still lit by the old lamps she had not yet let him take down, a carrier coming up the road in the dusk stopped his cart at the gate and sat looking at the house a long moment before he drove in, and told her, when she asked him what had held him, that he had thought for a moment he had come to the wrong inn, the yard being lit in a way he had never known it.

"You have not," she said. "Come in and I'll show you the account for it, if you doubt me."

When her cousin presented his account for the work and the lamps together she read it through twice, ran her thumbnail down the column as she always did, found no error in it, and paid it without a word of complaint, which her cousin said afterwards was the strangest part of the whole business, stranger even than the lamps themselves. She kept the bill pinned inside the cover of that year's ledger, where a curious carrier who asked to see the house's books could still find it, the whole cost written plain: a year's takings from the oil trade, to the shilling, spent all at once to be rid of the trade that had earned it.

The old oil lamp over the taproom door she did not keep burning beside the new ones, as the Lion's landlord kept his; she took it down the same evening the new lamps were lit, cleaned it, and set it on the shelf above the till, where it stood empty from that day, and where more than one carrier, seeing it there years after and asking after it, was told only that the house kept its reckonings where it could see them.

## V. Of the Two Houses and the Carriers' Song

Farther north, on the old coal road above Cuan chrom, the house called An Taigh-seinnse Mòr had done what few of the smaller inns could afford to do, and built rather than merely lit: a second hall, set back from the road behind the old one, raised over the summer of the ninth year and opened in an Dàmhair, lit throughout with dubhan lamps set into the walls themselves rather than hung from chains, so that the hall showed no lamp at all to a stranger's eye, only a steady even light with no flame anyone could point to. The landlord let the new hall for weddings and for wakes, at a price the old taproom could never have commanded, and that same spring, when Comann nan Gualadairean, its own hall at Achadh dhomhain put up for sale for want of members to keep it, asked whether it might hold its meetings there until it found a roof of its own, he let the hall to the guild as well, at less than he might have asked of a wedding party, because his father had hewed coal on that road before he ever kept an inn on it, and he said he would not charge a guild dying of the very trade his family had left for its own last meetings under his roof. The guild's rolls were thin by then and its meetings shorter than they had once been, but for two years and more the hall above Cuan chrom heard the old business read out under new lamps, by men whose fathers had cut coal by nothing brighter than a wick clipped to a cap.

The guild's master, an old hewer whose name the hall's own account did not trouble to keep, thanked the landlord at the first meeting held there, standing under lamps set into a wall his own trade had never built with, and said that a hall was still a hall whoever's light it burned. The landlord answered only that he hoped the guild would have the use of it a good while yet, though both men in the room that evening knew, from the guild's own thinning rolls, that the hope was more kindly meant than likely to be kept.

Farther east, on the south-east road near Cnoc dhìreach, a smaller house called An Taigh-òsta Grianach, went further than any inn on any road that year. Its landlady, widowed young and running the house alone with two grown sons, rebuilt it entire over the winter, lamps in every room down to the meanest, a pump of its own set into the yard wall where a carrier low on fuel could fill his barrel before he had so much as taken a room, and a sign painted new over the door that named, under the house's old name, what a traveller could buy there: *beds and fire*. No house on any road had sold fuel alongside a bed before that spring; within the year half the great houses did the same, but hers was first, and the carriers said of her, for as long as the house stood, that she had understood before any of them what a road ran on now, and had simply built her house to match it.

It is from the carriers, in the end, more than from any house's own book, that the fullest account of that year along the roads survives, for they alone travelled the whole length of them and saw every house in its turn, bright or dark, new-lit or old, and carried word of one house to the next faster than any clerk of Comhairle nam Mèinnean ever carried a report. In the tenth year, at a fair where carriers of half a dozen roads met as they did every spring to trade news and hire and complaint, someone set a verse to a tune the carriers already used for a droving song, about the wick kept burning over a door for no more use than the memory of it, and the tune caught before the words were even settled into their final order, so that within a season it was sung, in one form or another, from the north-east road to the south-west, by carriers who had never seen An Leòmhann Buidhe and did not always trouble to get its name right. It runs four lines and a turn, and says only that the old light and the new light burn side by side a while in every house before the old light goes out for good, and that a wise house keeps one wick a little longer than it needs to, so as not to forget too quickly what it burned before.

No one along the roads could say, by the time the tune was old, who had made the words first, and no house claimed the making of it, though more than one landlord hummed it without noticing he did, filling the new lamps by their own steady light with the old song about the wick going on in his mouth.

# Chapter Twelve: Of the Engines Laid Up and the Pit Quarter Emptied

*DE 10 – 11*

## I. Of the Long Siding

By the tenth year of Linn an Dubhain there were nine coal engines at the yard of Muileann chrom, and in the space of one autumn all nine went into the long siding by the river and none of them came out again.

It was not done at a stroke. Through the summer Comhairle nam Mèinnean had run them where it could, on the shorter hauls up to An Sloc Mòr and back, while the single dubhan engine took the long run to Cathair dhearg twice in the week and grew, in the yard's mouth, from a thing to be pointed at into a thing to be reckoned with. A coal engine wanted a fireman as well as a driver, coal by the ton got up from the pit and carted to the yard and shovelled twice over before it burned, and water besides, taken on at every second stop; the dubhan engine wanted a man to open a valve. By harvest Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerk had stopped writing coal orders for the shorter hauls at all, because there was no longer coal enough coming up from An Sloc Mòr to be worth ordering by the ton, the pit itself running three days in the week where it had run six.

Eachann mac Ruairidh drove the dubhan engine those months, as he had all that year, and watched the coal engines come in from their last runs one behind another through an t-Sultain and an Dàmhair, until by the feast of Samhain there were nine of them standing cold in the long siding with their fires drawn and their tenders empty, in a row under the rain, and no order came to light them again.

Comhairle nam Mèinnean did not say the word laid up. The notice on the shed door, when it came at the end of an Dàmhair, said that the coal engines of the yard were stood down pending Comhairle nam Mèinnean's further order, and that the men who had driven and fired them would be entered for instruction on the new engines, at the driver's rate while they learned, as Eachann had been the spring before. It did not say what would be paid to a man who did not learn, nor what was to be done with the engines standing in the siding, and the rows read both silences the same way.

Some of the older men put their names down. More did not. Two firemen younger than Eachann, brothers named Somhairle and Uilleam Frisealach, came to him at the shed door the week the notice went up and asked him plainly what the new engine was like to drive, since he was the only man at Muileann chrom who could tell them from having done it a year, and he told them as well as he could: that there was less to it and more to it both, less strength wanted and more watching, that a man came off shift cleaner than he had ever come off a coal engine and slept worse the first month for want of knowing why. They put their names down together. Their father, who had fired for thirty years and was near the end of driving, did not, and said nothing to either of them about it, which the rows understood, having heard the same silence in Eachann's own house the year before.

The instruction, when it came, fell to Eachann, since Comhairle nam Mèinnean had no one else at Muileann chrom who had driven the dubhan engine a full year and knew its temper. He took the Frisealach brothers out on it through the slack hours of a fortnight in an Dàmhair, and found them apt enough, being young and used to trusting a gauge over a feeling; the harder teaching was with the older men, four of them who had put their names down against their own better judgement because a driver's wage was a driver's wage whatever pulled it, and who came to the footplate each with thirty years of a coal engine's habits already set hard in their hands.

One of these was a man named Dòmhnall Ruadh, who had fired and then driven on Slighe a' Ghuail since before Eachann was born, and who stood at the new engine's controls the first morning turning the valve this way and that with the same slow, testing pressure he had always used on a regulator, waiting, Eachann saw, for some resistance in it that would tell him how hard he might press; and there was none, the valve turning as easily open as shut, giving him nothing back to read. He drove it badly that week and worse the next; his hands carried a kind of grief they would not put down, whatever care he gave the work, and on the ninth day he came off shift, hung up his coat in the shed for the last time, and told the clerk to strike his name from the instruction list.

"I can drive anything with a fire in it," he said to Eachann afterwards, not unkindly, the two of them standing by the cold rank of coal engines while the rain came down. "Show me a boiler and I'll tell you its mood before it tells me. This thing has no mood. It only has a setting, and a man who reads moods all his life makes a poor hand at reading settings." He looked along the siding at the engines he would never drive again. "I'll go to the sidings, or the stores, or wherever they'll have a fifty-year-old man who knows every mile of this line and nothing of the thing that's replacing it. It's more than some are given."

Ruairidh mac Eachainn, Eachann's father, had by then given up his chair outside the middle row's door for the worst of the cold weather and sat instead just inside it, where he could still hear the yard through the open half of the door but keep his knees out of the wind. He heard the coal engines come in one by one through the autumn, and he heard, because the wind off the river carried it into the rows most evenings, when the last one came in and did not go out again. He did not go down to look at the siding. Eachann offered, more than once, to walk him down of an evening, and each time his father said he had seen a coal engine and did not need to see nine of them standing idle to know what idle looked like.

"They'll scrap them," he said one night in am Faoilleach, when the fire was low and the girls were asleep and Seonaid had gone through to the back room. "Or they'll leave them to rust in that siding until somebody with more sense than Comhairle nam Mèinnean sells the iron. One or the other."

"Maybe," Eachann said.

"I drove on that line before the kingdom had a timetable of its own," his father said. "Before your time. I fired for a man who had fired for a human, and he told me things about the old running I never saw the like of again — signals given by flag in fog, a fireman who could tell you the load of a train by the sound of the wheels on the points before it was in sight. All that's gone into the ground with men now, and it never went anywhere. It just stopped being wanted, the way this is stopping being wanted." He looked at the fire. "I don't grudge you the new engine, Eachann. That should be said plainly, since I may not say it again. What I grudge is Comhairle nam Mèinnean's silence. A thing that has carried men and coal and the kingdom's post for sixty years is owed better than a notice on a shed door."

Eachann did not answer that, because there was no answer that would not have sounded like an argument, and he did not want to argue with his father in am Faoilleach over a thing neither of them could mend. He banked the fire instead, and helped his father through to his bed, and went out to clean his boots in the cold of the yard, which he did every night whatever the day had been, the one habit of his that Seonaid still called vain.

In the spring Comhairle nam Mèinnean sent a clerk with a book to walk the long siding and write down the number and condition of each engine, and after that nobody at Muileann chrom saw the clerk again, or the book, or any order touching the nine engines at all. They stood there through that whole year and the next, and the grass came up between the sleepers under them, and children of the rows who had never fired a coal engine and never would climbed into the cabs to play at driving, until the paint wore off the footplates where their boots had stood. The oldest of the drivers who had put their names down for instruction and been turned away for age, a man named Ailean Frisealach, uncle to the two brothers, used to walk down to the siding of a Sunday and stand by the engines a while before he came home, and would not say to anyone what he did there, and nobody in the rows asked him.

## II. Of the Reek at An Taigh-seinnse Reòta

On the north road above Muileann fhada, a day's ride from the yard, stood An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the coldest of the old coaching inns on that side of the country and, by its own landlord's telling, the last that still lit its rooms with oil and wick from end to end. Eachann had never seen the place himself; he heard of it from a guard who rode the carriers' coach on the north road and stopped there most weeks to change horses.

The landlord of the Reòta, a heavy, slow-spoken man named Murchadh Frisealach, no kin to the brothers at Muileann chrom though the name was common enough on that road, had written to Comhairle nam Mèinnean in am Faoilleach of that year to say that he would not put dubhan lamps in his rooms, because the reek of the stuff drove custom from an inn the way smoke drove bees from a hive, and he had seen it happen at three houses on the coast road and would not have it happen at his own.
