The letter was read out, so the guard said, at more than one fireside between Muileann fhada and the capital before it ever reached anyone at Comhairle nam Mèinnean with the standing to answer it, and for a season or two it was repeated as a kind of proof that a house could hold to the old ways if it had the will.

It did not hold. The lorries that ran past his door every day of the week brought him more custom in a month than the old coaching trade had brought him in a season, and every one of the drivers who stopped there asked, the first night, why the rooms stank of tallow and smoked worse than the yard they had just come from, and more than a few did not stop a second time. By the following winter Murchadh Frisealach had put dubhan lamps in the taproom and the two best rooms, telling anyone who asked that it was only for the drivers' comfort and that his own rooms upstairs kept the old lamps still; and within the year after that the old lamps were gone from the whole house but one, kept over the stable door out of what he called habit and everyone else called defeat. The guard told it as a joke against himself as much as against the landlord, since he had been one of those who complained of the reek the first night and had gone on stopping there anyway, for want of anywhere else to change horses on that road.

Eachann heard the tale from the guard one evening at the yard, over nothing more than the ordinary talk of men waiting on a delayed load, and thought little of it at the time beyond a moment's fellow feeling for a landlord who had written Comhairle nam Mèinnean a letter that changed nothing. It was only afterwards, in the autumn that followed, that it came back to him and stood for something larger than an innkeeper's stubbornness; but that is properly told with what happened at Muileann dhearg, and not before.

## III. Of the Last Face

Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh had been master of Comann nan Gualadairean for eleven years, and in all that time he had buried more of the trade than he had bound to it. He was a broad, grey man, not far off seventy, with a cough that had settled into his chest a dozen years before and never wholly left it, and hands that still knew a seam of coal by feel through a glove better than most young hewers knew it by lamplight. He had cut coal himself at Muileann dhearg as a boy, before the guild had thought to make him a master of anything, and it was to Muileann dhearg that the guild's last close business called him in an Dàmhair of that year.

The pit at Muileann dhearg had worked one face only for three years past, the rest of its galleries stood and flooding slowly from below, and the one face left had been thin and poor coal for most of that time, cut more because a town needs its pit to still be a pit than because the coal paid for the cutting. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyor came up from Cathair mhòr in the first days of an Dàmhair, walked the face with the pit captain and two of the older hewers, and wrote in his book, which Tormod was shown afterwards and never forgave himself for reading, that the seam was spent below the value of working it, and that the pit should close.

It closed on 10 an Dàmhair, DE 10, on a morning of thin rain with the wind off the moor above the town. Tormod came up from Seann Toll the day before, on a carrier's cart with his own coat over his knees against the wet, because it seemed to him, though no rule of the guild required it, that the master ought to be there for the last shift of a pit that had made hewers of three generations of his own family before him, and he was not a man to reason himself out of a thing that seemed to him owed.

He stood at the pit-head from before light with the pit captain, a heavy, silent man named Gilleasbaig Ruadh, and watched the cage come up for the last time a little after the ninth hour, twelve men in it, black to the eyes, none of them speaking. They had known, going down that morning, that they would not go down again; the last coal had been cut two days before and the shift had spent its hours drawing the props and the rails that could still be sold for scrap, which is bitter work for a hewer, being the taking apart of what better men had built rather than the getting of anything new. The twelfth man out, a boy not yet twenty named Aonghas Dubh, carried up the last lamp used on the face, and stood at the cage door with it in his hand and looked about him for someone to hand it to, the way a lamp was always handed on at the end of a shift to whoever waited to go down next; and there was no one. The next shift had not been called, because there would be no next shift, and the boy stood there with the lamp until Gilleasbaig Ruadh, without a word, took it from him and hung it on the rack himself, in its place, where it stayed unlit.

Tormod watched that and said nothing for a long while, though of everything he saw that winter it was the thing he spoke of oftenest, to Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's clerk among others, when the guild's own end came to be written down. He had seen pits close before, in his years as master, and had always thought the worst of it was the wages stopped and the families scattered; he had not before stood at a pit-head and seen a lamp with nowhere to go.

"There'll be work," Gilleasbaig Ruadh said, when the last man was up and the cage stood empty and swinging a little in the shaft-draught. "Comhairle nam Mèinnean says it. The river landing wants hands for the tanks, and the boats at Cill ghlas are hiring, some of them."

"Some of them," Tormod said.

"It's not nothing."

"No," Tormod said. "It is not nothing. I did not say it was nothing." He looked back at the pit-head, at the winding gear standing idle over the black mouth of the shaft, at the rain running off the roof of the engine-house where no engine now turned. "I have watched three pits close in my time as master, Gilleasbaig, and I have made the same speech at each of them, and each time it has been a smaller speech than the last, because there were fewer men to hear it. There is no speech left in me for this one. I am only glad I came."

## IV. Of the Walk to Seann Toll

Comhairle nam Mèinnean's word was that the families who remained at Muileann dhearg, some forty households by then, the rest having gone south or to the works before them in the years the pit had been failing, would be found places at Seann Toll on the Abhainn uaine, some five miles off by the river road, where Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's tanks and the dubhan works along the landing were taking on hands as fast as the river towns could send them. No cart was sent for the families' goods, Comhairle nam Mèinnean's letter having spoken of places found and said nothing of a removal paid for, and it was Tormod, hearing of it at the pit-head that same wet morning, who went from door to door in the pit quarter through the rest of that day and the next to say that the guild, though it had next to nothing left to give, would find carts for what could not be carried on a back, and that he would walk the road with them himself.

They went on the third day of an t-Samhain, forty households in a straggling line along the river road, with what they could carry and what four hired carts could hold besides, the children walking or riding on the carts by turns, the old carried when they must be. It was five miles, but the road was wet the whole way and the carts slow in the mud, and it took them from first light until well past dark. Tormod walked the whole of it, though Gilleasbaig Ruadh offered him a seat on a cart more than once and was refused each time, on the grounds, which he gave once and would not repeat, that a master who could not walk the road his people were walking had no business calling himself their master.

Seann Toll took them in without much ceremony. The town had land enough on its edge, low ground by the river that flooded in the worst winters and had never been built on for that reason, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean, which owned the land, had begun a row of houses there against just such a removal. They were not finished; the families lay that winter in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's sheds by the landing and went into the row as each house was roofed, the last of them in the high summer after. They were plain slate-roofed houses in a single street with a well at either end, no different in their building from the rows at Muileann chrom save that the walls were thinner and the chimneys smoked worse in a south wind. The town's own people, who called every new thing by the plainest name that came to hand, called it Sreath nan Gualadairean before the last house was roofed, and the name held, and within the year it was the only name anyone used for it, in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own letters as much as in the town's mouth.

Few of the families found work on the river, as Gilleasbaig Ruadh had hoped. The boatmen of Seann Toll were their own close trade, river-bred for generations, and took on outsiders slowly if at all; two or three of the younger men were hired as deck hands over that winter and no more. Most went instead to the dubhan tanks at the landing, where the works wanted hands to roll barrels and mind the pumps and needed no river craft to do it, only a strong back and a willingness to learn a trade that had not existed when they were born. It was, as more than one of them said afterwards, not so different from the pit in the way it used a man, though the coal it moved was not coal and did not come up out of the ground under their own town.

Tormod did not stay at Seann Toll past the first fortnight, his guild's business calling him elsewhere and his chest not standing the damp of the river well, but he came back twice more that winter to see how the row did, and it was on the second of those visits, walking the street with Gilleasbaig Ruadh in a hard frost, that he said the thing Eachann mac Ruairidh, hearing it that same winter from the coach guard, turned over and came at last to understand.

"I keep thinking of the lamp," Tormod said. "The boy with nowhere to hand it. I have turned it over all winter and I think now it was not the pit closing that undid me at the pit-head. Pits close; I have seen it before and lived through the seeing. It was that there was no one coming down to take the lamp from him. A trade can lose its work and still be a trade, so long as the work is only gone for a season, or gone from one place and waiting in another. What I saw that morning was a trade with nowhere left for the work to go at all. The landlord on the north road who will not light his rooms with the new stuff — I heard of him this summer, and I thought him a fool, holding to an old thing out of pride. I think differently of him now. There is no trade left in his hands to hold together. He keeps one lamp lit that he need not, because somewhere in him he cannot bear to be the last man in the house who does not."

Gilleasbaig Ruadh had no answer to that, and did not try to make one, and the two men walked on down the frozen street of Sreath nan Gualadairean in silence, past the well and the first roofed houses, where forty households were to live that had not lived in that place a year before, until they came to the landing where the dubhan tanks stood in a row on their stone piers, and the river ran black and cold beneath them, going down, as it had always gone down, to the sea.

## V. Of the Druid House Left Standing

Above the emptied pit quarter of Muileann dhearg, on the rise where the winding gear could still be seen from the moor road, stood the druid house that had served the pit families since the town was young, a low building of the same grey stone as the pit-head, with its own small burial ground behind it running back toward the moor. When the last households went down the river road to Seann Toll, the house went neither with them nor into Comhairle nam Mèinnean's keeping, but to a caretaker, an old man named Pàdraig Iarna who had swept its floor and rung its bell for thirty years and had no family left in any of the towns the pit had scattered its people to.

Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean, which held the charge of such houses as had lost their congregations, wrote to say that a teacher would come once a year to give what lecture the empty quarter still had ears for, and did come, in the autumn after, a young man who found four old people and Pàdraig Iarna himself waiting in the cold hall and spoke to them for the better part of an hour on a text none of them had chosen and none of them afterwards could say they remembered. He did not come oftener than once a year after that, there being little in the empty quarter to draw him back sooner, and the house stood the rest of each year with its door locked and its bell silent, kept only by the old man's daily round, the graves behind it tended as they had always been tended, the town below it going about its business at Seann Toll with no more thought for the hill than the hill, in its long patience, seemed to ask of it.

Eachann mac Ruairidh never went to Muileann dhearg himself, that year or any year after, his own road running the other way along Slighe a' Ghuail to the capital and back; but he carried the tale of it, as the yard carried every such tale sooner or later, in the guard's telling and in Tormod's own words repeated at secondhand, and he thought of it, when he thought of it at all, alongside the nine cold engines standing in the grass of the long siding at Muileann chrom, each of them waiting, as the lamp at Muileann dhearg had waited on its rack, for a hand that was not coming to take them up again.

# Chapter Thirteen: Of a Name that Went before the Fuel

*DE 11 – 13*

## I. Of the Slip-box

Sìleas nic Rath came to an Leabharlann in the wet spring of the eleventh year of Linn an Dubhain, a niece of a copyist at Àth dhìreach with a fair hand and no family living close enough to keep her from a post so far up the valley. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh had asked the council for a clerk three times in as many years and been answered twice with silence and once with a letter regretting that the office's charge did not run to it; in the end it was Raghnall mac Mhuirich who found the money, out of the keeper's own small fund for binding, and told the council afterwards rather than before. Sìleas was two-and-thirty that spring, narrow-shouldered, quick with a pen, and she arrived at the old building on a wet Tuesday with a single box tied with string and a letter of introduction she never had cause to show, because Beathag met her at the door before she had raised her hand to knock.

"You'll want dry stockings before anything else," Beathag said, and that was the whole of her welcome, and Sìleas took it for kindness, which it was.

She was set, that first month, to nothing grander than copying the shires' returns into the year's ledger in a hand the council's clerks could read without complaint, work any careful child could have done and few had the patience for; but she had, from the second week, a habit of her own that nobody had asked of her and nobody thought to stop. She kept, in a cigar-box begged from Ailig mac Thormoid, who had no more use for it than she had for the cigars that had come in it, a set of slips, one to a scrap of paper, on which she wrote down every spelling she met of the word that was now on every second letter that came up the library road.

There was no one spelling to meet. The council's own minute, the autumn before, had set it down twice in two lines as *dubhan* and *dùbhan*, the second with the grave accent moved a place, as though the clerk who wrote it had not been certain where the weight of the word should fall and had guessed twice rather than once. A letter from the maor of Cathair mhòr wrote it *dùban*, dropping the h entirely, which Sìleas thought at first a slip of the pen until she found it done the same way three letters running from the same clerk's hand, and understood it for a settled habit rather than an accident. Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's own minute-book, which came up twice a year for an Leabharlann's copying, wrote it once, in an t-Ògmhios of that year, as *An Dubhan*, with the article and a capital letter, as though the word had become, in that one entry, less a kind of fuel and more a name for a thing there was only one of; and a fortnight later, in the same book and the same clerk's hand, it went back to the small letter and no article, as though the writer himself had thought better of it, or simply forgotten what he had done a fortnight before.

"It's not the spelling that wants marking," Beathag said, the first time she found Sìleas at the box after the day's copying was done, sorting slips by the little pile they made rather than by any order a stranger could have followed. "Any fool can misspell a word. It's that they're spelling it at all, and not the man's name. Read me the maor's letter again — the one from Cathair mhòr, in am Faoilleach."

Sìleas found it and read: "'The price of dùban at the fair here has held above the coal ceiling the court set for it, there being no ceiling yet set for dùban, the court holding it no fuel of the old kind and so no matter for the old order.'"

"There," Beathag said. "A year ago that letter would have said Dubhan's fuel, or the black stuff a Tuathach makes, or some such circling of a thing the writer had no settled word for. Now it has a word, and the word has parted from his name. He is going out of the sentence, the way a man's name goes out of a coin once the coin has been struck long enough. I want every letter marked, from now, the first time it happens in each hand, so we can say when. I don't think why is a thing that can be dated."

Sìleas kept the box faithfully after that, and by the time the box would hold no more slips without a second box beside it, which was some time in the fourteenth year and so beyond the telling of this chapter, she had marked the turn in forty-one hands out of the sixty or so that wrote regularly to an Leabharlann, each at its own month, none of them together, as though the word had come up out of the ground in a hundred kitchens and market squares at once and needed no one to carry it from one to the next.

She wrote her own small note at the front of the box, in the careful hand she kept for anything she thought might one day be read by someone other than Beathag, saying only what the box held and by whose asking; and under it, because she could not quite stop herself, a line that was hers alone and went into no ledger: that a word which does not need a man's name behind it any longer has become, whatever the court of the fair or the council's minute chooses to call it, a thing of its own. Beathag, finding the note some weeks later while looking for a slip out of order, read it twice, put it back exactly as she had found it, and never said a word to Sìleas about it at all, which Sìleas took, rightly, for the nearest thing to praise the chronicler knew how to give a clerk not yet three months in her post.

## II. Of the Letter from Caol shean

In the same spring a letter came from Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean, addressed to Raghnall mac Mhuirich as keeper and copied, by his own note in the margin, to Beathag as chronicler, because it concerned, the school's letter said, a matter an Leabharlann might in time wish to have on its shelves rather than in a schoolman's private word.

The school at Caol shean had long been near empty for the better part of two generations, its halls built for three hundred pupils and holding, in most years since the humans' time, fewer than forty; and the letter, which ran to four close-written pages before it came to its point, spoke first and at some length of the school's own poor fortunes before it turned to the matter at hand, in the manner the letter itself called an old habit of scholars, of saying the discouraging thing before the useful one, so that the useful one should not be mistaken for good news undeserved.

The point, when it came, was a word. The school's masters, discussing among themselves — the letter did not say over what occasion, though Sìleas guessed, reading it aloud to Beathag by the window that afternoon, that it had been over supper, there being a lightness to the sentence that no committee minute ever carried — had found themselves in want of a word for a particular kind of thing: an attempt that looked, at the time it was made, like one more failure among many, and proved afterwards, when nothing else had come of the years around it, to have been the one attempt that mattered. The masters had turned the word over among themselves for the school's own case, which had tried and failed at a dozen small revivals over the generations and did not yet know, the letter said with what Sìleas took for a schoolman's dry honour, whether its own latest effort at taking pupils again would prove another failure or the one that held; and out of that turning they had made, from the old root for a first working and the word the north now used for the fuel, a single coined term: *dubhan-tùsail*, a first-attempt-that-was-the-one, which they offered to an Leabharlann, the letter said, for one reason alone: that a word made in a small room ought to be sent somewhere it might be kept even if it was never used.

"They want it in the record," Raghnall said, when Sìleas brought it to him. He turned the page over, as though the back of it might have more to say than the front. "For a word about their own school."

"They want it kept," Sìleas said. "I don't think they much care whether it's used."

Raghnall looked at her a moment, the way a man looks at someone who has said, without meaning to, a truer thing than he had said himself. "No," he said. "I expect that's exactly it." He copied the word into the day's page in his own hand, under the entry that had already noted the letter's coming, and did not use it again that year in anything he wrote. It sat on in an Leabharlann's word-list where he had set it, unused and uncorrected, the one entry on that page that nobody troubled to strike or to build upon.

## III. Of the Line and the Coal Line

Up at Muileann chrom the next year Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's own minute-book, the one Sìleas had marked for its wandering article, was making a smaller change than any word of Dubhan's, and one that touched Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own name for its own road.

The line from the capital to An Sloc Mòr had been called, since it was laid, Slighe a' Ghuail, in every timetable Comhairle nam Mèinnean had printed and every mouth that used it; and in the spring of the twelfth year Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerks, drawing up the new season's card, printed it for the first time as only *an t-slighe*, the line, with no coal in it at all. Nobody at Comhairle nam Mèinnean wrote to say why, and no order that Sìleas ever found in the returns explained the change; the timetable simply came up to an Leabharlann in an Cèitean with the old name gone from its own cover, though every entry inside it still spoke, as it always had, of trains and hours and the fare by the mile.

It made no difference to anyone who rode the thing. The drivers at Muileann chrom, who had never in living memory called their road anything but Slighe a' Ghuail, went on calling it that in the yard and at their own firesides, whatever Comhairle nam Mèinnean's printer set on the card; and the carriers who used the road, and the farmers whose fields it ran through, and the clerks at Cathair dhearg who booked freight on it, all went on saying coal line as they always had, so that within the year Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own new name existed nowhere but on the printed cards themselves, a name with no mouth to carry it, while the old name it had tried to set aside went on being spoken by everyone who had any daily business with the road at all.

Beathag, reading the new timetable when it came up with the spring's papers, laughed once, shortly, and set it on the pile with the rest.

"They can print what they like," she said. "A road keeps the name the men on it give it, not the name Comhairle nam Mèinnean puts on the card. I'd sooner trust the drivers." She looked at Sìleas over the pile. "Mark that too, if you're marking such things. Not the word for the fuel this time. The word for what the fuel is taking away."

## IV. Of the Last Roll

Comann nan Gualadairean dissolved itself in an Cèitean of the twelfth year, in the hall it rented at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr above Cuan chrom, by a vote its own last minute recorded as unanimous among the eleven masters who came to cast it, out of a roll that had once numbered more than sixty.

Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, who had been master eleven years and buried, by his own reckoning given at the pit-head at Muileann dhearg the autumn before, more of the trade than he had ever bound to it, brought the guild's last goods to an Leabharlann himself, on a hired cart, in the first week of an t-Iuchar: its rolls of binding going back to the guild's chartering in the early years of the restored custom, its sick-roll, thin now, with the names of the last dozen hewers it still paid a shilling a week to for the black cough that had ended most of their working lives, and the oath-stone itself, a flat grey block no bigger than a hearthstone, worn smooth on its upper face where two generations of thumbs had rested while a boy or a girl swore the guild's old words over it, words that had promised, among other things, that the swearer would never cut coal for any hand but the guild's own and would die, if it came to dying, with the guild's black on their own.

Sìleas met the cart in the yard and signed for the goods herself, Beathag having gone that week to Àth dhìreach to see her sister, who was unwell; and it was to Sìleas, not to the chronicler she had come to see, that Tormod handed the rolls one by one, naming each as he gave it over, as though a thing so long kept ought not to change hands without at least that much ceremony.

He was three days coming, and had stopped, she guessed from the mud on his coat, more than once on the road to rest a chest that no longer let him ride a full day without it; but he would not sit while the goods were handed over, and stood the whole of the unloading with his hat off in the rain, though she asked him twice to come in out of it and wait by the fire in the porters' room while the men carried the heavier things.

"I've stood at worse handings-over than this," he said, when she asked a third time. "I'll stand at this one too, and then I'll come in, and gladly."

"You'll want a receipt," Sìleas said, when the cart was empty, and felt the word wrong in her mouth as she said it, a thing too small for what had just been handed over.

"I want nothing of the kind," Tormod said. "I want it kept, and I want it said, when anyone asks, that it came here whole and not begged for. That's receipt enough for me." He looked at the oath-stone, which stood now on the yard's flagstones between them, too heavy for either of them to have carried far alone, waiting for the two men Raghnall had sent down to bring it in. "I've sworn eleven masters on that stone in my time, and had eleven sworn on it themselves before that. I don't know what it's for now, in a room with nobody to swear on it. But it oughtn't to be broken up for a doorstep, which is what would happen to it at Achadh dhomhain inside five years, now the hall's sold."

He gave her, last of all, a single folded letter, addressed to no one in particular, which he asked her to see copied into an Leabharlann's record rather than filed loose among the guild's other papers, because he said he had written it to be read, not kept.

Sìleas read it that evening, by the last light at her own small desk in the room she had been given off the old building's stair, and copied it herself into the day's page before Beathag came home, in a hand as close to Beathag's own settled hand as she could make it, because it seemed to her, reading it, a thing that should sit in the record as though the chronicler herself had taken it down. It was not a long letter. It said, among lesser things about what the sale of the hall had fetched and the disposal of what small funds remained, that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience; that a trade bound to a thing in the ground could not outlast the vein by more than a generation or two of pretending otherwise, and that the guild, in dissolving itself before it was dissolved by want, had done the one dignified thing left to it to do.

Beathag read the copied page the morning after she came back from Àth dhìreach, standing at the window with the light behind her the way she always stood to read anything she meant to think hard about, and said nothing for a long while.

"You copied it well," she said at last.

"I tried to make it sound as you would have made it sound."

"You made it sound as he made it sound, which is better." Beathag folded the page back into the ledger and set the ledger on the pile with the others. "There's not a hedging word in the whole of it. Most men, writing the end of a thing they'd given their life to, would have found some way to say it wasn't really ending, or asked to be remembered for it, or promised better days for it yet. He didn't trouble himself with any of that. He said the thing was over and gave the reason and stopped." She looked at Sìleas a moment. "That's a rarer gift than you'd think, in a chronicler's clerk as much as in a guild master. Keep it, when your own time comes to write things down."

## V. Of the Bath-house below Muileann ruadh

Among the guild's smaller goods, listed at the foot of Tormod's own inventory almost as an afterthought, was a bath-house the hewers had built two generations before over Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh, for the ease of men whose chests the coal-dust had ruined; a low stone building over three basins fed straight from the ground at a heat no fire needed to raise, kept by an old woman of the town on the guild's small wage and open, until that year, to none but hewers and their families on the guild's own card.

The house passed, with the rest of the guild's holding, to the custodians of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail at the southern Seann Skell, the guild having named no other body fit to take a charge it could no longer keep; and the custodians, who owned already the greater bath-houses of the south coast and had never had much use for a small one so far inland, opened it that same summer to any who could pay the old woman's modest fee, hewer's card or none.

It was in an Lùnastal of that year, by the letter the keeper of the house sent up to an Leabharlann at Raghnall's own asking, that a Tuathach family came to the basins for the first time in the house's history: a woman of Doire ghlas, brought south by a married daughter for a chest complaint the northern doctors had no more to offer against, and the daughter's own two children, who had never in their lives been let past the door of any house of the old faith on any errand at all. The keeper's letter said only that she had taken the woman's coin, which was good coin and no different from any other, and shown her to the basin as she would have shown anyone, and that the woman had stayed the better part of an hour and come out saying something to her daughter in a tongue the keeper knew nothing of, though she took it for thanks by the way it was said, and it made the daughter laugh and put an arm round her mother's shoulders in the cold of the yard outside.

"She asked no leave of the custodians," Raghnall said, reading the letter to Beathag and Sìleas both, "and none was asked of her. I don't know that either side thought of it as a thing needing leave at all. The water doesn't know whose chest it's easing."

"Write it down as she wrote it," Beathag said. "Not a word more."

## VI. Of the Damp at Seann Toll

Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh did not long survive the guild he had dissolved. His own chest, which had troubled him for a dozen years before that summer and troubled him worse after it, kept him from the road for most of the autumn that followed; but in am Faoilleach of the thirteenth year, against the plain advice of a doctor at Cathair mhòr who told him a river town in winter was the worst place a man with his cough could choose to visit, he went down once more to Seann Toll, to see, he told the doctor, how Sreath nan Gualadairean did in its first hard frost, and would hear no argument against it.

He was three days at the Row, by Gilleasbaig Ruadh's own account sent up afterwards to an Leabharlann at Beathag's asking, walking the frozen street each morning as he had walked it the winter before, and taking, on the third evening, a fever that settled in his chest within a day and would not lift. Gilleasbaig sent for the nearest doctor, who was at Muileann chrom, half a day off by the river road in the worst of the weather, and sat with him himself through the two nights that came between the sending and the doctor's arrival, in a house of the Row no better built than any other, with a single dubhan lamp burning low on the sill because the fire, Gilleasbaig's letter said, gave less heat than the lamp and Tormod had asked, more than once in his wandering, that the lamp be kept lit and the fire let go out, though he never said why and Gilleasbaig never asked.

He died a little before dawn on the sixth day of an Gearran, in the Row he had walked his people into, among people who were no longer, by any charter, his to answer for. Gilleasbaig Ruadh's letter, which reached an Leabharlann a fortnight later, the river road being what it was in that season, said only that he had gone quietly, that he had spoken little in the last day beyond asking twice after the oath-stone's safekeeping and being told, both times, that it was safe; and that the Row had buried him themselves, in the ground at the edge of the flood-plain that Seann Toll kept for those it had no older claim on, because there was no guild left to claim him and no family near enough to send for in the time the weather allowed.

Beathag entered his death in the day's page herself, in her own hand, the last entry Sìleas ever saw her make without asking the clerk to make it first and copy it after; and she wrote beside the bare date, which was all the entry strictly needed, the one line from his own letter that Sìleas had copied the summer before, that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience, and under it, in a hand smaller than her usual hand, as though she had thought better of writing it large: that he had not.

The hall at Achadh dhomhain, which the guild had sold before it dissolved itself, changed its trade on 1 am Màrt, DE 13, three weeks after he was buried. Its buyer, a dealer of the town, had the long room cleared of its benches and set two dubhan pumps in the doorway where the masters had once come in to sit, and a tank in the yard behind; and because the lintel over the door was one great stone, and cutting it out would have brought the front of the house down with it, the lintel stayed where it was, with the guild's oath cut into it in letters a hand high, above the pumps. The carters who filled their barrels there read it every time they looked up, those who could read, and the ones who could not had it read to them once and did not ask again.

# Chapter Fourteen: Of the Charter Rule

*DE 13 – 14*

## I. Of the House of Mac Ùisdein

The stone house at Cathair mhòr had been built, four generations back, of the spoil of An Sloc Mòr: grey rubble from the tips that no mason would otherwise have troubled to dress, hauled up from Achadh dhomhain on An Crùn's own carts because the first Mac Ùisdein to hold the concession had wanted it said that his hall was built of the very stuff that paid for it. It was said still, by anyone who wanted to flatter the house, and by a good many who did not.

Coinneach mac Ùisdein sat in that hall in am Màrt of the thirteenth year with the pit's returns open on the table before him and did not need his clerk to tell him what they meant. He had read An Sloc Mòr's returns every quarter of his life since he was old enough to be shown the ledgers, first at his grandfather's knee and then at his father's, and he knew the shape a failing seam took on a page before he knew what most of the words on it were for: fewer tons at greater cost, more days lost to water, a gallery abandoned here, a face condemned there, and under it all the same steady, patient arithmetic that had been eating the house's fortune for thirty years and showed no sign of tiring of the meal.

"How much is left in it," he said, not as a question, to the clerk who had brought the returns.

"A fifth of what it gave in your grandfather's day, sir. Less, this last twelvemonth."

"And An Crùn's share still comes off the top before ours."

"It does, sir. It always has."

Coinneach closed the ledger. He was a broad, unhurried man of five-and-forty who had never in his life cut coal or gone down a shaft, and whose whole knowledge of An Sloc Mòr was the knowledge of a man who owns a horse he has never ridden: he knew its habits, its ailments, its cost, and nothing else. His grandfather Alasdair had borrowed against the house's share to meet its debts in a bad year and never fully paid the loan off; his father had sold half the share outright to An Crùn rather than see the whole house go under with it. Coinneach had grown up hearing both transactions spoken of at table as wounds the house had suffered and survived, and he had grown up, too, hearing his father say, more than once and always at the end of a long evening, that a house too proud to sell the rest when the time came would end by having nothing left to sell at all.

He thought the time had come. He did not think it with any great grief, which surprised him a little when he noticed it in his own chest; he had expected to feel the weight of four generations when he finally sat down to write the letter, and instead he felt mostly the relief of a man setting down a sack he has carried a long way past the point of needing it.

Even so, he gave the matter a week more than it needed, out of respect for his father's memory rather than any doubt of his own mind, and spent part of that week walking the tip-heaps above Achadh dhomhain with the clerk who had brought him the returns, looking at ground he had inherited a right to and never once in his life had reason to stand on before. The heaps were higher than he remembered from his grandfather's telling of them, grey and terraced, with a thin scurf of gorse taking on the older slopes where the spoil had lain undisturbed longest; a boy with a barrow was picking over the newest tip for lumps still black enough to burn in a poor man's grate, and looked up at the two strangers in good coats without much curiosity and went back to his picking.

Coinneach wrote to Comhairle nam Mèinnean offering what remained of the house's share in An Sloc Mòr's spoil and quarry, the stone-cutting and the tip-rights that had come down with the coal, at a price he judged fair and expected to be haggled down from. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's answer came inside a month and haggled him down by less than he had expected; Comhairle nam Mèinnean, he understood without being told, was glad to have the whole of a great pit in its own hand at last, and had no wish to argue long over the last piece of it. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerks took the summer over the papers, and the sale was signed at Cathair mhòr on 4 an t-Sultain, DE 13, with two witnesses and a fee to Cùirt na Fèille, and Coinneach mac Ùisdein put what it brought him, and a good part of what the house had besides, into an account with the shipmasters at Ros dhomhain, against the building of three dubhan hulls.

He rode down to see the first of them on her slip in an Dàmhair: a coastal trader of the middling size, her ribs up and her planking half on, smelling of new pitch and sawdust in a yard that smelled of nothing else for a quarter mile around. The master shipwright walked him round her twice and answered his questions plainly, in the way of a man who has been asked the same questions by a great many new owners that year and does not resent it yet.

"She'll carry dubhan or anything else you like," the shipwright said. "The tank sits amidships, out of the way of cargo, and she'll do without it besides, burning wood in the old grate if it ever came to that, though I don't know why it would." He looked at Coinneach a moment. "Your house held coal a long time, I hear."

"It did," said Coinneach.

"And now hulls."

"Now hulls." Coinneach put his hand on the new wood of her side, which was still rough where the adze had left it. "The coal held us as long as it had anything to hold us with. I'd sooner move the house's money before the seam moves it for me."

The shipwright nodded, as if this were the most ordinary thing in the world, which by that year it very nearly was.

## II. Of the Bridge at Cathair dhearg

Coinneach had come up to the capital that summer, while the sale was still in the clerks' hands, to see them about its paperwork, and found the road changed since his last visit two years before. A dubhan bus now ran between Cathair dhearg and Inis mhòr twice a day, a long closed carriage on iron-shod wheels with a driver's box at the front and benches down each side inside, and it went the eleven miles in under an hour where the old coach had taken the better part of the morning. Another line ran out to Cathair mhòr itself, his own town, though he had come up by his own horse this time and had not thought to look for it at the bridge.

The word for the thing, he noticed, was not a Dia-thìris word at all. Men called it *bus*, flat and short, the same sound the humans of an Tìr Thall were said to use for it in their own tongue, and nobody troubled to find another. There had been words made, in the early years of the fuel, for the engine and for the trains that ran on Slighe a' Ghuail and now the dubhan tanks beside it, careful compounds out of old roots that Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerks were proud enough of. The bus and the hired car that waited for a fare at the foot of the bridge, its driver leaning on the door with his cap pushed back, had come into the tongue with their humans' names still on them, the way a thing arrives faster than the word-makers can catch up to it. *Tacsaidh*, the hired car was called, and the men who drove them took the name for themselves as well, and neither word troubled anyone enough to be replaced.

Coinneach stood at the foot of the bridge a while, watching the bus load. Six passengers went up the step, a basket of hens tied under one of the benches, a woman with a child on her knee paying her fare in coin new enough that Coinneach could see, when she opened her purse, that it still bore the coal-inked seal. He thought that the change he had made in his own house's fortune was a small thing set against the change the whole kingdom was making around him: a bus line and a hired car and a word borrowed rather than coined, none of it decreed by anyone, all of it happening because it was easier than not happening.

The coal caste of the capital, the old families who had held the mines and the mine-rights since the first grants, said nothing that anyone troubled to write down. Coinneach knew a dozen of them by name, had sat at table with half of them, and heard from none of them any word of complaint at the bus or the tacsaidh or the fuel that ran them; the ones who still held a working seam held their tongues because the pits still paid, however little, and the ones whose seams were spent, like his own family's, had for the most part already begun doing what he had done, quietly, each house in its own time, none of them wishing to be first and none, now, minded to be last.

## III. Of the Court of the Sea

He was at Ros dhomhain in that same autumn, when the first of his hulls had her engine in, and watched her go off on a trial, a short coasting run to Cuan shean and back with a cargo of nothing more than barrels of dubhan for the harbour lamps, and stayed to watch the kingdom's own patrol boats put out on the same tide.

They had been refitted that summer, the whole small fleet of them, and it showed in the way they took the harbour mouth: quicker off the mark than Coinneach remembered patrol boats ever being, with none of the labouring plume of smoke a coal-fired hull threw up, and gone round the headland almost before the gulls that always followed a boat out had settled which one to follow. A harbour-master's clerk, standing near Coinneach on the quay with nothing better to do than talk to a stranger, said they had run down two raider hulks that same month that would have got clean away from them the year before.

"Never used to catch them," the clerk said. "Coal boat's slower off the mark and slower to answer the helm both, and by the time she's got up her head of steam the raider's half over the horizon. These new ones are away before he's well started."

Both hulks, taken under tow, lay at the harbour wall when Coinneach walked down that way in the evening. Their crews lay the winter in the town's gaol, for Cùirt na Mara sat only at midsummer; and in an t-Iuchar of the fourteenth year, when Coinneach came down again to see his second hull launched, the court sat on them in the long room above the customs house, a room Coinneach had been in once or twice before on his own house's business and never for anything so grave. He went in out of curiosity more than anything else, and found the room fuller than he had expected: the raiders' trial was, that year, still enough of a novelty — the fleet's new speed being novel, and the catching of two crews in a month being novel with it — that half the town's idle men had come to watch.

There were eleven of the two crews together, ragged, salt-marked, answering the magistrate in a mixture of tongues that his clerk translated as it came. The oldest of them, a scarred man who gave his name as Callum of no fixed harbour, said through the clerk that he had followed the raiding trade twenty years and had never before this season had a boat of An Crùn come up on him faster than his own could run, and said it, Coinneach thought, less as a confession than as a kind of professional complaint, the grievance of a man whose trade has changed under him without his leave. Three of the eleven, it came out in the course of the morning, were Tuathaich, taken on for the voyage at some northern harbour for want of better work and knowing, by their own account, nothing of where the boat's takings were meant to go once she had them. One of the three, a boy who could not have been past sixteen, wept through most of his own questioning and had to be told twice to speak up, until the magistrate, not unkindly, said there was no need of him to speak at all if the other two would answer for him, which they did.

The magistrate heard the whole of it out at length, conferred with his own clerk over a paper Coinneach could not see, and in the end hanged none of the eleven: he sent the eight Dia-thìrich among them to the quarries at Achadh dhomhain, the same quarries whose stone had built the house Coinneach had grown up in, and told the three Tuathaich, the boy among them, that they were free to find their own way home, north, by whatever road would have them, and that the court had no charge to hold against a man for want of choosing better company to sail in.

Coinneach watched the three go out of the room together, saying nothing to each other or to anyone, and thought it an odd smallness of the world that the sentence on the guilty should send eight men to break the stone his own family had lived four generations off, in the same season his own family's money had gone the other way, into hulls that had helped catch the men now sentenced to break it. He turned the thought over once, the way a man turns a coin he has found in the road, and put it away with the rest of the day's business, and rode home to Cathair mhòr well pleased with his hulls.

## IV. Of the Chartering at Seann Skell

Peigi nic Ascaill had been master-fitter at the shipmasters' works for seven years by the summer Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail were chartered, and she had known the charter was coming, in the way anyone in the trade had known it, for the better part of a year before it came. Comann nan Sciobairean had wanted it: a guild of its own, rolls that could bind an apprentice and set a wage and keep a bad fitter's name off any yard's books, the ordinary machinery of a trade grown too large to run any longer on a handful of masters' say-so. Every craft in the kingdom that had ever grown large enough to need binding had ended, sooner or later, chartered; nobody at the works had thought the fitters would be different, and nobody was much surprised, in the spring, when word came that An Crùn had granted it.

What surprised Peigi, though she told herself afterwards that it should not have, was the single clause near the foot of the grant that fixed the rolls to Dia-thìrich alone.

She read it three times at her desk in the works' office before she understood that she had not misread it the first time. It was not a new kind of clause; every guild chartered in her lifetime carried some version of it, Comann nan Gualadairean before their own dissolving, Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's drivers, the masons, the smiths; she had simply never before had cause to read one with her own hand about to be asked to enforce it. She sat with the letter a long while after she had finished reading it, and then she did what she had always done with a hard thing since she was a girl learning her trade under men who thought a woman had no business at a lathe: she got up and went to see it done, because putting it off would not make it easier and might make it worse.

The chartering itself was held at the southern Seann Skell on 29 an Lùnastal, DE 14, in the works' own long shed with its doors thrown open to the harbour for air, before a clerk of An t-Ionmhas sent down from the capital to read the grant and a custodian of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail to bless the guild's new banner, a black swan on grey. Twelve masters were sworn that day, Peigi among the first six called, and she said the words of the oath — to bind no hand outside the roll, to teach the trade truly to those admitted to it, to answer to the guild's own court for any fault in her own work or her apprentices' — in a clear voice that did not shake, because she had decided beforehand that it would not, whatever else happened that day.

What happened that day, for the men she had brought south from Caol mhòr seven years before, was that their names could not go on the roll being read at the same hour in the same shed, and every man in the yard who had worked beside them for those seven years knew it without needing to be told twice.

She found Joe Ashby that evening at the forge where he had a room, sitting on the step with his tools laid out on a cloth beside him, already half packed though the chartering was not four hours old.

"You'll have heard," she said.

"I heard it read." He did not look up from the wrench he was wrapping. "Sworn among Dia-thìrich only. It's plain enough. I've heard plainer things put worse."

"I argued it, Joe. Before the grant went up, and again this spring when I knew it was coming. I went to the company's masters and I told them what losing you and Ned and Abel would cost the works, in plain trade terms, because I judged that was the argument likelier to move them than any other, and I was wrong that it would move them at all." She stood in the doorway with her hand on the frame, not coming further in, as though she had not decided whether she had the right to. "I'm a master of the guild that's put you out of the yard. I don't know how to say that to you in any way that makes it smaller than it is."

"Don't, then," said Joe. "Say the other thing you came to say."

She had a purse in her coat pocket, which she had counted out herself that afternoon rather than leave it to the works' clerk, and she set it down on the step beside him. "A month's wage over what's owed you. For all three of you, the same. It's the company's money by rights, not the guild's, and I got it out of them by telling them it was cheaper than the trouble of a bad name up and down this coast, which is also true, though it isn't why I asked for it."

Joe looked at the purse and did not touch it for a moment. "Why did you ask for it, then."

"Because I fitted a burner beside you for two winters before either of us had a guild to answer to, and I don't know how else to say I haven't forgotten that, since the guild I've just sworn into won't let me say it in the only way that would mean anything, which is keeping you on." She said it fast, in one breath, the way a person says a thing they have rehearsed and are afraid of losing their nerve over before the end of it. "I know a month's wage isn't that."

"No," Joe said. "It isn't." He picked up the purse, weighed it once in his hand, and put it in his coat. "I'll take it, because it's owed and because Ned's got a debt at the smith's that wants clearing before we go, and pride's a poor thing to leave a debt unpaid for. But I'll tell you plainly, since you've been plain with me: I'd sooner you hadn't come tonight at all than come and stand in that door and not come in."

Peigi did not come in. She stood a moment longer, and then she said, "I know," and went back up the yard to the office, where there was a night's paperwork waiting that she was, for once in her working life, glad of the excuse to lose herself in.

## V. Of the Boat without a Guild

Joe Ashby went home to Caol mhòr in the first days of an t-Sultain with the Fowler cousins beside him and Will Tanner's letter in his pocket, which had reached him at the works a fortnight before and said only that there was work at the harbour for any man who could still fit an engine, guild or no guild, and that Will had kept the room over his own boat-shed empty on the chance.

Caol mhòr's harbour had grown since Joe had left it seven years before: more dubhan hulls at the moorings than he remembered coal-burning boats ever standing there at once, and a new shed at the harbour's north end with a sign that named it, in the Dia-thìrich tongue only, a depot of the fleet's provisioning, though the men who worked it, Joe saw within a day, were Tuathaich to the last one, paid by the fleet and answering to no guild the fleet had ever heard of asking after.

He fitted his first engine at Caol mhòr inside the week, a small fishing boat belonging to a widow named Jean Fisher whose husband had drowned two winters before and who had been putting off the cost of a proper engine ever since on what a widow's share of a fishing boat brought in. Joe fitted it for less than the southern works would have charged and took his payment half in coin and half in fish, which he judged, correctly, would see him through the winter better than coin alone in a town where every boat had fish to spare and coin was the scarcer thing.

There was no guild roll to enter his name on, north of the boundary stones, and no guild court to answer to if a burner he fitted failed; there was, instead, the harbour, which knew within a season whose engines ran true and whose did not, and told it plainly enough in whose boat a man trusted his own family to. By the turn of the year Joe had fitted engines in eleven boats at Caol mhòr and two at Baile chrom, working from a bench in the corner of Will Tanner's shed with tools he had bought from the smith of Baile chrom who had once straightened Peigi's burner with him on the anvil, at a price the smith called fair and Joe suspected was less than fair, out of a kindness neither of them named.

Ned Fowler took work on the harbour depot's own boats, minding the pumps that filled the fleet's tanks, and his cousin Abel went further, out past the mill country to Muileann bheag, where Calum Bàn the keeper still remembered the four fitters of the rain-soaked week and put in a word that got Abel taken on to help a farmer mend a threshing engine none of the district's own smiths would touch. Will Tanner, who had never gone south at all, said to Joe more than once that winter that the works at Seann Skell had done the north an unintended kindness in casting its fitters back onto it, since the harbour now had, for the price of nothing, four men who could fit an engine to a standard the south's own guild would have been glad to swear by, and answered to no one for it but the boats they served.

He did not write to Peigi, and she did not write to him, though a letter did come that winter, forwarded from the assembly's house, from the master of the guild's court at Seann Skell, informing any who fitted a dubhan engine north of the boundary stones without the guild's leave that they did so at their own risk and without the guild's protection should the work fail. Joe read it once, by the light of the shed's single lamp, and pinned it to the wall above his bench, not out of defiance exactly, though it did the office of defiance well enough, but because Will Tanner said it would make good kindling for the winter and Joe found he did not want it burnt.

## VI. Of the Walk-Out

Tional nan Tuathach met at Caol mhòr on 24 an t-Samhain, DE 14, under Martha Greaves in her seventh year as speaker, to settle a question that had been put off, by common consent, through two summers of the fuel's spreading: whether the north should take the new fire up for its own use, as the south had, or hold to its own seams as long as those seams had anything left to give.

It was not, in the letter of the thing, much of a question by then. Half the roofs of Caol mhòr already burned dubhan lamps bought off the harbour depot, and the mill at Doire ghlas had run its winter looms on it two years running for want of coal cheap enough to buy from the south. What Tional nan Tuathach's vote settled was not whether the north would use the fuel, which it plainly already did, but whether it would say so, in its own minute-book, as a thing decided rather than a thing that had simply happened around everyone the way the bus and the tacsaidh had happened around Coinneach mac Ùisdein at the foot of the capital's bridge.

The delegates spoke through the better part of a short winter afternoon, the hall lit early against the failing light by dubhan lamps hung from the same beams that had once held tallow, which more than one speaker remarked on without needing to labour the point. When the vote was called near dusk it went eleven towns for taking the fuel up and five against, the five being the delegates of the western pit towns, whose own seams still worked, however poorly, and who had not come to Caol mhòr that day expecting to be outvoted by towns that had never cut coal in their lives.

It was among the five that a young woman stood to speak before the vote was carried, whom few in the hall had heard address Tional nan Tuathach before: Ruth Calder, sent that year in her father's stead from Àth leathan, where he still held the pit captain's place though his chest had kept him above ground since the winter before, and where she kept his books and did his business for him by no rule anyone could point to but the hewers' own custom.

She was not long on her feet. Tional nan Tuathach's own minute gave her, as it gave every delegate that day, no more than a line: that the western towns had cut coal for their own hearths and their neighbours' since before there was a Moot to vote on anything, and meant to go on doing it as long as the seams allowed, and did not ask Tional nan Tuathach's leave to do so, only its patience while they did. When the vote was carried against her she rose again, with the four other delegates of the five towns beside her, and walked out of the hall before the clerk had finished writing the count into the book, not in anger that anyone present could afterward describe as anger exactly, but in the manner of people who have said what they came to say and see no further use in staying to hear it argued over.

Martha Greaves let them go without calling after them, and said only, to the hall that remained, that the minute would show the five towns' dissent recorded and their delegates withdrawn, and that Tional nan Tuathach's granaries, whatever else the vote had settled, remained open to any household of the north that came to them hungry, coal-burning or dubhan-burning alike, and always would. A delegate of Doire ghlas asked her, once the hall had quieted, whether the granaries' word applied equally to a household of Àth leathan as to one of Caol mhòr, since the five towns had that day, in effect, declared themselves apart from the rest of Tional nan Tuathach's business. Martha answered that a hungry household was a hungry household in whatever town Tional nan Tuathach's charter covered, and that she did not propose to begin sorting granary sacks by how a man's delegate had voted, and the question was not put to her again that year.

The clerk wrote it down as Martha said it, word for word, and under it, in the day's last light before the lamps were trimmed for the evening, wrote the names of the five towns that had walked out, Àth leathan first among them, in a hand no different from the hand he had used for every other name in the book that year. Outside, in the yard, the five delegates stood a while by the lit windows before starting for the western road, none of them in any great hurry to begin the walk home in the dark, and it was there, by Ruth Calder's own later account, that Tom Varley of Cnoc thais said to her that she had spoken better than her father ever had, which she took, she said, for the kindest thing anyone said to her that whole hard year.

# Chapter Fifteen: Of the Fifteenth Year

*DE 15*

## I. Of the Northern Depots

The letter from Doire ghlas came up the library road in the last week of an Giblean, water-stained at one corner where the carrier had let his bag swing against a puddle, and Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh read it twice before she set it on the day's pile.

It was Martha Greaves's own hand, which had grown no neater in seven years of writing Cuimhne-coinneimh an Tionail and had, if anything, grown faster and less patient, so that whole words leaned into one another like men crowding a doorway out of the rain. A dubhan depot had opened that month at Doire ghlas, she wrote, supplied by sea from the south, and word had come the same week of two more, at Caol mhòr and at Ceann mhòr, both stocked from the same boats. The figures followed as Comhairle nam Mèinnean's agent had given them to her: so many casks a fortnight, so much a cask, a scale of credit for any household that could not pay outright and would work it off at the mill. All this she set down as a minute sets a thing down, plainly, one fact behind another, and then, at the foot of the page, in a line apart from the rest as though she had thought about it before she let herself write it, came what the minute did not ask her to say. *The north now buys its fire from the south. I do not say whether this is a good thing or a bad one. I say only that it is the case, and that it was not the case a year ago.*

Beathag copied the letter whole into the day's page, the figures first and Martha's own line last, exactly as it stood, and did not add a word of her own beneath it. She had learned, in her years at the desk, that some sentences wanted nothing added to them, and this was one; anything she might have said herself would only have blunted the plain fact Martha had already sharpened for her.

Doire ghlas she knew a little, from letters if from nothing else: a mill town on the north coast, its people Tuathaich of the old northern congregations, whose great church under the grey oaks the north calls the heart of its faith. She had never been there and did not expect now that she would be. It came to her plainly enough from Martha's figures all the same: the casks coming off a boat at a quay that had never before unloaded anything but wool and salted fish, a queue of townsfolk with their own carts and barrows, a clerk with a scale of credit written on a board because half of them could not pay outright and the mill would stand for them if they could not; and somewhere in the queue, an old man or an old woman remembering the coal fires their own fathers had burned, coal that had never once, in all the years of the kingdom, come north of the boundary stones to warm a Tuathach hearth, because the vein was the kingdom's and the north had never held any part of it. Now the north was buying fire it had made no part of either, only bought it from a different hand.

She wrote nothing of this in the record. The carrying of it belonged to Martha's own line, and Martha's line was enough.

Three days later a shorter note came up from Raghnall mac Mhuirich's own desk, though he sat not six feet from her own, because he had taken to leaving her such notes when he thought a thing wanted saying and did not want to interrupt her at the page. It read only: *Ask Sìleas to mark the depots on the map in the front room. Three dots, close together on the coast. It will want marking again before the year is out, I think, though I could not tell you why I think it.*

She did not ask him why. His hunches about the shape a year would take, she had learned, were more often right than wrong, and he liked least to be asked to account for them before they had proved themselves one way or the other. She called Sìleas from the copying-room and gave her the note, and watched the girl's quick hand set the three dots on the old map that hung in the front room, close together on the coast as the note said, small and black and, for the present, no more than three dots among a hundred others.

## II. Of the Fifth of an Cèitean

The council sat on the fifth of an Cèitean, and what was done at that sitting reached an Leabharlann three ways within the week: the council's own minute, sent as a matter of course to every office of record; a private letter from a clerk of An t-Ionmhas who owed Raghnall a kindness from some years before and thought the chronicler's desk should not wait on the formal copy; and, last and slowest, the printed proclamation, posted up in the market towns and brought to an Leabharlann folded inside a farmer's almanac by a carrier who had torn it from a post at Cathair dhearg because he thought Beathag would want to see the thing as the crowd had seen it, creased and a little torn at one corner where someone's thumbnail had caught it pulling it down to read.

She read the clerk's letter first, because it came first and because it was the plainest telling of the three. He wrote that the council, sitting the whole of the forenoon and part of the afternoon on nothing else, had resolved two things at one stroke, as though An t-Ionmhas's masters had judged that two changes made on the same day would be easier for the kingdom to swallow than the same two changes made a month apart, each with its own weight of argument. The first: that the coin of the Rìoghachd, which since Fearchar Bonn's own day had rested on the stores of coal held against it, would rest from that day on the making of dubhan, the mint's reserve counted now in casks of the new fuel and not in coal at all. The second, moved by a councillor whose name the clerk did not think it his place to give, though Beathag guessed from the wording of the motion that it had come from one who had argued it before and lost: that the age of the kingdom, which had run since An Dealachadh under its own count of years, was ended, and that a new count began from the day of the first working dubhan, fourteen years gone and more, so that the year now standing, which the mint's own ledgers and the council's own minutes had been calling the eighty-fifth of the old count, was to be entered thereafter as the fifteenth year of Linn an Dubhain, the era of Dubhan.

The clerk added, in a line he had crossed out and then, thinking better of the crossing, written again below it so that both stood: that the proclamation had passed by a show of hands with no count taken, which was not the council's custom in a matter of such weight, and that he did not know whether this meant the matter was thought too plain to need counting, or too awkward to want a number set against it that some other year might be held up and compared.

The printed proclamation, when it came, said nothing of the vote at all, only the two resolutions themselves in the flat language proclamations use, and, at the foot, the line that was carried to every market town on the same sheet: *from the day of the first dubhan the years shall be counted anew.* Beathag read it standing at the window with the creased sheet held to the light, the tear at its corner letting a thin blade of sun through onto the page, and thought that a single sentence had just done to fourteen years of her own record what an Leabharlann's reckoners had done, three generations before her time, to the ages before An t-Aiseag, folding a stretch of lived years into a new count as though the years themselves had always belonged to it and only wanted the right hand to say so.

"They have moved the ground under every date I have ever written," she said to Raghnall, who had come to stand at her shoulder, though she was not sure until she had said it whether she meant it as complaint or as plain description, and found, turning the sentence over once it was out of her mouth, that she meant it as both at once and saw no reason to choose between them.

"They have," Raghnall said. "It was always dubhan that moved the ground. This is only the council saying so out loud, which it does seldom enough that I own I did not expect it from them this cleanly."

## III. Of the Fourteen Years Re-headed

The work fell to her alone, because it was a chronicler's work and no clerk's, however careful the clerk's hand; a clerk might copy a line, but only the chronicler who had written the fourteen years in the first place could say, of each one, where its true head now stood.

She began the evening the proclamation reached her, by a single lamp at the long table in the room behind the front room, with the fourteen ledgers stacked at her right hand in the order she had written them and a fifteenth, the year now running, open before her with its first four months already filled under the old heading. Sìleas offered to sit with her and hold the lamp steady, or fetch fresh oil when the first measure burned low, and Beathag let her, though there was little enough the girl could do beyond that; the turning wanted one hand and one memory, and Sìleas's memory did not go back far enough to be trusted with it.

It was not hard work in the doing, only slow, and slower than she had thought it would be when she sat down to it. Each ledger's first page carried, at its head, the year of the old count, *SE* and the number, in the same square hand she had used for fourteen years running because she had never in that time had reason to write it any other way; and beside each old heading she now set the new, *Linn an Dubhain*, the year in its place, first, second, third, and so down the stack to the fourteenth, which was the year just closed, and the fifteenth, which was the year she sat in as she wrote. She did not strike out the old headings. She had thought, before she began, that she might, and had decided against it somewhere in the walk from the front room to the long table, on no better ground than that a thing once written into the record was the record's own and not hers to unwrite, however the council chose to count it afterward; so she set the new heading beside the old, in a smaller hand, with a line drawn between them, and let both stand.

Between the sixth ledger and the seventh, some time past midnight by the state of the lamp, she stopped long enough to look back over what she had already turned, and found, reading the years in their new order, that she remembered them differently set out so. The sixth year of Linn an Dubhain had been, under its old heading, the seventy-sixth of the kingdom, a year she remembered chiefly for the cold spring and a fever that had gone through Muileann chaol's own streets and taken two children from the copyists' row; set now under the new count it was the year the coastal lights first burned dubhan, and she found she had to search her own memory for the fever and the cold spring, which had not moved an inch in the record but seemed, set beside the new heading, to have slipped a little further back than they had stood the night before.

"It is a strange thing," she said to Sìleas, somewhere past the ninth ledger, "to find that a year does not change by being renamed, and yet somehow does."

"Which is the truer year, then," Sìleas asked, "the one you lived, or the one the council has just given it?"

Beathag considered this longer than the question perhaps deserved, turning her pen between two fingers the way she did when a thing wanted more thought than the first answer she could have given it. "Both," she said at last. "I lived the year I lived, cold spring and fever and all, and no proclamation touches that. But I did not live it knowing what it was, and the council has just told the whole kingdom what it was, all at once, fourteen years after the fact. I expect that is what a proclamation is for. It does not change what happened. It only tells the ones who lived through it what they were living through at the time, which they could not have known, being in the middle of it."

She finished the fourteenth ledger a little before the light came up, and set it on the pile with the others, and sat a while with her hands flat on the table before she drew the fifteenth toward her, which wanted no turning, only a new heading at its head to match the fourteen behind it. She wrote *Linn an Dubhain, a' chòigeamh bliadhna deug* at the top of the open page, the fifteenth year of Linn an Dubhain, in the same square hand as always, and found, setting the pen down, that her hand was not quite steady, though she could not have said whether it was the hour or the work.

At the foot of that same page, under the day's entries, which were themselves nothing more than the depot letter she had copied the week before and a note of a birth at Muileann chaol she had taken down for the town's own roll, she wrote one line more, in a hand smaller than her working hand, as though she meant it less for the record than for herself, though she let it stand once written and never struck it: *Cha b' fheudar dhomh riamh roimhe bliadhna a ghluasad 's mi beò innte.* Never before have I had to move a year I was living in.

Sìleas, reading it over her shoulder as she blotted the page, said nothing for a moment, and then asked whether it was meant to go into the fair copy that went up to the council each quarter.

"It can go in," Beathag said. "I've no wish to hide it. But copy it exactly as it stands, and don't smooth the grammar. I wrote it tired, and I'd sooner the council saw that I wrote it tired than have it think a chronicler writes such a thing at her ease."

## IV. Of the Plain Seal

The letter from the mint at Cathair dhearg came up a month later, in the first week of an t-Ògmhios, over the signature of its master but in a hand Beathag recognised before she reached the signature at all, because she had had one letter from that hand before, three years past, asking whether an Leabharlann kept any record of the old ink-recipe's origin, and had answered that it did not, only the recipe, which the mint already had.

Gille-Easbaig Bàn wrote now to say that the mint had cut new dies for the coin's seal, the first change to the seal since Fearchar Bonn's own day, and that the coal ink, ground from vein coal at a cost that had climbed every year of his own service at the mint until it stood, that spring, higher than the seal's whole worth in coin, was pressed into no die of the new coinage at all. The new seal showed the kingdom's mark plain, in the same silver as the coin, with no colour worked into it, and he wrote, in a line Beathag thought carried more feeling than the rest of the letter allowed him to show, that he did not know whether he was glad of it or sorry, having spent twelve years grinding an ink he would now never grind again, and having no pupil of his own yet to whom the losing of that knowledge might matter one way or the other.

He wrote last, as though it were an afterthought and not, Beathag thought, the true reason he had troubled to write to her at all rather than let the council's own notice carry the news: that Fearchar Bonn's first dies, the ones that had struck the kingdom's very first coin in the old counting-house at Cathair dhearg, and had been kept at the mint ever since, more relic than tool, past any use but the honour of having been first, were the council's to dispose of now that the seal they had cut was no longer the kingdom's seal, and the council had ordered them sent to an Leabharlann, to be kept there rather than melted, because a die that had struck the kingdom's first coin was thought worth more as a kept thing than as the little weight of silver it would fetch broken up.

They came up ten days later, wrapped in oiled cloth in a box no bigger than a loaf, carried by a mounted courier of An t-Ionmhas who would not leave them with anyone but the keeper himself and made Raghnall sign a paper before he would hand the box over, though what the paper said neither Raghnall nor Beathag could afterward agree, having both signed it without reading it closely in their eagerness to open the box.

The dies themselves were smaller than either of them had expected, two flat discs of worn steel, the king's old mark on one face of each so shallow with age and use that it wanted a slant of lamplight to read at all. Raghnall turned them over twice in his hands before he set them, at Beathag's own suggestion, in the glass case in the front room where Clach-mhionnan nan Gualadairean already stood, the two things side by side under one pane of glass, a stone worn smooth by two generations of hewers' thumbs and a pair of dies worn smooth by more strikings than any ledger had troubled to count, neither of them any use now to the trade that had made them.

"It is a strange sort of case we are building," Raghnall said, setting the last of the dust from his hands. "Everything that comes into it has just stopped being used."

"That is what a library is for, in the end," Beathag said. "Not only the things still in use. Someone has to keep the things that have stopped."

## V. Of the Two Letters

The Àrd-choimheadaiche's letter reached an Leabharlann in the last week of an t-Iuchar, sent, as his letters always were, over the seal of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail at the southern Seann Skell and in his own close, old-fashioned hand, which Beathag had come, over the years of her office, to read almost as easily as her own.

Alasdair mac Ìomhair wrote to the council, and sent a copy, as courtesy required, to an Leabharlann for its record, protesting the plain seal in terms he had plainly weighed with some care, for the letter carried none of the heat his earlier letters, on lesser matters, had sometimes shown.
