The coal ink pressed into every coin the kingdom had struck since Fearchar Bonn's day, whatever the mint's masters might now call it in their accounts, was a mark, he wrote: every hand that touched the coin, market-woman or minister, had touched it knowing that the kingdom's own wealth rested, in the last account, on the vein An Creideamh Sean had always held sacred. A seal struck plain, in silver alone, with no colour of the coal in it anywhere, said to every hand that touched it thereafter that the kingdom no longer held that to be so, whatever the council's clerks might answer if asked outright. Withdrawal of the seal he did not ask. He asked only that the council say, in its own words and not through a mint-master's accounting, whether it meant by the change what he took it to mean.

The council's answer came within the fortnight, shorter than the custodian's own letter by more than half, over the signature of the councillor Beathag guessed, from the clerk's earlier letter of an Cèitean, had moved the proclamation in the first place, though the answer named no mover, only the council as a body. It said that the coin's seal had never, at any sitting of the council since the mint was first set up, been declared a holy thing by any resolution the council's own minutes could show; that the coal ink had been pressed into it because coal was, at the time, the surest reserve the kingdom held to stand behind its coin, and for no other reason the record kept; and that the council, in changing the reserve to match the fuel the kingdom now in fact used, had changed nothing it had ever said was sacred, because it had never said any such thing to begin with. The letter closed with a single sentence that carried, Beathag thought reading it the first time and thought again reading it the fifth, more weight than its own plainness seemed to want to admit: that the council held no vein and no fuel sacred, and never had, and that if the custodian's houses had taught otherwise these fourteen years, the teaching was theirs, and not the kingdom's.

She copied both letters whole into the day's page, the custodian's first and the council's after it, in the order they had come to her, and set no note of her own between them or beneath them, though she sat a long while at the table after the second was copied, the pen dry in her hand, before she blotted the page and closed the ledger for the night.

It was, she thought, setting the ledger back on its shelf among the fourteen others and the fifteenth still open beside them, one of the few places in the whole of her record, in all her years at the desk, where the kingdom had been asked outright what it held to be true, and had answered the question rather than let it stand unanswered as such questions were more often let stand; and it had answered, when it came to it, that it had never held what everyone had long taken it to hold, coal or council or custodian alike, and had never troubled, until a plain-seal coin and a custodian's letter forced the words out of it, to say so.

She did not write that thought into the record. It was only her own reading of a fact, and she had long held that a chronicler's readings belonged in her own head, not in the ledger, however much they might colour the choosing of what she set down and what she let pass. But she thought it again, walking back from the front room to her own small chamber under the eaves, the last light of an t-Iuchar still pale in the sky though the hour was late, and thought that a kingdom that had just said, in writing and for the first time, what it did not believe, might in time be asked what it did, and that she did not know, setting her lamp down for the night, whether that question, when it came, would be as easily answered as this one had been.

# Chapter Sixteen: Of the Meeting at Muileann àrsaidh

*DE 16*

> **Part Three: Of the Holdouts of the Western Hills**
>
> *B' fheàrr leinn a bhith fuar còmhla ri ar nàbaidhean na blàth leinn fhèin.*
> We would sooner be cold with our neighbours than warm alone.
>
> — the delegates of Àth naomh, DE 16

## I. Of the Pit Captain's Daughter

In the western hills they still tell it that Calder of Àth leathan went down to his own pit for the last time in the dark of an Gearran, three weeks before he died, and would let no one carry his lamp for him though his hands by then shook too much to trust with a naked flame. He had cut coal at Àth leathan for six-and-thirty years, boy and man, and captained the pit for twenty of them, and the black cough that took him in the end was no stranger to that village; it had taken his own father before him, and it would take others after, and nobody in the hills thought to call it anything but the price of the seam.

Ruth was with him when the last of it came. She had kept his tally-books since she was twelve, first because her hand was steadier than his after a day underground and later because it was simply understood between them that the books were hers to keep; and she sat by his bed those last nights with the ledger open on her knee more from habit than any thought that the work in it still wanted doing, while her mother, dead herself these nine years, was spoken of only once, near the end, when Calder said her name and then said nothing else that Ruth could make sense of. He died a little before first light on the ninth day of the month, in the small stone house above the pit-head that had been his father's before him, and the village buried him two days after in the plot behind the chapel where the Àth leathan dead had been laid since before anyone living could say.

It was at the pit-head, not the chapel, that the choosing was made, on the evening of the burial, with the light going and the wind coming up cold off the hills. There was no guild left in the west to make it formal; Comann nan Gualadairean had dissolved itself four years before, and the western pits, small and poor and half-forgotten by any board that might once have cared, had never troubled the guild's rolls much in any case. What there was instead was thirty-one hewers of Àth leathan standing about the pit-head in their working clothes because they had come straight from the last shift, and old Angus Rennie, who had cut coal longer than any man there but Calder himself, saying what everyone had already half decided among themselves in the two days since Calder took to his bed for good.

"He kept the books and he kept the peace," Angus said, "and he knew every seam in this hill better than any man breathing, saving one." He kept his own eyes on the pit-head's winch as he said it; every other eye in the crowd turned to Ruth. "I'll not stand up here and pretend I know another man fit to take his place at short notice. But I know who kept his books alongside him five years and more, and knows the seams near as well as he did, and I'll stand behind her if the rest of you will."

Nobody spoke against it. The hewers of Àth leathan had, Ruth understood afterward, no settled notion at all of a woman standing where her father had stood; what they had was a memory of her running messages down the pit road with her father's dinner in a cloth as a child, and of watching her keep his books through two winters when his eyes had begun to fail him, and too little time, with the light going and the ground cooling under their feet, to think of anyone else to ask. Ruth said yes because there was nothing else to say, standing at the pit-head in her father's own worn coat, which she had put on that morning without thinking because it was cold and it was there, and because a man handed her, without a word, the small brass lamp that had been Calder's own since his own father died, its case dented from thirty years of being carried down and up again. She took it because there was nowhere else for it to go.

Sleep would not come to her that night. She sat up instead with the ledger open before her, as she had a hundred nights before, and found that for the first time in her life there was no one to hand it to when the figures were entered and the page was done.

## II. Of Sarah Dunmore's Kitchen

Word of the meeting at Muileann àrsaidh had been going round the western hills since the turn of the year, carried by carriers and by the hewers who still walked between the pit towns on Sundays to see kin, and by the time Ruth set out on the hill path in the first week of am Màrt, ten miles by the short way over the shoulder of the moor, she went as Àth leathan's delegate without having asked to be one or having been asked in any form she could afterward have pointed to. It was simply understood, the way the choosing at the pit-head had been understood, that the pit captain went where the pit towns' business was done, and that this was pit towns' business if anything in the hills was.

She had never before walked so far alone. The path ran up over open ground where the wind had nothing to break it and down again through a stand of birch where the last of the winter's snow still lay in the shadow of the trunks, and she came into Muileann àrsaidh a little after noon with her boots wet through and her father's lamp, unlit, swinging from her hand because she had brought it without quite deciding to and had not liked to leave it behind once it was in her pocket.

Sarah Dunmore's house stood at the foot of the town's one street, a stone house no larger than its neighbours, with a good peat fire already going in the kitchen grate when Ruth came to the door and a smell of broth that told her the house had been feeding people for some days before she arrived. Sarah herself, a broad, plain-spoken widow of some thirty years past her own husband's death under a fall of stone at the Muileann àrsaidh pit, had put her kitchen at the meeting's disposal without being asked twice, on the reasoning, as she gave it to Ruth within an hour of her arrival, that a kitchen fed people and a hall did not, and that men who had walked ten or fifteen miles over hill paths in the wet would talk better with something hot in front of them than they would in a cold room with nothing but a table.

There were seven of them crowded round that table by the time the light began to go: two from Muileann àrsaidh itself, an old hewer named Fraser and a younger man called Meikle who did most of the town's writing; a heavy, careful man named Drummond who had walked over from Cnoc thais that morning on Tom Varley's errand, Varley himself being kept at home by a knee that had never mended right since a fall the winter before; a thin, watchful woman called Nan Ross who spoke for the few families left at Tobar dhearg of the hills, where the one pit barely kept forty hewers in work; and Sarah Dunmore herself, who was no delegate of anywhere but sat at the head of her own table as though the question of whether she belonged in the talk had never once occurred to her.

Ruth said little that first evening. She was the youngest at the table by a dozen years and more, new to the captaincy by less than a fortnight, and she had come, she told herself, to listen before she spoke; but she listened hard, and what she heard, under the talk of prices and the talk of the south and the talk of what Tional nan Tuathach might or might not do, was that none of the six people in that kitchen had any clear notion yet of what they wanted the towns to agree to, only a clear and common notion of what they would not agree to, which was to fold their pits and buy their fire from the south like every other town in the north had done.

"We're none of us saying we won't sell to the south's fuel-men, mind," Fraser said, late in the evening, with the fire down to embers and Sarah moving quietly about the room banking it for the night. "Only that we'll keep cutting what we cut, and sell it to whoever in the north still wants coal, and not be told by any charter that we've no business doing it."

"That's a thing worth saying," Ruth said, the first full sentence she had put into the room all evening, "but it wants saying plainer than that, or it'll be argued over as long as it's talked and never once written down." She felt every face at the table turn to her, and pressed on before she could think better of it. "My father kept books thirty years. A thing not written down plain enough to read back is a thing that gets remembered five different ways by five different people inside a twelvemonth."

Sarah Dunmore, from the hearth, laughed once, short and approving. "There's Calder's own daughter talking," she said. "Well. If it wants writing plain, who's for the writing of it?"

Nobody answered for a moment. Then Drummond nodded slowly across the table at Ruth, and Fraser after him, and Ruth understood, with something between pride and a plain cold weight settling in her chest, that the pen, like the lamp, had been handed to her before she had thought to reach for it.

They talked past midnight, though little more of it went into any settled shape that night. Meikle set down on a scrap of paper, for his own memory more than the meeting's, the figures Drummond had brought from Cnoc thais: what a sack of dubhan cost delivered to a northern door against what a sack of their own coal cost cut and carted, and how the second sum had crept up year on year as fewer hands stayed to cut it, until it stood now not far below the first. Nan Ross said little beyond agreeing that Tobar dhearg's forty hewers would go on cutting whatever the meeting decided, since forty hewers with nothing else to do were no argument at all; and Sarah, setting bread and a jug of milk on the table without being asked, said once that she had buried a husband under this town's coal and would sooner see her neighbours burn it than see the pit stand idle over his grave, which nobody in the kitchen thought needed answering. Ruth slept that night in a box-bed off Sarah's own kitchen, with the fire's last heat coming through the wall behind her, and lay a long while listening to the house settle before sleep took her, turning over in her mind the shape of a paper that did not yet exist.

## III. Of the Pit-shed and the Agreement

The kitchen held them well enough for talk, but by the second day word had gone round the town and more had come than Sarah's table would seat: hewers from Muileann àrsaidh itself who wanted to hear with their own ears what was being said in their name, two more men down from Cnoc thais on Tom Varley's second errand once his knee let him send them, and, on the third morning, a boy on a borrowed pony from Tobar dhearg with a note in Nan Ross's own hand asking that nothing be signed before she'd had the chance to read it over once more herself, which raised a laugh even from Nan when it was read aloud, since she was sitting at the table not three feet from where the note was opened.

They moved the talk to the pit-shed above the town, a long low building of stone and turf where Muileann àrsaidh kept its winches and its spare timber and, in the corner nearest the door, a bench worn smooth by three generations of hewers changing their boots before a shift. It smelled of tar and damp rope and old coal-dust, and it held, once the benches were cleared and set in rows, near forty people at a squeeze, which was more, Ruth thought, looking round it on that first morning, than she had ever seen gathered in one room in her life.

She wrote the agreement's terms on three sheets of Meikle's paper over the course of that day and the next, crossing out more than she kept, while the room argued each line before it was let stand. It was slower work than she had thought book-keeping had prepared her for; a line she thought plain enough to need no more discussion could still draw an hour's argument from men who had different notions of what "the seams" meant, whether it took in Tobar dhearg's single pit as well as Cnoc thais's dozen workings, or whether "any household in the north that will buy" meant houses in the south too if a southern buyer somehow wanted northern coal, which nobody thought likely but several thought worth saying plainly all the same.

The hardest of it, in the end, was the leaving out. A man from Muileann àrsaidh's own row of hewers, a squat, red-faced man called Dodds, stood up on the second afternoon and wanted a line put in naming the fuel-fitters of the south by name, and the charter that shut Tuathaich hands out of the new trade besides, so that whoever read the agreement after would know exactly whose doing the five towns' trouble was. Ruth let him talk himself to a stop before she answered, because she had learned already, in two days of it, that the room argued better with a thing than against a man. "Name them," she said, "and the paper stops being about coal and starts being about grievance, and a grievance is a thing folk argue with. Five towns cutting their own coal and selling it plain is a thing folk can only agree to or leave be." Dodds sat down without much grace, but he signed the sheet three days later along with the rest of Muileann àrsaidh's hewers, which Ruth took, privately, for the better half of an answer.

What stood, in the end, in the hand Ruth had written it in, was shorter than any single hour of the argument that had shaped it. The five towns of the western hills — though only four were named in that first writing — would go on working their seams as they had always worked them, taking up no man's charter and asking none, and would sell their coal to any household of the north that came to buy it, at whatever price buyer and seller could agree between them, and to no household that did not come freely asking. It said nothing against the fuel from the south, and nothing for it. Of Tional nan Tuathach, which none of the four towns present had asked to be part of the meeting, it said nothing at all, and none proposed to write to it now. Its last line, which Ruth added herself and read aloud to the shed before anyone else saw it, promised that the towns signing it would stand by each other in the keeping of it, for as long as any of them had coal left to sell.

Fraser signed for Muileann àrsaidh, Drummond for Cnoc thais, Nan Ross for Tobar dhearg once the boy had ridden the finished sheet back to her and she had, true to her note, read it over twice before putting her own mark beside her name. Ruth signed last, for Àth leathan, in the same hand she had used for her father's tally-books, on a morning in the third week of am Màrt with the pit-shed's one small window letting in a grey light that had not yet decided whether it would rain, and felt, setting her name under the others, that she had put more of herself into those three short sheets than into anything she had done in her life before that week.

## IV. Of the Town that Would Not Be Warm Alone

Àth naomh sent no one to the meeting at Muileann àrsaidh that am Màrt, and for the better part of a month afterward the agreement stood signed by four towns and spoken of by the fourth as though it were finished business. It was in an Giblean, with the pit-shed's turf roof dripping steadily under a fortnight of rain, that two delegates came over the hill path from Àth naomh on a wet Tuesday and asked, without much in the way of preamble, to be let sign what the others had already signed.

Àth naomh had the least to offer of any of the five: a handful of old shafts worked thin, a temple and a citadel from an older age that the town's few hundred souls now kept more from habit than any wealth to defend, and coal enough, by its own delegates' plain accounting, to warm perhaps two winters more before the seams gave out entirely. It would have cost the town nothing, several in the shed pointed out, and might have spared it a hard winter or two, simply to go over to the south's fuel as every other northern town but these four already had; and it was the elder of the two delegates, a stooped, grey-bearded man named Ferguson who had walked the hill path with a stick in either hand, who answered that argument standing in the middle of the pit-shed floor with the rain loud on the roof above him.

"We could burn dubhan same as any town in the north," he said. "We've thought on it, don't doubt that we have, thought on it hard through two cold winters running. But we'd be burning it alone among our own hills, with every neighbour we've got still cutting coal at the seam, and I'll tell you plainly what we decided, the whole town of us, over it." He looked round the shed, at faces he mostly did not know, and said the thing as though he had carried it the whole ten miles from Àth naomh rehearsing exactly how he would say it. "We'd sooner be cold with our neighbours than warm alone."

Nobody in the shed answered that at once. Ruth, sitting near the front with the signed agreement still in its folder on her knee, found that she had nothing to add to it that would not have made it smaller, and said only, after a silence that went on long enough to be its own kind of answer, that there was room on the sheet for a fifth name, and would he care to write it himself or have her write it for him. He wrote it himself, in a hand less steady than Ruth's own but legible enough, and his companion after him, and by the time the two of them set off back over the hill path that same wet afternoon, unwilling to be a night's board and lodging on a town no better off than their own, the agreement of Muileann àrsaidh carried the names of all five.

By an Cèitean, with the worst of the spring rain past and the hill paths dry enough to walk without ruining a pair of boots in an afternoon, the five towns had become, in the mouths of everyone in the western hills and a good many people well beyond them, simply the holdout towns, and Ruth Calder, one-and-forty years old and less than three months a pit captain in her own right, had become, without any second choosing to mark the change, the person whose name was given when anyone from outside the hills asked who spoke for them. She had not asked for that either. It came to her the way the lamp had come to her, and the pen after it, because there was no one else at hand when the asking was done, and because she had shown, in the writing of three short sheets, that she could put a thing down plainly and stand behind it after.

Tional nan Tuathach, when word of the agreement reached it, did neither of the two things the five towns had half expected it might do. It did not send a delegate north to add Tional nan Tuathach's own name to the sheet, as one or two in the pit-shed had hoped it might; and it did not send word condemning the towns for standing apart from a trade the rest of the north had gone over to whole. It sent nothing at all, so far as Ruth or anyone in the hills ever learned, beyond a bare line in its own minute-book, copied out for her by a carrier some weeks later at her own asking, that noted the towns' agreement had been reported to Tional nan Tuathach and that Tional nan Tuathach, having heard it, saw no cause to act upon it either way. She read the line twice, standing in her own kitchen at Àth leathan with her father's lamp on the shelf where she had set it the night of his burial, and understood it for what it plainly was: the sound of a door being left exactly as it stood, neither opened nor shut, by people who had decided that the five towns' trouble was, for the present, none of theirs to have an opinion about.

## V. Of the Two Shafts at Cnoc thais

Tom Varley's knee mended slowly through the summer of that year, and it was not until an t-Samhain, with the first hard frosts already whitening the moor grass in the mornings, that he was fit again to walk the length of his own pit workings at Cnoc thais without a stick; and it was in that same month, once he could stand a full day underground, that he set two dozen of his hewers to opening again a pair of shafts on the hill's northern face that had lain shut, by every account the town could give of them, since before An Dealachadh, when the men who dug them had been of another people entirely and the coal they left behind had been thought too thin and too far in to be worth a second working.

It was thin, when Varley's men reached it, and it was harder cutting than the town's main seams, and the first cartload brought up from it, in the last week of the month, burned with more smoke and less heat than any coal Cnoc thais had cut in living memory. Nobody in the town complained of it. It was set that same week on a dozen hearths across Cnoc thais, in houses that had been buying their fire in from Muileann àrsaidh at a price the winter made harder to bear each year, and the town's own account of it, which reached Ruth by way of a letter from Varley himself a fortnight later, said only that the coal was poor, and that it was theirs, and that a poor fire of one's own cutting warmed a house no worse than a good one bought dear from a neighbour.

Varley wrote, too, that the two old shafts had given up more than coal in the opening of them: a broken pick-head of a make none of his hewers knew, and, in the second shaft, a length of rotted timber shoring still holding the roof up after however many years it had stood there, which his men had left untouched rather than risk the roof coming down on the strength of curiosity alone. He asked, half in earnest, whether Ruth thought it worth writing to Leabharlann Muileann chaol about the pick-head, and answered his own question in the same letter before she could: that a chronicler's clerk two days' ride away would take more interest in an old iron head than any of the five towns could spare the time to satisfy, and that the shaft wanted working, not wondering over, with the winter coming on and Cnoc thais's own hearths waiting on it.

Ruth read the letter at her own table at Àth leathan on an evening in the first week of an Dùbhlachd, with the year's business behind her and the next year's not yet begun, and found in it, more than in anything that had happened since the pit-shed at Muileann àrsaidh, the whole of what the five towns had agreed to be. It was not a victory, Varley's letter said as much as it said anything; it was thin coal from an old working, burning worse than the coal it replaced, in houses that would rather have had better. But it was the hills' own, cut by the hills' own hands, out of ground the hills had never given up, and Ruth understood, reading it a second time by the last of the evening light, that this was the whole of the bargain the five towns had made with each other in am Màrt and would go on making, winter after winter, for as long as any seam among them held coal enough to be worth the cutting.

She sat a long while at the table after the letter was folded away, with her father's lamp burning low on the shelf and a fresh sheet of paper set out in front of her, blank, because Fraser had written from Muileann àrsaidh that week asking whether it would not be worth a letter to one or two of the northern towns still undecided about their fire, laying the five towns' case out plain the way the agreement had been laid out plain, in case there were households elsewhere in the north still minded to buy coal from a neighbour rather than dubhan from the south. It was, Ruth thought, turning the pen over once in her fingers before she began, exactly the kind of asking her father would have turned to her without a second thought, the way every asking since the pit-head in an Gearran had come to her without her once being asked whether she wanted it; and she understood, dipping the pen at last, that there would be a great many more such letters before the seams at Àth leathan or Cnoc thais or any of the five towns ran thin enough to end the need of them, and that she, and no one else, would be the one sitting at a table some cold evening each year of it, finding the words.

# Chapter Seventeen: Of the Eleven Books

*DE 17*

## I. Of Cathair gheal

Tobar dhearg of the hills was the least of the five holdout towns, and knew it, and made no complaint of it. It had one pit and forty hewers, a red well the Dia-thìrich had dug long before An Dealachadh and the Tuathaich had kept digging after, and a track down through the western hills that a cart could just take if the carter walked at the horse's head the whole way. What the pit raised was poor coal, sooty and quick to crumble, no match for the seams of Muileann àrsaidh or Cnoc thais; but it burned, and the walled town of Cathair gheal on the coast below had no coal of its own at all, only boats. So twice in the month, when the weather served, a cart went down from Tobar dhearg loaded with sacks, and came back loaded with fish salted in barrels, and the arrangement had held so long that nobody in either town could have said which had thought of it first.

Ellen Marsh came down to Cathair gheal on the carrier's cart that brought the fish north, in the raw first days of an Gearran, with her satchel on her knees and her notebook wrapped in oilcloth against the spray off the harbour road. She had made the journey a dozen times in as many years, for one reason or another, and always for the same true reason underneath the others: there was, in that walled town of white stone with the sea on three sides of it, an old woman named Annie Drew who had been a child at An Dealachadh, and who had said, the last time Ellen sat with her, that she did not think she would keep another winter.

She had kept it. Ellen found her sitting up in the kitchen of her daughter's house by the harbour wall, wrapped to the chin though the fire was well built with Tobar dhearg's coal, her hands gone to knuckle and vein, her eyes still quick. She was ninety-one that winter, the oldest soul in Cathair gheal by some years, and the only one left who had been more than an infant when the parting came.

"You're earlier than I looked for," Annie said, by way of greeting, "or I'm later than I looked for. One or the other."

"The fish cart wanted an early tide."

"It always does." Annie nodded at the stool by the fire, which had plainly been set there for her before Ellen arrived, and Ellen sat and unwrapped the notebook and found the place where the last visit had left off, a third of the way down a page, in her own small hand: *she was five, or near it. her mother would not let her look back at the smoke.*

"You'll want the rest of that," Annie said.

"If you're willing."

"I said I'd give it you before I die, and I mean to keep to that whatever else I don't keep to." She was quiet a moment, working her hands together in her lap, and then she began, in the humans' tongue, which she kept to by long habit and never troubled to leave for Dia-thìris even with those, like Ellen, who had both equally. Ellen wrote as she talked, in Dia-thìris, since that was the hand she wrote fastest and truest, and stopped her now and again only to ask a name again, or a distance, or which of two roads.

It was not a long telling, in the end, though it had taken eleven years to get the whole of it, a little at a time, out of a woman who did not care to dwell on it and would not be hurried past it either. The smoke over the fires they had left burning to make the parting look sudden, though it had been three weeks in the planning by the time the household stirred that night. The stones set new along the road, white and raw, not yet grown over, that her father called the boundary though there had been no boundary the week before. A soldier at the last of them who had given her mother bread out of his own satchel and would not meet her mother's eye while he did it. The long walk after, and the fires lit along it each evening smaller than the one before, until by the fourth night there was coal enough only for a handful of families to share one fire between them, and the rest went cold, and nobody spoke of that afterward either, not for years, not until an old woman sat by a stranger's fire built of Tobar dhearg's crumbling coal and found she had, after ninety winters, one telling left to give away.

"That's the whole of it," Annie said, when she had done. "You've the bones of it from me twice over already. This is only the flesh."

"It's the flesh I wanted." Ellen read the last page back to her, low, so as not to wake the sleeping cat that had climbed into Annie's lap somewhere in the telling, and Annie listened with her eyes shut and said, at the end, that it would do, and that Ellen had got the soldier's bread right, which was the part she had always feared losing between one visit and the next.

"That's the last of them, isn't it," Annie said then. "You've been round the whole coast for it. There's none left older than me this side of Muileann àrsaidh, and she's simple, poor soul, hasn't known her own name since the fever three winters back."

"You're the last," Ellen said. She did not pretend otherwise; Annie was not a woman it did any good to spare.

"Well." Annie stroked the cat once, the length of its back, and looked into the fire a while. "I've kept my word, then. See you keep yours."

"I mean to."

"Mean isn't do. But I'll not live to see which, so you may tell me what you like." She said it without bitterness, the way she said most things, as a fact laid down and left to lie, and Ellen closed the notebook over the last page and did not answer that, because there was no true answer to give her that was also a kind one.

She stayed the night, as she always did, in the loft above the kitchen, and in the morning she walked down to the harbour before the fish cart was loaded and stood a while at the wall in the cold light, looking out past the white walls to the grey water. A boat was coming in from the night's fishing, low and slow, and up on the hill road behind the town a cart was coming down from Tobar dhearg with its load of sacks, the carter walking at the horse's head. She watched the two of them come toward each other, the boat and the cart, as they had come toward each other, she supposed, a thousand times before her, and thought of Annie Drew asleep in the house behind her with the cat still warm in her lap, and of the notebook wrapped in oilcloth in the satchel at Ellen's own feet, and of how little either the boat or the cart, going about their trade, cared for the telling folded inside it.

## II. Of the Eleventh Book

The schoolroom at Doire ghlas, by the time Ellen came home, had gone back nine years to being nothing but a schoolroom, the tables in their rows again under the alphabet painted round the walls in both hands, the stove drawing well, no smell of paste in it any longer to speak of. But in the low cupboard at the back, under lock, stood ten books, bound in plain grey board by her own hand over eleven winters, each lettered on the spine with a year and nothing more, and it was to these that Ellen went first, before she had so much as taken off her coat, to lay the notebook from Cathair gheal on top of them and stand looking down at the row.

She had begun the work almost by accident, the year she came to teach at Agnes Pike's old school, when an old man of the parish had stopped her in the lane to correct something she had told the children about An Dealachadh, a small thing, a date got wrong by a generation, and had gone on, once started, to tell her the true year and a good deal besides that she had never read in any book because it was written in none. She had gone home that evening and set it down before she forgot the half of it, and the next week had asked another, and the week after another, and had not, in eleven years, found a way to stop, though she had several times found reasons she ought to.

What she had, by the winter that closed the seventeenth year, was eleven books: the tellings of some two hundred old men and women of the north, taken down as near their own words as her pen could keep pace with, town by town, coast to hill, An Dealachadh and the years straight after it, the first winters, the boundary stones, the names of those who had not lived to cross them. No two tellings agreed in everything. She had learned early to let that stand rather than smooth it, and had written, in the front of the first book, a line to say so: that where two witnesses differed she had set down both, and let the reader judge, as a court would.

She worked through the first week of an Gearran binding the eleventh volume herself, at her own table by lamplight, with the flat bone folder Daniel Frayne's eldest binder had given her nine winters before, when the two of them had sat up late in this same room over Tional nan Tuathach's own sixty-three books and Ellen had asked, more from curiosity than any plan, to be shown how the stitching went. The binder had shown her, and left her the folder after, saying that a body who kept books ought to know how to mend one, and Ellen had used it every winter since on her own small work, though never so fine as the binder's own.

She had thought, more than once through those years, of asking the binders of Muileann leathan to do this last one properly, since they were near and willing and it would have taken them an evening where it took her three, but had always come back to doing it herself. It seemed to her, though she could not have said quite why to another person, that a book made of other people's own words asked to be sewn by the same hand that had taken them down, and not passed on for finishing to someone who had never sat by any of those fires.

When it was done she laid it at the end of the row, and it was, by an inch's difference in the grey board, exactly the same as the other ten, and the row of eleven stood the length of a hand-span on the cupboard shelf, and held, she reckoned without troubling to count it exactly, the better part of two hundred lives that would otherwise have gone into the ground with nothing to show that they had been lived at all.

She wrote the letter to an Leabharlann the same evening, at the same table, in a fair hand she kept for such things and did not often need. Four sentences held the whole of it. It set down what An t-Aon Leabhar Deug were and how they had been gathered, over how many years and from how many mouths, and asked, in the plain form such requests took, that Leabharlann Muileann chaol receive them and keep them beside its own record, as a thing belonging to the shires as much as any royal minute or council return. Nowhere did it ask that the books be believed over the written record where the two crossed; the whole of the asking was that they be kept where a person who wanted to know might come and find them, the way a person could come and find the reign of any king. Ellen read it over twice, found nothing in it she wished to soften, sealed it, and sent it north the following week by the library carrier who came through Doire ghlas each month with the shires' returns, An t-Aon Leabhar Deug wrapped together in oilcloth and tied with the same waxed thread the binders of Muileann leathan had taught her to use.

## III. Of the Letter Laid on the Table

The answer was five months in coming, which did not surprise her, since she had asked five months' worth of a plain answer and had not, in her heart, expected one at all.

It came in an Lùnastal, on a hot still evening when the children had long since gone home and Ellen was alone in the schoolroom totting the term's slates before she put them away for the summer. The carrier brought it up from the harbour road himself rather than leaving it at the school gate, a courtesy he did not often trouble with, and stood a moment at the door turning his cap in his hands before he gave it over, as if he had already guessed, by its weight or its seal, that it was not the kind of letter a man handed across a threshold and walked away from.

It was in Raghnall mac Mhuirich's own hand, which she knew from the flyleaf of every one of her own books, since he had written a line in each on the day it was carried in, acknowledging its receipt, always the same few words. This was longer. Her request, he wrote, and An t-Aon Leabhar Deug with it, had been laid before the keepers of an Leabharlann in the spring, read entire, and set upon the table of the council's business, where it remained, not refused. The question the request raised, as he set it out, touched the books themselves hardly at all, since he did not doubt they were honestly made; it turned instead on what standing an Leabharlann ought to give to witness that came by the mouth and not by the pen, set down at second or third hand by one recorder's own judgment of what to keep and what to leave. This was a question Comhairle na Rìoghachd had not yet given its view on, in this matter or in any other that had come before it in like form, and until it did, Neach-gleidhidh an Leabharlainn had no more authority to shelve eleven books of spoken telling beside the shires' own returns than he had to strike a line through any of those returns on his own word that they were wrong. Sorry to send so little for so much labour, he hoped she would believe the labour was not lost for being unanswered, since a thing once written did not become less true for waiting.

Ellen read it twice at the window, where the light was better, and then sat down at the nearest table with it still in her hand.

She was not, in the ordinary way, a woman given to sitting idle over a letter. But there was, in the reading of it, a particular kind of stillness that came over her, not anger exactly, or not only anger, more the stillness of a sum that has been added correctly and come out wrong. She thought of Annie Drew's hands working together in her lap, and of the soldier's bread that Annie had feared losing between one telling and the next, and of the ninety winters it had taken to bring that one small true thing to a page, only to have it weighed now, by a kind man in a good hand, against a standard it could never by its nature meet, since a soldier's bread given at a roadside leaves no return for any clerk to enter.

She did not doubt that Raghnall mac Mhuirich meant every word of his sorrow, nor that he had done, within the room he had, as much as the room allowed; she had heard, from more than one quarter, how the man had found money out of his own small fund to keep a girl clerk in dry stockings when the council would give him none for the purpose, and she did not think a man of that stamp wrote *not refused* as a way of refusing. That was, in its way, the worst of it. There was no one person in the whole chain of it to be angry at. The letter simply said, in its careful sentences, that An t-Aon Leabhar Deug would lie on a table until a council that had not been asked to look at them chose to, and that no one, not the keeper, not the council, not Ellen Marsh herself, could say when that might be, or whether it ever would.

## IV. Of the Census Clerks

She wrote her reply the same night, before the stillness had time to cool into something more governable and less exact.

She did not write in anger, or not in any anger a reader could have pointed to in a single line; she was too careful a hand for that, and too old a teacher of grammar to let a sentence run away from her meaning. But she wrote, plainly, that she did not think the standing of spoken witness was so untried a question as the council supposed. She reminded the keeper — though she did not think he needed reminding, and said so — that when Cunntas nan Làmh was last taken in the shires, the clerks who came north to count the northern towns had counted nothing, but had taken the figures of every town from Tional nan Tuathach's own mouth, written them down on their own authority with no other proof asked or given, and that this spoken tale, and no other kind, was the figure entered afterward in the kingdom's own returns and used by Tional nan Tuathach in its dealings with the council to this day. She had seen the page herself, she wrote, in Tional nan Tuathach's own minute-book, the year the figures were read into the room and the two words written under them that were the whole of what the room had thought fit to say. If spoken witness had stood good enough, without question, to fix what a shire owed and what it was owed, she did not see by what rule it stood too uncertain to be shelved, unweighed against nothing, beside a written return that no one had ever asked to prove.

She wrote that she would not press the council to believe An t-Aon Leabhar Deug over anything an Leabharlann already held. She asked only, again, that they be kept where they could be found, and left the rest, as she had the first time, to whoever came after her with the patience to read them.

Nobody saw the letter before she sent it, not even Martha, who would have read it with approval and said so and perhaps, being Martha, have found some way to make it the mills' business as well as her own; Ellen wanted no more behind it than her own name. She sealed it and gave it to the carrier the next market day, and went back to the term's slates, and did not, in the weeks after, ask whether an answer had come, because she had already had the only answer there was going to be, and a second letter would only have dressed the same one differently.

## V. Of the Parsing

The children came back to their benches the first week of an t-Sultain, brown from the summer and restless at their letters, and Ellen, who had spent eleven years deciding what was worth a class's morning and what was not, took Raghnall mac Mhuirich's letter out of her satchel on the second day and read it to them entire, standing at the front of the room with the sun coming in low and yellow through the tall north windows.

She did not tell them, at first, what it was about, only that it was a real letter, lately received, and that she wanted their ears on the words and not the matter, since the matter was hers to carry and the words were a lesson any of them might use. She read it through once without stopping, and then began again from the top, slower, and stopped this time at the end of nearly every sentence to ask a child to say what it did: here was the subject, here the thing done to it, here a clause that leaned on another and would fall without it, here a word chosen, she said, because it let a man say a great deal while appearing to promise nothing at all.

"What does 'not refused' mean?" she asked, at the sentence that held it, and a girl near the stove, quick with her tongue and quicker with her temper, said at once that it meant *no*.

"It doesn't say no."

"It means no all the same, missus."

"Then why doesn't it say so?"

The girl thought about that longer than she thought about most things, turning her slate over in her lap. "Because," she said slowly, "if he said no, you could ask him why. And there's no answering 'not yet.'"

Ellen let that stand a moment before she went on, because it was, she thought, as exact a piece of parsing as she was likely to get out of any of them that year, truer to the letter's working than half the grammar she had meant to teach from it. She showed them the long sentence in the middle, the one that turned on itself three times before it came to rest, and had them find where the turns were, and asked whether a shorter sentence could not have said the same thing, and whether, if it could, there might be a reason a careful man chose not to say it shorter. A boy at the back, who rarely had much to offer on any morning that did not involve sums, said that his father had told him once that a long fence took longer to climb than a short one, whatever height it stood, and the room laughed, and Ellen let them, and did not correct him, because he had not, in her judgment, said anything that wanted correcting.

She did not tell them, that morning, what had become of the request, only that it concerned some books she had made herself over many years, and that the letter was the answer she had had about them; and when the quick girl by the stove asked outright whether the books would go to an Leabharlann or not, Ellen said, in the same plain voice she had used all morning on subjects and clauses, that she did not know, and that not knowing was itself a thing worth being able to say plainly, since a great many grown people spent a great deal of ink trying not to.

The lesson ran past its hour, and she let it, since the day was long and the harvest not yet calling any of them away. When at last she sent them out to the yard she folded the letter back into her satchel, along with the fair copy of her own reply that she had kept for her own record beside the eleventh book, and stood a while at the window watching them scatter across the grass in the last of the low sun, loud and unhurried, as children are who have not yet been told that a table is a place where a true thing can be laid down and left to lie.

# Chapter Eighteen: Of the Leòid Ruling

*DE 18*

## I. Of the Wool Contract

The letter that began it was not addressed to Seumas mac Eachainn at all, and he read it only because the clerk whose table it belonged to was down with a chest cold and had asked him, as a favour between neighbours at the long table, to sort what came in until she was back on her feet.

It was from Tional nan Tuathach's wool mills at Doire ghlas, a contract of the plainest kind, three lines longer than it needed to be only because the mill's clerk had been taught to write a full sentence and could not bring himself to stop short of one: that the mill would take its winter coal from Cnoc thais and Muileann àrsaidh, at the price those towns asked, and no longer from Comhairle nam Mèinnean's yard at Cathair mhòr, Comhairle nam Mèinnean's price having risen twice in two years while the fires under the mill's own vats burned no hotter for it. Seumas read it twice, because the first time he did not believe the figure at the foot, and filed it in the tray marked for the master's own hand, because it plainly was not his to answer.

He was forty that spring, and had been four years Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerk at Cathair mhòr, a post he had not asked for and had not thought, at four-and-twenty riding north with Iain Ruadh mac Nèill to watch a northern fire go out, that he would ever hold. Iain Ruadh sat two tables down still, grey now past red, half deaf in the ear nearer the door, and looked at the world through the coal he had spent his life measuring and found it, on the whole, unimproved by dubhan. He had not been north again since that first ride. He said the road was longer than it used to be, by which he meant that he was.

"There'll be more of those," Iain Ruadh said, when Seumas told him what the letter held, not looking up from the return he was totting. "The pit towns sell dear to us and cheap to their own kind. It's not a mystery. A man sells cheap where he must live after."

"It's the mills I'm thinking of. If Doire ghlas buys northern coal—"

"Then Cathair gheal will, and Cathair mhòr's own tanners after that, and in a twelvemonth every mill from here to the strait is burning coal that never paid An Crùn's fifth to anybody, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's yard stands full and nobody comes for it." Iain Ruadh set down his pen. "I've seen a seam go like that. Not all at once. A gallery here, a gallery there, until one quarter you look at the returns and the whole face is gone and you cannot say the day it went."

Seumas did not answer that, because there was no answer in it that would not sound as though he were arguing with a man thirty years his elder about a mountain the man had walked underground before Seumas was born. He went back to the tray, and by the time the regular clerk was back at her table the letter from Doire ghlas had three more like it behind it, from Cathair gheal, from a tannery at Ros gheal, from a brewer at Baile ìseal who wrote that he saw no shame in warming his own vats with whatever coal came cheapest and would take no lecture on the matter from a Board that had never once, in thirty years, carried coal north of the boundary stones for a Tuathach hearth to burn.

Seumas kept that last one on his own table longer than the others.

## II. Of the Quarter

The master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean at Cathair mhòr was Fearghas mac Aonghais, a broad, short-necked man of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own service who had risen to the mastership from the yard rather than from the mine office's tables, and who trusted a column of figures the way other men trusted a priest. He called for the northern returns himself in the third week of am Màrt, which he had not done in Seumas's four years at the table, and Seumas carried them in and stood while the master read.

It took him the better part of an hour to draw them properly: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's takings from every northern account, set against the same quarter of the year before, town by town, with the wool mills' new contract entered where it belonged and a note beside it in his own hand, because a note seemed to him owed. When the sum stood at the foot of the page it was down by a quarter on the year before, and by more than a quarter against the quarter before that, and no part of the fall lay anywhere but in the five holdout towns' own coal finding buyers that had once bought from Comhairle nam Mèinnean and now did not.

"A quarter," Fearghas said, when Seumas laid the page before him, and said nothing else for a while, turning the page as though a second look might find him a different sum on it. "In how long?"

"Eighteen months, master, near enough. It was steady until the wool mills went over, and it has moved faster from that month on."

"Since when has anyone in the north had coin enough to buy coal at all, that An Crùn never saw a fifth of?"

"Since the fuel came, master. They sell the dubhan they cannot use themselves, and buy each other's coal with the coin it brings." Seumas had thought about how to say this on the ride in, turning the sentence over as a man turns a coin to see it is not counterfeit, and it came out flatter than he had meant it, which he thought afterwards was as well. "It's an honest trade between them. I've no figures that say otherwise."

Fearghas mac Aonghais looked at him for a moment in a way Seumas had not been looked at before in that office, the way a man looks at a tool to see whether it will do the next job as well as it did the last.

"Nobody asked you whether it was honest," he said, and it was not said unkindly either. "You're asked what it costs Comhairle nam Mèinnean. You've told me. Go and find me Breith Leòid. The whole of it, not the digest. I want the words she used."

## III. Of the Ruling Read Again

Breith Leòid had lain in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own press for eighty years, copied twice since, once when the press at Seann Bhral burned and once, later, for no reason the docket gave, and Seumas found the newer copy within the hour and carried it to the master's room himself rather than send it by a runner, because he wanted, without admitting it even to himself, to hear how it was read.

Eilidh nic Leòid had ruled, sitting at Seann Bhral in the eighth year of the old count, that the land the Tuathaich held under the humans' title passed to An Crùn, and that the right to work it stayed with the holders and their heirs. The rulings of the circuit that followed on it, copied into the margin of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's press copy in three different hands, had settled the rest: that the holders' right ran with the payment of An Crùn's fifth and failed with it; and that nothing in the ruling bound Comhairle nam Mèinnean to carry any holder's coal it did not choose to carry. It had been written, Seumas judged from the language, to settle where the north should stand when the humans' titles fell, and it had gone on being cited for eighty years in every land case the north had brought, because it gave the holders their right in one clause and, read with its margins, let Comhairle nam Mèinnean withdraw its custom and keep its claim both.

Fearghas mac Aonghais read it through once, slowly, moving his lips over the harder clauses as a man does who reads more figures than sentences, and set it down.

"Comhairle nam Mèinnean stopped carrying from the western pits when the branch to Àth leathan was closed," he said. "Before the fuel."

"Twenty years, master, near enough. The branch closed in the sixty-eighth year of the old count. They went on paying the fifth all the same, by cart and by boat, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean entered it as arrears, until the agreement."

"And since the agreement?"

"Not from the western towns. Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh, Tobar dhearg and Àth leathan have paid nothing to Comhairle nam Mèinnean's account since the agreement they signed among themselves. I have the ledger, if the master wants the figure."

"I don't want the figure. I know the figure." Fearghas mac Aonghais stood, which he did not often do at his own table, and went to the window, which looked out over the yard where a dubhan tank stood being filled from a cart, and said nothing for long enough that Seumas began to wonder whether he was dismissed. "Under her ruling, the right lapsed the day the fifth stopped, whatever the reason it stopped. It doesn't ask whether Comhairle nam Mèinnean's reason for not carrying was a good one. It only asks whether the fifth came in. It didn't."

"They would say Comhairle nam Mèinnean stopped carrying first, master, and the fifth was owed on carrying."

"They can say what they like. It isn't in the ruling. I've read it twice now and it isn't in it." He turned back from the window. "Write the report. The northern revenue down a quarter in eighteen months, the cause named plain: the holdout pits underselling Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own coal to Tuathaich buyers who were Comhairle nam Mèinnean's custom until they had somewhere cheaper to go. And the remedy, since the council will ask for one whether I give it or not: that under Breith Leòid the western seams are An Crùn's to take back, the holders having let the fifth lapse these two years, and that Comhairle nam Mèinnean declare them so and order the pits shut until such time as they are worked again under An Crùn's own hand."

Seumas wrote it that same evening, at the long table after the others had gone, with the lamp turned low to spare the oil, and every figure in it was true. He had drawn them himself and checked them twice, and he would have sworn to any of them before the council or before Manannan's own altar. It was only when the report was fair-copied and sealed, and he sat looking at his own name at the foot of it as the hand that drew the figures, that he let himself think, for the length of one candle burning a finger's breadth, about what a true figure could be made to carry that the man who drew it had never meant it to carry. He had written that the north bought its own coal with dubhan's coin. He had not written that Comhairle nam Mèinnean had itself stopped carrying that coal first, and taken the western towns' custom away before it complained of losing it; that sentence was in the ruling and not in his report, because the master had not asked for it, and a clerk's figures went where he was told to send them and no further.

He thought of the brewer's letter at Baile ìseal, still in his own tray, that no coal had gone north of the boundary stones in thirty years, and put the thought away, because there was nothing to be done with it that would not cost him his place and change nothing else at all.

## IV. Of the Order Carried North

Comhairle nam Mèinnean's decree went out under Fearghas mac Aonghais's seal on the twentieth of an Giblean: that the western seams, their right to work them lapsed under Breith Leòid for two years' unpaid fifth, were declared An Crùn's; that the pits at Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh, Tobar dhearg and Àth leathan were ordered shut from that day; and that any coal raised from them after the order was coal of An Crùn, taken without right, and answerable at law.

It went north by Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own courier to the maor of the western Seann Skell, who read it standing at his own door because the courier would not wait, and who sent for the town's clerk before he had finished reading it a second time, because he judged, rightly, that a paper of that weight wanted two witnesses to its arrival rather than one.

"They'll not shut," the clerk said, when he had read it in his turn. "Not for a paper."

"No," said the maor. "I don't suppose they will."

He was right in both halves of it. The word reached Muileann àrsaidh within the week, by a carrier who had it from a Cnoc thais man who had it from the maor's own clerk, and the five towns' answer, when it came, came not to Comhairle nam Mèinnean but to each other, in the form of a letter passed hand to hand and signed by none of them formally, that the pits would go on working until the seams themselves were spent, An Crùn having never carried their coal, never paid a wage in their pits and never, in all the years since the agreement, sent so much as a surveyor to say what it thought the seams were worth. They had stopped paying the fifth, the letter said, when Comhairle nam Mèinnean stopped earning it. If Comhairle nam Mèinnean wished the fifth restored, it might restore the carrying first, and the fifth would follow the same week.

Both were true, and both sides knew both were true, and neither the truth of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's claim nor the truth of the towns' answer moved either an inch from where it had stood since the wool mills of Doire ghlas first went over to northern coal. The letter never reached Cathair mhòr in any form Comhairle nam Mèinnean would call an answer; it was read at Muileann àrsaidh, at Cnoc thais and at Àth leathan, and its substance, rather than its words, made its way south by the same carriers' road the order had come north on, so that within a month it was generally known at Cathair mhòr, without ever having been formally received, that the western towns did not mean to obey.

The five towns met, as they had met before, in Sarah Dunmore's kitchen at Muileann àrsaidh and then in the pit-shed when the kitchen would not hold them all, and Ruth Calder read Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order aloud from the paper a carrier had brought, twice through, once fast and once slow, so that no one in the shed could afterwards say he had not heard every word of it. Tom Varley wanted the letter answered line for line, clause against clause, in the manner of a man who has read a great many contracts and does not trust a paper that goes unchallenged. Ruth said Comhairle nam Mèinnean had not asked for a clause-by-clause answer and would not read one if it were sent; Comhairle nam Mèinnean had asked for the pits shut, and the only answer that mattered was whether the coal came up on the morning after the order's date. It came up. Nobody at Muileann àrsaidh put down a tool, and the shed voted, without much debate and without a show of hands anyone troubled to count, to go on as before and let Comhairle nam Mèinnean make the next move, since it plainly meant to make one regardless of anything the towns wrote in reply.

"They'll send men," said Sarah Dunmore, who had said little through the meeting and was heard the more for it. "A paper that isn't obeyed gets men sent after it. It always has."

Nobody answered her, because nobody could say she was wrong, and the meeting broke up into the wet evening with the matter no further settled than it had been when it opened, except that every person in the shed now carried, alongside the day's ordinary work, the private certainty that the paper nailed to nothing yet would shortly be nailed to something.

## V. Of Somhairle mac Lachlainn

Somhairle mac Lachlainn had come up through Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers by the same road most of them came, from a farm too small to keep a second son, into a company that had existed for forty years to see harbour-dues paid and smugglers' coal weighed at Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own scale. In eighteen years he had made himself the man other captains sent for when a thing wanted doing quietly, whether or not it stayed quiet once he had started on it. He was two-and-forty that autumn, broad through the shoulder in the way a farm makes a man rather than a drill-yard, with a scar through one eyebrow from a fight at Ros dhomhain's quay he never spoke of and a reputation, among the men under him, for giving an order once and expecting it obeyed without a second telling.

He was sent for at Cathair mhòr in the last week of an t-Sultain, called before Fearghas mac Aonghais and a councillor of the Rìoghachd he did not know by sight, and told, in fewer words than he had expected the matter to take, that a company of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers was to go north to the western Seann Skell before the winter closed the roads, and that he was to command it.

"How many men, master?"

"Forty. What Comhairle nam Mèinnean can spare from the southern stations without leaving them bare."

"And their orders, once we're there?"

"To see the shutting order held. No pit at Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh, Tobar dhearg or Àth leathan is to raise coal after the day you arrive. You'll post men at the pit-heads. You'll not close the town, nor the road, nor any house that isn't a pit-head. That's the whole of it."

"And if they raise coal anyway."

The councillor answered that one, before Fearghas mac Aonghais could. "Then you'll have shown Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order cannot be held with forty men and a captain, and the council will decide what it wants to do about that. Your business, mac Lachlainn, is to hold the order, not to fight a war nobody has declared."

Somhairle mac Lachlainn took the order as it was given, because it was not his place to say that a company sent to stand at five pit-heads in a country that had buried its dead against Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own kind within living memory was already more than a policing matter, whatever the council chose to call it. He asked for, and was given, forty men of his own choosing rather than whoever the southern stations cared to spare, choosing men who had served under him before over younger men who had not, which the master noted and did not question.

Two days ahead of the company he rode north alone, to see the ground before he brought men onto it, and crossed the boundary stones on a grey morning with rain coming and going in the west, much as another man had crossed them sixteen years before on a different errand. He did not stop at the stones. He had crossed them a dozen times in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's service, weighing coal at a scale or carrying a summons, and had never yet been north of them with a company at his back, and he found, riding alone through the same bare ridges Seumas mac Eachainn had ridden as a young man, that the difference sat on him more heavily than he had thought it would.

He lay that night at a road-house south of the western Seann Skell, a low place with a dubhan lamp over the door and a landlord who asked no questions beyond what he was owed for the bed, and lay awake a while going over the ground he had ridden and the ground still ahead of it, in the way a man does the night before a piece of work he has not done before, whatever its size. He had put men in harm's way often enough, at a smuggler's landing or a quay brawl gone past reason, and had never yet lost one; he set some store by that record, privately, the way another man might set store by a relic, and did not care to think too closely about how far it could be made to stretch. Forty men at five pit-heads in a country that had not seen a company under arms since before his own grandfather's time was not a smuggler's landing, and he knew it, and had said as much to the councillor at Cathair mhòr in words careful enough not to sound like a refusal, because refusing had never once, in eighteen years of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's service, been a road that led anywhere he wanted to go.

He thought, before he slept, of the scar over his eyebrow, taken at Ros dhomhain's quay from a smuggler's boat-hook in a scuffle that had gone wrong in the space of ten seconds and never once, in the years since, made him careful in the way other men's scars seemed to make them careful. It had taught him instead to move first and explain after, which had served him well enough among smugglers and harbour thieves, men who understood a blow and a purse and little else. He did not know yet what it would teach him among five towns that understood a great deal more than that, and meant, plainly, to go on understanding it in their own time and by their own lights, whatever paper Comhairle nam Mèinnean sent north to tell them otherwise.

## VI. Of the Company at the Western Seann Skell

The company came up the western road on the sixteenth of an Dàmhair, forty men and their baggage-carts, in a rain that had set in for the day and showed no sign of lifting, and the western Seann Skell watched them come from doorways and from the harbour wall without a stone thrown and without a word of welcome, which Somhairle mac Lachlainn, riding at their head, judged the worse of the two receptions a town could give.

He quartered them at the old customs shed above the harbour, the only building in the town large enough and empty enough to hold forty men, and paid the maor's clerk for the use of it out of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own purse rather than requisition it, which the clerk noted in his book without comment and which Somhairle did for reasons he would not have found easy to set out plainly even to himself, beyond a sense that a company that paid its way stood on firmer ground than one that did not, in a country where it had no ground of its own to stand on.

He sent men to Muileann àrsaidh, to Cnoc thais and to the three smaller towns within the week, not to close the pits by force, which forty men scattered across five towns could not have done in any case, but to stand at each pit-head with Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order nailed to the winding-gear and to report, twice weekly, whether coal came up. At Cnoc thais, Tom Varley met the two men sent there at the pit-head himself, read the order nailed to the post without a word, and told them they were welcome to stand there as long as they liked, the coal coming up whether they stood or not, and that he would see they were given tea at midday like anyone else standing about in the wet, since it was no fault of theirs that they had been sent.

They took the tea. The coal came up.

Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, at Muileann chaol, wrote the whole of it into the day's page when word reached her, some ten days after the company had marched, in fewer words than the matter seemed to her to deserve, and added at the foot of the entry, in the small close hand she kept for the things she judged worth remembering past their own day, that it was the first company the kingdom had sent armed toward the north since An Dealachadh itself, near ninety years gone, and that no one now living who had signed the truce at the boundary stones was left to say whether it was meant as more than a policing matter, or whether anyone, on either side of the stones, still believed that it could stay one.

Seumas mac Eachainn read the report of the company's quartering at his own table at Cathair mhòr, three weeks after he had written the figures that had, by a road he had not chosen and could not now shorten, put it on the road north, and found in himself no surprise at all, which troubled him rather more than surprise would have done. His figures had been true. He had drawn them carefully, checked them twice, and would draw the next quarter's the same way, because that was the whole of his office and he did not know how to hold any other. But he understood now, reading of forty men quartered above a harbour he had once ridden into as a young man with Iain Ruadh's mare setting the pace, that a true figure asked to serve a purpose would serve it faithfully, and that the purpose was never his to choose, only the figure, and that he had known this from the evening he sat with the report before him and the candle burning down, and had sent it anyway.

He wrote the next quarter's returns without adding anything the master had not asked for. It was, he told himself, the whole of what a clerk owed the truth: to draw it exactly, and to leave what was done with it to hands that were not his.

# Chapter Nineteen: Of the Depot Nobody Would Bless

*DE 19*

## I. Of the Ground by the River

Somhairle mac Lachlainn had been a soldier of paper before he was a soldier of anything else, and it showed in the way he laid out the depot: string and pegs first, then the foundations, then the men. He walked the ground above the river at Seann Skell in the west on a grey morning in am Màrt with Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyor's plan under his arm, and where the plan said the wall should run he set a peg, and where it did not he let the whin stand.

The company had been three months in the town by then, quartered in the old customs shed above the river harbour, which Comhairle nam Mèinnean paid for and nobody else wanted, and in three months Somhairle had learned the shape of the place the way he had once learned the shape of a muster roll: the citadel on its rock, empty since before his grandfather's time, its gate rehung with new iron; the river road running north to Muileann àrsaidh and the pit towns, ten miles and more, climbing all the way; the quay where the coal barges had once tied up three deep and now lay two, and those two waiting on cargo that did not come. He had learned, too, which doors opened to him and which did not, though nobody in the town had struck him or thrown a stone at him yet, in am Màrt. That came later, and by a different road than he expected.

The depot was Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own notion, and a plain one: the enforcers' lorries wanted dubhan, and dubhan wanted a tank, a pump, and a roofed place to keep the barrels dry between the boats that brought it up from the south and the wagons that would carry it on to wherever Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order sent it next. Somhairle had built worse things with less. He set the masons on the tank's foundations first, six courses of dressed stone with a puddled clay lining that Comhairle nam Mèinnean's engineer swore by, and while they worked he rode the ten miles to Muileann àrsaidh and back twice a week to see what the pit towns were doing, which for the most part was nothing he could report, since a wall of spoil and timber going up slowly, a cart at a time, over a winter, does not look like defiance until it is finished.

He wrote his first report on the fourteenth of am Màrt, three plain paragraphs: the depot's ground broken, the quay's second berth cleared for the dubhan boats, no incident at Muileann àrsaidh worth Comhairle nam Mèinnean's attention. Every word of it was true, and he sealed it believing so. Some months would pass before he learned that a report could be true in every sentence and still be a kind of lie, a thing a man came to by doing it, not by being told.

The masons finished the tank's stonework by the middle of an Cèitean, and the carpenters raised the roof over it the same month, a long shed of tarred boards not unlike the shipmasters' sheds Somhairle had seen once at the southern Seann Skell, save that this one had no chimney and no smell but pitch and new-cut wood. The lorries themselves had not yet come; two were promised from the capital for midsummer, the first the western Seann Skell had ever seen, and the town's children had already worked out where they would stand to watch them arrive, a fact Somhairle knew because his corporal reported it to him with more relish than he reported most things.

He had come to the west with forty men and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's authority to shut what Breith Leòid had declared shut, and had expected, from what he had read at Cathair mhòr, a fight or the threat of one within the month. What he found was a town that answered him in two tongues and told him nothing in either, pit towns above him on the river road going on hewing coal as though no ruling had been made at all, and a season of building instead of a season of soldiering, which suited him less than he would have said aloud to any of his officers. The depot itself he had not asked for. It came down to him in an order three lines long, much like the note the house of Òrd Mhanannain would send him in return before the season was out, and he built it because it was built, the way a man drills a company because the drilling is ordered, without troubling himself overmuch about what it would be used for once it stood.

The town watched him build it. Seann Skell in the west was not a large place, three thousand and more souls between the quay and the citadel, but it had eyes enough, and Somhairle came in the first weeks to know which of the faces at the market stalls and the bridge-end were merely curious and which were counting: the courses of stone as they rose, the size of the tank, the number of men set to the work each week. He did not think, that spring, that the counting meant anything he needed to answer. It was a plain building. He never understood, afterwards, why it was the building nobody would bless.

## II. Of the House That Would Not Bless

The custom of the town, and of every town on that coast so far as Somhairle had troubled to learn it, was that a new roof got a blessing before it was worked under, the way a new boat got one before it was launched: a house of the old faith sent a man to walk the ground and say the words, and the town's masons would not lay a floor inside walls that had not had it. Piety was too grand a word for it, most of them would have said; it was the same caution that kept a farmer from ploughing a field on the wrong day of the moon. Somhairle had watched it done for the customs shed's new door the winter before, a custodian of Òrd Mhanannain come down from the house on the hill with a bowl of sea-water and a few words nobody troubled to explain to him, and thought no more of it than he thought of any other local weather.

He sent his corporal to the house of Òrd Mhanannain in the last week of an Cèitean, with a civil note asking that a custodian come and bless the depot's roof before the tank was filled, and naming a day that suited the masons. The note came back within the hour, in a hand Somhairle did not know, three lines long: the house of Òrd Mhanannain at Seann Skell did not bless what was built for Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers, and hoped the captain would trouble it no further on the matter.

Somhairle went himself the next morning. It was not pride so much as disbelief; he had asked leave to be refused things before, by councils and by weather, but never in three lines from a house he had never troubled.

The house stood on the rise behind the citadel, a low grey building with a well in its yard and a single window facing the river, unglazed, the shutter folded back. The man who came out to him at the gate was younger than Somhairle had pictured from the hand of the letter, thin, sunburned across the nose the way a man gets who works outdoors and forgets his hat, in the plain grey the order wore.

"I had your note," Somhairle said, "and I came to ask it again myself, in case the corporal put it badly. It's a roof over a tank, nothing more. I'm told the custom is to bless a new roof before the town's men work under it, and my masons are the town's men."

"Your masons are the town's men," the priest said. "What's under the roof is Comhairle nam Mèinnean's, and what will stand beside it before the year's out is yours." He did not raise his voice.
