"We bless a boat because the sea doesn't ask whose it is before it drowns a man. We bless a roof because rain doesn't ask either. I'll not pretend the same of a depot built to keep your lorries fuelled on the road to Muileann àrsaidh, captain, because you and I both know the rain isn't the thing I'd be blessing it against."

Somhairle had heard evasions dressed as plain speaking often enough to know the difference, and this was not that. He stood a moment with the morning coming up warm off the river behind him and found he had no answer that was not either an argument about theology he had no standing to make, or a threat he had no wish to make.

"Then I'll trouble you no further," he said, and did.

He wrote of it to Àrd-choimheadaiche at the southern Seann Skell that same afternoon. The house of Òrd Mhanannain answered to no one outside itself, being its own master under a different order entirely; he wrote to Alasdair mac Ìomhair anyway, for want of anyone else in the whole of the old faith who might see the thing plainly and not as a quarrel between the enforcers and the north. He set down the refusal in the priest's own words, as near as he could remember them, and asked, since the house on the hill would not come, whether some other house might, so that the masons would work under a blessed roof as any other masons on that coast expected to.

The answer came back inside the fortnight, over Alasdair mac Ìomhair's own hand, and said less than Somhairle had hoped and more than he had expected. The Àrd-choimheadaiche would not command a house of Òrd Mhanannain, he wrote, no more than the priest's own master could command a custodian of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail; but Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail blessed what it was asked to bless, north or south, Board or town, and if the depot's roof wanted the words said over it, a custodian of the southern house would come and say them.

He came in the first week of an t-Iuchar, a young custodian named Pàdraig, sent the two days' road from the south with a letter of introduction and nothing else, no escort, riding a hired horse he did not know how to manage and arriving stiff and saddle-sore an hour after the masons had given up expecting him. He said the words over the depot's roof at evening, with Somhairle and half a dozen of the enforcers standing by and none of the town's own people, though a good many watched from the bridge and further off, at a distance that made plain it was watching and not attending. The words themselves were nearer to what Somhairle had watched said over the customs shed's door than he had expected, the same bowl carried out and the same slow walk round the four corners of the building, and he found himself, standing bare-headed in the last of the evening light with his men behind him, oddly moved by a thing he had asked for chiefly as a matter of custom and had not thought to feel anything about at all.

Pàdraig ate with the officers that night, a quiet young man who asked Somhairle a great many questions about the road north, how far it ran, how the towns along it stood, whether Comhairle nam Mèinnean's writ carried past Muileann àrsaidh or stopped short of it, and answered none of Somhairle's questions in turn about the house of Òrd Mhanannain or why the southern house had sent a man two days' ride when a house on the hill above the depot could have walked down in a quarter of an hour. He rode south again the next morning, stiff still, and thanked Somhairle for the horse's keep in a way that made plain he did not expect to be sent north again on such an errand, and he was not.

The masons worked under the blessed roof without complaint, being, as the priest had said, the town's men and glad of the wage whoever paid it. But it was noticed, and remembered, that the depot had been blessed by a stranger's hand from the south, and not by the house that stood in sight of its own roof, and the town had a name for the building inside the month that was not Comhairle nam Mèinnean's name for it, though Somhairle never learned what it was, his corporal having more sense than to tell him.

## III. Of the Letter Filed

What Somhairle did not see, and could not have, was the letter Martha Greaves wrote from Caol mhòr at the summer's end, though it touched his depot as nearly as anything in that year.

She wrote it at Tional nan Tuathach's table, with Peter Hale reading over her shoulder and putting in a word here and there that she mostly did not take, because the letter was hers to write as speaker and she had turned it over in her mind on the road down from Doire ghlas until she had it by heart before she set pen to paper. It said, in substance, what Tional nan Tuathach's delegates had been saying to one another in the corridor outside the hall for a month: that the five towns of the western hills would not shut their pits for a letter carried by a Board's clerk, whatever Breith Leòid said the seams now were; that Tional nan Tuathach was no party to the quarrel and wished to be none; and that a year's delay, while Tional nan Tuathach itself sent men to treat with the towns, would cost Comhairle nam Mèinnean nothing it had not already lost, and might cost the kingdom a great deal less than the alternative.

She did not write the word the alternative meant, having no wish to be the one who first put it on paper, and Peter Hale, reading the sentence over her shoulder, said nothing about the omission either, though both of them understood it.

The letter went up to the capital by the ordinary post, and was read, Tional nan Tuathach's minute later recorded, at a sitting of the council in the first week of an t-Sultain, at which Somhairle mac Lachlainn was not present and of which he knew nothing beyond what his own masters chose to tell him, which was nothing at all. The council's clerk entered it as received. No answer was sent. It went, with the rest of that quarter's correspondence, into the press where such letters were kept, in a folder with a paper label in a clerk's hand that said only *Tional nan Tuathach, western towns*, and there it lay through the autumn and the winter that followed, read again, so far as the record shows, by no one until long after the matter it asked about had been settled by other means.

Martha Greaves learned, some weeks later, that the letter had been received and filed, and no more than that; the phrase itself, filed, has stood ever since in the north for an answer that is not one.

Peter Hale, who had wanted a harder letter and had said so at Tional nan Tuathach's table before Martha wrote the one she meant to write, told the delegates at the next sitting that a filed letter was better than a refused one, since a refusal closed a door and a filing merely left it shut, which was not the same thing and might yet be opened. Ruth Calder, who had walked out of Tional nan Tuathach five years before and sat now among the western towns' own people rather than among Tional nan Tuathach's, heard him say it, and said nothing back. Tional nan Tuathach's letter went into the record as its own act, the last it would take in that quarrel that asked for anything so plain as a year's grace, and it is remembered in the western hills, where such things are remembered exactly, for what it asked and for the single word that answered it.

## IV. Of the Stones on the Road

The first skirmish that An Clàr Foscailte does not name happened on the Muileann àrsaidh road in the second week of an t-Sultain, and the north tells it thus.

A lorry of the enforcers, one of the two promised in midsummer and only lately come, was sent up from the depot with a load of timber for the post Comhairle nam Mèinnean meant to build on the road below Muileann àrsaidh, the same post whose foundations had not yet been dug. It went up the river road in the early morning with two men in it, a driver and a corporal, and it did not come back by dusk, when it was looked for. It came back after dark instead, one wheel stove and the timber gone, and the corporal with a cut over his eye he would not say how he came by, though the driver, a Seann Skell man with kin in the town, was not so close-mouthed among his own people, and what he told them, in the way of such things, went from the depot's yard to the quay to the whole town inside two days, and from there, by the carriers who worked the river road, to Muileann àrsaidh itself before the month was out, told there a little differently than it was told at the depot, as such things are.

The telling that held in the pit towns says that the lorry came up past the second milestone below the town in the grey of the morning, and that word of it had gone ahead by whatever road word travels faster than a lorry on a bad surface, so that by the time it reached the narrow place where the road runs between the old spoil-heap and the river, there were men on the heap above it, not many, the telling says, and none of them known to any teller who did not already know them before that morning. Most of them had nothing to fire with that year, and none fired. They threw stones, and rolled two loosened boulders down from the heap into the road ahead of the lorry, and stood where they could be seen and counted, though the telling is careful never to give a number, until the driver turned the lorry about in the narrow place, no easy thing, and took it back down the way it had come, the corporal's cut earned, the telling says, by a stone and not by a blow, though it does not press the point.

The enforcers' side of it, as a man of the depot told it afterwards, to another man who by then had his own reasons to ask, runs shorter and says less. He said they had gone up with the timber as ordered, had found the road blocked above the spoil-heap by stones that might have fallen or might not, had turned back rather than clear it themselves with no escort and no orders covering the case, and that somewhere in the turning the corporal had taken a knock he made light of. He did not say he had seen anyone on the heap. Asked directly, years afterwards, by someone who had reason to press him, he said he had not looked up at the heap at all, being occupied with the lorry. The man who asked him did not press further, though he did not look wholly satisfied either.

Neither telling gives a name. An Clàr Foscailte gives none either: it was not written down at the time, being, in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own later word for such things, not great enough to name, and it was one of a dozen or a score that autumn on that road and others like it, none counted, none put in any report that reached beyond the depot's own book, until they had between them made a thing too large to call by any of their separate names.

There was a second such meeting on the same road before an t-Sultain was out, and a third on the shorter track above Àth leathan that the escorted wagons had begun to use instead, and Somhairle came, over that month, to recognise the shape of the thing before he had words for it: a load sent up, a delay reported, a man come back with a graze or a fright or nothing at all beyond a story he told differently each time he told it. None of it was war. He would have said so himself, that autumn, and believed it. The wall at Muileann àrsaidh grew a little higher through the same weeks, a cartload of spoil and a length of timber at a time, and no one on either side of the shire line called that war either, though it was built for nothing else.

Somhairle heard of it from the corporal himself that same night, the cut still open, the man more shaken by the stove wheel and the lost timber than by the blow, or saying so. He asked him three times whether he had seen who threw the stones, or how many there had been, and got, each time, a slightly different answer. Somhairle judged it no lie: a frightened man in a turning lorry on a bad road in poor light does not see clearly, and does not know afterwards how much of what he remembers he has built since. That judgement went into the report he began that night and did not finish until the following morning.

## V. Of the Report That Said Less

He wrote three drafts.

The first said what the corporal had told him, in the corporal's own uncertain words, three men seen or perhaps five, stones and two boulders, the lorry turned back, the timber lost, no shots fired on either side, no man badly hurt. He read it over and struck out *seen or perhaps five*, because he did not believe the corporal had seen anything of the kind, and wrote instead *a number not established*.

The second, written the next morning with a clearer head, said less again: an obstruction on the Muileann àrsaidh road, the lorry returned undamaged beyond a wheel, the timber not delivered, to be sent up again under escort. He looked at *undamaged* for a long while, the wheel in fact having cost three days at the wheelwright's, and let it stand, because a stove wheel was a fact Comhairle nam Mèinnean's engineer would ask after in a way a captain's judgement of a crowd on a spoil-heap would not be asked after at all, and Somhairle had begun, without quite deciding to, to weigh his sentences by what question each one would draw down on him, and to prefer the ones that would draw down none.

The third was the one he sent. It said that a lorry sent to the Muileann àrsaidh road with timber for the new post had met an obstruction and returned; that the timber would go up again under proper escort; that there had been no engagement. The word stones did not appear in it, nor the corporal's cut, which had by then closed and would leave, the surgeon said, no scar worth the noting. Somhairle read the third draft over twice, found nothing in it that was false, and sealed it. Riding out the next morning to see the escort chosen for the timber's second try, he told himself that a report existed to answer the questions a superior officer needed answered, and that a captain who filled every page with every uncertain thing a frightened corporal half remembered was not doing his superiors a service, whatever he was doing for the truth of the matter.

He believed this for the length of the ride, more or less, and found, dismounting at the depot's gate, that he no longer entirely did, though he could not have said where in the three miles the belief had worn through.

It was some weeks after, at the foot of the year, that Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerk at Cathair mhòr forwarded to Somhairle, without comment, a copy of a letter that had come up from Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd at Muileann chaol, asking Comhairle nam Mèinnean for its returns of the incidents on the northern roads that autumn, so that the record might be kept as fully as the record was kept of everything else the kingdom did. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh had written it herself, in the same plain hand she had used for every such asking in the four-and-twenty years she had kept the kingdom's chronicle, believing, as she wrote it, that the office she wrote to would answer as every office had always answered a chronicler's plain question, with what it had, no more and no less; that had always been the custom of the kingdom's record, and she had not yet had cause to doubt it held. She set the letter down among the day's other copying and thought no more of it than the fifty other such letters she sent out in an ordinary year.

It was Sìleas nic Rath, reading the returns as they failed to come through the following weeks, who first said aloud in an Leabharlann's upper room that Comhairle nam Mèinnean's silence on this one letter did not feel like the ordinary silence of an office too busy to answer. The old woman at the next desk told her she was young yet, and would learn in time the difference between a thing not answered and a thing refused; it generally took longer to learn than a body would like.

Comhairle nam Mèinnean did not answer it, that year or the next. Somhairle never learned the letter's fate after it left Cathair mhòr, whether it went unread into a press like Martha Greaves's, or was read and answered with a silence someone had chosen rather than a silence that simply happened; he was not, that autumn, high enough in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's counsel to be told which. He knew only that no order came down to him changing anything in the reports he sent, and that he went on writing them as he had begun to, three drafts to one, the first honest and the third sent, and that by the time the first snow of that winter closed the higher road above Muileann àrsaidh, he had stopped noticing that he did it at all, which was, though he did not think of it in these words and would not have thanked anyone who put it to him so plainly, the whole of what the habit was for.

He rode out on the last clear day before the snow to look at the depot's roof, blessed by a stranger's hand and standing sound, and the tank full under it, and the two lorries in their shed, and thought, as near as the matter can be told, of nothing at all worth the writing down. That, too, went into no report.

# Chapter Twenty: Of Ruth Calder's Letter

*DE 19*

## I. Of the Wall and the Trench

The frost came early to Muileann àrsaidh that year, hard enough by the third week of an t-Samhain to ring under a boot on the spoil-heaps before the sun was properly up, and Ruth Calder, who lodged at Sarah Dunmore's that winter to see the walling done, was out among the pit-heads in it most mornings before the men were, walking the line as her father had walked the line at Àth leathan, though he had walked it to see that the timbering held and she walked it now to see that the wall did.

It was not much of a wall to look at, and she knew it. A cartload of spoil tipped and levelled, a length of pit-timber laid along the top of it and pegged, a gap left for the cart-track and nothing more, built a load at a time through the back end of the autumn by men who came to it after their shift underground and worked it by lamplight when the days ran short, so that it had grown the way a coral grows, she thought, without anyone in particular deciding on its shape, and stood now waist-high the length of the pit-yard and higher than a man's head where it crossed the old cart-road into the town. It would not have kept out a company of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers with proper tools and half a morning to spend on it. It kept out nothing but a lorry, and a lorry was, in the end, the only thing that had come up that road in eighteen months that anyone in Muileann àrsaidh had cause to keep out.

Old Fraser had the digging of the trench across the southern road, being the best hand in the town with a spade and the only one old enough to remember, from some tale of his own grandfather's, that a road dug across at the right place could be made near as good as a wall for a fraction of the labour. He stood in it to his knees that morning, breath smoking, and called up to her as she came along the bank.

"Another two days and she's done, captain. Deep enough a cart won't chance it and narrow enough a man on foot needn't get his boots wet crossing, which I make out to be about right, since it's carts we're stopping and not men."

"You'll want it filled with water before the frost sets it solid, or it's a bridge by am Faoilleach and not a ditch at all."

"I'll want a great many things I'm not like to get." He leaned on the spade a moment, looking up at her with the particular squint he kept for anything he thought worth saying plainly. "You know what this is, the pair of us standing here talking about drainage. It's not a ditch for keeping the wet out of a cellar."

"I know what it is."

"I only say it because there's men down there" — he tipped his head toward the pit-shaft behind them, where the morning cage was just then coming up with its first load of the poor Cnoc thais coal that Muileann àrsaidh had taken to burning itself since Comhairle nam Mèinnean stopped carrying the good — "who'd tell you it's only a fence, the way a man tells himself a dog's only barking at the wind. It isn't only a fence, Ruth. You want to have your mind made up what it is before somebody else makes it up for you."

She had thought, more than once through that autumn, that old Fraser said more true things to her in a morning's digging than the whole of the letters that came up from the south said in a twelvemonth, and this was one of them. She let it sit a moment before answering, since any answer she could find that morning ran either smaller than the trench deserved or larger than she was ready to speak aloud.

"It's a wall and a ditch," she said at last, "same as it looks. What anybody south of it chooses to call it is their own business."

old Fraser went back to his digging without pressing her further, being a man who knew the difference between a question worth a second asking and one that was not, and Ruth went on along the bank to the pit-head, where the day's shift was already gathering at the cage with their lamps, and took out her father's tally-book, which she had carried over the hill with her and had kept, in one hand or another, every morning for going on four years now, and began the day's count of coal raised, coal burned, coal owed, the same three columns she had kept since the week they buried him, in a hand that had grown, she thought sometimes without much pleasure in the noticing, very nearly as neat as his.

The word from the south that autumn came thin and came late, by whatever carrier still troubled to climb the hill road once the weather turned, and most of what it carried was not news so much as the absence of it: no answer from Comhairle nam Mèinnean to the collective letter the five towns had sent in the summer, unsigned by any one name and carried hand to hand, that said only that the pits would go on until the seams themselves were spent; no word of the enforcers at the western Seann Skell beyond the plain fact of their being there still, quartered in the old customs shed above the river harbour, building something by the river that the carrier's talk called a depot and could not say more of than that; no sign, from Caol mhòr or from Cathair dhearg either, that the winter now closing in on the hills was expected, by anyone south of them, to end in anything but more of the same silence it had been given all that year.

It was into this silence, and not out of any clearer counsel, that Ruth began, in the last week of an t-Samhain, with the trench half dug and the wall not yet finished, to write.

## II. Of the First Drafts

She did not tell anyone at first what she meant to do, partly because she had not yet decided to do it and partly because she had learned, in four years of keeping a pit captain's books, that a thing said aloud too soon in Muileann àrsaidh came back to you by evening in a shape you no longer recognised, with three opinions attached that you had not asked for and could not now easily set down.

The first attempt was made at her father's table, in the stone house above the pit-head at Àth leathan, on a Sunday home, on a night when the wind was coming hard enough off the hill to want the shutters latched twice, with the tally-book put away and a single sheet of the good paper in front of her that she kept for the collective letters and had, until that night, always used for someone else's words and never her own. She wrote the salutation first, *To the Council of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr*, and looked at it a long while, because it seemed to her a great thing to have written at the top of a page in a pit captain's kitchen, and then she wrote nothing else that night at all, and went to bed with the sheet still lying there, the ink dry and the rest of it blank, and told herself in the morning that a letter begun and not finished was no different from a letter never begun, which was not, she found, much comfort.

The second attempt, a week later, she tore across before it was a third done, because she had written three long paragraphs on the history of the agreement at Muileann àrsaidh and the wrong done the towns by Breith Leòid, and reading it back she heard, under every sentence, her own voice raised the way it rose at the pit-shed meetings when Tom Varley or one of the Cnoc thais men said a thing she thought unjust, and she knew, without anyone having to tell her, that a letter written in that voice would be read by whoever read it at an Leabharlann as one more northern grievance among the hundred they must have on file already, and set beside the rest, and answered, if it was answered at all, the same way.

"You're writing it like a complaint," Sarah Dunmore said, the one evening Ruth brought the torn half-sheets to her kitchen and laid them out on the table where the towns' agreement had first been drafted three years before, in much the same seats, with much the same tea gone cold between them. "And they've a great many complaints. What they haven't got, I'd wager, is an offer. Nobody in four years has offered them anything. Everybody's told them what's owed, or what's been done wrong, or what they mean to keep doing whatever's said against it. Nobody's put a thing on the table and said, here, take this, and we'll both be the better for it."

"There's not much on our table to offer. We've coal and nothing else."

"Coal's what they want. It's the only thing anybody in this quarrel has ever wanted from us, whatever else they've said about seams and rulings and An Crùn's own right. Offer them the coal, on your own terms, and let them see whether they'd rather have it that way than not at all."

Ruth turned the idea over through the whole of that week, at the tally-book in the mornings and at the table above the pit-head in the evenings, and came, slowly, to see that Sarah Dunmore had put her finger on the one thing the four years of letters, hers and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's and the council's between them, had none of them yet tried. Every letter she had read or heard read aloud at the pit-shed meetings had been an argument about a right: whose the seams were, whose the fifth was, who had broken faith with whom first, and each argument had answered the last with a sharper one, until the whole exchange had the shape less of a negotiation than of two men shouting the same three sentences louder each time, in the hope that volume alone might eventually pass for proof. She did not think she could win that argument. The towns' case was sound, she still believed that; the trouble was that nobody who had the power to answer it was troubling any longer to listen to it as an argument at all.

An offer was a different thing. An offer did not ask to be believed. It only asked to be weighed.

## III. Of the Terms

She wrote the third draft in a single sitting, on the last evening of an t-Samhain, with the trench filled and frozen behind the pit-yard and the wall finished but for a length at its northern end that old Fraser had left off out of what he called simple exhaustion and what everyone privately understood to be the same caution he had shown her that morning in the ditch, a wall built all the way round a town being, in his private judgement, a thing too near a boast to finish.

This one did not begin with the history. It began with the thing itself.

*We will pay An Crùn's fifth in coal, the same fifth Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own ruling names, on every load raised from the seams at Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh, Tobar dhearg and Àth leathan, from this day until the seams themselves are spent, if Comhairle nam Mèinnean will carry that coal to market as it carried it before, and make no further claim upon the pits while the fifth is paid.*

She read that sentence back four times before she let herself write the next, because it was, she understood even as she set it down, a very great deal to offer and a very little to ask in return, and she wanted to be certain, before she went further, that this was truly what she meant and not merely what desperation had put into her pen. The fifth had gone unpaid for four years, by Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own reckoning, and Breith Leòid made a great deal turn on that unpaid fifth; to offer it now, in coal and not in coin, backdated to nothing and forward-looking only, was to give Comhairle nam Mèinnean the one thing its own ruling said it wanted and to ask, in exchange, only that the pits be let alone to work until they were worked out, which was, on the towns' own reckoning, a matter of years and not of generations, the seams at Muileann àrsaidh being already thin in places and Cnoc thais's reopened shafts thinner still.

It was, she thought, setting the pen down a moment to warm her hand over the fire, a bargain Comhairle nam Mèinnean ought by any sane reckoning to take, since it lost nothing it had not already lost and gained the fifth back besides. She knew, even as she thought it, that sane reckoning was not the only reckoning a council weighed a matter by, and that a body which had already sent a company of armed men north over a fifth part of a coal seam was not, perhaps, a body that could be counted on to want the quarrel settled quietly and without a victory to show for it. But she wrote the offer anyway, because it was the true offer, the one Sarah Dunmore had asked her to find, and because a letter that asked for what she privately expected to be refused was still, she judged, worth more than no letter at all.

She went on from there more plainly than she had written anything before: that the five towns had never sought to take from Comhairle nam Mèinnean what Comhairle nam Mèinnean itself had ceased to want, Comhairle nam Mèinnean having stopped carrying northern coal to southern markets long years before the towns stopped paying for the privilege of a carriage that no longer came; that the coal raised in the western hills, being poor coal by any southern measure, fetched no price outside the north that would tempt any buyer Comhairle nam Mèinnean itself still served; and that the wall now standing round Muileann àrsaidh's pit-yard, which she did not doubt some report had already carried south in a shape larger than the thing itself, was built to keep out lorries and not men, and would come down the day a lorry had no further reason to come up that road.

She did not write the word war, in that draft or in any of the three that followed it over the fortnight after, though she thought it, reading each draft back, more times than she would have owned to any of the pit-shed meetings. The same thin carrier-talk that brought every other scrap of southern news that autumn had brought word that regiments not called out since An Dealachadh were being spoken of again at Cathair dhearg, spoken of and not yet raised, which was, she told herself, still a distance short of raised; and into the space that distance left she wrote her letter, believing, or choosing to believe, that a plain offer honestly meant might yet close it before it closed on its own account.

## IV. Of Christmas Day

The chapel at Àth leathan kept its service on the morning of the twenty-fifth as it had kept it every year Ruth could remember, the small stone building above the ford road filled to its narrow doors with the town's own people and a good number come down from Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais besides, since the western hills had never troubled themselves greatly with the difference between the two faiths the island kept, most households along that coast holding to both without much sense of contradiction, a custodian of Òrd Mhanannain and the humans' own priest sometimes standing at the same graveside within a season of each other and neither thinking it strange.

Ruth walked down from Muileann àrsaidh the evening before with Tom Varley and a dozen others of the pit towns, the road frozen hard and easy underfoot for once, the whole company more cheerful on that walk than she had seen any of them in months, singing a little in the last stretch coming down into Àth leathan, where the chapel lamp showed early through the bare trees. She had not meant, setting out, to finish the letter that day. She had meant only to keep the feast, as her father had kept it and his father before him, and to let the letter lie another week in the drawer where it had lain, in one draft or another, since an t-Samhain began.

The chapel was cold, the small dubhan stove at the back doing little against a building built for a warmer age, and Ruth stood through the service between Sarah Dunmore and Tom Varley with her hands deep in her coat, her mind for once on her father, who had stood in that same pew every an Nollaig of her life until the last one, and on the particular quiet that came over a small crowded room when the whole of it, for the length of a carol, wanted nothing from any of the others in it but to be there together, warm or cold.

It was afterward, walking back up from the chapel in the thin winter light with the congregation breaking up into its knots of neighbours and kin, that the thing came clear to her, not as a new thought so much as an old one finally allowed to finish: the crowded chapel, the carrier's road frozen and passable for once, the whole of the five towns keeping one feast together whatever else divided them from the country south of the wall, was the plain thing her letter was asking Comhairle nam Mèinnean to leave alone, standing for an hour in front of her on the one day of the whole turning year best fitted to send it.

She did not go up to her own cold house that afternoon. She went instead to the kitchen of Tom Varley's sister, who had married at Àth leathan and kept a room for her brother when the roads were bad, and took out the last draft, and read it through once more by the window in the fading light, and found, this time, nothing in it she wished to soften or to harden either.

The fair copy took her under an hour, set down in the same hand she kept for the towns' ledgers, plain and even, with no flourish at the start or the close; a letter asking to be weighed and not believed, she had decided somewhere in the reading, ought to look like a ledger and not like a plea. She dated it at the top, the twenty-fifth of an Dùbhlachd, and signed it with her own name and the names of the pit captains of the other four towns beneath it, Tom Varley's among them. None of the four had seen the final draft, Sarah Dunmore alone excepted; their names stood there because she had asked each of them, weeks before, whether she might sign for them if the letter, when it came, said nothing they would not themselves have said, and none of them had refused her.

She sealed it with the same wax she used for the tally-book returns, there being no other in the house, and sat a while at the window with it finished in her lap before she carried it down to find Tom Varley.

## V. Of the Post at the Western Seann Skell

He was in his sister's kitchen when she found him, half asleep by the fire with a cup of something warm going cold at his elbow, and he came fully awake the moment she set the letter on the table in front of him, because he had known, better than most of the others, what she had been carrying in that drawer all through an t-Samhain, and had asked her twice already, without pressing, whether it was done.

"That's it, then."

"That's it."

He turned it over once in his hands, reading the address on the outside without opening it, since it was not his to open, and set it down again with a care she noted and was grateful for. "You want it to the post at the western Seann Skell, I expect, and not the Muileann àrsaidh carrier, since he's not been up the hill in a fortnight for the drifts."

"The Seann Skell post. It's the only office this side of Cathair dhearg that still keeps regular hours, whatever else sits beside it in that town now."

He did not ask her what she meant by that, both of them knowing well enough what else the western Seann Skell now held, the depot by the river and the company quartered in the old customs shed, and he did not, she noticed, offer to have someone else carry it, though the five miles down from Àth leathan to the town were not, on an evening of an Nollaig with the light already going, a walk either of them would have chosen for its own sake.

"I'll go tonight," he said. "It'll be there before the office shuts if I go now, and I'd sooner it were posted before I've had time to think better of the terms myself, which I haven't, mind, but I'm an old man and old men change their minds in the night for no reason they can afterward name."

"You've not seen the terms."

"I've seen enough of you these two months to trust the terms, Ruth Calder, whatever they say, which is more than I'd have told your father I'd say of anyone twenty years back, him included." He said it without much ceremony, pulling on his coat as he spoke, and she did not answer it, because there was, again, no answer that would not have made more of the moment than either of them wanted made of it on a feast day.

He walked the five miles down to the western Seann Skell in under two hours, by his own account afterward, the road clear and the frost holding, and found the post office lit and open as she had said it would be, kept that evening, as it happened, by a clerk who had stayed past his hour rather than leave a stack of an Nollaig letters to wait another day, and who took Ruth Calder's letter across the counter without any particular notice of it among the dozen others in his hand that evening, weighed it, entered it in his book, and told Tom Varley it would go north with the regular carrier in three days' time, the roads and the holiday allowing.

It went, as promised, three days after, by the ordinary carrier and no other, folded in among the season's other correspondence with nothing about its plain sealed outside to mark it apart from a hundred like it, and it travelled the length of the island by the same slow stages any letter travelled that winter, town to town, hand to hand, until it came, in the second week of am Faoilleach following, to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, where it was read, entered in the day-book in Raghnall mac Mhuirich's own clerk's hand, and laid, as Ellen Marsh's An t-Aon Leabhar Deug had been laid two years before it, upon the table of the council's business, to wait there beside whatever else waited.

A copy of it went, by a slower road still, into Tional nan Tuathach's own minute at Caol mhòr, carried by one of the western towns' own people who thought Tional nan Tuathach ought at least to have the sight of it, whatever Tional nan Tuathach chose to do or not do with the sight once it had it; and there, in Tional nan Tuathach's own hand, it is recorded to this day, four short paragraphs and five names, under a heading that says only what it was and when it came.

No answer to it came from the council, that winter or the next. Ruth did not, in the weeks after, ask whether one might yet. She had learned enough, in four years of keeping her father's book, to know what a silence of that length generally meant, and she went back to the tally-book and the pit-yard and the wall's unfinished northern end with no great expectation stirring in her that the offer she had spent a season making plain would be met with anything plainer in return.

She did not wish it unsent. Setting it down that an Nollaig evening with her father's tally-book closed on the shelf behind her, she knew it for a fair offer honestly meant, the fairest either side of that quarrel had yet put forward; and she knew, just as plainly, folding it into its seal by the last of the daylight, that a generous offer was not, of itself, a thing that had ever yet been enough to answer for.

# Chapter Twenty-one: Of the Granaries and the New Chronicler

*DE 20*

## I. Of the Nine Votes

The room over the net-lofts at Caol mhòr was colder than Martha Greaves had known it in twelve years in the chair, and she had known it in every kind of weather the north could send. The driftwood fire at the near end had been built up twice before the sitting and still could not warm the far wall, where the ice on the inside of the panes had not melted by noon. Forty-one delegates had come through snow that had closed Rathad na Fèille three days before and was not yet done falling, and five benches along the harbour wall stood empty, as they had stood empty for five years now, since the day the western delegates had risen without a word and gone down the outside stair and not come back. Nobody moved to fill those places. Thomas Rook kept them chalked in the roll all the same, under the towns' names, with nothing after them.

She had not meant to bring the matter before the room herself. It was Peter Hale, delegate of Caol mhòr these dozen years and long-armed and fair still though there was grey now at his temples, who rose first and said that Tional nan Tuathach had sat three sittings running without a word said of the western hills, and that a room which called itself the gathering of the northern towns and would not speak the plainest fact in the north was not doing the thing it was built to do. There was a murmur along both walls at that, not agreement exactly, more the sound of men and women glad to hear said aloud what they had each been keeping to themselves.

"Say it, then," Martha told him, from the chair.

He said it. The pits at Muileann àrsaidh were walled now, he said, against Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own order, the road into the town dug across so that nothing came in or out but what a man could carry on his back over the spoil. The letter Ruth Calder had sent south at an Nollaig, offering An Crùn's own fifth in coal if only Comhairle nam Mèinnean would carry it, had gone to an Leabharlann and had had no answer, not a refusal even, only silence, and a silence from that quarter, he said, looking round the room as if daring anyone to contradict him, generally meant one thing when it went on long enough. He did not say the word war. Nobody in the room that morning said it, though it sat in the middle of the trestle as plainly as the ice on the far window.

Martha herself had had her own silence to weigh against his, though she did not put it before the room, having no wish to make the matter more hers than it already stood: the letter she had sent the autumn before, asking Comhairle nam Mèinnean for a year's delay while Tional nan Tuathach talked with the western towns, had gone the same road as Ruth Calder's and come to the same end, received and filed, no more said. She had not looked for anything better of it. She looked now, hearing Peter Hale lay the two letters side by side without knowing he had done it, at the plain shape the pattern made when two requests from two different hands met the same wall in the same season, and found she believed him a good deal more readily for the coincidence than she would have believed either letter alone.

"And what would you have the room do," asked the delegate of the farm towns, an old woman named Christina Munro who had sat on that bench longer than Martha had sat in the chair, "that it has not tried already? We sent a letter. It was received and filed, same as the last."

"I'd have the room say plainly what it is," Peter Hale said. "Not a fighting man's ally and not Comhairle nam Mèinnean's either. Say it, and put it in the book, so that whatever comes after, no one can claim Tional nan Tuathach was ever asked and never answered."

It went round the trestle after that in the old way, each delegate free to speak once before any speak twice, and Martha let it run longer than she generally let anything run, because she judged, rightly as it turned out, that the room needed to hear itself say the thing from every corner before it would agree to say it once, together, in the book. A fisherman of Cathair gheal, whose town sold its catch up the coast for the last poor coal of the hills, said he for one would not have his name set down as neutral between men who dug and men who came with lorries to stop them digging, whatever the word neutral was made to mean in a minute. A miller of the eastern towns, whose trade touched the western hills not at all, said the room had no army to send and no coal to spare and had best say what it could truly do and no more, or it would find its own word worth as little as Comhairle nam Mèinnean's. Martha wrote none of it down herself. That was Thomas Rook's work, and he kept at it with his head bent and his pen scratching, filling three pages before the room came, of its own accord and without her steering it there in words, to the shape of the thing Peter Hale had wanted from the start: that Tional nan Tuathach was no party to the quarrel between Comhairle nam Mèinnean and the western towns, and would take no side in it by word or by deed; and that it would feed, from its own stores, any soul who came to any of its towns hungry, of whatever town, without asking first what side that soul had stood on.

She called for the show of hands herself, as speaker, standing so the room could see her count and know it was honestly done. Nine hands went up along the near wall for the motion as Thomas Rook read it back, Peter Hale's among them, and not one hand rose against it, though a good many arms stayed folded and a good many faces looked at the table rather than at her, Christina Munro's among those. She waited the space of three breaths, in case any of the folded arms meant to unfold, and none did.

"Nine for," she said. "None against. Carried." And Thomas Rook wrote it in, the day, the count, and the two clauses entire, no party to the quarrel and feed the hungry, in his small careful hand, and the room broke into its usual noise of benches scraping and voices low and urgent, already arguing over what feeding the hungry would want in barley and where it would come from, before the ink on the page was dry.

Christina Munro caught Martha's sleeve on the way down the outside stair, the last of the room ahead of them already scattering into the snow. "Nine," she said, not unkindly, "out of one-and-forty. You'll not tell me that's the whole room's mind."

"I'll tell you it's the whole room's vote," Martha said, "which is the only thing the book can hold. A man's mind is his own to keep."

"And is it yours as well? Nine, and you the tenth, and never raised your own hand at all."

"The chair doesn't vote," Martha said, "except to break a tie, and there was none to break." She said it as she had said it a hundred times before, in a hundred sittings where the rule had never once troubled her to explain further, and saw, in the way the old woman's mouth set, that this time it had not answered the question that was actually being asked. She did not answer that one either, there on the stair with the snow coming down between them, and Christina Munro, who had sat in that room longer than Martha had sat in the chair, let her sleeve go and said no more about it, then or after.

Martha sat on a while after the others had gone down the stair into the snow, as she had sat on the evening of her own first sitting, twelve years before, gathering Walter Hale's loose pages square on the table though there were no loose pages now to gather, only the habit of sitting still a little while in an empty room before she had to be Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas again and not merely Tional nan Tuathach's speaker. Nine votes would not carry so much as a bag of meal to Muileann àrsaidh, walled as it was, nor buy Ruth Calder's letter an answer it had not had. That much she had known before she ever called for the hands. What she had wanted was the thing in the book, in Thomas Rook's own careful ink, because a thing once written did not, whatever else befell it, become less true for having been carried by only nine.

## II. Of the Wool Mills' Takings

She did not speak again of what the nine votes would mean in barley until the carding-sheds at Doire ghlas were running full summer hours and the fleece was in from the spring clip, weighed and sorted and already turning, under her own hand at the tally-desk, into the figures that told her each year what the mills had made and what they had left over. That summer left over a good deal, the fleece having come in heavy after two mild winters and the price holding at the fair better than it had in some years, and Martha sat with the figures a whole evening in the counting-house with the window open on the grove and the grey oaks going gold-green in the long light, before she wrote, at the foot of the mill's own book and not Tional nan Tuathach's, an order to the miller at Caol mhòr and a second to her own granary-keeper at Doire ghlas, that the stores of both towns be filled that autumn beyond the ordinary wont, and paid for out of the mills' own takings, and no other fund drawn on.

She could have laid it before the room first. She was speaker, and the room had voted the feeding of the hungry into its own minute not six months before, and by every custom of the office she might have brought the figures to the next sitting and let the delegates argue, as they argued over everything, how much grain and which towns' stores and whose purse. That she chose not to. Instead she told herself, turning the reasons over on the ride home that evening with the oilcloth over her knees against a shower that never quite came, that a granary filled in am Faoilleach when the need showed itself would be six weeks too late for whoever needed it first, and that the mills were hers to spend as she judged, being no part of Tional nan Tuathach's own purse; and both of these were true reasons, and neither was the whole of it. The whole of it she did not put into words even to herself that evening, only felt it, the way a person feels the weight of a decision already made and only waiting to be carried out: that if the wall at Muileann àrsaidh meant what Peter Hale had said it meant, then a granary at Caol mhòr and another at Doire ghlas, standing full and unremarked through an ordinary summer, might in a year's time be the only thing in the whole north that stood between some family walking down out of the hills with nothing and a winter they did not live through.

The carts began coming up from the coast in the last week of an t-Iuchar, grain bought quietly through three different factors so that no one merchant should wonder aloud why Tional nan Tuathach's towns wanted so much of it in a year when the harvest promised well enough on its own account, and Martha stood in the yard at Doire ghlas most of one long afternoon watching the sacks go up into the loft above the old mill store, counting them herself against the factor's tally the way she had once counted fleeces that the mill's own tally said were forty and her own eyes said were thirty-eight. The granary-keeper, a broad quiet man named John Skinner who had kept that loft for eleven years and had never in all that time seen it filled past two-thirds before the frost, asked her once, straightforwardly, whether he ought to enter a reason in his own book against the extra, since his book was looked at by the room's auditors each spring and a figure without a reason drew a question sooner or later.

"Enter the weight and the date," Martha said, "and no reason at all. If anybody asks you why, tell them to ask me."

John Skinner wrote it so, and asked nothing further, being a man long used to taking a plain instruction plainly and leaving it there. He did, over the weeks the carts kept coming, take to walking the loft himself of an evening after the last sack was up, counting the rows against no tally at all but his own memory of how the place had stood in other autumns, and once, near the end of it, he remarked to Martha, in the mild way he remarked on weather, that he could not recall the loft standing so full at harvest-time in all his eleven years, not even the year of the good barley when Tional nan Tuathach had sold the surplus south at the fair. Martha said only that it was a good year for fleece as well as barley, and let it go at that, and John Skinner, who had his own family in the mill cottages and his own notion of what a full loft might be wanted for before winter was out, let it go with her.

Nobody asked her, that year or for some while after. Tional nan Tuathach's own minute, when Thomas Rook came in the autumn to make the autumn entry of the granaries' state, as he made it every year without any particular interest in the figures, recorded that the stores at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas stood fuller than the five years' average by a good half again, and gave, because none had been given him to give, no reason for it at all. Martha read the entry over his shoulder when the book came round the trestle for the room's inspection, as it did each autumn, and said nothing, and signed under it in her turn, and passed the book on down the bench to Peter Hale, who glanced at the figure, and then at her, and did not ask either, though something in the set of his mouth said plainly enough that he had done the same sum in his own head and come to the same answer she had, and had chosen, as she had, not to write it down.

Martha was one-and-seventy that year, broad still in the shoulder though the years had begun to stoop it a little, and had managed the mills at Doire ghlas since before most of the delegates now sitting on the benches around her had been born. In the quiet after a sitting her mind went sometimes to Daniel Frayne, dead these twelve years, who had kept the room's minutes for twenty-three years and never once, that she had heard, put a private reason into a public book where a plain figure would do as well alone. She understood him, she found, a good deal better now than she had while he lived.

## III. Of the Desk, the Ink and the Key

It is told at Muileann chaol, in an Leabharlann's own upper room, that the handing-over took the better part of an afternoon and would have taken less had either woman been willing to let it go quickly, and that the keeper Raghnall mac Mhuirich, who had found the money for Sìleas's own hiring nine years before out of his own small fund and told the council afterward rather than before, kept well away from the room the whole of that day, saying to anyone who asked that a chronicle changed hands better without a keeper standing over it.

Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh had written to the council in the spring of that year, in her own plain hand and no other's, that she asked leave to lay down the office of royal chronicler at the close of the summer, being nine-and-sixty that year and finding the winters harder on her eyes than the summers, and that she named, as the office's custom allowed a retiring chronicler to name, her own clerk of near nine years' standing, Sìleas nic Rath, to take up the desk after her, subject always to the council's own leave, which the council gave without discussion in a single line at the foot of a sitting given over mostly to other matters. Sìleas learned of it, in the end, from Beathag herself and no letter of the council's, on an ordinary wet morning in an Gearran, over the same pot of tea they had shared at the same hour for nine years, when Beathag set down her cup and said, in the same voice she used for the weather, that she had written to the council, and what she had written, and that Sìleas had until an Lùnastal to decide whether she still wanted the desk once she had heard the whole of what it cost.

Sìleas thought afterwards, more than once, that she ought to have asked then what Beathag meant by cost, and had not, partly from the surprise of the thing and partly because some instinct told her that whatever the answer was, she would learn it better by waiting for it than by asking for it before she was ready to hear it.

The last afternoon came in an Lùnastal, a still hot day with the river low and slow past the old building's windows and the paper-mill's wheel barely turning for want of water to drive it. Beathag had cleared the desk herself over the week before, a little at a time, so that there should be no single day when the room looked stripped, and by the last afternoon there was little left on it but the inkstand that had been Tormod Pinn's before her, the day's page half-written in her own hand, and a small iron key on a loop of waxed thread.

"The ink first," Beathag said, and pushed the stand a hand's breadth across the desk, though it had stood in that same spot, Sìleas knew, since before either of them had been born. "It was Tormod's. It will outlast the both of us if nobody drops it. Don't clean the well too often. A little of the old ink left in the bottom keeps the new from going thin."

Sìleas said she would remember it.

"The page next." Beathag turned the half-written sheet so it faced the chair Sìleas had not yet sat down in. "I've left it short. You'll finish today's entry in your own hand, not mine, so that the book shows the change where the change was made, and not hidden in the middle of a sentence as if nothing had happened. That's the office's own rule, and a good one. Write in your own hand today, and every day after, and don't trouble yourself trying to write like me. Nobody thanks a chronicler for pretending to be the last one."

Last of all she took up the key, and held it a moment in her closed hand before she gave it over, and Sìleas understood, without being told, that this was the part of the afternoon Beathag had least wanted to hurry.

"This opens the press where the sealed things go," Beathag said. "Not the day-book. The day-book is open to any soul who comes and asks, and so it should stay, whatever the council or anyone above the council would rather. This is for the other kind. You'll know the difference when it comes to you, and it will come to you, sooner than you'd wish, if the roads north stay as they are this autumn." She closed Sìleas's fingers over the key with her own thin ones. "Write what you are let, Sìleas, and write it as fully and as plainly as if no one would ever grudge you a word of it. But write down, too, what you are not let, and where, and by whom, and on what day, even if all you can write is that a letter went out and a silence came back. A chronicle that only shows what it was free to show is no chronicle at all in the end. It is a fair copy of somebody else's leave."

"And if the leave never comes?"

"Then the silence is the record," Beathag said, "and you set it down as carefully as you would set down a battle, because it very likely is one, only fought with paper instead of anything sharper, and paper battles are the ones that get lost soonest if nobody minds to keep the score."

She said little else. She looked once round the room, at Tormod Pinn's chair that neither of them had ever used, and at the window on the paper-mill's wheel, and picked up the small bag she had packed the evening before for the carrier who would take her north-east to Àth dhìreach and her sister's house the following morning, and went to the door, and there stopped, and turned back only far enough to say that Sìleas should not get up, since a chronicler did not rise for a chronicler, only for the office, and the office had already changed hands and was sitting, at that moment, in the chair behind the desk.

The carrier's cart stood waiting in the yard below when Beathag came down the outside stair the next morning, the bag already stowed under the seat and a rug laid ready across the boards, and there was nobody there to see her off but the carrier himself and, at the last, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, who came out from the door of the reading-room in his shirtsleeves with ink still on his fingers and said only that he hoped the road stayed dry as far as Àth dhomhain, since the low ford there was no friend to a laden cart in wet weather. Beathag said she had crossed that ford in every kind of weather it owned and did not expect this crossing to be the one that taught her anything new about it. He handed her up himself, though the carrier stood ready to do it, and stepped back, and the cart went out under the arch and down toward the river road, and that, so far as an Leabharlann's own telling goes, was the whole of the leave-taking: a dry ford wished for, and a hand given, and no more said than the road wanted.

Sìleas sat where she was told to sit until the door had closed and the footsteps had gone down the stair and out into the yard, and then a good while longer, with the key still warm from Beathag's hand and the pen dry in the stand before her. When at last she drew the half-finished page toward her and dipped the pen, her own hand, she noticed, ran a shade smaller and a shade more upright than Beathag's, and she let it run so rather than try to match the older woman's slant, remembering what she had been told about pretending. She finished the day's entry, the ordinary business of an ordinary summer's day at an Leabharlann, in her own hand entire, and at the foot of it, where the office's custom asked for nothing more, she wrote one further line, because it seemed to her, sitting alone in the room for the first time as its chronicler, that the custom had left a silence exactly where Beathag had told her a chronicler ought never to leave one.

*This day the office passed from Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh to Sìleas nic Rath, by the council's leave and the outgoing chronicler's own naming. What follows in this book is written by the second hand, and the reader is told so here, once, so that it need not be said again.*

She read the line back twice, found nothing in it she wished to soften, and set the pen down beside the inkstand that had been Tormod Pinn's and was now, in the way such things become true only by being used, her own.

# Chapter Twenty-two: Of the Old Names Read Aloud

*DE 20*

## I. Of the Rolls Brought from the Chests

The order came up from Cathair dhearg in an Dàmhair, and it said nothing of war. It said that certain companies, disbanded since An Dealachadh, were to be reformed for the guarding of the coal roads and the dubhan depots against disorder, and it named no enemy, because to name one would have been to say aloud what everyone from the clerk who copied it to the boy who carried it already knew and none of them, that autumn, would yet say.

Somhairle mac Lachlainn read it twice at the depot below the western Seann Skell, standing in the yard among the barrels his own company had built the shed to hold, and put it in his coat and went on with the day's business as though it changed nothing, the kind of thing he had learned to do in eighteen years among Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers. A man who showed what an order meant to him before his own men had time to decide for themselves what it meant lost a measure of trust he did not get back. He had learned that on the road to Muileann àrsaidh with stones coming out of the dark, and he had learned it again writing the report of that night, choosing each word the way a man picks his footing on wet rock.

He was summoned to the capital three weeks after, in the first cold week of an t-Samhain, and rode down by Slighe a' Ghuail with a corporal and a leather satchel of the depot's returns he did not expect anyone to ask for. Nobody did. He was taken instead, the morning after he arrived, to an old drill hall behind the council's own rooms, a building he had never had reason to enter, long and low, of dressed stone, its high windows gone grey with age and cobweb; used in his own lifetime, so far as he knew, for nothing grander than the storing of the city watch's spare pikes.

Three men were waiting for him there: the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, a clerk he did not know with an ink-stained sleeve, and an old soldier called Cormac Liath whom Somhairle had met twice before at musters and taken, both times, for a man kept on past his use out of courtesy. It was Cormac Liath who did the talking that morning, and Somhairle understood before the man had said three sentences why he had been wrong to write him off.

"You'll have command," Liath said, without any of the preamble Somhairle had braced for. "Of what there is to command, which by spring will be more than there is now. The council has not said war, and will go on not saying it as long as the word can be kept out of a minute. You'll say muster, and mobilisation, and the guarding of the roads, and you'll be right to, because those are the true words for what you're doing this month. Whether they're the true words for what you'll be doing by harvest is not for you or me to say today."

"And the men?"

"That's why you're here." Liath nodded to the clerk, who set his satchel on the long table that ran the hall's length and began, with the particular carefulness of a man handling a thing he has been told is old and is not sure how old, to lift out ledgers bound in board gone soft and dark at the corners.

They were the rolls of Buidhnean an Dealachaidh, and Somhairle had heard of them the way a man hears of a relic kept behind glass in a chapel he does not often visit: known to exist, never expected to be taken down and read. Ninety years they had lain in the council's chests, through reigns and rulings and the slow forgetting that overtakes any roll nobody calls, and the ink in some of them had gone the colour of weak tea, and in one, near the bottom of the stack, whole pages had stuck together and had to be worked apart with a blunt knife, the clerk's hands not quite steady at it, so that Somhairle found himself wanting to take the knife from him and could not, from his place at the far end of the table, have said whether it was patience or unfitness that kept him from offering.

"These name the companies," Liath said. "Not by number. By what they were called when they were raised, which was mostly for the town that raised them, or for whoever led the raising, or once or twice for a reason no living man can now explain, so that you'll find a company of An Dealachadh called simply the Grey House, and nobody in this room can tell you why, and neither could the last three clerks who had charge of this hall before this one." He laid his hand flat on the topmost ledger, not turning it. "The council wants the new companies to carry the old names, when a name can be matched to a town still standing and willing to give men. It will do the recruiting more good than any bill posted at a market cross. Men come readier to a name their grandfathers marched under than to a number stamped fresh on a drumhead."

Somhairle thought, though he did not say it, that the council wanted one thing more besides, to make the thing feel less new than it was, to dress a war nobody had yet agreed to call a war in the coat of something the kingdom had done before and survived; but he had learned, in the same eighteen years, when a thought of that kind was worth the saying and when it was better kept behind the teeth, and this, with Liath's hand still on the ledger and the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean watching him with the patient, unhurried attention of a man who has already decided what he thinks of you and is only waiting to see whether you will confirm it, was plainly not a morning for saying it.

"Read them, then," he said instead.

It took the rest of that day and most of the next. Liath read, in a voice gone dry and even with age but not weak, town by town, company by company, and the clerk set down beside each name whether the town it had been raised from still stood, still had men of an age to carry arms, and still lay within a day's reach of a road Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's dubhan carts could use, for a company that could not be supplied might as well not be raised. Some towns answered to their names still and would send men gladly, the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean said, reading from a paper of his own; the fisher towns of the east coast, quick to feel any threat to their harbours, and the market towns of the centre that had grown fat on the coal trade and now stood to grow fatter still on the trade that had replaced it. Other names on the roll answered to nothing at all, because the town was gone, swallowed into a larger one or fallen to a scatter of farms with no muster-ground left standing, and those were struck through in the clerk's hand and set aside, and nobody in the room remarked on it, though Somhairle noticed that Liath's reading grew a shade quieter over each one, as a man's voice does at a grave he did not expect to be asked to visit.

By the second afternoon the light in the high windows had gone from grey to the deeper grey that in that month passed for evening, and lamps were brought in, four of them, hung from iron brackets along the wall that Somhairle guessed had not held a flame in years, because the first one smoked and stank before it caught and burned clean. It was dubhan in the lamps, of course; there was no coal issued to a drill hall that had stood empty a generation, and Somhairle watched the black smoke go up in a thin curl to the rafters and thought, not for the first time that autumn, how strange a thing it was that the fuel a man in the north had made to warm his own hearth now lit the room where his own people's old names were being taken down off a shelf to be used against, whatever the council chose to call it this month, his own people's children.

The last of the rolls was read as full dark came on outside, by lamplight that threw the four men's shadows long and doubled up the hall's stone walls, and when Liath's voice stopped at the final name, a company once raised at a town on Slighe a' Ghuail whose muster-ground, the clerk found on checking, was now a rail siding with three sheds and a signal box, the room held a silence that none of the four men seemed in any hurry to break. It was Somhairle who broke it at last, because someone had to, and because command, he was beginning to understand, meant chiefly that whichever silence nobody else would break fell to you.

"How many companies stand, once the dead towns are struck out?"

The clerk added a column that had lain untotalled since the reading began and gave him the figure. It was not a large one, set beside what the roll had once named, ninety years before, when the whole of the kingdom's strength had stood behind Cogadh nam Beann; but it was more than Somhairle had commanded at any one time in his years with Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers, and he found, hearing it said aloud in that cold hall by lamplight that smelled of the fuel a Tuathach had made, that it settled on him with a weight he had not braced for. The number did not frighten him. What weighed was that it was his, from that evening, to answer for, in a way that the depot and its barrels and the road below the western Seann Skell had never quite been.

"Then we begin with those," Liath said, and closed the topmost ledger, and Somhairle understood that the reading was over and the rest, whatever it turned out to be called, was now his own to carry.

Before the clerk began to pack the ledgers away, Somhairle asked to see the list of the towns still standing, and read it through himself by the last of the lamplight, slower than Liath had read it aloud, because a name on a page took longer to settle in the mind than a name spoken once and moved past. He knew most of the towns for what they were now rather than what the roll called them, market towns grown fat on the coal trade that had since gone south, fishing harbours that had never had much cause to think of the western hills at all until a company was named for them ninety years before and left, since, to gather dust; and he found himself doing, without quite meaning to, the same sum the clerk had done all afternoon with his careful column of struck-out names, setting each town against what he remembered of it from his own years riding the coal roads, and asking of each, silently, whether the men it sent him now would know, or care, what their grandfathers' company had once been called.

"You've a corporal of your own with you," Liath said, watching him at it. "Bring him in tomorrow and let him hear the names as you heard them today. A man who has heard a thing said once in a lamplit hall carries it differently to his own company than a man only handed a paper."

Somhairle thought of the corporal who had ridden down with him, a steady, unremarkable man named Iain Dòmhnallach who had served two years under him at the western Seann Skell without once, so far as Somhairle knew, asking why any order he was given had been given, and wondered whether that was the kind of man the old rolls wanted brought in to hear them, or whether it was precisely the kind that did not need to be, having never in his service shown any sign of asking the questions a hall full of ninety-year-old names was meant, Somhairle supposed, to answer before they were asked.

"I'll bring him," he said, and left it there.

## II. Of the Bench in the Passage

Martha Greaves kept the feast that year in a hired carriage on the northern road south, with a rug over her knees that did little against the cold coming up through the floorboards and a basket at her feet holding bread and a cold fowl that Ellen Marsh had pressed on her at the last that she had not yet found the heart to eat. She had left Doire ghlas two days before an Nollaig, when Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail was at last agreed word for word after a sitting that ran past midnight, and had travelled since by whatever the season offered: a carrier's cart as far as the boundary of the shires, a dubhan coach from there, and this last hired carriage, its wheels loud on the frozen ruts, for the stretch into the capital that no coach ran on an Nollaig Eve.

She had never in her life kept the day travelling, and she did not, in the small hours somewhere south of the boundary stones with the carriage jolting and her breath showing white even under the rug, allow herself to think overmuch about what her mother would have said of a woman who did. The Dia-thìrich kept no feast that day at all, which was one small mercy in a season that had offered her few, since it meant the roads she travelled were not crowded with those keeping it properly, at home, by a fire, as she should by rights have been keeping it herself.

The petition rode in her lap the whole way, in a leather folder Peter Hale had made her promise to guard as though it were the crown, which she had thought at the time a young man's overstatement and had come, somewhere past the second night without proper sleep, to find less funny than he had meant it. It asked one thing only, in words Tional nan Tuathach had turned over for the better part of a fortnight until every clause said exactly what it meant and no more: that the western pits be let alone to work out their own seams, since by every honest reckoning the coal in them would be spent within a handful of years regardless of what any board or council did about it now, and that the kingdom, having already the whole of the south's new fuel to warm it, might find in its own patience a cheaper peace than in any company it could raise to enforce the alternative.

She came into Cathair dhearg in the grey forenoon of an Nollaig, with frost lying white and undisturbed on the parapet of the bridge because so few feet had crossed it that morning to wear it away, and paid off the carriage driver, who wished her the day's blessings in the human way out of what she took for simple habit and then looked faintly embarrassed at himself for it, as a man does who has said a thing to the wrong company. She found the council's building without difficulty, having been given careful directions by Peter Hale from a visit of his own some years before, and was shown by a porter, once she had stated her business and waited while he went to ask whether her business was in fact wanted, to a bench in a stone passage off the main hall, where she was told the council would see her when it saw fit and not before.

More times than she could easily have counted, from her years managing the mill at Doire ghlas and her years since in Tional nan Tuathach's own chair, she had sat waiting on hard benches, and had thought, before this morning, that waiting was a thing she had grown past minding. The cold of the stone under her had little to do with it, nor the ache of two nights without a proper bed still in her back; it was the particular smallness of sitting in a passage that was not built to hold anyone for long, with nothing on the walls to look at but a row of framed grants she did not trouble to read and a single high window that showed her nothing of the sky but a strip of flat white cloud. Sitting there, she thought of the morning twelve years before when Thomas Rook had read Daniel Frayne's death into Tional nan Tuathach's own minute and the room had stood for the space of a breath and sat down again, and how strange it was that the office that morning had handed her without her asking for it should end, or at least come to this particular passage, on a bench built for men who did not expect to be kept waiting and had never once, in the building of it, thought to ask whether a woman from the north might someday be.

She waited the better part of an hour. The bench was cold enough that she kept her cloak about her the whole time, and the passage carried, faintly and by turns, voices from the chamber at its end, none of them clear enough to make out a word, only the rise and fall of men taking turns to speak and be answered, which told her nothing except that the council was, in fact, sitting, and had not, as she had half feared through the last two days of travel, adjourned for the feast after all and left her to have come all this way for a locked door. Twice in that hour she took the petition out of its folder, her hands wanting a thing to hold besides their own stillness, and twice she put it back unread, since she had written half of it herself and could have said it from memory standing on her own doorstep at Doire ghlas without troubling to look.

A clerk came out at last, a young man with the particular brisk courtesy of someone who has been told to be courteous and has not yet had time to make it his own, and asked her name. She gave it, and he wrote it on a small paper he carried, and went back in, and she heard, a moment later, her own name said through the door in a voice not his, in a shape she did not at first know for hers at all: the surname set first, in the way of the island's own houses, and the whole of it given the turn of the tongue that made every foreign name that passed through this building sound, by the time it reached the room, a little more like the island's own. She sat a second longer than she meant to before she understood that it was her they were calling, and stood then quickly, gathering the folder and her cloak together in a way that felt, to her own eye if to nobody else's, less composed than she had meant to arrive.

The chamber, when she came into it, was smaller than she had pictured it in the two days of travelling here, and warmer, with a dubhan stove set in an alcove at one side throwing a heat she felt at once after the cold of the passage, so that for the first few moments she was more aware of her own numbed hands beginning to prickle back to life than of the room. It took her a breath or two to see it properly: a long table, twelve chairs about it, and in every chair a face turned toward the door, toward her, with the particular stillness of people interrupted in the middle of business they had expected to finish uninterrupted.
