She knew none of them by sight save one, Anna nic Phàil, whom she had met once at a market charter's signing three years before and who gave her now, across the width of the table, the smallest incline of the head, not quite a greeting, more an acknowledgement that the room held one other person who had not always sat in rooms like this one.

She was the first speaker of Tional nan Tuathach, in all the years since Walter Hale had first gathered the northern towns to speak with one voice, to walk into this chamber at all. Nobody told her so; she understood it crossing the floor, from the feel of a room that did not often see a stranger cross it, the twelve faces following her the whole short distance from the door to the place, some six feet short of the table's head, where the same clerk who had called her name now stood waiting with a look that told her, plainly enough, that this was as far as she was meant to come. She learned afterward that she had understood rightly, and was not surprised.

"You may read it," said the man at the table's head, an old man she did not know, his voice carrying easily in a room built, she thought, for exactly that kind of voice.

She read it standing, holding the leather folder open in both hands because her hands, still not quite recovered from the cold, did not entirely trust themselves with a single sheet. She read it through without hurrying, though every instinct in her wanted to hurry, to be done and out of the room and back on the cold road north where she understood, at least, the weather and the company; she read it the way Peter Hale had made her practise it twice in Tional nan Tuathach's own hall before she left, slowly enough that no clause outran its own sense, pausing where the sentence paused and nowhere else. The room heard her out in a silence she could not read at all, twelve faces giving back nothing she could carry home and tell Tional nan Tuathach she had seen, no nod, no frown, nothing but the ordinary attention of people listening to a thing they had already, she suspected, been told the substance of before she ever crossed the bridge that morning.

She came to the last line, the offer of patience in place of a company, and let it stand a moment in the warm air of the chamber before she folded the paper closed and stepped forward the last few feet to lay it on the table, in the space the old man at its head cleared for it with one hand without otherwise moving.

"Received," said the clerk at her side, and wrote it down.

That was the whole of the answer the room gave her that morning: one word, said by a man who was not one of the twelve, and the small dry sound of a pen crossing paper. Nobody at the table spoke to her directly, then or after; the old man at its head inclined his own head slightly, in a gesture that might have been thanks and might only have been the signal that her business was finished, and the porter who had shown her in was already at her elbow to show her out again, as though the room's whole business with her had been measured beforehand to the minute and now, that minute spent, must close over the gap she had made in it and go on to whatever had stood next on its morning's list before she came.

Crossing back to the door, she thought of the letter she would have to write Tional nan Tuathach when she came home, and of how little there would be to put in it beside the one word and the small dry sound that had followed it. A room capable of measuring a stranger's whole business to the minute, she thought too, though she did not let it slow her step, was not a room that had been surprised by anything the petition asked of it, which meant that whatever answer the western towns were eventually to have, it had very likely already been settled, in some other room than this one, before she had ever climbed into the hired carriage two mornings before.

The cold struck her at once through the door before it had even fully shut, back in the passage, and there she let herself, for the first time since Doire ghlas, feel the whole distance she had come to hear one word said once. Weeping had never in her life answered anything, and she did not begin now; but she stood a while by the cold bench she had waited on, not sitting again, only standing, with the empty folder under her arm and her own breath white in front of her, until the porter, waiting with the particular patience of a man paid to wait, asked whether she wished him to find her a carriage back north, and she said that she did, and let him.

The petition she never saw again. It went, she supposed, wherever a filed thing goes in a room she had been in only the once, into some clerk's press among the year's other business, to be found, if it ever was found, by whoever next had reason to open that drawer and ask what Tional nan Tuathach had wanted, that an Nollaig, and what the council had answered it. She thought of it, on the long cold road back, less as a paper than as the one word the room had spent on it, turned over so many times in the two days of travel that had brought her here and the two more that would take her home again that by the time she came in sight of Doire ghlas's own lit windows, late on the second night after, she had almost stopped hearing it as a word at all, and heard instead only the sound the clerk's pen had made, crossing the paper, once, and then lying still.

# Chapter Twenty-three: Of the Arms Trains

*DE 21*

> **Part Four · Of Blàr Àth leathan and the First Summer**
>
> *Airson ùine.*
> For a time.
>
> — the council's word on Deachamh a' Chogaidh, DE 21

What is told here of the war comes from An Clàr Foscailte, the towns' reports and Sceulachdan nan Tuathach; the rest is sealed. What follows is what was seen and what was written down at the time: from a footplate on Slighe a' Ghuail's western branch, and from a trestle table above a pit village where a woman kept a list.

## I. Of the Trains That Ran by Night

Eachann mac Ruairidh had driven on Slighe a' Ghuail for three-and-thirty years and the dubhan trains for thirteen of them, and in all that time he had never once been asked to carry a crate he was not told the weight of. That changed on the second night of am Faoilleach, when the yard foreman at Muileann chrom came down the line with a paper in his hand and a lantern that threw more shadow than light and told him his engine would take on eight wagons before dawn, loaded by Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's own men, and that he was not, this once nor any night after, to ask what was in them.

"Weight's on the manifest," the foreman said, holding the paper up rather than handing it across, as though the handing across were itself a thing to be careful of. "That's all the manifest's for, this trip. You'll sign for the weight and not the goods."

Eachann had signed a good many papers in his time on the footplate without reading past the figure at the bottom, and he signed this one the same way, though he noted, as a man notes weather he means to remember, that the foreman did not meet his eye while he did it. The eight wagons came on through the small hours behind a screen of tarpaulin that Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's men kept up even inside the shed, working by shuttered lamps and speaking to one another, when they spoke at all, in the flat short sentences of men who have been told exactly how much to say and have decided to say less than that. Eachann's own second man, a broad quiet man of Muileann chrom who had ridden with him three years and asked him nothing that night either, watched the gauges in silence and once, when a case slipped an inch on its rollers and struck the wagon's floor with a sound too dull and too heavy for tools, looked across at Eachann in the lamplight and looked away again without a word passing between them.

They ran west before first light, Slighe a' Ghuail proper past Muileann mhin and the goods-sheds at Cathair dhearg, and beyond the capital onto the western branch, single-tracked and slower, that Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn had laid twenty years before to carry lime and slate down to the coast and had carried little enough of either since. It was dubhan in the tank now as it had been for thirteen years, and Eachann had long since stopped missing the coal's particular heat, though he still, on a cold footplate in the first mile, found himself listening for the crackle of a fire that was not there and hearing instead the flat, steady beat of the engine. The branch ran through country he had known since he was a boy riding with his own father on the coal trains, low hills going up into the higher ones, farms and a scatter of pit villages whose lamps, this deep in winter, were most of them out before his engine passed, and he drove it that first night, and every night after through the rest of the month, at a speed the branch's condition did not properly allow, because the manifest that rode with him now, whatever else it did not say, said plainly enough that speed mattered more than the branch's rails did.

By the middle of the month it had become his run and no other's, given him, he understood without being told outright, because the yard's masters had found him steady and asked no questions of him twice, which in that season had come to count for more than the years he had spent learning every gradient of the line by feel. He ran the double shift the yard had gone to that winter, out on the down run with the wagons and back light before noon, and slept what hours he could in the drivers' room at Muileann chrom with the other men of the arms trains, none of whom spoke much of the work either, though Eachann noticed that they had all, every one of them, taken to a particular silence about the eight wagons that was not quite the silence they kept about anything else, a silence with a kind of care folded into it, the way a man is careful crossing ice he has been told will bear him and has not tested for himself.

He did not open the crates. That, he told himself those first weeks, was no more than the ordinary discipline of the line, the same discipline that had him signing for coal tonnage he never counted sack by sack; and it was only later, well into the month, hauling the same eight wagons west through a night of driving sleet with the branch's rails slick under him and the manifest folded in his coat where it had ridden since the foreman first handed it across, that he let himself think plainly what any man on that footplate would have known from the weight alone and the care Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's men took loading it, that he was carrying arms west to Seann Bhral, and that a man does not load arms onto a train bound for a river port below the western hills unless he means, before long, to use them on the hills themselves.

At Seann Bhral, those first nights, he saw little of where the wagons' cargo went once it left his own charge. The quay there was new work, built out over the tidal mud in the two years since the river port had grown from a lime-boat's stopping-place into something Comhairle nam Mèinnean thought worth a covered shed and a length of proper stone, and Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's men unloaded by lantern into a lorry that always stood waiting with its engine already turning over, so that the whole business, from the last wagon's door swung open to the lorry's tail-lamp vanishing up the coast road, took less time than it took Eachann to turn his engine on the triangle below the shed and see it faced back east. He asked, the second week, where the lorry went, of a stevedore he had exchanged a civil word with more than once over a winter of shared cold mornings, and got for his answer only a look that told him plainly enough the question had been heard, weighed, and judged not worth the trouble of an answer, and he did not ask it a second time.

He thought of this the way he thought of the manifest, which was to say he thought of it and put it from him, because the alternative, the thing his thinking kept circling toward and would not quite land on, was to ask himself what he owed the men whose hills the line ran under, and he found, turning that question over on a cold footplate at three in the morning with thirty miles of bad rail still ahead of him, that he did not know the answer and was in no great hurry to find it before he had to. A driver of Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn since he was nineteen, and his father before him a driver of coal for the same line under the same board, he had never in either man's time on the footplate known it to be any part of a driver's trade to know what his cargo was for. He told himself this on the second night, and again on the ninth, and by the seventeenth had stopped telling himself anything at all, and drove.

The eighteenth night brought him, an hour past the second lamp-post below the capital's edge, a company on the branch road below the line, marching in the dark with lanterns swung low against the wet and a corporal at their head whom Eachann, slowing for the level crossing at that point, recognised by the set of his shoulders before he made out his face: a steady, unremarkable man he had carried west once before on an ordinary passenger working, three years and more back, a man he had exchanged no more than a dozen words with in that whole journey and remembered chiefly for having asked him, once, an intelligent question about the line's gradients that most passengers never thought to ask. He did not know the man's name then and did not learn it now; he only lifted a hand from the regulator as the engine passed above the marching company, an old habit from lonelier runs, and the corporal, glancing up at the sound of the engine, lifted his own hand in answer without breaking step, and the company went on into the dark toward the west, and Eachann's train went on into the dark toward the west a little faster, since arms do not wait on marching men and the manifest in his coat had never once, in eighteen nights, allowed him to slow for anyone.

It was the night after that, the third-from-last night of the month by his own count, though he had by then stopped keeping the calendar with any care, that he came, an hour before the false dawn that time of year brings before the true one, upon the family walking north along the line.

He saw them a long way off, the way a man on a footplate sees anything on a straight run at night, as a paleness first and then a shape and only at the last a family: a man and a woman and, between them, two children small enough to be half-carried, walking the cinder path beside the rails because the branch road that season was deep in mud and the cinder path, packed hard by generations of platelayers, was not. They had a handcart with them, piled with what a family carries when it is carrying everything it owns at once, and they walked, Eachann saw as his lamp swept over them, with the particular steadiness of people who have already walked further than they meant to and have found that walking, once begun, is easier kept up than stopped. He knew them for Tuathaich before his lamp had fully passed over them, by the cut of the man's coat and by the way the woman carried the smaller child against her hip, a way of carrying he had seen at Caol mhòr's harbour a hundred times and never once, until that morning, seen on Slighe a' Ghuail's western branch, going north, away from the hills the arms in his wagons were bound for.

He did not stop. In the half-second such things take a man on a footplate doing forty miles an hour with thirty more still to run and a manifest in his coat that named a time at Seann Bhral he could not miss, the reasons came to him ready-made: that a train running arms west did not slow for anyone on the line whatever the hour or whoever they were, that the family, whatever had put them on that path at that hour, were plainly bound the opposite way from wherever his own night's work would end, and that whatever had set a family walking north with a handcart in the dark of am Faoilleach was no business a driver could mend from a moving footplate in any case. All of this was true, and none of it, he found afterward, sitting in the drivers' room at Muileann chrom with a mug of something hot going cold in his two hands, was the reason he had not stopped, and the reason he had not stopped was one he did not put into words that night nor for a good while after, though he came, in the months the arms trains ran, to know it well enough by the feel of it, which was that stopping would have meant knowing something about the family that not stopping let him not know, and that a man who has agreed to sign for weight and not for goods finds, given the practice of a few weeks, that the same discipline serves for a good deal else besides.

He did not look back. The line ran straight enough there that he could have, in the lamp's last light before the curve, but he kept his eyes on the rail ahead and his hand on the regulator and let the family go by behind him into the dark, and drove on to Seann Bhral, where Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's men were waiting on the quay with lanterns and a covered lorry, exactly as they had waited every night that month, to take the eight wagons' cargo off his hands and into their own keeping, and ask him, as they always did, for nothing but his signature on the manifest, which he gave them, and turned his engine, and ran light back east before the true dawn came up grey over hills he had, by then, stopped letting himself look at from the footplate at all.

## II. Of the List at Àth leathan

Ruth Calder had kept lists her whole life, first her father's tally-books and then, these five years past, Còrdadh Muileann àrsaidh's own accounts, and she had thought, before the last week of am Faoilleach, that she knew the shape a list could take. She learned otherwise standing at the mouth of the road into Àth leathan on a morning so cold the ink in her pen thickened between names, watching the hewers of five towns come down out of the hills by paths no cart had ever used, with their pit-lamps lit at noon.

They came first from Cnoc thais, forty men and more under Tom Varley, down the drove track that ran along the ridge and had not carried so many feet at once, Ruth thought, since An Dealachadh itself; then from Àth naomh, a smaller company but no less determined, the men walking two abreast where the path allowed it as though even now, arriving at another town's pit-head with nothing to defend but their own presence, they meant to be seen keeping order; then, through the afternoon and into a second cold dusk, the men of Muileann àrsaidh and Tobar dhearg of the hills in smaller parties, some of them boys of fourteen who had never cut a working face in their lives but whose fathers or brothers or, in two cases that Ruth wrote down and did not trust herself to think about further, whose whole households had already come, so that there was nobody left at home to keep them from it.

Sarah Dunmore sent down from Muileann àrsaidh, with the second of her town's parties, two cartloads of oatmeal and a barrel of salted fish that her own kitchen could ill spare, with a note pinned to the barrel's lid in a hand Ruth knew for hers, saying only that a company that had not eaten would not stand the walk home again whatever else the week brought, and asking no thanks and expecting, Ruth judged from the note's shortness, none given. Ruth set a boy to portioning it out at the pit-shed door, one bowl to a name checked off her own list, and found, doing the sum of oatmeal against mouths on the second evening, that Sarah's two cartloads would carry the gathering perhaps nine days at the ration she judged safe to set, and said nothing of that figure to anyone, since a number a company cannot mend by any labour of its own is not a number worth handing round a cold pit-shed at dusk.

Tobar dhearg's men, last of the five towns to arrive and fewest, came down a path so little used that two of the older hewers had to be sent ahead the day before to cut back the whin that had grown across it in the years since anyone had walked it in company; there were but eleven of them in all, every man the hill town's one pit could spare and still keep a face working, and their captain, a stooped man older than Tom Varley and older, Ruth thought, than the walk down should rightly have let him manage, set his lamp on her trestle table before he gave her his own name, as though the lamp itself, and not the man carrying it, were the thing that most wanted counting.

Why the lamps, lit and carried at noon when there was no working face at the end of any of these paths to light, Ruth did not ask any of them, because she did not need to. She had grown up among hewers and knew a hewer's habits the way she knew her own hands: a lit lamp carried openly, at noon, on a hill path, was not light a man needed to see by, it was a thing said without saying it, the way a company musters under its own colours rather than marching bare, and she understood, watching the first of Cnoc thais's lamps come down off the ridge in the grey early light, that the men carrying them meant the whole of the western hills to see, from every farmhouse window between here and the sea, that the pits' own men were coming to Àth leathan and coming as pit men, lamps lit, not as anything the council or Comhairle nam Mèinnean might afterward choose to call them.

She kept her list at a trestle table set up in the lee of the Àth leathan pit-shed, with Tom Varley beside her the first two days until Cnoc thais's own numbers were fully in and he judged his own presence better spent seeing to the byres, and she wrote down every name that came to her, town by town, with the age of each man or boy where she troubled to ask it and a mark against those who had brought their own tools, since tools, in the weeks that followed, proved harder to find than men willing to carry them. By the fourth day the pit-sheds at Àth leathan, three of them standing since before her father's father worked the seam, were full to their rafters with men sleeping on straw laid over the old floor timbers, and the byres behind the chapel, given over by families who had, most of them, already sent a son or a husband to be counted at her own table, held the overflow, cattle moved out into whatever shelter a hedge or a drystone wall could offer in a month that gave them precious little of either.

She did not, in all those days, let herself think overlong about what the list was for. It was, on its face, no more than a count: how many men, from which town, with what tools, so that whoever came after her with the harder questions, feeding them, arming what few of them could be armed, finding them somewhere to stand when the day came that everyone at Àth leathan now spoke of only as "when it comes" and never named further, would have a true number to work from rather than a guess. She told herself this each evening, going back over the day's names by lamplight in the small room above the pit-shed office that had been given her for the writing, and she believed it, mostly, and it was only on the sixth evening, with the list grown past four hundred names and the ink gone thick again in the cold, that Tom Varley came in from checking the last of the byres and told her, in the flat voice he had taken to using for anything he judged she needed to hear and would not thank him for, that Comhairle nam Mèinnean kept a list too.

"Whose is it," she asked, though she had already half guessed the answer from his voice before he gave it.

"Comhairle nam Mèinnean's, out of Cathair mhòr," he said. "A clerk of Seumas mac Eachainn's office let it slip to a carter at Seann Skell, and the carter told it to a man at Cnoc thais, and the man at Cnoc thais told me on the drove path coming down. Two names on it above every other, he said. Yours and mine."

She sat with the pen still in her hand and did not write anything for a moment, looking at the page of names she had taken all that week, four hundred and some men and boys of five towns who had walked to Àth leathan carrying lit lamps at noon because a lit lamp said what none of them had the words, or perhaps only the wish, to say outright; and the thought that had circled her all that winter came to her now fully formed, that a list is a strange kind of thing to be the author of, since the same discipline that let her set down four hundred names in a clean careful hand for the hills' own use was, on some other table in Cathair mhòr, being used to set down two names, hers and Tom's, for a use she did not need Tom to spell out further.

"Then they'll know where to look for us," she said, "when it comes."

"They knew that already," Tom said. "It's not as though we've been hiding at Àth leathan." He said it without much heat, the way a man states a fact he has already made his peace with, and went to see about the last of the straw for the newest arrivals, and Ruth sat on a while longer with her own list open before her, running her thumb down the column of names as though the touch of the page might tell her something the ink itself did not, before she closed the book and blew out the lamp and went down to see that the pit-shed fires, banked low against the cold, were not banked so low that a man might wake in the night and find himself colder than the walk down from his own hill farm had already left him.

Word of the regiments' setting out reached Àth leathan on the six-and-twentieth of am Faoilleach, carried up the western road by a carter who had watched them pass below Cathair dhearg on the three-and-twentieth and made the walk north as fast as a laden cart could manage once he had seen enough to know it was worth the telling. They had gone by the western road, he said, companies enough to fill it from verge to verge for the better part of an hour, their lorries running on dubhan the whole column's length, so that the road smelled, he told it, of a fuel the western hills had never burned a barrel of and never meant to, going west now ahead of the men who were to use it, to Seann Skell in the west where the enforcers had sat quartered these two years and more waiting for exactly this company to come and join them.

Ruth heard it standing at her trestle table with the day's last names not yet entered, and found, hearing it, that she felt none of the surprise she might have expected of herself a month before, only a kind of settling, the way a held breath settles once the thing waited for has at last, for good or ill, arrived. She looked down the pit-shed row at the lamps still burning here and there among the sleeping men, small steady flames against a cold that showed no sign yet of any spring; and she opened her book to a clean page, dipped her thickened pen, and began, because it was the only work she properly knew how to do and the only answer she had left to give a Board that had already, by its own list, given its answer to her, to count once more, town by town, how many men Àth leathan now held who had come to it carrying a lit lamp at noon and meant, whatever the road below Cathair dhearg was now carrying west to meet them, to be there still when it came.

# Chapter Twenty-four: Of Blàr Àth leathan

*11 an Giblean DE 21*

## I. Of the Burn in Spate

The three months since the regiments went west had been the slowest Ruth Calder had ever lived through, and also, she came to think afterward, the fastest, in the way that a long wait can be both at once: slow in the living of each single day at the pit-shed office with the fires banked and the ink freezing, and fast in the looking back, so that am Faoilleach and an Gearran together seemed, from the far side of them, to have gone by in the time it took to draw one long breath. Word had come up the western road twice a week or better, carried by carters who had their own reasons to travel Slighe a' Ghuail's western branch and their own reasons, most of them, to be glad of the coin Ruth paid for a true account rather than a rumour dressed up as one: that the enforcers held the western Seann Skell in strength; that the regiments camped beside them through the worst of the winter and drilled, when the ground allowed it, on the flats above the river; that the manor house had been made a headquarters and the maor's own hall a store for the lorries' fuel. None of it told her a day or an hour, only the slow gathering of a thing readying to move, and she had learned, through those weeks, to read it the way her father had taught her to read a seam before it gave, from the sum of many small signs taken together.

She had not looked for the thaw to come so fast. Through am Faoilleach and into an Gearran the snow had lain deep enough on the hill paths that the companies coming in from Muileann àrsaidh and Tobar dhearg of the hills went a full day slower than the walk should have taken, and she had grown used to a world of white fields and black timber and a cold that got into the ink and stayed there. Then in the first week of an Giblean the wind came round to the south-west and did not go back, and within four days the snow was gone off every slope but the north faces of the higher hills, and the burn below Àth leathan, which she had crossed dry-shod as a girl in most winters, came up brown and quick and loud enough that she heard it from her window in the pit-shed office before she was properly awake.

She went down to look at it on the tenth, the evening before, with Tom Varley beside her because he had taken to walking the ground with her most evenings that month, the two of them saying little and looking hard at whatever there was to look at. The ford below the pit-heads, which any cart had crossed dry in a normal spring, was gone under two feet of brown water moving fast enough to turn a stick end over end, and the flat meadow beyond it, the one everyone at Àth leathan still called the fair field though no fair had been held there in three years, lay soft and dark with the last of the melt still standing in its furrows.

"They'll not bring a lorry over that," Tom said, meaning the ford, and meaning by it more than the ford.

"They'll not need to," Ruth said. "The road from Seann Skell doesn't cross it. It comes down the near side and stops at the pit-heads. Whatever they bring, they bring it dry."

She had walked that road herself twice that winter, once as far as the river and once, in secret and against Tom's counsel, most of the way to Seann Skell, to see with her own eyes what the carter's word had already told her: the regiments quartered beside the enforcers, their lorries drawn up in rows under canvas, more of them than she had troubled to count past a hundred because the counting past a hundred did not change what she meant to do about it. She had not told the five towns the whole of what she saw, only Tom, and Tom had told the pit captains, who told their own companies only so much as steadied a man rather than loosened his knees, which was the same discipline she had grown up watching her father keep about a bad seam or a flooding gallery, and which, standing at the swollen ford with three months of waiting behind her and a night before whatever the morning brought, she still knew how to keep.

The five towns had been at Àth leathan since the last week of am Faoilleach, near enough four hundred names on her first count and closer to five hundred and fifty by the time the last of Tobar dhearg's boys came down with their fathers in an Gearran, once the whole matter had stopped being a gathering and become, in everything but the word for it, a muster that would not disperse. Through the waiting months she had done the thing that a captain's daughter does without being taught it in so many words, which was to turn a crowd of men and boys glad of one another's company into a body that could be told where to stand: five companies, one to a town, each under its own captain and answerable, in the matter of where the whole body moved and when, to Tom Varley, whom the five towns had agreed on without much debate once it was plain nobody much fancied the office and Tom least of anyone.

Cnoc thais's company was the largest, near a hundred and sixty under Tom himself, most of them hewers of his own two reopened shafts and the families that had followed the coal down from the ridge. Àth naomh's sixty-odd kept their two-abreast order even at the pit-head, a habit Ruth had stopped remarking on by the second week. Muileann àrsaidh sent the most of any single town, near two hundred, Sarah Dunmore's oatmeal carts having by then made three further journeys down from the mill, each one shorter than the last as the mill's own reserves thinned. Tobar dhearg of the hills sent, in the end, near forty, every man and boy the hill town's one pit could spare and a dozen more besides who had walked down all the same, leaving the pit worked by old men and women for the season. Àth leathan's own company was Ruth's, by the same accident of a dead father that had made her the towns' spokeswoman, and it stood at ninety hewers of the town's three pits, with a scatter of wives and elder daughters who had, by then, made themselves as much a part of the muster as any man with a pick, carrying water and dressings and, where a household had a fowling piece from before An Dealachadh and no man left to carry it, carrying that too.

Nine hundred souls, near enough, stood at Àth leathan by the tenth of an Giblean, counting the carriers among them, and Ruth's list, grown thick with names crossed through and names added, held every one. Against them, by every account the carters brought up from the river, the kingdom would send near fourteen hundred, drawn from the companies quartered at Seann Skell and the enforcers already settled there, with lorries enough to carry them the five miles from the river port to the pit-heads in a single morning's work. Ruth had done that sum more than once through the winter, turning it over the way she turned over any figure that would not come out even, and had found, each time, that it changed nothing about what the five towns meant to do, only the manner of doing it.

The waiting months had worn the gathering thinner in ways no muster roll troubled to record. Two of Sarah Dunmore's cart-horses had gone lame on the Muileann àrsaidh road and were not replaced; a fever had gone through the byres behind the chapel in an Gearran and taken an old woman of Cnoc thais who had come down only to be near her grandsons; Ellen Marsh, teaching still at Doire ghlas, had sent up through the winter two letters that Ruth kept folded inside the same list-book as the names, neither of them saying anything Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own censors would have troubled to strike out, both of them saying, in the plain way Ellen wrote everything, that the school's benches were being kept ready should any family need them. Ruth had not answered either letter. She was grateful for both, and she had found, by the second month of the muster, that she no longer trusted her own hand to write anything short enough to be worth the carter's trouble.

They had picks and shovels and the hewers' own short axes, sharpened that winter past any use a coal face had ever asked of them. They had, among the whole nine hundred, perhaps sixty firearms fit to be called such, most of them fowling pieces older than any man carrying them, a dozen better rifles bought or begged from who knew where and never asked after too closely, and four kegs of blasting powder from the pits themselves, which Tom Varley meant, if it came to that, for the narrow places where the road from Seann Skell ran between the spoil-heaps and the flooded lower galleries, where a charge set right might do more than sixty fowling pieces together.

"You'll not fire the powder unless I say," Tom told her that evening at the ford, not for the first time. "A charge set too soon warns them off the ground we want them on."

"I know it," Ruth said. "I've known it since you first told me, and the second time, and the third."

"I'll go on telling you," Tom said, "because it's the one thing between us and a rout, and I'd sooner bore you with it than have you forget it at the wrong minute." He said it without much heat, the way he said most things that winter, and Ruth, looking at the brown water going by faster than either of them could easily have swum it, found she was glad of the boring, glad of anything said plainly and repeated, because the alternative, she had learned these three months, was a silence in which a person's own thoughts ran on faster than the burn.

She did not ask him, that evening, what he thought the morning would bring, because she had asked him some version of that question most evenings for a fortnight and had stopped expecting an answer different from the last. He only looked a while longer at the water, and then at the dark shapes of the pit-heads against a sky gone the colour of a struck match, and said that they should get what sleep the night would give them, because the towns' companies would want their captains steady in the morning whatever the morning brought.

On the way back she passed Tobar dhearg's captain, the stooped man who had brought his own lamp down off the hill path in am Faoilleach and set it on her trestle table before he gave his name, sitting outside his men's fire with a cup he was not drinking from. He asked her, in the flat way he asked most things, whether the chapel at Àth leathan would be open before light, and she told him it would, since the priest had said as much himself, and the old man nodded and said that a man ought to have been inside a chapel at least once before a morning like the one coming, whatever else the morning held, and that he meant to see to it his own men had the chance of it too, those who wanted it. Ruth said she would pass the word along the line, and did.

Walking back up to the pit-shed office with the ford's noise falling away behind her, she thought that Tom's answer, plain and repeated and not much of an answer on its own terms, was as near to one as she was likely to get, and found, turning it over, that it was answer enough.

## II. Of the Word Ruth Gave at Dawn

She woke before light, as she had every morning that month without needing anyone to rouse her, and went out into a cold that had lost, overnight, the last hard edge of winter and taken on instead the raw, wet cold of a spring morning after rain, the kind that gets into a coat faster than any frost. The sky to the east, over the road from Seann Skell, was going from black to a grey the colour of wet slate, and the burn, louder now than it had been the evening before, ran on unseen below the pit-heads with a sound like water that had somewhere particular to be.

The companies were mustering already, town by town, along the low ground between the pit-sheds and the fair field, exactly as she and Tom had marked out the ground for them three evenings before: Cnoc thais on the left flank nearest the flooded lower gallery, where the ground did most of a wall's work; Àth naomh in the centre, keeping their two-abreast order even now, forming and re-forming it as their captain called them into it as though the order were a kind of armour worn; Muileann àrsaidh on the right, where the road from Seann Skell came down between the spoil-heaps into the narrowest ground of the whole field, the ground Tom's blasting powder was laid to answer if it came to that; Tobar dhearg's forty held back a little, by their own captain's word and not by anyone else's ordering, at the mouth of Àth leathan's own pit, where a man too old for the front line could still see what came and send word of it; and Àth leathan's ninety in the last gap between Àth naomh and the pit-heads proper, Ruth's own place among them though she carried, that morning, no pick and no fowling piece, only her list, folded small inside her coat where it had ridden for three months, and a lantern not yet lit.

She thought, standing a moment at the pit-shed door before she started down the line, of her father, five years dead now and buried at the chapel she had just sent word about, and of the last thing he had ever told her of the seam under Àth leathan, which was that a working face tells you what it means to do a long while before it does it, if you trouble to listen, and that the trouble of listening is most of what a captain is for. These three months she had listened to as much as the north's own carters and her own eyes could tell her, and this morning found she had run out of anything further the listening could give her; what was left was only the doing.

She went down the line as the light came up, as she had gone down it every morning of the muster, though this morning she found herself looking at faces rather than counting them, which she had not let herself do before: a boy of fourteen from Tobar dhearg whose father had come down with him and whose name, she remembered without needing the list, was the last one she had taken on the sixth evening of the gathering; one of Sarah Dunmore's carters, too old by rights for the front line and standing in it anyway because his two sons stood either side of him and he would not be parted from them; a woman of Àth naomh, no older than Ruth herself, with a fowling piece across her back and a baby not eight months born left, that morning, in the care of an aunt at the pit-shed, whose name Ruth had entered on her list under the mother's own insistence, since the child was to be counted as being of the muster too, in some fashion the woman had not troubled to explain and Ruth had not troubled to question.

Along the line she passed the Muileann àrsaidh company forming up on the right, where Sarah Dunmore's carter stood between his two sons as he had every morning that month, and past him the company's own captain, a mill-hand turned pit-hand named for the season only as Muileann àrsaidh's captain, since he had never troubled anyone with more of a name than that and nobody had troubled him for it, checking the priming of the dozen better rifles one by one down the front rank with the same unhurried care Ruth had watched a smith give to a set of new-forged tools. He told her, as she passed, that the ground below the spoil-heaps was as good as it would ever be, the road narrowed there to less than a cart's width by the heaps on either hand, and that if Tom's charge went off true it would do the work of fifty men. Ruth said she hoped he was right, and went on.

She found Tom at the centre of the line, where he had gone to speak with Àth naomh's captain about the ground below the spoil-heaps, and she came to him not with any speech prepared, because she had tried, the night before, to write one in her head and found every version of it either too grand for what the morning was or too small for what the last three months had been, and had given it up.

"They'll be in sight within the hour," Tom said. He had a spy-glass, an old thing of his grandfather's that had done service, he'd told her once, watching for An Dealachadh's ships that never came a second time, and he had it trained now on the road below the spoil-heaps, where nothing yet moved but the light. "Dust first, if the road's dried enough. Then the column."

"And after that," Ruth said, "it's yours to give the word, not mine."

"It was always going to be," Tom said, not unkindly. "You kept the list. I keep the line. That's the shape it's taken, and I'll not pretend either of us chose it different from how it fell." He lowered the glass and looked at her a moment in the grey light, and whatever he had meant to say next, he did not say it, and instead put out his hand for the plain clasp two people give each other before a thing neither can promise the shape of, and Ruth took it.

"Tell them," she said, meaning the five towns' companies both, "that whatever comes of today, the list stands. Every name on it, town by town. Whoever comes looking after, for whatever reason they come looking, the list will say who stood at Àth leathan and who they stood beside."

"I'll tell them," Tom said. "Go back to your own company now. They'll want to see you standing with them when it starts, not off talking to me."

She went back down the line to Àth leathan's ninety, and took her place among them, not at their front, since she carried no weapon and had never claimed to be any kind of soldier, but near enough the front that any man there could see her if he turned his head, which several of them did, briefly, as the light came fully up and the grey overhead thinned toward a colour that might, on another morning, have been called a fair sky.

For a while, standing there, there was nothing to do but wait, and the waiting had a shape of its own that Ruth had not met in three months of waiting for other things: the burn loud below them, a lark going up somewhere over the higher ground as though the morning were an ordinary one, one of the Àth leathan hewers beside her murmuring the numbers of a psalm under his breath without seeming to know he did it, and, from along the Tobar dhearg line, the sound, thin on the wind, of the old captain's men singing something low in An Eaglais's own words, which she followed only in part and understood well enough for what it was. She found she was glad of it, the singing, in the same plain way she had been glad of Tom's repeating himself the night before: a thing said or sung that steadied more by its saying than by its sense.

The dust came first, as Tom had said it would, a pale smear along the road below the spoil-heaps where nothing else moved, and then, before the dust had well settled in her sight, the column itself came, dark and long and closer than Ruth had let herself think it would be so soon, moving at a steady pace that had nothing hurried and nothing hesitant in it, the pace of men who had been told exactly where they were going and saw no reason to arrive there other than on time.

Ruth Calder stood at the front rank of Àth leathan's company, in the raw cold of a spring morning with the burn loud behind her and the dust of the regiments' coming rising pale along the road ahead, and watched them come on, and this is where her own account of that day ends, because after this hour no page in her own hand, nor any word set down as hers by anyone who stood beside her, tells what she said or thought or did when the column reached the ground below the spoil-heaps and the first order, whoever gave it and on whichever side, was given.

## III. Of What the North Tells

So the people of the five towns tell it, those who stood in one company or another that morning and lived to walk home from it, and those who had it from them at their own hearths.

They tell that the regiments came on past the dust and did not slow at the ford, because the ford was not their road, and that the fighting began at the spoil-heaps rather than the ford, where Muileann àrsaidh's company held the narrow ground and Tom Varley's charge, when at last he gave the word for it, brought down enough of the loose spoil to check the column's head for the better part of an hour, though it did not turn them back, because a column of fourteen hundred does not turn back for the loss of its head, only slows, and re-forms, and comes on again by a wider way round the fallen ground.

They tell that the fighting spread from there along the whole line through the morning, Cnoc thais holding longest on the left where the flooded gallery did a wall's work as Tom had judged it would, Àth naomh's two-abreast order breaking at last into no order at all when the regiments' own line reached and passed it, and that the fair field, the soft dark meadow beyond the ford that Ruth and Tom had looked at the evening before, was by noon a ground no one who stood on it that day has ever agreed to call by its old name again.

Cnoc thais tells its own part of that morning apart from the rest, as a town will keep the telling of its own dead closer than it keeps any other part of a shared grief, and its telling holds that Tom Varley was seen three times in the worst of the fighting by the flooded gallery, each time carrying a wounded man or boy back from the line with his own hands before going forward again, and that it was Tom who at last called the retreat toward Cnoc thais and Muileann àrsaidh when the gallery's ground could no longer be held. Muileann àrsaidh's own telling, kept separately again, holds to the charge below the spoil-heaps and to little else, as though the town had decided, without ever quite deciding it aloud, that the one thing it had done that day was worth the telling and the rest belonged to other towns to keep.

They tell of the pit-heads changing hands more than once before the day was out, of men fighting with picks and axes against rifles because that was what the five towns had brought to fight with, of the boy of fourteen from Tobar dhearg whose father would not let him past the pit-shed door and stood in the door himself the whole of the morning, and of the woman of Àth naomh with the fowling piece, whose name is remembered in that town still, though not written here, because the naming of her is the north's to keep and not this book's to spend.

Doire naomh, whose grove lies within sight of the field though its own people took no part in the fighting, tells only what could be seen from that distance: smoke over the pit-heads by mid-morning, though nothing there had been fired that either side has ever owned to setting; the sound of it carrying on a south wind as far as the grove, so that the grove's own people, going about their ordinary morning, heard the whole of it without seeing more than the smoke; and a silence, toward evening, that some of them said afterward was worse to hear than the noise had been.

They tell that by early afternoon the five towns' companies, what remained whole of them, gave up the ground below the pit-heads and the fair field both, and fell back in a scatter of smaller bodies rather than one, along the hill paths that had brought them down in am Faoilleach and up again now in the opposite direction, toward Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais and the higher ground the regiments' lorries could not easily follow. Of the nine hundred who had stood at dawn, the towns' own reckoning, made afterward and never once written down together in a single tally, holds that something under two-thirds came home to one hill town or another by the second evening; what happened to the rest is the part of the telling that varies most from mouth to mouth, since a scattered retreat over broken ground in failing light leaves as many questions behind it as a battle does, and the north's telling does not pretend to answer them all.

They tell the dead in the hundreds, and they do not agree past that on any closer number, because no one town's count was ever set beside another's, and because more than one family of the five towns lost, that single day, every name it had sent to Àth leathan, so that there was no one left of that household to be asked how many, or which, or when.

Of Ruth Calder herself the north tells nothing certain. Some say she was seen at the pit-head door in the worst of the afternoon, calling names from memory to men who could no longer answer to them. Others say she went down with Àth leathan's company when it broke, and was carried off the field by two of her own hewers who did not themselves come home to say so. A few, the fewest, say she was seen on the Muileann àrsaidh path that evening, walking, her list gone from her coat, though every teller who says this admits in the same breath that they had it third-hand or fourth, from someone who was not there to see it either. No teller in the north, asked plainly, will say for certain which of these is true, or whether none of them is, and the north has learned, in the years since, to let the question stand unanswered rather than choose among three stories none of which any single mouth can swear to.

## IV. Of What the Open Record Gives

An Clàr Foscailte, kept that year by Sìleas nic Rath at an Leabharlann in Muileann chaol from the regiments' own returns, says a good deal less, and says it more plainly.

It gives the day, 11 an Giblean DE 21, and the place, the field below Àth leathan, and it gives the kingdom's dead by name and by company, thirty and eight in number, the returns of that day counted and signed by officers whose own names stand beside the count. Somhairle mac Lachlainn's own return, written from Seann Skell within the week, names the companies that had marched from Cathair dhearg the winter before and does no more than name them; it says which held the ground below the spoil-heaps and which came up after, and says nothing of how any man among the thirty and eight came to be counted, only that he was. The west-coast levies who had guarded the road behind the column are named among the dead too, a dozen of them, men the return does not yet call by any regiment's number, since none of the companies that fought at Àth leathan had, on that day, been given one. The rest of the thirty and eight are scattered among the capital's own companies, drawn from Cathair dhearg and Inis mhòr, ordinary men whose names, set down in a clerk's even hand on a return meant only to balance a muster roll, are the fullest account An Clàr Foscailte gives of anyone who died at Àth leathan that day.

The return notes, in the same even hand, that the kingdom's host had been victualled through the campaign from Inis àrsaidh, the river town nearest the field by water, and that its stores had held good through the fighting and after; it is the only line in the whole return that speaks of anything going right for anyone, and it speaks of bread and salt fish rather than of men.

Of the holdouts' dead An Clàr Foscailte gives no number at all. It notes only that the field was held by evening, that the pit-heads of Àth leathan passed into Comhairle nam Mèinnean's keeping, and that the companies of the five towns, what remained of them, had withdrawn toward Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais by nightfall. It does not say how many withdrew, nor how many did not.

Ruth Calder's name does not stand among the thirty and eight, which is no matter, since she was never of the kingdom's regiments for An Clàr Foscailte to count. It does not stand anywhere else in An Clàr Foscailte either, that day or after. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own list, the one Tom Varley had word of on the drove path months before, does not appear in what an Leabharlann was given to keep; if it survives, it lies where the rest of the war's sealed record lies, and no one now living has read it. Every page an Leabharlann holds open of that spring, and every page after, is searched in vain for her name. Sìleas nic Rath, taking down the regiments' returns that season in a hand still new to the office, wrote once, in a private note kept with her own papers and not with Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd proper, that she had looked for the name a second time and a third, thinking she had missed it among so many others, and had not found it any of the times she looked.

She wrote, in that same private note, that she had thought once of asking Somhairle mac Lachlainn directly whether his own return, or any paper that had passed under his hand, named a woman among the dead or the taken, and that she had not sent the question, because a chronicler new to the office learns early which questions the office will let her ask and which it will not, and this, she judged, was one of the second kind.

Near Àth leathan, in the grove the Dia-thìrich of Doire naomh keep closed to strangers, many of the field's unclaimed dead were laid that week and after, the grove's own people going out onto the ground once the regiments had passed on toward Muileann àrsaidh, and carrying what they found. The town of Àth chrom, a short way off at the bent ford, sent its own people to carry others, its own drovers going out along the road with carts they had until then used only for coal and salt. Neither town's record says whose dead they carried, of which side, or how many, only that they carried them, and that the grove has kept its graves since, closed to strangers, as it kept them before. Baile fhiadhaich, further off on the west-coast harbour road, sent no one to the field, lying further off than the others, but its own people took in what wounded reached that far, and the town has kept the remembering of that day in its own way since, apart from any teller's account written down elsewhere.

The field, the fair field below the pit-heads where nine hundred souls of five towns had stood at dawn, lay empty by the time the last light went out of that day, the burn still running loud and brown below it, the spoil brought down by Tom Varley's charge still lying where it had fallen across the narrow road, and no plough has turned that ground since.

# Chapter Twenty-five: Of the Field Left Unploughed

*DE 21*

## I. Of the Carriers on the Ridge Path

Tom Varley did not see the battle end. He saw it break, which is a different thing, and he saw it from the wrong side of a drystone wall with a boy of Tobar dhearg bleeding through both hands pressed to his own thigh, and after that he saw very little that a man could afterward set down in an orderly way. The burn was in spate below the pit-heads, brown and quick with the last of the snow-melt, and it was the burn he remembered most clearly once the day was done: the sound of it under the other sounds, going on the same before, during and after, as if the water had somewhere better to be than any of them.

They had held the southern pits until the light began to go, longer than anyone at the pit-shed table had thought they would, and then word came down the line from company to company, not an order so much as a thing everyone understood at once the way a flock understands weather, that the southern ground was not to be held any further, and the hewers of five towns began to come back off it in the dusk in the way men come back from a thing that has gone against them, walking fast in twos and threes, turning now and again to look behind at nothing in particular.

Tom took the wounded. It was not a duty anyone gave him; he found himself doing it the way he found himself, most days of his life, at the head of whatever needed a head, and by full dark he had six men and the Tobar dhearg boy on hurdles and handcarts and, in one case, on the back of a Cnoc thais man built broad enough to carry his own cousin the better part of two miles without setting him down. They went up by the drove path along the ridge, the same track Cnoc thais's forty had come down by in am Faoilleach with their lamps lit at noon, and this time no lamp was lit at all, because a lit lamp on that path that night would have told the whole of the low country exactly where to look.

The boy from Tobar dhearg was called Rab, though Tom did not learn that until they were an hour up the path and the boy, half out of his senses with the cold and the loss of blood, began saying it over to himself, quietly, as though it were the one word left to him that still meant anything sure. Tom knelt by the handcart twice in that hour to press the dressing tighter, cloth torn from his own shirt-tail since the proper dressings had gone with the men still fighting, and both times the boy looked at him without seeming quite to see him and said his own name again, Rab, Rab, and Tom said it back to him, which was the only medicine he had to give.

They did not stop at Àth leathan. That was the hardest thing Tom did that night, harder than the carrying: to come within sight of the pit-shed roofs where four hundred men had slept on straw two months before, and to keep walking past them into the hills, because word had already reached him, passed hand to hand up the column of carriers, that the southern approach was cut and the town would not hold a night's stand against what was coming up the road behind them. He looked once at the dark shape of the pit-shed roof against a sky just beginning to lighten in the east, and thought of Sarah Dunmore's oatmeal carts and the boy who had portioned it out one bowl to a name, and did not let himself think further, because there was a cart-wheel stuck in a rut just then and six other men waiting on him to set his shoulder to it.

By the grey hour before true dawn they had come up over the saddle between two hills and down the far side toward Muileann àrsaidh, where fires had been lit, small and shielded, in the lee of the walled pit-heads, and women came out along the last half-mile of the path to take the hurdles from the carriers' shoulders without being asked. Sarah Dunmore herself was among them, in a coat thrown on over a nightgown, and she took one look at the Tobar dhearg boy's leg by the light of a shaded lantern and sent a girl running for the woman who set bones and stitched wounds for half the western hills, and said nothing to Tom at all beyond a hand laid once, briefly, on his arm as he went by her with the next hurdle, which was thanks and welcome and a question all in the one touch, and which Tom had no words to answer that night and did not try to find any.

He counted them in at the pit-head gate the way Ruth had counted them out at the trestle table two months before, though his list was shorter and kept in his head and not on paper, because there was no paper to hand and, he thought, setting the last hurdle down inside the wall as the sky went from grey to a thin cold white, perhaps no great wish in him to see the number written where anyone could count it against the number that had gone down to Àth leathan.

Six on hurdles, one on a cart, one carried the last mile on a cousin's back, and himself walking, which was nine souls got up off a field that had held nine hundred, and he knew, doing that sum in his head at the gate the way he had done Sarah's oatmeal sum two months before, that it told him nothing at all about the wider field, since a man who carries the wounded off a battle carries only those near enough his own place on it to be carried, and the rest of the field, wherever it lay and whatever it held, was no more open to him that night than the far side of the sea. He had heard, going up the path, two other parties of carriers ahead of him and behind, their voices carrying strangely in the wet air the way voices do on a hill at night, and did not know, and would not know for some days, how many souls those parties had brought off between them, or from how far along the line they had gathered them.

The woman who set bones came within the hour, an older woman named for nothing but her trade in every mouth on that hillside, Bonesetter, and worked on Rab's leg by lamplight at Sarah's own kitchen table while Sarah held the boy's shoulders and Tom, having no other use just then, held the lamp steady and watched a stranger's hands do to a stranger's boy the sort of careful violence that saves a leg or does not, and found himself, watching it, thinking less of the boy than of every other hand at that moment doing the same work on some other kitchen table in some other hill town, work he could not see and would only hear of, in pieces, over the days that followed.

Ruth's name was on neither list, in his head or on any paper. He had last seen her before first light the day before, at the pit-shed table with her own book open, telling off the companies by town as they formed on the road below the pit-heads, and had not seen her again once the light came up and the morning's work began in earnest. He told himself, standing inside the Muileann àrsaidh wall with the last of the wounded seen to and the dawn fully come, that she was one woman among nine hundred and the field was wide, and a man does not see everyone on a field that wide in a single day's fighting, and this was true, and it did nothing at all to loosen the particular tightness that had settled behind his breastbone somewhere in the small hours and had not left him since.

## II. Of the Pits Taken and the Water Let In

What happened at Àth leathan after the hewers went out of it, Tom Varley did not see, because by the time it happened he was two hills away with a wall between himself and the road, seeing to the last of the wounded and to Sarah Dunmore's fires. It came to him afterward the way most of that spring came to him, in pieces, carried up the hills by men who had themselves had it third-hand from a carter or a shepherd or, once, from a Dia-thìrich quartermaster's clerk who talked more than his orders allowed to a woman selling eggs at the western Seann Skell market and did not know or did not care that the woman's cousin kept sheep on the Àth leathan road.

The town was taken without a shot fired in it, or so every account that reached the hills agreed, a strange thing to Tom, turning it over afterward: that a town four hundred men had gathered to hold could pass from one hand to another in an empty street with nobody left inside it to say either yes or no to the taking. The regiments came up the road that same evening, the accounts said, and found the pit-shed doors standing open on their straw, the byres empty of the cattle that had been driven off into the hills days before by anyone who thought to do it, and the chapel bell still hanging in its little tower, untouched, because nobody on either side that week had found it in himself to ring a bell for any reason at all.

The order to flood the pits came from Comhairle nam Mèinnean at Cathair mhòr, and it came, by every account Tom heard, within days of the town's falling, as though the order had been drawn up and left ready in a drawer against exactly this day and wanted only the day's arriving to be sent. The shafts at Àth leathan were old, older than Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own charter, cut into a seam that had fed three generations of the town's hewers before it fed the war that ended their holding it, and the engineers who came up with the order did their work in an afternoon: the pumps that had kept the lower galleries dry for sixty years were stopped, and the water that the hills had been shedding all that wet spring, the same brown quick water that ran in the burn below the pit-heads, was let down into the workings by a sluice cut for the purpose, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's report, which Tom heard of long before he ever saw a word of it, gave the flooding as complete within the week.

Tom had gone down those shafts himself as a boy, visiting a cousin's family at Àth leathan the summer he turned eleven, and he remembered them chiefly for the cold and the smell of wet stone and a hewer, his cousin's father, showing him a seam of coal by candlelight with the particular pride of a man showing off a thing he has spent his whole life inside of. He thought of that seam now, drowned, dark water standing where the candlelight had been, and found that the thought did not move him the way he might have expected it to a year before. He had reopened his own two shafts at Cnoc thais five winters before with exactly this in his mind, that the coal under the western hills was the hills' own and answered to nobody's charter but the hewers who cut it, and he had known, taking that first cartload up out of the ground, that a day might come when somebody with more men than argument decided otherwise. It had come. He found he was less surprised by the water in the Àth leathan shafts than by how little, in the end, the surprise of it cost him, set against everything else that week had already cost.

What he could not get past, turning the reports over at Sarah Dunmore's kitchen table in the evenings that followed, was the emptiness of it: a town taken by nobody, from nobody, its pits drowned by an order signed in an office two days' ride away by a man who had never, so far as anyone in the western hills could learn, set foot within a mile of the place. Sarah said, the third evening, stirring a pot that had less in it than either of them would have wished, that it was the emptiest thing she had heard of in a long war already thick with empty things, and Tom, who had by then heard the word field left unploughed passed from mouth to mouth among the men who had come up from the south with him, though nobody yet knew quite what lay under the phrase, said only that an empty town was easier held than a full one, which was true, and was also, he knew even as he said it, no kind of answer to what Sarah had actually asked.

She pressed him on it a second time, the fifth evening, with the kitchen quieter than it had been all week and the last of the wounded moved to beds found for them among the town's own houses. What she wanted to know, she said, setting two bowls down and sitting rather than standing over the pot as she had every night before, was not whether the pits were flooded, which every carter on the road had told her twice over by then, but whether flooding them served any purpose beyond the purpose of telling the hills plainly that the seams were done for good and no agreement, however generous, would ever open them again. Tom turned that over a while before he answered her, because it was, he saw, the better question of the two he had been asked that week, sharper than his own about the field, and he said at last that he thought it served exactly that purpose and no other, since a flooded shaft cost Comhairle nam Mèinnean more to pump dry again than the coal in it would ever be worth to a kingdom that no longer burned coal for anything but its altars, and that a Board which meant only to hold the seams against some future need would have sealed the entrances and left the water out, not let it in. Sarah nodded at that, slowly, and said that she had thought as much herself and had wanted to hear it said by somebody who had gone down those shafts as a boy, so as to know the saying of it cost him something and was not merely a guess offered cheap.

## III. Of the Returns at the Western Seann Skell

Somhairle mac Lachlainn had been two years and more learning to write a report that said less than he had seen, and by the second week after Àth leathan he had learned it well enough that the returns crossing his desk at the western Seann Skell read, to a man who did not know how to read them, like the dullest paperwork any army had ever generated: musters, rations issued, a bridge repaired, a company's boots replaced. He knew how to read them, and what he read in the returns that fortnight was a victory that had cost more than the figure at the bottom of any single sheet would say, and a countryside behind his own lines that had gone, in the space of a battle, from watchful to silent in a way he did not entirely trust.

The order for An seachdamh rèisimeid was dated the day of the battle itself, drawn up, like the order to flood the pits, before the day it answered; it reached him on the fourth day, carried down from Cathair dhearg by a rider who had changed horses twice and looked it. It was raised, the order said, from the levies of the west coast, fishermen and small tenants and the sons of the river-port families who had never before been asked to stand a muster, and it was to be quartered at Seann Skell, the port nearest the western hills, with instructions Somhairle himself had a hand in drafting once the order's bare bones reached him: to hold the road behind the army and to hold, in particular, the field below Àth leathan, until such time as the council's further pleasure was known.

He had its rolls filled in a week, which was faster than any regiment before it had been raised in the whole course of the war, and he raised it, he told the returns and told nobody else, because the west coast had men enough idle at that season, between one fishing and the next, to fill the rolls without stripping a single farm of its labour, and because a regiment recruited on the coast and not from the capital's own companies was a regiment whose loyalty, in a countryside as unsettled as this one had lately become, he judged less likely to be tested by a cousin or a brother found on the other side of a wall. He kept this second reason out of any return, the kind of thing a commander thought and did not set down, the same discipline, though he would not have put it to himself in these words, that had a driver on Slighe a' Ghuail signing for weight and not for goods.

The regiment's first task, once mustered, was simple enough to state and dull enough in the stating that the return recording it ran to four lines: patrols on the Àth leathan road, morning and evening, to keep it open for the army's supply and to report anything found upon it. Somhairle read the first week's patrol reports at his own table in the requisitioned merchant's house at Seann Skell, by a dubhan lamp that burned steadier than any coal flame he had known as a young man, and found in them exactly what the order had asked for and nothing more: the road clear, the weather wet, a cart met and let pass, a farm gate found open and shut again.

It was the second week's reports that gave him the phrase that stayed with him longer than any other that spring. A patrol sent out on the fifth day past the town, along the road that ran below the old pit-heads and on toward the hills proper, returned with nothing to report but the field, and the officer writing it up, a young man new to his rank and not yet schooled in the discipline of saying less than he had seen, wrote more than the form strictly required: that the field where the battle had been fought lay as it had been left, that no one had come to it since, and that it had not been ploughed, though the season for the first ploughing was well begun on every other field the patrol had passed that morning.

Somhairle read that line twice. He had seen, in the years since he had first marched a company toward the west, a great many things he had chosen not to set down, and he had grown, without quite meaning to, careful of the things other men chose to set down when he was not looking over their shoulder to stop them. The field left unploughed was, on its face, no more than an agricultural fact, the kind of detail a farmer's son turned soldier notices because farming is the trade he was bred to before soldiering was. It sat with Somhairle longer than that, through the evening and into the night, because he understood, better perhaps than the young officer who had written it, exactly why no farmer within five miles of that field had put a plough to it, and he found himself unwilling, turning the return over by lamplight, to write the reason into any report of his own, and equally unwilling to let it pass from his mind as easily as the form he was filing it under seemed to want him to.

He sent the same officer out again three days later with instructions, given verbally and not in writing, to walk the field ground rather than the road beside it, and to bring back word of what, if anything, the ground still held. The officer went, and came back within the day, and what he brought back Somhairle wrote into the return in the fewest words the form would bear, and no fewer, because there are things a report can carry and things it cannot, and he had by then two years' practice in telling one from the other.

The musters that same fortnight gave him a second figure he found himself turning over as often as the first. The seventh's rolls, drawn from the coast towns and the river-port families, ran to some four hundred and twenty men by the second week, short of the full regiment the order had called for, and the shortfall, when he asked after it through the maor of Seann Skell rather than through any officer of his own, came back to him as no more than the ordinary business of a fishing season not yet done and boats still out that a levy could not properly reach until they came home to harbour. He accepted this answer because there was no other readily to hand and because pressing harder on a levy already raised faster than any before it seemed to him, weighing the whole of that fortnight's business, more likely to cost him goodwill on the coast than it would buy him bodies for the muster roll. He wrote the shortfall into his own return to Cathair dhearg as a seasonal matter, to be made good by midsummer, which was true as far as it went, and left out of it the maor's further remark, offered over a glass of something the maor's own cellar had not paid Deachamh a' Chogaidh on, that a coast town asked to fill a regiment's ranks against its own hill neighbours might be forgiven for finding its boats a week longer at sea than the weather strictly required.

## IV. Of the Answer Nobody Could Give

Tom Varley began asking after Ruth Calder on the third day at Muileann àrsaidh, once the last of the wounded were settled and Sarah Dunmore's kitchen had stopped needing every pair of hands in the town at once. He asked first the men who had come up the ridge path with him, one by one, in the flat unhurried way a man asks a question he has already asked several times and expects, each time, the same answer he has had before. None of them had seen her past the grey hour of the morning, when the companies were still forming on the road below the pit-heads and her own book was still open on the trestle table, her thickened pen going down the last names before the light was properly up.

He sent word out from Muileann àrsaidh to every hill farm within a day's walk, not by any formal order, since he held no rank that could give one, but in the way word travels among people who have known each other's families three generations back: a boy sent here, a cousin asked there, a message left with a shepherd whose flock ranged close enough to the old battle-ground that he might, in the course of an ordinary week's work, see something worth the telling. Has anyone seen Ruth Calder, the message ran, in one form or another, carried by a dozen different mouths into a dozen different farmhouses over the course of that week, and the answer, when an answer came at all, was always some version of the same thing: that nobody now working that ground since the battle had seen a woman of her description, alive or otherwise, and that the battle-ground, by the regiments' own patrols and by the few shepherds bold enough to walk near its edge, appeared to hold nothing that anyone had found worth reporting.

A woman from a farm below the ridge, whose husband had gone down with the Cnoc thais men and come back with a wound in his shoulder that Tom himself had dressed on the path, sent word that she had heard, from a niece married into a family nearer the town, that some of the field's own dead had been carried off in the days just after the battle by people from the hills who came down at night and went again before light, and that if Ruth Calder had fallen there, she might have been carried with the rest and be lying now in ground no list on either side would ever hold a name for. This was not an answer either, though it was closer to one than anything else Tom heard that week, and he found himself, hearing it, unable to decide whether it eased the tightness behind his breastbone or drew it tighter, and settled, after turning it over two full days, on the second.

He asked, too, at the pit-shed table, once word came that a handful of Àth leathan's own people, those who had not come north with the hewers, had begun slipping back down under cover of dark to see what remained of their own doors and byres, and had themselves been asking after faces they knew and not finding them.
