One such, an old woman who had kept hens at the edge of the town and gone up into the hills with a cousin's family rather than stay to see what the regiments made of her yard, sent word by the same chain of boys and shepherds that she had seen, the morning after the battle, before the regiments' patrols came out onto it, a party of women from the hill farms out on the field with handcarts of their own, moving among the fallen in the grey light, and that she had not looked long enough, or near enough, to say whose faces she had seen among either the carriers or the carried, because a woman alone at the edge of a battlefield the morning after learns quickly not to look too long at anything. Tom heard this and thanked the boy who brought it and gave him nothing further to carry back, because there was nothing further to ask that the old woman's account had not already, in its own way, answered as fully as it meant to.

He walked out himself on the eighth day, alone, along the ridge path he had carried the wounded up, and down the far side toward the field, going as near it as An seachdamh rèisimeid's patrols allowed, which was not very near, a sentry turning him back at a stone dyke a quarter-mile short of the ground with a civility that Tom, for all his anger at the turning back, could find no fault with; the man was young, and cold, and doing exactly what his own officer had told him to do, no more and no less. From the dyke Tom could see the shape of the field, a long slope running down from the pit-heads to the road, empty under a grey sky, no plough mark on it anywhere that he could make out at that distance, the grass beginning already, in the way grass will, to come up green over ground that had held, eight days before, nine hundred men and more with their carriers.

He looked at it a long while, until the sentry, not unkindly, told him the light was going and the patrols came round again at dusk and would not be so civil to a man found standing at the dyke after dark. Tom thanked him, which cost him something to do and he did it anyway, and walked back up the ridge path in the failing light with no more of an answer than he had carried down it, and no less, and told himself, coming over the saddle with Muileann àrsaidh's few fires showing small below him, that a field left unploughed keeps whatever it keeps whether or not a man stands at its edge asking it to give an account of itself, and that he would go on asking all the same, because asking was the one thing left to him that Ruth Calder's own book, four hundred names taken down in a clean careful hand, would have understood as work worth doing, and he was not yet ready to set it down.

# Chapter Twenty-six: Of the Tithe and the Fleets

*DE 21*

## I. Of the Clerk beside the Pump

Ùna nic Ailein had kept Cùirt na Fèille at Muileann òg for four-and-twenty years, and in that time she had written into its books every kind of sale a market town on Rathad na Fèille might see: cattle, cloth, coal by the cartload and then by the sack, dubhan by the barrel and then by the tank, a woman's dower, a dead man's debts. She had not, until the second week after Àth leathan, written a tax.

The order came down from the capital with the same rider who brought word of the battle, so that the town had the two together before it had properly finished with either: the field lost and won in the same breath as the clause that would pay for the losing and the winning both. It was short, as such orders went, and plain in the way orders are plain when the thing behind them is not: for the war's sake, and for so long only as the war should last, every sale of dubhan within the kingdom was to bear a tithe of one part in twelve, taken at the point of sale and not after, and a clerk of An t-Ionmhas was to sit at every depot and every fair-court pump where dubhan changed hands, to see it taken. The word the order used, twice, was *for a time*.

Muileann òg's own pump stood in the yard behind the toll-house, where the fair's dubhan tank had been sunk the year the town gave up its last coal cart, and it was there, on a wet morning three days after the order reached her, that Ùna met the clerk An t-Ionmhas had sent to sit beside it.

He was a young man named Cailean Ros, thin in the wrists, with a ledger of his own bound in An t-Ionmhas's grey boards and a stool he had brought with him because nobody had thought to leave one for him. He set the stool down in the lee of the tank, where the drip from the eaves did not quite reach, and opened his ledger on his knee, and looked up at Ùna with the particular unhappiness of a man sent a long way from home to do a thing he had not chosen and could not undo.

"I'm told to sit here," he said, "and mark what's drawn."

"You'll want the tank's own book as well as your own, then," Ùna said, "or your figures and mine will never agree, and one of us will be made to answer for it before the year's out."

He had not thought of that. She saw him not think of it, in the way his face did nothing at all for a moment before it did something. He wrote her name down, and the tank's, and Cùirt na Fèille's, in his grey book, under a heading that said only *Muileann òg*, and asked her, civilly enough, whether she would show him how the tank's own draw was measured, since nobody in the capital had thought to tell him that either.

She showed him. It took the better part of the morning, in the rain, the two of them bent over the tank's brass cock and the marked rod that measured what came out of it, and by the end of it Cailean Ros had learned to read the rod as well as she could, and had written, in a hand still stiff with being taught something new, the first entry of the tithe ever taken at Muileann òg: eleven gallons drawn to Seumas Buidhe the smith, at the market price, and one part in twelve of the price set aside before the coin changed hands, and Seumas Buidhe standing by with his hands in his apron looking at the young clerk as though a second smith had set up shop in the yard without asking anyone's leave.

"Where does it go," Seumas asked, when the counting was done, "the twelfth part?"

"To An t-Ionmhas," said Cailean Ros, "for the war."

"And when the war's done?"

The clerk looked at his own ledger as if the answer might be written in it, and it was not. "I couldn't say," he said, which Ùna judged, watching him, to be the truest thing he had said all morning, and also the thing that would serve him worst in the weeks to come, because a smith who has just paid a twelfth of his coin to a stranger from the capital wants an answer, even a false one, more than he wants an honest silence.

Seumas Buidhe took his eleven gallons and went home without another word, and Ùna wrote the sale into Cùirt na Fèille's own book below the line where the tithe was noted, in the plain hand she used for every sale, because a smith's dubhan was a smith's dubhan whatever An t-Ionmhas took off the top of it, and the court's book did not change its manners for a war.

She wrote, too, in the margin, the thing she had not been asked to write and wrote anyway, as she had once written that a coal cart was the last of its kind: *Cailean Ros of An t-Ionmhas sat first at this pump on the thirtieth of an Giblean, and the first tithe taken here was one gallon in twelve of Seumas Buidhe's eleven.* It was no more than Cùirt na Fèille's habit of a hundred years, to set down what was new the day it was new, before the newness of it wore smooth into simply the way of things. She did not think, writing it, that anyone but the court's own clerks would ever read it. Eighteen years before she had thought the same of a margin note about a coal cart, and had been wrong about that too.

Cailean Ros came back the next market day, and the one after, with his stool and his grey ledger, and by the third week he had stopped setting the stool in the lee of the eaves and had asked the toll-house keeper, through Ùna, whether a corner of the upper room might be spared him against the worst of the weather, since a wet ledger served An t-Ionmhas no better than a dry one served the king's enemies. The toll-house keeper, who was Ùna's own second cousin and disliked strangers on principle, gave him the corner nearest the door, which was the coldest in the room, and Cailean Ros took it without complaint, and Ùna, watching him take it, thought that a man who does not complain of the corner he is given generally means to stay in it a good while.

## II. Of the First Complaint

The complaint came in the fourth week, on a market day with the first real heat of the year in it, and it came, as most complaints at Muileann òg came, from a woman who had waited a fortnight to be sure she was not merely in a temper before she brought it to the court.

Her name was Barabal nic Rath, and she kept three looms in a shed behind her house and sold cloth at the fair every second week, and she had bought dubhan for her looms' small engine from the fair pump since the engine was fitted, four years before, because a loom that ran on dubhan wove faster than a loom worked by foot and hand, and a woman with three looms and no sons old enough to work them had needed the faster weaving or given up two of the three. She came up the toll-house stair with her ledger under her arm, a thin cloth-bound book she kept herself in a hand less fair than Ùna's own but every bit as careful, and she set it down on the court's table and opened it to a page marked with a scrap of blue thread.

"I've kept my own count," she said, "these four weeks, against the pump's, because I didn't trust my own arithmetic to hold a grudge fair, and now I've kept it long enough to be sure the grudge is honest."

Ùna looked at the page. Barabal nic Rath's count agreed with the tank's own book, gallon for gallon and tithe for tithe, to the last measure; there was no cheating in it, no clerk's thumb on the scale. What the page showed, set down in the woman's careful hand week by week, was the twelfth part alone, added up: what her looms had paid An t-Ionmhas since an Giblean, against what she had earned by them in the same four weeks, and the second figure was not large enough, set beside the first, to leave her easy about the six weeks still to come, or the six after that, if the order's *for a time* meant what she was beginning to suspect it meant.

"I'm not asking the court to strike the tithe," she said. "I know the court's no more power over a Treasury order than I have myself. I'm asking that it be written down, here, in this book, that a woman of Muileann òg brought a complaint against it in the fourth week of its taking, and what the complaint was, so that when the *time* it was laid for is over, and somebody asks whether the time was long or short, there'll be a paper that says when the asking began."

Ùna took up her pen. Cailean Ros, in his corner, had stopped writing in his own ledger and was watching the table with the stillness of a man who knows a thing is being made that will outlast him in that room whichever way the war goes.

"I'll write it," Ùna said, "as you've said it, no more and no less, unless you'd have me soften it."

"I'd have you write it as I said it."

She wrote it as Barabal nic Rath had said it, in Cùirt na Fèille's book, under the day's date, the first complaint the court had recorded against Deachamh a' Chogaidh: the weaver's name, the looms, the four weeks' figures set down from the woman's own ledger and checked against the tank's, and the plain sentence the woman had asked for, that the complaint stood against the tithe's silence on its own ending, and left its justice, which she did not judge, alone. Ùna turned the book round, as she had once turned it for a carter who could not read, and Barabal nic Rath read her own words back in the court's fairer hand and nodded once and went down the stair to her cloth.

Cailean Ros came over from his corner once the woman was gone and looked at the entry a long while without asking to.

"Will you send a copy to An t-Ionmhas?" he said at last.

"I'll send a copy where the court's book always sends copies, which is nowhere, unless it's asked for. It's the court's book. It answers to the fair, not to the capital." She closed it and set it on its shelf. "If your masters want to know whether the tithe is loved, they can ride down and read it for themselves, or they can ask you, since you sit beside the pump five days in the six and would know better than any letter could tell them."

"They haven't asked me," Cailean Ros said, "what I think of it."

"No," Ùna said. "They wouldn't."

He went back to his corner, and Ùna, setting the day's other business in order, thought that a young man sent a long way from home to sit beside a pump and mark what was drawn from it was learning, faster than she had expected, the one lesson Cùirt na Fèille's own books had taught every clerk who ever kept them: that a thing written down plainly outlives the mood that made someone want it written, and outlives, sometimes, the very order that called the writer into being. She did not know, setting the ink-horn back under its cloth against the evening damp, how many other pumps in the kingdom that week had a Cailean Ros beside them, or how many other women had kept a ledger of their own four weeks running against a grudge they meant to be sure of before they brought it up any stair. There were a good many, she supposed. What was before her she wrote, as the court had always done, and the rest she left to whoever, someday, might read every such book at once.

## III. Of the Boats Come Home Late

Joe Ashby heard of the tithe before he felt it, because a fitter who buys no dubhan to sell, only to burn in his own forge and pour into other men's tanks at a price he set himself, was a step removed from any pump. What struck Caol mhòr's harbour first that spring, and struck it hard, were the ships.

A' chiad rèisimeid, raised at Inis mhòr from the capital's own companies to stand about the council and the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain, meant nothing to a harbour four days' sail to the north and was three weeks old before word of it reached Will Tanner's shed at all, brought by a carter who had it third-hand from a corn-factor at Cathair mhòr. The fleets meant a great deal more, and meant it sooner. Within the month a fleet was raised from the south-west harbours and stationed at Àth gharbh, its hulls lying at Doire shean a short walk along the shore, and sent round the western cape; and hard on it a fourth fleet out of Cuan shean joined the first off the Tuathaich coast, and between the two of them the sea-reach of the western Seann Skell and the waters off Cnoc bhàn in the north-west were closed to every hull that was not a fishing boat, and the fishing boats themselves were searched.

Caol mhòr's own boats were fishing boats, in the main, whatever engine Joe had fitted under their thwarts, and it was the searching, not the closing, that came first to the harbour wall.

The first of the king's boats to put in was a low grey hull out of An ceathramh cabhlach, with a lieutenant aboard her young enough that his coat still looked new on him, and she came alongside the wall on a morning with the herring boats half unloaded and their crews still at the baskets. The lieutenant came ashore with two men behind him and a paper in his hand, and read from it, in Dia-thìris, that every hull of the harbour was to be boarded and its hold and its bilges searched, by the order of the fleet, for coal or dubhan carried contrary to the closing of the western waters, and that any master who refused the search would have his boat's papers taken and his name sent to the maor.

Nobody refused. It was not, Joe thought, watching from the shed door with a wrench still in his hand, that anyone at the wall had anything to hide; it was that a harbour which had spent seven years learning to answer a fleet clerk's letters with silence had not yet learned how a young lieutenant with two men and a paper was to be answered at all, and silence, this time, would not do, since the man was standing on the wall asking, plainly, to be let aboard.

They boarded Jean Fisher's boat first, because it lay nearest the steps, and the two men went down into her bilges with a lantern and came up black to the elbow and found nothing but bilge-water and a winter's rust, and the lieutenant wrote something in his own book and moved on to the next. It went that way down the whole of the wall through the morning: down into the bilges, up black to the elbow, a line in the book, the next boat. Will Tanner's own boat took the longest, because Will had, in an idle winter three years before, built a false locker under the stern thwart to keep a jar of the smith's own spirit out of his wife's reach, and the men found the locker and opened it and found the jar and nothing else, and the lieutenant, to his credit, laughed once, briefly, and wrote nothing about it at all.

They came to the engine-boats last, the half-dozen hulls in the harbour that Joe himself had fitted with a dubhan engine under the stern rather than oars alone, and here the lieutenant's manner grew careful, gentle still but slower, the way a man's manner slows when he has been told, before he ever left the fleet's own harbour, that this was the true business of the day and the bilges only the excuse for it. He asked, of each engine-boat's master in turn, who had fitted the engine, and when, and whether the fitter held any guild's leave to do it, and each master gave him the same answer in the same flat voice, that the engine was fitted by Joe Ashby of this town, guild or no guild, and the engine ran true, which was more than any Seann Skell guild's own work could always promise, and the lieutenant wrote that down too, without comment, in the same book as the bilges.

He came to Joe himself at the shed door before he left the wall.

"You're the fitter," he said. It was not quite a question.

"I am."

"You hold no guild's paper."

"There's none in this harbour would give me one."

The lieutenant looked at him a moment, and at the shed behind him, the bench with its rows of tools and the half-stripped engine laid out on sacking that Joe had been working over when the boat came alongside. "The fleet's own hulls run on engines fitted by men who do hold the guild's paper," he said, "and half of them, by what I've seen this year, run worse than the ones I've just come off. I'll write what I've seen, and no more, and what's done with it after that is the fleet's business and not mine." He touched his cap, in a way that was neither quite courtesy nor quite its opposite, and went back down the steps to his boat, and by noon the grey hull was gone round the point, north, toward whatever other harbour's wall was next on his own book's list.

## IV. Of the Hull Nobody Would Name

The letter came to Will Tanner's shed a fortnight after, carried up from Caol mhòr's own harbour depot by a boy who would not say who had sent him, only that he was to wait for an answer and bring it back the same day.

It was short, and it named no fleet and no rank, only that a hull now lying at the depot's own jetty had an engine that would not answer past half its speed, that the depot's own men had looked at it twice and could not say why, and that whoever could put it right, guild or no guild, would be paid in coin at the harbour's own rate and asked no question the work did not answer of its own accord. A mark stood where the signature should have been, no name under it anywhere.

Joe read it twice, standing in the shed door with the boy waiting on one foot and then the other, and then he asked the boy plainly whose hull it was, since a letter that would not say so plainly meant to be read carefully by whoever it was sent to.

"The depot's," the boy said. "One of the fleet's."

Joe folded the letter and put it in his apron pocket and stood a while without answering, and the boy, who had been told only to wait, waited. It took him no time at all to know his own mind; he knew it inside the first reading, the way a man knows before he has finished a sentence whether he means to say yes or no to the end of it. The while he stood there went instead into weighing what the deciding would cost against what the refusing would cost, setting the one sum beside the other until he was satisfied neither would grow smaller for further looking.

A fleet hull was a fleet hull, whatever coin it paid in, and the fleet that hull served was the same fleet that had closed the western Seann Skell's waters to keep dubhan from going where the western hills wanted it, and had raised a tithe on every gallon a Muileann òg weaver drew for her looms, and would, before the year was out, though Joe did not yet know the shape of what was coming, carry arms and men to towns whose names he had heard all his life without ever once thinking of them as places a Caol mhòr man's own hands might help to reach. He thought of Baile chrom's report, pinned outside the custom-house fourteen years before, that had named a town and not a man; he thought that a fleet which could not be bothered to name the fitters of a lighthouse was not likely to trouble over-much with the conscience of the fitter it now wanted for an engine none of its own men could mend.

He thought, too, and did not let himself think it away, that Ned Fowler's boy was down with a chest complaint that winter's damp had settled into him and had not yet loosed, and that the harbour's own rate for an engine's mending, paid straight and without argument, was the kind of coin a man in Joe's own trade did not often see offered without three months' haggling first; and that a boat's engine, once he had it in pieces on his own bench, would tell him nothing at all about where that boat had been or where it was bound next, being made, as every engine he had ever fitted was made, of iron and copper and a burner's throat, and answering to nobody's flag once it was stripped down to its own parts on a sheet of sacking.

"Tell them," he said at last, "that I'll come and look at her. I'll say what I can do once I've seen her, and not before."

The boy went, and came back within the hour with word that Joe was to come to the depot's jetty in the morning, and that the depot's own men would clear the shed for him and ask no questions of anyone he brought with him, if he wanted a second pair of hands.

He took Ned Fowler, whose own hands were as good as any at the pumps and better than most at a stripped engine, and the two of them walked down to the depot in the grey of a morning with the tide half out and the gulls loud over the mud. The hull lay at the jetty's outer end, low and grey like the lieutenant's own boat had been, with the fleet's mark painted small on her bow where a merchant hull would have carried her name, and no name of her own anywhere on her that either man could find, fore or aft, though every fishing boat in the harbour behind them wore its own painted plain for any child to read.

"No name," Ned said, looking her over from the jetty.

"No," said Joe. "Nor any it'll answer to, once she's running again, that either of us will ever hear."

They went aboard, and down into the engine well, and by noon Joe had the fault in his hand, a valve seated wrong from the yard that built her, the kind of small blind error that a rushed builder leaves behind in a hundred engines and a careful fitter finds in one, and he sat over it the rest of the short afternoon with Ned beside him passing tools, the two of them saying little, because there was little that wanted saying about a valve's seat that the valve itself did not say plainer, and because both men knew, without either putting it into words on the jetty that day, exactly whose engine they were mending and to what further use, unnamed and unasked-after, the mending would be put.

By evening the valve was seated true and the engine answered past half speed and on to its full, and the depot's own men, who had stood back the whole day watching two Tuathaich fitters do in an afternoon what their own hands had failed twice to do in a week, paid Joe at the harbour's own rate, in coin, and asked him nothing at all, as the letter had promised, and Joe took the coin and put half of it, that same evening, into Ned Fowler's own hand for the boy's chest, and said nothing about where it had come from beyond that it had been fairly earned, which was true, and which he told himself, walking home along the harbour wall in the last of the light with the grey hull already standing out past the point on the evening tide, was the whole of the answer he owed anyone.

## V. Of Two Books That Would Not Meet

Will Tanner asked him, over the bench a few evenings after, whether he meant to do it again, if the depot's boy came back with another letter and another mark instead of a name, and Joe said he supposed he would, if a chest wanted clearing or a boy wanted mending or the coin was fair, and that he did not see how a man in his trade was to run a harbour's worth of accounts on a war he had had no hand in starting and no vote in ending. Will said nothing to that, because there was nothing in it he could rightly argue with, and the two of them went on stripping a winch that had nothing to do with any fleet at all.

No paper anywhere on the island set the two of that spring's small transactions side by side: Cùirt na Fèille's book at Muileann òg, where a weaver's complaint against a twelfth part in twelve stood written under the day's date for anyone who cared to climb the stair and ask for it, and the depot's own tally at Caol mhòr, unsigned, which recorded only that an engine had been mended and a sum paid out, and named, in its own hand, no fitter at all. Ùna's book meant to be read; that was the whole of Cùirt na Fèille's hundred-year habit, to set a thing down so that someone, someday, asking after it, would find an answer waiting rather than a silence. The depot's tally meant the opposite, and meant it just as carefully, a mark standing in for a name the way the sea-reach off the western Seann Skell now stood closed to every hull that could not prove itself a fishing boat, which was its own kind of writing, done in absences instead of ink.

Between the two books, that spring, ran the whole distance of the tithe and the fleets both: an order that named itself only for a time, taken at every pump the kingdom had thought to guard, and answered, in the fourth week, by a woman with a ledger of her own; and a fleet that closed a coast to keep dubhan from the hills that had first made it, and came, before the season was out, to need the very hands it would not put a name to. Neither book troubled over the other, and no one that spring stood in any office of the kingdom with both open on the same table, to ask what the war had cost, taken all together, in coin drawn at one end of the island and coin paid out, unnamed, at the other.

# Chapter Twenty-seven: Of the Siege of Muileann àrsaidh

*DE 21*

## I. Of the Wall Fraser Did Not Finish

They tell it in the western hills, those few of that town's own people left to tell anything at all, that the regiments came up the southern road on the twenty-first day of an Cèitean in the grey hour before a full morning, and that the first anyone in Muileann àrsaidh knew of it was the sound of the ditch-bridge going down under wheels that were not a carrier's cart. Old Fraser had dug that ditch himself the autumn before, on his knees in the cold with his own breath smoking, and had said to Ruth Calder at the time that a road dug across at the right place could be made near as good as a wall for a fraction of the labour; and it had held a season and more against nothing heavier than a lorry turned back with stones. It did not hold against men with timber and their own backs to lay it. By the time the sun was properly up, the bridge was down and a company of the regiments' advance stood on the wrong side of Fraser's ditch looking in.

Sarah Dunmore heard it from her own kitchen, where she had been feeding porridge into a boy of nine who did not want it, and knew before she reached her own door what the sound under the other sounds was, because she had spent the better part of two years by then learning the particular weight of a great many boots moving together, a sound no cart or drove of cattle ever quite made, however you tried to tell yourself otherwise in the first half-minute of hearing it. She set the boy's bowl down, told him to stay where he was in a voice that made him mind her for once without an argument, and went out into the street in her apron with her hair still not properly pinned, because there was no time left that morning to be a woman who minded such things.

The town had known the regiments were coming for the better part of a fortnight, in the way a town in the western hills always knew such things before anyone official troubled to tell it: a carter's report, a shepherd who had seen dust on the southern road that no drove of sheep raised, a cousin's letter from the western Seann Skell saying that men and wagons had been moving north out of the port in numbers nobody there had counted before. What the town had not known, and could not have known short of standing on the road to see it, was which of the wall's several weak places the regiments' engineers had marked for their own use, and it was, as it happened, the same stretch at the northern end that old Fraser had left unfinished the autumn before, out of what he had called simple exhaustion at the time and what the whole town understood privately to be his own unwillingness to finish a wall built clean round a town, that being, in his judgement, too near a boast for any hill town to make. He was an old man now, older than he had been that autumn by a year of siege already half begun in everyone's mind if not yet in fact, and he stood that first morning at the gap in his own unfinished work with a mattock in his two hands and eleven other men and women about him, none of whom had slept, and none of whom had any clear notion of what a mattock would do against a company of riflemen beyond the small comfort of having something in the hands.

It did nothing, in the end, because the regiments' officers, whoever they were and whatever their orders said, chose that first morning to do no more than close the gap from the outside and set a picket on it, rather than force it with men still forming up from a night's march; and Sarah, coming up the street in time to see the last of that decision made, understood, watching soldiers she had never before seen stand still and businesslike on ground that had been Muileann àrsaidh's own pit-yard the evening before, that the town was not being taken that morning so much as it was being shut, the way a hand closes slowly round a thing it means to keep rather than crush.

By noon the southern road was cut as well, a second company come up behind the first and dug in across it a half-mile below the town where the ground rose enough to give a clear sight of anyone coming or going, and by the end of that first day Muileann àrsaidh, which had built its wall against a lorry and never seriously against an army, found the wall mattered little either way, because the roads it stood beside were closed at both ends and the hills behind it, steep and trackless enough that no regiment had thought them worth a picket, offered no way out that a cart or a wagon of stores could use, only paths a person on foot might take by night and at some risk. Tom Varley came to Sarah's kitchen that evening, his knee long since mended and his face the grey of a man doing sums he did not like the answer to, and said, standing in her doorway with his cap still on because he had forgotten to take it off, that he had walked the whole ring of it that afternoon, as near as the pickets would let him go, and that there was no gap in it he could find that a man might drive a cart through, only the hill paths, and those good for nothing heavier than what a back could carry.

"How long have we coal for," Sarah asked him. She kept the answer herself, to the sack, and asked it all the same, the way a person sometimes wants a bad sum said aloud by another voice before they will properly believe it.

"Weeks," Tom said. "Coal and potatoes both, if it's managed right, which it will be, because Meikle's already at the counting of it and Meikle counts things carefully." He looked at her a moment longer than the answer needed. "Weeks isn't long enough, Sarah, not truly, and we both know it. It's more than I'd have said we had a year ago, before any of us thought to lay any of it by."

She did not ask him the other question in her mind that evening, which was how many weeks a town of six hundred souls, swollen now by however many of Àth leathan's own people had come up the ridge path with him in the spring and stayed on rather than go further, could hold water and grain and courage all together before one or another of the three ran short first; she had learned, in the two months since the battle, that Tom Varley answered a plain question honestly and a question dressed as despair not at all, and she had need of him answering plainly rather more than she had need of comfort. She put the kettle on instead, because it was the one thing in the house that still worked exactly as it always had, siege or no siege, and set it to boil over a fire built, that evening and every evening after for weeks to come, out of the last of Cnoc thais's poor black coal.

## II. Of the Pit-heads Taken One by One

The dressing-station had never properly closed since the spring, Sarah's own kitchen having done service for the wounded of Àth leathan before it ever needed to do service for a siege, and it filled again within the first week, though more slowly than it had after the battle, a man brought in with a shoulder opened by a stray shot from the northern picket, a girl who had put her foot wrong on the hill path carrying water up from the one spring inside the ring the regiments had left them, an old woman whose heart, already failing before any of it began, gave out entirely on the third night of the siege in a way that had nothing to do with soldiers at all and everything, Sarah thought privately, to do with the sound of the bell.

The bell of Muileann àrsaidh's own small chapel had rung for weddings and for burials the whole of Sarah's life and her mother's before her, a single note struck by hand from a rope in the porch, since the town had never run to more than the one bell and had never, until that spring, needed to ring it for anything but the ordinary business of being born and married and dying. It was Meikle, of all people, the same careful man who kept the town's writing and now kept its counting of coal and potatoes both, who proposed that the bell be rung once for every pit-head the regiments took, on the reasoning, offered to the town gathered in the pit-shed on the fourth evening of the siege, that a town under siege wanted some way of knowing plainly, all at once, what had been lost that day, rather than hearing it piecemeal from whoever happened to have been nearest the fighting and was willing to talk of it.

The pit-heads went one at a time, through the last week of an Cèitean and on into an t-Ògmhios, not all at once and not, so far as anyone in the town could afterward make out a pattern to it, in any order that served the regiments' convenience over the town's, but simply as each fell in its turn to whatever pressure was brought against it that day: the northern head first, nearest the unfinished stretch of wall, taken on the sixth day after a fight that lasted the better part of an afternoon and cost the town two men Sarah had known since they were boys; then, a week later, the eastern head, given up rather than fought for, on Tom Varley's own counsel, because the ground about it could not be held without stripping men from the wall that mattered more; then a long stretch of near a fortnight in which nothing at all was taken and the town began, cautiously, to let itself believe the regiments had decided the remaining ground was not worth the cost of it, a hope Sarah did not share aloud though she felt the pull of it same as anyone, because she had watched, from her own doorway, the number of tents on the ridge above the southern road grow rather than shrink through that fortnight, and knew what a growing camp generally meant.

The bell rang twice on a single evening in the third week of an t-Ògmhios, for the southern head and the smaller working above it both, lost within an hour of each other in a fight Sarah heard more than saw, being at that hour elbow-deep in a wound at her own table and unable to leave it; and it was that evening, with the second stroke of the bell still going out over the roofs and the light failing fast the way it does in that month even at its longest, that she understood, setting a dressing in place with hands that did not shake though she had expected by then that they might, that the town's own reckoning of the siege, which had begun the first week with plain sums of coal and potatoes, had somewhere in the weeks between become instead a reckoning of pit-heads, the way a body counts down from a full hand of fingers, and that there were, by her own count kept without meaning to keep it, three left standing of the six the wall had once been built to hold.

Tom Varley came to her kitchen most evenings a fight had happened, some to be tended himself, though only twice was the tending more than a scratch, and the rest of the evenings simply because there was nowhere else in the town a man wanted to sit out the day's end but somewhere with a fire and another living person in the room. He rarely spoke of Ruth Calder that summer, having by his own telling asked every question there was to ask of every farm within reach months before, and had every answer there was to have, none of them an answer worth the name; he spoke of her once, late in an t-Ògmhios with the bell silent for three days running and the whole town holding a stillness that felt, Sarah thought, heavier in its way than the ringing had been, saying only that he found himself glad, in a way he could not properly account for even to his own self, that whatever had become of her, she was not inside this particular ring counting down pit-heads along with the rest of them, since a person could only be asked to carry so much ground in her own chest before something in her gave the way a shaft-timber gives, all at once and with little warning beforehand. Sarah said nothing to that beyond setting another cup of what passed, by then, for tea in front of him, judging rightly that he had not said it wanting an answer.

The stores held better than the fear had, through those first weeks, Meikle's counting proving out as careful as his reputation, and the town settled, as towns under siege will, into something that was not quite ordinary life and was not quite anything else either: a rota for the water, a rota for the walls where walls still stood, the chapel's one service a week kept as it had always been kept though the congregation that came to it grew thinner by attrition to the walls and to the dressing-station both, and Sarah's own kitchen, feeding fewer mouths now on smaller portions than it had fed at Ruth Calder's meeting five years before in what felt, to everyone who remembered it, like another age of the world entirely.

Children still played in the one street those first weeks, in the way children will play under almost any roof so long as somebody keeps the worst of the fear from their own faces, a game of counting pit-heads themselves that Sarah overheard one afternoon from her own doorway and had to go inside for a moment rather than let the children see what it did to her, four small voices chanting the names of the six pit-heads in a rhyme none of them could afterward say who had made up, with a hand slapped down at each name the way a hand slaps down at a lost point in any other game, and no understanding at all, mercifully, of what the game's own ending would mean once the last name in it had been slapped down for the last time. Sarah never told Meikle of it, nor Weir either, judging that a thing children had made of their own fear to carry it was not a thing grown people ought to take from them before the fear itself was done.

## III. Of the Sunday Kept and the Grave Behind the Chapel

The one thing the siege did not ration, Sarah came to think through those weeks, was Sunday, and she was glad of it more than she ever said aloud, because a town that had given up counting the days of the week by anything but the bell's tolling for a pit-head needed, she judged, some other reckoning left over that had nothing to do with what had been lost. The priest of Muileann àrsaidh's own small congregation, an elderly man named Weir who had buried Sarah's husband under the fall of stone and married a good half the town besides, kept his one weekly service through the whole of the siege without missing a Sunday, though the benches held fewer each week as men were called instead to the walls and the dressing-station both, and though the bread on the little table by the door, kept there since before Sarah could remember for whoever in the parish had none of their own, stood empty for the first time in her recollection by the fourth week, there being nobody left in Muileann àrsaidh with bread enough spare to leave any on a table.

Weir preached short that summer, shorter each week if anything, on the plain reasoning, which he gave to Sarah once over the graveside of the old woman whose heart had failed the third night, that a congregation standing a siege wanted its comfort given briefly and its own strength left for the rest of the day's work, and that a long sermon on a short summer's morning was, in his judgement, a kind of vanity no man of his trade could properly afford that year. He read the same psalm three Sundays running in the second month of it, the one about a strong tower and a very present help, without any comment on the reading at all beyond the reading itself, and Sarah, sitting in her usual place near the back with her hands raw from the dressing-station's work, found that she did not need the comment, the psalm having said, plainly enough for anyone in that room to hear it, exactly the thing the room had come needing to hear.

The graves went in behind the chapel through those weeks at a rate the town had not seen since the fever year Sarah's own grandmother used to speak of, though never so fast that the ground itself grew short, the western hills having buried their dead in that same plot since before An Dealachadh and having, by Weir's own dry reckoning, ground enough behind the chapel wall to serve three towns the size of Muileann àrsaidh twice over before it wanted extending. The old woman went in first, in the second week, and after her the two men lost at the northern head, and after them a scattering through the rest of the summer that Sarah, standing at the graveside for most of them because there was seldom anyone left in a household to stand there otherwise, found herself keeping a private count of without ever meaning to, the way she kept the pit-heads' count without meaning to either, until the two counts together sat behind her breastbone most evenings like a second and a third heartbeat she could not still by any effort of her own.

Meikle's rationing held through it all with a steadiness Sarah came, by midsummer, to depend on the way a person depends on weather holding fair through a hay-making: a set weight of meal to a household by the week, a set weight of coal to a hearth by the day, a smaller portion again once the second month of the siege began and the town's own store of the year's potatoes, laid by against an ordinary winter and not against a siege at all, began visibly to shrink in the pit where it was kept. He came to Sarah's own kitchen twice a week with his figures written small on a scrap of paper, not because her table needed watching over more than any other in the town but because he had, she came to understand, nowhere else he wanted to sit with the figures once they were done for the day, and she fed him from her own reduced portion without remark either way, since a man who kept a whole town's counting straight through seven weeks of siege had, in her private reckoning, earned rather more than his own strict share of whatever there was left to give.

## IV. Of the Third and the Fifth

Word of what moved beyond the ring came into the town the way most news came into a besieged place, in pieces, carried by whoever had last spoken to whoever had last spoken to a man who had actually seen the thing himself, so that Sarah learned of An treas rèisimeid and the fifth both from no report she could have set any store by, only from a picket's own boast, shouted across the gap where the northern head had been to two of the town's own men on watch there, that the town might as well open its gates now as later, since Cathair mhòr had sent a whole regiment north under the Mac Ùisdein's own cross to see the business finished, and Seann Warr another besides, and that between the two of them and what already sat on the southern road, there would shortly be more soldiers ringed about Muileann àrsaidh than the town had ever had people in it at any one time in its history.

It was old Fraser, of all people, standing his watch at the gap he had once dug and never finished walling, who brought that boast back down into the town and set it before the pit-shed that evening as plainly as he had once set his mattock down at the same spot, saying only that a boast shouted across a gap by a bored picket on a slow evening was no thing to build despair on; still, he had counted the smoke of new fires on the southern ridge for three mornings running and there were more of them than there had been the week before, which was a thing a man's own eyes could tell him and no picket's boasting was needed to confirm. Sarah, sitting near the back of the shed with a mending she had brought to keep her hands from idleness, thought that this was Fraser through and through, to distrust the shouted word and trust the smoke, and thought also, though she said nothing of it aloud, that a regiment raised at Cathair mhòr under a house's own cross and another raised on a lake shore two days' ride away, both sent north in the same fortnight for no other business she could imagine but this one, told her something the boast alone would not have: that whatever Muileann àrsaidh's few hundred souls had thought they were worth to the kingdom that besieged them, the kingdom, spending two regiments' raising and marching on the answer, plainly thought them worth rather more.

What came of the third and the fifth, once they came, Sarah never afterward learned in any order she trusted, the pit-shed's evening talk through the last weeks of the siege being less a council by then than a place where rumour was aired and mostly, though not always, found wanting: that the new men had been set to strengthen the southern road rather than force any new ground, which Tom Varley judged likely, from what little he could see of their dispositions on his own watches; that a company of them had been sent instead down toward the coast to see to some trouble with the fishing boats that had nothing to do with Muileann àrsaidh at all, which Meikle judged less likely, though he could not say why beyond a general distrust of any rumour that made the town's own trouble smaller than it felt; and that Somhairle mac Lachlainn himself, whose name the town knew by then the way a town under siege learns the name of whoever commands the ring around it, without ever having laid eyes on him, had come up from the western Seann Skell to see the reinforced lines himself, which nobody could confirm and everybody, in the way of these things, half believed regardless of the confirming.

It was in that same stretch of weeks, from a man taken briefly at the wall and let go again the next morning under some understanding between the two sides that Sarah never fully grasped the shape of, that word reached the town of the capital's own streets going dark again, the poorer ones at least, the dubhan that had once lit them being taken now, as coal once had been taken before it, for the army's own use first and the ordinary lamp-houses after, if anything was left over to give them; and Sarah, hearing this third or fourth hand in her own kitchen from a man still shaking with the two nights he had spent not knowing whether he would be let go or kept, found in it a small, cold satisfaction she was not proud of and did not try hard to be rid of, that the fuel the kingdom had taken up in place of coal, and had sent an army north to make sure the western hills took it up too, could not after all light every street it claimed to serve once that same army wanted feeding first.

## V. Of the Door Nobody Was Left to Hold

By the second week of an t-Iuchar the bell had rung for five of the six pit-heads, and the sixth, the one nearest the town's own street and nearest, therefore, to Sarah's own kitchen door, stood behind a line of men and women so thinned by the weeks before it that Tom Varley, walking it on what would prove to be his last full round of the walls before the end, told her plainly that evening, sitting at her table with a cup he did not drink from, that he did not think the line would hold a second real push, and that he had told the same to Meikle and to old Fraser both, and that neither of them had disagreed with him, which from either man was as near to a confession of the same fear as either was ever likely to give.

The push, when it came, came in the grey hour before a full morning, the same hour the whole siege had begun in seven weeks before, and it came not with any great weight of shot or shouting, so far as Sarah afterward could piece it together from the little she saw with her own eyes and the rather more she was told by others in the days just after, but with a quietness that frightened her more, in the moment, than noise would have done, the line at the last pit-head simply giving way in the dark the way a rope gives that has been fraying for weeks and finally parts on no particular pull heavier than any that came before it. She woke to Tom Varley's own voice at her door, not loud, saying only her name and then that it was over, that the last of the pit-heads was taken and there was no line left anywhere in the town for anyone to hold, and that she should open her door before someone with less patience than the men who had let a prisoner go free a fortnight before came and opened it for her. He did not stay to say more than that. He had kin still at Cnoc thais, he told her once, months back, over the same table, and a shaft of his own there he meant to see fired by his own hand and no other's before any regiment came near it, and Sarah understood, watching him go back out into the dark toward the hill path rather than toward the street where the soldiers would shortly be, that he meant to keep that word if the hills would let him, and did not try to keep him from it.

She dressed and went down and found the street already full of a grey, tired quiet that was not quite surrender and not quite anything a person could properly name, townsfolk standing in their own doorways or sitting on their own steps because there was, in the end, nowhere left to go and nothing left to hold, and soldiers coming up the one street in no great hurry, as men come who have already won a thing and know it and see no cause to make more noise about the winning than the winning required. Sarah stood in her own doorway with her hair, as on the first morning, not properly pinned, and watched them come, and found, when the first of them reached her, a young man with a face no older than her own son's would have been had her son lived past his second winter, that she had nothing in her to meet him with beyond the plain fact of the open door behind her, opened by her own hand before he could think to ask, there being no one left in the town, herself included, with the strength or the reason left to keep it shut.

He asked her, in Dia-thìris first and then, when she did not at once answer, in the humans' own tongue, whether there were arms in the house, and she told him there were none beyond a kitchen knife she had used that morning to cut bread, and stood aside to let him look, which he did, briefly and without unkindness, before going on to the next door, and the next, the whole street being worked through in that same brief, businesslike way by men who had, she understood watching them, done this same work in other towns before this one and would likely do it again in others after, and found in that thought, standing in her own doorway with the morning coming up grey and ordinary over a town that had held for seven weeks and now, in the space of a single dark hour, had nothing left to hold with, neither comfort nor its opposite, only a kind of tiredness too complete to hold either.

What An Clàr Foscailte gives of that day, Sìleas nic Rath's own hand setting it down some months later at Muileann chaol from whatever report crossed her desk, is the day, and nothing more: that Muileann àrsaidh fell on that date, after a siege of some weeks, and was found, on the regiments' own taking of it, to hold nothing further worth a report. Of the bell, and of Fraser's unfinished wall, and of Meikle's careful counting of coal and potatoes both, and of a kitchen table that had been a dressing-station through a whole spring and half a summer, An Clàr Foscailte says nothing at all, having no way of knowing it, and Sarah Dunmore, telling it afterward to whoever in the hills still cared to ask her, never troubled herself greatly over An Clàr Foscailte's silence, having long since learned, in seven weeks of counting pit-heads by the striking of a single chapel bell, that a thing could be entirely true and entirely unwritten both at once, and that the second did not, in the end, make the first any less so.

# Chapter Twenty-eight: Of the Benches at Doire ghlas

*DE 21*

## I. Of the First of Them

They came down out of the hills the way water comes down a hill after rain, Ellen Marsh thought, watching the first of them from her own gate on a wet morning in an Giblean: a trickle at first, no order to it that a person could have foretold, and then, before you had rightly marked the trickle had begun, more than the ground about you seemed able to hold. The first family she saw with her own eyes was five people and a handcart, a woman and three children and an old man too stiff in the knees to have walked the whole way on his own legs, though he had, the woman said, because there had been no cart to spare for him and no time to wait for one.

"Àth leathan," the woman said, when Ellen asked her, the one word and no more, standing in the lane with the rain running off her shawl and her eyes gone past Ellen to the grey roofs of Doire ghlas beyond her, as if she could not yet quite believe a town still stood whole anywhere on the island. She did not say the battle's name. Nobody who came down that spring said the battle's name, not for weeks yet; they said the town's name, Àth leathan, and let the listener supply the rest, because the rest was a thing that did not want saying twice by the person who had walked out from under it.

Ellen took them in that first night, the five of them and the handcart both, her own house being the nearest with a fire lit, and gave them what she had, which was porridge and a corner of the byre for the old man's knees to be spared the floor, and did not ask them any of the questions her notebook wanted asked, because a woman who has walked three days with three children and a father-in-law who cannot bend his own legs is not a woman a schoolteacher puts a pen in front of on the first night. She asked instead where they meant to go on, and was told nowhere, that Caol mhòr was said to have work on the boats and Doire ghlas was said to have the mill, and that one or the other would have to do, since there was no third place left in the world that anybody in that family could name with any certainty of finding it standing.

More came the next week, and more the week after, along the same road down out of the western hills that had never in Ellen's memory carried more than a carrier's cart and a drover's cattle at any one time, walking now in twos and fives and, once, a whole clutch of eleven from three farms near Muileann àrsaidh who had left together in the night before the ditch-bridge went down, having judged, rightly as it turned out, that a siege was coming and having no wish to be inside the ring when it closed. They did not all come to Ellen's own gate. Most went on into the town proper, to whatever door had a fire showing through the shutter-crack and a face behind it willing to open, and by the month's end there was hardly a house in Doire ghlas that did not have some part of a stranger's family sleeping on its floor, nor a house in Caol mhòr either, by what letters told her, the two towns between them having taken in, by a count nobody had troubled yet to make formal, some hundreds of souls who three months before had never set foot north of the western hills in their lives.

Ellen kept her school running through all of it, mornings at least, judging that the children who were left to her, her own town's children and now a growing scatter of the newcomers' besides, wanted the one ordinary thing in their days more than they wanted a holiday from it; and she found, teaching sums and letters to a room grown suddenly half again its size, that the new children learned quick and said little, and that the ones from Àth leathan in particular would not, for weeks, be drawn into games that ran too near the door, as though a door left standing open behind them at speed was a thing their bodies had not yet finished expecting.

It was from one of the mothers, a woman named Nell Forbes who had taken the empty half of the net-mender's cottage two doors from Ellen's own, that she first heard the word used plainly, in the humans' tongue and then again in Dia-thìris as though the woman wanted to be sure of being understood in both: that the town they had left had been taken, and its pits, which had fed three generations of her own house, filled with water on the regiments' own order within a day of the fighting's end, so that there was, in the plainest sense a person could mean it, nothing left in Àth leathan for any of them to go back to even had they wished it. She said this without much weight in her voice, the way a person reports a fact they have said over often enough to themselves already that the saying of it aloud costs less than it once did, and Ellen, writing nothing down that evening, only listening, thought that this was itself a kind of telling, the flat voice as much a record as the words it carried.

The old man who had ridden the handcart the whole way, whose name Ellen learned only in the third week, when he judged himself sufficiently recovered in his own dignity to give it, was called Hugh Ferris, and had been forty years a hewer before his knees gave out and ten more a keeper of the pit-shed's own small library of tallies and wage-books, so that of all the household he alone had thought, in the handful of minutes the leaving allowed him, to bring away a single ledger under his coat rather than any clothing or food, on the reasoning, given to Ellen without apology, that clothing could be begged from any charitable house on the road but a hewer's forty years of wages, owed and part-paid and disputed, existed nowhere but in that one book, and a man who let a debt owed him go under the water along with the pit that owed it was a man choosing, in his own small way, to let the water win more than it had already won. He showed her the ledger once, dried by the fire and swollen at the spine from a wetting it had taken somewhere on the road, and asked her, in all seriousness, whether the schoolteacher thought a book of wages owed by a flooded pit to a hewer three months gone from the town that pit stood in was a book worth keeping any longer, or only a thing an old man carried because he had carried it too far already to set it down. Ellen told him she did not know, which was true, and that she would keep it for him regardless, which was also true, and put it on the shelf in her own front room beside the wrapped and waiting eleventh book, where it stayed the whole of that summer, two ledgers of two different kinds of debt standing side by side and neither of them yet called in.

## II. Of What the Room Did with Its Own Vote

Martha Greaves had sat in the chair at Caol mhòr the day the room voted nine to none that Tional nan Tuathach was no party to the quarrel and would feed any who came hungry, and she had known then, better than most of the room had troubled to know it, that a vote is a promise made to a future the room cannot yet see the shape of, and that the shape, when it comes, generally asks more of the promise than the promise-makers quite bargained for at the trestle. She was proved right of that within the year, and found, proved right, that she took no satisfaction whatever in the proving.

The granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas had been kept full since the summer before on the wool mills' own takings, against a want Martha had not named aloud even to Thomas Rook, who kept the books and asked no questions she did not care to answer. She fed the first comers from the mills' own kitchens that spring, the same weeks the first families reached her own town's gates, and did the plain arithmetic of the granaries at her own kitchen table by candlelight because she trusted no clerk's sum on this particular matter but her own, and found that what she had laid by would carry the towns' own people and a few hundred more through to the next harvest, provided the few hundred did not become a few thousand, and provided the harvest came in as it generally did.

She said as much to the room at the next sitting, standing in the cold over the net-lofts with the same ice on the same far window that had not properly gone since the winter she called the nine votes, and found the room readier than she had looked for to hear it. Peter Hale moved that the granaries be opened without further vote needed, the nine votes of the year before being, in his own words, a promise already made and now only being kept rather than a new thing the room had to decide over again, and the room agreed to that reading of it with less argument than Martha had braced herself for, and the granaries were opened to the families of the west in the middle of an t-Iuchar, when the mills' own kitchens could stretch no further, though Christina Munro, from the farm towns' bench, asked plainly what would be done if the harvest failed to come in as it generally did, and got no better answer than that the room would cross that ground when it came to it, which satisfied nobody, Martha least of all, but was the truest answer there was to give.

What she did not put before the room, because it was not the room's business to weigh and she had already weighed it herself in the small hours more than once, was the shape of the choice underneath the vote: that the council in the capital, whose regiments had emptied the western hills of the people now filling her own town's spare rooms, had sent nothing north to feed them and had forbidden nothing that Tional nan Tuathach chose to do about it either, the silence on both counts being, as she had come to understand silences of that particular kind, its own sort of answer. She wrote to Sìleas nic Rath at an Leabharlann that same week, less to ask anything of an Leabharlann, which she knew by then had no more power over the council's silence than Tional nan Tuathach did, than to have the fact set down somewhere outside her own kitchen table that Tional nan Tuathach had acted and the council had not, in case a day came when that difference wanted proving to someone who had not been there to see it for themselves.

Thomas Rook kept the register from the first week, a plain ledger bought for the purpose and ruled by his own hand into columns, name, town of origin, family, and a last column headed simply *taken in*, which he filled with whichever house or hall had found room for the family named on that line. He came to Martha near the end of an Cèitean with the ledger open at the last written page and his face doing the sum before his voice did.

"Three hundred and forty," he said. "As near as I can make it, and I'll not swear to the last ten, because a family that moves house twice in a fortnight, as more than a few have, is a family a ledger has trouble keeping honest count of."

"Three hundred and forty," Martha said, "out of two towns that between them held four thousand souls at the last count the head-due took."

"Aye."

"And the harvest not in yet."

"Aye," Thomas Rook said again, and closed the ledger over his thumb rather than let it fall shut on its own, the way a man closes a door he means to open again shortly rather than one he is done with, and Martha understood, watching him do it, that he had come to her not to be told what to do about the number, which neither of them could yet do anything about, but only to have another living person hear it said aloud before the writing of it went back into the dark of the ledger's covers where numbers lived until somebody needed them again.

She went down to the harbour that same evening, as she had taken to doing when the day's business would not let her sleep on it plainly, and stood a while watching the boats come in against a wind that had turned since noon, the fishing families of Caol mhòr going about the ordinary business of their own trade as though the town behind them had not doubled its trouble in the space of a season. A boy she knew, one of the harbourmaster's own, ran past her with a coil of rope over his shoulder and called out, in the way of a child who has heard a grown thing said at his own table and repeats it without yet weighing it, that his father said Tional nan Tuathach would beggar itself feeding half the western hills before the year was out and serve the council right if it did, since it was the council's own regiments had made the beggars in the first place. Martha did not correct him, a boy of ten owing no speaker of Tional nan Tuathach a careful answer, and she carried the sentence home with her all the same, turning it over the way she turned over most things said plainly by people who had not troubled to soften them for her hearing, and found, weighing it against her own kitchen-table arithmetic, that she could not honestly call it wrong, only early, the beggaring being a thing that had not yet happened and might yet be held off, granary by granary, harvest by harvest, so long as the towns that had voted the promise kept finding, each season, some new way to make good on it.

There was a second sitting of the room in an t-Iuchar, called at Peter Hale's own asking rather than by the calendar, at which the delegate of the eastern towns, a quiet man named William Reid who had said little at the first sitting and less since, rose to ask whether the room had considered that feeding the west's own people indefinitely, without any word from the west's own towns as to how long the feeding was likely to be needed, was a promise the room had made without a floor under it, in the sense that a floor is a thing you can at least say how far down it lies. Martha, from the chair, answered him herself rather than let the room answer for her, saying only that she had asked herself the same question at her own kitchen table more nights than she cared to number, and had found no better answer to give the room than the one she gave herself, which was that a promise made without knowing its own floor was still a promise, and the not knowing was no excuse the room had ever offered itself before for breaking one that mattered less. William Reid sat down at that without pressing further, and Christina Munro, two benches along, said nothing at all, which Martha took, rightly or not, for the nearest thing to agreement the farm towns' bench was likely to give her that year.

## III. Of the School's New Trade

The school that Agnes Pike had built at Doire ghlas thirty years before, out of her own money and her own stubbornness against a Moot that had not, in that generation, thought a mill town's children wanted more schooling than their trade required, was given over, a room at a time from the last week of an Cèitean and wholly in the last week of an t-Iuchar, to whatever families still had no roof of their own, its four rooms and its long hall together holding, by Thomas Rook's count, near sixty souls by midsummer, the benches Ellen had taught sums on for a dozen years serving now, pushed together in twos and threes with a blanket over the gap, for beds.

She kept teaching in the one room the families had left her, mornings still, the room crowded now with children who slept twenty feet from where they learned their letters and seemed, on the whole, none the worse for the closeness of it; and in the evenings, when the lessons were done and the hall had settled into whatever a room full of displaced families settles into once the day's small business of eating and washing and quarrelling mildly over blankets has run its course, she took her notebook, the twelfth after the eleven she had already filled and offered an Leabharlann, which had answered, by Raghnall mac Mhuirich's own letter, with no promise of taking them up, and began, without quite deciding to begin it, to write down what the families told her.

It was not the same work as An t-Aon Leabhar Deug had been. Those had been given slowly, over years, by old people with a whole life's telling saved up and offered a little at a time to a listener they had come to trust; this was given fast, in the first raw weeks of a loss too near to have found its proper shape yet, by people who had not asked to be listened to and in some cases did not want to be, and who told her, when they told her anything, not the long considered account an old woman gives at the end of her life but the sharp particular things a person cannot help saying because the mind will not put them down of its own accord: the exact word a neighbour had used, standing at his own door, when he chose to stay rather than come; the weight of a handcart's one wheel going soft in a rut two miles from anywhere; a hen someone had carried the whole way in a basket and would not now eat, keeping it instead as though the keeping of it were the last unbroken thing in the house.

Ellen wrote all of it down, in Dia-thìris as she had always written, and found that this book, unlike the eleven before it, grew a name of its own within the first month without her choosing one for it: the families themselves, hearing that the schoolteacher kept a book, began to call it, among themselves, the war-book, and to bring things to her for it the way a person brings a thing to be weighed, half in the hope of having it made lighter by the telling and half only because there was, in a hall crowded with strangers and grief both, nowhere else the thing could properly be set down.

Nell Forbes's own contribution to it, given one evening in an t-Iuchar with her three children long asleep on the bench behind her, was the shortest and, Ellen thought afterward, the truest thing anyone gave her that whole summer: that she had left her own kitchen dresser standing, plates and all, because there had been no room on the cart for it and no time to choose what to save from what to leave, and that she thought of the dresser now, of all the things she might have thought of, more often than she thought of the house itself, because a house, once you have walked far enough away from it, becomes a thing your mind can hold whole and finished, but a dresser with the plates still on it stays, somehow, unfinished, a thing still happening somewhere without you.

Hugh Ferris gave her something for the war-book too, near the end of an t-Iuchar, once he had settled enough into the hall's own rhythm to think the giving worth his while: not an account of the leaving, which he would not be drawn on beyond what he had already told her of the ledger under his coat, but a description, exact to the number of steps, of the pit-shed at Muileann àrsaidh where Ruth Calder had once stood to read out the agreement the five towns signed, a building he was certain by then stood no longer, or stood flooded to the rafters if it stood at all, and which he wished, he said, set down somewhere in a book with his own name attached to the setting-down, on the reasoning that a pit-shed a man has stood inside forty years deserves one more accounting before it goes under, whatever becomes of the coal beneath it. Ellen wrote the shed down as he gave it, the bench along the north wall, the tally-board by the door, the smell of the lamp oil that never quite left the timbers, and thought, copying his exact steps into her own exact hand, that this was the nearest thing to an epitaph the man was ever likely to compose for a building, and that it would have to do, there being, as with so much that summer, no better one on offer from anywhere else.

Not every family that came to the hall gave the war-book anything at all, and Ellen made a point, from the first week, of asking nobody twice who had once turned the asking aside; there were households who ate at the long table and slept behind their own blanket and spoke to her only of the weather or the children's sums for the whole of their time under Agnes Pike's roof, and she let them, judging, as she had judged of the family at her own gate the first wet morning, that a book kept by a schoolteacher was a use for the telling and not a debt the telling owed.

## IV. Of the Name a Child Gave Her

It was a girl of no more than eight, one of the Muileann àrsaidh eleven who had left in the night before the ditch-bridge fell, who came to Ellen at the school in the last week of an t-Iuchar, after the evening's lessons and before the hall's evening business had properly begun, and asked her, without any of the preamble the older families generally gave their askings, whether the war-book had names in it.

"Some," Ellen said. "The names of the people who tell me things, when they want their own name kept with what they've said. Not always. Some would rather the telling stood alone."

"Would you put a name in it that I gave you," the girl said, "even if I can't tell you anything true to go with it? I don't know anything true. I only know the name."

Ellen set down her pen, because she had learned, in eleven years of taking down old women's tellings, that a question asked in that particular flat, careful way was not a question to be answered with the pen already moving. "Whose name is it?"

"Ruth Calder's," the girl said. "My mother knew her. Everyone in Muileann àrsaidh knew her, or knew of her, which my mother says is near the same thing in a town that size. Nobody's put her name anywhere since the spring. My mother says An Clàr Foscailte has all the dead of the battle written down proper, every one, but Ruth Calder isn't dead, or isn't known to be, so she isn't in the dead ones' list, and she isn't in anything else either, because nothing else got written down about her at all, not since, and my mother says that's not right, a person going about not dead and not written down anywhere as if she'd never been a person in the first place."

Ellen looked at her a moment, and then picked the pen back up, because there was, in the end, no true reason not to, and turned to a clean page near the back of the book, the pages she kept for things given without a full telling behind them, single lines standing alone the way a stone stands alone in a field that has otherwise been cleared. "Tell me what your mother says, then," she said. "Not what you think I want. What she says."

"She says Ruth Calder drafted the agreement at the pit-shed five years back, the one that let the five towns work their own seams and sell to whoever'd buy honest coal from them. She was chosen to speak for the towns because nobody else wanted the work of writing the letters, and she wrote them anyway, every one, and the last one on an Nollaig after church, and nobody answered it. My mother says she was at Àth leathan the morning of the battle with a list in her hand, counting who'd come to fight, and that's the last anyone from Muileann àrsaidh saw of her or heard of her, and that's all. That's the whole of it. I don't know anything else, because there isn't anything else to know."

Ellen wrote it down exactly as the girl gave it, in the girl's own order, changing nothing, adding nothing, and did not write beneath it any of the things her own mind wanted to add, that An Clàr Foscailte's silence on the matter was likely to be permanent, that a name once dropped from every list a kingdom keeps rarely finds its way back onto one, that she herself, in eleven years of this same work, had never yet taken down a telling that ended in anything so plainly unfinished as this one did. She closed the book instead on the girl's last line, *that's all, that's the whole of it, I don't know anything else, because there isn't anything else to know*, and thought, walking home along the lane past the school's lit windows with the hall's evening noise going up behind her, of Thomas Rook's ledger and its last column, *taken in*, and of how many things a town could be asked to take in that a single ruled column had no proper heading for at all.

She wrote nothing more in the war-book that night. The girl's line stood alone on its page, as she had meant it to stand, and Ellen, closing the cover over it, found she had no wish, that evening or any evening after, to be the one who decided what ought to be written beneath it.

# Chapter Twenty-nine: Of Cnoc thais and the Windy Coast

*DE 21*

> **Part Five · Of the Regiments in the North**
>
> *Cha deach dad a lorg.*
> Nothing was found.
>
> — a regimental return, DE 21

## I. Of the Road They Cut

Tom Varley had reopened the two shafts at Cnoc thais with his own hands five winters before the war came looking for them, and he had known even then, hauling the first cartload of poor coal up into daylight with three other men and a borrowed windlass, that a seam a town cuts on its own account without a charter is a seam some day somebody with more men than argument will want back. He had said as much to Sarah Dunmore once, at her own kitchen table, and she had not disagreed with him; and he thought of that unremarkable evening a good deal in the middle weeks of an t-Iuchar, hard on his own coming home from Muileann àrsaidh, when the word came up the hill paths, farm to farm the way word always came in that country, that the road below Cnoc thais was cut.
