It was cut the way the road to Muileann àrsaidh had been cut earlier that summer, a company dug in across the cart track where it left the last of the flat ground and began to climb, and a second company working along the ridge to close the hill paths one by one, so that within a fortnight a man could still walk out of Cnoc thais on his own two feet, by paths only the town's own people rightly knew, but nothing on wheels could come in or go out, and nothing at all could come in that the regiments below did not first choose to let by. Tom had seen a siege from the inside once already that year, at Muileann àrsaidh, from the wrong side of a wall with a boy's blood on his hands, and he had carried the wounded of it up a ridge path in the dark and left a woman he could give no better answer than silence. He had told himself, walking home from Muileann àrsaidh to his own shaft-head with that behind him, that he would not stand inside a second wall and watch it close a second time, and he found, when the road below Cnoc thais was cut in earnest, that he still held to it.

The town itself was smaller than Muileann àrsaidh and had held out longer than anyone below it in the low country had troubled to expect, for the plain reason that Cnoc thais had never been much of a town to begin with, a scatter of houses about two shaft-heads and a chapel too small for half its own dead, and a company sent to take a place that size does not, in the ordinary way of war, hurry. The regiment below spent the better part of three weeks doing nothing that Tom's own watchers on the ridge could make out as an attack at all: digging, mending a bridge the spring floods had taken, drilling in a field the townsfolk had sown that year with oats they would not now live to cut. Tom used the weeks as they were given him. He walked the two shafts with the men who had cut them beside him, old Angus Rennie's cousin among them, and worked out between them, in the evenings, by a single shaded lamp in the room behind the chapel that served the town for a council when it needed one, exactly how much powder the lower galleries would want to bring the roof down clean and how much less than that would only crack the timbering and leave a seam half open for whoever came after to clear.

"You'd know that better than any man here," Angus's cousin said to him, the second evening, meaning it kindly and meaning also, Tom understood, that the work of ruining a thing you had built with your own hands was not work any man should be asked to reckon twice over if once would serve. Tom did not answer that directly. He said only that he had gone down those shafts as a boy to another man's coal before he ever cut a foot of his own, and that a shaft, when all was said, was a hole in a hill and would still be a hole in a hill when the war that wanted it closed was three generations forgotten, which was less an answer than a thing he told himself to make the reckoning bearable, and both men in that room knew it for what it was and let it stand.

The council, such as it was, met most evenings in that same chapel room, five men and two women who held no charter for the holding of it beyond the town's own custom of asking the oldest and the steadiest to sit and hear a thing out before anybody acted on it, and Tom sat with them though he had never been asked to and nobody had ever thought to tell him not to. The talk those evenings ran the same ground over and over, the way talk will when a town is waiting on a thing it cannot hurry and cannot put off: whether to send the children down to kin in the low country while the road still allowed it, whether a message to Muileann àrsaidh's own remnant might bring help that did not exist to bring, whether the regiment below meant to starve the town out slow or take it quick, a question none of them could answer and all of them asked all the same, the way a man worries a loose tooth with his tongue for the plain reason that it is there to worry.

It was old Mary Kessock, the eldest of the two women and a widow of a hewer dead these twenty years, who said, the second week of that waiting, the thing Tom found himself turning over longest after. She had lived through An Dealachadh as a girl, or near enough to it that her own mother had, and she said that a town threatened by soldiers it cannot fight had, in her mother's telling of the old days, exactly two ends open to it: to be taken whole, houses and all, for whatever use the takers wanted made of it, or to leave the takers nothing worth the taking and go. Cnoc thais, she said, looking round the room with an evenness that Tom thought afterward had cost her a good deal to keep, was too small and too poor to be worth much taken whole, and that left, by her own reckoning, only the second end, whenever the soldiers finally troubled to come up and prove her right or wrong of it. Nobody in the room argued with her that evening, though nobody voted on it either, there being nothing yet to vote on; but Tom saw, watching the faces round the shaded lamp, that the room had, without a word more being said, already begun quietly making ready to leave rather than be taken, each in whatever way each household judged it could manage the leaving.

## II. Of the Firing

Cnoc thais fell in an Lùnastal, on a morning grey with the kind of low cloud the western hills keep long past the season the low country calls summer, and it fell, by every account An Clàr Foscailte afterward gave and every account Tom himself carried away from it, without the town ever properly deciding to let it. The regiment came up the last of the road at first light, having found, two days before, a shepherd's path along the northern ridge that the town's own watchers had judged too steep for anything but goats and had, for that reason, left unwatched; and by the time word of soldiers on the ridge reached the chapel room where the council sat, the thing that wanted deciding had already, in the plainest sense, been decided for them.

Tom fired the shafts himself. He would not let Angus's cousin do it, though the man offered, twice, and Tom found afterward that he could not entirely say why he had refused the offer beyond a feeling, not fully reasoned, that a thing built by one pair of hands ought if it must be unbuilt to be unbuilt by the same pair and no other. He went down the first shaft alone in the grey hour with the powder already laid and the fuse cut to the length he had reckoned the night before, and stood at the shaft-head afterward with the second fuse in his hand and the sound of the first charge still working its way up through the rock underfoot, a sound less like an explosion than like a very large door being shut a long way off, and thought, watching the smoke come up thin and grey against the greyer sky, that he had heard that same sound described to him as a boy, by the man who first showed him a seam of coal by candlelight, as the sound a hill makes when it decides a thing is finished.

The second charge went the same way. By the time both shafts were sealed, timber and rubble packed down hard enough that no summer's digging would open them again without more men than the regiments below had any reason to spend on a played-out western seam, the soldiers were already coming through the town's one street, and Tom stood at his own shaft-head with the smoke still drifting and watched them come without any clear notion in his own mind of what he meant to do next, until Angus's cousin took his arm, not roughly, and said that a man who had just spent his morning burying his own coal had done the day's work the hills would remember him for, and that the rest of the day's work, whatever it turned out to be, could be done walking.

Mary Kessock was not among those who went up into the hills that morning. Tom saw her, in the last moments before he and the others took the rabbit path, standing at her own door with a shawl about her shoulders and a look on her face that he read, at the time and again many times after, as a woman who had already made her own reckoning of the two ends she had named three weeks before and chosen, for herself and no one else, the first of them, being too old by her own account to walk a hill country she had not walked in forty years and unwilling to be the weight that slowed six younger men's going. She raised a hand to him as he passed, not a wave so much as an acknowledging of him, one person to another, and he raised his own hand back, and that was the whole of the parting between them, no more words spent on it than the moment could properly hold.

An Clàr Foscailte, when it came to be written, gave the number of Cnoc thais's holdouts taken that morning as forty-one, a figure Sìleas nic Rath's clerks drew from the regiment's own muster of prisoners marched down to the low country in the days that followed, and it gave no figure at all, then or ever, for how many of the town's people had not been taken because they were, by the time the regiment reached the chapel room, already some hours gone up into the hills behind the town by paths the shepherd who had shown the soldiers one path had not, in the end, shown them all. Tom was among those not taken. He left the town by a path he had walked as a boy after rabbits and had not walked since, with Angus's cousin beside him and, within the first mile, four more of the town's own hewers who had judged, watching the soldiers come up the street, that a man taken at Cnoc thais that morning was a man who would not see his own hill again for a good while, if at all, and had chosen, each in his own time and by his own reckoning, to take the path instead.

## III. Of Those Who Went On

They did not stop in the near hills, where a dozen other small parties out of Cnoc thais and the last of Muileann àrsaidh's own scattered folk had by then made a kind of ragged half-camp among the shielings the summer herding used and abandoned every autumn regardless of any war. Tom had thought, the first night out, that the near hills would do, that a man could sit quiet enough among the shielings through the worst of the weather and wait to see what the peace, whenever it came, would leave standing for him to go back to. It was Angus's cousin, of all of them, who said otherwise, on the second night, with the six of them crowded round a fire small enough that its smoke would not carry far and a sky above them clearing, for once, to more stars than any of them had troubled to look at in a year.

"They'll not let the near hills be," he said. "This year or next, it makes no matter. They'll come up after the shielings same as they came up after the town, once some clerk in the low country works out there's men here still breathing that the muster roll never caught." He had no more certain a reason for the saying of it than any other man's guess that autumn, and he offered none, but the six of them sat with it a while in the firelight, turning it this way and that the way men turn a coin they cannot yet decide is counterfeit, and found, each in his own private accounting, that none of them could put forward a better guess to set against it.

Tom said little that night himself, though he had thought, before Angus's cousin spoke, that he might argue for the shielings after all, on the plain ground that a man's legs tire and a winter in open country asks a great deal of legs that had spent a life underground and not on a hillside. He did not argue it. He found, turning his own reasons over by the fire, that he trusted the other man's guess more than his own wish, and a guess trusted over a wish was, he had learned that year if he had learned nothing else, the surer thing to build a winter's walking on.

So they went on, past the near hills and the shielings and the last of the drove paths any Cnoc thais man had a name for, into ground that the town's own oldest hewers spoke of only at second or third hand, a country of low scrub and standing water and, at last, a wind that Tom found did not properly stop from the day they first felt it on their faces to the day, weeks later, that he stood at the edge of the sea and understood why every teller who had ever spoken of that coast to him as a boy had called it, without needing to say more, an Oirthir Ghaothach.

The walking took the better part of three weeks, by Tom's own count of nights slept under whatever cover the ground offered, and it was not, he found, a country that made the walking easy for the reward of its emptiness. The scrub tore at boots already worn thin from a summer's siege-work, and the standing water, brown and cold and often deeper than a man's first step into it judged it to be, cost them one bad night when Angus's cousin went in to the knee in what had looked, in the failing light, no more than a puddle, and came out with a chill that kept him shivering by the fire two days running before it passed. They ate what the country gave them and what little they had carried, birds taken with a sling two of the party had thought to bring, and once, memorably enough that it was spoken of round the fire for a week after, a hind that one of the Àth naomh men, met on the path by then and fallen in with them, brought down with a single cast of a spear he had carried the whole way from his own dissolved town for no better reason, he said, than that a man walking into country he did not know felt easier walking into it armed with anything at all, even a spear no soldier on either side of the war would have troubled to call a weapon.

They crossed one another's paths with the other six parties by a kind of slow accretion rather than any single meeting, a fire seen at a distance one evening and approached cautiously by both sides until a shout in Dia-thìris settled what a shout in no tongue at all might not have, two families falling in together for a day's walk and then parting again toward different stretches of coast, word of a third party carried forward by whichever traveller had last spoken with them. Tom found, doing this slow arithmetic of meetings as the weeks went on, that he had come to know the shape of the whole scattered company, seven parties and something short of two hundred souls, before he had ever stood in the same place as more than a dozen of them at once, a kind of knowing at second hand that put him in mind, more than once, of Ellen Marsh's books of Tuathaich accounts, gathered the same slow way from people who had not set out meaning to be gathered into anything at all.

They were seven parties in all by the time word of one another reached them on that ground, seven separate handfuls out of Cnoc thais and the last stragglers of Muileann àrsaidh and, it was said though Tom never met the man himself, one small party out of Àth naomh that had come the longest way round of any of them, and between the seven parties they made, by nobody's exact count, somewhat short of two hundred souls sitting on ground that belonged, by any charter the low country kept, to nobody at all. The regiments followed them as far as a boundary stone at the edge of what the old province rolls called the shire of Seann Vell, a stone none of the seven parties had known was there until a patrol's officer, come up to within shouting distance of it one grey morning, called across that he was under orders to go no farther, the ground beyond being outside any shire Comhairle nam Mèinnean's writ ran in, and that his own commander wanted no part of a war fought on ground his own maps did not properly own.

It was that same officer's report, copied afterward into An Clàr Foscailte and from there, in time, into every account the low country ever kept of that autumn, that gave the seven parties the name they carried thereafter in every paper that troubled to name them at all: Muinntir gun Siorrachd, a phrase the officer had reached for, Tom thought later, hearing it repeated back to him by a trader who had heard it from a soldier who had heard it from the officer himself, because a man writing a report wants a name for the thing he is reporting, and the ground those seven parties sat on had, in the plainest sense the officer's own maps could give him, no name of its own to lend them. The phrase said nothing of Cnoc thais and nothing of the western hills either, and Tom, hearing it named back to him for the first time by a stranger's mouth at a stranger's fire, felt the particular smallness of a man who learns that the ground he stands on has been written down by somebody who has never stood on it at all.

## IV. Of the Fleet Sent South and the Boats That Burned

What word reached an Oirthir Ghaothach of the rest of that autumn's business came slowly, and came sideways, carried by traders who came up the coast path from the south with salt and needles and, now and again, a barrel of dubhan oil to sell to fisherfolk who had burned fish-oil in their own lamps since before any of the seven parties' grandfathers were born, and who took, in exchange for their goods, whatever news the traders judged worth the telling. The fisherfolk themselves took the seven parties in without much asking, in ones and twos and small households, the way Tom had heard the north coast generally took in whoever a hard season washed up on it, and he and Angus's cousin and the others of the Cnoc thais six came, before the month was out, to a widower named Calum Odhar who fished a two-man boat out of a cove Tom never did learn a proper name for, and who gave them the byre behind his own house to sleep in and asked, in the whole of the first fortnight, exactly one question of them, which was whether either could mend a net, and neither being much use with a net, set them instead to hauling driftwood for the winter's fires and troubled them with nothing further.

It was one such trader, a woman named Cairstine who walked the coast path twice a year and had done so, by her own account, since before the war had a name, who first told Tom and the others, sitting over a fire in Calum Odhar's own byre with the wind working at the thatch above them, that the fleets in the south had been thinned to keep the north-west shut, and that the raiders of the eastern water, who had troubled nobody in living memory while the fleets stood full, had come out from their own islets that same autumn and found the southern water emptier than it had been in a generation. She told it plainly, the way Tom came to understand was her whole manner of telling anything, sitting cross-legged on a creel with her pack still on her back because she meant, she said, to be gone again before the tide turned, and she took a long pull from the cup Calum Odhar's own daughter set by her before she went on, as though the telling were thirsty work and wanted wetting partway through.

An dàrna cabhlach, Cairstine said, had been raised that same season at the southern Seann Skell, out of the harbour towns and Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's own boatmen, to hold the eastern and southern water while A' chiad chabhlach and the fourth kept the north-west shut against nothing that anyone on an Oirthir Ghaothach could rightly say deserved the shutting; and the raising of it had not been quick enough, or not full enough, or simply not lucky enough, to keep two salt-boats out of Àth bheag from being taken clean out of the water one grey morning and a third burned to the waterline within sight of its own harbour mouth, the crew of the burned boat put ashore, some days after, at the light of Baile ìseal, more by luck than by any rescue An dàrna cabhlach could rightly claim credit for. The fleet did run one of the raiders down in the end, off that same light, a fortnight or more after the burning, and brought her in with what was left of her crew for Cùirt na Mara to deal with in its own time and its own way; but Cairstine, telling it, gave the running-down less weight in the telling than the burning that came before it, in the way a teller weighs a thing by what it cost rather than by how it ended, and Tom, hearing it, found himself thinking less of the raiders or the fleet than of a woman he had never met, put ashore at a light he had seen only from a boat's deck once as a boy, with nothing left of her own boat to show for a season's work but the clothes she stood up in.

He asked Cairstine, when she had done with the telling, whether the fleet's thinning and the raiders' coming were spoken of, in the low country, as one thing or two, and she said she could not properly answer that, not being a woman the low country's own clerks troubled to ask; but she said that a fisherman of Baile ìseal, from whom she had the tale in the first place, had put it to her plainly enough over a cup at his own hearth, that a kingdom which sent its ships to shut a door on nothing much would some day find another door, one it had not thought to watch, standing open behind it, and that this was not, in his own telling of it, a new thing under any sky, only a thing kingdoms went on forgetting each in their own turn.

Calum Odhar, who had sat through the whole of Cairstine's telling without a word, said only, once she had gone on her way north the next morning with her pack lighter of goods and heavier, he judged, of nothing at all, that a man who fished a two-man boat out of a cove with no name learned early not to trouble himself over which of a kingdom's doors stood open or shut, since the sea took no more notice of a kingdom's doors than it took of a kingdom's charters, and a fisherman's whole trade was learning to read the one door the sea kept, which no fleet anywhere had ever yet managed to shut for a single season together. Tom thought that a fair answer, turning it over afterward, and thought too that it was the kind of answer a man could only give who had never had a shaft of his own to fire, or a book of names taken down at a trestle table that he could not stop, some nights, from counting over in his head.

## V. Of the Edge of the Sea

Tom kept, through that autumn and into the first hard weather of an Dàmhair, a private reckoning of his own, not written down anywhere, since there was no paper on an Oirthir Ghaothach that any of the seven parties troubled to carry and no ledger a man could rule columns in even had he carried one, but held instead the way a man holds a tally he means to keep straight in his own head against the day somebody asks him for it. He counted, that autumn, the men who had come out of Cnoc thais with him and were still, by his own eye, breathing and whole; he counted, separately, the ones the regiment had taken at the town and marched south, whose names he knew and whose faces he could still call up plainly enough by firelight; and he counted, last and longest, a column that had nothing to do with Cnoc thais at all, a woman's book of names taken down at a trestle table two seasons before, and a field left unploughed below Àth leathan that he had stood at the edge of once, at a sentry's leave, and looked at a long while without finding an answer his own eyes could bring back with him.

He did not find, that autumn, any word of Ruth Calder on an Oirthir Ghaothach, nor any reason to think a word of her would ever reach so far a shore, and he had by then stopped expecting one in any place he came to, the way a man stops expecting rain in a season that has already, by every sign the sky gives, gone dry for good. Angus's cousin asked him once, mending a net neither of them was much use at, whether he still meant to send word north to the hill farms the way he had that first fortnight at Muileann àrsaidh, boy to shepherd to farmhouse, and Tom said he did not, this coast having no chain of boys and shepherds a message could travel by, and no farmhouse within it that had ever heard Ruth Calder's name to begin with; and having said it aloud he found it settled a weight in him that had ridden there unspoken the length of the walking, not so much an ending as a putting-down of it he had carried the length of the walking without once setting it aside to rest his arms.

What he found instead, in the last clear evening before the weather turned for good, was the sea, and he stood at the edge of it on a strand of black shingle with the wind coming off the water hard enough to take a man's breath if he stood square into it, and the light going down grey into grey without any proper sunset to mark the day's end, the way the low country's own evenings marked it with colour and this coast, by every account the seven parties had of it, never troubled to. Calum Odhar had told him, the week before, that an Oirthir Ghaothach kept no calendar of feast days the way the low country did, the weather here being too much its own master to be told when a season was meant to turn, and that the fisherfolk marked their year instead by the boats that went out and the boats that came back, a reckoning Tom found, turning it over, not so very different from a hewer's own way of marking a year by the coal that came up and the coal that did not.

He stood there a while, with Angus's cousin some way off along the shingle doing the same thing in his own silence, and thought, watching the water come in flat and grey and endless, of a burn in spate below a pit-head, brown and quick with snow-melt, going on the same before, during and after a battle as if it had somewhere better to be than any of the men fighting beside it; and he thought that the sea before him now was the same water, in the end, only grown too large for any man to hear it the way he had heard that burn, and that a man could stand at its edge his whole life and never once persuade it to answer a question he had not thought to ask it plainly. The wind did not let up. It had not let up, by his own reckoning, since the day the seven parties first felt it on the far side of the near hills, and Tom Varley, watching the light go out of a grey sky over a grey sea on ground that belonged, by any charter the low country kept, to nobody at all, found he had stopped expecting it to.

# Chapter Thirty: Of the Ships Round the North

*DE 21*

## I. Of the Regiments Called Again

The rolls that had lain in the council's chests since An Dealachadh, brought out once already that autumn to arm the regiments that went west to Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais, were not yet put away when the second half of them was wanted, and by the middle of an Dàmhair the calling went on across the whole island rather than the west alone, so that a man might now be summoned to a war he had thought, until the summons found him, a quarrel of the pit towns and no business of his own province at all.

The sixth was raised first, at Cnoc bheag, the great river port of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in the north-central country, on the seventeenth of the month, and of all the regiments called that autumn it alone had its colours blessed before it marched, Òrd an t-Seabhaig keeping still, in that one town, the custom that had gone out of fashion at the capital three reigns before. The priest who blessed them was an old man, by every account that reached an Leabharlann afterwards, and he blessed the cloth and not the men who would carry it, saying, as the custom asks, that Mòd's hunger fed on what marched under an unblessed flag sooner than on what marched under a blessed one, which the regiment's own clerk wrote down as said and did not trouble to explain further, it being no part of a clerk's office to explain a priest to a reader who had not been there to hear him. The colours, when they went north-west a week later to hold the road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, were new cloth on an old staff, one that had stood in Òrd an t-Seabhaig house's own keeping since a war none of the men now carrying it could have named. The blessing was done at first light on the quay steps, the cloth laid across the priest's own two hands and the whole regiment drawn up in three sides of a square about him with the river fog still lying on the water behind, and the townsfolk who had turned out to watch it, being a river port and used to the sight of soldiery coming and going on Comhairle nam Mèinnean's business, stood a good deal quieter than Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own returns of the day thought worth remarking, as men and women commonly do at the start of a thing whose end they have no way yet of guessing.

The regiment's own clerk, a careful young man new to the office, wrote in his first report that the ceremony had taken the better part of an hour on account of the tide, the colours needing to be blessed and the boats loaded on the same ebb, and that the priest had shown no sign of hurrying it for the tide's sake or anybody else's, which the clerk set down without complaint, having been told by his own captain, before ever they reached Cnoc bheag, that a blessing rushed for the convenience of a schedule was a blessing better not asked for at all.

Eight days after that the second was raised at Àth dhìreach, in the east, and set to guard Slighe a' Ghuail and the library road together, the two roads running so near each other along that stretch that one company could watch both without doubling its marches. It was the first soldiery the town of Muileann chaol had seen in any living memory, and Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, who had kept Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd for five-and-twenty years before she laid the office down and asked nothing of her retirement but her sister's house at Àth dhìreach, watched the camp go up from the garden wall with the particular attention of a woman who had spent a working lifetime writing down what other people did and had never once, until that autumn, had it done under her own window.

She wrote to Sìleas nic Rath, her old clerk and the chronicler now in her place, a letter that said less than a letter from Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh might have been expected to say, on the reasoning, she told Sìleas plainly, that the office was no longer hers to fill with her own judgements, only her own eyes, which the office had never asked to be idle even when the pen that once served them had been laid aside. The camp was orderly, she wrote; the tents stood in rows a surveyor might have set out; the company's captain, a young man not long out of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own service, had called on her within the first week to ask, civilly enough, whether her garden wall marked ground he needed for a picket line, and had accepted her answer, which was that it did not, without argument. She wrote that the town had given the company no trouble and the company had given the town none, and that this, in a year when other towns nearer the fighting could say no such thing, seemed to her worth the setting down, whatever anyone at an Leabharlann chose to make of it.

She added, at the foot of the second page, a line she struck through once and then let stand, the ink of the strike-through thin enough that Sìleas read the words under it without difficulty: that she had spent five-and-twenty years writing down what a kingdom did in its own name, and had come, in the six months since she laid the pen aside, to find she trusted her own eyes on a garden wall rather better than she had ever quite let herself trust the reports that used to reach her desk from towns she had never once had occasion to stand in. Sìleas kept the letter among her own papers, and it is one of the few private hands of that autumn that anyone kept by nobody's order but its writer's own habit of writing things down.

Away in the north-east, at Caol bheag, the fourth was raised on the second of an t-Samhain, and of the four companies mustered that season it was the fourth's road that ran longest and strangest before it ever came within sight of a field it might have to hold.

## II. Of the Voyage Round the North

Dùghall mac Iain was twenty-three that autumn and had been three years a soldier without, until the muster bell rang at Caol bheag on the last day of an Dàmhair, ever once expecting to be one anywhere but at home. He was a corporal because a sergeant who had known his father thought him steady, and steady he had been, in the way of a young man who has never yet been asked to prove it: he kept his kit in order, said little in the mess that he had not first turned over twice in his own head, and had, before that autumn, gone no farther from Caol bheag in the whole of his soldiering than the shire's own boundary stone, twelve miles out on the Ros chiar road, where the company sometimes marched of a summer to keep its legs in practice and its officers' reports supplied with something to report.

The order that came down named the fourth for the north-west, without saying at first how a company was to reach a coast that no road on the island ran the whole way to, and it was two days before the answer came down after it: they were to go by water, down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar, and from Ros chiar round the north coast in whatever hulls Comhairle nam Mèinnean could hire on short notice, there being no fleet of An Crùn's own idle enough that season to spare for the carrying of one regiment when four others wanted moving besides.

They marched down to the river on a grey morning with the frost still on the grass verge and the town's whole population turned out along the road to see them go, which Dùghall found harder to bear than he had looked for, the cheering of people he had known his whole life being a different thing entirely from the cheering he had imagined, in the idle way a young soldier imagines such scenes before he is given one, of a crowd that did not know him and so could cheer him without also, in the same breath, wondering aloud to each other whether he would come home. His own mother stood at the corner by the mill with her shawl pulled tight and said nothing at all as he passed, which he understood, without either of them needing to say it, as the greater kindness.

The barges that carried them down the Abhainn ghorm were coal barges once, by the look of the tar still black in their seams, refitted since with plank benches down both sides and not much else, and the river ran high and quick with the autumn rain so that the two days' journey the maps had promised was done in a day and a half, the barge-men steering more than rowing, and Dùghall, who had never in his life been afloat on anything larger than a fishing coble, spent the better part of that first day learning the particular misery of a barge deck in a following current, which pitches a man's stomach in ways no cart on a rutted road had ever taught him to expect.

The men of his own file passed that first day poorly, the way soldiers pass any day with nothing asked of them but to sit still and be carried, in fits of talk that ran out and started again over nothing much: a game with pebbles and a chalked board one of them carried folded in his kit for exactly such an idleness, an argument over whose home town brewed the better ale that neither side had any way of settling on a barge deck and so carried on for the better part of an hour regardless, and, once the light began to go, a song two of the older men knew between them and the rest picked up by the second verse, a harvest song their own mothers might have sung, which struck Dùghall, listening to it carry out flat over the water in the dusk, as a strange thing for men bound to a war to be singing, and a right one all the same.

His own corporal's charge, a file of nine, was young for the most part, three of them not yet twenty and none, Dùghall among them, ever before asked to do more soldiering than a summer's drill and the keeping of a quiet road. He found himself, without quite choosing it, the file's steadiest hand by simple virtue of being the one among them who had worn the corporal's own mark longest, a matter of eight months and no more, and spent a good part of that first night's watch answering questions from the youngest of them, a lad named for his own father and called by nobody the whole voyage but that same father's name, about what a battle was likely to be like, questions Dùghall had no truer answer to than the lad had himself, and answered anyway, as steadily as he could make his voice go, because a corporal who let his own voice shake in the dark was no use to a file with nothing else that night to hold steady by.

Ros chiar, when they came to it, was a walled town smaller than Caol bheag and built entirely, so far as Dùghall could see from the barge, around the business of getting things onto and off ships, its whole waterfront one long clutter of hoists and rope-walks and sheds smelling of tar and salt fish, and it was there, tied up three deep along the outer quay, that he had his first sight of the hulls that were to carry the regiment the rest of the way: squat, broad-beamed vessels with tanks built into their holds where cargo should have gone, hired, the quartermaster said, from whatever shipmaster on that coast owned a hull already fitted to carry dubhan and was willing, for Comhairle nam Mèinnean's money, to carry men instead for one voyage.

Comhairle nam Mèinnean's money was good money, and the shipmasters who took it asked no questions Dùghall's officers troubled to answer, but the men who crewed the hulls asked plenty among themselves, in the hearing of soldiers standing at the rail with nothing else to do but hear them, and Dùghall learned in this way, before any officer told him so directly, that they were going round the north cape and down the far side to a coast the fourth's own quartermaster had needed a chart to find, a coast whose towns the crew named as easily as Dùghall could have named the streets of Caol bheag, and spoke of, he noticed, in the plain flat voice of men speaking of somewhere they had traded in for years and expected no trouble in trading in again, whatever cargo they carried this particular voyage.

They put out from Ros chiar on the fourth of an t-Samhain into a sea already turning, the shipmasters said without much comfort in the saying, and it was a hard passage by any account Dùghall heard given afterwards, five days round the north cape in hulls built for dubhan and not for men, the tanks below decks giving off a smell that got into a man's kit and did not come out of it again for weeks, and the north cape, when they rounded it on the second night, showed Dùghall a sea he had not known the island's own coast could make: grey water running in ridges taller than the barge that had carried him down the river, and beyond it, for the better part of a watch, nothing at all to be seen in any direction but that same grey water going on to a horizon a man could not find the edge of. He was sick over the rail twice that night, along with the better part of his own file, and heard, above the wind, one of the older soldiers laughing at nothing in particular in a way Dùghall came in time to understand: a man keeping his own voice going so as not to have to listen too closely to the sea.

They lost no man on that passage, though a boy of the second company went overboard reaching for a line that had come loose and was hauled back in half-drowned and shaking, and one hull, separated from the others in the worst of the second night's weather, put into a cove on the far side of the cape and lost two days finding the others again, arriving at Ceann mhòr three days behind the rest with its whole crew and cargo safe but its captain, by every account, considerably older in the face than he had been when he set out.

## III. Of Ceann mhòr

Ceann mhòr stood at the head of a long inlet on the Tuathaich coast, a port town of some size by the standard of that country, its grey stone houses climbing the slope above the harbour in the close-built rows Dùghall had already learned, from what the older men of the company said of Tuathaich towns, to expect of that people's building, and its church, the largest structure the town owned, standing above the harbour where a Dia-thìrich town would have set its temple, which struck Dùghall, seeing it for the first time from the deck of the hull that carried him in, as a small and useless thing to notice and one he found himself noticing anyway.

The regiment was quartered on the tenth of an t-Samhain in the old human magistrate's house, a low, thick-walled building above the quay that the town's own maor, a Dia-thìrich man of An Crùn's appointing named for that office alone, had kept as his own residence since the shires were first drawn, on the reasoning, handed down with the office itself, that a house built by the humans to hold the humans' law was as good a house as any to hold An Crùn's, and better than most, being stone through and cheap to warm. The maor gave up the greater part of it without complaint that Dùghall's own captain reported hearing, and moved his own household into the two upper rooms the regiment had no use for, and it was noticed by more than one man of the fourth, in the way soldiers notice such things without being told to, that the maor's clerk, a Tuathaich woman who had served the office for years under three maoir running, addressed the captain in Dia-thìris without once stumbling over it and addressed her own townsfolk, when they came to the house on the office's business, in the humans' tongue exclusively, as though the two languages belonged, in her own ordering of the world, to two entirely different kinds of transaction and were not to be let mix.

The house, once four hundred men had been fitted into what had held one household and its servants, kept a smell about it for the whole of that winter that Dùghall came to think of as the particular smell of soldiery indoors, wet wool and boot-blacking and the tallow of too many lamps burning too long into too short a day, laid over whatever the magistrates who had built the place had meant it to smell of, and the maor himself, a heavy, unhurried man who had held the office since before Dùghall was born, took to walking the two upper rooms' own narrow gallery of an evening with his pipe, looking down into the courtyard at the drill his house had been given over to, and saying, to whichever officer happened to be crossing below him, some version of the same dry observation: that he had held this house forty years against damp, and the army had done in a fortnight what forty winters of the sea air had not managed, which the captain, by the third or fourth telling of it, had learned to answer only with a nod, there being no answer to a landlord's joke that does not also concede the landlord's point.

Tional nan Tuathach's protest reached the house within the fortnight, carried up from Caol mhòr by whatever carrier still worked that coast road in the season's worsening weather, a single sheet in Martha Greaves's own hand asking, in terms Dùghall's captain read aloud to the assembled company on the theory that men quartered somewhere ought to know what was being said of the quartering, that An ceathramh rèisimeid be lodged at its own charge and not the town's, the town having neither asked for soldiers nor been offered the choosing of them. It was received, the captain's own note back to Comhairle nam Mèinnean said, and forwarded, and there the matter rested, as such matters generally did, Comhairle nam Mèinnean's reply, when it came near the year's end, saying only that the arrangement stood until the campaign's needs changed it, which answered the letter's words without answering anything the letter had actually been written to ask.

It was in those same weeks, though a good way farther west along that same coast, that the fleets off Cathair gheal took up the searching of the fishing boats that put out from that harbour every morning the weather allowed it, a measure Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order named necessary against the carrying of arms or men under a full boat's catch, and one the fishermen of that town, within a month of its starting, had put into a petition of their own, carried to Tional nan Tuathach by a delegation of six, and by Tional nan Tuathach on to the council with no more comment attached than the plain fact of its having been forwarded. The searching went on the same as before the petition and the same as after it, a boat held at its own quay of a morning for the better part of an hour while two of the fleet's own men went through its nets and its fish-hold both, and it was said afterwards, by the fishermen themselves and by nobody troubled to deny it, that not one weapon and not one man beyond the boat's own crew was ever found in the whole course of that searching, which Comhairle nam Mèinnean's returns record without remark and without, so far as the record shows, any change of order following from it.

The petition, when it came to be written, was drawn up at a meeting held on the quay, in the cold, before the boats went out one morning, the six men chosen to carry it agreeing between them on no more than the plainest facts a petition could safely carry: the number of days the searching had run, the number of hours a boat was commonly held, and the plain observation, set down without complaint attached to it because none of the six judged a complaint likely to travel any further than the facts alone, that a fish left too long in a held net spoiled before it ever reached a buyer, spoiled fish being spoiled fish whichever tongue the boat's crew happened to curse it in. It went to Caol mhòr folded inside a barrel of salt cod consigned, quite genuinely, to Tional nan Tuathach's own stores, on the reasoning of the man who carried it that a petition riding inside an honest cargo drew less notice at the searching than a petition riding in a man's coat.

Dùghall heard of it third-hand, from a corporal of An dàrna cabhlach billeted for a night at Ceann mhòr on his way to somewhere else, who told it as a piece of dry entertainment over the two men's shared supper and nothing graver than that, a fish barrel and a folded letter being, to a man who had spent that autumn searching nets for muskets and finding none, the sort of story a soldier keeps by him for its comedy rather than its weight. Dùghall laughed with him at it that night, and thought little more of it at the time beyond the ordinary soldier's thought that another man's orders were another man's trouble and not his own, a thought he had occasion, before that winter was out, to think a good deal less easily than he thought it that first night.

Farther east again, on the sixteenth of the month, the eighth was raised at Inis uaine on the Abhainn chaol, to stand guard over the dubhan depots of the eastern ports against a burning the council feared more than it ever quite said aloud it feared, the holdouts having, by every report that reached the capital, neither the means nor, so far as anyone could show, the least intention of firing a depot the width of the island from any field they had yet fought on, which did not stop the eighth from being raised and posted regardless, on the reasoning, as sound in its own way as the reasoning behind the searching of Cathair gheal's nets, that a fear a council could not quite prove groundless was a fear it generally chose to arm against rather than argue with.

## IV. Of the Widow's House

The billeting of the company's men among the town's own houses, once the magistrate's house was full past any further stretching, was done by the maor's clerk from a list of the town's rooms to spare, a list she kept, Dùghall came to understand, with the same flat and even hand she gave to every other business of that office, naming which house had a room over its byre or a loft above its kitchen and how many a household could be asked to take without more hardship than the office judged fair to ask of it. Dùghall's own name came down against a house two streets back from the harbour, kept by a widow named Barbara Keir who had a loom set up in the room behind her kitchen and worked it, he came to learn, most of the daylight hours a fishing town's own work left her free for.

She opened the door to him the first evening with no more welcome in her face than the clerk's list had shown in its own writing, looked him over the way a woman looks over a stranger she has been told to house and not asked whether she wanted housed, and showed him the room she had made ready without a word in either tongue, only a hand toward the stair and, once he had climbed it and set down his kit, a plate of bread and salt fish left at the stair's foot without his hearing her come up to bring it. It was, he thought that first night, no worse a billet than a soldier had any right to expect in a town that had not asked for him, and he was three years too well trained in the plainer disciplines of soldiering to expect a hostess's warmth on top of a dry roof and a full plate, and told himself so, and slept.

She answered him readily enough in Dia-thìris, he found within the first week, a civil word for a civil word, the accounts of the billeting-due settled between them without friction on either side, and it was only some evenings later, meaning no more by it than the ordinary courtesy a guest owes a house not his own, that he tried the few words of the humans' tongue he had picked up from men of his own company with kin among the Tuathaich, and got, for his trouble, nothing at all: not so much as a shake of the head, only the same flat and even look she had given him at the door that first evening, as though he had not spoken. He heard her, within the same week, across the yard wall, giving that same tongue easily enough to a neighbour who had called something over about the weather, quick and unhesitating and without the smallest trip in it, so that he came to understand, before he ever properly asked himself why, that the withholding lay in whose ear the words were meant for, and nowhere in her own mouth.

He tried it again, once or twice, in the weeks that followed, telling himself each time that a man ought to be let learn the tongue of a house he ate bread in, and got, each time, the same flat civility that was not quite unkindness and was not, either, anything he could rightly call an answer, until he came, by the third or fourth trying, to understand it for what it was: a door she had shut on him alone, and kept open, plainly and without apparent effort, to every other soul in the town who was not wearing the regiment's own coat.

Why, he did not ask her. The question he turned over instead, those first weeks at Ceann mhòr, the way he turned over most things he had not been given orders about, slowly and without arriving anywhere he was satisfied to call an answer, got him only as far, most nights, as the plain fact that a woman who gave a soldier her own kingdom's own tongue for the plain business of bread and billeting-dues, and would not give him her own people's, had drawn a line somewhere in her own reckoning that was hers to draw and none of his to cross uninvited, whatever the drawing of it cost either of them. He went on eating her bread and sleeping under her roof through the weeks the billeting list kept them so, and she went on answering him in Dia-thìris exactly as far as the house's own business asked and no further, keeping the humans' tongue for the yard wall and the neighbour's voice and every ear in Ceann mhòr but his, and neither of them, in all that time, ever once said to the other what either of them understood the silence to mean.

# Chapter Thirty-one: Of the Dark Town

*DE 21*

## I. Of the Third Fleet

An treas cabhlach was raised at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast on 1 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21, out of a fishing town that had never, so far as anyone at Ceann mhòr could say, raised so much as a harbour-watch before that winter, and Dùghall mac Iain saw the first of its hulls a week later, from the quay at Ceann mhòr, where she came in round the point on a grey forenoon riding low and black in the water with the dubhan sloshing audibly in her belly whenever the swell took her. She had no name on her bow. A clerk of the fleet had chalked *Trì* there, for the fleet's number, for want of any properer name yet given her, and the chalk had half run in the spray of the passage.

She had come the whole length of the west coast in four days, up from Baile ghorm past the capes and the closed water off the western Seann Skell, carrying the army's dubhan to the regiments in the hills and on the northern coast, and nothing else. That was the whole of An treas cabhlach's business, her master said, a man named Griogair who had fished the south-west waters forty years before the fleet ever thought to want him: to carry fuel north, since a regiment that could not light its own lamps or run its own lorries was no regiment at all, whatever guns it carried. Dùghall was on the quay with a file to see the barrels ashore, and Griogair, who had little enough to do once his hull was made fast, stood with him at the tank-cock through the better part of the unloading and talked, when he talked at all, in the manner of a man laying down one plain fact at a time and leaving the hearer to make of it what he would.

It was Griogair who told him that the fleet's hulls were fitted, every one, with the same tanks a lorry carried, only built larger and set low in the belly for the ballast the fuel's own weight gave her, so that a hull running full rode lower and steadier than one running light, and a crew learned within a season to judge a fair-weather passage by nothing more than how much dubhan she still had aboard. He told him too, without being asked, that he had buried two brothers and a father to that sea in the ordinary course of a fishing life, and that a war which asked him only to carry fuel rather than to fight was, by his own reckoning, the easiest service any kingdom had yet asked of him, whatever else might be said of it. Dùghall thought, hearing it, of the coal engines laid up in the Muileann chrom siding that he had heard tell of from a driver's son in his own company, and of how strange it was that a war fought in the hills should turn, in the end, on fishing boats fitted with tanks. He found he had no answer ready for Griogair, and gave none, and Griogair did not seem to want one.

The town was little changed since the regiment had landed: the fourth still quartered in the old human magistrate's house on the rise above the water, Tional nan Tuathach's protest against that quartering still, so far as Dùghall could learn, sitting wherever the council kept protests it did not mean to answer, and the widow he was billeted on, a Tuathaich woman named Barbara Keir who kept a loom in the room behind her kitchen, still answering him in Dia-thìris when he spoke to her in it and in nothing at all when he tried, of an evening, the few words of the humans' tongue he had picked up from men in his own company, though he had heard her, more than once, speaking that same tongue easily enough to her own neighbours across the yard wall.

## II. Of Barbara's House

Barbara's house stood two streets back from the harbour, a low stone building with the loom-room built on at the back in a later age than the rest of it, by the look of the joists, and Dùghall had been billeted on her since the regiment first came to Ceann mhòr, an arrangement neither of them had asked for and neither, so far as he could tell, much liked, though both had settled by then into the kind of wary household truce that two people keep who share a roof without ever agreeing to share anything else. She fed him at the same table she fed herself, plain fare and not much talk over it, and took the billeting-due the regiment's quartermaster paid her without comment, the way Dùghall supposed she took a good many things that autumn without comment, having no clear way of refusing any of them.

He had tried, early on, to make some small conversation of an evening in what little of the humans' tongue he had picked up, thinking it might ease the two of them into something more than a silent table, and had found each attempt met with the same flat courtesy: a nod, perhaps, or a word in Dia-thìris that answered the sense of what he had asked without troubling to answer it in the tongue he had asked it in, so that he came, after the third or fourth such evening, to let the matter drop rather than go on pressing a door she had made plain enough, in her own quiet way, she did not mean to open to him. He had heard her, once, through the wall between the kitchen and the loom-room, singing some low tune to herself at her shuttle in that same tongue she would not use to him directly, and had stood a moment in the passage listening before he thought better of it and went on to his own room, feeling, without quite being able to say why, that he had come near to overhearing something he had no right to.

## III. Of the File to Baile chrom

In an Dùbhlachd, with the days grown so short that the regiment's patrols went out and came back by lamplight both, Dùghall was given a file of six men and an order to go north along the coast road as far as Baile chrom, a bent little town on the far headland that the regiment's own maps marked only as the seat of a shire and the site of one of the five lighthouses, and that no patrol of the fourth had yet troubled to visit in the two months since the regiment had come to Ceann mhòr. The order named no particular business at Baile chrom beyond the general one every patrol that autumn carried, which was to search whatever ground it covered for arms, for men of the western hills who might have come so far north, and for anything else a report could usefully call *nothing found*, since nothing found was, by then, the commonest single line in every regimental return Dùghall had ever been made to copy fair.

He chose his six men the evening before from among those of his own company least likely to make trouble of a night's search, and found himself, going down the roll in his own head, settling more than once on men from the river towns rather than the coast ones, on no better ground than a private feeling that a river man would carry himself quieter in a stranger's house than a man used to the rough manners of a fishing harbour, a feeling he did not trouble to examine any further than that, since the order asked him only to bring back a report and not an account of his own reasons for choosing one soldier over another. The regiment's quartermaster gave him three days' rations for the file and a lamp apiece, the days by then being short enough that a patrol which meant to search a town properly could not count on daylight to do it in, and told him, handing over the last of the lamps, that Baile chrom lay far enough round the headland that no patrol before his had troubled to go so far, the town having sent in no complaint, raised no trouble, and given the regiment, in four months of war, no reason at all to spend a file's time on it.

The road north ran along the shoulder of the coast the whole way, with the sea on the left hand and, on the right, a country of low stone walls and thin pasture that put Dùghall in mind, more than once, of the ground round Caol bheag before the strait widened into the river proper, though the light here was flatter and greyer than any light he had known at home, coming off a sea that his father, a river man all his life, would have called no proper sea at all but a doorstep to one. They marched two days by way of the headland farms, which the order bade them visit on the road, to cover what the map called four miles straight, the light failing early both days, and slept the one night between in a drover's bothy that had plainly not sheltered a drove in some years, its thatch gone soft with damp and its single hearth cold enough that two of the men spent the night's watch arguing, in low voices Dùghall pretended not to hear, over whose turn it properly was to have thought to bring dry kindling.

They passed, on the second day's march, two farms and a mill whose wheel stood idle for want of water, the burn that turned it run low with the season's dry spell, and at each the file was watched from a doorway by whoever stood in it but never once hailed, the watching itself carried on in a silence Dùghall found he minded more, by the second farm, than any shout would have troubled him. One of his men, a stolid soldier named Cailean who had said little the whole march, remarked at the mill that a Dia-thìreach farm on the same road would have had a child out asking them their business inside a minute, favourable or not, and that a farm which only watched and said nothing was a farm that had already decided, before the file came in sight, exactly how much of itself it meant to show a soldier of the regiments, which Dùghall thought a fair enough observation and did not add to.

He knew, coming up the last rise before the town, that it was the eve of some observance of Eaglais nan Tuathach, having heard two of his own men, both of them river-born like himself and neither much given to piety of any kind, mention in passing that the north coast kept a vigil that night which the low country's own Christian houses did not, a Grey Night, one of them called it, without being able to say much more of it than that his own grandmother, who had come south from somewhere near this coast before Dùghall was born, used to go quiet and short-tempered for the length of one evening every year without ever properly explaining why, and that the family had learned, long before he was old enough to ask, simply to leave her be until morning. Cailean, who had grown up nearer the capital and knew the coast towns only by their trade, said he had heard the priests of Manannan at Ceann mhòr call it a prayer of their own gone astray in the north, kept there for a bird the church itself no longer named the same way the south did, and that the two houses disputed the matter without either, so far as he knew, troubling to settle it; Dùghall said only that he supposed a file ordered to search a town on the one night of the year it kept its silence deliberately had drawn, among the whole regiment's patrols that season, a particularly poor lot, and none of the six men with him disagreed.

## IV. Of the Unlatched Door

Dùghall had come up the coast road that autumn expecting, if he expected anything in particular, the kind of welcome the regiment's other patrols had reported from other Tuathaich towns: shutters put up at the first sound of boots on the road, a dog or two set loose to bark the length of a street, a woman calling a warning from an upper window to whoever in the town most needed the warning carried to them first. He had heard all three from men of his own company who had searched other coast towns that season, and had gone north with some private notion, never spoken aloud even to himself in so many words, that a night search would at least give a man something to push against, some sound or sight that told him the town knew he was there and minded it.

Baile chrom gave him none of that. The file came down off the last rise into the town's one bent street a little after full dark, the road following, as one of his men remarked, no straighter a course than a burn finds down a hillside, and not a single lamp showed in any window the whole length of it. No dog barked, not from the first house nor the last, and the only sound the whole way in was the sea working at the stones below the headland and, nearer at hand, his own men's boots on the road, which began, without any order given, to fall softer of their own accord the further into the town they came, as men will when a silence asks something of them that no order has yet put into words.

He tried the first door himself, a low house set back a little from the street with a byre built on to its gable end, and found it unlatched, the way a door is left in a house that expects no visitor and fears none either. Inside, by what grey light came through the one small window, he made out a man and a woman and three children, the youngest of them no more than five or six by his own guess, sitting round a hearth gone entirely cold, their hands folded in their laps in a stillness that put him more in mind, oddly, of a church he had once been made to sit through as a boy at his mother's insistence than of anything a soldier searching a house for arms had any right to expect. None of them spoke. None of them, so far as he could tell in that light, so much as turned a head toward the door.

He asked them, first in Dia-thìris and then, haltingly, in the little of the humans' tongue he carried, who else was in the house, and whether there were arms kept anywhere on the ground. The man only shook his head once, slowly, the whole weight of the gesture in its slowness rather than its motion, in the particular way, Dùghall thought afterward, that a man shakes his head at a child in church who has asked a question the room itself has already answered by staying quiet, a headshake that asked nothing further and offered nothing further either, and that closed the matter, so far as the man plainly judged it closed, more completely than any word could have.

It was the same at the next house, and the one after that, through the small hours of the night: unlatched doors, cold hearths, families sitting in a stillness Dùghall came to think of, by the fourth or fifth house, not as fear exactly, though he supposed fear was somewhere in it, but as a thing closer to a held breath that the whole town had agreed, without ever agreeing it in his hearing, to hold together until the file had passed through and gone. He found no arms in any house he searched that night, and no man or woman of an age to fight who was not already sitting, hands folded, in that same stillness.

The house nearest the lighthouse road, the last but one on the file's way through the town, held only a single old woman, sitting alone at a hearth as cold as every other, her hands folded the same way and her eyes open and steady on the doorway before Dùghall had so much as raised his hand to knock, as though she had heard the file's boots on the street some houses back and had settled herself, in her own time and by her own choosing, to receive whatever came through the door before it came. She gave her name when he asked it, the first person in the whole town that night who answered him at all beyond a headshake, and gave it plainly, in Dia-thìris, as Margaret Crane, and said nothing further, neither complaint nor welcome, only that same steady look that Dùghall found harder to stand under than any of the silences that had gone before it, a look that seemed to him less to be asking what he wanted than to have already decided, before he had finished asking it himself, what she meant to give him and what she did not.

He asked her, as he had asked at every other house, whether there were arms kept on the ground, and whether any man of the town was elsewhere that night who ought properly to be accounted for; and she answered only that the town kept its vigil that night as it kept it every year, and that she herself kept it in that house as she had kept it, she said, since before the war had a name to be kept from, and that a soldier was welcome to search the house from floor to rafter if the order he carried required it of him, since she had nothing in it he need trouble himself to hide from a searching. It was, of the whole night's houses, the one answer that gave him more words than any other and told him, when he came afterward to turn it over, no more than the rest had told him with none at all. He searched the house as she had bid him, finding nothing, and one of his own men, the same soldier who had walked heel first past the threshold at the house before, set his own lamp down of his own accord in the passage outside her door rather than carry its light in past her, a small courtesy Dùghall had given no order for and did not afterward ask the man to explain.

He learned only much later, from a clerk at Ceann mhòr who had served two seasons on that coast before An ceathramh rèisimeid ever came to it, that the vigil the old woman kept was held, in that one town before any other on the island, by the greater part of its people rather than the lesser, a night of silence kept, the clerk said, for some bird of their church that the south's own house of the same faith no longer named the same way, and that the whole town's custom, on that one night of the year, was to sit each in their own house with hearth and lamp alike unlit and speak no word aloud until the vigil's morning released them from it, a custom no soldier of the regiments coming up that coast in ignorance of the calendar could have known to expect, and no order Dùghall had been given had troubled to warn him of.

## V. Of the Report That Said No More

In the end he wrote the report every patrol that autumn had learned to write, that the town had been found dark and silent throughout, that it had been searched house by house, and that nothing was found: no arms, no men of fighting age unaccounted for, no sign that Baile chrom held or had ever held anything the regiment's order had sent him north to look for. The file's own clerk copied it fair the next morning at the bothy where they slept the second night, a younger man than Dùghall who had joined the fourth straight from a shipwright's yard at Ceann mhòr and had not yet lost, in Dùghall's private judgment, the habit of asking questions an older soldier learned to leave alone; folding the report into the satchel that would carry it back to the regiment's own returns, he asked whether there was more to be said of the night than the three lines it held.

Dùghall told him there was not, which was true in the only sense the order had asked him to make it true, and did not tell him of the man who had shaken his head once, slowly, nor of the very old woman his own soldier had stepped past on his toes, nor of the particular sound the sea had made on the stones below the headland while the file stood a long moment outside the last house before turning back for the road, a sound he found, walking south again the next day with the report already gone ahead of him, he could not afterward call to mind without the whole of that night coming back with it entire, the unlatched doors and the cold hearths and the headshakes, in a way three written lines had done nothing at all to put down or settle.

The file marched south again the next morning, the vigil's silence lifted by then, or so Dùghall judged from a single lamp he saw lit at last in a window as they left the bent street behind them, and he found the walk back to Ceann mhòr passed in a quiet among his own six men greater than any that had marked the march north, none of them offering much conversation and none pressed to, as though the town they had left behind had asked something of the file's own tongues as well as the town's. Cailean broke the silence only once, on the second day, to say that he had searched a good many houses that autumn on a good many coasts and had never yet come away from a search feeling, as he put it, that the house had searched him back, and that he did not care to go north to Baile chrom again if the regiment could find another man to send.

Word came to the regiment, a week after Dùghall's own report went in, that Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg of the hills, the last two of the five towns still holding out, had opened their own roads to the regiments that same week without so much as a shot fired on either side, their pits flooded on Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order the same day the roads opened, and An Clàr Foscailte, when Dùghall came to see a copy of it some weeks later pinned in the guardroom at Ceann mhòr, named no holdout taken prisoner at either town, the same three words, nothing found, standing in the place where a longer account might have stood had there been one to give. He thought, reading it, of Baile chrom's own cold hearths, and found himself wondering, not for the first time that winter, whether a return that named nothing found was a return that had looked in the right place to begin with, or only a return written by a man who had learned, as he himself plainly had, to stop asking a question once the room had already answered it by staying quiet.

He mentioned Àth naomh's opening to Barbara one evening over the plain fare she still set before him without much talk to go with it, thinking she might have some word of her own on it from whatever channel carried news among the Tuathaich households of the coast faster than any regimental return carried it among his own kind, and she told him only, in Dia-thìris, that a pit flooded was a pit flooded whichever order flooded it, and asked nothing further, and offered nothing further, and took up her mending again in a silence he had by then learned not to press. Watching her needle go in and out by the one lamp she allowed herself of an evening, he found himself thinking that the whole coast, Dia-thìreach and Tuathaich both, seemed that winter to have settled on the same three words the regiment's own returns had settled on, each in its own house and its own tongue, and that a war fought mostly in silence on both sides was, whatever else might be said of it, no easier a thing to carry home at night than one fought with any noise at all.

On an Nollaig that year An naoidheamh rèisimeid was raised at the southern Seann Skell, to stand guard over the dubhan works the shipmasters had built there, and Dùghall heard the news of it read out at Ceann mhòr's own guardroom two days after, one more line in a winter that seemed to him, turning the last months over as he lay awake in Barbara's back room with her loom silent behind the wall and the widow herself long asleep, to have been made up of nothing but such lines: a fleet raised here, a regiment there, a town's roads opened without a fight, a report that said no more than three words allowed it to say. He had not slept well since Baile chrom, waking most nights somewhere in the small hours with the sea-sound of that headland in his ears though Ceann mhòr's own harbour lay near enough that he could not always be sure, half waking, which shore the sound in fact came from; and he did not know, lying there with the winter's short daylight still some hours off, what exactly it was about that one bent street that would not let him sleep the way the other towns his file had searched that autumn had let him sleep easily enough, only that it would not, and that no line he could write in any report, then or afterward, was going to tell him why.

He thought, more than once in those wakeful hours, of trying the words for it in the humans' tongue, the few he carried, as though a thing that would not settle in Dia-thìris might yet settle in the other, and found each time that he did not have the words at all, in either tongue, for a stillness that had asked nothing of him and given him, in the asking, nothing to answer with; and he let the matter lie, the way the town itself had taught him, without much hope by then that letting it lie would do any more for him than it had plainly done, over some longer span of years he could not guess at, for Margaret Crane's own steady, waiting look.

# Chapter Thirty-two: Of the Quartered Year

*DE 22*

> **Part Six · Of the Quartered Year, the Column and Blàr Muileann ghlas**
>
> *Chaidh am fadachadh.*
> They got long-warred.
>
> — a saying of the north

## I. Of the Pass at the Harbour Wall

The regiments did not fight that year. Martha Greaves came to know it the way the whole north came to know it: from the plain evidence of a winter passing into a spring and a spring into a summer, with no name added to any list she had not already entered by hand, and by the middle of am Màrt she had stopped waiting for the next battle the way a woman stops listening for a caller who has twice failed to come, without ever quite deciding to stop, only finding one morning that she no longer did it.

What came instead of battle was the quartering, and the quartering asked more of the harbour at Caol mhòr, in its own quiet way, than any single engagement had asked of the hill towns. A patrol boat lay off the harbour mouth through that whole spring, always of the same low grey build though seldom the same hull twice running, and a soldier stood at the head of the harbour steps from first light to last with a book under his arm and a list of names in it that grew longer by the week; and any man or woman of the town who meant to go beyond the harbour road, to a farm inland or a market at Doire ghlas or a burial two parishes off, learned to come to that soldier first and show him the small square of paper Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own office had begun, that spring, to issue against a name and a face and a stated errand, which the townsfolk had taken, within a month of the first of them being handed out, to calling simply the pass, though the paper's own heading gave it a longer name that nobody troubled to read past the first line.

Martha came to the harbour herself on Moot business three times that spring, carrying Tional nan Tuathach's papers down from her own mill at Doire ghlas in the same worn satchel Walter Hale had carried them in before her, and each time she showed her own pass to the same soldier, a stolid young man from one of the southern shires who plainly found the asking as tiresome as she found the answering, and each time he wrote her name in his book beside the hour, though he had by the second visit ceased to trouble her further than that, the way a toll-keeper ceases, after enough passings, to weigh a coin he already knows to be sound.

It was on the third of these visits, in the last week of an Cèitean, that she came down to the wall in time to watch the same soldier's own captain board Joe Ashby's boats.

She knew Joe Ashby, as the whole Moot knew him, for the fitter who had turned the Baile chrom light on Tional nan Tuathach's own coin and now held no guild's paper and answered to none, and she watched now from the head of the steps as two of the captain's men went down into the bilges of a hull she took, by its lines, for one of the half-dozen the town's people called the engine-boats, and came up black to the elbow, and found, so far as she could tell from where she stood, nothing that troubled the captain's own book beyond a line written and the next boat called for. The fitter himself stood at his shed door through the whole of it with a wrench still in his hand, watching in the particular stillness of a man who has done this dance before and knows every step of it, and when the captain came to him at the last and asked, as Martha heard it carried on the wind off the water, whether he held any guild's leave for the engines he fitted, Joe Ashby answered that there was none in that harbour would give him one, in a voice that carried no more heat than a man remarking on the weather.

Martha did not speak to him that day, having business enough of her own with the harbour-master over a Moot petition on the tithe, but she wrote the whole of it into her own private book that evening, the one she kept apart from Cuimhne-coinneimh an Tionail and showed to no council, because it seemed to her a thing worth setting down: that a harbour a year clear of any battle could still be searched, boat by boat, on the strength of an order nobody at the wall had asked to see written out in full, and that the town bore it the way it bore the pass and the soldier at the steps and the patrol hull off the mouth: without gladness, and without much noise, the plain unspectacular labour of a people getting on with a war that had stopped fighting and had not yet stopped asking.
