She heard, some weeks later, from the same harbour-master, that the depot's own men had sent for Joe Ashby again before the summer was out, a fleet hull this time whose engine no guild-trained fitter at Seann Skell could put right, and that he had gone and mended it and taken his coin and asked no more of the matter than the coin required, which struck Martha, hearing it, as neither a betrayal of anything nor a submission to it, only the same plain labour again, carried on wherever the labour was wanted and paid for, war or no war.

The pass, small square paper that it was, reached further into the harbour's ordinary year than Martha had looked for when she first watched it handed out. A carter of the town buried his own father in am Màrt at a parish two roads inland, and stood at the harbour steps the morning of the burial with the whole of his family's mourning black already on him, showing his paper to the same stolid soldier as any market-day errand, because the office that wrote the passes had made no separate provision for a burial and the carter had not thought to ask one of it; and Martha, hearing the tale from the harbour-master over the same tithe business that had first brought her down, found she could not say afterward which struck her the harder, that the office had thought so little of a burial's difference from a market errand, or that the town had by then stopped expecting it to think of any such difference at all.

By the height of summer the soldier at the steps had learned most of the harbour's own faces well enough to wave the plainest of its errands through with no more than a glance at the paper held up, and the town, for its part, had settled into carrying the little square papers the way a fisherman carries a knife, without remarking on it, only reaching for it when the moment asked; and it was this settling, more than any single search or any single asking, that Martha found hardest to set down plainly in her own private book, since a thing borne quietly enough for long enough ceases, in the telling, to look like a thing borne at all.

## II. Of the Names Added at Àth leathan

Tional nan Tuathach kept its register in the same low room behind its own house at Caol mhòr where it had kept it since An Dealachadh, a single long shelf of bound books running back further than any living speaker could put a date to without consulting them, and it fell to Martha, in the second week of an Giblean, to open the current volume to the column headed the dead and the maimed and enter, at last, the names of Àth leathan.

The battle was thirteen months gone by then. An Clàr Foscailte had counted the kingdom's own dead at the field below the town the spring before, thirty-eight by its last tally, and had let the holdouts' dead go uncounted, as An Clàr Foscailte let a great many things go uncounted that Tional nan Tuathach's own register did not; and it had taken Tional nan Tuathach's own clerks the better part of a year, working from what letters and lists the hill towns themselves would send south under the disarming, to put together a fuller reckoning than An Clàr Foscailte had ever meant to give. Peter Hale, who by then carried the rebound minute-books through half Tional nan Tuathach's own business the way his great-grandfather Walter had carried the first of them, brought the western list to her himself on a morning of steady rain, a single folded sheet in a hand she did not know, and told her only that it had come up from Cnoc thais by three hands and a fortnight's delay, and that he had checked it twice against the letters already filed and found no name in it that any other list contradicted.

She read the names aloud to herself before she wrote them, a habit she had kept since her first year at the desk, on the private reasoning that a name spoken once by a living voice was less entirely lost than a name only ever set down in ink; and she found, reading the Àth leathan list through for the first time, that Ruth Calder's own name stood nowhere on it, neither among the dead nor the maimed nor, so far as the list troubled to say, among the living, which told her, as it had told every clerk who had looked for that name in the year since, precisely nothing at all.

The names went in through that whole wet morning, in the same clear hand the register had always been kept in, a column of them running to the foot of one page and the head of the next, and she thought, dipping her pen for perhaps the fortieth time, that a register was a strange kind of mercy: too slow to comfort anyone in the year a death happened, and yet, a year on, still willing to receive it when nothing else on the island any longer was.

It was an Giblean too, in that same fortnight, that she went up to the old chapel above the mill at Doire ghlas on the morning Eaglais nan Tuathach kept its Easter, less from any faith of her own in An Eaglais's rite than from a long habit of standing at the back of whatever house of worship her own town's people kept, to see for herself how a thing was borne rather than take another's word for it. She found the chapel fuller than she had looked for, the whole small congregation of Doire ghlas's own Tuathaich households gathered in, and a single soldier of the regiments standing at the door through the length of the service, not unkindly, only present, the way the soldier at the harbour steps was present, a book under his arm in which he wrote, so far as Martha could see from where she stood, nothing at all, the whole service passing without a word exchanged between the door and the altar. Before the last hymn was sung she left, having seen what she had come to see, which was that the north kept its own feasts that year under watch and kept them anyway, and she carried the sight back to Doire ghlas with her the way she carried most such sights, unspoken to anyone, set down only in the private book Tional nan Tuathach never saw.

She wrote the register's own list closed that same week, ruling the double line the book's own form asked of a finished column and setting the date under it in the same hand she had used for every name above; and she found, ruling it, that she had grown, over the year of no battles, into a kind of clerk she had not set out to become when Tional nan Tuathach first gave her Daniel Frayne's own chair: still the speaker who carried the north's grievances south to a council that mostly did not answer them, and now, besides that, a keeper of a book that answered, in its own slow and unhurried way, what the council never troubled to. How many further columns the same book would ask of her before the war she had not yet learned to call ended was done asking, she could not say, closing the Àth leathan column; only that the book would take them, page after ruled page, whatever the council chose to do about the asking.

## III. Of the Women from Cnoc thais

Ellen Marsh had turned Agnes Pike's old schoolroom over to the families from the west the summer before, and when Cnoc thais fell its people too came down out of the hills with what they could carry, and by the second spring of their sheltering there she had come to know most of the women of that town by name, sitting three and four to a bench in the evenings after the day's small work was done, while she went from bench to bench with her own ink and paper and took down, in the plain hand she had used for eleven books before this one, whatever each woman judged worth the telling.

Peggy Innes, who had kept a byre of six goats above the second shaft before the road was cut, told her, on an evening in an t-Ògmhios, of a farm two ridges back from the town's own ruin where the wife still baked twice what her own household could eat and left the second baking on the sill overnight, and where the loaves were always gone by morning and the sill never once watched to see by whom; and she told it, Ellen noted, in the flat unhurried voice of a woman reporting a fact of the weather, neither boasting of the farm's courage nor fearing to name it, since every woman on that bench already knew, without needing to be told, that a war which had stopped its battles had not stopped its hiding, and that the hills above Cnoc thais still held men who had gone up into them the year the road was cut and had not yet, whatever the disarming at Muileann àrsaidh and Àth leathan had settled for the towns themselves, come down.

Ellen wrote the farm's telling into her own twelfth book without a name attached to it, on the same private rule she had kept through all eleven books before, that a fact could be kept and a name spared where the naming would cost the teller more than the telling was worth; and she was still turning that rule over in her own mind three weeks later when word came up from the hill country, carried by a carter's boy who had it from a cousin still at Cnoc thais, that a patrol of the regiments had found a farm much like the one Peggy had named, though not that one, close enough to it that the whole schoolroom bench went quiet at the telling, and had put its thatch to the torch on the strength of a barn found half full of grain no ration book of the district could account for.

No one was killed at that burning, the boy's own telling said, the family having been turned out of the house before the thatch was fired and left standing in their own yard to watch it go; but the byre went with the house, and the season's hay with the byre, and Ellen set the whole of it down in her twelfth book that same week in the same flat voice the women themselves used for such tellings, because she had learned, over eleven books and the better part of a life spent taking down what the north would tell her, that the flat voice was very often the only one a fact of that kind could safely be carried in.

Marion Kenny, who sat the bench nearest the door most evenings and said little until the room had thinned to two or three, told her own account of the same burning some weeks after the carter's boy had first carried it down, having had it herself from a sister still living within sight of the ruin, and her telling added only one thing the boy's had left out: that the family put out into their own yard that morning had been given time, before the thatch was fired, to carry out what they could of the house's own goods, a chest and a loom and the year's stored meal, by the very patrol that had come to burn it, and that no one on the bench that evening could rightly say whether this was mercy in the men who did the burning or only the ordinary carefulness of soldiers who had learned, over a long year of finding nothing, to make what small amends they could within an order they had not written themselves. Ellen set that down too, unresolved as it stood, since she had come to think, closing in on her twelfth book what her first had taught her at the very start of the gathering, that a full account left its own contradictions standing rather than smooth them away for the sake of a tidier page.

She finished the twelfth book in the first week of an Dàmhair, closing it on an evening when the schoolroom benches held fewer of the west's own women than they had a year before, some gone home already to whatever their own hill towns had left standing, some gone nowhere anyone at Doire ghlas could say; and she sat a long while with the finished book closed on her own table before she wrote, on its last blank leaf, a single line that owed nothing to any woman's telling but her own: that the war her first eleven books had never troubled themselves to speak of had, by the time this twelfth one closed, written its own record into the north as plainly as An Dealachadh had, and that she did not yet know, closing it, which of her twelve books a reader two generations off would find the harder to believe.

## IV. Of the Hymn Through the Wall

An ceathramh rèisimeid kept its patrols on the Ceann mhòr road through the whole of that year, in a rhythm Dùghall mac Iain had come, by the spring, to know almost without troubling to think of it: a file out at first light, a file in at dusk, the same stretches of coast and hedgerow walked and walked again until the road seemed, some evenings, to walk the file rather than the other way about. No arms were found on any of those patrols after the winter's search of Baile chrom, and no man of fighting age was taken up who could not give some account of himself that the file's own corporal, whoever he was that week, judged worth passing without further trouble; and the regiment's returns, which Dùghall still copied fair as often as any other corporal of his own company, settled by the spring into the same three words that had closed every report of the autumn before, so that a man reading a twelvemonth of them end to end, as Dùghall once did on a wet afternoon with nothing else to fill it, would have found a year's patrolling summed up in little more than a list of dates against which nothing had been found.

The farms along that road told their own year plainer than any return did. A byre Dùghall's file had passed shuttered in the winter stood open by the summer with a boy of ten or eleven driving the same three cows out to the same field each morning, and the boy came, by the second season of the same patrol going by, to lift a hand to the file as it passed, not quite a greeting and not quite its refusal, a small loosening Dùghall noticed and did not remark on to the men behind him, judging that a thing noticed aloud too soon had a way of curdling before it could properly set. Other farms kept the same watching silence they had kept the year before, the door held to and the field worked in a stillness that asked the file nothing and gave it nothing, and Dùghall had stopped, by the spring, expecting either kind of farm to become the other, having learned that a household's own manner toward a patrol was no more likely to change for a year's quiet than a man's manner toward the sea was likely to change for a calm summer, both being founded on a memory no summer could touch.

He was still billeted on Barbara, the arrangement having become, over the better part of a year, less a wariness endured than a plain fact of his own days, the two of them keeping the same table and the same thin courtesy across it without either, so far as he could tell, wanting it otherwise or expecting it to become anything more. She fed him, and took the billeting-due without comment, and answered him in Dia-thìris when he spoke to her in it and in nothing at all when he tried, of an evening, the little of the humans' tongue he still carried, though he had long since stopped minding that particular silence the way he had minded it the first autumn, having come to understand it, or think he understood it, as a boundary she kept for reasons that were hers to keep and none of his to press.

It was on an evening of an t-Sultain, with the regiment's patrols grown so much a matter of habit by then that even the men who walked them had stopped remarking on the empty houses they no longer troubled to search, that Dùghall heard, through the wall between his own room and the loom-room, a hymn he did not know sung low and unhurried in the humans' tongue, a different air from the shuttle-song he had overheard the autumn before and heavier in its cadence, the kind of tune a house keeps for its own church rather than its own work. He stood a while in the passage as he had stood the first time, and went on to his room as he had gone on then, telling himself it was no more his to overhear a second time than it had been the first.

The same air came again a fortnight later, and again after that, always of an evening, until by the second week of an Dàmhair he found he could carry the whole of its shape in his own head without meaning to have learned it, the rise and fall of it if not the words, the way a man comes to know the toll of a bell he has lived long enough beside without ever climbing the tower to see it rung. He did not ask Barbara what the hymn was called, judging, by then, that the asking would cost more of the household's thin peace than the answer was worth; but he found himself, walking the Ceann mhòr road of a morning with his own file strung out behind him, humming a bar or two of it under his breath before he caught himself at it, and stopping, each time, with the particular unease of a man who has found a stranger's coin in his own pocket and cannot say how it came there.

He mentioned it, once, to Cailean, who had marched with him to Baile chrom the winter before and had said little of that night since; and Cailean, hearing two bars of it hummed low over a cold supper, said only that his own grandmother had kept a tune very like it, and that he had never asked her the words of it either, and that a man billeted long enough on a house not his own generally came away, whether he meant to or not, carrying some small piece of it home in him that no order and no regiment could ever quite account for in its returns.

## V. Of the Word That Came to Caol mhòr

Through that whole quartered year, from the harbour at Caol mhòr to the schoolroom at Doire ghlas to the coast road above Ceann mhòr, ran a single rumour that none of them, telling it to one another across the width of the island in letters and carters' talk and a soldier's idle word over a cold supper, could ever quite run to ground: that something was gathering in the western hills that the disarming had not reached, and had not been meant to reach, and that no report from any regiment's own patrol, searching the same empty farms and the same silent doorways it had searched for a year without once finding arms or men to answer for them, had troubled to explain.

Martha heard a version of it from a letter out of Cnoc thais that reached Tional nan Tuathach's own house in the last week of an t-Sultain, a plain note from a clerk of Comhairle nam Mèinnean stationed there that said only that the hill paths above the town carried more foot-traffic by night than any patrol's own daylight counting could make sense of, and that the clerk did not know what to make of it and set it down all the same, since a fact unexplained was, in his own judgment, still worth Comhairle nam Mèinnean's having. Ellen heard it in gentler form from the last of the Cnoc thais women still on her own schoolroom benches, a shrug more than a telling, that the hills had always kept more than any regiment's list could count and would go on keeping it whatever the disarming said. Dùghall heard it from Cailean, who had it from a corn-factor at Ceann mhòr who had it, in turn, from nobody he could rightly name, that the western hills were said to be emptying of something, though of what, and toward where, the corn-factor himself could not say and did not, by Cailean's own account, seem greatly troubled not to know.

None of the three of them, in all that quartered year, ever heard the rumour told twice the same way, and none of them, telling it on in turn, thought to connect it with any other thing they themselves had seen: not with the farm above Cnoc thais that fed a night's coming and going the disarming had never quite ended, not with the hymn Dùghall had learned without meaning to through Barbara's own wall, not with the pass a soldier at the Caol mhòr steps still asked of every fisherman and carter who wanted the harbour road. It was simply the one thing that whole year that would not settle into any report's three closing words, the one line no regimental clerk and no Moot's register and no schoolroom's twelfth book could make read as nothing found, because nothing, in this one matter alone, had ever been offered for the finding.

Word came to Caol mhòr in the first days of an t-Samhain, brought up the harbour road by a Board carrier who had ridden two days without pausing to change his own horse twice over, that a company of some hundreds, out of no town the carrier's own dispatch troubled to name, had come down out of the western hills and turned south-east across the middle of the island, keeping to no road the regiments had thought to watch, and bound for no destination the dispatch would guess at. Martha read the carrier's note at her own desk in Tional nan Tuathach's low room, with the register's current volume still open on the shelf beside her at the page she had closed that spring over the names of Àth leathan, and found, reading it, that the rumour the whole quartered year had carried without ever once running to ground had, in the space of one carrier's ride, stopped being a rumour and become, instead, the first plain fact any report that autumn had troubled to set down.

She did not yet know, folding the note away to lay before the room in the morning, how long the road the company had chosen would run, nor where it would end, nor what name, if any, An Clàr Foscailte would ever trouble to give the man the western hills' own tellings were already, by every account reaching her desk, calling their own. She knew only, sealing the note into her satchel beside the papers that had carried Tional nan Tuathach's whole quartered year, that the year of nothing found was over, and that whatever came after it would not, this time, close on three words and a clean page.

# Chapter Thirty-three: Of the Column's Road

*DE 22*

Nobody at Cathair dhearg saw it start. That is the first true thing to say of it, and the last, since everything between is town report and hill telling, and the two do not always agree even on the weather. What An Clàr Foscailte gives is this: that in the last week of an Dàmhair a company of some four hundred came down out of the western hills where the holdouts had sat quartered a year and more under the regiments' watch, and went south-east across the middle of the island by roads that had carried nothing heavier than a drover's cart in living memory, and that six weeks later it stood on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from the capital, with two regiments come down Rathad na Fèille to meet it. Why it went is not in An Clàr Foscailte, nor in any town's report, nor, if Sceulachdan nan Tuathach are to be believed on this one point, in the column's own knowledge past the man who led it, and he left no account behind him that anyone has found. The tellings give his name as Owen Barrow. An Clàr Foscailte gives no name at all, only "a column of the western hills," as though the hand that wrote it had decided, or been told, that a name was one thing too many to set down.

## I. Of the Ford at Àth bheag

Àth bheag stands where the old drove road crosses the upper water on its way down from the western hills to the plain, a burg of not much above two hundred souls with a mill, a smithy and a bridge too narrow for two carts abreast, and it had seen nothing of the war since the second summer's musters except the soldiers who came through now and again on the road to the Seann Skell garrison and never stayed the night. Its report to Comhairle nam Mèinnean, dated the thirtieth of an Dàmhair and copied afterward into an Leabharlann's file on the column, says that a company of armed men, not fewer than three hundred and by the reckoning of two who counted them from the mill loft nearer four, crossed the ford below the bridge in the grey of a Tuesday morning, in good order and without haste, and that they did not use the bridge, which would have brought them through the heart of the town, but forded the water a field's length below it, wet to the knee, and went on south without stopping.

The maor of Àth bheag, a man named Cailean mac Griogair who had held the office nine years and buried, in that time, two wives and one son to the winters the western hills give a small town on short rations, wrote his report the same evening by his own hand, and it is the fullest of the whole road because he wrote it while the thing was still new to him and had not yet learned, as later towns learned, how little a report of this kind was wanted to say. He had been woken before light by the smith's boy hammering at his door, and had come down to the bank himself in his nightshirt and a borrowed coat, and stood a good while at the field's edge watching the last of the column cross before he judged there was anything in it worth the walk back up to his own desk to set down. He set down the hour, the number as near as two men's counting could give it, the road they took and the road they did not, the state of the water (in spate from three days' rain, and cold enough that he wondered, watching them wade it, that no man of them cried out), and one thing more that Comhairle nam Mèinnean's copyist struck through in the file copy and that survives only because Cailean kept his own draft: that the miller's wife, watching from the loft with the two who counted, said afterward that she had seen no banner among them and no drum, only a man walking at the head of the column with nothing about him to mark him out from the rest except that the others left him the whole width of the road to himself, and that this, more than the guns some of them carried, was what had made her certain the company kept some errand of its own, and no design on the mill's stores.

Cailean added, in his own draft and nowhere else, that he had thought of going down to the ford himself and asking the man at the head of it plainly where he was bound, and had not done it, and could not afterward say why not, except that the width of road the column had left the man made him think a question put across it would not be answered, and a maor of Àth bheag who had spent nine years keeping the peace between drovers and millers without once having to draw a sword saw no profit in learning that for certain at a river crossing before breakfast.

Cailean's report went by carrier the next morning to Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerk at the western Seann Skell, and from there, in the slower way such things travel once they are no longer news to the man carrying them, to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, where Sìleas nic Rath entered it in the file she had begun to keep of the column's road the week the first report of it reached her desk. She had asked, by then, for every town's account of it that could be got, and had been given leave to keep them, which was more than she had been given for the war four years before; the difference, she wrote once in a private note that never went into any file, was that a column marching in the open through country at peace was a thing a chronicler might be let see, where a war fought in the hills was not, and she did not know, setting that down, whether it comforted her or not.

Àth bheag's report ends with a line that Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own men, reading it afterward, took for a maor's caution and that Sìleas took, copying it in, for a plainer thing: that the column had asked nothing of the town, taken nothing from it, and left nothing behind but the wet marks of its crossing on the near bank, which the next rain washed out within the week.

## II. Of the Bread at Muileann mhin

A few days on, and a few miles by the road the column seemed to be keeping, though no report survives to say exactly where it slept those nights, Muileann mhin had its own turn: not the lamp-makers' town of that name east of the capital, but the small mill town of the same name under the western hills, a place of some two hundred souls. Its report to Comhairle nam Mèinnean, signed by its miller rather than its maor, who was from home that week at a wedding in Cathair mhòr, has a different temper from Àth bheag's, less the note of a man watching a company pass and more the note of a man doing sums.

Two men came into the town on the morning of the second of an t-Samhain, the report says, ahead of the column by some hours, and went to the baker nearest the bridge, a widow named Mòrag nic Fhearghais who had kept the ovens since her husband's death. The two men asked for bread, as much as the ovens held and as much again as could be baked fresh by noon, and asked the price, and paid it in full in the coin of the realm, counted out on the counter in front of three other customers who had come in for their own morning loaves and stood back, the report says, "not from fear so much as from a wish to see the thing done properly, as men will stand back from a fair bargain struck in the street." Mòrag, by the miller's account, asked the older of the two whether he meant to feed a garrison or a wedding, meaning it, she told him afterward, half as a joke to ease her own daughters' nerves at the size of the order, and he answered only that he meant to feed men who had walked a long way and would walk further, which was no answer at all and satisfied her, she said, better than one would have.

Mòrag baked through the morning with two of her own daughters to help her, and the column, when it came through a little after noon, sent no more than a dozen men into the town to carry the loaves away, the rest passing on the road below without turning aside, and the dozen who came for the bread paid again, a small sum over the first price, which Mòrag's own account, kept separately from the miller's and sent to Comhairle nam Mèinnean a week later at his asking, gives to the last farthing.

The miller's report does not say what the two men looked like, beyond that one was young and the other not, nor whether either was the man the tellings name; it says only that they spoke the humans' tongue between themselves and Dia-thìris to the widow, civilly, and that neither gave a name when Mòrag, by her own account, asked for one to set against the sale in her book. She wrote instead, where a name should have stood, "bread, to the western company, paid in full," and that is the line Comhairle nam Mèinnean's file preserves, copied twice more before it reached an Leabharlann, the wording unchanged each time, as though no clerk who handled it had found anything in it worth altering.

The miller's own closing line, which Sìleas kept without comment in her file, notes that the town's takings for that week showed no loss against the ordinary, the bread having been paid for at a fair price and the company having troubled nobody's stock beyond it, and that he set this down not to speak for the column, which was no business of his, but so that Comhairle nam Mèinnean should not suppose, from the mere fact of an armed company passing through a working town, that the town had suffered by it. Whether Comhairle nam Mèinnean read that line as the warden meant it, or otherwise, the file does not say; but a second hand, in a different ink, has added below the miller's signature a single further note, unsigned, that the loaves were good loaves and the widow well paid for them, which is either a clerk's private aside or, as Sìleas herself once wondered, a line the miller thought better to add without his own name against it.

## III. Of the Barn on the Capital's Edge

The country between Muileann mhin and the capital's own fields is the quietest stretch of the whole road, farms and hedgerows and the low rise of ground that a man from the hills would hardly call a hill at all, and it gave, in the fortnight the column crossed it, only one report of any substance, from a farmer named Aonghas mac Cuinn whose steading lay a mile off the road proper, close enough that a company passing would have seen the barn's roof plain against the last light, and far enough that Aonghas, by his own account, thought at first they would go by without troubling him.

They did not. A party of perhaps thirty came to his gate an hour after dark on a night of driving rain, in the second week of an t-Samhain, and asked, through the same young man who had asked at Muileann mhin, or one enough like him that the two reports, set side by side in an Leabharlann's file, read as though they might be the same man, whether the barn stood empty and whether they might have the use of it for one night against the weather. Aonghas, who had a wife and four children under his own roof and no love, he wrote afterward, for having armed strangers so near either, stood in his own doorway with a lamp held up between himself and the gate long enough to count the shapes waiting beyond it, and told them the barn was theirs for the night and nothing more, and asked no payment, thinking a company of that size would take what it wanted whether he named a price or not. His wife, listening from the passage behind him, asked once he had barred the door again whether he had done right, and he told her, by his own account, that he did not know, only that thirty armed men asking leave at a gate were thirty armed men who had not simply taken it, and that this seemed to him, that night, worth more than an answer to whether he had done right.

In the morning he found, weighted under a stone on the barn's threshing floor where the party had slept, a sum in coin that by his own reckoning came to more than a fair week's rent of the barn in any ordinary season, and a note, in a clear hand and in Dia-thìris, that read only: *For the barn, and thanks. We have asked nothing else and will leave nothing else asked of you.* The barn itself they had left swept cleaner, his wife said, than his own boy generally left it of a Saturday, the straw restacked and the door barred from the inside as they had found it, so that but for the coin and the note a stranger coming after might have thought no one had lain there at all.

Aonghas kept the note. It went, eventually, by way of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's local clerk, into an Leabharlann's file with the rest, and Sìleas, reading it the first time, found it the strangest paper the whole road had given her, stranger than the widow's uncompleted line at Muileann mhin, because it was the only piece of writing anywhere in the file that could be set down, without much doubt, to a hand inside the column, and it said, in the end, almost nothing: no reason, no name, no word of where the company was bound or why, only the plain courtesy of a debt paid and a boundary kept. She copied it into her file exactly as it stood, spelling and all, and noted beside it only the date and the finder's name, and did not, in all the years she kept the office after, ever find another line to set beside it.

The column crossed the last of the open country in the third week of an t-Samhain, keeping, so far as the scattered reports of small farms and a single toll-keeper at the edge of the fair country can be made to agree, a road that ran wide of every town of any size, as though whoever led it had studied the ground beforehand and meant to be seen only where seeing could not be helped. No report from that stretch tells of trouble, of begging, of theft, or of any word exchanged beyond what the day's business required; the column asked lodging where lodging was offered, paid what was asked and sometimes more, and went on, and the towns it passed, having nothing worse to report than a night's noise and a morning's quiet going, mostly did not trouble to report it at all until Comhairle nam Mèinnean, hearing by then from Àth bheag and Muileann mhin both, sent word down the whole line of the western road asking every maor to say what he had seen.

## IV. Of the Booths Taken Down

Ùna nic Ailein had kept the books of Cùirt na Fèille at Muileann òg for the better part of thirty years by the time the first word of the column reached the toll-house, and in all that time, through Riaghailt na Cairte and the granary votes and the long quiet stretch of the war years when nothing crossed Rathad na Fèille but the ordinary carts, she had never once been asked to close the year's books before the last market of an Dùbhlachd, and she found, when the asking came, that she did not much like being the one to do it.

It came from A' chiad rèisimeid's quartermaster, a brisk youngish man she had dealt with twice before over billeting matters and found, both times, civil enough for a soldier, who came up the toll-house stair on the seventh of an Dùbhlachd with an order under the council's own seal requiring the fair-ground at Muileann òg, its booths, its standings and its cleared ground, for the use of the first and third regiments from that day until further notice. Ùna read the order twice, the second time aloud, half to herself and half, she supposed afterward, to give the quartermaster the chance to say it was some mistake, and he did not take it, only stood at the foot of her desk with his cap under his arm and said that he was sorry for the short notice and that the order was not his to argue with any more than it was hers.

"Two regiments," she said. "On my fair-ground."

"On the whole ground between here and Muileann ghlas, if it comes to that," he said, "though I'll own the fair-ground's the flattest and driest piece of it, which is why it's yours the order names first." He had the grace, she thought, to look at his own boots saying it, as though the flatness and dryness of another town's market ground were not a compliment he much enjoyed paying.

"The market's set for the ninth," she said. "There's stalls booked from three towns."

"Then they'll book them somewhere else this year," he said, not unkindly, "or not at all. I've a thousand men and more coming down this road inside the week, and nowhere else in twenty miles flat enough to camp them and near enough water."

She went down herself on the ninth, the day the market should have stood, to see the booths taken down, because it was, she told the justice when he asked why she had not sent a clerk, the kind of thing the court's own book ought to have set down by someone who had seen it rather than been told of it, and she stood at the fair-ground's edge in a wind that had turned from the west that morning and watched men she had known for years, stall-holders and their sons, working under the quartermaster's own soldiers to strike the timber frames that had stood on that ground, some of them, since before her own time at the desk. Fionnlagh Dubh, who had sold ironmongery from the same standing for thirty years and whose father had sold it there before him, took his own frame down with more care than the soldiers gave theirs, numbering each pole with chalk before he stacked it, and told Ùna, passing her with an armful of them, that he supposed he would want the numbers again come spring, though neither of them, standing there, much believed it. Behind him the eel-woman was packing her tub onto a handcart with two of the soldiers lifting the heavier end for her, not unkindly, and further off a boy who sold ribbons and thread from a tray sat on an upturned crate with the tray still on his knees, watching the frames come down around him as though he had not yet decided whether there was any longer a market for a boy to sell ribbons in.

By dusk the ground stood cleared from the toll-house arch to the river bend, a long bare stretch of trampled grass and mud where a fair had stood every market day for longer than the court's own books went back, and the first companies of An treas rèisimeid came onto it before full dark, pitching their tents in rows where the ironmonger's stall and the eel-woman's tub and the cheese-sellers' shaded row had stood a day before, their fires lit against a cold that Ùna, watching from the toll-house window, thought looked, in the last of the light, very much like any market night the town had ever known, and nothing at all like one.

A' chiad rèisimeid came down the same evening, in better order and, Ùna thought, watching them from the same window, in greater numbers than she had believed a thousand men could be, filling the fair-ground and the water-meadow beyond it and spilling into the lanes above the mill, so that for those nights Muileann òg held more soldiers under canvas than it had held its own people the whole year round. The town's two inns filled with officers and the mill's own loft was given over to stores; a picket stood at the toll-house arch by the second night, civilly enough, and asked her name each morning going up to her own desk as though she had not kept that desk longer than the sentry had been alive, and she gave it each morning without complaint, judging it no great cost against the larger thing the whole camp was asking of the town without asking at all.

She kept Cùirt na Fèille open through it, as the justice bade her, hearing what small business came, a dispute over a strayed cow, a complaint against a soldier who had taken firewood without asking that the regiment's own officer settled before she need write a word of it down, and she watched, from her desk under the window, the road that ran south from the fair-ground toward Muileann ghlas fill and empty and fill again with companies going down to the fields there, where word had it that the column lay, camped in the open on the far side of the river from the town of that name, a day's walk from the capital's own gate and no farther, and showing, by every account that reached the toll-house, no sign of moving on.

She did not go to see it. Enough, she told the justice, watching the fair-ground go, and it was true enough as far as it went, though the truer reason, which she kept to herself, was that she did not want the picture in her own head to stand beside the fair-ground's own emptiness when she came to write the year's closing entry; and by the second week of an Dùbhlachd she knew there would be a closing entry to write, and that it would not read like any before it.

She wrote it on the last evening of the month the market should have run, sitting at the same desk where she had written the last cartload's sale nineteen years before, in the same clear hand, though slower now and with more pauses than that earlier page had needed. She set down the year's takings to the date the order came, which were ordinary enough, and the names of the three towns that had booked stalls and not had them, and the order, copied whole under the council's seal, and then she found, dipping her pen for the line that every year's book before this one had carried, the plain sum of the market's takings struck and totalled and the court's seal set under it, that she did not know what figure to write, because there had been no market, and a book cannot close on a sum that was never taken.

The pen stayed dry above the page some while. Outside the window the fair-ground's fires burned in their long soldiers' rows where the stalls had stood, and somewhere beyond them, past the river and the low dark shoulder of the land, other fires burned on the fields by Muileann ghlas that she had not gone to see and did not mean to, and the road between the two, Rathad na Fèille her own court's charter took its very name from, lay empty in the last of the light, waiting, though for what, and for how long, and with what end, was no more hers to know, sitting at her own desk with her own dry pen, than it was the miller's wife of Àth bheag's to have known, six weeks and near sixty miles before, watching a column with no banner and no drum go down into the water and up the far bank and on, south, without once turning to look back at the town it left behind it.

In the end she wrote nothing under the year's takings. She ruled the line the court's own form required, and left the space above it blank, and set the year's date under it, and closed the book, and it stands so in the court's own press at Muileann òg to this day: of all the years she has kept the desk, the only one with no closing entry.

# Chapter Thirty-four: Of Blàr Muileann ghlas

*DE 22*

> First and third regiments on the field. The enemy's dead not counted.
>
> — An Clàr Foscailte, 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22

## I. Of the Field

The tenth of an Dùbhlachd came up grey and stayed grey, the kind of short northern day that seems to give its light back almost as soon as it has lent it, and by the middle of the morning below Muileann ghlas the frost had not lifted from the furrows so much as thinned, so that the ground under the first and third regiments' boots was neither hard nor soft but something between the two that took a print and held it. The mill town, three hundred souls and a green-slated roof or two among the thatch, stood a little apart from its own fields that day, its doors shut, its one bell not rung, as if the place had drawn itself in the way a snail draws in its horn at a footstep. Its river, the small one that turned the mill and gave the town half its name, ran high and brown with the autumn's rain, and made, all that morning and into the early afternoon, the only steady sound on the field besides the guns.

An Clàr Foscailte, which is what this book must mostly follow here, since the rest is kept from it by an Leabharlann's own hand, gives the day in the manner it gives every day of that war: plainly, and without the years the north would spend telling it over. A' chiad rèisimeid held the ground nearest the river, the third the rising ground to its right, where the old byre stood; the column, which the record calls, when it calls it anything, Muinntir gun Siorrachd, held the line of a low bank and a stand of thorn along the field's northern edge, dug in as well as a fortnight's marching and two nights' frost had let them dig. They had come from the western hills the best part of two months before, some four hundred strong at their setting out, fewer by the day they reached the fields at Muileann ghlas, for the road south-east through the middle of the island had cost them men to sickness and to loss of heart in about equal measure, and had cost them, too, whatever hope any of them had carried that the towns they passed would rise and join them. Muileann mhin had sold them bread. Àth bheag had reported them, honestly and at length, to the first clerk of Comhairle nam Mèinnean its maor could find. No town on the whole of that road had done more than watch them go by and write down what it saw.

The regiments opened the day at first light with the guns, four pieces An treas rèisimeid had brought down from the capital on Slighe a' Ghuail and hauled the last two miles by hand through ground too soft for the horses, and An Clàr Foscailte gives their number and not their effect, which is the record's way with most things that would otherwise need a harder word than it cares to spend. What is told in the north, from those who stood near enough to that field to have some right to speak of it, is that the guns found the thorn stand within the first half-hour and did not need to find it twice; that the column's line broke there first, for a stand of thorn on a low bank is no cover at all against a gun that has found its range, whatever the will of the men behind it, and that what held after that held along the bank, in the frozen mud, hand to hand and at close range, through most of the short forenoon. An Clàr Foscailte says only that the field was carried by early afternoon, which is a sentence long enough to hold a great deal of a morning and says nothing of what it holds.

Three-and-twenty of the kingdom's dead were named that week in the register the regiments keep for their own, a list drawn up by a corporal of An treas rèisimeid at a trestle table in the mill itself, with the miller's own ledger turned backward and his account of grain crossed through to make room for it, since no other paper could be found in the town that morning and the corporal, a careful man by the look of his list, would not wait for one to be sent for. Twenty-three names, each with a town beside it and, where it was known, an age, written in a hand that grew smaller as the page filled and the light went, so that the last few names on it are barely legible at all, as if the man writing them had begun, by the end, to write mostly by feel. The column's dead An Clàr Foscailte does not count. Some tried to count them: the regiments' own burial parties, working through what light the short day still had and then by lantern into the evening, are known from a single surviving requisition to have asked the quartermaster for more lime than twenty-three graves would need, a good deal more, and that requisition, filed and answered and forgotten in the ordinary way of requisitions, is the nearest thing An Clàr Foscailte holds to a number for the column's own loss. No number stands in its place. Only the shape one leaves, once it has been taken out of a record and something quieter put where it stood.

The mill changed hands twice before noon, by the surgeon's later account, once when the column drove out a picket A' chiad rèisimeid had set in it before dawn and once when A' chiad rèisimeid took it back with the guns already turned on the byre beyond, and each time the miller's wife, who would not leave her own kitchen for either army, is remembered by the surgeon to have gone on quietly moving her pots and her flour sacks out of whatever corner the fighting had lately occupied and into whatever corner it had lately left, as if the day were no more than an unusually thorough cleaning forced on her by two sets of careless lodgers. She fed the surgeon a bowl of broth some time in the afternoon, without being asked and without, so far as he could tell, distinguishing in her own mind between the man who ate it and the uniform he wore, and this too he has set down since, among the handful of things about that day he found himself still able to speak of plainly.

The colonel of A' chiad rèisimeid, who is not named twice in An Clàr Foscailte and whose own report of the day survives only in the quartermaster's copy of it, wrote that the column had held the bank longer than any force he had faced in two years of the war, and set this down for one reason only, that a commander who does not tell his own council the truth of what he found on a field does that council no service at all; praise the record was never made to give, and he gave none. It is one of perhaps three sentences in the whole open record of the war that reads as though a man wrote it for himself and not for the file it was put into, and this book has chosen, of the little that record allows it, to keep this one.

This was not the first battle fought below Muileann ghlas. An old man of the town, brought before the regiments' officers that evening to answer for a store of grain they wanted and he was reluctant to give up, told them, when he had given it up and was let go, that his grandmother's grandmother had shown him, as a boy, the low place in the same field where men of Cogadh nam Bràithrean had fought two centuries and more before, and that the town still called it, in the old way, the taken ground, for a captain of that older war had been taken alive there rather than let escape across the river, which ran the same course then as now. The officer who heard this wrote it down, more from a wish to have something in his own notebook besides the day's dead than from any use he could see in it, and it is by that accident, and no better reason, that the two battles of Muileann ghlas are set beside each other in this book at all. The island's fields do not choose to be fought over twice by design. They are simply not so many, in the end, as its history is long.

By the day's short dusk the guns had stopped, and what remained of the fighting had gone to ground in the mill and the two barns nearest it, where perhaps sixty of the column held out past dark rather than come out into a field the regiments now commanded on every side. A' chiad rèisimeid's colonel, whose name An Clàr Foscailte gives once and not again, sent in word before full dark that any man who came out unarmed would be marched, not shot, to the capital's gaol, and had the word carried by a Tuathach prisoner already taken, under a white cloth tied to a byre-fork, since no one else on the field that evening could be found who both peoples would trust to carry it and bring back an honest answer. The sixty came out a little after full dark, in ones and twos at first and then in a body, into a cold that by then had begun to bite in earnest, and were counted, and searched, and marched under guard to the mill floor for the night, where the regiments' own surgeon, a Dia-thìreach of Cathair dhearg two years out of his training and new enough to the work that his hands, by his own account written since, would not stop shaking until well past midnight, did what could be done for wounded of both sides by the light of two lanterns and a banked fire, and made no distinction between them that An Clàr Foscailte, at least, thought worth setting down.

By the day's end, when the ground had gone from grey to black and the two lanterns in the mill were the only light for a mile in any direction, the surgeon's tally, kept on the back of the same requisition that had asked for the lime, stood at three-and-twenty of the regiments buried or dying and near ninety of the column's wounded brought in, some by their own side before the field was carried and some, after, by the regiments' own burial parties, who are recorded, in a note the surgeon thought worth adding though no one had asked him to, as having carried in the column's hurt with no more roughness than they used on their own, which he set down, he wrote, because he had gone into that day expecting otherwise and had been glad, once, to be wrong.

## II. Of the Tellings

This much the north keeps of that day and gives it, as it gives most of its history, from mouth to hearth to grandchild, a telling handed on at the turn of the year when the fire is banked and the youngest in the house has been let stay up past its hour for once, the teller beginning, as often as not, with some such plain word as *my sister stood on that ground*, which is a kind of proof An Clàr Foscailte cannot offer and does not try to.

What is told in the north of that day begins, in nearly every version this book has been able to gather, with the frost before it begins with the guns, for it was the cold, the tellers say, that the column felt first and longest, two nights of it in the open with fires kept low or not kept at all for fear of what a fire on that flat ground would show the regiments below. A woman of Cnoc thais, who was a girl of sixteen on that column and carried a message twice between the bank and the byre before the guns opened, has told it more than once since to her own people, and it has been taken down, in the north's own way, by more than one hand since: that the last night before the battle the column sang, low and by turns, company after company. It may have served them for courage, she allows, though that was never her own reason for it: a body that is singing cannot easily be heard to be afraid, she says, and there were children on that field, brought by mothers and fathers who had nowhere else on the whole island to leave them, and the singing was as much for the children's sake as for the men's.

The tellings give the column's leader a name An Clàr Foscailte never once sets down: Owen Barrow, a man of the west hills who is said, in the tellings, to have walked the whole line himself in the last hour before first light, speaking to every company by name and by name to a good number of the men and women in each of them, and to have said, to more than one teller's memory, much the same short thing each time, that the hills were behind them now and could not be walked back to before the guns found them on open ground either way, and that a man who has come this far owes it to himself to be found, if he is to be found at all, facing the way he came and not the other. Whether he said any such thing, or said it in those words, this book cannot know and does not pretend to; what it can say is that the saying is told the same way in three towns that have, so far as the record shows, had no occasion to agree it between them, which is as much as the north's own memory usually offers by way of proof, and more than it often troubles to give.

Of the fighting the tellings are, in their way, both more and less than An Clàr Foscailte. They are less because no teller who was in the thorn stand when the guns found it has left more than a handful of words about it at all; the girl of Cnoc thais, asked directly, by her own mother among others, what it had been like, answered only that it had been loud, and then quiet, and that she did not care to say more; and that this is the whole of her answer every time she has been asked it since is a kind of telling in its own right, though not one that fits easily into a book. They are more because they keep, where An Clàr Foscailte does not, the names of those who did not come back from the bank and the thorn: not all of them, for the fighting scattered families as well as companies and not every name found its way home to be kept. A good many did, kept in the way the north keeps its dead, spoken at firesides and at the turn of the year, without a stone to hold them and without, until this book, any page in the kingdom's own record to be spoken in.

It is told, too, of the byres, where the sixty held out past dark, that among them was a boy of no more than fourteen who had carried water to the thorn stand all that morning rather than carry arms, being thought too young for arms even by a column that had by then grown short of grown men to bear them, and that when the white cloth went up on the byre-fork it was the boy who asked, of the man beside him, whether the marching to the capital's gaol that the colonel's word had promised them was truly better than staying where they were, and was told, by the same man, that a boy who lives to ask a foolish question in a gaol has done better for himself than one who dies asking a wise one in a field, which the tellers offer, more often than not, without further comment, as if the answer needed none. The boy is not named in any telling this book has found. Whether he lived out that winter in the capital's gaol, or after it, this book cannot say, and no teller in the north has claimed to know.

## III. Of the Roads Home

Word of the field reached the western hills before the wounded did, carried by men who had broken from the fighting early enough to run and had run without stopping, by the tellers' own account, for the better part of two days on tracks the regiments did not know to watch. It found, in the hills, not an army so much as what an army leaves behind it when the greater part of it has already marched away to be broken elsewhere: old men and women who had kept the last of the flocks through two summers of war, a scatter of the sick and the maimed too far gone to walk south with the column in the autumn, and here and there a handful still under arms, holding a pass or a spring that no one on either side had thought worth fighting over directly, because it fed a dozen families and not a regiment.

To these the news came, in every telling this book has gathered, without argument attached to it. No one is remembered to have proposed holding the hills a season longer, or waiting for a spring that might bring the column's survivors back to them, or sending word south to ask what terms, if any, the regiments would give. What is remembered is simpler and, in its way, harder to set down plainly: that within a matter of days, in ones and twos and small parties, without much speech between them and none at all, so far as any telling says, with the regiments, the last of the hills' people came down out of the high ground and along the Àth leathan road to where An seachdamh rèisimeid had kept its posts through two summers of a war it had spent mostly waiting, watching a road that had, until that week, carried very little for it to watch.

An seachdamh rèisimeid's own return for those days, which survives in full where a great deal else of the war's paperwork does not, is a document of a particular kind: a list, kept post by post along the road, of those who came down, their town where it could be got from them, and the arms, if any, they carried and surrendered, drawn up by the post's own sergeant in a hand a good deal steadier than the corporal's list at Muileann ghlas, for An seachdamh rèisimeid's war had been, whatever else it had been, a long watch on a quiet road rather than a morning of guns and dead by a river, and the men who kept it had time, that week, to do the counting properly. The weapons came in a strange mixture even for a war that had, by its last year, armed itself from whatever could be found: fowling pieces older than any man then living, two or three rifles of a pattern the regiment's own quartermaster did not recognise and noted as such, pikes made in the first months of the trouble from scythe blades and ash poles, and, from more than one post's list, nothing at all, for a good number of those who came down that week had carried no arms in the first place and had followed the column, or stayed in the hills that kept it fed, without ever once being asked to fight.

Among those who came down to the northernmost post on the second of those days was a man of Cnoc thais, past sixty by his own reckoning and lame in one leg from an old fall down a shaft years before the war, who had carried no weapon at all and told the sergeant so before he was asked, and who had with him, on a rope halter, the one cow his family had kept through two summers of soldiers moving over their ground, on the plain reasoning, as he gave it to the sergeant and the sergeant set down more or less word for word, that a man might be let go home with an empty rope and starve there just as surely as he might be shot for coming down armed, and that he had thought it worth the asking either way. The sergeant let him through with the cow, noted the exchange in full, being, as his list shows throughout, a man who set down more than his orders strictly required of him, and added nothing further, though this book, reading his hand now, finds in that one unnecessary sentence more of the war's true cost, and more of its end, than in a page of the guns' account from Muileann ghlas.

They were disarmed at the posts, searched, and sent home rather than to the capital's gaol, as the sixty from the byres had been, to whatever the hills' towns still had standing for them, which in more than one case, Muileann àrsaidh chief among them, was not a great deal. An seachdamh rèisimeid's sergeant at the northernmost post, whose own list this book has followed more than any other for the plainness of its hand, noted at the foot of his last page, after the final name was entered and the last weapon counted, that no more had come down the road since noon of that day, and that he took this to mean the counting was done. It is the whole of his comment on the matter, and it is, so far as An Clàr Foscailte allows this book to say, very nearly the last entry made anywhere on the island in the name of An Cogadh Fada, which had begun on a bitter morning at Àth leathan nearly two years before, and ended, as such things end, with a sergeant deciding, on the evidence of an empty road, that there was nothing left for him to count.

## IV. Of Somhairle After

Somhairle mac Lachlainn was not himself at Muileann ghlas that day. He had commanded the regiments from the capital through the better part of that autumn, by then, at a table in a room Comhairle nam Mèinnean had given over to him near Slighe a' Ghuail's own offices, and An Clàr Foscailte's silence on his own movements through those two years, a silence this book has met before and will meet again, holds here as everywhere else: what he did in the rooms where the war was made this book cannot tell, because the record of it went into Ciste-chuimhne Dhùinte with the rest, and the man himself, in the years since, has kept to it as closely as an Leabharlann does.

He would say, in the one account of that day this book has found written down, given since the peace, that he had heard the guns were done at Muileann ghlas from a clerk who came into his room without knocking, an hour or so past the short day's dusk, and that his first thought on hearing it, before any other, had been for Slighe a' Ghuail's timetable, whether the wounded could be got up to the capital that same night or would have to wait for morning, and that it was some while later, sitting alone in that room with the lamp burned low, before he let himself think of the day in any other terms at all. This is the whole of what he is remembered to have said of it, told to a councillor since, who set it down more or less as he heard it, and it is offered here for one reason: it is the nearest this book can come to Somhairle's own voice on the one day of the war that ended it, and because a man who spent two years commanding a war from a room he never once, by his own account, thought to leave, is entitled to be heard, at least, on what it was he thought about when word came that the room's work was done.

He was given a seat on the council the following year, the first soldier so honoured since An Dealachadh, and he sat in it, by every account this book has, without once speaking of Muileann ghlas from that chair, nor of Àth leathan before it, nor of any of the two years between. What he did instead, in the first weeks of that peace, by his own clerk's later account, was to have Slighe a' Ghuail's schedule for the wounded checked twice against the surgeons' own returns, to be certain that no man carried north that winter had been carried on a train meant for something else. It is a small thing to be remembered for, out of two years of war; it is the thing this book has found, and a chronicle that has so little else of the man cannot afford to leave it out.

So ended An Cogadh Fada, twenty months from the bitter morning at Àth leathan to the sergeant's empty road, and it left behind it, standing to this day, nine regiments and four fleets, each carrying still the name of the town where it was first raised, whether or not that town had cause, before the war, to think of itself as a soldiering place at all. It left behind, too, a mill at Muileann ghlas with a floor that had held both armies' wounded in one night and a miller's wife who is not remembered to have spoken of it again to any stranger who asked; a corporal's list, twenty-three names long, kept afterward at the capital and copied onto a stone the following year; and a requisition for lime that outlived, by the accident of a filing clerk's carelessness, every grander paper the war produced, and says, to anyone who reads it rightly, more than most of them do.

At Caol mhòr, in the days after, where word of the field reached the harbour before it reached most of the north by any road, an old Tuathach standing at the fish quay with the news new in his ears is remembered, by more than one who was there, to have said, to no one in particular and to everyone near enough to hear him, that they had got long-warred, chaidh am fadachadh, meaning it, the tellers agree, as a joke against his own people and no one else's, for a fadachadh is what the north calls the waiting a fisherman does for a boat that is not coming back, drawn out past all sense until the waiting becomes the thing remembered, longer than whatever it was waiting for. He said it, by every account, as a man says a thing he has said before about smaller griefs and finds, to his own surprise, still fits a larger one. Those near him on the quay that day are not remembered to have laughed, then or after, though the saying has been carried the length of the north since, and is said still, of any hope held too long past the day it was worth holding, always as a jest, and never, in this book's hearing, by anyone who laughed while they said it.

# Chapter Thirty-five: Of the Stations Kept

*DE 23*

> **Part Seven: Of Peace**
>
> *Leigeadh leis bàsachadh.*
> Allowed to die.
>
> — Tional nan Tuathach's minute on Tagradh na h-Èirig, DE 25

## I. Of the Capping

The council did not stand the regiments down, and Somhairle mac Lachlainn, reading the minute that said so in the first week of am Faoilleach, understood before he had finished it why the thing had been done, and understood also that no one in the room where it was decided would ever say the reason aloud. A regiment sent home was a regiment that had to be raised again from nothing if the hills gave any more trouble than a farmer's grumbling, and raising nine regiments once had cost the kingdom the better part of two years and more men than An Clàr Foscailte cared to total in one place; keeping them, at their own stations, on Deachamh a' Chogaidh that had been laid on every barrel of dubhan sold since the second month of the fighting, cost a line in An t-Ionmhas's book and nothing else that anyone in that room was minded to count. The tithe had been called, when it was laid, a thing for the war's sake and for a time only. Somhairle had heard the phrase often enough that winter, from men who plainly believed it and from men who as plainly did not, to know by now which kind of man was speaking by the speed with which he said it.

He kept, that first spring of the peace, to the rooms near Slighe a' Ghuail's own offices that Comhairle nam Mèinnean had given him through the war and had not yet asked back, and it was there, at a table too large for the papers he had to put on it, that the reports of the western seams first came to him, forwarded by Fearghas mac Aonghais, master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean at Cathair mhòr, with a covering note two lines long: the seams were An Crùn's by Breith Leòid, as Comhairle nam Mèinnean had declared them five years before, the holders had stopped paying when Comhairle nam Mèinnean stopped carrying, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean saw no profit and considerable risk in leaving open ground that had lately held an army. The order that followed asked for nothing subtler than concrete and men enough to pour it, and An seachdamh rèisimeid, quartered at the western Seann Skell since before the fighting began and idle now in a way that Somhairle suspected its own colonel found harder to bear than the siege had been, was given the men.

He went himself to the first of the cappings, at Àth leathan, in am Màrt, for no better reason he could have given anyone than that he had commanded the taking of the ground and felt it owed him, or he it, the seeing of what came after. The pit-head stood much as the battle had left it, the winding-gear still up though the wheel no longer turned, the spoil-heaps gone green at their lower slopes with the first of the year's grass and black and bare higher up where nothing had yet had time to take. A company of the seventh worked the shaft mouth with barrows and a mixer brought up from the western Seann Skell on a lorry that ran, as every lorry on the island now ran, on the fuel a Tuathach had made two-and-twenty years before at a fire he had banked in the dark for reasons the record did not give and Somhairle, standing at the shaft's edge with the smell of the wet mix in his throat, found he did not much want to guess at either. The concrete went down grey and thick and, poured, lay still in a way that struck him, watching it, as unlike the seam it covered, which even flooded had never once in the whole history of the pit lain entirely still.

A sergeant of the seventh, a broad man named Iain Mòr who had held Freiceadan Àth leathan's ground since the last month of the war, stood by him at the shaft's mouth and told him, without being asked, that this was the fourth such capping his company had stood by that month, the others at Muileann àrsaidh, at Cnoc thais, and at a smaller working near Àth naomh that had never had a name outside its own valley. "Tobar dhearg of the hills we've still to do," he said, "and after that there'll be nothing left in the west for a man to be sent to guard, unless the council finds him something new to guard." He did not say this bitterly. He said it the way a man reports weather, a fact to be noted and then let go, and Somhairle, who had by then spent the better part of two years learning to hear what a soldier did not say along with what he did, understood that Iain Mòr had already begun, in his own mind, to wonder what An seachdamh rèisimeid was for, now that the war it had been raised to fight had ended and the ground it had fought over was being filled in under his own boots.

Word came to him that same week of a small matter from the eastern side of the island that had nothing to do with the west at all and everything to do with what the peace was already turning into: Caol ruadh, whose harbour had fed the garrisons and An dàrna cabhlach through both years of the fighting with more salt fish and biscuit than any town its size had ever been asked to victual before, had been granted, by a council minute so short Somhairle read it twice to be sure he had not missed a clause, a market right of its own for the strait below it. It was the sixteenth town so chartered on the island and, the minute noted in its last line, as if the fact carried some weight worth setting down, the last that would be. Somhairle, who had never in his life had cause to think about market charters one way or the other, found himself thinking of it now chiefly as a kind of book-keeping: the kingdom settling its accounts with the towns that had fed the war, town by town, in whatever coin came cheapest to it, a charter here, a contract there, nothing that could not be filed and forgotten once given.

By the month's end the last of the western workings that were not Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own was capped, and Fearghas mac Aonghais's office at Cathair mhòr sent out, without much ceremony, a further note that the trade in coal-fuel, outside what Comhairle nam Mèinnean itself still cut for its own account at An Sloc Mòr, was at an end on the island; no law had ever been troubled to forbid it; it ended all the same, the way a road empties when, at last, nowhere along it is left that anyone still wants to go. An Sloc Mòr's own galleries were named nowhere in the note, and Somhairle understood the omission for what it was: a mine close enough to the capital for Comhairle nam Mèinnean to keep an eye on it directly was one matter, and the western hills, a two days' ride from anyone minded to ask an awkward question, had plainly been another.

Somhairle read that note at his own table with the lamp lit, for the days were still short, and found his thoughts turning, for reasons he did not examine closely, away from the western pits and toward the poorer streets of the capital as he had last walked them as a young man newly with Comhairle nam Mèinnean, dark from the lamp-houses' rationing, and of how thoroughly, in the years since, that darkness had been undone by the very fuel that had just finished undoing the last of the trade it replaced. Every lamp in the capital now burned on dubhan, every lorry and every engine of Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn besides, and a man could go the length of the island, he supposed, and not find so much as a coal fire outside a smith's forge or Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own hearths, and yet no council minute, so far as he had read, had ever once said in plain words that lighting, moving and warming the whole kingdom on dubhan was now simply how things stood; it had become true the way the western seams had become quiet, by a hundred small orders that never once named the whole of what they added up to. He wrote nothing of this thought down. It was not the kind a report had room for.

## II. Of the Boundary Stones

Martha Greaves had sat as speaker of Tional nan Tuathach long enough by then to have learned that most of what came to her desk in a given month could be answered by a clerk, and that the little which could not was, in the end, simply lived through and not answered at all; so that when the letter came in an t-Iuchar from the capital's gaol, by way of the council's own office and not, as everything else from that quarter usually came, by way of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, she read it twice before she understood that this was neither kind, and that it would want, of her, more than a signature.

The letter said that the holdouts taken at Muileann ghlas the Dùbhlachd before, some four score of them who had come out of the byres unarmed on the promise A' chiad rèisimeid's colonel had given them that night, were to be released and sent north under guard, as far as the boundary stones, where they would be handed over to whatever authority the shires beyond chose to send to meet them. It named a day. It did not say what the men and the handful of women among them were to do once handed over, nor who, if anyone, was to feed them on the road, nor whether their own towns, most of them long since walled with spoil and flooded, would know what to make of men coming home a year and more after the fighting they had left them in had ended. Martha read all this standing at her own window with the letter in her hand, and then sat down and wrote to Peter Hale, who had carried the rebound minute-books through half the war on his own back and had earned, she thought, more say in how Tional nan Tuathach's part of this ended than any other man in Caol mhòr, asking him to come north with her to the stones.

They went down the northern road in a hired carriage, on a morning with the first real heat of the year in it, the kind of morning that in another year would have had the hill farms turning hay and did that year too, Martha noted from the carriage window, as if the land had not been told a war had passed over it. The boundary stones stood where they had always stood, set some ninety years before at An Dealachadh and never once, in all that time, moved by so much as a foot, low grey markers a man could sit on and often did, worn smooth on their upper faces by generations of shepherds waiting out a shower. A company of A' chiad rèisimeid was drawn up on the southern side of them when Martha and Peter arrived, and beyond, on the northern side, a scatter of Tuathaich had already gathered, word of the day having travelled ahead of the letter by roads the council's own office never troubled to use.

The prisoners came up the road on foot, in a column no longer than the fourth part of a mile, and Martha, watching them come, found she had braced herself for men marked by a year's close keeping in a way that none of them, when they were near enough to see plainly, quite were; thinner, most of them, and slower on their feet than men of their years should have been, but walking under their own strength and looking, more than anything else, like men who had stopped some time before expecting to be looked at as anything worse than tired. The colonel in charge read out a paper at the stones that said, in the dry way such papers said everything that year, that these were released on the council's order and were Tional nan Tuathach's charge from this point north; and it was at that word, charge, that Martha understood what her own part in the day was to be, and stepped forward with the register she had brought up from Caol mhòr in her own bag rather than trust it to a clerk.

Tional nan Tuathach had kept, since An Dealachadh, one long list of its dead and its maimed, added to every year the war or the pits or the fever took a name from the north, and it was to the foot of this list, in a fresh column ruled that morning by Peter's own hand because no other paper in the party would serve, that Martha now added, one by one, as each man or woman came forward and gave a name and a town, the names of those who had gone into the byres at Muileann ghlas and come out again.
