She wrote plainly, town beside name as the corporal's list of the regiments' own dead had been written the Dùbhlachd before, though she did not know that list existed and would not, this book must say, ever come to read it; and more than one of those who gave her their name that morning gave, along with it, some further word she had not asked for and set down anyway, because it seemed to her wrong to take a name and refuse whatever the man attached to it, that morning of all mornings, wanted said with it. A woman of Cnoc thais gave her son's name and then, unbidden, the words he is not among these, meaning that her son had not come out of the byres at all, and Martha wrote both the name given and, beside it in a smaller hand, the four words, because she judged, rightly or not, that the register would be a poorer thing without them.

Peter Hale stood at her shoulder through the whole of it and said little, though Martha noticed, more than once, that his own pen had gone still over the page at a name he seemed to recognise, and it was only afterward, on the carriage south, that he told her the fourth man to come up had been apprenticed, before the trouble began, to the same binder at Muileann leathan whose old pupils had rebound Tional nan Tuathach's minute-books at Daniel Frayne's dying wish, fifteen years before, and that the man had not known him, or had known him and chosen, that morning, not to say so. "I could not have said which," Peter told her, "so I let it go unasked. It did not seem a morning for asking a man to remember more of himself than he had already been asked to give up that day." Martha thought this the truest thing said to her the whole of that summer, and told him so, and neither of them spoke of it again.

Not every man who came up the road that morning gave his name readily. One, older than most, stood some while before the register without speaking at all, and Martha, who had by then learned in her years as speaker not to press a silence that might yet fill on its own, waited with her pen lifted until he said, at last, that his name would mean nothing written down beside a town that no longer stood in any shape a name could be sent back to, Muileann àrsaidh having been, by the last report she had herself read, more spoil-heap than street by the war's end; and Martha told him, as truly as she knew how, that the town would stand again in whatever shape its own people chose to build it in, register or no register, but that the register would hold his name either way, against the day it did. He gave it then, and his town with it, and walked on north without waiting to hear whether she believed her own answer, which she was not, in fact, entirely sure she did.

By the time the last name was taken the sun stood well past noon, and the released men and women had already begun, in ones and twos, to go north past the stones under no guard at all, A' chiad rèisimeid's company having no order to do more than see them handed over and no great wish, that Martha could see, to linger on a road that led nowhere its own men wanted to walk. She closed the register at last with some four score names added to its foot, a column of its own beside the long column the war before this one had begun, and rode back to the carriage with Peter beside her and the book on her knee, and found, somewhere on that road south, that she could not have said with any confidence whether the day had been a mercy or only the last administrative act of a war that had run, by then, so long past any single act's power to end it that mercy and book-keeping had come, in practice, to look much the same thing.

## III. Of the Seat and the Post

The council's summons to Somhairle came in an Lùnastal, three lines on a single sheet, inviting him to take a seat among the twelve at the next sitting after harvest, and he read it, when it came, with less surprise than he thought a man ought to feel at being asked to sit among the twelve who had, for two years, decided from a room he had never once been admitted to what his own regiments were to do and where. He had commanded a war, by then, longer than most of the twelve had held their own seats, and it occurred to him, folding the letter and setting it under the ink-stand for want of anywhere better to keep it, that a soldier given a seat on the council was less an honour done to the soldier than an insurance the council was taking out against its own next reckoning, so that the next war, should the island ever raise another, would be made by men who had at least once stood close enough to a field to know what the word cost in more than coin. He did not refuse it, having not, by then, refused much that the council had asked of him in three years, and saw no cause to begin with the one thing it offered rather than demanded.

The autumn sitting seated him, the first soldier to hold a chair there since the captains of Cogadh nam Beann, whose own names, he had occasion to remember, he had himself read aloud from the council's chests not two years before to raise the very regiments he now, as a councillor, would help to keep or stand down. He said little at that first sitting, by his own later account, chiefly because the twelve about him, Anna nic Phàil among them, spoke that day mostly of the harvest tithe and Slighe a' Ghuail's autumn schedule and other matters a soldier had no particular fitness to weigh, and he judged it wiser, in a room he did not yet know the temper of, to listen a full season before he ventured a view the others might have cause to remember against him.

Anna nic Phàil was the one member of the twelve who spoke to him directly that day, catching him at the chamber door as the sitting broke, to say, without much preamble, that she had sat among the twelve an Nollaig three years before when Martha Greaves carried Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail into that same room, and had voted, since, for every small mercy the council's own business allowed her to move, and meant to go on doing so, and thought a man who had commanded the regiments ought to know it before he had sat among them long enough to suppose the room held only the twelve kinds of silence he had likely met there that first day. Somhairle thanked her and said little more, less from want of an answer than because he had not yet decided, in his own mind, which of the twelve kinds of silence he had in fact met that morning was hers, and did not think it a courtesy to guess wrong to her face on the first day of their both sitting there.

An seachdamh rèisimeid, meanwhile, having capped the last of the western seams by midsummer, was set that autumn to a work of its own choosing rather than the council's, though the council's leave was asked and given readily enough: a post of stone and timber on the road below Àth leathan, at the crossing where the holdouts had once formed on the morning of the battle, built by the regiment's own hands over six weeks with materials carted up from the western Seann Skell. It went into the regimental returns under the plain name the lists had used from the first order that raised it, Freiceadan Àth leathan, and Somhairle, reading that return at his own table in the same room where he had once read the order to march on the town, found that the name sat oddly with him, a name so exactly what the thing was, a post kept at Àth leathan, that it told a reader nothing at all of what had been fought for on that ground or what had been lost taking it.

He learned, from a report of Iain Mòr's some weeks later, that the town itself, the four-and-thirty souls who had come back to what was left of it since the pits were flooded, called the post something else, though the report did not say what, Iain Mòr having judged, in his own words, that it was not a soldier's business to carry a name like that back to his own colonel to be entered anywhere the council might one day read it. Somhairle did not press him for it. He had learned, in three years, to recognise the shape of a thing a man had decided not to tell him, and had learned, too, that pressing rarely got him more than a different silence dressed as an answer; and there was, besides, some part of him, which he did not examine too closely that autumn any more than he had examined the thought at the capping in am Màrt, that judged the town's own name for the post, whatever it was, none of the council's proper concern, and least of all his own, now that he sat among the twelve who might, given the chance, ask him to have it struck from every mouth that used it.

## IV. Of the Stone and the Sown Field

The plough had gone into the field at Muileann ghlas that same spring, while Somhairle was still watching concrete settle at Àth leathan and Martha had not yet had the letter from the gaol, for the farmer who held the ground, a broad quiet man named Aonghas mac Phàdraig who had worked that field and his father's before him, saw no reason a battle fought on it once should keep it from feeding his own house a second winter running, and turned the first furrow in am Màrt as he had turned it every spring of his life. He found the first of the iron before the furrow was half done, a bayonet gone to rust, turned up whole and lying across the share as if it had been laid there rather than buried, and he stood some while over it, by his own account given afterward to more than one neighbour, before he judged there was nothing to be done but finish the furrow and carry the thing home at the day's end, which he did, and gave it, some weeks later, to a corporal of A' chiad rèisimeid who came through the district collecting rents on Comhairle nam Mèinnean's account and had, it turned out, no better notion than Aonghas himself of what ought to be done with a rusted bayonet turned up by a plough, but took it anyway and entered it, for want of any other heading that suited, on a list he kept for exactly such things. The corporal has kept that list since, adding to it each season as Aonghas and his sons turn up more of the same, a bayonet, a broken rifle stock, once a whole cartridge box gone green with the years in the ground, and no two men who ever saw that list agreed, when asked, on what it was truly a record of: the dead, who could not be counted any other way, or only the ground, giving back, in its own slow time, what two armies had once been in too great a hurry to stop and gather.

Clach nan Rèisimeidean was raised in an Dùbhlachd, a year to the week since the battle it named, beside the market cross that Taigh Mhic Ùisdein had kept at the town's centre for longer than anyone now living could say, and Somhairle, seated by then among the twelve, was asked, as the regiments' own councillor, to stand at its unveiling and read the names cut into it aloud before the town. He had not sought the office. He had not, if the truth were told, much wanted it, having spent two years reading rolls of names in halls and camps and once, at Muileann ghlas itself by report only, at a trestle table turned to a desk by a corporal with no other paper to hand, and finding each reading harder than the last rather than easier, as he had once supposed such things grew with use. But the council had asked it of him as it had asked the seat, and he had learned by then which of the council's askings a man in his place could safely decline, and this, he judged, standing before the stone in the cold with the town's whole population, or near it, gathered in the square before him, was not among them.

The stone bore one-and-sixty names, eight-and-thirty of Àth leathan and three-and-twenty of Muileann ghlas, cut in two columns under a single heading that gave neither battle nor date but only, in the plainest words the mason's letter to the council had proposed and the council had accepted without change, the regiments' dead. Somhairle read them from a paper copy rather than from the stone itself, the light being poor and his own eyes, he supposed, no longer what they had been at thirty, and read them slowly, town by town as the corporal's list and the sergeant's return had first set them down, a boy of Cathair mhòr's own western quarter, two brothers of Seann Bhral who had enlisted together and died, the return noted, within the same hour of the same morning, a man of Inis mhòr old enough to have a grown son of his own already serving in the same company. The square kept a silence through the whole of the reading that Somhairle, listening to his own voice fall into it name after name, found harder to bear than any noise the crowd might have made instead, for a silence like that asked nothing of him and gave him, in return, nothing to answer, only the sound of his own voice going on alone until the last name was said and there was, for one long moment before anyone in the square moved or spoke, nothing left to read.

He stood a while longer at the stone after the crowd had begun to break up and go home to its own suppers, the paper still in his hand, and thought, as he had half expected he would from the moment the council first asked him to do the reading, less of the one-and-sixty names he had just given back their voices for the length of a winter afternoon than of the others the stone did not carry and never would: the column's own dead, buried in more lime than three-and-twenty graves could need and never once counted by any hand An Clàr Foscailte trusted; the sixty who had come out of the byres and gone, some of them, into the register Martha Greaves had carried up to the boundary stones that summer with four words written beside one name that was not, in the end, among those released; a woman's son of Cnoc thais who was not among these, and whose own stone, if his mother ever raised one, would stand nowhere the council's own mason had been asked to cut, in a field or a chapel yard An Clàr Foscailte had no occasion ever to visit. Sixty-one names were a great many to read aloud in one winter afternoon, and Somhairle, folding the paper at last and turning for Slighe a' Ghuail's carriage that would carry him home to the capital and the twelve who waited there to hear how the unveiling had gone, found that the number staying with him longest, walking away from the stone in the last of that short day's light, was the one no mason on the island had yet been asked, or would ever be asked, to cut anywhere at all, and never the one already cut into it.

# Chapter Thirty-six: Of the Sealed Room

*DE 24*

> Let the whole record of the war be shut against every reader for fifty years, and let the keeper hold the one key.
>
> — the council's order, am Faoilleach, DE 24

## I. Of the Key

The order came up to Muileann chaol in the first days of am Faoilleach, carried by a rider who had changed horses twice at Àth dhomhain and once more at the ford, and who told Raghnall mac Mhuirich, handing it over on the doorstep of the old building with the snow still on his shoulders, that he had been given no leave to wait for an answer, only to see it delivered and ridden back. Raghnall read it standing in the doorway, in the cold, because the rider would not come in out of it, and read it a second time at his own desk before he sent for Sìleas.

It was four lines long and said what it meant to say without any of the softening a council's clerk usually gives an order of that kind. The whole record of An Cogadh Fada, from the first muster to the last, was to be put out of the reach of every reader, of whatever office or standing, for fifty years from that day. A room was to be found for it in an Leabharlann's own keeping, and the key was to be held by the keeper and by no one else, and the keeper was to answer to the council, and to no reader, for what was done with it. There was no reason given. There never is, in an order of the council's own hand; the reasons, when there are any set down at all, go in a minute Tional nan Tuathach's own clerks never see and this book may not read.

Raghnall had kept an Leabharlann five-and-twenty years by then, and had seen, in that time, one chronicler lay the office down and another take it up, and he read the order through twice and said, when he had finished, only that it was the first time in the kingdom's whole history that any part of the record had been shut against its own chronicler, and that he did not think Ailean Leabhar, who had said once that an Leabharlann settles nothing and only keeps, would have thought much of the distinction the council's clerk had just drawn between keeping a thing and keeping it from a reader.

"He said it settles nothing," Sìleas said. "Only keeps."

"He never foresaw an order asking an Leabharlann to keep a thing from its own reading-room."

She asked him, because there was as yet no clerk of her own in the room to ask it in her stead, whether he meant to argue the order, and he said no, in the same flat voice he had read it aloud in, and when she asked why not, since he had argued smaller things with the council before and won, he told her that a keeper who argued an order of this kind risked being answered with a second order naming a different keeper, and that he had rather keep the room himself, badly if it came to that, than hand the key to some clerk of the council's own choosing who might not trouble to keep it at all. She had no answer to that, and did not try to make one; she only asked, before she left his room, whether she might at least be told who at the council's table had proposed the sealing, and he said he did not know, and that the order, as she had already seen, gave no name for anything, not the reason, not the proposer, not even, in its own four lines, the war it meant.

There was a room at the end of the new wing's lower gallery that had held nothing for years but the broken binding-press nobody had troubled to carry down to the smith, and a scatter of tallow ends, and the smell, in wet weather, of the river coming up through the stone. Raghnall had it cleared in a day, the press dragged out and the tallow swept up and burned, and a mason sent for from the town to fit a door of oak two inches thick where a plank door had stood since the wing was built, with a lock the smith made new to no other key in the kingdom. It took the mason and the smith between them the better part of a week, working through the worst of the month's weather with a brazier for warmth and their breath standing white in the room even so, and Raghnall stood over the fitting of the lock himself on the last morning, because he judged, he told Sìleas afterward, that a thing built to keep a secret from the whole kingdom for fifty years deserved at least one pair of eyes on it who meant to keep the secret honestly and not merely competently.

Sìleas brought her own record to the door on the appointed morning herself, and would let no clerk carry it for her. It was the fuller record she had kept beside the open chronicle since the first year of the war, four boxes of it by then, close-written and cross-referenced in her own hand, everything An Clàr Foscailte left out set down in it as plainly as she had been able to set anything down while the war still ran: the regiments' movements she had not been let publish, the numbers of the column's dead that the corporal's requisition for lime had only hinted at and that she had gone back afterward and tried, as honestly as the surviving papers allowed, to reckon for herself; three letters from Doire ghlas that Ellen Marsh had sent her under seal and asked her to keep rather than print, because the families named in them were still living and had not asked to be read by strangers; a single page, unsigned, that had come to her by a hand she never learned, setting out what a boy of the western hills had told a stranger at a market about the last night before Muileann ghlas, which she had judged too near the tellings and too far from proof to put in any chronicle bearing an Leabharlann's own name, and had kept anyway, because she judged also that a thing might be true and still unfit to print, and that a chronicler's business was to keep both kinds and know which was which.

She had carried the four boxes up from her own room herself, one at a time, on the two days before, and set them just inside the new door, and on the morning of 14 am Faoilleach, DE 24, she stood in the doorway a while before she went in to lay the last of her own working papers on top of them, not because she doubted what she had decided to give up, she said afterward, but because a woman does not often get to stand at the door of the one room in the kingdom built to keep her own hand's work from her, and she thought it worth a moment's looking before she went in and did it.

Raghnall turned the key himself, in the new lock, with the smith and the mason gone and no one else in the gallery to see it done. It was a plain iron key, longer than most, and it turned with a sound neither of them had thought to ask the smith to make quieter, a single hard click that ran the length of the stone gallery and came back to them off the old wing's far wall before it died. Raghnall put the key on its own cord round his own neck, under his shirt, and has worn it there since, by every account this book has found, and he has been seen, more than once, by copyists who worked late enough to see him lock the reading-room for the night, to lay his hand flat against his own chest for a moment before he blew out the last lamp, as a man does who is making sure of something he has already made sure of a hundred times before and cannot quite stop checking.

## II. Of the List She Was Allowed

What stayed open, when the door had been shut on the rest, was less than a chronicler of thirteen years at the desk might have wished to keep and more, Sìleas has told her own clerk since, than she had expected the council to leave her. Three things: a list of the places the war had touched, town by town and post by post, with no number of dead set against any of them; a list of the regiments and fleets present at each place, by name and by date; and the counts she had already been permitted to give in the open chronicle before the order came, which stood as they stood and were not called back, though nothing was to be added to them from that day.

It was a narrow allowance, and Sìleas kept to the letter of it with a care her own clerk, a girl of nineteen new to the copying that winter, found at first hard to understand, since the girl could see for herself, reading the open list over Sìleas's shoulder some months into the work, that the same list, read carefully enough by a reader who already knew the places and the regiments both, told a good deal more than its own bare columns seemed to say. Sìleas did not deny it. She told the girl, the one time the girl asked her outright, that the council had shut the drawer, not the shape of the room the drawer stood in, and that a chronicler who kept an honest list of places and regiments, and let a reader's own wit do the rest, was keeping the letter of an order she had never been asked to keep in spirit as well, because no order had troubled to ask that of her, and she did not propose to offer it unasked.

The list, as it stands, runs to some forty places by name, from Àth leathan where the war had opened to Muileann ghlas where it had closed, each with its regiments set against it in the order they had come and gone, and against each place, where she had been let give it, the count the council had allowed before the sealing and not one figure more. Cnoc thais, taken in an Lùnastal of the second year, kept the number of holdouts An Clàr Foscailte had always given for it. The thorn stand at Muileann ghlas kept the three-and-twenty the corporal's list had named. Nowhere on the whole open list did any number stand for the column's own dead, because no number had ever stood there before the sealing either, and Sìleas judged, setting the list to rights that first week, that an order telling her to add nothing was no bar to her leaving a blank space exactly where a blank space had always been, in case some later hand, fifty years on, cared to ask why it was blank and went looking, as she had gone looking herself, for the requisition that answered it without quite saying so.

She wrote, at the head of the open list, a single line she had not been asked to write and did not strike out when she had written it: that this was the whole of what an Leabharlann's own chronicle held open for the war years, and that the rest of the record existed, and was kept, and would be given to whoever asked for it honestly on the day fifty years should end. It was, she said to Raghnall when he read it over her shoulder, the nearest thing to a promise she was able to make to a reader she would not live to meet, and she thought a chronicle owed its readers that much honesty about its own gaps, whatever it owed the council about filling them.

Raghnall let the line stand. He told her, folding the page back into its place among the day's other returns, that he had once told a young chronicler new to the office that an Leabharlann keeps and does not chase, and that he stood by it still. Keeping a thing honestly, he had come in five-and-twenty years to think, sometimes meant telling a reader plainly that a thing was being kept from them, and where, and until when, rather than letting the gap in the shelf speak for itself and be taken, by some later hand with less patience than hers, for carelessness or for shame.

## III. Of the Cairn and the Tithe

The Tuathaich of the western hills had begun, before the frost was properly out of the ground that spring, to carry stone up to the field at Àth leathan where the first great battle had been fought three years before, and by the time the snow was gone from the higher ground they had a cairn there taller than a standing man, raised without any leave asked of An seachdamh rèisimeid whose post lay not half a mile below it on the road. The regiment's captain, a Dia-thìreach of Cathair dhearg new to the post that year, wrote to Comhairle nam Mèinnean asking whether he was to move it, and was answered, some weeks later and in terms that told him a good deal less than he had hoped, that Comhairle nam Mèinnean saw no charge laid on him to move stones off a field An Crùn had no present use for, and that he might use his own judgment in the matter so long as no arms were found under them.

He used his own judgment, and it was, by every account this book has found, a plainer thing than Comhairle nam Mèinnean's letter had troubled to be: he told his patrols to walk past the cairn as they walked past any other stone on that road, and to count the stones if they had a mind to, and to report nothing of it unless they found something under one worth reporting. The patrols have walked past it since, and it has grown, by ones and twos, every time they passed, until it stands, by the reckoning this book has had from a corporal who serves at that post, higher than any stone the regiment had ever troubled to raise for its own dead, though it carried no names, and no plaque, and nothing at all to say whose field it stood on or why.

A woman of the town, who had lost a brother to the fighting on the bank there and would not say, when asked, which side he had died fighting for, was seen more than once by the same corporal to walk out to the cairn alone in the early morning before the patrol came by, and to set one stone on it, never more than one, and to stand a while afterward with her hand flat against the top of the pile before she walked back down to the town. The corporal never asked her name, and never reported the visits, holding, as he told it afterward, that a woman who carried one stone at a time to a field where her own brother might or might not lie was doing nothing his captain's letter had told him to trouble himself over, whichever side the stone was meant to answer for.

At Cathair dhearg that same spring An t-Ionmhas carried Deachamh a' Chogaidh forward on the pumps for another year, as it had carried it forward every year since the war's first month, and no minute of the council records that anyone there so much as raised the question of letting it lapse. A tithe laid for a war's sake and never once revisited once the war was won is not, Sìleas wrote in the open chronicle that year, a thing this book need call by any harder name than the plain one; it is enough to set down that it was never struck out, and to let a later reader draw whatever conclusion the plain fact seems to want drawn.

In the same season An t-Ionmhas's clerks fixed the market-due, on every sale a town made into its own market and on every sale carried between one market and the next, at seventeen in the hundred, and set a clerk of their own in each of the sixteen chartered market towns to take it and keep the town's own roll of what was sold and by whom. Caol ruadh, whose charter the council had granted the year before, the sixteenth and the last such charter the kingdom would grant, had its first An t-Ionmhas's clerk that spring, a young man out of Cathair dhearg who lodged, his own letters home say, over the harbourmaster's own storeroom for want of any better room in a town that had never before had cause to house an officer of An Crùn at all. Deachamh a' Chogaidh on dubhan An t-Ionmhas kept apart from the new market-due, on its own line at the pumps, as it had kept it from the first month of the war, so that a barrel of fuel paid twice over before it left the pump, once to the war that had made the fuel's price what it was and once to the market that sold it on, and no clerk of An t-Ionmhas's, so far as this book has found, ever wrote a word to say the two payments sat oddly together on the same barrel.

## IV. Of the Contracts

Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail took, that same spring, the contract for every engine the nine regiments kept and every hull the four fleets ran, and doubled its own rolls within the year to answer it. Peigi nic Ascaill signed the contract on the guild's behalf at Cathair dhearg on a morning in an Cèitean, in a room of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own offices with a clerk on either side of her to witness it, and she told her own under-fitter afterward, in words the under-fitter thought worth keeping and set down in a letter home, that she had signed a good many papers in her working life and never one before that she was certain, signing it, would put more Dia-thìrich boys and girls into a trade her own charter had once shut its Tuathaich fitters out of, without a single line in it anywhere that named the Tuathaich at all. Riaghailt na Cairte held under the new contract exactly as it had held under the old: every fitter taken on to answer the regiments' work was Dia-thìrich, as the law had required since the charter's first year, and Peigi signed to it, her under-fitter said, with the same hand and the same care she gave any other clause, neither faster nor slower for what the clause meant.

The forges of Àth naomh in the west and of Caol ìseal on the north coast, which had smelted the bog-iron of their own districts since before the war began, took An Crùn's contract that same season for the regiments' small arms and field-pieces, and every forge-town of the old vein country that could turn a hand to iron followed them into it within the year, so that by the autumn arms had become, in every market of the kingdom, the dearest common goods a household could buy, dearer than grain in a bad year and dearer, in the pit towns especially, than the fuel it was bought to burn. A smith of Àth naomh, writing to his own brother at Cathair dhearg that winter, said that he had turned out more musket-stocks in the six months past than he had turned out ploughshares in the six years before the war, and that he did not know, setting his tools down at the day's end, whether to call that a smith's good fortune or a kingdom's bad one, and had decided, by the time he sealed the letter, that a man in his trade was not the one who ought to have to choose between the two words for it.

At Caol ìseal the same trade came to a smithy that had cast little before the war but nails and pot-hooks and the odd gate-hinge for the farms round about, and its master, a woman who had inherited the forge from a father with no son to leave it to and had spent her first years in it proving to every customer in the district that a woman's hand could hold a hammer as true as a man's, told Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own inspector, when he came to see the new contract's terms met, that she had taken on four boys and a girl that winter who had never before been let near a forge fire, and meant to keep every one of them past the contract's own term if the trade would bear it, war or no war, because a hand once taught a trade does not forget it merely because the reason it was taught has passed. The inspector wrote her answer down more or less whole in his own return, adding nothing to it, which this book takes for as plain a mark of respect as an inspector's report is ever likely to give.

## V. Of the Fleets

Of the four fleets that the war had raised and the peace had not stood down, three had work that spring that An Clàr Foscailte was glad enough to set down in full, having no cause to shut any of it away. An dàrna cabhlach, working the eastern water off Baile ìseal through that summer, ran down at last, in the first days of an Lùnastal, the raiders who had taken the salt-boats off Àth bheag three years before and burned a third, and brought their two remaining hulls into Seann Skell under guard, their crews to the capital's gaol and their own account of themselves, such as it was, to a court that this book has found no full record of. Seonag nic Thòmais, keeper of the trial lamp at Baile ìseal's own lighthouse and mother, by then, to a daughter old enough to keep the watch with her on the worse nights, kept in her own log, alongside her plainer entries of wind and tide, an account of the chase that An dàrna cabhlach's own captain thought worth copying whole into his return to Comhairle nam Mèinnean: that she had seen the raiders' sail from the lamp-room two hours before the fleet's own lookout raised it, by the set of a light she had learned, watching that coast for near thirty years, to know from an honest fisherman's by nothing she could easily put into words beyond the plain fact that an honest boat runs before a squall and a raider runs across it, and that she had lit the second lamp, the one kept unlit in ordinary weather and meant only for a warning, a full hour before the fleet came up, on her own judgment and without waiting to be asked for it by any signal from the water.

An ceathramh cabhlach, kept on the Tuathaich coast in the north-west since the war's last summer, searched through that same spring the bays off Cathair gheal where the raiders had been thickest in the war years, and found them, to the last cove, empty. The fishermen of Cathair gheal, questioned by the fleet's own officers as to where the raiders had gone, gave an answer more than one of the officers set down in almost the same words in their separate returns, as though the town had agreed it beforehand, though this book takes it rather for a saying already old among them than for any planned answer: that the raiders had left when the fleets came, and would be back when the fleets went, and that a fisherman of that coast had learned, over a good many years of both, not to trouble himself overmuch about which was doing at any one time, since the sea, in his experience, always found some use for an empty bay before long, whichever side filled it.

An treas cabhlach, at Baile ghorm on the western strait, kept the tank-hulls it had built for the war's own carrying and turned them, that spring, to running dubhan up the coast to the Tuathaich depots at Doire ghlas and Caol mhòr, on a contract Tional nan Tuathach had asked for itself and Tional nan Tuathach's own purse paid the freight of, purse for purse, out of what little Tional nan Tuathach's fund had left over from feeding the war's own families three years before. It was, so far as this book has found, the first contract in the whole of the war's long accounting that the Tuathaich had asked for and paid for themselves rather than had laid upon them, and Tional nan Tuathach's own minute on it, brief as its minutes generally are, records only that the freight was agreed at a fair rate and that An treas cabhlach's captain, a Dia-thìreach who had run the same water for the war's own carrying and asked, this once, to be told plainly what he was carrying and to whom, was told, and carried it, and made no complaint of the cargo that this book has found, though more than one Dia-thìreach captain of that same fleet, in the years before, had grumbled loudly enough about carrying dubhan north at all that his grumbling had gone into Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own returns.

## VI. Of the Morning After

Sìleas came to her own desk on the morning after the lock was turned at the ordinary hour, before the copyists were properly at their tables and before the market bell had rung in the town below, and opened the day's page as she had opened it every working morning for thirteen years, with the date set at its head in her own hand and the weather noted under it, because a chronicle that means to be read fifty years on, she had told her own clerk more than once, ought to be able to tell its reader, at the very least, whether it was raining. It had not rained that morning. She wrote that it had not, and then the day's first ordinary business, a letter from a mill at Muileann leathan asking after a copyist's fee, exactly as she would have written it on any other morning of the thirteen years before, and did not write, anywhere on that page or any page that followed it, one word about the room at the end of the new wing's gallery or the key that hung, from that day, under Raghnall's own shirt.

It was not, she has told her clerk since, that she had put the sealing out of her mind; a woman does not carry four boxes of her own work to a locked door and then forget, by the next morning, that she has done it. It was rather, she said, that a chronicle which stopped, even for a day, to say to its own reader, here is a thing we are no longer able to tell you and here is why, more than the bare line she had already set at the head of the open list, was a chronicle that had begun to write about its own troubles rather than about the kingdom, and she had watched enough chronicles in an Leabharlann's own stacks fall into that habit, in years when their keepers grew tired or frightened or merely old, to know it for a slow way of ceasing to be a chronicle at all while still filling pages. So she wrote the mill's letter, and the fee, and closed the page at the ordinary hour, and began the next morning's page the same way, the date, the weather, the day's first ordinary business, as if the room at the end of the gallery held nothing more than the broken binding-press it had held the winter before, and went on writing that way, morning after ordinary morning, for the years the rest of this book has still to tell of her.

Raghnall, for his part, was seen that same first morning to open the reading-room at the usual hour and set the fire and lay out the day's returns for the copyists exactly as he had laid them out every working morning since before Sìleas came to an Leabharlann at all, and if he laid his hand against his own chest that morning for the first time, no one who was in the room to see it thought it worth writing down, there being, that early in the thing, nothing yet in the gesture to mark it out from any other habit a keeper might fall into without quite meaning to. It was only later, once the habit had held for a season and then for a year, that a copyist or two began to notice it and to wonder, without ever quite asking him outright, what it was a man checked for so often in a key he had never once, by any account this book has found, mislaid.

# Chapter Thirty-seven: Of the Motion Allowed to Die

*DE 25*

## I. Of the Thing Off the Cape

An ceathramh cabhlach's log for that year, kept as every fleet's log was kept, in a hand that set down wind and sail and little else, carries one entry that its own captain thought worth underlining, twice, before he sent the book south with the winter's returns. On a clear night off the north-western cape, with no sea running to speak of and the moon most of the way to full, the watch on the *Bratach Ghlas* reported a thing longer than the hull under their own feet moving under the water off the starboard bow, showing neither fin nor spout that any man aboard could swear to, and gone before a second man could be fetched to see it. The captain wrote what his watch told him and no more, and then, because a log is not a place for a captain's own fancies and he knew it, added underneath, in the same hand: *called it a whale.*

It was not the first such thing seen off that cape. The Tuathaich fishermen of an Oirthir Ghaothach had a name for whatever it was, and a telling to go with the name, that ran back at least to the years when Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill kept Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd, for she had set down a sighting of it from the fishermen's report, and she was the first chronicler of the restored kingdom; the telling said only that the thing came seldom, and always in fair weather, and that it had never yet been known to do harm to any boat that let it pass unremarked. An ceathramh cabhlach's own men, being Dia-thìrich and mostly from towns that had never had cause to fish that coast before the war stationed them there, knew none of this, and called it a whale because a whale was the largest thing any of them had a name for, and because a log, once a captain has written a word in it, is generally left to stand.

Nothing came of the sighting. No boat was lost that year off the north-west cape, and no fisherman of an Oirthir Ghaothach troubled to ask An ceathramh cabhlach what its log said, there being little, by then, that the two sides of that water had fallen into the habit of asking each other about anything at all.

## II. Of the Motion Anna Brought

Anna nic Phàil had kept a copy of Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail in her own writing-case for four years and more by the time she brought her motion, at last, before the twelve, and she could have told anyone who asked her, though nobody did, the exact words of its closing clause without once looking at the paper, having read it over to herself so many evenings at her own table in Cathair dhomhain that the words had worn a groove in her the way a cart-track wears a groove in a soft road. *The kingdom, having already the whole of the south's new fuel to warm it, might find in its own patience a cheaper peace than in any company it could raise to enforce the alternative.* She had watched, in the years since Martha Greaves carried it into the chamber, one small mercy after another pass the council's table and be granted or refused on its own account, a capping here, a register there, a released man handed over at a boundary stone, and had come to understand that the petition, the whole of it, asked payment rather than patience for a season the petition had not foreseen, and would need a new clothing before the room would so much as look at it straight.

She wrote the motion herself, through the early months of that year, at her own table by her own lamp, in the plain hand she used for every paper she meant the council to take seriously, and she wrote it three times before she judged it fit, cutting from the second draft a whole page of what the war had cost the western towns in named figures, granaries filled and pit-heads flooded and a stone with one-and-sixty names on it at Cathair mhòr, because she had sat at that table long enough to know that a room grows deaf to a column of figures faster than to almost anything else a petitioner can bring it, and that the figures, however honestly reckoned, would only give the twelve a thing to quarrel over instead of a thing to answer. What she kept, in the end, was short: that the Tuathaich towns had borne the war's cost in flooded seams and burned farms and men not come home, that the kingdom's own Treasury carried a tithe laid for the war's sake two years after the war had ended, and that a sum, once, out of that same tithe, paid to the towns that had borne the worst of it, would cost the kingdom less than the war itself had cost and would settle, at least in part, an account that every year left standing only grew harder to close.

She brought it to the council in an t-Ògmhios, on a morning warm enough that the dubhan stove in its alcove stood cold and unlit for once, and the twelve sat, as they always sat, about the long table with the light coming down grey and even from the high windows, Somhairle mac Lachlainn among them now these two years, a soldier's stillness about him that Anna had come, in that time, to read as attention rather than indifference, though she could not always have said which of the two it truly was. She read the motion standing, as the room's custom required of any member bringing new business, and she read it slowly, the way she had read the petition to Martha Greaves's own draft years before it ever came to this table, pausing where the sense paused and nowhere else, because a room that has decided in advance what it thinks of a thing will hear a hurried voice as an apology and a slow one, sometimes, as a fact it cannot so easily set aside.

"You have heard it," said the old man at the table's head, when she had finished and laid the paper down, in the same voice that had told Martha Greaves, four Christmases before, that she might read. "Does any member speak to it?"

Anna spoke to it herself, since custom allowed the bringer one further word before the table's own business took it up, and she kept that word shorter even than the motion: that she did not ask the council to say the war had been wrong, only that a kingdom rich enough to raise nine regiments and four fleets in twenty months was rich enough to spare, once, a sum smaller than a single season's tithe for the towns that had not raised them; and that she brought it now, and not before, because two years of watching what the peace was turning into, capping by capping and contract by contract, had taught her that a thing left unasked past its season is rarely asked at all. She sat down when she had said it, and the room, for the length of perhaps ten breaths, said nothing back to her at all, twelve faces giving her exactly the silence Martha Greaves had once described to her over a cup of tea at Doire ghlas as the room's whole answer to anything it had not yet decided how to refuse.

It was the master of An t-Ionmhas who spoke first, a heavy, careful man named Uisdean Dubh whom Anna had sat beside at that table for six years without ever once hearing him raise his voice, and he asked, in the flat tone he asked every question in, whether the mover had costed the sum she proposed against An t-Ionmhas's own roll for the year, since a council that granted a payment without a figure attached to it granted, in his experience, a habit rather than a mercy, and habits, once granted, were harder to unmake than the wrongs they were meant to answer. Anna had expected the question and answered it plainly: a sum, she said, was for An t-Ionmhas's own clerks to set, being their trade and not hers; her motion asked only that the principle be granted, that some amends were owed, and left the reckoning of how much to the room better fitted to reckon it. Uisdean Dubh wrote this down, or wrote some other thing down, in the small notebook he kept always at his elbow, and said nothing further that morning, and Anna, watching him write, could not have told anyone afterward whether she had answered him or only given him a longer sentence to carry back, unresolved, to whatever room he next carried his notebook into.

## III. Of the Eight Days

What she had not expected, and what she found hardest afterward to set in any order she could report to Martha Greaves, was how little the eight days that followed resembled a refusal of any kind she had met before at that table. No member spoke against the motion. Nobody rose, in that sitting or the one that followed it three days later, to say that the western towns had brought the war on themselves by holding their pits against Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own ruling, though she had braced for exactly that argument from at least two of the twelve and had an answer ready for it that she never, in the end, had cause to give. Nobody said that An t-Ionmhas's roll could not bear it, though Uisdean Dubh's question had seemed, that first morning, to open the door to exactly such an answer. The motion simply sat, on the table's own business-paper, at the foot of each day's list, carried forward morning after morning under the small clerk's notation *held over*, the same two words she saw written against it on the second day and the fourth and the sixth, until she came to recognise the phrase the way a woman recognises a neighbour's knock, by its shape alone before the door is even opened.

She spoke to three of the twelve privately in those eight days, in the corridor outside the chamber where such talk was neither forbidden nor encouraged, only tolerated the way a draught under a door is tolerated, too small a thing to be worth the mason's trouble of stopping it. The first, a woman of the eastern fisher towns whom Anna had counted, before that year, among the table's fairer members, told her that she saw the justice of the thing plainly enough and would vote for it gladly when it came to a vote, which was, Anna understood only some days later, not quite the same promise as a promise to see that a vote was called. The second, a man of the coal-line towns whose own seat depended, Anna knew without being told, on merchants who had done well enough out of the war's freight to want no new tithe laid anywhere near their own ledgers, said only that the times were not easy for asking An t-Ionmhas for anything new, and left the sentence exactly there, without saying which times he meant or when, in his own reckoning, easier ones might come. The third was Somhairle mac Lachlainn himself, whom she caught at the chamber door on the sixth day much as he had once caught her at it, two autumns before, and asked him plainly, since he alone among the twelve had once commanded the very regiments the motion's figures would have been measured against, whether he thought the sum too great.

"I think," he said, after a pause long enough that she wondered whether he meant to answer her at all, "that I have read a great many rolls of names in the last four years, and that I have never once been asked, reading them, whether the towns they were raised from could bear the cost of the raising. Why a roll of the dead should be easier to ask a kingdom to pay for than a roll of the living, I don't know. That it has been, I know well enough." He said nothing further, and Anna, walking back to her own lodging that evening past the mint where Gille-Easbaig Bàn's dies still struck the plain seal into coin pegged, now, wholly to a fuel a Tuathach had made, found she could not decide whether what he had given her was an answer, a confession, or only the same kind of silence dressed, this once, in more words than the others had troubled to use.

## IV. Of the Line Allowed to Die

On the eighth day the motion did not appear on the business-paper at all. Anna saw its absence before she saw anything else that morning, scanning the short list a clerk laid at each member's place as the twelves' custom was, and she asked the clerk, a young man she had seen carry that same list to that same table for the better part of three years without once, so far as she knew, being asked to explain an omission from it, where Tagradh na h-Èirig had gone. He told her, in the brisk apologetic voice of a man repeating something he had been told rather than something he had decided, that the master of An t-Ionmhas had asked that it stand over to the autumn sitting for want of the figures the mover had declined to bring, and that the request had been granted the evening before, in a short session Anna had not been told was sitting, by a vote of the members present, of whom she had not been one.

She understood, hearing this, with the particular clarity that comes to a woman only after the thing she has feared has already happened rather than before it, that a motion stood over to a sitting nobody troubles to call is a motion granted every appearance of patience and refused every substance of a decision, and that the room had found, in the space of eight days and without a single member ever once saying plainly that the Tuathaich towns should have nothing, a way to give them nothing that left no single hand answerable for it. She asked whether the autumn sitting had in fact been set a day, and was told that it had not, An t-Ionmhas's figures being, the clerk understood, still some way from ready. When they might be ready she did not ask him, having learned enough that week to know the question would only be answered with another true thing that answered nothing.

Tional nan Tuathach's own minute on the matter, when word of it reached Caol mhòr some weeks later and Thomas Rook's successor set it down in the book that had run unbroken since Walter Hale's wet afternoon, gave the whole of what had happened in one line, in the plain hand the minute-book had always used for a thing too large for the room to say more about: *Leigeadh leis bàsachadh.* Allowed to die. Anna read a copy of that line herself, sent her by Martha Greaves under a short cover note that asked nothing and accused nobody, and found that it said, in three words, everything her own two years of drafting and cutting and reading slowly at a long table had failed, in the end, to say in any number of words at all.

She went back over the sittings in her own mind afterward, more than once, in the way a woman goes back over a fall to find the exact stone her foot had caught on, and could not, however she counted it, find the single vote that had killed the thing, because no single vote ever had. She counted instead the faces: the woman of the eastern towns who had promised a vote and never once, in eight days, asked that one be called; the man of the coal-line towns who had spoken of hard times and let the phrase stand for an answer; six more of the twelve who had said nothing to her at all, in the corridor or at the table, and whose silence she had at first taken, in her own hopefulness, for simple caution and had come, by the eighth day, to read for what it plainly was; and Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who alone of them had given her an answer with a shape to it and had, in the end, no more moved to call the vote than any of the rest. Twelve chairs, and not one hand raised against the motion, and the motion dead all the same. She thought, counting them over that last time, that a room could look away from a thing together more thoroughly than any single member of it could ever have managed to look away from it alone.

## V. Of the Chair Laid Down

Martha Greaves heard of the motion's fate at Doire ghlas, from the same letter of Anna's that had carried the minute's four words to her, and read it standing at her own kitchen table with the morning's mail still in her other hand, and found, reading it, that she felt less anger than she had expected of herself and more a kind of tiredness that had, she understood only slowly, been gathering in her for the better part of two years without her once giving it a proper name. She had sat as speaker of Tional nan Tuathach since the winter Daniel Frayne died, seventeen years by then, through the fuel's whole rise and the whole of the war and the whole of the two years' peace that had followed it, and she found, folding Anna's letter back into its envelope, that she no longer wanted, in any way she could put a plain word to, to be the one who wrote the next letter asking a room that had just let this one die to look at anything else Tional nan Tuathach might bring it.

She told nobody of the decision for a fortnight, turning it over at her own table much as Anna had turned over the motion's own wording at hers, and when she did tell someone it was Peter Hale, in the delegates' room over the net-lofts at Caol mhòr on an ordinary sitting day, with the fire of driftwood and turf doing as little for the far end of the room as it always had. In the same voice she had used to read Ellen Marsh's registers and the census figures and every other hard thing the chair had asked her to read aloud over seventeen years, she told him plainly that she meant to lay the chair down that year, and that she thought him, of every delegate she had sat among, the fittest to take it up, having carried the rebound minute-books through half the war on his own back and having, besides, a great-grandfather's name that the room's own oldest members still remembered without being told whose grandson he was.

Peter Hale did not answer her at once, and when he did it was not to refuse, though Martha had half expected refusal from a man past fifty who had never, in all the years she had known him, put himself forward for anything Tional nan Tuathach had to give. He asked her instead whether she thought the chair worth taking up, after what the council's own table had just shown the whole north it thought of anything Tional nan Tuathach troubled to bring it, and Martha, who had asked herself the same question at her own kitchen table more than once that fortnight, told him what she had come, by then, to believe: that a chair worth nothing to the room across the boundary stones was worth a good deal more than nothing to the room it actually sat in, since Tional nan Tuathach's own minute-books, unbroken since Walter Hale's wet afternoon, were the one record on the whole island that had never once, in ninety years, needed the council's leave to be kept honestly, and a man willing to keep them honestly for another seventeen years was doing work that mattered whether or not any table south of the stones ever troubled to read it. Peter Hale sat with that a while, in the way Martha had seen him sit with hard things before, and said at last that he would take it, if Tional nan Tuathach itself, and not only its outgoing speaker, judged him fit for it, which she thought, hearing him say it, as good an answer as the chair had ever been given by anyone who had held it.

She sat one last sitting that autumn, in the same room over the net-lofts, with the same trestle down the middle and the same plain high-backed chair of ship's oak that Thomas Rook had once laid a cushion on for a man too ill to sit in it, and read out, as her last act in it, the year's register of the dead and the maimed with its new column of released names from the boundary stones added at the foot, and then the short business of the day, a roof at the school at Doire ghlas, the price of wool at the fair, a complaint from a mill at Muileann leathan about the coal-line's freight rates, ordinary things that the room had gone on discussing, she thought, listening to herself read them out for the last time, through a war and a siege and a sealed archive and now a motion allowed to die, because a people does not stop needing its roofs mended and its wool priced merely because the larger account it also keeps refuses, this year, to be settled. When the business was done she said, in the same voice she had used for the roof and the wool, that she laid the chair down, and that Tional nan Tuathach's own custom, unbroken since its first speaker's death, asked it now to choose whoever it judged fittest to take it up; and the room, after a silence shorter and warmer than any the council's own table had ever given Anna nic Phàil, chose Peter Hale by acclamation, without so much as a show of hands being called for.

She went home to Doire ghlas the next morning on the ordinary carrier's cart, her own baggage no more than it had been the year she first came to the mill as a young woman, and found, coming up the last rise before the town with the mill's own smoke rising grey against the hill behind it, that she did not know yet what a woman who had been Tional nan Tuathach's own voice for seventeen years was meant to do with her mornings now that the voice was no longer asked for, and thought that she supposed she would learn it the way she had learned everything else in that chair, one ordinary day at a time, without being told in advance how the learning was to go.

That same autumn, while Tagradh na h-Èirig still sat, unsummoned, on whatever shelf the council's own clerks had at last found for it, three lesser accounts of the war's long tail were closed with rather less ceremony than either the motion or Martha's own chair had been given. At Seann Warr An còigeamh rèisimeid, quartered there since the war's first summer under canvas and borrowed roofs, raised through that season a barracks of dressed stone on ground the town gave it freely, judging, as its own delegates told the maor plainly enough, that a regiment likely to stay was worth more to a harbour town's trade settled than tented. At Inis uaine An t-ochdamh rèisimeid's watch on the eastern dubhan tanks, set there against fire in the war's second year and never yet stood down, was made lasting by a council order that gave it, for the first time, officers' houses in the town rather than quarters borrowed year by year from the tank-yard's own sheds, and the house of Na Seann Spioradan in that town, whose prayers had never before had cause to name any company of soldiers at all, added the regiment to its Sunday round. And at Ceann mhòr, in an Dùbhlachd, An ceathramh rèisimeid marched out of the old magistrate's house it had held since the war's first winter and went home at last to Caol bheag, its own colours cased for a journey the men had waited four years to make; Tional nan Tuathach asked, as it had asked once before and been answered with nothing, that the house be given over to the town it stood in, and this once, the council's answer came within the season and was granted; Tional nan Tuathach's own letter had asked the house for the town, and the order gave it instead to the maor who governed the town in the kingdom's name, so that the house passed, in its plain wording, from one hand of An Crùn to another, and the town that had housed the regiment through four years of quartering found itself no nearer owning the old magistrate's house than it had been the morning An ceathramh rèisimeid first marched in under it.

# Chapter Thirty-eight: Of the Old Reckoning and the Last Hewers

*DE 26*

> **Part Eight · Of the Present Year**
>
> *Tha clàr na rìoghachd slàn anns gach pàirt ach dhà: an cogadh, a tha dùinte, agus an àird a tuath, nach deach fhaighneachd.*
> The kingdom's record is whole in every part but two: the war, which is sealed, and the north, which was not asked.
>
> — Sìleas nic Rath, DE 27

## I. Of the Word Nobody Had Coined

No one afterward could say who had said it first, or where, though a dozen towns of the north claimed the saying for their own before the year was out, each with a different mouth to hang it on: an old woman of Doire ghlas selling eggs at her own door, a boatwright of Caol mhòr with his hands still black from a hull's engine, a schoolboy at his slate who had heard the two words joined at his own supper table and brought them back to his class the next morning as though he had made them himself. What was certain, by the time Sìleas nic Rath came to set the matter down at Muileann chaol, was only that the word had not existed at the turn of the year and could not, by its end, be kept out of any Tuathaich mouth that spoke for more than a minute together of An t-Aon Leabhar Deug Ellen Marsh had asked an Leabharlann to keep, or of Tagradh na h-Èirig that Anna nic Phàil had carried into the council the year before and that no vote had ever come to answer.

Seann-chunntas, they had begun to call the two things together, the tabled request and the dead motion, as though a single word could hold what two separate papers, filed a year apart in two separate rooms, had somehow failed between them to close. The old reckoning. No one in the north claimed to know what settling it would look like, or who would be the one to say the account was even; it kept, rather, the shape of a wrong no court had ever been asked to try, carried forward from one year's ledger to the next, the line never struck because no one on either side had found a way to strike it without first owning that the line had been drawn at all.

Sìleas heard the word first from a carrier who came up Slighe a' Ghuail road with salt fish for an Leabharlann's own kitchen and stood talking a while in the yard with the porter before he went on, and she heard it again within the month from a letter of Ellen Marsh's that reached her desk unbidden, a short civil note asking after nothing more than the eleventh book's binding, in which the schoolteacher had used the word twice in passing, as a woman uses a word she has stopped noticing is not yet in general currency. She copied both instances into her own working notes, as she copied any word she had not met before, meaning at first only to ask Raghnall, when the season allowed, whether an Leabharlann's own glossary of the north's speech ought to carry it. It was some months before she understood, turning the carrier's yard-talk and the schoolteacher's letter over together on a wet afternoon with little else on her desk to occupy her, what the word truly was: a name the north had given to something the kingdom's own record had never troubled to name, and the giving of it, whatever the council's twelve made of it, an entry that belonged somewhere in the open chronicle, though she was hard put, that same afternoon, to say under what heading a chronicler ought properly to enter a word.

She entered it, in the end, under no heading at all, in a single line at the foot of a page otherwise given over to a Board return on Slighe a' Ghuail's autumn schedule, noting only that the word had been heard that year in more than one northern town, joining an Leabharlann's tabled request of nine years before with the council's dead motion of the year past, and that no Dia-thìreach in office, so far as her own hearing of the council's business went, had yet used it or shown any sign of having heard it. She wrote the line, she has told her clerk since, less because she supposed it would matter to any reader fifty years on than because a chronicle that let a whole people coin a name for its own grievance and troubled to record everything else that year, the fair's takings, the regiments' postings, the price of salt at Àth bheag, but not that, would have failed, in her own judgment, at the one thing a chronicle was for.

## II. Of the Last Twelve

The order to shut the upper galleries of An Sloc Mòr came down from Comhairle nam Mèinnean to the maor of Achadh dhomhain in an Cèitean, four lines on a single sheet not unlike the order that had sealed an Leabharlann's own war record two years before, and it gave, as that order had, no reason beyond the plain fact of the thing required: the upper workings, which had given the kingdom the greater part of its coal before the vein began to fail and gave it now, by Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own reckoning, less than the cost of keeping the pumps running against the water, were to be closed, the timbering left standing and the shafts capped against a day Comhairle nam Mèinnean did not trouble to name. One face only was to be kept, the deepest and driest of the old workings, and that face was given over entire to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, to cut altar-coal for the houses of Brìde's order, a few baskets a year, no more, and no less either, than Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's own accounting required.

Twelve hewers were kept to work it, chosen by the maor from among the few dozen still living who had learned the trade before Comann nan Gualadairean dissolved itself fourteen years before, and Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, having no oath of its own ready-made for coal-cutters, took the guild's dissolved rolls, which Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh had carried to an Leabharlann with his own hands in the year of the dissolution, and drew from them a form of words the Àrd-choimheadaiche's own house judged fit for men who cut fuel for an altar rather than a market. The twelve were sworn at Achadh dhomhain on a clear morning of an t-Ògmhios, in the yard above the one shaft still open, by a priest sent down from the southern Seann Skell for the purpose, who read the oath from a single sheet and set his own hand to a second copy that went back south with him, while the twelve stood bareheaded in a line that had not, within living memory of the oldest among them, been drawn up for any purpose but a shift's muster.

They were, by every account this book has found, an ill-assorted dozen for so solemn a swearing: two brothers who had cut coal together since boyhood and would go on doing so, the elder said afterward, until the vein or their own backs gave out, whichever came first; a widow's son barely twenty who had never worked any face but the one now shut and had asked to be kept on the altar-face less from love of the trade than from want of any other the maor's district could offer him; and, at the end of the line nearest the priest, an old man well past sixty who had hewed at An Sloc Mòr since before Cathal was crowned and who told the priest, when the oath was done and the man asked, out of ordinary courtesy, whether he had any words of his own to add to it, that he had sworn the guild's oath once already in his life and had thought, swearing it, that it would be the last oath a coal-cutter's trade would ever ask of him, and that he supposed a man in his years ought not to be surprised any longer at being wrong.

The eleven upper galleries were capped within the fortnight, the timbering left to rot in the dark as the order required, and the maor's own report to Comhairle nam Mèinnean that season noted, in the same flat hand it gave to every other return, that the old hewing families of Achadh dhomhain, who had worked no trade but the vein for as long as the town had stood, said nothing against the closing and asked nothing of Comhairle nam Mèinnean in its place, as they had said nothing and asked nothing at every turn the vein's failing had brought them these thirty years past.

## III. Of the Còmhrag and the Watch at the Library

Of two things that same summer An Clàr Foscailte kept a plainer account, and Sìleas entered both in the ordinary way, without the private line she had given the north's new word. At Ceann leathan, where the yearly melee had been fought every summer since before any Dia-thìreach now living could remember its founding, the regiments entered fighters for the first time, a company from each of the nine sending its own man to the field below the town where the fair-wardens had raised the gate-price twice already since the war's own gate-money first taught them how much a crowd would bear. An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man, a broad quiet Dia-thìreach of the southern Seann Skell who had refitted engines under Peigi nic Ascaill's own charter before the regiments took him, won it in the third bout of the afternoon, and the crowd, Sìleas's own return notes, cheered him no louder and no softer than it had cheered any winner of Còmhrag Ceann leathan in the years before the regiments had any part in it, which she took, setting the line down, for as plain a mark as any that some things in the kingdom had not yet troubled themselves to notice a war had been fought at all.

At Muileann chaol that same season An dàrna rèisimeid, quartered at Àth dhìreach to guard Slighe a' Ghuail and the library road as it had since the war's own first musters, was given a further charge the council's order did not trouble to explain: a guard of six men, stood at an Leabharlann's own gate through every hour of the day and night, over a room whose existence beyond an Leabharlann's own walls no more than a dozen people in the kingdom were supposed to know of at all. Raghnall mac Mhuirich watched the first of them take up the post from his own window on the morning they arrived, a sergeant and five men with a tent pitched in the yard where the copyists' own handcarts usually stood, and wrote to the council, within the week, in a letter Sìleas copied into the day's returns before she quite knew what to make of it herself, that an Leabharlann had not asked for a guard, had never in the whole of its history needed one to keep a room an Leabharlann's own lock already held shut, and would be glad of the council's reasons, whenever the council found leisure to give any.

No reasons have come. The guard has stood its watch since, relieved by An dàrna rèisimeid's own rota without a word from an Leabharlann's own gate to the soldiers' tent or from the tent to the gate beyond the ordinary courtesies a sentry and a porter exchange across a yard they must both cross a dozen times a day, and Raghnall, speaking of it to Sìleas at the year's end, said only that a man learns, keeping a library five-and-twenty years, to recognise the shape of an answer the council has decided not to give, and that he had stopped expecting this one.

The sergeant who stood the first watch, a young Dia-thìreach of Cathair dhearg new enough to the regiment to find the whole business as strange as Raghnall did, asked him once, crossing the yard on a wet morning with nothing better to fill the silence, whether the keeper knew what it was his own men were set to guard against, and Raghnall told him, with the same flat courtesy he gave every question he had no answer for, that he supposed the council knew, and that a keeper's own business was to keep the room shut whether the guard outside it stood there for a reason or for none. The sergeant thought this over a while, walking on toward his own tent, and said, before he was quite out of earshot, that it was a queer sort of soldiering, standing watch over a door that had never once, in a whole season, opened from either side while he was there to see it; and Raghnall, watching him go, judged it the truest thing either of them said to the other that whole year.

## IV. Of the Last Coal Train

Eachann mac Ruairidh drove Slighe a' Ghuail on the tenth of an t-Sultain as he had driven it, on and off, for fifty years and more, since a boy of nine had first been let up onto his own father's footplate at Muileann chrom to hold the whistle-cord and be told, each time he pulled it, exactly how long a blast the crossing ahead required. He was given the run three days before by the yard's own masters, who told him plainly, handing him the manifest, what no manifest of the arms years had ever troubled to tell him: that this would be the last train Slighe a' Ghuail carried under that name for coal's own sake, Comhairle nam Mèinnean having decided, after eighteen years of carrying dubhan under a name the line had never troubled to change, that the last few wagons still owed to the southern lamp-houses under an old contract might as well go down in one final working before the contract lapsed and the name lapsed with it in every mouth but the timetable's own.

He asked for no ceremony, and none was offered him. The engine that took the wagons out of Achadh dhomhain that morning was the same dubhan engine he had driven for eighteen years, its tank carrying the same fuel it had carried every working day since the coal engines were laid up in the Muileann chrom siding and never ran again, and the six wagons behind it held coal only because the contract said coal, a scant load by the standards of the trade's old years, the kind of load a driver of his father's generation would have called barely worth the coupling. He signed the manifest at the yard office in the grey hour before first light, in the same hand he had signed every manifest of the arms years in, and found, walking out to the engine across a yard he had crossed ten thousand times before, that his own legs carried him at something less than their ordinary pace, though he could not, questioned about it afterward by his second man, have said why a man ought to walk any slower to an engine he meant to bring home again by noon.

The run went as any ordinary run went, the line past Muileann mhin no worse and no better under him than it had been the week before, the crossings sounded at their proper distances, the gradient above Cathair dhearg's own goods-yard taken at the same careful speed he had always taken it since a boy on his father's footplate first watched the needle climb there and asked why the driver eased the regulator rather than pressing on. He thought, taking that same gradient for what he supposed, without quite letting himself finish the thought, might be the last time under that name, of his own father, who had driven coal on this same line for forty years and had told him, the year the dubhan engines first came to Muileann chrom, that he would not ride one, and had kept to it, so far as Eachann knew, to the end of his own working days; and he thought, too, though less clearly, of the yard family's son killed under a wagon in the changeover eighteen years gone, a boy he had known only by sight and by the single line the yard's own register had given him, and of how strange it was that a line as long as this one, carrying coal and then dubhan and then arms and now, for one last morning, coal again, should have so few names left along its own length that a driver crossing it could still call to mind.

At Cathair dhearg's own goods-yard, where the wagons were to be unshunted and the coal handed over at last to the lamp-houses' own carters, a small knot of men had gathered along the platform edge who had no ordinary business there, yard hands off their own shift and two or three of the older drivers who had heard, in the way such things were heard along a working line before any bell announced them, that this was Slighe a' Ghuail's last coal working under that name. They said little to him as he brought the engine in, no cheer and no speech, only a few raised hands and, from one old driver near retirement himself, a nod Eachann took, bringing the engine to its stand, for as full an accounting as the morning was likely to give of thirty years' worth of coal carried down that same line by men most of whom the register held no line for at all.

He unshunted the wagons himself rather than leave it to the yard hands, working the couplings in the cold with his own bare fingers gone stiff before he was done, and stood a while afterward at the head of the empty engine while the carters loaded the coal onto their own wagons for the last stretch to the lamp-houses, watching six wagons' worth of a trade that had built the kingdom's own coin and crowned its own kings go out of the yard behind horses rather than an engine, the lamp-houses having judged, that same week, that six wagons did not warrant the trouble of a second engine's steam merely to finish what one engine had already finished carrying.
