His second man, the same broad quiet man who had ridden the arms trains with him five years before and asked him nothing then either, stood beside him through the whole of the unloading and said only, when the last sack had gone over onto the carters' own wagon, that it was a poor sort of coal by the old reckoning, small stuff and dusty, the kind a hewer of thirty years before would have thrown back down the shaft rather than send up to the weigh-house at all; and Eachann, who had thought the same thing himself without troubling to say it, answered only that poor coal carried the same as good coal, so long as the wagon held together, which was as much of an epitaph as either man saw fit to give it.

He rode the empty train back to Muileann chrom that afternoon at the ordinary speed, no faster and no slower than any light working he had ever brought home, and signed the day's return at the yard office in the same hand, and told his second man, walking out into the last of the light, that he supposed the line would keep the name a good while yet in the timetables, whatever it carried, because a name, once printed often enough on enough paper, outlasts by some years the thing it was first printed to describe. He walked home by the yard rows that evening rather than by the shorter way along the embankment, past the siding where the old coal engines had stood laid up and rusting these sixteen years, their fireboxes cold and their own paint gone the colour of the ground under them, and stopped a while at the fence to look at them, as he had not troubled to do in some years, before he went on to his own supper and said nothing of the day's run to his own wife beyond the plain fact that Slighe a' Ghuail had carried its last coal, and that he had been the one to drive it.

## V. Of the Pass, the Wool, and the Foot of the Year

The returns that reached Sìleas's own desk through the rest of that autumn came, as they always came, in no order she would herself have chosen, so that An siathamh rèisimeid's northern posts and the fair's own wool-count arrived within the same week's post and lay together on her table some days before she found leisure to enter either. The sixth, quartered at Cnoc bheag since the war's own last musters, had begun that same month to keep posts of its own at the boundary stones on the northern road, the first stones Seumas mac Eachainn and old Iain Ruadh had ridden past four-and-twenty years before to learn whether a new fuel burned as men said, and for the first time since An Dealachadh itself a Tuathach going south past those stones was asked to show a pass, a single printed sheet the maor's own clerks had begun issuing that autumn from a table set up in the shadow of the stones themselves. The council's minute on it, when it reached an Leabharlann, called the passes a measure for a time only, in the same three words Deachamh a' Chogaidh had been given five years before and had not, in all that time, been taken away again, and Sìleas, copying the minute into the day's page, set down the three words exactly as the council had given them and added nothing of her own beside them, though she found, writing them, that her own pen paused a moment longer over that particular line than the rest of the page had asked of it.

Fèill Muileann òg that same season kept the shape it had kept since the first fair any record of the island remembered, traders of every shire the state now held bringing their own goods to the fair-ground by the ford, and Tuathaich wool sold there still, as it had sold every year since the truce, on its own northern day, through Dia-thìrich factors who took their own cut of every fleece before a northern seller saw the coin. Ùna nic Ailein's own court entered the day's takings in the ordinary column, no different in its figures from the year before or the year before that, and Sìleas, setting the fair's return beside An siathamh rèisimeid's own pass-list on the same page of her working notes, found herself thinking, though she wrote none of it into Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd proper, that a trade six generations old and a pass six weeks old had come, in that one autumn, to stand for the same plain fact from two different directions: that the north sold to the south as it always had, and crossed into the south, now, only by the south's own leave.

It was in the last week of the same month, with the year's ledgers still open on her desk and the fair's own figures not yet fully copied in, that the letter came up from Àth dhìreach in the hand of Beathag's own sister, saying that Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh had died in the night, quietly, in the room she had kept these six years past since laying down the chronicler's office, and that the household there had thought Sìleas would wish to know of it before the news reached her by any slower road.

Sìleas set the letter down and did not, for some while, take up her pen again. Beathag had been five-and-seventy years old, by her own sister's own reckoning given in the same letter, a span her own mother's people had thought a fair age and no more; and Sìleas, who had come to an Leabharlann at two-and-thirty with a fair hand and little else, and had been taught every stroke of the chronicler's craft by the same woman the letter now told her was dead, found that she could not, for the better part of that whole grey afternoon, set down in the open chronicle the one entry the day plainly required of her, though she had entered a hundred deaths of greater and lesser note in the fifteen years she had kept the record at that desk.

She wrote it, in the end, at the day's ordinary hour, in the same plain hand she gave every other entry: that Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, royal chronicler of the kingdom from SE 65 to DE 20, had died at her sister's house at Àth dhìreach, and that an Leabharlann owed to her hand the first note of the fuel that named this whole age, the re-heading of fourteen years of the kingdom's own record, and a great many questions that no chronicler after her, Sìleas included, had yet found the means to answer. She added nothing more, no word of grief and no word of praise beyond the plain accounting of what the dead woman's own hand had left behind her, holding, as she set the pen down at last, to the same rule Beathag herself had given her the day she laid down the office six years before: write what you are let, and write down what you are not.

Folding the letter away into the same drawer where she kept every private paper the open chronicle had no proper room for, she thought of the word the north had coined that same year for its own unsettled account, and found, turning the two things over together in the last light of that short autumn day, that she did not know whether a kingdom's own record could be said to keep an old reckoning of its own, in the way a family keeps one, or whether that manner of keeping belonged, as so much else that year seemed to belong, to the north alone. It was, she judged, closing the drawer, a question fitter for a chronicler with more years left to her than the one now sitting at this desk, and she returned, the next morning, to the day's first ordinary business, exactly as she had returned to it every morning since the door at the end of the gallery was shut.

# Chapter Thirty-nine: Of the Charter of Export

*DE 27*

## I. Of the Còmhrag and the Two Docks

Joe Ashby had fitted boats at Caol mhòr for thirteen years by his own count, and in all that time he had never once gone up to watch Còmhrag Ceann leathan, though the men he fitted for went every year, win or lose a shift's pay on it, and came back the next morning with their knuckles wrapped in whatever cloth their wives could spare. That year the fight went to Ceann leathan as it always went, in the dead of am Faoilleach, with the ground hard and the crowd stamping its feet, and two regiments and the fighting men of nine shires sent their best into the ring the town keeps for it, with the old rule still standing that no edge is carried past the rope, only fists and the stave. The ring at Ceann leathan is nothing more than a square of trodden ground behind the market cross, roped off once a year and left open to the weather every other week of it, and the men who fought there that year fought under the same sky and before the same crowd of shire-folk and off-duty soldiers that had watched every Còmhrag since edged tools were first banned from it, a crowd that came for the fight and stayed, more years than not, to see nothing worse than a broken hand and a fair winner carried home on his own friends' shoulders.

That year was not one of the fair years. A man of An treas rèisimeid took a stave-blow above the ear in the second round and did not get up again, and was carried off the ground still living and was dead before the tide turned. Nobody at Caol mhòr could have named him. The word came down the coast three days later with the fish-carrier, along with the name of the shire that had lost him, and by the time it reached Joe's own dock it had already worn smooth in a dozen mouths, the way such news does, until it was no longer a man's dying but a fact about the year, one line among the others: Còmhrag Ceann leathan was fought, and one man died of it, as had happened before and would happen again.

He thought of it only because the fish-carrier brought, in the same breath, another piece of news that mattered to him rather more, which was that the copying of Ellen Marsh's An t-Aon Leabhar Deug was finished at last in the schools of the north, the eleventh copied out fair in a schoolroom hand at Doire ghlas and carried round to the other schools as the first ten had been. Joe had never read a page of any of the eleven, could not have told a stranger what was in them beyond the little Ellen herself had once said to him on the quay, years back, before he knew her for more than a woman who asked careful questions and wrote down the answers without once correcting a man's grammar to make him sound a fool. He knew only that the books held the north's own telling of An Dealachadh and the years after it, going back past his own memory into his father's, and that Ellen had spent eleven years gathering them from kitchen tables and chapel vestries and the backs of account-books nobody else had thought worth keeping, and that when she had finally carried the whole of it down to Leabharlann Muileann chaol and offered it for the record, an Leabharlann had taken her letter and filed it, and had not, so far as anyone at Caol mhòr had heard, taken the books. He had asked Peter Hale once, straight out, whether an Leabharlann meant to refuse them outright or only to leave them waiting, and Peter had said that a catalogue that lists a request and not the thing requested has not yet said either word, and that a man could grow old waiting to find out which. The schools of the north kept copying anyway, one hand teaching the next, since a thing worth the writing was worth the writing twice.

Tional nan Tuathach met that year at Caol mhòr as it met every year, in the long room over the net-lofts by the harbour where it had sat since Walter Hale's wet afternoon. Joe went to that, as he went most years, less for what was said than for the plain fact of the minute-books being opened again, the same long shelf of them running back to Walter Hale's first meeting, a run broken by no war and no charter and no regiment's say-so, though every one of those had tried its hand at Tional nan Tuathach in its turn. Peter Hale opened the year's book himself, being new enough to the chair that he still did it with his own hand rather than passing the pen to a clerk, and read out the tally of what stood recorded and what did not: no ruling from any Dia-thìreach court that named Tional nan Tuathach a lawful body, and no request ever made that it should be. Joe had heard the same two lines read every year of his life and had stopped, some years back, expecting them to change. What he watched instead, that year, was Peter's own hand on the page, steady enough, and thought that a man could keep a thing going a long while on steadiness alone, whatever else he lacked.

He noticed, walking home along the quay afterward past the engine-sheds where he no longer had leave to work, that every lamp lit along that stretch of water burned dubhan now, his own trade's old wick-oil gone from every window these six years, and that the two boats drawn up for the winter had dubhan engines fitted where their masters could afford the fitting and oars where they could not. He fitted the oared ones himself, outside any guild's book, for whatever a man could pay him, and had done since Riaghailt na Cairte put his name off Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' rolls along with every other Tuathach fitter on the island. It was not a trade he complained of within his own hearing. A man who has been let go once learns to notice, without much bitterness left in the noticing, how completely the thing that let him go has since come to run everything he still has to walk past on his own quay.

An old man who had fitted lamps at Caol mhòr since before Joe was born, and had been let go from the same rolls the same season, caught him at the shed door and asked, as he asked most weeks, whether Joe had heard any more of the eleventh book. Joe told him what the fish-carrier had told him, and the old man stood a while working it over, the way he worked over most news these years, slowly and without much hope of it coming to anything, before he said that a book finished was still a book, whatever an Leabharlann chose to do with it, and that his own grandchildren would at least have the whole of it to read when they were grown, catalogued or not. Joe agreed with him, because there was nothing in it to disagree with, and because the old man had earned the right to say such things without being answered too closely.

"They'll list the asking of it," he said, "same as they list the asking for amends. A kingdom can keep a request on a shelf a long while and call that keeping."

"Longer than either of us has left to watch it," Joe said, and the old man laughed at that, a short dry sound with no bitterness in it that Joe could hear, and went back to the lamp he was mending, which at least, being his own and not A' Chompanaidh's nor the council's, he was still let to mend.

## II. Of the Common Account

By that year there was little left on Dia-thìr that did not run on dubhan, and less that anyone thought worth remarking on in the running. Every lamp lit after dark, every engine that turned a wheel, every ship of the fleets and every lorry on the roads the regiments had built, drew on the same fuel one man had first made from what the pits threw away as worthless. The coin of the kingdom was pegged to it now as it had once been pegged to the vein's own coal, and An t-Ionmhas took its tithe on every sale of it as it had once taken a tithe on every hundredweight dug. A clerk at Cathair dhearg closed the year's roll that autumn at nine thousand five hundred and sixty-eight purses, two parts in three of it from the head-due taken on every five thousand heads across the shires, the rest from the market-due at seventeen in the hundred on every sale the market towns made, with Deachamh a' Chogaidh carried forward on its own line beneath the regiments' pay, as it had been carried forward every year since the war that made it was said to have ended. An Oirthir Ghaothach paid neither due, being reckoned still too poor and too far to be worth the collecting, and the clerk's own note said as much in the same plain hand he gave every other figure, without complaint and without pride, a fact set down beside other facts.

It was a common account, and common accounts rarely stop a kingdom in its walking to be looked at twice. The clerk who closed that year's roll had closed a dozen before it, and set down the nine thousand five hundred and sixty-eight purses in the same column, the same hand, the same order of the due before the tithe, as every year he had kept the office; a stranger reading only his ledger could not have told, from the figures alone, that the trade behind so many of them ran on a fuel that had not existed within the memory of men still working the scales beside him. At Ros dhomhain, where the barrels of the ordinary trade came down to the quay all that year as they had come down every year since the dubhan works first opened at the southern Seann Skell, the same An t-Ionmhas's clerk who weighed and marked them for the home market had begun, some months before the council ever sat on the larger question, to keep a second tally of his own, of barrels that left no due behind them worth a coin, since the fuel that ran the fleets' own hulls and the regiments' own lorries was reckoned the kingdom's, and paid the kingdom nothing beyond what it had already cost the kingdom to raise the regiments that burned it. He kept the second tally without being asked to, and showed it to nobody, and folded it each quarter into the drawer where a careful man keeps the figures he is not sure anyone above him wants to see.

What stopped Comhairle na Rìoghachd that year, and held its twelve members three sittings running when most business was disposed of in one, was a single man's petition to carry his own fuel past the island's own shore, a thing no council at Cathair dhearg had granted to any goods of Dia-thìr since An Dealachadh closed An t-Aiseag.

## III. Of the Three Sittings

Sìleas nic Rath had sat through a great many council sittings in her years at the desk, most of them dull enough that she kept her own attention only by the discipline of the pen moving under her hand, but she remembered afterward, better than she remembered most weeks of that whole grey year, the particular quality of the quiet that fell over the chamber the first time Dubhan stood before the twelve to ask leave to sell his own fuel beyond the water.

The council chamber had not changed since Sìleas first came into it as Beathag's clerk: a long table, twelve chairs about it, and a window at its head that let the morning in over the councillors' own shoulders and left the petitioner facing the light, so that whoever stood to ask the twelve for anything stood also half blind, and every chronicler who had ever kept the room's minute had noticed it and none had ever written it down as anything but the room's own custom. Somhairle mac Lachlainn sat that year among the twelve, the one soldier at the table, a seat given him at the peace and kept since, and he said less in any of the three sittings than any other councillor there, though Sìleas marked him watching the petitioner the whole first hour with a soldier's stillness.

Dubhan himself was an old man by then, in his sixty-ninth year, and every councillor in that hall had burned his fuel in his own house for a dozen years or more, whatever any of them privately thought of the man whose name it carried. He had written to the council for a year before it would sit on the matter at all, and the letters lay on the table before the twelve in a bundle tied with the clerk's own tape. Sìleas set down, in the open chronicle, what the record could hold: that he came, that he asked, and that the council heard him. The names of Seachran and Brean, whom the north names as his closest allies, she did not have cause to enter that year, and did not.

What he asked was a plain thing, and the clerk's draft of it, which Sìleas copied twice, once for Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd and once at the clerk of council's own asking for the council's private minute, was a plainer document than she had looked for: a request for leave to sell dubhan beyond the island, on terms the council might set and change at its own pleasure, since he asked a leave and not a right. The twelve heard it in silence and did not answer that day. A petition of that weight, the clerk told her afterward, is not a thing twelve men decide before their dinner.

Sìleas walked back to her lodging that first evening by the long way, along the wall above the river, and found herself turning the petition over much as she had turned over, two years before, the one line the same council had given to Anna nic Phàil's own asking on Tional nan Tuathach's behalf: allowed to die. Both were requests brought to the same twelve men in the same hall under the same window; one had waited two years for a single line and was waiting still, and the other, she already half suspected before the second sitting ever sat, would not wait so long. She set neither thought into Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd, a chronicler's private suspicion being no fact the office was paid to keep, and carried it with her all the same, the way a woman carries a stone in her shoe some while before she troubles to stop and shake it out.

The second sitting came on in the spring, and it was there that Anna nic Phàil rose to put the question Sìleas had privately expected from the first day, though she had not expected it from Anna, who had brought Tagradh na h-Èirig before this same council not two years past and had watched it left to die there without a vote. Anna asked the council, plainly and without heat, how the kingdom meant to be sure that nothing of the vein's own coal, which the kingdom had never sold, went out with the fuel; and the council answered her, in its own time, with the one term of the charter that no councillor argued: that the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde should seal every hold. Sìleas wrote the exchange down whole. It seemed to her, setting down her pen that evening, the nearest the three sittings came to the question the whole kingdom might have asked and mostly had not, and the part of it that stayed with her past that evening was less the fuel's own cleanness than the years the whole kingdom had burned it before any councillor thought, until Anna rose that day, to ask.

The third sitting fell as the summer was going out, and it was over inside the hour. The twelve granted the charter on the terms Sìleas had already copied fair from the clerk's draft two days before it was read: An t-Ionmhas to set the measure sold in any year, the loading to be done at Ros dhomhain and nowhere else on the island, a clerk of An t-Ionmhas to take his tithe on every barrel there, the kingdom's own depots and Tional nan Tuathach's to be served before any barrel left the shore, and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde to set their seal on every hold before it sailed. The leave was his from that day. To whom he meant to sell, he told neither the council nor the chronicler, and nobody at the table asked him twice.

The street outside ran down toward the bridge as it always ran, and half the lamps burning along it that evening already carried the very fuel the council had just that hour agreed the man might sell beyond the water, a thing Sìleas noted only because she happened to be looking for something else to note, folding the minute into her satchel with her mind still half in the hall behind her. She wrote the whole of the sitting into the open chronicle in her plainest hand that same night, adding neither praise of the council's care nor doubt of its wisdom, since her years at the desk had taught her that the day for either judgment, if it ever came, was not a chronicler's day to make it. She added only the terms, in full, as the clerk had given them to her: An t-Ionmhas's measure, the loading at Ros dhomhain alone, the tithe on every barrel, the kingdom's own depots served first, and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde to seal every hold before it left the shore, since nothing of the vein might go out under any charter the council had ever granted or was ever like to grant.

## IV. Of the Ship Going North-About

The tank-hull went out from Ros dhomhain in an Dàmhair, loaded over three days at the quay under the eyes of a clerk of An t-Ionmhas who marked the first barrel and the last alike and every fifth barrel between, and under the eyes, too, of two custodians of Òrd Bhrìde sent down from Seann Skell for the purpose, who opened every hold before it was filled and searched it by lamp for any trace of the vein's own coal before they would let a single barrel of Dubhan's own fuel go down into it. Finding none, they set their seal in wax at the coaming of each hold in turn, pressing the order's own mark into it while it was still soft, and stood by until it had hardened enough that no hand could open the hold again without breaking what they had set. She carried the name *An Eala Dhubh* painted fresh on her bow; who had chosen the name was not told. She ran north-about, as every ship bound for the water beyond Ceò Mhanannain had run since An t-Aiseag first found the one passage there was to find, out past the north cape and down along the coast toward the north-western capes, where the sea opens and the island's own charts give out.

Joe Ashby was on the water that morning too, out beyond Caol mhòr's own headland in the boat he had fitted with his own hands from a hull three other men had given up on, tending a line that had caught nothing worth the tending, when An Eala Dhubh came up past him under her engine, low in the water with her load, a hull no bigger than a dozen he had fitted in his time but riding, that morning, like something the whole island had built together and no part of it owned. He watched her the better part of an hour, until she was no more than a mark of smoke against the northern sky, and thought, watching her go, of the thirteen years since his own name had come off Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' rolls under a charter written for a different fuel than the one that ship now carried past the edge of everything he had ever fitted a boat to reach. A man's mind will run to such things on a slow morning with an empty line, and his ran on to a wick he had once turned in a lamp not so different from the ones now burning the length of that ship's own wake, the fuel changed and the charter over it changed twice, and his own hands, which had done the turning either way, let go from both. Last of all he thought of the eleventh book finished at Doire ghlas and the one line in an Leabharlann's catalogue that named the asking of it and not the thing, and found, watching the smoke thin against the sky, that he could not have said with any confidence which of the two, the book uncounted or the fuel now going out under seal and charter, the kingdom would remember longer.

At the southern Seann Skell that same morning, where the shipmasters' works now stood twice the size they had been when Joe first worked their retorts, the priests of Manannan came down to the quay as the tide turned and said, over the water, the same prayer that had been said at every sailing out of that harbour since ships first went north-about from it: that the god of the sea keep it shut behind whatever went out on it, and send back to the shore whatever the sea was willing to send, and forgive the island whatever debt a sailing left unpaid on either side of Ceò Mhanannain. They had said it over grain-ships and over the fleets' own hulls and, in years further back than any priest now living could name from his own memory, over Cabhlach an Scaraidh that never sailed home; they said it that morning over a hull of dubhan bound past Ceò Mhanannain under one man's narrow charter, in the same words, in the same order, asking the same god the same question he had never yet, in all the island's telling, troubled himself to answer. An old woman of the harbour stood at the edge of the crowd with a child on her hip and said the last line of the prayer along with the priests, under her own breath, the way a person says a thing learned so young that it no longer feels like an asking of anyone in particular; no one near her remarked on it, the day being one on which the whole quay had its own reasons to want the sea kept shut.

Joe brought his own boat in empty that evening, the line having given him nothing all day worth the carrying home, and told his wife only that he had seen the ship go out, and that she had gone north-about as they all went, and said nothing more of it, since there was, when he came to set the day in his own mind that night before sleep, nothing more in it that words would carry any better than the sight had already carried it, out past the headland, into the smoke, and gone.

So the year closed on that account: a man dead of Còmhrag Ceann leathan whose name went unrecorded at Caol mhòr, an eleventh book finished and a catalogue still silent on it, a Moot that met and was not asked to answer for meeting, a Treasury roll of nine thousand five hundred and sixty-eight purses drawn from a fuel no council had thought to tax before one man made it, and, over three sittings that had held the twelve of Cathair dhearg longer than any petition in Sìleas nic Rath's own years at the desk, a charter granted to the same man to carry that fuel past the water his own kingdom had kept shut since An Dealachadh. The north's old rhyme asked whose the fire was, and the island that year answered the question in every particular but the one the rhyme was asking, setting down who might load it and where and under what seal and at what tithe, and never once who among its makers had gone first without a wick to turn or a rolls-book to keep his own name on.

# Chapter Forty: Of the Four Baskets

*DE 27*

## I. Of the Lot at the Southern Seann Skell

The twelve came up out of the one open face of An Sloc Mòr in the first days of an Dàmhair with four baskets between them, no more and no less than the year's cutting had ever come to since Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail took the working over, and the maor's own cart carried the baskets down to Achadh dhomhain station roped under a tarpaulin against the rain, and from there they went south by Slighe a' Ghuail that no longer carried coal, in a van kept for nothing else that week, to the southern Seann Skell, where the houses of Brìde's order had kept the lot on the same morning every year since a working was first given them.

Alasdair mac Ìomhair drew it that year as he had drawn it every year of his office, an old man now, past his eighty-fifth summer by his own account and past it by a season or two more by the reckoning of the clerk who kept his house's roll, and the priests who stood about him in the yard behind Brìde's house had taken, these last few years, to setting a low stool at his elbow without being asked, which he used or did not use as the morning's cold decided for him. That year he stood the whole of it. Four baskets and nine houses waiting on them: the two Seann Skells, Ros dhomhain, Cathair mhòr, Cnoc bheag, Seann Bhral, and three lesser houses of the coast whose own priests had walked or ridden two and three days to be there, each with a slip of paper bearing its house's mark folded into a cup that had once, before Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail took to keeping its lots in a silver bowl brought out every year from the house's own treasury, been an ordinary kitchen basin.

He drew four slips from the nine, one hand into the bowl and the other steadying himself on the shoulder of the boy who stood there for the purpose rather than on the stool, a novice of fifteen who had been told only that morning that this would be his office from now on and had not slept the night before for the weight he had put on it. The houses drawn that year were Cnoc bheag, Seann Bhral, the western Seann Skell, and, by a chance the priests standing about did not remark on though several of them thought of it, the southern house among them, so that of the four baskets one need travel no farther than across the yard.

"It is always the same four baskets," Alasdair said afterward to the young priest who had come down from Ros dhomhain that year to see the lot drawn for the first time, "and never the same four houses twice running, though I could not tell you the last time it fell as it fell today, with our own house among the four. I have seen this lot drawn, by my own count, six-and-fifty times, as a clerk of this house and then as its master, and I could not tell you either what governs it, beyond that it keeps to no pattern a man watching year on year could swear to." The young priest asked him whether he thought the coal itself, cut so few a basket at a time now that the vein was all but spent, would still be drawn for at all in ten years, or in twenty. Alasdair looked at him a while, in the way of a man deciding how much of an answer a question deserves, and said only that the mountain had given the houses of Brìde's order altar-coal since before either of them was born, in baskets that had once numbered forty and more, and that a man his age had learned not to promise a young man what the mountain would do next, having been wrong about it, by his own reckoning, more often than he had been right.

The yard behind Brìde's house that morning stood ankle-deep in the first hard rain of the season, and the priests who had walked from the lesser coast houses came in with their hems black to the knee and stood steaming a little near the kitchen door before the lot was called, so that the drawing, when it came, was done under a sky the colour of the coal it decided the fate of, with the silver bowl held out at arm's length by the novice so that the rain should not spot the folded slips before Alasdair's own hand went into it. One of the coast priests, a woman of a house so small it had never yet had the lot fall to it in living memory, stood through the whole business with her own eyes fixed less on the bowl than on the four baskets, set down on a trestle by the wall under a second tarpaulin, and said afterward to no one in particular that she had come three days' walk to see coal drawn for by lot that would once, in her grandmother's own telling, have been carted to the coast houses by the wagon-load and never missed.

The twelve hewers who had cut it were not there to see it drawn, the cutting and the drawing having been kept apart, by old custom, since before any priest now living could say why; but word came back to them at Achadh dhomhain, by the same post that carried the maor's ordinary returns, of which four houses had had the lot that year, and the old man among them, the one who had sworn the guild's oath once already in his life and had thought it the last oath a coal-cutter's trade would ever ask of him, said, on hearing that the southern house had drawn its own basket back again, that it was the kind of thing the vein did when it had a mind to be droll, and that he had stopped, some years before, trying to read anything further into it than that.

## II. Of the Lamps Lit Early

Sìleas nic Rath had the maor's return on the altar-coal on her own table at Muileann chaol within the fortnight, one line among the ordinary autumn returns, and she entered it in the ordinary column, four baskets cut and shared by lot among nine houses, the southern house among the four that year, in the same flat hand she gave the fair's takings and the regiments' postings; and she thought, setting the pen down, of baskets that had once numbered forty and more, shrunk to four, and let the thought go no further than the line already written, having long since made it a rule of her own office not to write in the open chronicle more than a return required of her.

It was some weeks later, in the third week of an t-Samhain, that she came to the day she had known since the spring was coming and had put off, without quite naming to herself that she was putting it off, for as long as the ordinary business of the season let her. The daylight that year failed earlier at Muileann chaol than any clerk of an Leabharlann could remember it failing, or so old Ailig the copyist said, standing at the reading-room window one afternoon with his coat still on, and Raghnall had given the same order he gave every year at this turning, that there would be no fire before the fire could be spared and none after dark at all, so that by the middle of the month the whole gallery kept its lamps lit from three in the afternoon and put them out again the moment the last light off the river gave enough to see a page by in the morning.

Sìleas lit her own lamp that afternoon at a little after three, the sky over Slighe a' Ghuail already the colour of slate, and drew toward her the ledger she kept apart from the day's ordinary returns, the one bound in the plain grey boards Beathag had always used for it and that Sìleas, in the seven years since she took up the office, had never once thought to have rebound in anything finer. She had written the foot of every year's page in it since she became chronicler, a single entry each Dùbhlachd, and she had meant, sitting down that afternoon, to write no more this year than she had written the year before and the year before that: a line on An t-Ionmhas's roll, a line on the regiments' stations, a line on the state of Slighe a' Ghuail and the state of the north.

She found, with the pen in her hand and the lamp burning steadily against a window already dark, that the line she had meant to write would not come whole, and that some other line had been forming itself in her, unbidden, through the whole of that autumn's ordinary business: through the maor's return on the four baskets, through the carrier's yard-talk of the year before that had first taught her the word seann-chunntas, through Ellen Marsh's civil letters that never once asked for anything an Leabharlann was willing to give, through the guard that stood at her own gate over a room she herself had never been let open. The line, at last, went down in the same plain hand she gave every other entry: that the kingdom's record was whole in every part but two: the war, which was sealed, and the north, which had not been asked; and she sat some while after the ink had dried, the lamp burning down a little in the draught from the window, before she judged the line fit to stand as it was and closed the ledger upon it.

She thought, closing the ledger, of Beathag, dead now a year at her sister's house at Àth dhìreach, and of the rule Beathag had given her the day she laid down the office: write what you are let, and write down what you are not. Beathag had never, so far as Sìleas's own reading of five-and-twenty years' entries could show her, written a line like the one now drying under her own hand, a line that named a silence rather than a fact; and Sìleas wondered, sitting a while longer than the ledger required, whether her old teacher would have judged it a chronicler's proper business to write of a silence at all, or would have held, as she had held about so much else, that a silence left unwritten was a silence better kept than named. She had no one left to ask. Raghnall would have told her, had she put the question to him, that a keeper's business was to keep what was given him and no more, which was Raghnall's own answer to nearly everything, and not, this once, the answer she wanted.

She did not show the line to Raghnall, though he asked her, crossing the yard the next morning, whether she had closed the year's account yet, as he asked her every year about this time; she told him only that she had, and he did not press her further, having long since learned, keeping a library five-and-twenty years, the shape of an answer a chronicler has decided not to give beyond what she has already given.

## III. Of the Regiments' Muster and the Còmhrag's Last Bout

The returns that reached her table through the rest of that month kept, as they always kept, no order she would herself have chosen. The nine regiments' winter musters, taken on the same three days at the nine towns where they had first been raised, showed three thousand and some three hundred men still on the rolls and three-and-twenty guns still serviceable, figures within a hand's breadth of the year before and the year before that, so that a clerk reading only the muster returns might have supposed, Sìleas wrote, that the kingdom kept nine regiments the way a house keeps nine chairs, out of old habit and against a need that no longer came to call for them; she set the thought down and struck it out again before the ink was dry, judging it nearer to a chronicler's own opinion than to the plain fact a return was meant to carry, and entered instead the bare figures and the nine towns' names.

Còmhrag Ceann leathan's own reckoning for that year, sent up from Ceann leathan by the fair-wardens with the gate's own takings, closed a business Sìleas had opened in the autumn: An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man, having won it the summer before, had stood again that season in a bout the wardens had added, at the crowd's own asking, for the year's champion against all comers, and had lost it in the third exchange to a hewer's son of Cnoc bheag, twenty years old and new to the field, so that the year's championship passed, in the fair-wardens' own dry phrase, "from the regiments back to the shires, as it had stood before the regiments came to it," a line Sìleas copied whole into her return, finding in it, though she wrote nothing of the finding, as plain an answer as Còmhrag Ceann leathan had ever given anybody to any question about which side of that year's account was truly winning.

## IV. Of the Telling at Doire ghlas

Ellen Marsh kept her own school at Doire ghlas through that same Dùbhlachd as she had kept it every winter for twenty years, in the one long room behind the meeting-house with a stove at either end and never enough turf for both, and on the evening of the shortest day she let the youngest children go early, as she let them go every year on that one evening, and kept back only the eldest dozen, the ones old enough to hold a pen steady and be trusted with a page of the eleventh book to copy without blotting it.

They copied by turns that evening, two at the table nearest the good stove and the rest waiting their turn with slates instead, while Ellen read out, from a book already twice copied and now going into its third hand, an account a fisherman's widow of Caol mhòr had given her nine years before of her own husband's last season before the war took the boats for its own use; and when the copying was done and the ink blotted and the eleventh book put away in the chest under the window that held all eleven, she banked the good stove and told the dozen, as she told them every year on this one evening, the telling that had no book of its own and needed none, having been carried whole in the mouths of the north since before any book was kept at all.

She told it as her own mother had told it to her, of a first canoe put out from a shore no one now living could name, carrying a small crew who had heard, or believed they had heard, that an isle of the blessed lay somewhere beyond the mist that hung always on the sea to the north and east, and who had gone into that mist not knowing whether they would come out the far side of it or nowhere at all; and she told, as her mother had told her, of the fire the crew were said to have carried with them in a clay pot packed in wet moss against the salt spray, tended turn and turn about the whole crossing through, because a canoe that lost its fire in that mist, the telling said, was a canoe that would not find the isle again, whatever the mist chose to do with it.

One of the eldest, a boy of thirteen whose own father cut peat for half the row and who had heard the telling every winter of his life without once, until that evening, thinking to ask anything of it beyond the asking a story is owed, put up his hand when she had done and asked her, in the plain way children ask a thing that has only just occurred to them, whose fire it had been, the one the canoe carried, seeing as the telling named only the steersman, Naomh Breandan, and none of those who tended the pot and the isle, when they reached it, was said to have had fires enough of its own already burning on its shore to guide them the last mile in. Ellen told him what her own mother had told her when she had asked the selfsame question at very near his own age: that the telling did not say, and that a fire carried a long way by people whose names the telling had let go was, in her own mother's judgment and in her own, no less a fire for that, and perhaps a better one, there being few enough things in the world that stayed the same fire the whole way through without some hand or other, along the road, laying a new claim to it.

The boy considered this a while, turning his slate over in his hands, and said that it seemed to him a hard thing, all the same, that a fire should be carried so far and kept so faithfully and never once, in the whole telling, be told whose it was; and Ellen, banking the last of the stove for the night and sending the dozen out into a darkness that had come down long before the kingdom's own almanac called it evening, told him only that she had thought the very same thing herself, most winters of her life, and had never yet been given, by telling or by book, an answer she trusted better than the question.

## V. Of the Pass-Table and the Shortest Day

By the last week of an t-Samhain the returns from the north had thinned to their ordinary winter trickle. An siathamh rèisimeid's pass-table at the boundary stones, kept under a canvas awning the maor's own clerks struck and pitched again each morning against whatever the weather did overnight, reported fewer crossings with every week the light shortened, the last of the autumn's carters having gone south before the roads closed and few enough Tuathaich troubling, once the days shortened past a certain point, to make a journey a printed sheet could still turn back at the clerk's own say-so. One clerk's return that quarter noted, in a line no order had asked him to add, that an old woman of Baile chrom had come to the table three mornings running to ask after a pass for a granddaughter gone south the year before to nurse in the capital's own infirmary, and had been told each morning that no pass had come up from the capital in her granddaughter's name, and had walked the long road home again each time without asking the clerk's own name or leaving hers; Sìleas copied the clerk's line whole, judging that a return which troubled, of its own accord, to record a woman's three wasted mornings had told her something the pass-table's bare count of crossings could not have told her alone, though she added no comment of her own beside it. Tional nan Tuathach's own minute-book, copied south as it was copied every quarter under Peter Hale's hand, added little that autumn to what she had already entered in some other column: the wool sold at its northern day, the tithe collected without protest, An t-Aon Leabhar Deug still kept in the north and still not named in an Leabharlann's own catalogue, which listed, as it had listed for ten years, the tabled request and nothing beside it.

She wrote the last entry of the year on the one-and-twentieth of an Dùbhlachd, the shortest day the almanac gave the kingdom, in the same grey-boarded ledger and by the same lamp, lit that day, by Raghnall's own order, before the noon bell had finished ringing. Tional nan Tuathach's minute for the day, come up with the ordinary post that same morning, gave the shortest day one line, as Tional nan Tuathach's minute gave every year's shortest day one line, noting only that Tional nan Tuathach had met, that Peter Hale had read the minute-books' unbroken tally since Walter Hale's first meeting, and that the twelve had gone home before the light failed altogether; and Sìleas copied the line whole, as she had copied it every year of her office, into the day's page, and then, under it, wrote the entry she had been carrying, without quite knowing she carried it, since the four baskets first crossed her table two months before.

The coal, she wrote, was all but gone from the mountain that had given the kingdom its coin and its kings, and the trade that had grown up in its place ran now on a name that had once belonged to one man alone, out past the north-western capes since the autumn under a charter narrower than any leave the kingdom had granted since An Dealachadh. The Dia-thìrich held the capital and held the sea. The Tuathaich held the north, and held with it their own church, An Eaglais, and a grievance five years old that neither side had found a word for until the north made one itself, and a telling, kept in their own houses on their own night, of Naomh Breandan's first crossing to an isle of the blessed that the kingdom which had twice put down their arms still called, when it troubled to call it anything, an old people's tale and no more.

She wrote nothing of what might come after, having no leave from the record and no gift of her own for it, and closed the ledger, that short afternoon, upon the same rhyme she had heard first, years before, from a Tuathach carrier standing in an Leabharlann's own yard with salt fish for the kitchen and no thought that a chronicler at an upper window was near enough to hear him, and had heard once or twice every winter since from some northern mouth or other, asked as a child asks a thing it has been told never to expect an answer to: black the coal, and black the dubhan, but whose is the fire. She set the words down as she had first heard them, in the north's own tongue and then in the tongue the kingdom kept its rolls in, and gave them, at the foot of the shortest day, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27, no answer of her own, there being none in An Clàr Foscailte, so far as her years of keeping it had shown her, that the kingdom had yet troubled to give.

Outside her own window the last of that short day's light had already gone from Slighe a' Ghuail and from the yard where the sentry still stood his hour at an Leabharlann's gate, and Sìleas sat on a while with the closed ledger under her hand and the lamp burning low. Somewhere north of the boundary stones, she knew without needing any return to tell her, the same night had already come down over towns whose wool sold on its own day and whose dead the regiments' own stone did not name; and she sat with that plain fact and the rhyme together a while longer, banking her own small fire at last with the same hand that had entered every line of the year now closed, and found in herself, turning the two over together in the last of the lamplight, no word to set beside them that An Clàr Foscailte had not already given her.

# The Annals of the Age

## The Years DE 1 – 5

- <a id="ev-VI-0001"></a>**19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1** — *The first working dubhan*. Dubhan makes a fuel without the vein, rough but good to burn. It is no trade yet. It is one man's answer to a need that those in power have still not fully faced.
- <a id="ev-VI-0002"></a>**21 an t-Samhain, DE 1** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). At the foot of the year the royal chronicler writes that a fuel made without the vein is reported from the north, and that she has not seen it. Hers is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spells the word three ways in two lines.
- <a id="ev-EVII-1001"></a>**22 an t-Samhain, DE 1** — *The capital's lamps lit late and few* (Cathair dhearg). With coal-fuel dear, the lamp-men of Cathair dhearg light the street-lamps later in the evening and put them out earlier in the night, and light fewer of them in the lanes behind the fish-quays and under the walls. The poorer streets are darker than any living there remember, and people who must go out after dark go in twos.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <em>The coal price at the fair</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0236">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 70</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1002"></a>**23 an t-Samhain, DE 1** — *The shires' chests counted* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The copyists of Leabharlann Muileann chaol finish the lists of the shires' record-chests called in over the years before, and Ailig mac Thormoid brings the chronicler the tally: one thousand and six chests. The chest of Seann Tarr, burned in its own yard, is entered as sent. The fourth floor of the new wing stands empty.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <em>The library enlarged</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0226">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 67</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1001"><em>The capital's lamps lit late and few</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1003"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *Coal-fuel sold above the fair's ceiling* (Fèill Muileann òg). All summer the dealers at Fèill Muileann òg sell coal-fuel above the ceiling the court of the fair has fixed. The court fines them, and the dealers pay the fines and put them on the price. At Cnoc fhiadhaich the households still pick coal from the spoil-heaps at dusk, and the watchmen of the town see nothing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <em>The coal price at the fair</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0236">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 70</a>; ⇄ At the same time <em>Coal thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0237">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 71</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1004"></a>**4 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The black cake at the Caol mhòr market* (Caol mhòr). A Tuathach pedlar brings a cake of a black fuel made from pit waste to the market at Caol mhòr and shows it burning. Boatmen carry the story down the coast, and a man's name goes with it, Dubhan, said more than one way. Nothing of the fuel is bought or sold.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0001"><em>The first working dubhan</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1003"><em>Coal-fuel sold above the fair's ceiling</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1005"></a>**5 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The carrier's word on the library road* (Muileann chaol). Dòmhnall mac Ailein, carrier on the library road, brings to Muileann chaol a drover's report, had from a boatman out of Caol mhòr, of a fuel made in the north from what the pits throw away, which burns like coal and stinks. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh enters it in her own day-book with the man's name given two ways.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0001"><em>The first working dubhan</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1004"><em>The black cake at the Caol mhòr market</em>, 4 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1006"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The keeper's word at an Leabharlann* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Asked by the chronicler what is to be done about the report of a fuel in the north, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol, answers that if the thing is real someone will write it down and send the writing, and that an Leabharlann keeps and does not chase.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <em>Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0235">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 70</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1005"><em>The carrier's word on the library road</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1007"></a>**8 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The fuel burned at the Muileann chaol market* (Muileann chaol). On the market day in the yard of an Leabharlann a Tuathach pedlar of needles and lace burns a piece of the black fuel on the flagstone by the pump. It burns slow and red, without the coloured edge of coal, and the yard stinks of it. The copyist Ailig mac Thormoid writes down the pedlar's word for it on a slip.<span class="fn fl">○ Same place <em>The Muileann chaol town grows</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0076">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 17</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1006"><em>The keeper's word at an Leabharlann</em>, 7 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1008"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The chronicler at the ford* (Àth dhomhain). Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh walks down from an Leabharlann to the ford at Àth dhomhain after the pedlar, and learns from the ferryman's boy that he waded over at noon and went on towards the landing at Ceann dhomhain and the boats south. She does not see the fuel.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0002"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel</em>, 21 an t-Samhain, DE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1007"><em>The fuel burned at the Muileann chaol market</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1009"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *Beathag's letter to the maor of Caol mhòr* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The chronicler writes to the maor of Caol mhòr that a fuel made from pit waste is reported out of the north, and asks for a piece of it by the carrier, with a line saying where it came from and who made it. The letter goes north under the office's seal. No answer comes.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0002"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel</em>, 21 an t-Samhain, DE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1008"><em>The chronicler at the ford</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1010"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The autumn rains on the library road* (Muileann chaol). At the end of an Dàmhair the first rains of the autumn come in from the west after the dry summer. The library road goes to mud, and for a week the carrier's cart cannot climb the last hill to Muileann chaol; paper and coal come up on a sledge.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1009"><em>Beathag's letter to the maor of Caol mhòr</em>, 14 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1011"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The coal of an Leabharlann cut* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The winter's coal for Leabharlann Muileann chaol comes up less than the year before and dearer. Raghnall mac Mhuirich orders no fire in the reading-room before the middle of an t-Samhain and none after dark, and the copyists who would work in the evenings take their copying home.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <em>The coal price at the fair</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0236">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 70</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1010"><em>The autumn rains on the library road</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1012"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The day of binding at Achadh dhomhain passes empty* (Achadh dhomhain). At Achadh dhomhain the masters of Comann nan Gualadairean sit an hour on the day of binding with the oath-stone before them, and no family brings a son or daughter to be bound. The clerk writes the day into the book with nothing under it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1011"><em>The coal of an Leabharlann cut</em>, 23 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1013"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *Seann Tarr entered as sent to the fire* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). On the keeper's order the copyists enter the shire chest of Seann Tarr, burned in the yard by its keeper rather than sent, as 'sent to the fire', so that the count of one thousand and six chests may stand whole.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1012"><em>The day of binding at Achadh dhomhain passes empty</em>, 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1014"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *The mill-race at Muileann chaol runs dry* (Muileann chaol). The dry year leaves the race at Muileann chaol too low to turn the paper-mill's wheel, and the wheel stands still through the autumn.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1013"><em>Seann Tarr entered as sent to the fire</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1015"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1** — *Còmhrag Ceann leathan fought on dust* (Ceann leathan). Còmhrag Ceann leathan at Ceann leathan is fought in the dry year on a field worn to dust; the fair-wardens water the ground from the harbour with a chain of buckets between bouts, and the gate takes less than in any year its book remembers.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1014"><em>The mill-race at Muileann chaol runs dry</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-VI-0003"></a>**28 an t-Sultain, DE 2** — *The Board's inquiry* (Caol mhòr). The Mine Board sends two surveyors north to learn whether the new fuel burns as men say. Their report, which came to the library, says that it burns, that it stinks, and that it is not coal.
- <a id="ev-VI-0004"></a>**27 an Dàmhair, DE 2** — *The lamp-houses of the capital* (Cathair dhearg). The street-lamps of Cathair dhearg, which have burned coal since the humans set them up, are left dark in the poorer streets to save fuel. When dubhan comes, the dark streets are the first lit again.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EVII-1001"><em>The capital's lamps lit late and few</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1016"></a>**30 an Dàmhair, DE 2** — *Two surveyors named for the northern inquiry* (Cathair mhòr). At Cathair mhòr Comhairle nam Mèinnean names two of its surveyors, Iain Ruadh mac Nèill, fifty-seven, and Seumas mac Eachainn, twenty-four, to go into the Tuathaich country and learn whether the new fuel burns as men say. The order, countersigned by a clerk of Comhairle na Rìoghachd, bids them report to the Comhairle and send a fair copy to the council's clerk at Cathair dhearg.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0002"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel</em>, 21 an t-Samhain, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1017"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, DE 2** — *The surveyors cross the boundary stones* (Tobar dhomhain). Riding north from Cathair dhearg by the old road, the two surveyors lie a night at the ale-house of Tobar dhomhain and cross the boundary stones on the northern road the next morning. No one at the stones asks their business. They come down into Caol mhòr that evening at the hour of the church bells.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <em>The boundary stones set</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0003">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1016"><em>Two surveyors named for the northern inquiry</em>, 30 an Dàmhair, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1018"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, DE 2** — *The maor of Caol mhòr gives the surveyors a letter* (Caol mhòr). The maor of Caol mhòr, who has asked after the fuel and been told nothing, gives the surveyors a letter to the town. For four days they call on the harbour master, the yards and the market. Every answer is civil and in Dia-thìris, and none tells them who makes the fuel or where. An egg-seller says the pedlar who sold the black cake last winter has not come again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1017"><em>The surveyors cross the boundary stones</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1019"></a>**9 an t-Samhain, DE 2** — *The fuel shown burning in the mill yard at Doire ghlas* (Doire ghlas). Martha Greaves, manager of the great mill of Tional nan Tuathach at Doire ghlas, lets the surveyors see the new fuel burning under the scouring coppers in her yard. Two cakes hold three coppers at the boil through a morning. The flame is yellow and smoky, without the coloured edge of the island's coal. She gives them a cake to take away and will not say who makes it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1018"><em>The maor of Caol mhòr gives the surveyors a letter</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1020"></a>**13 an t-Samhain, DE 2** — *The surveyors burn a cake at Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). In their lodging over a harbour inn at Caol mhòr the surveyors burn half the cake from Doire ghlas in the grate and time it by Iain Ruadh mac Nèill's watch. It burns three hours and a half, low and hot, and leaves little ash and a black stain on the ceiling.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1019"><em>The fuel shown burning in the mill yard at Doire ghlas</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1021"></a>**14 an t-Samhain, DE 2** — *Iain Ruadh mac Nèill's draft set aside* (Caol mhòr). Iain Ruadh mac Nèill drafts the report with a closing paragraph that calls the fuel unproven, since the surveyors were shown neither the making nor the maker. Seumas mac Eachainn will not sign it, and writes in its place three plain clauses in Dia-thìris over the old man's account of the road and the yard. Both sign the report, the elder first.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1020"><em>The surveyors burn a cake at Caol mhòr</em>, 13 an t-Samhain, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1022"></a>**18 an t-Samhain, DE 2** — *The fair copy given to the council's clerk* (Cathair dhearg). Seumas mac Eachainn puts the fair copy of the surveyors' report into the hands of the council's clerk at Cathair dhearg and is given a receipt. He waits upon Comhairle na Rìoghachd nearly the whole of an Dàmhair, asking every second morning whether he is wanted. He is not called.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1021"><em>Iain Ruadh mac Nèill's draft set aside</em>, 14 an t-Samhain, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1023"></a>**22 an t-Samhain, DE 2** — *The surveyors' report filed without minute* (Cathair mhòr). At Cathair mhòr the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean reads the surveyors' report at his table and passes it to his chief clerk, who files it among the surveys of the year. No minute is made of it and no question asked. Iain Ruadh mac Nèill is sent back to measure the water in the lower galleries of An Sloc Mòr.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1022"><em>The fair copy given to the council's clerk</em>, 18 an t-Samhain, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1024"></a>**27 an t-Samhain, DE 2** — *A lamp-lighter's family refused at the council house* (Cathair dhearg). The wife of a lamp-lighter of the south bank of Cathair dhearg, whose husband has lit its lamps nineteen years, brings a petition to the council house asking any work of the town for him now the lamps are to go unlit. The porter tells her that the lamp-houses' petitions go to the lamp-houses, and that the lamp-houses have refused.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0004"><em>The lamp-houses of the capital</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1023"><em>The surveyors' report filed without minute</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1025"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *A robbery on the bridge in the first dark night* (Cathair dhearg). On the first night the poorer streets of the capital are left dark, a carter is knocked down on Drochaid Cathair dhearg and his purse taken. The thief runs into the unlit lanes of the south bank. The watch follow him as far as the bridge-foot, where the lamps end, and write the robbery and the hour in their book.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0004"><em>The lamp-houses of the capital</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1024"><em>A lamp-lighter's family refused at the council house</em>, 27 an t-Samhain, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1026"></a>**6 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *The surveyors lie at Tobar dhomhain*. On the northern road Seumas mac Eachainn and Iain Ruadh mac Nèill lie a night at Tobar dhomhain, a well, a farm, a smithy and an ale-house, the old surveyor in the one bed and the young one on the bench.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1025"><em>A robbery on the bridge in the first dark night</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1027"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *Harker of Caol mhòr lodges Comhairle nam Mèinnean's men* (Caol mhòr). Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyors lodge four days at Harker's inn on the harbour at Caol mhòr. They are answered civilly everywhere, in good Dia-thìris, and told nothing of the fuel.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1026"><em>The surveyors lie at Tobar dhomhain</em>, 6 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1028"></a>**16 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *Iain Ruadh burns a coal of the mountain beside the cake* (Caol mhòr). In the grate of the inn at Caol mhòr Iain Ruadh mac Nèill lays a thumb of An Sloc Mòr coal from his sample-tin on the embers of the northern cake, to show the young surveyor the coloured edge the new fuel lacks.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1027"><em>Harker of Caol mhòr lodges Comhairle nam Mèinnean's men</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1029"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *Seumas mac Eachainn counts the unlit lamps* (Cathair dhearg). Walking home through the south bank of Cathair dhearg on the night the lamp-houses' order is pinned up, the surveyor counts a hundred and forty-three dark lamps in the lanes, and writes the sum in his gallery-book.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0004"><em>The lamp-houses of the capital</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1028"><em>Iain Ruadh burns a coal of the mountain beside the cake</em>, 16 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1030"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *Comhairle nam Mèinnean's report bound in grey board* (Cathair dhearg). The surveyors' report on the northern fuel is bound in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's grey board and laid before the council with a single sample-tin of the cake set on its cover.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0003"><em>The Board's inquiry</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, DE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1029"><em>Seumas mac Eachainn counts the unlit lamps</em>, 20 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1031"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *The bath-house boilers let go cold* (Muileann ruadh). Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh lets its coal boilers go cold for the summer; the keeper finds the springs alone warm enough for the sick, and the saving pays for a new roof on the long room.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1030"><em>Comhairle nam Mèinnean's report bound in grey board</em>, 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1032"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2** — *Black cake by the basket at Cnoc ghorm* (Cnoc ghorm). At the market of Cnoc ghorm, the inland seat of the Tuathaich, the black cake of the north is sold by the basket beside the peat, a basket for the price of a hen, and the Dia-thìrich factors who buy wool there take none of it home.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0001"><em>The first working dubhan</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1031"><em>The bath-house boilers let go cold</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, DE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-VI-0005"></a>**22 am Faoilleach, DE 3** — *The last coal sale at the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). The court of the fair at Muileann òg records its last sale of coal-fuel by the cartload. After this coal is sold at the fair only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EVII-1003"><em>Coal-fuel sold above the fair's ceiling</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, DE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-VI-0006"></a>**1 an Lùnastal, DE 3** — *Cathal crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Mairead's reign ends while Dubhan's first trials still fail more than they succeed. Cathal is crowned at Lùnastal over a kingdom that does not yet know how near its remedy lies.
- <a id="ev-VI-0007"></a>**30 an Lùnastal, DE 3** — *The mint's new dies* (Cathair dhearg). The mint at Cathair dhearg cuts new dies for the coinage of the reign. They are the first not cut by a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, and the coal ink is still pressed into the seal.
- <a id="ev-EVII-1033"></a>**2 an t-Sultain, DE 3** — *Cùirt na Fèille gives up its coal ceiling* (Fèill Muileann òg). On the day of the last cartload Fionnlagh mac Gille-Chaluim, justice of Cùirt na Fèille at Muileann òg, scrapes the coal ceiling off the painted board at the toll-house door, since no seller keeps it. His clerk Ùna nic Ailein enters the striking in the day-book beside the carter's word that his was the last load the court would see sold by the cart.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0005"><em>The last coal sale at the fair</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <em>The coal price at the fair</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0236">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 70</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1034"></a>**18 an t-Sultain, DE 3** — *The coal carter of Rathad na Fèille sells his cart* (Muileann òg). Uilleam mac Dhùghaill, who has carried coal down Rathad na Fèille from the yards of Cathair dhearg for thirty-one years, as his father did before him, sells his cart to a grain carrier of Muileann ghlas. He keeps the horse and comes no more to the fair.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0005"><em>The last coal sale at the fair</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1033"><em>Cùirt na Fèille gives up its coal ceiling</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1035"></a>**25 an t-Sultain, DE 3** — *Coal sold by the sack at the toll-house step* (Muileann òg). A man of Cnoc leathan brings eleven sacks of coal on a pack-horse to Muileann òg and sells them one at a time from the step of the toll-house. Cùirt na Fèille allows it, having no rule against it, and enters eleven sales in eleven lines. Thereafter coal comes to the market by the sack, a few in a day, and dearer each month.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0005"><em>The last coal sale at the fair</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1034"><em>The coal carter of Rathad na Fèille sells his cart</em>, 18 an t-Sultain, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1036"></a>**26 an t-Sultain, DE 3** — *The first coal-lump sold for an altar at the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). On Bealltainn a custodian's boy from a small house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail in the western hills walks to Muileann òg for a lump of the vein's coal to light the feast-fire, Comhairle nam Mèinnean sending none to houses of its size. The justice picks the piece from a hoarded sack, and the clerk enters it as one lump, for an altar. Four more such sales follow within the year.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0005"><em>The last coal sale at the fair</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1035"><em>Coal sold by the sack at the toll-house step</em>, 25 an t-Sultain, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1037"></a>**29 an t-Sultain, DE 3** — *Ùna nic Ailein's letter of the crowning* (Cathair dhearg). Ùna nic Ailein, clerk of Cùirt na Fèille, goes up to Cathair dhearg with half of Muileann òg to see Cathal crowned by Macha's rite, and writes that night to the justice what the street saw: the regalia, the grey mare and the black horse at the temple steps, the king crowned without a word. The letter is kept among the court's papers.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0006"><em>Cathal crowned</em>, 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1036"><em>The first coal-lump sold for an altar at the fair</em>, 26 an t-Sultain, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1038"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, DE 3** — *The coal ink for the new dies* (Cathair dhearg). The mint at Cathair dhearg buys coal of the vein from Comhairle nam Mèinnean to grind the seal-ink for the new reign's dies. Gille-Easbaig Bàn, who cuts them, reckons on the back of the answering letter that the price of the little pot of ink is a year of his wages. The mint pays it, and the recipe on the card by the grinding-stone is kept.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0007"><em>The mint's new dies</em>, 30 an Lùnastal, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <em>The mint at Cathair dhearg</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0024">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 5</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1037"><em>Ùna nic Ailein's letter of the crowning</em>, 29 an t-Sultain, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1039"></a>**22 an Dàmhair, DE 3** — *Cathal's coin comes to the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). Through an t-Sultain the first coin of the new dies comes down Rathad na Fèille in the purses of carriers and drovers. By the opening of Fèill Muileann òg half the coin that crosses the court's table bears Cathal's head, with the coal ink dark at its edge.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0007"><em>The mint's new dies</em>, 30 an Lùnastal, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1038"><em>The coal ink for the new dies</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1040"></a>**3 an t-Samhain, DE 3** — *The coal-sellers' row stands empty at the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). Fèill Muileann òg runs eleven days and is the thinnest in its clerk's memory. The coal-sellers' row, which once ran the length of the lower field with its wagons, has four booths, two of them selling turf. The booths go dark early for want of fuel to keep a brazier, and Cnoc leathan lets fewer beds.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <em>Fèill Muileann òg first held</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_VI/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_the_Kingdom.pdf#ev-V-0088">→ An Aois Rìoghachd, SE 21</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0005"><em>The last coal sale at the fair</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, DE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1039"><em>Cathal's coin comes to the fair</em>, 22 an Dàmhair, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1041"></a>**14 an t-Samhain, DE 3** — *Black cake entered at Cùirt na Fèille* (Fèill Muileann òg). On the northern day of the fair a Tuathach pedlar brings a creel of black cakes made from pit waste. Burned in the court-room stove, it glows hot and stinks. The justice will not have it entered as coal, and the clerk Ùna nic Ailein rules a new page for black cake, of the north, and enters its first sale, to a baker of Muileann ghlas, with the maker not named.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0001"><em>The first working dubhan</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0002"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel</em>, 21 an t-Samhain, DE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-1040"><em>The coal-sellers' row stands empty at the fair</em>, 3 an t-Samhain, DE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-1042"></a>**15 an t-Samhain, DE 3** — *The foot of Cùirt na Fèille's year* (Fèill Muileann òg). In the last week of an Dàmhair the clerk of Cùirt na Fèille reckons the year.
