Caught at the chamber door, Somhairle mac Lachlainn tells Anna nic Phàil that he has read many rolls of the dead and never once been asked whether the towns that raised them could bear the cost, and does not know why a roll of the dead should be easier to pay for than a roll of the living.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0137"><em>Anna nic Phàil's motion</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6038"><em>The motion held over, morning after morning</em>, 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6040"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *The motion stood over without a sitting called* (Cathair dhearg). On the eighth day Tagradh na h-Èirig is absent from the business-paper; a clerk tells Anna nic Phàil it was stood over to the autumn sitting the evening before, in a short session she was not told was sitting, by members' vote without her among them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0138"><em>The motion for amends</em>, 10 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6039"><em>Somhairle mac Lachlainn is asked whether the sum is too great</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6041"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *Anna counts the councillors who looked away* (Cathair dhearg). Going back over the eight sittings, Anna nic Phàil can find no single vote that killed the motion, only the faces of the twelve, one who promised a vote and never called it, one who spoke of hard times, six who said nothing to her at all, and Somhairle who gave her an answer and moved no more than the rest to call it to a vote.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0138"><em>The motion for amends</em>, 10 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6040"><em>The motion stood over without a sitting called</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6042"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *Martha Greaves tells Peter Hale she means to lay the chair down* (Caol mhòr). In the delegates' room over the net-lofts at Caol mhòr, Martha Greaves tells Peter Hale plainly that she means to lay down Tional nan Tuathach's chair that year, and that she judges him, of every delegate she has sat among, the fittest to take it up.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0139"><em>The Moot's minute on the amends</em>, 18 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6041"><em>Anna counts the councillors who looked away</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6043"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *Martha Greaves's last sitting* (Caol mhòr). Martha Greaves reads out the year's register and the ordinary business of the day, a roof at the school, the price of wool, a mill's complaint of the coal-line's freight, lays the chair down, and Tional nan Tuathach chooses Peter Hale by acclamation without a show of hands.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0139"><em>The Moot's minute on the amends</em>, 18 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6042"><em>Martha Greaves tells Peter Hale she means to lay the chair down</em>, 29 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6044"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *Martha Greaves goes home to Doire ghlas* (Doire ghlas). Martha Greaves rides home to Doire ghlas on the ordinary carrier's cart with no more baggage than she came to the mill with as a young woman, not yet certain what a woman who was Tional nan Tuathach's own voice for seventeen years is to do with her mornings now.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0139"><em>The Moot's minute on the amends</em>, 18 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6043"><em>Martha Greaves's last sitting</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6045"><em>Officers' houses at Inis uaine</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6045"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *Officers' houses at Inis uaine* (Inis uaine). By council order An t-ochdamh rèisimeid's officers at Inis uaine are given houses in the town in place of quarters borrowed year by year from the tank-yard's sheds.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0141"><em>The eighth regiment at Inis uaine</em>, 14 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6044"><em>Martha Greaves goes home to Doire ghlas</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6046"><em>The quarrymen of Seann Warr</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6046"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *The quarrymen of Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). The quarrymen of Seann Warr cut the stone for An còigeamh rèisimeid's barracks through the summer from the same face that gave the harbour wall, and are paid by An t-Ionmhas at a rate the town's masons call fair.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0140"><em>The fifth regiment's barracks</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6045"><em>Officers' houses at Inis uaine</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6047"><em>Cnoc bhàn's harbour opened again</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6047"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *Cnoc bhàn's harbour opened again* (Cnoc bhàn). The Tuathaich of Cnoc bhàn open their harbour again to boats they do not know, the raiders who took the salt-boats having been brought into Seann Skell.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0133"><em>The second fleet off Baile ìseal</em>, 2 an Lùnastal, DE 24</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6046"><em>The quarrymen of Seann Warr</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6048"><em>The springs of Muileann ruadh in a wet summer</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6048"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25** — *The springs of Muileann ruadh in a wet summer* (Muileann ruadh). Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh run so full in the wet summer that the bath-house's lower room floods, and the custodians carry the sick up to the long room.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6047"><em>Cnoc bhàn's harbour opened again</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>.</span>

## The Years DE 26 – 27

- <a id="ev-VI-0143"></a>**18 an Giblean, DE 26** — *Seann-chunntas* (Caol mhòr). Tuathaich speakers begin to name the tabled request to the library and the dead motion for amends together as 'seann-chunntas', an old reckoning that none in power will settle and none has cancelled. The Dia-thìrich in office do not take up the word.
- <a id="ev-VI-0144"></a>**17 an Cèitean, DE 26** — *The Sloc Mòr closed* (Achadh dhomhain). The Mine Board shuts the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr at Achadh dhomhain. One face is kept open in the Rite's keeping, to cut coal for the altars, a few baskets a year.
- <a id="ev-VI-0145"></a>**15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26** — *The last hewers* (Achadh dhomhain). Twelve hewers are kept at the Sloc Mòr to cut the altar-coal in the Rite's keeping. They are the last of their trade to work the vein on the island, and the Rite gives them its own oath, not the dissolved guild's.
- <a id="ev-VI-0146"></a>**14 an t-Iuchar, DE 26** — *The regiments at the Còmhrag* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). Fighters of the regiments are entered in the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan for the first time. The ninth regiment's man wins it. The fair-wardens raise the gate-price again.
- <a id="ev-VI-0147"></a>**12 an Lùnastal, DE 26** — *The second regiment's library guard* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The second regiment at Àth dhìreach keeps a guard at Leabharlann Muileann chaol over the sealed war archive. The keeper, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, writes to the council that the library did not ask for one.
- <a id="ev-VI-0148"></a>**10 an t-Sultain, DE 26** — *The coal line carries no coal* (Achadh dhomhain). The last coal train runs from Achadh dhomhain to Cathair dhearg. The coal line keeps its name and carries dubhan, wool and soldiers.
- <a id="ev-VI-0149"></a>**9 an Dàmhair, DE 26** — *The sixth regiment on the northern road* (Caol mhòr). The sixth regiment at Cnoc bheag keeps posts on the northern road where the boundary stones stand. For the first time since the Severance the Tuathaich going south must show a pass. The council's minute calls the passes for a time only.
- <a id="ev-VI-0150"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, DE 26** — *The fair of the present year* (Fèill Muileann òg). The fair at Muileann òg draws traders from every shire the state holds. Tuathaich wool is sold there on its northern day, through Dia-thìrich factors, as it has been since the first fair.
- <a id="ev-EVII-6501"></a>**15 an t-Samhain, DE 26** — *The word heard first in the yard at Muileann chaol* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). A carrier bringing salt fish to an Leabharlann's kitchen uses the word seann-chunntas in the yard within Sìleas nic Rath's hearing; she copies it into her working notes, meaning at first only to ask Raghnall whether an Leabharlann's glossary should carry it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0143"><em>Seann-chunntas</em>, 18 an Giblean, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6502"></a>**18 an t-Samhain, DE 26** — *Ellen Marsh's letter carries the word twice* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). A civil note from Ellen Marsh asking after the eleventh book's binding uses seann-chunntas twice in passing, as a word already in general currency in the north; Sìleas sets it beside the carrier's yard-talk and begins to understand what the word joins.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0143"><em>Seann-chunntas</em>, 18 an Giblean, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6501"><em>The word heard first in the yard at Muileann chaol</em>, 15 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6503"></a>**19 an t-Samhain, DE 26** — *Sìleas enters the word without a heading* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Sìleas nic Rath sets a single line at the foot of a Board return, noting the word heard that year joining the tabled request and the dead motion, and that no Dia-thìreach in office has yet used it; she gives it no category of its own.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0143"><em>Seann-chunntas</em>, 18 an Giblean, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6502"><em>Ellen Marsh's letter carries the word twice</em>, 18 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6504"></a>**21 an t-Samhain, DE 26** — *Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order to Achadh dhomhain* (Achadh dhomhain). A four-line order from Comhairle nam Mèinnean reaches the maor of Achadh dhomhain in an Gearran, closing An Sloc Mòr's upper galleries and the timbering left to stand, the shafts capped, the workings judged to cost more in pumping than the coal they still gave.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0144"><em>The Sloc Mòr closed</em>, 17 an Cèitean, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6503"><em>Sìleas enters the word without a heading</em>, 19 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6505"></a>**22 an t-Samhain, DE 26** — *The maor's report on the hewing families* (Achadh dhomhain). The maor of Achadh dhomhain reports that the old hewing families of the town said nothing against the closing of An Sloc Mòr's upper galleries and asked nothing of Comhairle nam Mèinnean in its place.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0144"><em>The Sloc Mòr closed</em>, 17 an Cèitean, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0145"><em>The last hewers</em>, 15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6504"><em>Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order to Achadh dhomhain</em>, 21 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6506"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, DE 26** — *Eachann given the last coal run* (Muileann chrom). The yard masters at Muileann chrom tell Eachann mac Ruairidh, three days before, that the run he is given will be Slighe a' Ghuail's last working under coal's own name, an old lamp-house contract closing after fourteen years of the line carrying dubhan under the unchanged name.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0148"><em>The coal line carries no coal</em>, 10 an t-Sultain, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6505"><em>The maor's report on the hewing families</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6507"></a>**5 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *The coal handed to carters, not a second engine* (Cathair dhearg). The lamp-houses judge six wagons not worth a second engine's steam and carry the last coal on by horse and cart from the goods-yard, so that the trade which crowned the kingdom's kings goes out under its own name behind horses at the last.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0148"><em>The coal line carries no coal</em>, 10 an t-Sultain, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6506"><em>Eachann given the last coal run</em>, 24 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6508"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *Sìleas copies the council's three words* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Sìleas nic Rath enters the council's minute on the northern passes exactly as given, for a time only, the same three words Deachamh a' Chogaidh was given six years before and has not since been taken away.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0149"><em>The sixth regiment on the northern road</em>, 9 an Dàmhair, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6507"><em>The coal handed to carters, not a second engine</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6509"></a>**8 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh dies at Àth dhìreach* (Muileann chaol). A letter in the hand of Beathag's own sister brings word that Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh has died quietly in the night at her sister's house at Àth dhìreach, five-and-seventy years old, six years after laying down the chronicler's office.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0150"><em>The fair of the present year</em>, 7 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6508"><em>Sìleas copies the council's three words</em>, 7 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6510"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *Sìleas writes the one entry the day requires* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Sìleas nic Rath enters Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's death in the open chronicle in the plain accounting the office requires, naming her the first hand to note the fuel and the re-header of fourteen years, and adds nothing of grief beyond it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0150"><em>The fair of the present year</em>, 7 an t-Samhain, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6509"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh dies at Àth dhìreach</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6511"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *An old hewer sworn a second time* (Achadh dhomhain). At the swearing of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's twelve hewers at Achadh dhomhain an old man who had sworn the guild's oath in his youth tells the priest he had thought it the last oath a coal-cutter's trade would ask of him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0145"><em>The last hewers</em>, 15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6510"><em>Sìleas writes the one entry the day requires</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6512"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *An Sloc Mòr's upper galleries capped* (Achadh dhomhain). Within a fortnight of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order the eleven upper galleries of An Sloc Mòr are capped, their timbering left standing in the dark.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0144"><em>The Sloc Mòr closed</em>, 17 an Cèitean, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6511"><em>An old hewer sworn a second time</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6513"></a>**24 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man at Ceann leathan* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). The winner of Còmhrag Ceann leathan in the regiments' first year is a broad Dia-thìreach of the southern Seann Skell who had fitted engines under Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' charter before the regiments took him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0146"><em>The regiments at the Còmhrag</em>, 14 an t-Iuchar, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6512"><em>An Sloc Mòr's upper galleries capped</em>, 23 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6514"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *A sentry's word at an Leabharlann gate* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The sergeant of An dàrna rèisimeid's first watch at an Leabharlann tells the keeper it is a queer sort of soldiering, standing watch over a door that has never opened from either side.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0147"><em>The second regiment's library guard</em>, 12 an Lùnastal, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6513"><em>An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man at Ceann leathan</em>, 24 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6515"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *The last coal carter of the north road* (Muileann fhada). The last carter to bring coal down the north road past An Taigh-seinnse Reòta above Muileann fhada carries a load of small coal for the landlord's own kitchen and none for sale.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0144"><em>The Sloc Mòr closed</em>, 17 an Cèitean, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6514"><em>A sentry's word at an Leabharlann gate</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6516"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *Achadh mhòr's harvest in the present* (Achadh mhòr). The harvest of Achadh mhòr goes down to the capital in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's lorries and the growers' own; the factors reckon it the heaviest in a generation and the dearest to carry.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6515"><em>The last coal carter of the north road</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6517"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26** — *An t-ochdamh rèisimeid at Inis uaine keeps a school* (Inis uaine). An t-ochdamh rèisimeid at Inis uaine keeps a school in its barracks for the soldiers' children and the town's, taught by a corporal who had been a copyist.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0141"><em>The eighth regiment at Inis uaine</em>, 14 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6516"><em>Achadh mhòr's harvest in the present</em>, 29 an Dùbhlachd, DE 26</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-VI-0151"></a>**19 am Faoilleach, DE 27** — *The Còmhrag of the present year* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). The Còmhrag at Ceann leathan is fought with staves and fists, as it has been since edged tools were banned. Two regiments and nine shires send fighters. One man dies.
- <a id="ev-VI-0152"></a>**17 an Gearran, DE 27** — *The eleven books* (Doire ghlas). Ellen Marsh's eleven books are copied by hand in the Tuathaich schools and kept in the north. The library's catalogue lists the tabled request, and not the books.
- <a id="ev-VI-0153"></a>**29 an Cèitean, DE 27** — *The Moot of the present year* (Caol mhòr). The Moot at Caol mhòr meets under Peter Hale. Its minute-books run unbroken from Walter Hale's first meeting. It has no standing in Dia-thìrich law and has never asked for any.
- <a id="ev-VI-0154"></a>**27 an t-Ògmhios, DE 27** — *The dubhan works of the present* (Seann Skell). Dubhan is made at Seann Skell on the southern coast and at works in the east and north. Every lamp, engine, ship and lorry on the island runs on it. The coin is pegged to it, and the tithe is taken on every sale.
- <a id="ev-VI-0154a"></a>**29 an t-Iuchar, DE 27** — *The Treasury's roll of the present year* (Cathair dhearg). The Treasury's roll for the year stands at 9,568 purses: 6,375 from the head-due, taken at eighteen purses on every five thousand heads, and 3,193 from the market-due, taken at seventeen in the hundred on every sale. The wartime tithe is carried on its own line under the regiments' pay. The windy coast pays neither due.
- <a id="ev-VI-0154b"></a>**7 an t-Sultain, DE 27** — *Dubhan's charter of export* (Ros dhomhain). Dubhan, who made the first working fuel and is now in his sixty-ninth year, wins from the council at Cathair dhearg, after a year of letters and three sittings, leave to sell dubhan beyond the island. It is the first leave the kingdom has given since the Severance for any good of Dia-thìr to pass beyond its waters. The charter is narrow. The Treasury sets each year's measure. The fuel is loaded only at Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel. The kingdom's depots and the Moot's are served first. Nothing of the vein goes with it: the vein's coal is not sold, and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold. Dubhan has told neither the council nor the chronicler who buys from him. In the autumn the first tank-hull loaded under the charter goes out past the north-western capes, and on the day she sails the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut.
- <a id="ev-VI-0155"></a>**6 an Dàmhair, DE 27** — *The altar-coal* (Seann Skell). The Rite's twelve hewers at the Sloc Mòr cut the year's altar-coal. It fills four baskets. The high custodian at Seann Skell shares it among the houses of the Rite by lot.
- <a id="ev-VI-0156"></a>**22 an t-Samhain, DE 27** — *The chronicler's note on the present* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Sìleas nic Rath writes at the foot of the year that the kingdom's record is whole in every part but two: the war, which is sealed, and the north, which was not asked.
- <a id="ev-VI-0157"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The present* (Cathair dhearg). The coal is all but gone. The trade of the island runs on a name that once belonged to one man. The Dia-thìrich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, a grievance five years old, their Church, and the memory of the First Canoe, Naomh Breandan's voyage to the Isle of the Blessed, which the people who have twice defeated them still call folklore.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6542"><em>Ellen Marsh tells A' Chiad Churach again</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6543"><em>A boy asks whose fire it was</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6544"><em>Sìleas sets down the rhyme unanswered</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6549"><em>The telling of the fire in the canoe</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6518"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Joe Ashby asks Peter Hale about An t-Aon Leabhar Deug* (Caol mhòr). Joe Ashby puts to Peter Hale the question of whether an Leabharlann means to refuse An t-Aon Leabhar Deug outright or only to leave them waiting; Peter answers that a catalogue naming the request and not the books has not yet said either word.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0152"><em>The eleven books</em>, 17 an Gearran, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6519"><em>Peter Hale opens Tional nan Tuathach's book in his own hand</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6519"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Peter Hale opens Tional nan Tuathach's book in his own hand* (Caol mhòr). At Caol mhòr, still new enough to the chair to write rather than pass the pen, Peter Hale opens the year's minute-book himself and reads the standing tally: no ruling of any Dia-thìreach court names Tional nan Tuathach a lawful body, and none has ever been asked.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0153"><em>The Moot of the present year</em>, 29 an Cèitean, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6518"><em>Joe Ashby asks Peter Hale about An t-Aon Leabhar Deug</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6520"><em>An t-Ionmhas's clerk at Ros dhomhain keeps a second tally</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6520"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *An t-Ionmhas's clerk at Ros dhomhain keeps a second tally* (Ros dhomhain). An t-Ionmhas's clerk who weighs and marks the ordinary barrels of dubhan at Ros dhomhain begins, unasked, a private tally of the fuel that leaves the quay for the fleets and the regiments and pays An t-Ionmhas nothing, and folds it each quarter into his own drawer.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154"><em>The dubhan works of the present</em>, 27 an t-Ògmhios, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154a"><em>The Treasury's roll of the present year</em>, 29 an t-Iuchar, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6519"><em>Peter Hale opens Tional nan Tuathach's book in his own hand</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6521"><em>The council hears the petition for export</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6521"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The council hears the petition for export* (Cathair dhearg). At the first of three sittings of the council at Cathair dhearg, in the winter, the petition for leave to sell dubhan beyond the island is read and heard in silence. The twelve give no answer that day. Sìleas nic Rath copies the clerk's draft twice.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154b"><em>Dubhan's charter of export</em>, 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6520"><em>An t-Ionmhas's clerk at Ros dhomhain keeps a second tally</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6522"><em>The custodians of Òrd Bhrìde search and seal An Eala Dhubh's holds</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6522"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The custodians of Òrd Bhrìde search and seal An Eala Dhubh's holds* (Ros dhomhain). Over three days at Ros dhomhain two custodians of Òrd Bhrìde search every hold of An Eala Dhubh by lamp for the vein's own coal before it is loaded, and set their order's mark in wax at each coaming once it is filled, waiting until the wax hardens past any hand's reopening.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154b"><em>Dubhan's charter of export</em>, 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6521"><em>The council hears the petition for export</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6523"><em>A clerk of An t-Ionmhas marks the first and last barrel loaded</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6523"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *A clerk of An t-Ionmhas marks the first and last barrel loaded* (Ros dhomhain). At Ros dhomhain a clerk of An t-Ionmhas marks the first barrel and the last of An Eala Dhubh's loading alike, and every fifth barrel between, keeping the tithe the charter sets before the custodians close each hold.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154b"><em>Dubhan's charter of export</em>, 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6522"><em>The custodians of Òrd Bhrìde search and seal An Eala Dhubh's holds</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6524"><em>Joe Ashby watches An Eala Dhubh pass off Caol mhòr</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6524"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Joe Ashby watches An Eala Dhubh pass off Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). Off his own headland with an empty line, Joe Ashby watches An Eala Dhubh pass under full steam bound north-about, and thinks of the six years since his own name came off Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' rolls under a charter written for a different fuel.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154b"><em>Dubhan's charter of export</em>, 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6523"><em>A clerk of An t-Ionmhas marks the first and last barrel loaded</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6525"><em>Anna nic Phàil asks how the vein is to be kept out</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6525"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Anna nic Phàil asks how the vein is to be kept out* (Cathair dhearg). At the second sitting on the petition for export, in the spring, Anna nic Phàil asks the council how the kingdom will be sure that nothing of the vein's coal goes out with the fuel. The council's answer is the term no councillor argues: the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde shall seal every hold.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154b"><em>Dubhan's charter of export</em>, 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6524"><em>Joe Ashby watches An Eala Dhubh pass off Caol mhòr</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6526"><em>The copying of An t-Aon Leabhar Deug</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6526"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The copying of An t-Aon Leabhar Deug* (Doire ghlas). An t-Aon Leabhar Deug of Ellen Marsh's gathering go from school to school in the north, each copied by the eldest children in a schoolroom hand before it passes on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0152"><em>The eleven books</em>, 17 an Gearran, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6525"><em>Anna nic Phàil asks how the vein is to be kept out</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6527"><em>A lamp-fitter of Caol mhòr on An t-Aon Leabhar Deug</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6527"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *A lamp-fitter of Caol mhòr on An t-Aon Leabhar Deug* (Caol mhòr). An old lamp-fitter of Caol mhòr, let go from Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' rolls with Joe Ashby, says a book finished is still a book, whatever an Leabharlann does with it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0152"><em>The eleven books</em>, 17 an Gearran, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6526"><em>The copying of An t-Aon Leabhar Deug</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6528"><em>The twelve hear the petition three times</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6528"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The twelve hear the petition three times* (Cathair dhearg). The council at Cathair dhearg sits three times on the petition for leave to export dubhan, in the winter, the spring and the summer's end, and grants it inside the hour at the third.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154b"><em>Dubhan's charter of export</em>, 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6527"><em>A lamp-fitter of Caol mhòr on An t-Aon Leabhar Deug</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6529"><em>An Eala Dhubh stands out of Ros dhomhain</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6529"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *An Eala Dhubh stands out of Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). An Eala Dhubh stands out of Ros dhomhain on the morning tide with An t-Ionmhas's seal on her hatches, and the harbour's children run the length of the mole beside her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0154b"><em>Dubhan's charter of export</em>, 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6528"><em>The twelve hear the petition three times</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6530"><em>A lamp for the Taigh-seinnse Mòr's gate</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6530"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *A lamp for the Taigh-seinnse Mòr's gate* (Cuan chrom). The landlord of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr above Cuan chrom hangs a dubhan lamp over his gate on the old coal road for the lorries that come by night, the last of the great inns but one to do so.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0025"><em>The inns take the new lamps</em>, 30 am Màrt, DE 9</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6529"><em>An Eala Dhubh stands out of Ros dhomhain</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6531"><em>The ferry of Àth gharbh fitted with an engine</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6531"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The ferry of Àth gharbh fitted with an engine* (Àth gharbh). The ferry at Àth gharbh is fitted with a dubhan engine and a chain across the ford; the old ferryman keeps his pole in the boat and says he will want it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6530"><em>A lamp for the Taigh-seinnse Mòr's gate</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6532"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The four baskets carried south* (Achadh dhomhain). An Sloc Mòr's twelve hewers cut the year's altar-coal in an Dàmhair; the maor's cart carries the four baskets to Achadh dhomhain station under a tarpaulin, and they go south to the southern Seann Skell in a van of Slighe a' Ghuail kept for nothing else that week.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6533"><em>The lot drawn in the rain at Brìde's house</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6533"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The lot drawn in the rain at Brìde's house* (Seann Skell). Priests of three lesser coast houses walk or ride two and three days to see the lot drawn in a hard autumn rain at the southern Seann Skell, the folded slips kept dry under a second tarpaulin while Alasdair mac Ìomhair draws.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6532"><em>The four baskets carried south</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6534"><em>Alasdair mac Ìomhair draws four houses</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6534"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Alasdair mac Ìomhair draws four houses* (Seann Skell). Past his eighty-fifth summer and steadied on a novice's shoulder, Alasdair mac Ìomhair draws Cnoc bheag, Seann Bhral, the western Seann Skell and, by chance, the southern house itself from the nine houses' slips.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6533"><em>The lot drawn in the rain at Brìde's house</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6535"><em>Alasdair mac Ìomhair on the lot's pattern</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6535"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Alasdair mac Ìomhair on the lot's pattern* (Seann Skell). Asked by a young priest whether the altar-coal will still be cut in ten or twenty years, Alasdair mac Ìomhair, who has drawn the lot six-and-fifty times, says only that he has learned not to promise a young man what the mountain will do next.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6534"><em>Alasdair mac Ìomhair draws four houses</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6536"><em>A coast priest measures the fall of the lot</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6536"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *A coast priest measures the fall of the lot* (Seann Skell). A priest of a house so small the lot has never before fallen to it walks three days to see the four baskets drawn for, and says afterward that her grandmother's telling remembered them carted to the coast houses by the wagon-load.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6535"><em>Alasdair mac Ìomhair on the lot's pattern</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6537"><em>The old hewer hears the lot fell home</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6537"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The old hewer hears the lot fell home* (Achadh dhomhain). Word reaches the twelve hewers at Achadh dhomhain that the southern house drew its own basket back to itself; the eldest among them, sworn once already as a young man to the dissolved guild, calls it the vein's own way of being droll.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0145"><em>The last hewers</em>, 15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6536"><em>A coast priest measures the fall of the lot</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6538"><em>Sìleas enters the altar-coal return</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6538"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Sìleas enters the altar-coal return* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The maor's return on the four baskets reaches Sìleas nic Rath's table at Muileann chaol within the fortnight; she enters it in the ordinary column and lets pass, unwritten, her own thought of forty baskets shrunk to four.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0156"><em>The chronicler's note on the present</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6537"><em>The old hewer hears the lot fell home</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6539"><em>Còmhrag Ceann leathan's champion falls to a hewer's son</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6539"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Còmhrag Ceann leathan's champion falls to a hewer's son* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). In a bout added at the crowd's asking for the year's champion against all comers, An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man loses to a twenty-year-old hewer's son of Cnoc bheag; the fair-wardens' own return calls the championship passed back to the shires as it stood before the regiments came to it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0151"><em>The Còmhrag of the present year</em>, 19 am Faoilleach, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6538"><em>Sìleas enters the altar-coal return</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6540"><em>An old woman of Baile chrom is turned back three mornings</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6540"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *An old woman of Baile chrom is turned back three mornings* (Baile chrom). A pass-table clerk at the boundary stones notes, unasked, that an old woman of Baile chrom came three mornings running to ask a pass for a granddaughter nursing in the capital, and walked eleven miles home again each time with no pass and no name given.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0149"><em>The sixth regiment on the northern road</em>, 9 an Dàmhair, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6539"><em>Còmhrag Ceann leathan's champion falls to a hewer's son</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6541"><em>Ellen Marsh keeps the eldest back on the shortest evening</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6541"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Ellen Marsh keeps the eldest back on the shortest evening* (Doire ghlas). On the evening of the shortest day Ellen Marsh sends the youngest children of her Doire ghlas school home early and keeps the eldest dozen to copy a page of the eleventh book into a third hand before the chest under the window is shut on all eleven.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0152"><em>The eleven books</em>, 17 an Gearran, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6540"><em>An old woman of Baile chrom is turned back three mornings</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6542"><em>Ellen Marsh tells A' Chiad Churach again</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6542"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Ellen Marsh tells A' Chiad Churach again* (Doire ghlas). Ellen Marsh tells her eldest pupils, as her own mother told her, A' Chiad Churach's crossing through Ceò Mhanannain with a fire tended turn and turn about in a clay pot of wet moss, kept faithfully the whole way for fear a canoe that lost it would not find the isle again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0157"><em>The present</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6541"><em>Ellen Marsh keeps the eldest back on the shortest evening</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6543"><em>A boy asks whose fire it was</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6543"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *A boy asks whose fire it was* (Doire ghlas). A thirteen-year-old asks Ellen Marsh whose fire A' Chiad Churach carried, since the telling names none of the crew; she answers, as her own mother once answered her, that the telling does not say, and that a fire no one hand still claims is no less a fire for it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0157"><em>The present</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6542"><em>Ellen Marsh tells A' Chiad Churach again</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6544"><em>Sìleas sets down the rhyme unanswered</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6544"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Sìleas sets down the rhyme unanswered* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Closing the year's ledger, Sìleas nic Rath sets down the rhyme she first overheard from a northern carrier in an Leabharlann's own yard, black the coal and black the dubhan, but whose is the fire, in both tongues, and gives it no answer of her own.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0157"><em>The present</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6543"><em>A boy asks whose fire it was</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6545"><em>A novice to hold the lot-bowl</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6545"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *A novice to hold the lot-bowl* (Seann Skell). A novice of fifteen is given the office of holding the bowl for the lot of the altar-coal at the southern Seann Skell and does not sleep the night before for the weight of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6544"><em>Sìleas sets down the rhyme unanswered</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6546"><em>The southern house draws its own basket</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6546"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The southern house draws its own basket* (Seann Skell). At the lot of the four baskets the southern house of Brìde at Seann Skell is drawn among the four, so that one basket goes no farther than across the yard.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0155"><em>The altar-coal</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6545"><em>A novice to hold the lot-bowl</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6547"><em>The lamps of Muileann chaol lit at three</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6547"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The lamps of Muileann chaol lit at three* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). At Muileann chaol in an t-Samhain the keeper orders the gallery lamps lit from three in the afternoon and no fire after dark.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0156"><em>The chronicler's note on the present</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6546"><em>The southern house draws its own basket</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6548"><em>The regiments' winter musters</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6548"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The regiments' winter musters*. The winter musters of the nine regiments show some three thousand three hundred men on the rolls and twenty-three guns serviceable.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0118"><em>An Cogadh Fada ends</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6547"><em>The lamps of Muileann chaol lit at three</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6549"><em>The telling of the fire in the canoe</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6549"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *The telling of the fire in the canoe* (Doire ghlas). On the shortest day Ellen Marsh tells the eldest children at Doire ghlas the telling of A' Chiad Churach and of the fire its crew carried in a clay pot through the mist.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0157"><em>The present</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6548"><em>The regiments' winter musters</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6550"><em>Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd's last page of the year left open</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6550"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd's last page of the year left open* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Sìleas nic Rath leaves Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd open on its stand at the year's end with the ink dry, as Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh had done before her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0156"><em>The chronicler's note on the present</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, DE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6549"><em>The telling of the fire in the canoe</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6551"><em>Cnoc ghorm's elders at the northern posts</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6551"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *Cnoc ghorm's elders at the northern posts* (Cnoc ghorm). Elders of Cnoc ghorm going south to the fair show their passes at An siathamh rèisimeid's posts by the boundary stones, and write in their own book that the sergeant wished them a good road.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0149"><em>The sixth regiment on the northern road</em>, 9 an Dàmhair, DE 26</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6550"><em>Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd's last page of the year left open</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVII-6552"><em>An Taigh-òsta Grianach in the present year</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVII-6552"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27** — *An Taigh-òsta Grianach in the present year* (Cnoc dhìreach). An Taigh-òsta Grianach at Cnoc dhìreach sells fuel at its yard, beds under its roof and suppers by a dubhan lamp, and its sign still names all three.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-VI-0029"><em>An Taigh-òsta Grianach</em>, 4 am Màrt, DE 10</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EVII-6551"><em>Cnoc ghorm's elders at the northern posts</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27</a>.</span>

# A Gazetteer of the Age

#### A

**Achadh dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 272. The deep-field town of the camps' granaries above An Sloc Mòr was the hewers' own. Comann nan Gualadairean kept its hall there and its day of binding, which passed empty in the first year with no son or daughter brought to be bound. The hall was sold before the guild was dissolved in DE 12, and became a dubhan depot with its carved lintel, the guild's oath cut in it, left above the pumps; the oath-stone went to the library. Comhairle nam Mèinnean bought the last private share in An Sloc Mòr when Taigh Mhic Ùisdein moved to shipping, and its pumps ran on dubhan from the thirteenth year. In DE 26 An Sloc Mòr was closed, one face kept for Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail, its upper galleries capped; twelve hewers were sworn at the town to cut the altar-coal, one an old man who had sworn the guild's oath in his youth, and in the present year the four baskets of their coal were carried south to the lot. Known for Comann nan Gualadairean' hall, An Sloc Mòr and the altar-coal.

**Achadh mhòr** (Achadh mhòr). Founded 2 an t-Samhain, GE 4,000. The town of the great granary fields in the south was the drovers' country. In DE 9 the drover families of Achadh mhòr, with no oxen left to drive, sold their teams to farmers of the granary country at the drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às, and the works at the southern Seann Skell took the price of the beasts against eleven lorries. The inn kept its trade by selling the drovers dubhan. The harvest of the fields went down to the capital's mills by lorry in eleven days the next year, the old drovers watching it pass from the field-gates. Its granary factors sold oats to the western pit towns through Tional nan Tuathach in the years of the holdouts, and wrote to Comhairle nam Mèinnean that they knew of no rule against it. In the present year its harvest is the heaviest in a generation and the dearest to carry. Known for the drovers who bought lorries.

**Àth bheag** (Baile fhiadhaich). Founded 14 an t-Samhain, LE 224. The small western crossing lay on the column's road. Its report in DE 22 is the first An Clàr Foscailte copies: the smith's boy woke the maor, Cailean mac Griogair, who stood at the field's edge in a borrowed coat and watched the column ford the water without going down to ask where it was bound, and the miller's wife, watching from the mill loft, saw no banner among them and no drum, only a man at the head whom the rest left the whole width of the road. It is a village of a mill, a smithy and a score of houses beside the ford, and its people had never, before that night, sent a report to Comhairle nam Mèinnean of anything. Its maor's report and the miller's wife's words stand together in the library's file, the first two papers of the column's road. Known for the ford the column crossed.

**Àth bheag** (Àth bheag). Founded 26 an Cèitean, GE 4,347. The ford town on the east coast, under the pirate watch, sent its salt inland on the drove road past Baile ìseal behind oxen for as long as anyone remembered, until a salt-master of Àth bheag bought a dubhan lorry in the eighth year and sent the first salt west by it. The salt reached the yard at Muileann chrom and went on to Cathair dhearg in a covered wagon behind the empty tanks, the first load the new engine carried toward the capital that was not dubhan. The last ox-drove on the eastern salt road went the next spring, and within a few years the drovers of the east coast had sold their oxen. Its tinsmith made the iron hood for the trial lamp at Baile ìseal. In the war raiders from the eastern waters took two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burned a third while the fleets were in the north-west. Known for the eastern salt-road, and the first salt carried by lorry.

**Àth dhearg** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 364. The town under Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape waited longest for its light's turning. The work took a month longer there than at the other beacons, for the stair of the tower was too narrow for the new tank, and a crane had to be walked from Seann Tarr to lift it to the lantern from outside, the rope-makers of that town having refused to hire out their cordage for it. Peigi nic Ascaill wrote from here to Caol mhòr for Tuathaich fitters. The keeper has written since for spare chimney-glass, the stair still too narrow to carry up more than one at a time. Through the autumn of the column's year his log records that no ship of the fleets passed the cape in three months. The crane that lifted the tank was left standing on the cape for a year afterwards, rusting, until Comhairle nam Mèinnean sent a wagon for it; the children of the town had meanwhile made it the gallows of a game whose rules none of their elders could follow. Known for the beacon whose tank went up the outside of the tower.

**Àth dhìreach** (Achadh chaol). Founded 8 am Màrt, AE 90. The small eastern town of An dàrna rèisimeid's garrison was quiet until the war. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, who had been royal chronicler since before Linn an Dubhain, laid down the office in DE 20 and went there to live, and watched An dàrna rèisimeid's camp being pitched from her garden wall when it was raised in the autumn of the war's first year, writing to Sìleas nic Rath of it. The regiment guards Slighe a' Ghuail and the library road. She died at Àth dhìreach in DE 26. The town is small, a street of houses on Slighe a' Ghuail's embankment and the regiment's camp on the water-meadow below it. The camp's first winter was spent under canvas; its huts went up the next spring from timber brought by Slighe a' Ghuail, and the town's one inn has taken the regiment's custom since. Known for An dàrna rèisimeid, and the old chronicler's last years.

**Àth gharbh** (Doire shean). Founded 28 an t-Sultain, FE 1,855. The walled ford town is A' chiad chabhlach's station, its hulls lying in the harbour of Doire shean a short walk away. Its ferry had carried coal across for the eastern farms every week until the fourth year, and carried grain and passengers after at a higher fare. When A' chiad chabhlach was raised in DE 21 from the south-west harbours, four of the ferrymen went into it, and the ferry was worked through the war by the oldest of them and his daughter. In the present year it is fitted with a dubhan engine and a chain across the ford; the old ferryman keeps his pole in the boat. Known for A' chiad chabhlach's station, and its ferry.

**Àth leathan** (Seann Skell). Founded 8 am Màrt, LE 1,303. The small Tuathaich pit town of the western hills was the first of the holdouts and the ground of the first battle of the war. Its pit captain Calder died in the sixteenth year and the hewers kept his daughter Ruth to speak for them; she wrote the letters of the five towns, and was their spokeswoman in Tional nan Tuathach until they walked out. In the war the hewers of the five towns came down to Àth leathan with their pit-lamps lit at noon, and her list at the pit-shed ran past four hundred names in six evenings and near nine hundred souls with their carriers by the battle's eve. The battle of Àth leathan was fought below its spoil-heaps; after it the town's pits were given as flooded. The western seams were capped by Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order in DE 23 with An seachdamh rèisimeid standing by, and the regiment built its post on the road below the town. On the field stands the cairn the Tuathaich families built without leave, and it has grown by a stone or two every time the patrols pass it. Known for Ruth Calder, Blàr Àth leathan and the cairn.

**Àth naomh** (Cuan shean). Founded 26 an Giblean, LE 900. The small town of the harbour carts in the Cuan shean shire blesses its carts every spring, horses and all, and in the seventh year its priest held a dubhan lamp on a tail-board blessed because it was on the cart. Its forges smelt the bog-iron of the district, and in DE 24 took the contract for the regiments' small arms and field-guns with Caol ìseal, the forge-towns of the old vein country following; a smith of the town counts his musket-stocks by the hundred. The town lies on the harbour road of the Cuan shean shire, where the carts of An ceathramh cabhlach's harbour go up and down all day; since the war its forges work by dubhan heat, and the blessing of the carts at the spring draws the regiments' own wagoners to stand with their teams among the town's. Known for its blessing of the harbour carts, and its forges.

**Àth naomh** (Cnoc thais). Founded 26 an t-Sultain, FE 2,780. The Tuathaich town of the citadel over the holy ford was the fourth of the western pit towns. Its two delegates walked the hill path to Muileann àrsaidh in DE 16, the elder with a stick in either hand, and signed the agreement in their own hands. Its company of sixty stood at Àth leathan. In the war it opened its road to the regiments without a siege, with Tobar dhearg of the hills, and its pits were flooded; An Clàr Foscailte names no holdouts taken there. A man of Àth naomh went with Tom Varley's six to an Oirthir Ghaothach. Its citadel over the ford, older than any pit, has the town's grain in it now, the pits being capped; the delegates who signed at Muileann àrsaidh were not asked by the regiments what they had signed, and the town has kept the copy of the agreement in the citadel's chest with its charter. Known for its citadel over the holy ford, and the road opened without a siege.

#### B

**Baile chrom** (Baile chrom). Founded 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464. The Tuathaich town under the Baile chrom light keeps Oidhche Glaise vigil. Its light was turned to dubhan in DE 7 by fitters of Caol mhòr, Comhairle nan Taighean-solais having none of its own to send so far north, and when the burner failed that winter it was mended on a smith's anvil in the town. In the war, in the first winter of the regiments in the north, a file of An ceathramh rèisimeid was sent round by the headland farms to search the town, and found it dark and silent on Oidhche Glaise, every door shut and every lamp out. The house of Margaret Crane on the lighthouse road kept the vigil alone; a soldier of the file set his lamp down in her passage rather than carry its light past her, and another said afterwards that the house had searched him back. The regiments reported the search, and that they found nothing. The town lies below its light on the headland, its houses of grey stone; Oidhche Glaise is kept in every house with its lamp out, as it was kept before the war. Known for Oidhche Glaise vigil kept against a search.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 622. The south-west anchorage of the wolf-post quays took up engines early: two of its skippers sent for burners and a boatwright of Caol fhiadhaich in the sixth year, and a dubhan pump was set on its quays in the fifteenth, the first on that coast. An treas cabhlach was raised there in DE 21 and took the quays for its own, the fishing boats going to the old beach with their pump; it carried the army's dubhan up the west coast in tank-hulls to the regiments in the hills. The quays were lengthened by forty paces for its tank-hulls in DE 24. The wolf-posts that gave the quays their name were cut down to make room for the tank-hulls' moorings, and one was kept, at the quay's end, for the town's sake. Known for An treas cabhlach's anchorage and tank-hulls.

**Baile ìseal** (Àth bheag). Founded 14 an t-Samhain, LE 197. The small town under Taigh-solais Baile ìseal gave the dubhan its first trial as a light. Twenty barrels were landed at its slip in the fifth year, and Peigi nic Ascaill set a burner of two wick-rings in the storm-lantern of the light and burned it on a stage below the tower, beside the coal light, night after night for more than three months. The retired keeper Murchadh mac Coinnich kept its log for her; a fisherman of the town, coming home in a haar, steered by the trial lamp when the tower's coal light was lost above him; and the keeper Seonag nic Thòmais, who had kept the fuel off her stair, came down at last to ask how the burner was made. The lights of the coast were turned by order the next year. The town's brewer bought the western holdouts' coal for his vats in the eighteenth year and told Comhairle nam Mèinnean he would take no lecture from it. In DE 24 An dàrna cabhlach ran down off Baile ìseal the raiders who had taken the salt-boats in the war, and the lighthouse log recorded the chase in the keeper's hand. Known for the trial lamp of the first dubhan light.

#### C

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 2,414. The river port of the north-east raised An ceathramh rèisimeid in DE 21. It marched down to the river and went down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar in old coal barges fitted with plank benches, in a day and a half on a high river, to be shipped round the north coast to Ceann mhòr. It came home in DE 25 after four years in the Tuathaich north, and lies at Caol bheag. The regiment's barracks are the old wool stores by the river landing, and the town, which had seen the regiment go out in coal barges, saw it come home by the road in lorries, its colours cased. The maor gave a supper for the officers and none for the men, and the town gave one for the men. Known for An ceathramh rèisimeid's home.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,547. The harbour of the strait-pilots and the wolf-stone was the first town to put an engine in a fishing boat. In the fifth year the boatwright Sorcha nic Dhùghaill, at her skipper's asking, bored the sternpost of the decked boat An Ròn Dubh to take a shaft, against the first rule of Comann nan Saor-luinge, Cha tollar an druim, the keel is not bored; the smith of the town made the burner for the engine bought at Ros dhomhain. An Ròn Dubh crossed the harbour under engine, came home against a south-westerly, and was taken through the strait by a pilot whose word at the wolf-stone settled the town. Within the season all four yards were fitting engines. The guild struck and fined them; they returned their papers; and when its court at Ros dhomhain offered Sorcha readmission in DE 6 she declined it. The boats of the strait took the new fuel before any other fleet of the coast, and the skippers of Baile ghorm and Seann Warr sent to Caol fhiadhaich for boatwrights who would bore a keel. Known for An Ròn Dubh, the first engine-boat, and the bored keel.

**Caol ìseal** (Caol ìseal). Founded 21 am Màrt, FE 1,450. The salt-pan town of the low strait on the north coast tried the northern cake under one of its pans in the fourth year and found it boiled the brine as well as coal. In the war a clerk of An t-Ionmhas sat at the pump by the pans to take the tithe, and the salt-boilers said salt paid twice. Its forge smelts the bog-iron of the district, and in DE 24 took the kingdom's contract for the regiments' small arms; the woman who keeps it took on four boys and a girl to answer it. The pans are boiled with dubhan now, bought at the pump An t-Ionmhas's clerk sits beside, and the salt of Caol ìseal goes east and west along the north coast in engine-boats of Caol mhòr's fitting. Known for its salt pans and its forge.

**Caol mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462. The chief harbour of the Tuathaich was the first town of the Dia-thìrich kingdom to see the northern fuel sold, a black cake at its market in the first year, and the first to be asked about it: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's two surveyors lodged four days at Harker's inn on the harbour, were answered civilly everywhere in good Dia-thìris, and were told nothing. Tional nan Tuathach sat at Caol mhòr through the whole age. Martha Greaves took its chair after Daniel Frayne's death; the rebound minute-books were laid in its press, the key on the speaker's ring. The fitters of Caol mhòr turned the light at Baile chrom, and when Riaghailt na Cairte let them go from the southern works they came home and fitted engines without a guild, so that within a few years the harbour held more dubhan boats than any port of its size in the south. The five western pit towns walked out of Tional nan Tuathach here in DE 16, and their benches were kept chalked in the roll with nothing after them. In the war An ceathramh cabhlach searched the harbour's boats and Tional nan Tuathach's granaries were opened to the families of the western hills, whose names Thomas Rook entered in a register that ran past three hundred. In the present year Peter Hale keeps the chair and opens Tional nan Tuathach's book in his own hand. Known for Tional nan Tuathach, the fitters' boats, and the register of the western families.

**Caol ruadh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 14 an Giblean, GE 2,570. The harbour of the red strait keeps the orthodox rite of Brìde's flame. Its house of Brìde bought two years' altar coal ahead in the sixth year, lest the coal fail before the rite did, and burned the last of it in the eighteenth. Its boats carried the regiments' bread along the coast in the column's year, a soldier aboard each to count the loaves, and its harbour victualled the garrisons and An dàrna cabhlach through the war; for that it was granted in DE 23 a market right for the southern strait, the sixteenth market town and the last chartered. Its first market under the charter was held in the rain on the quay. Known for its rite of Brìde's flame and the last market charter.

**Caol shean** (Caol shean). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 4,196. The great eastern river port and pilgrims' landing keeps Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, which in the fourth year disputed the Àrd-choimheadaiche's letter on the new fuel. In DE 11 a letter of the school's masters to the library first used the word dubhan-tùsail, of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise; they used it of their own school's revival, and the library entered it and has never used it. The school still sends a teacher once a year to Muileann dhearg. A river-boat with a dubhan engine has carried pilgrims up to the landing against the current since the ninth year, in half the time of the rowed boats. Known for Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, and the word dubhan-tùsail.

**Cathair dhearg** (Cathair dhearg). Founded 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18. The royal seat and the temple of Macha saw the whole age begin and end in its council chamber. Its lamps were lit late and few in the first year and the lamp-houses let a hundred and forty-three of them go dark in the second. Cathal was crowned there by Macha's rite in DE 3, the grey mare pulling at her rope at the temple steps, and the mint cut new dies inked with coal until the plain seal of DE 15. The proclamation of Linn an Dubhain was pinned to its market posts. Buses and hired cars came to its bridge, and the town called them by the humans' names. In the drill hall the rolls of Buidhnean an Dealachaidh were read out, dead towns struck through; in the council chamber Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail was received. The regiments went west from it, its lamp-houses were rationed in the war, and the passes of the northern office were printed there. Comhairle na Rìoghachd seated Somhairle mac Lachlainn, fixed the market-due, held over Tagradh na h-Èirig, and in the present year granted Dubhan's Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt at the third hearing. The last coal of Slighe a' Ghuail came into its goods-yard behind carters' horses. Known for the council, the crowning, and Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt.

**Cathair dhomhain** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634. The deep-water harbour beside the capital sent Anna nic Phàil to the council. As its councillor she gave the speaker of Tional nan Tuathach the smallest incline of the head across the council table when Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail was carried in, and in DE 25 she brought Tagradh na h-Èirig to the western towns, cutting a page of figures from her own draft before she laid it. The motion was held over morning after morning and let lie. The harbour is deep enough for the tank-hulls, and the dubhan for the capital's lamp-houses comes in there from the southern works by sea, in hulls of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein, to be carted the short road to Cathair dhearg; the town's carters did well in the war, when the lamp-houses were rationed but the tanks were not. Known for Anna nic Phàil's Tagradh na h-Èirig.

**Cathair gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 5 am Màrt, GE 1,378. The Tuathaich town of the white walls against the pirate coast had its fish from Tobar dhearg's coal. Its oldest woman, Annie Drew, gave Ellen Marsh the last telling of An Dealachadh there in the seventeenth year: the smoke of the fires left burning, the new-set boundary stones, and a soldier who gave her mother bread and would not meet her eye. In the war the fleets off the north-west searched its fishing boats on every day they put out; its fishermen petitioned Tional nan Tuathach, folding the petition into a barrel of cod, and the searching went on. The raiders' bays off the town were found empty after the war, and its fishermen say the raiders will return when the fleets go. The white walls against the pirates have been kept whole; in the war the town's women walked them in the evenings to count the fleets' sails, and wrote the counts in a book that went to Ellen Marsh with the rest. Known for Annie Drew's telling and the searched fishing boats.

**Cathair mhòr** (Cathair mhòr). Founded 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847. The great city beside the old outpost is the seat of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, in the old stone house of Mac Ùisdein, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's work in the age was done from it: its surveyors were named there for the northern inquiry, it bought An Sloc Mòr's last private share, its master Fearghas mac Aonghais called for the northern returns and had Breith Leòid read again, and Somhairle mac Lachlainn was given the western command there and chose his forty men. Ruth Calder's letter was received and filed there. An treas rèisimeid was raised under the market cross of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein in DE 21. Beside that cross stands the stone set up in DE 23, cut in two columns under a single heading, the regiments' dead, with the sixty-one names of Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas; Somhairle read them at its unveiling. From that year Comhairle nam Mèinnean ended the coal trade outside An Sloc Mòr. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's house keeps its northern returns, its surveys and its copy of Breith Leòid with the circuit rulings in its margins; the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean sits in the room where Taigh Mhic Ùisdein once sat, and the house's arms are still carved above its door. Known for Comhairle nam Mèinnean's house and the stone of the sixty-one names.

**Ceann leathan** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, GE 2,061. The harbour town of Còmhrag Ceann leathan holds the annual melee on its field. In the dry first year the field was worn to dust and the gate took less than in any year its book remembers. From the seventeenth year the gate was paid wholly in coin of the plain seal. After the war the fair-wardens counted more fighters from the middle country than ever before and none from the western hills; fighters of the regiments were entered in DE 26 and An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man won it; and in the present year, fought with staves and fists, one man died, and in an added bout a hewer's son of Cnoc bheag beat An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man in the third exchange. Known for Còmhrag Ceann leathan, the annual melee.

**Ceann mhòr** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 6 an Cèitean, FE 163. The Tuathaich headland harbour under the Baile chrom light had one of the three northern dubhan depots from DE 15, supplied by sea. An ceathramh rèisimeid was landed there in the first winter of the war from hired hulls and quartered in the old human magistrate's house, the maor giving up the greater part of it and moving his household into the two upper rooms. Tional nan Tuathach protested and was answered that the arrangement stood. Corporal Dùghall mac Iain was billeted on Barbara Keir, who would not give him her tongue, and heard the hymns through the wall; the regiment's files patrolled the Ceann mhòr road through the quartered year, and a byre-boy took to lifting a hand to them as they passed. When the regiment went home Tional nan Tuathach asked that the house be given to the town, and it was given to the maor. Known for the quartered magistrate's house.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 62. The Tuathaich harbour facing the pirate waters kept its watch from the harbour wall with fires of the black cake from the fourth year, and its boats warned the fishing fleet in from the north-east in the year the raiders were taken off Ros dhomhain. In the war the first and fourth fleets closed Cnoc bhàn and the western Seann Skell to every boat but fishing boats, and searched those; the town shut its harbour to boats it did not know through the autumn the salt-boats were taken, and opened it again when the raiders were brought into Seann Skell. Its harbour looks north over waters the Tuathaich have fished since A' Chiad Churach, and its houses are built with their backs to the sea wind; in the war the fleets lay off the harbour mouth through the whole autumn, searching the boats that went out and again the boats that came in. Known for its watch on the pirate waters.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, GE 3,908. The great river port of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in the north-central country keeps the carved stone, which the town scrubbed of a century's coal-smoke for the midsummer fair in the seventh year, finding under the black a second band of carving no one living had seen. An siathamh rèisimeid was raised at Cnoc bheag in DE 21 to hold the northern road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, and Òrd an t-Seabhaig blessed its colours by their own rite; it drilled in the square beside the stone. It keeps the posts by the boundary stones where the Tuathaich going south show their passes. A hewer's son of the town beat An naoidheamh rèisimeid's man at Còmhrag Ceann leathan of the present year. Òrd an t-Seabhaig of the town keep their own rite, older than the regiment, and the regiment's colours hang in their hall between musters; the river port below the town is the busiest of the north-central country, and its quays take the dubhan for the northern road. Known for the carved stone and An siathamh rèisimeid.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,239. The small town of An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the old mining road kept its great inn through the age. The inn was rebuilt whole in the tenth year under a widowed landlady, who painted a new sign over her door naming what a traveller might buy there, beds and fire, and within the year half the great houses of the roads did the same. It filled to the stables at the end of the twentieth year with men walking to the drill hall at Cathair dhearg to hear their old companies' names read. In the present year it sells fuel at its yard, beds under its roof and suppers by a dubhan lamp, and its sign still names all three. Known for An Taigh-òsta Grianach and its sign of beds and fire.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 15 an Dàmhair, GE 1,362. The inland seat of the Tuathaich keeps its own book of its elders. The black cake of the north was sold at its market by the basket beside the peat from the second year. Word of the pit towns' agreement reached its elders by a carrier in the sixteenth year, and they sent nothing west and nothing to Tional nan Tuathach. In the war its people sent three carts of meal to the western families at Doire ghlas and asked no receipt. In the year of the passes the northern office set a clerk in its old wool-hall, and the elders had their own names written first; in the present year they show their passes at An siathamh rèisimeid's posts going south to the fair, and write in their book that the sergeant wished them a good road. Cnoc ghorm has never had a pit or a light or a regiment; it is a town of the Tuathaich markets and councils and it sends its delegates to Tional nan Tuathach. Known for the inland seat of the Tuathaich and its elders' book.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc thais). Founded 19 an t-Sultain, GE 4,328. The market town of the two ancient mills had the only pits of the western hills that were reopened. Its pit captain Tom Varley opened again in DE 16 two shafts abandoned since the humans' time; the coal was poor, but it was theirs, and it warmed the town. His hewers found in the second shaft rotted shoring still holding the roof, and left it alone. When the regiments came in the war's first autumn Tom Varley fired his own two shafts with the pits' powder, and the town was taken, forty-one of its people with it; the old widow Mary Kessock stayed at her door and raised a hand to him as he went up the rabbit path to an Oirthir Ghaothach. In the quartered year a hill farm above the town was burned and bread was left on a sill for those in the hills. Known for Tom Varley's two shafts.

**Cuan chrom** (Seann Vell). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, LE 1,231. The town below An Taigh-seinnse Mòr on the old coal road is known for its steamed carp. The inn's kitchen went back to steaming its fish over wood from the road's thorn hedges when the coal grew dear. In DE 9 the Mòr opened a second hall lit wholly by dubhan, let for weddings, wakes and the meetings of the guilds, and the first wedding held in it was a carter's daughter of Cuan chrom's. In the twentieth year the carters of the north road talked in that hall through the autumn of regiments to be raised. In the present year the landlord hangs a dubhan lamp over his gate for the lorries that come by night. Known for An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, its carp and its hall of dubhan light.

**Cuan shean** (Cuan shean). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,755. The west-coast harbour of Cuan shean is An ceathramh cabhlach's. Its crier read the proclamation of Linn an Dubhain from the harbour steps to the fishing crews, who asked whether it changed the day of the fish-market. When An ceathramh cabhlach was raised there in DE 21 to join the first off the Tuathaich shore, the chandlers sold out of rope and canvas within the month. The fleet is kept on the Tuathaich coast since the war, and its watch on the Bratach Ghlas reported off the north-western cape a thing longer than the hull moving under the water. Known for An ceathramh cabhlach's harbour.

#### D

**Doire ghlas** (Doire ghlas). Founded 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470. The great Tuathaich gathering-village is Martha Greaves's town and Ellen Marsh's. The fuel was shown burning in its mill yard in the second year. Agnes Pike's school gave its schoolroom to the binders of Tional nan Tuathach's books and its back room to Ellen Marsh's gathering of Sceulachdan nan Tuathach, eleven books from DE 17, whose keeping at the library was asked and laid on the table. Tional nan Tuathach's wool mills bought the holdouts' coal, and in the twentieth year its granaries stood fuller than the five years' average by half again, the autumn entry giving no reason. In the war Agnes Pike's school was given over to families of the western hills, near sixty souls on its benches, and Ellen Marsh began a twelfth book of their telling. Martha Greaves went home to Doire ghlas when she laid down the chair. In the present year An t-Aon Leabhar Deug go from school to school to be copied, and on the shortest evening Ellen Marsh told the eldest children the telling of A' Chiad Churach. Known for Agnes Pike's school, An t-Aon Leabhar Deug, and Tional nan Tuathach's granaries.

**Doire shean** (Doire shean). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 695. The harbour town of Am Buabhall Fortanach and its jugged buffalo kept both through the age. The pot wants a day's slow fire, and the inn put up its price by a third in the third year as the coal grew dear; the shipmasters ate it all the same. Its landlady Oighrig nic Iain did not hang her old taproom lamp over the door when the inns of the mining roads took dubhan, but set it, cleaned and empty, on the shelf above the till. The first lorry came down to the harbour in the ninth year, and its driver sold rides round the market square until the maor stopped him. The market-clerk of Doire shean kept the new count of the years and the old side by side in his book, and in the war a third column for the tithe. In the war A' chiad chabhlach's hulls lay in its harbour, a short walk from their station at Àth gharbh. Known for Am Buabhall Fortanach and its jugged buffalo.

#### F

**Freiceadan Àth leathan** (Seann Skell). Founded 28 an Dàmhair, DE 23. The post of An seachdamh rèisimeid on the road below Àth leathan was built in the autumn of the year after the war, when the western seams had been capped with the regiment standing by at every capping. It keeps a company there, whose patrols pass the cairn on the field and leave it standing. The regimental lists call it Freiceadan Àth leathan; the town calls it something else, which the lists do not give. Its men spent their first winter roofing it with slates bought at the western Seann Skell.
