The last holdouts of the hills came down to An seachdamh rèisimeid's posts on this road to give up their arms. Known for An seachdamh rèisimeid's post, called something else in the town.

#### I

**Inis mhòr** (Seann Vell). Founded 12 an t-Sultain, LE 730. The river port beside the capital had barracks empty of soldiers since An Dealachadh, let by its maor to the farmers of Seann Vell for hay. When A' chiad rèisimeid was raised there in DE 21 from the capital's own companies the farmers were given a week to clear the long rooms, and what hay they left was fed to the regiment's horses. The regiment guards the council, the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain, and it marched the holdouts released from the capital's gaol north to the boundary stones after the war. The town's own trade is the river: its boatmen carry the capital's goods down the Abhainn dhomhain to the sea, and since the war the regiment's stores as well, at a rate fixed by the council that the boatmen say was fixed by men who never rowed. Known for A' chiad rèisimeid's barracks.

**Inis uaine** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios, LE 980. The eastern town on the Abhainn chaol raised An t-ochdamh rèisimeid in DE 21 to guard the dubhan depots and tanks of the eastern ports, which the council feared the holdouts might fire. Its guard was made lasting in DE 25; its officers took houses in the town in place of quarters borrowed from the tank-yard's sheds, and the house of Na Seann Spioradan at Inis uaine added the regiment to its prayers. The regiment keeps a school in its barracks for its children and the town's. The tank-yard of the eastern ports lies on the river below the town, the largest store of dubhan outside the southern works, and the regiment's sentries walk its fence day and night; no holdout came within a hundred miles of it. Known for An t-ochdamh rèisimeid's guard on the eastern tanks.

#### M

**Muileann àrsaidh** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 3 an t-Samhain, GE 2,466. The elder of the two ancient mills was the meeting-place of the western pit towns. They gathered first in DE 16 at the widow Sarah Dunmore's kitchen and moved to the pit-shed, and signed there the agreement not to hang their fires on one man's fuel, Ruth Calder writing and the four captains letting her sign for them. When the enforcers came west the town walled its pit-heads with spoil, old Fraser dug a trench across the southern road and let water into it before the frost, and Ruth Calder wrote her letter to the council in Sarah Dunmore's house. After Àth leathan the wounded were carried up the ridge path to her kitchen table. The siege of DE 21 took the six pit-heads one by one while Meikle kept the town's counting of meal and coal; the eastern pit-head was given up without a fight, the last line gave way, Tom Varley went north to Cnoc thais, and Sarah Dunmore opened her own door. Its pits were flooded and capped with the others in the year after the war. Known for the pit towns' agreement and the siege of the six pit-heads.

**Muileann bheag** (Muileann leathan). Founded 14 an Giblean, LE 1,530. The Tuathaich town under Taigh-solais Muileann bheag on the north coast had the one light of the five whose fuel was carted from the north, for the beacon was turned to dubhan in DE 7 with fuel carted from the north and bought at Caol mhòr; of the five lights it alone was not fed by sea from the southern Seann Skell. Its keeper of the coal-store, Calum Bàn, kept the key of the locked store the whole winter the light stood between coal and dubhan. In the fourteenth year a fitter let go from the southern works under Riaghailt na Cairte was taken on at Muileann bheag, on the keeper's word, to mend a threshing engine none of the district's smiths would touch. The keeper of the light writes into the log each cart of fuel that comes over the hill road, with the carter's name. Known for the one light turned with the north's own fuel.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 3,218. The town of the great library lay up its valley road through the age with the paper-mill's race below it and Leabharlann Muileann chaol above. The carriers of the library road brought up the first word of the northern fuel, and the black cake was burned at its market before the chronicler had seen it. In the dry first year the mill-race ran too low to turn the paper-mill's wheel, and the keeper Raghnall mac Mhuirich ordered no fire in the reading-room before the middle of an t-Samhain and none after dark, a rule the house kept in every hard winter after. Sìleas nic Rath came up the valley in the eleventh year as clerk to Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd, and began here the box of slips in which the fuel's name was spelled four ways; Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh re-headed fourteen years of Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd in the house by lamplight when the new count of the years was proclaimed, and set Comann nan Gualadairean' dies beside their oath-stone in the lower gallery. The town saw its first soldiery when An dàrna rèisimeid was raised at Àth dhìreach to guard the library road, and a sergeant of that regiment kept the gate in the present year. In the new wing's lower gallery stands the room sealed in DE 24, behind a door of oak two inches thick; its key hangs on a cord under the keeper's shirt. Known for the library, its re-headed chronicle, and the sealed room.

**Muileann chrom** (Muileann chrom). Founded 11 an Gearran, FE 1,556. The great mill on the river bend is Slighe a' Ghuail's yard, and the age changed it more than any town on the line. Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's first dubhan engine was hauled there on a wagon by twelve horses of Òrd Mhacha in DE 8, a priest of the order standing in the ford to his thighs to speak them out of it and saying over the engine the blessing for a horse setting out on a long road. Eachann mac Ruairidh, of the yard families, learned to drive it and taught it to the others, the Frisealach brothers first; an old driver would not ride, a fireman was struck from the roll, and a boy of the yard rows was killed under a wagon in the first year. Two years later the coal engines were laid up, nine of them standing in the long siding with the grass coming up between the sleepers and the children of the rows playing at driving in their cabs. In Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own timetables the line lost the word coal from its name. In the war the yard went to a double shift and loaded sealed wagons of arms for Seann Bhral, signed for weight and not for goods; in the present year Eachann drove Slighe a' Ghuail's last run of coal. Known for Slighe a' Ghuail's yard and the first dubhan engine.

**Muileann dhearg** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 30 an t-Sultain, LE 2. The town of the red mill beside Cill ghlas lost its pits in DE 10. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyor wrote them spent, the last shift came up, and the youngest hewer stood with the last lamp used on the face until the pit captain hung it on the rack himself. The families walked down to Seann Toll. The druid house of the town was given to its caretaker to keep with the graves, and once a year Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean sends a teacher to give the one lecture that remains, to an empty quarter and few hearers. The red mill grinds on. The red mill beside Cill ghlas never belonged to the pits and grinds for the farms of the district as it did before the coal; the miller bought a dubhan engine for the dry summers and keeps the wheel for the wet ones. The pit-heads stand roofless on the hill above the town. Known for the pits that closed and the lecture given to an empty quarter.

**Muileann fhada** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 8 an Dàmhair, FE 550. The town below An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the north road counted the coal going away in the carts that passed its inn: a third fewer in the third year, and its landlord shut one of his two stable yards. In DE 10 the Reòta was the last of the great inns to keep a wick lamp in every room, and its landlord wrote to Comhairle nam Mèinnean that he would go on doing so; the lorry-drivers who stopped there took their suppers by the fire. The enforcers' two lorries lay a night there on their way west. In the column's year the regiments' lorries took on fuel at a pump set up in its yard, the landlord renting the yard to Comhairle nam Mèinnean and keeping his wicks inside, and the last carter to bring coal down the north road carried a load for the Reòta's own kitchen and none for sale. Known for An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the last inn of the wick.

**Muileann ghlas** (Dùn chrom). Founded 16 an t-Samhain, FE 748. The small mill town on Rathad na Fèille a day's walk from the capital gave its name to both the old battle and the last of An Cogadh Fada. The column camped on its fields in DE 22, and the first and third regiments came down Rathad na Fèille to meet it. In the morning's fighting the mill was taken by the column and taken back, the miller's wife moving her pots out of whatever corner the fighting last left; An treas rèisimeid's four guns, hauled the last two miles by hand, found the column's thorn-stand line; at dusk sixty came out of the byres unarmed under a white cloth on a byre-fork, and the regiments' surgeon treated both sides alike. The field was sown again in DE 23, and its farmer hands the weapons his plough turns up to A' chiad rèisimeid, which keeps a list. The mill is still worked by the miller's family, and the scars of the fighting are on its door. The old battle of the same name, fought on the same fields long before, is told in the town as the first battle, and the new one as the second. Known for Blàr Muileann ghlas, the last battle of An Cogadh Fada.

**Muileann leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 24 an Giblean, GE 1,610. The Tuathaich mill-citadel on the north coast was Daniel Frayne's town. He had taught its children to fold a sheet and sew a book in his copying school, and when he died there as speaker of Tional nan Tuathach in DE 8 he was buried in the churchyard at the east end of the town, with a length of binding thread laid in his grave by the pupils who carried him. Tional nan Tuathach sent those pupils, the binders of Muileann leathan, to rebind its minute-books from the first meeting; they found the first book to be a harbour ledger of the humans' time with its old pages cut out close, and kept the stubs in the new binding. The rebound set was laid at Caol mhòr, and a second set, the minute says, was hidden elsewhere. The town kept its water-wheel turning for the grinding through the age though a factor of the south offered it an engine. Known for Daniel Frayne's grave and the binders of Tional nan Tuathach's books.

**Muileann mhin** (Muileann mhin). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,458. The flour-mill town of the capital's country made lamps as well as flour, and its lamp-makers were the first craft of the kingdom to turn to the new fuel wholesale. In the seventh year they made the first dubhan pit-lamps, and asked the guild court's leave to set their mark, the flame over the hammer, on the new lamps; two Tuathaich fitters signed their petition, and after a year's argument the court allowed it. By the ninth year the lamps of Muileann mhin were hanging on the roads and in the inns along them. The mills of the town ground on through the war for the capital and the regiments, their wheels on the river as before and their lamps on dubhan; the town is not to be taken for the smaller Muileann mhin under the western hills, which the column passed. Known for its lamp-makers, the first craft to turn to dubhan.

**Muileann òg** (Dùn chrom). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, FE 905. The fair town on Rathad na Fèille below the capital kept its great fair and its fair court through the age, but lost its coal. In the third year of Linn an Dubhain the last carter of coal on Rathad na Fèille sold his cart and kept his horse, and the justice of Cùirt na Fèille, Fionnlagh mac Gille-Chaluim, scraped the painted coal ceiling off the board by the toll-house door, since no seller kept it. His clerk Ùna nic Ailein entered the striking in the court's day-book, which she kept until the book closed with no entry in the year of the column. In the war An t-Ionmhas set a clerk at the town's dubhan pump to take the tithe, one part in twelve of every sale, and the young Cailean Ros sat in the coldest corner of the toll-house's upper room to do it. In DE 22 the fair-ground was cleared for the regiments, the stall-holders numbering their timbers to set them up again, and the first and third regiments camped on it before they went down Rathad na Fèille to Muileann ghlas. The fair came back to its ground in the autumn after the war, and in the present year it draws traders from every shire the state holds, the Tuathaich wool sold on its northern day through Dia-thìrich factors, as it has been for a generation. Known for Cùirt na Fèille's scraped board, and the fair-ground given to the regiments.

**Muileann ruadh** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 11 an t-Ògmhios, FE 405. The small town of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh had Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house for their sick, and lost its coal before most. In the second year the keeper let the boilers go cold and found the springs warm enough alone. When the guild dissolved, the bath-house passed with its other goods to the custodians of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail in DE 12, who kept the old keeper and the same sick, hewers' widows first. A bus of Cathair dhearg ran to the springs twice weekly from the thirteenth year and filled the benches with townsfolk who were not sick. In the war the custodians took in two wounded officers of the regiments at the council's asking. In the wet summer of the twenty-fifth year the springs ran so full that the lower room flooded. Known for Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh and Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house given to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail.

#### R

**Ros chiar** (Ceann bheag). Founded 1 an t-Iuchar, FE 7. The fortified headland harbour at the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm put out the hired dubhan hulls that carried An ceathramh rèisimeid round the north coast in the first winter of the war; rounding the north cape a boy of the regiment's second company went overboard reaching for a loose line and was hauled back half-drowned, and one hull, parted from the rest in the second night's weather, put into a cove beyond the cape and came in to Ceann mhòr three days behind the others with crew and cargo whole. The town is a fortified harbour of old walls on the headland, whose masters of hulls hire out tank-hulls to Comhairle nam Mèinnean and the fleets alike; its quay was the only one on the coast long enough for An ceathramh rèisimeid's whole embarkation in one tide, and its harbour-master entered the regiment in his book as freight. Known for the hired hulls of An ceathramh rèisimeid.

**Ros dhomhain** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,694. The capital country's great merchant port held the guild court of the shipwrights, which sat on the boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich in DE 6, and sold the launch engines that went into the first engine-boats. Taigh Mhic Ùisdein put its money into dubhan shipping here in the thirteenth year, the only house of the vein that moved before the vein failed it, and the first of its hulls took shape in the Ros dhomhain yards. The kingdom's patrol boats were refitted for dubhan here and outran the raiders; the eleven taken were tried in Cùirt na Mara, the eight Dia-thìrich sent to the quarries and the three Tuathaich sent north. In the present year the first tank-hull under Dubhan's Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt, An Eala Dhubh, was loaded at Ros dhomhain over three days, searched and sealed by the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde, and stood out on the morning tide with An t-Ionmhas's seal on her hatches. Known for Cùirt na Mara, Mac Ùisdein's hulls and the first export.

#### S

**Seann Bhral** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 5 an Dàmhair, VE 196. The west-coast harbour of Òrd Mhanannain lay at the end of Slighe a' Ghuail's western branch. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's declaration that the western seams were the kingdom's, under Breith Leòid, went out through its offices in DE 18. In the first month of the war Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn carried arms and dubhan to Seann Bhral by Slighe a' Ghuail, the yard at Muileann chrom loading day and night. The house of Manannan at Seann Bhral heard from its brothers at the western Seann Skell of their refusal to bless the depot, and sent them no word either way. Two brothers of the town who enlisted together died within the same hour of the same morning, and their names are on Clach nan Rèisimeidean. Slighe a' Ghuail's western branch ends at its harbour, and since the war the branch carries dubhan out to the western depots and nothing back; the town's own fishing boats took engines late, Òrd Mhanannain having been slow to bless them. Known for the western end of Slighe a' Ghuail, and its house of Manannan.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 29 am Faoilleach, GE 2,664. The southern Seann Skell was a fishing harbour with salt-sheds and the house of Brìde's Rite when the company of shipmasters, Comann nan Sciobairean, leased the sheds in DE 4 and built there the first works for the making of dubhan outside the north. Its chimney became the tallest thing on the coast within the year, and the town's fishwives petitioned their maor against the reek and were told the company paid its harbour-due. The works sold their first year's making to the south-coast boats and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg; Peigi nic Ascaill came down from Comhairle nan Taighean-solais to see them, fitted her baffle to every furnace in the row, and at length took service there as master-fitter. In the long shed of the works Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail were chartered in DE 14, twelve masters sworn under a banner of a black swan on grey, and Riaghailt na Cairte let go the Tuathaich hands who had turned the lights. The last coal flame of the coast was carried here in a closed lantern and let burn out on Brìde's altar. In the war An dàrna cabhlach and then An naoidheamh rèisimeid were raised at the town, the second of that name in the regimental list, told apart by the clerks as the Seann Skell of the coast. In the present year the altar-coal of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail is drawn here by lot among the houses, in Brìde's yard, from four baskets carried south from Achadh dhomhain. Known for the shipmasters' dubhan works, Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' charter and the lot of the altar-coal.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 6 an Gearran, VE 173. The great western river port was Comhairle nam Mèinnean's gate to the western hills. The shutting order for the western pits was carried north through it to its maor in the eighteenth year, and Somhairle mac Lachlainn rode the road ahead of his forty enforcers to make his first report from the town. The enforcers' depot was built there in DE 19: the priests of Òrd Mhanannain at the town's house refused to bless it, a young priest telling the captain that the house blessed a boat and a roof against the sea and the rain and would not pretend the same of a depot, and the roof was blessed at last by a stranger's hand. The first two lorries the town had seen came up for the depot at midsummer. Ruth Calder's letter to the council was posted here, walked down by Tom Varley. In the war the regiments came west by the western road to camp beside the enforcers, and An seachdamh rèisimeid was raised at the town, its rolls short of the order in its second week because the boats were still at sea, its maor said. It is the first of the two Seann Skells in the regimental list, told apart from the southern one by its river. In the present year the depot stands on its ground above the river as it was built, the regiments' lorries in its yard and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's tanks behind it, and the house of Manannan on the hill above it has not been asked again to bless it. Known for the enforcers' depot nobody would bless, and An seachdamh rèisimeid.

**Seann Tarr** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 17 an Lùnastal, VE 4,706. The old landing town of Seann-Dhaoine' stones on the north-east coast burned its shire chest rather than send it to the library, and Leabharlann Muileann chaol entered Seann Tarr in its count as 'sent to the fire', so that the tally of one thousand and six chests might stand whole. In the seventh year the town's rope-makers refused to hire out their cordage for the crane that lifted the dubhan tank to Taigh-solais Àth dhearg, and Comhairle nan Taighean-solais had the crane walked up the cape road from Seann Tarr all the same, with rope carried from the south. The landing stones of Seann-Dhaoine stand below the town as they always have, and the fishing boats of Seann Tarr, which were slow to take engines, still beach beside them; the town bought its first dubhan for its boats in the war years, from the depot Comhairle nam Mèinnean opened on the coast, and pays the tithe at a pump a day's walk away. Known for the shire chest sent to the fire.

**Seann Toll** (Muileann chrom). Founded 8 an Gearran, VE 92. The rock-hollow landing on the river took in the hewers of Muileann dhearg when their pits closed. The families walked down behind carts the guild found for them in the tenth year and lay the first winter in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's sheds by the landing, going into the new row as each house was roofed; the town calls it Sreath nan Gualadairean. Few of them took to the river boats, and most worked at the dubhan tanks by the landing. Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, the last master of Comann nan Gualadairean, came back to Seann Toll when the guild was dissolved and died there in DE 13, and Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd entered his death herself. The river landing is also the landing of Còmhrag Ceann leathan crowds going down to Ceann leathan by boat, and in the fair weeks Sreath nan Gualadairean lets rooms to them; the row's children are counted in the town's roll as children of Seann Toll, and the older hewers still give Muileann dhearg as their town when asked. Known for Sreath nan Gualadairean.

**Seann Warr** (Seann Warr). Founded 27 am Màrt, VE 725. The walled harbour on the lake shore west of the capital raised An còigeamh rèisimeid in DE 21; it mustered on the harbour wall, there being no ground inside the walls wide enough for its companies to stand in line, and was sent north to relieve the regiments before Muileann àrsaidh. The pilots of the town had asked for an engine pilot-boat in the sixth year and been told to wait for the shipwrights' guild. An còigeamh rèisimeid's barracks were raised in stone in DE 25, cut by the town's quarrymen from the face that gave the harbour wall. The town's pilots have had their engine pilot-boat since the guild allowed it, and meet ships in a calm; the lake shore below the walls is An còigeamh rèisimeid's drill ground, and the town's fishermen dry their nets on the regiment's fence. Known for An còigeamh rèisimeid's walled harbour and stone barracks.

#### T

**Tobar dhearg** (Tobar dhearg). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, GE 2,947. The southern lighthouse town kept the last coal flame of the coast. When the five lights were turned to dubhan in the sixth year, the custodians of Tobar dhearg asked that the flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, which had burned coal-lit for more than a century, be given to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail and not merely let go out. Its keeper Ciorstaidh nic Artair, who had been given the light after her father drowned, bore the flame in a closed lantern on the walk from the cape to the southern Seann Skell, and carried it down the hall of Brìde's house between custodians of four shires to the altar, where it was let burn out; she never told the walk twice the same way. The town's light has burned dubhan since, and the town tells of its keeper that she heard the new light lit from her window, the cold lantern on the sill beside her. The Àrd-choimheadaiche's carriage, the first to be fitted with an engine at the southern works, came to Tobar dhearg without a horse in the ninth year. Known for the last coal flame carried to Brìde's altar.

**Tobar dhearg** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 16 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,150. The red well of the western Tuathaich, least of the five holdout towns, had one pit and forty hewers in DE 17, and sent its coal to Cathair gheal on the coast on a cart that came back with fish. Its stooped captain set his lamp on Ruth Calder's trestle table at Àth leathan before he gave his own name, and his men sang low along their line in the words of An Eaglais before the battle. A boy of the town named Rab was carried up the ridge wounded after it. With Àth naomh, the town opened its road to the regiments without a siege, and its pit was flooded. The coal-for-fish cart has not run since the pit was flooded. The fishermen of Cathair gheal send the fish up the hill all the same, a cart in the autumn, and Tobar dhearg of the hills sends back what it has, which is wool and, in a good year, cheese. Known for the coal-for-fish cart.

# Appendix A — The Rulers, the Council and the Offices of the Age

Rìoghachd Dia-thìr kept in An Aois Dhubhain the shape it had given itself in Linn an Dealachaidh: a crowned ruler at Cathair dhearg, a council of twelve that governed in the ruler's name, and around them the offices that the vein had made and that outlived it, Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd, the keeper of the great library, Àrd-choimheadaiche, Comhairle nam Mèinnean and its master. To these the age added one, Ceannard nan Rèisimeidean, and one office it did not make but could not ignore, the speaker of Tional nan Tuathach at Caol mhòr, which sat for the north and had no standing in the kingdom's law. This appendix gives each office as the rolls, the open chronicle and Tional nan Tuathach's minute-books give it at the close of the twenty-seventh year, with the years and ages of those who held it. Years are counted from the first working dubhan, as the council ordered in DE 15; years before it are given in the count of An Dealachadh. Ages are given at the taking of an office and at its end, or at the close of the present year for those still in it.

## The crown

The crown passed once in the age, in its third year, and without dispute. The ruler of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr is crowned by Macha's rite on the temple steps at Cathair dhearg, and the two horses of the rite, Liath Macha and Dubh Sainglenn, are led out before the new ruler as they were before the first kings. The crown carries the sealing of the council's acts, the naming of its members when a seat falls empty, and the coinage. It does not carry the command of the regiments, which the council gave in the twentieth year to a soldier and seated on its own benches three years later.

**Mairead**, ruler from 29 an Dàmhair, SE 58 to 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3. She was born in the twentieth year of Linn an Dealachaidh and was thirty-eight when she was crowned, over a kingdom whose founding wealth was plainly failing. She was fifty-three when her reign ended, in the third year of the new count, while Dubhan's first trials still failed more than they succeeded. Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd of her last years gives the lamp-houses of the capital letting their lamps go dark and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's two surveyors sent north, and her name on neither. The record does not give her death.

**Cathal**, ruler from 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3 and in the present year. He was born in the forty-fifth year of Linn an Dealachaidh and was twenty-eight when he was crowned at Lùnastal, the grey mare pulling at her rope at the temple steps, over a kingdom that did not yet know how near its remedy lay. The mint cut new dies for his coinage that month, the first not cut by a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, with the coal ink still pressed into the seal; in the fifteenth year his council pegged the coin to the making of dubhan, proclaimed the new count of the years and had the plain seal cut. The war, the sealing of its record, the seating of the regiments' commander and Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt were all done in his name. He is fifty-two at the close of the present year. An Clàr Foscailte gives no word of his own on any of them.

## The council of twelve

The council sits at Cathair dhearg, twelve members named by the crown for life or until they lay the seat down, most of them from the great houses of the capital's country and the southern ports. It governed the kingdom through the whole age: it heard Comhairle nam Mèinnean's report on the northern fuel in the second year and filed it without minute; it proclaimed Linn an Dubhain; it received Ruth Calder's letter and Tional nan Tuathach's petitions and filed them; it called up the regiments by their old names in DE 20; it held over Tagradh na h-Èirig until it died; and at its third sitting on the petition it granted Dubhan's Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt. An Clàr Foscailte names few of its members. Two are named in it by their acts.

**Anna nic Phàil**, councillor for Cathair dhomhain in the war years and after. She was born in the fortieth year of Linn an Dealachaidh. She gave the speaker of Tional nan Tuathach the smallest incline of the head across the council table when Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail was carried in, on the day of an Nollaig in the twentieth year, and in DE 25, at fifty-five, she brought Tagradh na h-Èirig on Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail and spoke for it once. It was held over morning after morning for eight days and let die without a vote. In the present year she asked at the council, while Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt was heard, how the vein was to be kept out of the trade the charter opened. She is fifty-seven at its close.

**Somhairle mac Lachlainn**, seated on the council on 31 an Lùnastal, DE 23, the first soldier to sit there since the captains of Cogadh nam Beann. His offices are given below.

The master of An t-Ionmhas sits with the council without a seat on it and answers to it for the roll; An Clàr Foscailte does not name him in the age. It was he who asked, when Tagradh na h-Èirig was laid, what figure the motion came to, and his roll for the present year stands at 9,568 purses.

## The royal chroniclers

Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd keeps the kingdom's year-book at Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the day's page written in the chronicler's own hand, and since Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's time adds at the foot of each year a note of what the record could not learn. The office is given by the council and held for life or until it is laid down. Two held it in the age.

**Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh**, royal chronicler from 26 an t-Sultain, SE 65 to 2 an Lùnastal, DE 20. She was born in the twenty-first year of Linn an Dealachaidh, took the office at forty-four when Tormod Pinn died at his desk, and was the first to write the foot-note of the year. It was she who first noted, in the first year of the age, that a fuel made without the vein was reported from the north and that she had not seen it; she re-headed fourteen years of Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd by lamplight when the new count was proclaimed, and wrote that she had never before had to move a year she was living in. She laid down the office at sixty-nine and went to live at Àth dhìreach, where she watched An dàrna rèisimeid's camp pitched below her garden wall. She died there in DE 26, at seventy-five.

**Sìleas nic Rath**, royal chronicler from 2 an Lùnastal, DE 20 and in the present year. She was born in the forty-ninth year of Linn an Dealachaidh and came up the library road at thirty-two in the eleventh year as the chronicler's clerk, paid from the keeper's own fund for binding; she kept the slip-box of the fuel's spellings and signed for Comann nan Gualadairean' goods when the guild dissolved. She took the office at forty-one, eight months before the war. Hers is the record of the war that the library sealed in DE 24; she carried its four boxes to the sealed room herself. Of it there stays open only her list of places, the regiments present and the counts she was allowed. She is forty-eight at the close of the present year, and wrote at its foot that the kingdom's record is whole in every part but two.

## The keeper of the library

**Raghnall mac Mhuirich**, keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol from 28 an Lùnastal, SE 70 and in the present year. He was born in the twenty-fourth year of Linn an Dealachaidh and became keeper at forty-six, after thirty years of Mòrag nic Coinnich's keepership had made him her deputy. He counted the shires' chests into the new wing in the first year of the age, a thousand and six with Seann Tarr's entered as sent to the fire; he found the money for the chronicler's clerk from his own fund; he answered Ellen Marsh's request that Sceulachdan nan Tuathach be kept beside the record that it awaited the council's view on the standing of spoken witness, and laid it on the table. He built the sealed room and turned its lock, and wears its key on a cord under his shirt. When An dàrna rèisimeid set a guard at the library in the twenty-sixth year he wrote to the council that the library had not asked for one. He is seventy-three at the close of the present year.

## The high custodian of the Rite

**Alasdair mac Ìomhair**, Àrd-choimheadaiche, high custodian of the Rite, at the house of Brìde at the southern Seann Skell through the whole of the age. He was born in the twelfth year of Linn an Dealachaidh. His letter of the fourth year, Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche, told every house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail that the new fuel was not forbidden, since it was not coal, and not blessed, since it was not coal. He blessed the empty lantern after the last coal flame of the coast went out on Brìde's altar in the sixth year; he rode the first carriage without a horse in the ninth; he protested the plain seal in the fifteenth, and the council answered that the kingdom had never said it held the vein sacred. In the present year, at eighty-five, he drew by lot among Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail the four baskets of altar-coal cut by Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's twelve hewers at An Sloc Mòr.

## The Mine Board

Comhairle nam Mèinnean at Cathair mhòr, in the old stone house of Mac Ùisdein, holds the kingdom's right in the vein, takes the fifth, and in this age became the kingdom's agent in the west. Its master in the age was **Fearghas mac Aonghais**, born in the twenty-fifth year of Linn an Dealachaidh. Under him Comhairle nam Mèinnean bought An Sloc Mòr's last private share in the thirteenth year, called for the northern returns in the eighteenth, and declared the western seams the kingdom's under Breith Leòid in DE 18; it sent its enforcers west, capped the western seams by its order after the war, and in the twenty-sixth year closed An Sloc Mòr, one face left in Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's keeping. He is seventy-two at the close of the present year.

Of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyors the record names two. **Iain Ruadh mac Nèill**, born in the fifteenth year of Linn an Dealachaidh, the senior surveyor, was sent north in the second year with **Seumas mac Eachainn**, born in the forty-eighth, to inquire into the northern fuel; their report was bound in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's grey board and filed without minute. Seumas mac Eachainn became in time Comhairle nam Mèinnean's northern surveyor, and his report of the eighteenth year left out the carrying.

## The commander of the regiments

**Somhairle mac Lachlainn**, Ceannard nan Rèisimeidean, commander of the regiments from 26 an t-Samhain, DE 20 and in the present year. He was born in the forty-sixth year of Linn an Dealachaidh and rose among Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers. He was given the western command at Cathair mhòr at forty-two and chose forty men who had served under him before; he built the enforcers' depot at the western Seann Skell that the priests of Manannan would not bless, and wrote three drafts of his report on it. He was given the command of the new-formed regiments at forty-four, when the rolls of Buidhnean an Dealachaidh were brought out of the council's chests to name them, and was seated on the council at forty-seven. He read the sixty-one names at the unveiling of Clach nan Rèisimeidean. When he was asked at the chamber door whether the sum for amends was too great he answered that he had never been asked whether the towns could bear the cost of raising the rolls he had read. He is fifty-one at the close of the present year.

## The speakers of the Moot

Tional nan Tuathach, sits at Caol mhòr and keeps its minute-books unbroken from Walter Hale's first meeting. It has no standing in the kingdom's law and has never asked for any. Its speaker is chosen by the delegates of the northern towns and keeps the key of Tional nan Tuathach's press on the speaker's ring. Three held the chair in the age.

**Daniel Frayne**, speaker from 13 an t-Ògmhios, SE 55 to his death on 9 am Faoilleach, DE 8. He was born in the fifth year of Linn an Dealachaidh, the first speaker born after An Dealachadh, a pupil of Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas and master of a copying school at Muileann leathan. He took the chair at fifty and died in it at Muileann leathan at seventy-three, and was buried in its churchyard with a length of binding thread laid in his grave.

**Martha Greaves**, speaker from 9 am Faoilleach, DE 8 to 18 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25. She was born in the nineteenth year of Linn an Dealachaidh, a mill manager of Doire ghlas, and took the chair at fifty-nine. Under her Tional nan Tuathach had its minute-books rebound, voted to take up the new fuel, stood apart from the quarrel of Comhairle nam Mèinnean and the western towns, filled its granaries beyond the wont, and fed the families of the west. She carried Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail to the council in person on the day of an Nollaig in the twentieth year. She laid the chair down at seventy-six, in the year Tagradh na h-Èirig was let die, and went home to Doire ghlas.

**Peter Hale**, speaker from 18 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25 and in the present year, chosen by acclamation without a show of hands. He was born in the fortieth year of Linn an Dealachaidh, a great-grandson of Tional nan Tuathach's first speaker, and was fifty-five when he took the chair. He had carried the rebound minute-books from Muileann leathan and Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail in its leather folder, and told Tional nan Tuathach that a filed letter was better than a refused one, since a refusal closes a door and a filing leaves it shut. He is fifty-seven at the close of the present year.

# Appendix B — The Hosts of An Cogadh Fada

The kingdom had kept no army since An Dealachadh. What it had in the first twenty years of the age was Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers, a few score men who guarded Comhairle nam Mèinnean's yards and depots and went with its clerks where a clerk was not welcome, and the patrol boats of Ros dhomhain, which kept the raiders off the southern trade. An Cogadh Fada was fought in two summers, the twenty-first and twenty-second years, and in it the kingdom raised nine regiments and four fleets, each named for the town where it is stationed. All of them stand in the present year. This appendix gives the hosts as the regimental lists and An Clàr Foscailte give them: the enforcers and their depot, the regiments and fleets in the order of their raising with their musters at the close of the present year, the companies of the western towns as Sceulachdan nan Tuathach count them, the campaign in outline, the counts An Clàr Foscailte allows, Clach nan Rèisimeidean, and the posts and passes that the war left. Of the war's full record, which lies in the sealed room at Leabharlann Muileann chaol, nothing is given here, because nothing of it can be.

## The enforcers

Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers were given a western company in the eighteenth year, when the western seams were declared the kingdom's and the pits ordered shut. Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who had risen among them, was given forty men and chose men who had served under him before. They posted two men at each pit-head of the five towns with Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order nailed to the winding-gear, to report twice weekly whether coal came up. It came up. In DE 19 the company built its depot at the western Seann Skell, whose roof the priests of Manannan would not bless, and brought up the first two lorries the town had seen. From the autumn of that year its wagons met stones and trenches on the roads into the hills. None of the skirmishes of that autumn is written down, and none was great enough to name.

## The regiments

The regiments were called up in the twentieth year by the names of the companies of An Dealachadh, whose rolls were brought out of the council's chests at Cathair dhearg and read in the old drill hall, the dead towns struck through. They were formed and armed openly, months before any in power would own that war was coming, and their command was given to Somhairle mac Lachlainn. Every regiment has foot, horse, riflemen and guns; every one of its carts and lorries runs on dubhan, which is carried up to it by Slighe a' Ghuail, the western branch and An treas cabhlach's tank-hulls. The musters below are those of the winter of the present year.

**A' chiad rèisimeid**, A' chiad rèisimeid, raised at Inis mhòr on 7 an Cèitean, DE 21, from the capital's own companies. It guards the council, the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain. It fought at Muileann ghlas and marched the released prisoners north to the boundary stones. It musters 248 foot, 174 horse, 119 riflemen and 4 guns: 545 men.

**An dàrna rèisimeid**, the second, raised at Àth dhìreach in the east on 25 an Dàmhair, DE 21 to guard Slighe a' Ghuail and the library road. Its camp was the first soldiery Muileann chaol had seen, and since the twenty-sixth year it keeps a guard at the library over the sealed room. It musters 259 foot, 70 horse, 146 riflemen and 3 guns: 478 men.

**An treas rèisimeid**, the third, raised at Cathair mhòr on 5 an t-Ògmhios, DE 21, under the market cross of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein. It fought at Muileann ghlas, its four guns hauled the last two miles to the field by hand. It musters 220 foot, 91 horse, 94 riflemen and 2 guns: 407 men.

**An ceathramh rèisimeid**, the fourth, raised at Caol bheag in the north-east on 2 an t-Samhain, DE 21. It went down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar in coal barges, was shipped round the north coast in hired dubhan hulls, and was quartered in the old magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr for four years before it went home. It musters 205 foot, 80 horse, 109 riflemen and 2 guns: 396 men.

**An còigeamh rèisimeid**, the fifth, raised at Seann Warr on the lake shore west of the capital on 13 an t-Ògmhios, DE 21, and sent north to relieve the regiments before Muileann àrsaidh. Its stone barracks at Seann Warr were the first lasting quarters any of the nine had. It musters 184 foot, 108 horse, 96 riflemen and 4 guns: 392 men.

**An siathamh rèisimeid**, the sixth, raised at Cnoc bheag on 17 an Dàmhair, DE 21, its colours blessed by Òrd an t-Seabhaig by their own rite. It holds the northern road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, and keeps the posts by the boundary stones. It musters 149 foot, 58 horse, 92 riflemen and 2 guns: 301 men.

**An seachdamh rèisimeid**, the seventh, raised from the levies of the west coast at the western Seann Skell on 11 an Giblean, DE 21, the day of Àth leathan. It holds the road behind the army and Àraich Àth leathan, stood by at every capping of the western seams, and keeps a company at Freiceadan Àth leathan, its post on the road below the town. Its rolls ran short of the order in its second week. It musters 131 foot, 67 horse, 69 riflemen and 2 guns: 269 men.

**An t-ochdamh rèisimeid**, the eighth, raised at Inis uaine on the Abhainn chaol on 16 an t-Samhain, DE 21 to guard the dubhan depots and tanks of the eastern ports. Its guard was made lasting in the twenty-fifth year. It musters 142 foot, 28 horse, 84 riflemen and 1 gun: 255 men.

**An naoidheamh rèisimeid**, the ninth, raised at the southern Seann Skell on 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21 to guard the shipmasters' works; the regimental clerks tell the two Seann Skells apart by river and coast. Its man won Còmhrag Ceann leathan at Ceann leathan in the twenty-sixth year and lost the championship in the present one. It musters 135 foot, 20 horse, 96 riflemen and 3 guns: 254 men.

Together the nine regiments muster 1,673 foot, 696 horse and 905 riflemen, some three thousand three hundred men, with twenty-three guns serviceable.

## The fleets

**A' chiad chabhlach**, A' chiad chabhlach, raised on 13 an Cèitean, DE 21, from the south-west harbours and stationed at Àth gharbh, its hulls lying in the harbour of Doire shean. It was sent round the western cape to stop the coal going out by sea from the Tuathaich ports. It has two hulls.

**An ceathramh cabhlach**, An ceathramh cabhlach, raised at Cuan shean on 20 an Cèitean, DE 21. With the first it closed the western Seann Skell and Cnoc bhàn to every boat but fishing boats, and searched those, and the boats of Caol mhòr and Cathair gheal on every day they put out. It is kept on the Tuathaich coast since the war. It has one hull, the Bratach Ghlas.

**An dàrna cabhlach**, An dàrna cabhlach, raised at the southern Seann Skell on 23 an t-Sultain, DE 21 to keep the eastern and southern waters while the first and fourth were in the north-west. It ran down one of the raiders who took the salt-boats off Àth bheag in the war, and the rest of them off Baile ìseal in DE 24. It has two hulls.

**An treas cabhlach**, An treas cabhlach, raised at Baile ghorm on 1 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21. It carried the army's dubhan up the west coast in tank-hulls to the regiments in the hills, and since the war runs dubhan to the Tuathaich depots on the council's contract, Tional nan Tuathach paying the freight. It has one hull, and the tank-hulls it hires.

## The companies of the western towns

An Clàr Foscailte names the holdouts only as Muinntir gun Siorrachd. Their companies are known from Sceulachdan nan Tuathach, from Ruth Calder's list at the pit-shed of Àth leathan as the families at Doire ghlas remembered it, and from Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own list, which named her and Tom Varley among them. By the eve of Àth leathan the muster there counted near nine hundred souls with their carriers, in five companies: Muileann àrsaidh near two hundred, Cnoc thais a hundred and sixty, Àth leathan ninety, Àth naomh sixty and Tobar dhearg of the hills forty. They had among them some sixty firearms, most of them fowling pieces older than any man carrying them, a dozen rifles, picks and short axes, and four kegs of blasting powder from the pits. They had no guns, no horse and no fuel but their own coal.

The column of the second summer, which left the western hills and marched south-east through the middle of the island toward the capital, is given in An Clàr Foscailte as some hundreds strong. Who led it is named only in Sceulachdan nan Tuathach, as Owen Barrow. Why it marched is not told.

## The campaign in outline

*The first summer.* The regiments set out from Cathair dhearg by the western road on 23 am Faoilleach, DE 21, their carts and lorries on dubhan, and joined the enforcers at the western Seann Skell. On 11 an Giblean, DE 21, they met the five towns' companies below the spoil-heaps of Àth leathan, the first great battle of the war. The holdouts gave up the southern pits and fell back into the hills about Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais; the pits at Àth leathan were taken without a fight and flooded. The regiments laid siege to Muileann àrsaidh on 21 an Cèitean, DE 21; the town held for weeks on stored coal and potatoes while its six pit-heads were taken one by one. Cnoc thais was taken on 2 an Lùnastal, DE 21, Tom Varley firing his own two shafts, and some of its people went on beyond the hills onto an Oirthir Ghaothach of the far north-west; the regiments followed to the edge of the shire of Seann Vell and no farther. Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg of the hills opened their roads without a siege on 17 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21.

*The quartered year.* Through the twenty-second year An ceathramh rèisimeid patrolled the Ceann mhòr road, the sixth held the northern road, and the seventh the western hills, and the northern office issued passes. In the autumn the column went south by Àth bheag in the west, the smaller Muileann mhin and the edge of the capital's country, and camped on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from Cathair dhearg. The first and third regiments were brought down Rathad na Fèille from their camp on the fair-ground of Muileann òg to meet it.

*The second summer's end.* On 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, the column was broken at Muileann ghlas, the second great battle of the war and the last; sixty came out of the byres at dusk under a white cloth. Word of it reached the hills, and on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, the holdouts still there came down to the posts of An seachdamh rèisimeid on the Àth leathan road and were disarmed. The war was declared ended that day.

## The open record's counts

An Clàr Foscailte counts the kingdom's dead at Àth leathan and not the holdouts'; Sceulachdan nan Tuathach put theirs in the hundreds. At Muileann ghlas it lists the first and third regiments on the field and gives no count of the column's dead. Of Sèist Muileann àrsaidh it gives the day the town fell and nothing else. Of Cnoc thais it gives forty-one taken. Of Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg it names no holdouts taken at either. The regiments' surgeon's tally for the night after Muileann ghlas, which the regiments allowed, stands at twenty-three of the regiments buried or dying and near ninety of the column's wounded brought in. Some four score holdouts taken at Muileann ghlas were held in the capital's gaol until 4 an t-Iuchar, DE 23, when A' chiad rèisimeid marched them north and handed them to Tional nan Tuathach at the boundary stones, and Tional nan Tuathach entered their names in a column of their own in Clàr nam Marbh is nan Leòinte, its register of the dead and maimed.

## The stone at Cathair mhòr

The regiments' dead are named on a stone set up at Cathair mhòr on 15 an Dùbhlachd, DE 23, beside the market cross of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein. It is cut in two columns under a single heading, the regiments' dead, and gives neither battle nor date. It carries sixty-one names: thirty-eight of Àth leathan and twenty-three of Muileann ghlas. Among them are two brothers of Seann Bhral who enlisted together and died within the same hour of the same morning. Somhairle mac Lachlainn read the names at the unveiling. No stone names the dead of the western towns. Their cairn stands on Àraich Àth leathan, built by the Tuathaich families without leave in DE 24, and grows by a stone or two every time the patrols pass it.

## The posts and the passes

After the war the regiments stayed on their stations, as the council ordered on 13 am Faoilleach, DE 23. The seventh built Freiceadan Àth leathan on the road below Àth leathan in the autumn of the twenty-third year and keeps a company there; the town calls it something else. The sixth keeps posts on the northern road by the boundary stones, where from the twenty-sixth year the Tuathaich going south show Cead an Rathaid, the pass of the northern office, printed at Cathair dhearg on grey card with a space for a name and none for a trade, and good for a time only. The second keeps its guard at the library, the eighth at the eastern tanks, and An ceathramh cabhlach on the Tuathaich coast. The war's cost is carried on An t-Ionmhas's roll as Deachamh a' Chogaidh, one part in twelve of every sale of dubhan, laid for a time in the twenty-first year and never lifted; it stands on its own line under the regiments' pay.

# Appendix C — The Dubhan Trade, the Guilds and the Dues of the Kingdom

The coal made the kingdom and the kingdom made its trade in the coal's image: a vein held by a few houses under Comhairle nam Mèinnean's fifth, a guild of hewers sworn on an oath-stone, carters and a coal line to carry it, lamp-houses to burn it in the capital's lanes, and a coinage whose seal was inked with it. In twenty-seven years every one of those things changed hands. This appendix gives Malairt an Dubhain, as it stood at the close of the present year: the fuel and its making, the works and depots, the guilds that rose and the guilds that went, the carrying, the peg of the coin, the dues the kingdom takes, and Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt. It is drawn from Comhairle nam Mèinnean's returns and An t-Ionmhas's roll as the library holds them, from Cùirt na Fèille's books at Muileann òg, and from Cuimhne-coinneimh an Tionail.

## The fuel

Dubhan is made from what the mines throw away. The first working fuel was made on 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1, by the man whose name it now carries, a Tuathach of the north, rough but good to burn; it was no trade then, but one man's answer to a need that those in power had not yet faced. What came south in the first years was a black cake, sold by the basket at the markets of Caol mhòr and Cnoc ghorm beside the peat, which burned without the coloured edge of coal. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyors, sent north in the second year, burned a cake beside a thumb of An Sloc Mòr coal in an inn grate at Caol mhòr and reported what they saw, and the council filed the report without minute.

The trade's fuel is finished in retorts: the spoil is heated in closed furnaces and the fuel drawn off and barrelled. It is burned in lamps with a burner of wick-rings and a warming coil, in the engines of boats, lorries, carriages and the line, under pans and boilers, and in the forges. By the present year every lamp, engine, ship and lorry on the island runs on it. The word for the fuel was the man's name before it was the thing's; the library's slip-box found it spelled four ways in the council's letters before it settled.

## The works

**Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell**, the works of Comann nan Sciobairean, the company of shipmasters, on the salt-sheds of the southern Seann Skell, founded 20 an Gearran, DE 4, the first on the island outside the north. On what terms the shipmasters had the making of it is not told. Its chimney has been the tallest thing on the coast since its first year, when it sold its making to the south-coast boats and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg. Its making-shed is kept under a padlock the size of a man's fist; its retort furnaces carry the baffle Peigi nic Ascaill sent round unsigned after the retort burst of the fourth year. Its hulls wear the company's black ring on their bows.

**The northern works**, the Tuathaich makings of the first years, which supplied the cake of the markets and the fuel carted to Taigh-solais Muileann bheag.

**The works of the east and north** of the present year, named in Comhairle nam Mèinnean's returns among the works where dubhan is made; Comhairle nam Mèinnean gives their making and not their owners.

## The depots and pumps

Dubhan is sold at depots, each with its pumps, and from the twenty-first year a clerk of An t-Ionmhas sits beside every pump. The first depots were the harbour tanks of the south coast and the lamp-houses' stores at Cathair dhearg. Comann nan Gualadairean' hall at Achadh dhomhain became a depot in DE 13, the guild's oath cut in the lintel above its pumps. The Tuathaich depots were opened at Caol mhòr, Doire ghlas and Ceann mhòr on 8 am Màrt, DE 15, supplied by sea; Martha Greaves wrote in Tional nan Tuathach's minute that the north now bought its fire from the south, and did not say whether this was good. The tank-yard of the eastern ports at Inis uaine is the largest store of dubhan outside the southern works, and An t-ochdamh rèisimeid guards it. The inns sell it too: An Taigh-òsta Grianach near Cnoc dhìreach was the first on the island to sell fuel as well as beds, in DE 10, and the drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às kept its trade by selling it to the drovers who had bought lorries.

## The guilds that went

**Comann nan Gualadairean**, Comann nan Gualadairean, which bound the hewing families' sons and daughters on its oath-stone of coal at Achadh dhomhain. Its day of binding passed empty in the first year of the age. It sold its hall in the ninth year and dissolved itself on 30 an Cèitean, DE 12; its last master, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, brought its rolls, its sick-roll and Clach-mhionnan nan Gualadairean, the oath-stone, to the library, and asked no receipt but that it be said they came whole and not begged for. His letter said that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience. Its bath-house at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh passed to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail.

**The coal carters**, never a guild, who carried the coal on Rathad na Fèille, the north road and the old mining roads. The last carter of Rathad na Fèille sold his cart in the third year; the last to bring coal down the north road carried a load for the Taigh-seinnse Reòta's kitchen in the twenty-sixth. The last coal on Slighe a' Ghuail went the last stretch from the goods-yard at Cathair dhearg behind carters' horses in DE 26.

## The guilds that stayed and the guilds that came

**Comann nan Saor-luinge**, Comann nan Saor-luinge' Guild, whose first rule is Cha tollar an druim, the keel is not bored. When the boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich bored their keels for engines in the fifth year it called the work unlawful, struck them and fined their yards; they returned their papers. Its court at Ros dhomhain ruled on 23 an Giblean, DE 6, that the fitting of an engine was no shipwright's work and so outside its charter, and readmitted them. They declined.

**Comann nan Lòchran**, the lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, the first craft of the kingdom to turn to the new fuel wholesale, on 28 an Dùbhlachd, DE 7. They asked leave to set their guild mark on the new lamps, and two Tuathaich fitters signed their petition; after a year's argument the guild court allowed it, and the flame over the hammer was kept. Their lamps were on the roads by the ninth year.

**Comann nan Sciobairean**, Comann nan Sciobairean of the southern works, which is a company and not a guild, and makes the fuel.

**Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail**, chartered at the southern Seann Skell on 29 an Lùnastal, DE 14, twelve masters sworn in the works' long shed under a banner of a black swan on grey. The fitters of dubhan engines had worked outside every guild; the charter gave them one, and Riaghailt na Cairte kept its rolls, like those of every guild before it, to Dia-thìrich only. The Tuathaich fitters who had turned the lights and the first engines were let go. Peigi nic Ascaill, a master of the new guild, paid Joe Ashby a month over. The fitters let go went home to the northern towns and fitted engines there without a guild, so that within a few years Caol mhòr held more dubhan boats than any port of its size in the south. On 26 an Cèitean, DE 24, the guild was given the contract for the regiments' engines and the fleets' hulls and doubled its rolls; all its new fitters are Dia-thìrich.

**The forges** of Àth naomh in the Cuan shean shire and Caol ìseal on the north coast, which smelt the bog-iron of their districts, took the kingdom's contract for the regiments' small arms and field-guns on 20 an t-Ògmhios, DE 24; the forge-towns of the old vein country followed, and arms became the dearest common goods in every market.

## The carrying

Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's line from Achadh dhomhain by Muileann chrom to Cathair dhearg and Ros dhomhain took its first dubhan engine on 1 an Cèitean, DE 8 and laid up its coal engines on 2 an Giblean, DE 10. In DE 12 its timetables dropped the word coal from the line's name, and everyone else went on calling it Slighe a' Ghuail. It carries dubhan, wool, salt and soldiers, and ran its last coal in the twenty-sixth year. The first lorries carried salt from Àth bheag inland in DE 8; the drovers of the east and of Achadh mhòr sold their oxen and bought lorries; buses and hired cars came to the capital in DE 13. At sea the south-coast boats took engines first, then the patrol boats at Ros dhomhain, which outran the raiders; Taigh Mhic Ùisdein put its money into dubhan shipping in DE 13, and An treas cabhlach's tank-hulls carry the fuel up the west coast to the Tuathaich depots, Tional nan Tuathach paying the freight.

## The coin

On 5 an Cèitean, DE 15, the council pegged the coin to the making of dubhan, at the same sitting that proclaimed the new count of the years. On 3 an t-Ògmhios, DE 15, the mint ceased to press coal ink into the seal of the coinage; the new seal is plain, and Fearchar Bonn's first dies went to the library, in the case beside Clach-mhionnan nan Gualadairean. The coin is reckoned in purses. At the fair of Muileann òg Cùirt na Fèille had kept a painted coal ceiling on its board by the toll-house door; it was scraped off in the third year, since no seller kept it.

## The dues

**The fifth**, the kingdom's old right in the vein, taken by Comhairle nam Mèinnean from those who held seams. The western holders ceased to pay it, they said, when Comhairle nam Mèinnean ceased to carry their coal; under Breith Leòid Comhairle nam Mèinnean declared the right lapsed and the seams the kingdom's. Ruth Calder offered to pay it in coal if Comhairle nam Mèinnean would carry it. With the seams capped and An Sloc Mòr closed, the fifth is taken on nothing in the present year.

**Deachamh a' Chogaidh**, one part in twelve of every sale of dubhan, laid for a time on 21 an Giblean, DE 21 and taken at the pumps by a clerk of An t-Ionmhas; within a month Cùirt na Fèille at Muileann òg recorded the first complaint against it. It was never lifted. On 27 an Giblean, DE 24, An t-Ionmhas's accounts carried it forward as a standing line under the regiments' pay, and no minute of the council records a choice to keep it.

**The market-due**, fixed on 22 an Cèitean, DE 24, at seventeen in the hundred on every sale a town makes into its market and on every sale between markets, taken by a clerk of An t-Ionmhas in each of the sixteen market towns. Caol ruadh, whose harbour victualled the garrisons and An dàrna cabhlach through the war, was granted the sixteenth and last market right on 26 am Faoilleach, DE 23.

**The head-due**, taken at eighteen purses on every five thousand heads.

**An t-Ionmhas's roll** for the present year, on 29 an t-Iuchar, DE 27, stands at 9,568 purses: 6,375 from the head-due and 3,193 from the market-due. Deachamh a' Chogaidh is carried on its own line under the regiments' pay. An Oirthir Ghaothach pays neither due.

## The charter of export

Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt was won on 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27, by Dubhan, who made the first working fuel and was then in his sixty-ninth year, after a year of letters and three sittings of the council at Cathair dhearg. It is the first leave the kingdom has given to sell dubhan beyond the island. Its terms are narrow: every barrel measured by An t-Ionmhas's measure; loading at Ros dhomhain only; the tithe taken on every barrel; the home depots served first; and every hold searched and sealed by the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde before a hull sails. The first tank-hull under it, An Eala Dhubh, was loaded at Ros dhomhain over three days, a clerk of An t-Ionmhas marking the first barrel and the last and every fifth between, and stood out on the morning tide past the north-western capes with the seal on her hatches. At the southern Seann Skell the priests of Manannan said over her the prayer to keep the sea shut.

| Due or measure | Laid | Rate | Taken by | The present year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The fifth | before the age | a fifth of the coal | Comhairle nam Mèinnean | taken on nothing |
| Deachamh a' Chogaidh | 21 an Giblean, DE 21 | one part in twelve of every sale of dubhan | An t-Ionmhas's clerks at the pumps | its own line under the regiments' pay |

# Appendix D — The Faiths in the Age of Dubhan

The orders of An Creideamh Sean came into the age as they had come through An Dealachadh: Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail of the custodians, whose Àrd-choimheadaiche sits at Brìde's house at the southern Seann Skell and who kept the vein holy while it lasted; Òrd Mhacha at the capital, which crowns the rulers and keeps the horses; Òrd Mhanannain in the harbours; Òrd an t-Seabhaig of the north-central country; Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean; and the houses of Na Seann Spioradan in the east. The Tuathaich of the north keep An Eaglais, the church of Naomh Breandan and A' Chiad Churach, and at Baile chrom Oidhche Glaise. None of them was put down in the age, and none was asked what it thought of the fuel before the kingdom took it up. What each said, and what each did with an engine when one came to its door, is given here as the letters, Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd and Sceulachdan nan Tuathach give it.

## The Rite and the new fuel

Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail had kept the vein sacred for as long as there was a vein, and the coal flame on its altars was the vein's flame. The fuel made without the vein put to it a question it had no teaching for, and its Àrd-choimheadaiche, Alasdair mac Ìomhair, answered it in DE 4 in a letter to every house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail: the new fuel was not forbidden, since it was not coal, and not blessed, since it was not coal. Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche was read in the houses and argued in Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean, which disputed it the same winter. It governed Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's dealings with dubhan for the rest of the age. Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail blessed no lamp, engine or depot of the new fuel, and forbade none; its custodians rode behind an engine from the ninth year, when the fitters of the southern works set a lorry's engine under the Àrd-choimheadaiche's closed carriage and the carriage's matched greys were retired.

**The last coal flame.** When the five lights of the coast were turned to dubhan by order in the sixth year, the custodians of Tobar dhearg asked that the flame of its light, which had burned coal-lit for more than a century, be given to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail. On 19 an t-Iuchar, DE 6, the keeper Ciorstaidh nic Artair bore it in a closed lantern on the walk from the cape to the southern Seann Skell and down the hall of Brìde's house between custodians of four shires, and it was let burn out on the altar. The Àrd-choimheadaiche blessed the empty lantern. The song of the last flame was first sung at the southern Seann Skell that year.

**The bath-house.** Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh passed to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail with the guild's other goods on 28 an t-Ògmhios, DE 12. Its custodians kept the old keeper and the same sick, and opened it to the Tuathaich; the first Tuathaich family was bathed there that year. In the war they took in wounded officers at the council's asking.

**The protest on the seal.** When the mint ceased to press coal ink into the seal of the coinage in the fifteenth year, the Àrd-choimheadaiche protested to the council that the kingdom had taken the vein out of its own coin. On 31 an t-Iuchar, DE 15, the council answered that the kingdom had never said it held the vein sacred. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh copied both letters into Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd.

**The altar-coal.** When An Sloc Mòr was closed in DE 26, one face was kept in Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's keeping, and on 15 an t-Ògmhios, DE 26, twelve hewers were sworn at Achadh dhomhain to cut the altar-coal. They are the last of their trade to work the vein on the island, and Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail gave them its own oath, not the dissolved guild's; one of them, an old man, had sworn the guild's oath in his youth. In the present year the coal they cut was carried south in four baskets, and on 6 an Dàmhair, DE 27, the Àrd-choimheadaiche drew by lot in the rain in Brìde's yard which of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail should have the four baskets. A novice of fifteen held the bowl. The southern house drew its own basket, so that one basket went no farther than across the yard. The coal is sold at the fair only by the lump, for altars.

**Òrd Bhrìde.** The custodians of Brìde search and seal every hold that sails under Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt, and set their seal on An Eala Dhubh's hatches at Ros dhomhain in the present year. It is the only office in Malairt an Dubhain that Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail holds.

**Caol ruadh.** The house of Brìde at Caol ruadh keeps the orthodox rite of Brìde's flame. It bought two years' altar coal ahead in the sixth year, lest the coal fail before the rite did, burned the last of it in the eighteenth, and wrote to the Àrd-choimheadaiche asking where the next was to come from.

## Òrd Mhacha

Òrd Mhacha crowns the rulers at Cathair dhearg and keeps the two horses of the rite, Liath Macha and Dubh Sainglenn, which were led out at Cathal's crowning on 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3. It has always blessed roads and those who set out on them. When Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's first dubhan engine was hauled to Muileann chrom on a wagon by twelve of the order's horses, a priest of Macha walked at the leaders' heads and stood in the ford to his thighs to speak them out of it, and before the first dubhan train left the yard he said over it the blessing for a horse setting out on a long road, there being none made for an engine. The order has made no blessing of its own for an engine since.

## The order of Manannan

The priests of Manannan bless boats, harbours, roofs and carts against the sea and the rain, and keep houses at Seann Bhral and the western Seann Skell and in the harbour towns. Their houses were slow to bless the engine-boats. In DE 19 the house at the western Seann Skell refused to bless Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers' depot: a young priest told Somhairle mac Lachlainn that the house blessed a boat and a roof against the sea and the rain, and would not pretend the same of a depot built for Comhairle nam Mèinnean's lorries. The roof was blessed at last by a stranger's hand. The house at Seann Bhral heard of the refusal and sent no word either way. At Àth naomh in the Cuan shean shire the harbour carts are blessed every spring, horses and all, and a dubhan lamp on a tail-board is blessed because it is on the cart. When An Eala Dhubh sailed under Cairt na h-Às-mhalairt in the present year, the priests of Manannan at the southern Seann Skell said over her the sailing prayer that asks the sea to stay shut.

## The Hawk houses

Òrd an t-Seabhaig of Cnoc bheag and the north-central country keep their own rite, older than the kingdom. When An siathamh rèisimeid was raised at Cnoc bheag on 17 an Dàmhair, DE 21, they blessed its colours by that rite, and the colours hang in their hall between musters.

## The druid school and Na Seann Spioradan

Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Caol shean disputed the Àrd-choimheadaiche's letter in the fourth year, and in DE 11 its masters, writing to the library of their own school's revival, made the word dubhan-tùsail, of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise. The school sends a teacher once a year to give the one lecture that remains at the druid house of Muileann dhearg, which was given to the town's caretaker with the graves when the pits closed. Pilgrims have gone up to its landing by engine since the ninth year.

The house of Na Seann Spioradan at Inis uaine added An t-ochdamh rèisimeid to its prayers when the regiment's guard on the eastern tanks was made lasting on 14 an Dùbhlachd, DE 25.

## An Eaglais of the north

The Tuathaich keep An Eaglais, the church of Naomh Breandan, whose telling of A' Chiad Churach, Breandan's voyage to Inis nam Beannaichte, is the north's own telling of how its people came. The Dia-thìrich in office call it folklore. Its hymns are sung in the humans' tongue that the Tuathaich keep, and its services are kept on the Sunday. The five western towns kept an Nollaig together at Àth leathan's chapel in the nineteenth year; in Sèist Muileann àrsaidh Weir kept the Sunday service through the whole of it and the graves were dug behind the chapel; before Àth leathan the men of Tobar dhearg of the hills kept the chapel and sang low along their line in the words of An Eaglais. At Ceann mhòr, in the quartered year, Corporal Dùghall mac Iain heard the hymns of Barbara Keir's house through the wall of his billet. At Doire ghlas, on the shortest evening of the present year, Ellen Marsh told the eldest children the telling of A' Chiad Churach and of the fire its crew carried in a clay pot through the mist, and a boy asked her whose fire it was. The rhyme of the north asks the same.

An Eaglais has no office in the kingdom and has asked for none. It was not asked for its witness when the war was sealed, nor was its register of the dead of the western towns kept at the library; Clàr nam Marbh is nan Leòinte is kept by Tional nan Tuathach.

## The Grey Night

Oidhche Glaise sect at Baile chrom keeps its vigil once a year with every lamp in the town out and every door shut. On 9 an Dùbhlachd, DE 21, the regiments quartered along the coast reported a night when the whole town was dark and silent; a file of An ceathramh rèisimeid searched it and found nothing. The house of Margaret Crane on the lighthouse road kept the vigil alone; a soldier of the file set his lamp down in her passage rather than carry its light past her. The vigil is kept every year as it always was.

## The faiths in the present year

| Order or faith | Seat | Its dealings with dubhan | In the present year |
|---|---|---|---|

| Òrd Mhacha | the temple at Cathair dhearg | the blessing for a horse said over the engines | crowns the ruler; blesses the line's engines |
